<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of a scholarly edition of the New Testament. While the previous page contained library stamps and cataloging information from Toulouse, this page begins the formal Latin preface by the editor, Constantin von Tischendorf, explaining the five-year progress of his work since 1864.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<sig>a *</sig>

After the start of this new edition was made in the year 1864, it is only now, five years later, that I have succeeded in bringing the four gospels to completion. This delay seems to find its excuse not only in the sheer scope and difficulty of the work, but it also had two other causes. For within these five years, several journeys had to be made—or rather repeated—for the purpose of visiting libraries in England, Paris, Rome and Naples, Saint Petersburg and Moscow; furthermore, several books which I had to bring to completion demanded care for publication. These included two volumes of the *Sacred Unpublished Monuments* <note>original Latin: *Monumentorum sacrorum ineditorum*</note>, the *Vatican New Testament* <note>original Latin: *Novum Testamentum Vaticanum*</note> with its Appendix, an Appendix of the most famous codices—the Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus—and the *Apocryphal Apocalypses* <note>ancient Christian writings not included in the standard Bible</note>, for the most part published now for the first time. There were also the *Philonea* <note>works related to Philo of Alexandria</note>, with one part previously unpublished and the other now finally correctly extracted from the ancient script; the one-thousandth volume of the Tauchnitz collection of British writers, titled: **The New Testament: the authorised English version; with introduction and various readings from the three most celebrated manuscripts of the original Greek text**; that short defense of the Gospels which I titled: **When Were Our Gospels Written?** <note>original German: *Wann wurden unsere Evangelien verfasst*</note>, which was published four times and rewritten three times; and a fourth edition of the *Old Testament according to the Seventy Translators* <note>the Septuagint, or LXX</note>, among others.

Although these interruptions could hardly occur without occasionally departing from the consistency of the work, nevertheless—and this gives me great joy—they served to enrich the <term>critical apparatus</term> <note>the technical footnotes documenting variations in different ancient manuscripts</note> in many ways. The Vatican Codex <note>one of the oldest and most important Greek Bible manuscripts</note> indeed, to mention this first, demanded studies far different from those of Angelo Mai <note>a Roman Catholic Cardinal who had previously edited the manuscript, often criticized for lack of precision</note> in order to satisfy the requirements of modern criticism. With difficulty, however...

<summary>In this preface, the scholar Constantin von Tischendorf explains that his five-year delay in finishing the four gospels was due to extensive travels to European libraries and the publication of several other major biblical and apocryphal works.</summary>
<keywords>Constantin von Tischendorf, New Testament, scholarship, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus, Angelo Mai, Septuagint, 19th-century biblical criticism</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Tischendorf’s preface to his major critical edition of the Greek New Testament. On the previous page, he explained the five-year delay in publication due to his travels to European and Russian libraries and his work on other projects like the Codex Sinaiticus. Here, he begins to discuss his methodology, specifically how he has overhauled his scholarly approach since his previous edition in 1859.</meta>

<page-num>IV</page-num>

I must bear this fact: that I did not think it necessary, right from the very beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew, to provide the same abundance of scholarly preparation that I employed once the work had progressed a little further.

Since it is well established that the excellence of an edition of the New Testament books consists chiefly in two things—the <term>critical apparatus</term> <note>the collection of variant readings from different manuscripts, usually found at the bottom of a page</note> as it is called, and the skill by which the actual words of the sacred writers are determined—I must speak briefly about both. Regarding the apparatus, I did not consider it enough merely to transfer the material from my "seventh major critical edition" (which appeared at the beginning of 1859), adding bits here and there to expand or correct it; rather, the whole thing has been prepared entirely from scratch through renewed study. For whatever evidence was to be brought forward—whether from Greek <term>codices</term> <note>ancient handwritten books</note>, from early translations, or from ancient Christian writers—pains were taken to record it more accurately than had ever been done by anyone before. In that seventh edition, I had already corrected a flaw found in all the older editions—those of Wetstein, Griesbach, Schulz, and Scholz—namely, that authorities were only cited when their readings differed from the so-called <term>Received Text</term> <note>original Latin: *vulgato textu*; the standard printed Greek Bible used since the Reformation</note>. However, beyond this, the notes regarding early translations and ancient writers still required much work. This issue stems from the fact that it was not yet fully understood how much authority the oldest translations—among which the Latin, Syriac, and Coptic hold the primary place—possess in the search for the true writings of the apostles. But I shall speak more precisely about these and similar matters in the *Prolegomena* <note>the formal introductory essay of a scholarly work</note>. For the present, it seems sufficient to indicate briefly which codices written in <term>uncials</term> <note>large, capital-letter handwriting used in the earliest Greek manuscripts</note> have been added to the critical apparatus since the year 1859, and what labors I have undertaken regarding the primary authorities so that they might be used with confidence.

Therefore, eighteen manuscripts <note>original Latin: *hi 18*</note> have been added to the uncial codices already used for the Gospels in the seventh edition<sup>1</sup>: **$\aleph$** <note>The Hebrew letter Aleph, the symbol for the **Codex Sinaiticus**</note> (of which a far greater part of these fragments has been added; for 12 leaves have been increased by another 33); **o<sup>f</sup>** (hymns from the psalter of Abraham de Noroff); **R** (ac—

Furthermore, from the remaining parts of the New Testament, we have published D (the Claromontanus) of the letters of Paul, M (fragments of the letters of Paul), P (Acts, epistles, and the Apocalypse), and B (the Basilian-Vatican Apocalypse); we have designated for publication from our own transcripts E of Acts, G of Acts, H of the letters of Paul, and N O Q. In addition to H of Acts, K of the epistles, and L of Acts and epistles, we have also recently investigated E (the Sangermanensis) of the letters of Paul more accurately in St. Petersburg.

Now, from these facts, it will be sufficiently clear how much the <term>critical apparatus</term>—which in the editions of Wetstein, Griesbach, Scholz, and even Lachmann, was filled with the defects of imperfect collation—has advanced over these last ten years and more, both in its abundance and its reliability. Indeed, it has also received other reinforcements, both from <term>minuscule</term> <note>manuscripts written in smaller, cursive-like Greek script, generally later than the capital-letter uncials</note> codices and especially from ancient versions and the Church Fathers; those who are accustomed to using critical editions will easily notice this by examining the book. Thus, the evidence of the Latin codices, and—

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Tischendorf’s explanation of the sources used for his "critical apparatus." He transitions from listing specific Greek manuscripts to discussing the ancient versions (translations into Latin, Armenian, Ethiopic, etc.) and the writings of the Early Church Fathers, emphasizing how these sources help confirm the oldest possible Greek text.</meta>

<page-num>VI</page-num>

Evidence for the **Old Latin** and **Vulgate** versions <note>original: *Italae et Vulgatae rationis*; the 'Itala' refers to the various Latin translations that existed before Jerome’s late 4th-century Vulgate</note> has been presented here more fully than by any previous scholar. However, at the beginning of this work, the edition of the **Vratislav manuscript** <note>also known as Codex Vratislaviensis</note> was not yet available, nor was the **Fulda manuscript** <note>Codex Fuldensis, an important 6th-century manuscript containing a Harmony of the Gospels</note>. Likewise, for at least the second part of the Gospels, it was possible to draw the **Jerusalem Lectionary** <note>a book of Gospel readings for church services</note> from the Verona edition. We have taken the Armenian version not only from those notes which Griesbach wrote by hand in the margin of Wetstein’s edition, but also from a <term>collation</term> <note>a word-for-word comparison of different manuscripts to identify variations</note> performed by Charles Rieu for the use of Tregelles. Furthermore, the efforts of Thomas Pell Platt have increased the number of readings from the Ethiopic version. ^1 Regarding the Greek **Fathers** <note>influential early Christian theologians whose quotations of the Bible provide evidence for ancient readings</note>, we have consulted—with tireless study—Irenaeus, Clement, Origen, Hippolytus, Eusebius, Basil, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Cyril of Alexandria, among others; of the Latin Fathers, we have used Tertullian, Cyprian, Lucifer <note>Lucifer of Cagliari, a 4th-century bishop known for his strict adherence to scripture</note>, and others. Just as these two types of evidence—the ancient versions and the writings of the Fathers—have been applied to the <term>critical apparatus</term> <note>the scholarly footnotes documenting every variation found in ancient sources</note> much more diligently than before, they have also gained far greater authority in our work for restoring the most ancient text than is usually the case.

This was not done without good reason. It has been clearly demonstrated through numerous examples that the most ancient translators agree so closely with our oldest Greek manuscripts that they must be considered to have drawn from the same or very similar sources. In this regard, nothing is more significant than that remarkable relationship which exists between the **Sinaitic manuscript** <note>Codex Sinaiticus, the 4th-century Bible discovered by Tischendorf</note> and the Old Latin witnesses, a connection often reinforced by the agreement of the **Curetonian Syriac** <note>an ancient Syriac translation of the Gospels discovered in the Nitrian Desert of Egypt</note>. Indeed, quite a few readings which one might have suspected the Sinaitic or the **Palatine manuscript** <note>Codex Palatinus, an Old Latin manuscript designated as 'e'</note>—to mention this one specifically among the others—of preserving through some individual whim, have been proven to originate from an even older Greek source when the two manuscripts are compared.

Now, having surveyed all the sources from which the history of what they call the Sacred Text can be understood, two things especially [become clear]...

^1 We preferred to exclude most of the Arabic and Slavonic readings from the apparatus because of the ambiguity with which they are burdened and the meager value they possess.

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Tischendorf’s discussion of his methodology, moving from the specific versions and Church Fathers mentioned on the previous page to his broader philosophy of "textual criticism"—the science of determining the original words of the New Testament. He concludes the sentence from the previous page by stating that his investigations into these sources have been completed.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

...have been brought to completion. Just as it cannot be doubted that in the very earliest times of the Christian era there were many departures from the pure writings of the apostles—though in this matter there was no wickedness or deceit intended—so too, by wisely and skillfully using the most ancient witnesses we still possess, the form of the apostolic books that was most widely in use in the second century can, for the most part, be probably restored. 

I believe everyone who applies themselves to this work will understand that this form of the text comes much closer to the actual integrity of the Sacred Scriptures than those books which were circulated through the Byzantine Church after about the fifth century and were soon afterward propagated almost exclusively. The only exceptions are those who, led by a false sense of piety, have forgotten how to distinguish custom from truth, or those who remain captivated by the theories regarding the <term>recensions</term> <note>theories that group ancient manuscripts into "families" based on shared characteristics and geographical origins</note> of the **New Testament** books devised by **Griesbach**, **Hug**, **Scholz**, and others. 

In order that both groups may be led toward a truer opinion and a fairer judgment of textual criticism, I intend to treat everything relevant to this matter clearly and in detail in the **Prolegomena** <note>a formal introduction or preliminary discussion to a scholarly work</note>, which will comprise the third volume of this edition. For now, I would like to draw attention to those passages where we have shaped the apostolic text based on a small amount of Greek authority—small, I mean, in the number of witnesses, but greatest in their weight—usually supported by testimony from the **Latin** <note>original: *Italis*; referring to the Old Latin versions used before the Vulgate became standard</note> sources. 

This has often been done in such a way that it carries a remarkable recommendation of probability. Yet it must not be forgotten that those who place their own judgment before the authority of the witnesses are deeply mistaken. This authority must be judged not by the number of witnesses, but by their antiquity. Furthermore, our most ancient witnesses—despite the ignorance of the Greek language shown by the **Alexandrian scribes** <note>original: *Alexandrinorum calligraphorum*; the professional copyists in Egypt who produced early manuscripts like Codex Vaticanus</note>—did not so much follow the linguistic customs of their own age as they did faithfully, however imperfectly, repeat much older copies.

Indeed, as I myself have repeated what I said elsewhere recently—in the critical comparison of the **Sinaiticus manuscript** <note>original: *codicis Sinaitici*; a 4th-century Greek Bible discovered by Tischendorf at Saint Catherine's Monastery</note> etc., page 13—while the **Vatican manuscript** <note>original: *Vaticanum*; another of the oldest surviving Greek Bibles, held in the Vatican Library</note> and a few other similar Greek manuscripts...

<summary>Tischendorf argues that the oldest available manuscripts, though few in number, allow us to reconstruct the New Testament as it existed in the 2nd century. He rejects the later "Byzantine" text in favor of these ancient witnesses, emphasizing that their age and faithfulness to even older copies outweigh their occasional scribal errors.</summary>
<keywords>textual criticism, Byzantine text, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Griesbach, recensions, Alexandrian scribes, New Testament manuscripts</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page concludes the preface to the eighth edition of Constantine von Tischendorf’s Greek New Testament. It continues his argument that scholars should prioritize the oldest available manuscripts and the writings of the early Church Fathers over the vast majority of later, more common medieval copies. He aligns his methodology with the pioneering work of Richard Bentley and Karl Lachmann.</meta>

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

supplemented by the consensus of several very ancient translators—most notably the **Latin** ones—and supported throughout by the testimony of the **Church Fathers**, we believe that these ancient sources alone, or nearly so, should be employed to restore the original writings of the evangelists and apostles. In doing so, we set aside the vast number of later manuscripts, regardless of how remarkably they agree with one another <note>Tischendorf refers here to the "Majority Text" or "Textus Receptus," which was common in his day but based on much later medieval copies</note>. In this approach, we are greatly encouraged by the judgment of **Richard Bentley** <note>1662–1742; an English scholar who was the first to propose using ancient manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate to reconstruct the oldest possible Greek text</note>. For he—whose footsteps **Karl Lachmann** <note>1793–1851; a German philologist who applied rigorous scientific methods to create the first New Testament text entirely independent of traditional medieval editions</note> also followed—when he devoted himself one hundred and fifty years ago to correcting, or rather restoring, the words of the sacred writers, judged that nearly the same path as our own must be taken. 

In this endeavor, Bentley (whom Lachmann followed in turn) believed one should rest satisfied with the version of the text that was commonly read by the Church at the time of the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The first ecumenical council of the Church in 325 AD</note>. However, by the most fortunate providence of God, it has come to pass that we are now permitted to return even further back, at least to the era of **Irenaeus** <note>c. 130–202 AD; a prominent early Christian theologian whose writings provide a window into the New Testament text used in the 2nd century</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Written at **Leipzig** <note>original: "Lipsiae"</note> on the day of the **Ascension of Christ**, in the year 1869.

<summary>Tischendorf aligns his text-critical methods with scholars like Richard Bentley and Karl Lachmann, claiming that modern discoveries now allow us to reconstruct a New Testament text dating back to the 2nd century (the time of Irenaeus).</summary>

<keywords>textual criticism, Richard Bentley, Karl Lachmann, Irenaeus, Council of Nicaea, Leipzig, New Testament manuscripts, church history</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the general methodology of the preface to specific technical descriptions of the primary manuscripts used in the edition. It identifies the most important ancient Greek codices—Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus—which form the foundation of Tischendorf’s critical apparatus for the Gospels.</meta>

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

# PRELIMINARY NOTES

## REGARDING MATTERS THAT SEEM ESPECIALLY NECESSARY 
## FOR THOSE INTENDING TO USE THE CRITICAL APPARATUS OF THE GOSPELS.

**א** **Codex Sinaiticus Petropolitanus** <note>The Sinai Codex, now in St. Petersburg</note> from the middle of the 4th century. It contains the entire New Testament in its complete form. **אᵃ** hardly differs in age from the original scribe; whatever readings we have marked with the sign **אᵃ** certainly belong to the same 4th century. **אᵇ** is to be considered as dating from approximately the 6th century. Aside from Matthew, whose first pages he treated with greater care, he touched upon only a few passages. **אᶜ** dates from approximately the beginning of the 7th century, and **אᶜᵇ** is not separated by a long interval from **אᶜᵃ** (whom we call **אᶜ** unless **אᶜᵇ** differs from him). I published the entire codex in four magnificent volumes in 1862; likewise, I published the *Sinaitic New Testament* for general use in the following year. After all copies of that edition were exhausted in the same year, there followed in the autumn of 1864 (though the title page says 1865) the *Greek New Testament from the Sinaitic Codex*, the most ancient of all, with the Vatican and Elzevir <note>The "Elzevir" refers to the standard "Textus Receptus" printed by the Elzevir family in the 17th century</note> readings noted.*

**A** **Codex Alexandrinus** of the British Museum, from the 5th century and specifically towards its end. It contains gaps <term>lacunae|physical missing sections in a manuscript</term> in the Gospels from the beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew until 25:6 <note>original: *Biblos - ho nymphios*</note> "Book — the bridegroom," and likewise from John 6:50 until 8:52 <note>original: *ina - legei*</note> "that — he says." C. G. Woide published a magnificent edition in 1786. B. H. Cowper reprinted this edition for general use in 1860, with corrections made throughout.

**B** **Codex Vaticanus** number 1209, from the 4th century. It hardly differs in age from the Sinai Codex. It contains the Gospels complete; however, it is lacking from the Epistle to the Hebrews 9:14 onwards, with the loss of four of Paul's epistles (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus, and Philemon) and the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>.* More than 400 errors in the editions of Angelo Mai <note>1782–1854; an Italian Cardinal and philologist who produced the first printed editions of the Vatican Codex</note> (Rome, 1857 and 1859**) have been cor-

---

\* To this edition was added a Supplement in May of this year, which pertains primarily to the Vatican readings.
\*\* Almost all the errors that Mai had made also passed into the editions modeled after Mai’s version. Among these, none is worse than—

<page-num>IX</page-num>

we corrected in the *Vatican New Testament*, which we published in 1867. This edition was followed in mid-1868 by the *New Testament* printed at Rome using my "Sinaitic" typefaces. Carlo Vercellone and Giuseppe Cozza edited it using my research notes from 1866. Once this volume (the fifth part of the edition of the entire codex) was released, at the beginning of 1869 we issued the *Appendix to the Vatican New Testament*, noting both the items that supplemented our edition and those that corrected the Roman one. \* B² differs hardly at all from the original hand (B) in age; B³ is later by 6 or 7 centuries.

<margin>c</margin>
**Codex Ephraemi Syri**, a rewritten manuscript <term>palimpsest|a manuscript where the original text was scraped off and overwritten with new text, in this case the works of Ephrem the Syrian</term> now in Paris, from approximately the middle of the 5th century. The hand marked c² appears to be from the 6th century, and c³ from the 9th century. In 1843, we published a facsimile-style edition of all the New Testament books it contains. It includes the following fragments of the Gospels: Matthew 1:1–5:15; 7:5–17:26; 18:28–22:20; 23:17–24:10; 24:45–25:30; 26:22–27:11; 27:47–28:14. Mark 1:17–6:31; 8:5–12:29; 13:19 to the end. Luke 1:1–2:5; 2:42–3:21; 4:25–6:4; 6:37–7:16; 8:28–12:3; 19:42–20:27; 21:21–22:19; 23:25–24:7; 24:46 to the end. John 1:1–41; 3:33–5:16; 6:38–7:3; 8:34–9:11; 11:8–46; 13:8–14:7; 16:21–18:36; 20:26 to the end. However, small portions of these have perished here and there, such as the first verses of each book which were originally written in red ink <note>original: "minio"</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
**Codex Bezae** of Cambridge, containing both Greek and Latin text written line-by-line <term>stichometrically|an ancient layout where lines were divided according to the sense of the words to aid in public reading</term>, dating from approximately the middle of the 6th century. It is damaged <note>mutilated</note> at Matthew 1:1–20; 6:20–9:2; 27:2–12; John 1:16–3:26. Supplements were added after roughly the 10th century (marked D<gloss>supplement</gloss> or supp): Matthew 3:7–16 (and in the Latin from 2:20–3:8, supplemented around the 9th century); Mark 16:15 to the end (the Latin from 16:6 to the end, supplemented as before); John 18:14–20:13 (the Latin from 18:2–20:1, supplemented as before). It appears, however, that the Greek supplements (though not the Latin ones) were derived from the original ancient leaves themselves, especially those pertaining to the Gospel of John.

<margin>E</margin>
**Codex Basileensis** K IV. 35. It appears to date from the middle of the 8th century. It contains the Gospels in their entirety, except for Luke 3:4–15 and 24:47 to the end. Additionally, three leaves were supplemented in small cursive letters: Luke 1:69–2:4.

...to the London edition (from the Teubner workshop in Leipzig), which increased the faults of the Roman version it followed with innumerable errors.

<header>XV</header>

## ON ANCIENT VERSIONS.

The manuscripts of the <term>Itala|The "Old Latin" versions of the Bible used before St. Jerome produced the Vulgate in the late 4th century</term> (produced in Africa during the second century) are: **a** the Vercelli manuscript, 4th century; **b** the Verona manuscript, 5th century; **c** the Colbert manuscript, 11th century; **d** the Cambridge manuscript, 6th century; **e** the Palatine manuscript of Vienna, 5th century; **f** the Brescia manuscript, 6th century; **ff^1.** and **ff^2.** manuscripts formerly belonging to Corbie <note>original: "Corbejenses"</note> (**ff^1.** is now in St. Petersburg); **g^1.** and **g^2.** the Saint-Germain manuscripts; **h** the Clermont manuscript, now in the Vatican, 5th century; **i** a Vienna manuscript of the 5th or 6th century; **k** the Bobbio manuscript, now in Turin, 5th century; **l** the Rehdiger manuscript of Breslau, roughly 7th century; **m** signifies the readings of the *Speculum* <note>The "Mirror," a collection of biblical quotations</note> which is usually attributed to Augustine (roughly 6th century); **n** the St. Gall manuscript, 5th century; (**o** a St. Gall fragment of Mark 16:14–20, roughly 7th century; **p** a St. Gall fragment of John 11:14–44, roughly 8th century); **q** the Munich manuscript, 6th century; **s** the Ambrosian manuscript, roughly 6th century.

Several of these contain only parts of the Gospels, such as **i, k, m, n, s**; **h** uses the Old Latin text only for the Gospel of Matthew, while for the remaining three, which have not been published, it follows the <term>Vulgate|The late 4th-century Latin translation by St. Jerome which became the standard Bible of the Western Church</term>. Indeed, none except the very late manuscript **c** has reached us in its entirety. They were published as follows: **a, b,** and **f** by Bianchini <note>original: "Blanchinum"</note>; **c** by Sabatier; **d** by Kipling and Scrivener; **ff^1.** by Martianay and others; **h** (the Gospel of Matthew with gaps) by Angelo Mai; **i** by Alter (though Bianchini had already compared it before Alter, hence the label *iblanc*); **l** by Friedrich Haase; **s** by Ceriani*; **e** and **k** by myself <note>Tischendorf refers here to his own editorial work</note>. For the purpose of publication, I have transcribed the whole of **n** (including **o** and **p**) and **q**. Only **ff^2.** (by Sabatier and Bianchini, hence *ff^2. sab* or *ff^2. blan*) and **g^1.** and **g^2.** (both by Sabatier) have been collated <note>Compared against other texts to note differences</note>.

The oldest manuscripts of the Vulgate are **am, fu, san, for, prag, reg, pe, fos**; likewise **gat, harl, ing, mm, mt, taur, tol**. To these are added the <term>lectionaries|Books containing Gospel readings arranged for the church calendar</term> **flor, gue, lux, mar, mich**.

**aeth** i.e., Ethiopic, from the Roman and Polyglot editions and P. Platt; **arm** i.e., Armenian, from the editions of Uscan (1666) and Zohrab (1789, 1805); **cop** i.e., Memphitic <note>Now usually called Bohairic Coptic</note> from the editions of Wilkins and Schwartz; **sah** i.e., Sahidic <note>A dialect of Coptic from Upper Egypt</note>; **basm** i.e., Basmuric (Schwartz used both Sahidic and Basmuric, but we have also frequently cited Sahidic from Woide and Münter); **syr^cu** i.e., Curetonian Syriac from a Nitrian manuscript of the 5th century; **syr^sch** i.e., Peshitta Syriac from the edition of Schaaf; **syr^p** i.e., Later Syriac <note>The Philoxenian or Harclean version</note> from the edition of Joseph White; **syr^hr** i.e., Syriac from the Jerusalem lectionary; **go** i.e., Gothic from the edition of Loebe and Gabelentz; **fr** i.e., Frankish <note>Old High German</note> (for the Gospel of Matthew) from the edition of Schmeller; **sax** i.e., Anglo-Saxon (this flowed from the Latin Vulgate and therefore is to be compared with its older manuscripts) from the edition of Benjamin Thorpe. Rarely on—

Then we employed Arabic readings (**ar arr**), Persian readings (**persp**, i.e., from the Polyglot Bibles; **pers whe**, i.e., from the Whelock edition), and Slavonic readings (**sl**, **sl¹**, **sl²**, etc.). The Syriac Curetonian (**syr cu**) appears to date to roughly the middle of the 2nd century; the Syriac Schaaf (**syr sch**) to the end of the 2nd century; the Syro-Hierosolymitan (**syr hr**) to the 5th century; the Philoxenian (**syr p**) to the years 508 and 616; the Egyptian <note>Coptic</note> to the 3rd century; and the Armenian (**arm**), Ethiopic (**aeth**), and Gothic (**go**) to the 4th century.

The names of the **CHURCH FATHERS** will mostly be clear on their own. But in the Prolegomena <note>the introductory preface to the volume</note>, everything concerning the usage of the Fathers will be illustrated with the utmost accuracy. **Naas**¹⁰⁹ i.e., the Naassenes in the first edition of Hippolytus's *Philosophumena*. Likewise other similar names. **Marctert** i.e., Marcion as cited in Tertullian; **Marcepiph** i.e., as cited in Epiphanius. **Chrgue** i.e., Chrysostom from a 6th-century Wolfenbüttel codex <note>original: "cod. Guelf."</note>. **Dampar cod** i.e., John of Damascus’s *Sacra Parallela* <note>a theological florilegium</note> from a La Rochefoucauld codex <note>original: "cod. Rupefuc."</note> dating to roughly the 8th century. **Eusmar**²²⁶ i.e., Eusebius's *Questions to Marinus* in Angelo Mai's *New Library of the Fathers*, Vol. IV.

**al** i.e., others; **aliq** i.e., some or sometimes; **c.** and **cum** signify "with the authority of." Thus, **Gb⁰ c. A** means Griesbach recommends omission based on the authority of Codex A. **mu** i.e., many; **pm, permu** i.e., very many; **pler** i.e., most; **pauciss** i.e., very few. **et.** (with a period) i.e., also. **evgg** or **evg ll** i.e., <term>evangelistaries|Church service books containing Gospel lessons arranged by the calendar</term>. **rell** i.e., the rest. **49ev** etc. i.e., evangelistary number 49, etc. **min** i.e., <term>minuscules|Greek manuscripts written in a smaller, cursive script, generally from the 9th century onward</term>. **mg** i.e., margin. **unc** i.e., <term>uncials|Early Greek manuscripts written in large, formal capital letters</term>. **yscr** etc. are manuscripts <term>collated|The process of comparing a manuscript word-for-word against a standard text to note differences</term> by F. H. Scrivener. **2pe** etc. are St. Petersburg codices collated by Ed. de Muralt. **cat** i.e., a <term>catena|A "chain" of interpretations from various Church Fathers written in the margins of a Bible</term>.

**ς** <note>the "stigma" symbol used here for the "Received Text"</note> i.e., the Elzevir edition of 1624, along with Robert Estienne's edition of 1550. Where these differ, **ς** refers to Robert Estienne, and **ςᵉ** to Elzevir.

**Ln** i.e., Lachmann’s larger edition (1842, 1850). Lachmann agrees with me <note>the editor, Tischendorf</note> if he is not specifically named.

**Sz.** i.e., Scholz’s edition (1830, 1836).

**Ti** i.e., Tischendorf’s edition of 1859.

**Gb** i.e., Griesbach’s edition of the Gospels, 1827 (prepared by David Schulz). **Gb⁰** and **Gb⁰⁰** indicate an omission that Griesbach saw as probable and highly probable, respectively; likewise, **Gb'** and **Gb''** indicate a reading recommended and highly recommended by Griesbach; **Gb +** indicates something admitted into the text by Griesbach with some doubt. **Schu:** i.e., David Schulz in his 1827 edition of Griesbach’s Gospels. Griesbach and Scholz agree with the Received Text (**ς**) if they are not named. **ς (— Gb Sz)** i.e., the Received Text except for Griesbach and Scholz.

Pages 1—2 and 15—16 of the first bundle <note>original: fasciculi</note> were incorrectly transcribed in several places (for example, in Matthew 1:2, "Phares" <note>original: Φαρεσ</note> for "Judah" <note>original: Ιουδαν</note>). ### THE REMAINING VERSIONS:

**aeth** — Ethiopic, i.e., from the Roman editions, the Polyglot, and P. Platt.
**arm** — Armenian.
**arr** — Arabic.
**cop** — Memphitic <note>also known as Bohairic, a Coptic dialect from Lower Egypt</note>.
**sah** — Sahidic <note>a Coptic dialect from Upper Egypt</note>.
**basm** — Basmuric <note>a minor Coptic dialect</note>.
**syrcu** — Curetonian Syriac, from a 5th-century Nitrian manuscript.
**syrsch** — Syriac, from the edition by Schaaf.
**syrᵖ** — Syriac, from the edition by White.
**syrhr** — Syriac, from the Jerusalem manuscript.
**persᵖ** — Persian, from the Polyglot.
**persʷʰᵉ** — Persian, from Whelock’s edition.
**go** — Gothic.
**fr** — Frankish <note>an early Germanic language</note>.
**sax** — Anglo-Saxon.
**sl** — Slavonic.

---

The names of the **CHURCH FATHERS** will mostly be clear on their own.
**Naas** <note>original: "Naas"</note> — the Naassenes <note>an early Gnostic sect</note> as cited in the first edition of Hippolytus's *Philosophumena*. Other similar abbreviations follow this pattern.
**Marctert** — Marcion <note>a 2nd-century teacher later declared a heretic</note> as quoted in Tertullian.
**Marcepiph** — Marcion as quoted in Epiphanius.
**Chrgue** — Chrysostom, from a 6th-century Wolfenbüttel manuscript.

---

**al** — others.
**aliq** — several, or several times.
**c.** — with the authority of. Thus, **Gb⁰ c. A** means Griesbach recommends omission based on the authority of Codex A.
**mu** — many.
**pm** — very many.
**pler** — most.

<column-break/>

**pauciss** — very few.
**et.** (with a period) — also / even.
**evgg** or **evgll** — evangelistaries <note>books containing the Gospel lessons for liturgical use</note>.
**rell** — the rest.
**49ᵉᵛ** etc. — evangelistary number 49, etc.
**barb** — the Barberini evangelistary, a 7th-century palimpsest.
**carp** — the Carpentras evangelistary, 9th century.
**ven** — the Venice evangelistary, an 8th-century palimpsest.
**min** — minuscules <note>manuscripts written in a smaller, cursive Greek script</note>.
**mg** — the margin.
**unc** — uncials <note>manuscripts written in large, formal capital letters</note>.
**yˢᶜʳ** etc. — manuscripts collated by F. H. Scrivener.
**2 peᵉᵗᵉ** — St. Petersburg manuscripts collated by Ed. de Muralt.
**cat** — a catena <note>a "chain" of commentary from various Church Fathers written in the margins</note>.

---

**ς** — the Elzevir edition of 1624, together with Robert Estienne’s (Stephanus) edition of 1550. Where they differ, **ς** refers to Stephanus and **ςᵉ** refers to Elzevir. <note>The symbol ς (stigma) is often used to denote the "Textus Receptus," the standard Greek text of the era.</note>
**Ln** — Lachmann’s larger edition (1842, 1850). Lachmann agrees with my reading if he is not specifically named.
**Sz** — Scholz’s edition (1830).
**Ti** — Tischendorf’s edition of 1859.
**Gb** — Griesbach’s edition of the Gospels (1827).
**Gb⁰** and **Gb⁰⁰** — indicate an omission that Griesbach saw as probable and highly probable, respectively.
Likewise, **Gb'** and **Gb''** — a reading recommended and highly recommended by Griesbach.
**Gb+** — something received into the text by Griesbach, though with some doubt.
**Schu:** — David Schulz in the 1827 Griesbach edition.
**Gb** and **Sz** agree with **ς** <note>the standard text</note> if they are not specifically named.
**ς (= Gb Sz)** — means the standard text except for Griesbach and Scholz.

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW.

## I.

<margin>1 see Luke 3:23—38</margin>
1 $^{1. 8}$ The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. <margin>2—6 1 Chronicles 2:1—15</margin> 2 Abraham begat Isaac, and Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob begat Judah and his brothers, <margin>3—6 Ruth 4:18 ff</margin> 3 and Judah begat Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez begat Hezron, and Hezron begat Ram, <margin>Genesis 38:16 ff</margin> 4 and Ram begat Amminadab, and Amminadab begat—

---

<note>This horizontal line separates the biblical text from the "critical apparatus," where the editor lists variations found in different ancient copies of the Bible.</note>

<margin>*</margin> *According to Matthew:* <note>original: "κα. μαθθ. c."</note> This spelling with a double "th" is supported by Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus <note>two of the oldest and most important Greek Bibles from the 4th century</note>. This same very ancient form is confirmed by several Old Latin and Vulgate manuscripts; for example, manuscript *e* at the end of Matthew has *the end of according to Matthew, the beginning of according to John*, and manuscript *q* has *the end of according to John, the beginning of according to Luke*. Also, Codex Bezae (like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) has nothing at the top of the page except "According to Matthew." Other editions <note>like those by Griesbach, Scholz, and Lachmann</note> include the word "Gospel," following manuscripts C, E, K, and others, some of which add "The reading of the holy gospel."

1. **David:** <note>original: "δαυειδ"</note> This spelling occurs everywhere in the primary manuscripts <note>Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.</note>. Editors like Griesbach and Scholz use "David" <note>original: "δαυιδ"</note>, as it is written here and there in later manuscripts. Most capital-letter manuscripts <note>uncials</note> usually write it as a shorthand "DAD" with a line over it. The traditional Greek text <note>the Textus Receptus, marked here as ς</note> uses "Dabid."

2. **Abraham:** Written thus in most manuscripts. | **Isaac:** Codex Sinaiticus and the Latin manuscript *k* write "Isak" twice. | **and (the first):** <note>original: "δε pr"</note> Omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus and several Old Latin manuscripts. The Curetonian Syriac version omits it here and in the following verses; manuscript *k* uses "and" throughout (*and Judah begat Perez and Perez begat...*), but omits it in verse 4 after Ram. In verse 12 it has "Jeconiah however" and in verse 13 "and Abiah however." | Some manuscripts add "the" before Judah.

3. **the (second):** Manuscript *v* omits this. | **Zerah:** <note>original: "ζαρα"</note> Codex Vaticanus has "Zare." Other Latin versions vary between *Zarad, Zaret, Zara,* and *Zaram*. The Latin manuscripts *g¹* and *k* omit the phrase "and Zerah by Tamar." | **Hezron:** <note>original: "εσρωμ"</note> Thus in most manuscripts; however, the Latin Vulgate and some others use "Esron" (matching the spelling in the Gospel of Luke).

4. **Amminadab:** <note>original: "αμιναδ-"</note> This spelling is found in many manuscripts. Tischendorf <note>Ti</note> prefers "Ammeinadab" <note>original: "αμειναδ-"</note> based on Codex Vaticanus and the Sahidic Coptic version, following the oldest copies of the Greek Old Testament. The name ends in "b" in most copies, but some have "m" (Amminadam).

### ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 1, 17.

...the deportation to Babylon. <margin>Ezra 3:2</margin> **12** And after the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah begat Salathiel, and Salathiel begat Zerubbabel, **13** and Zerubbabel begat Abiud, and Abiud begat Eliakim, and Eliakim begat Azor, **14** and Azor begat Zadok, and Zadok begat Achim, and Achim begat Eliud, **15** and Eliud begat Eleazar, and Eleazar begat Matthan, and Matthan begat Jacob, **16** and Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus who is called Christ. **17** <insert>2. 10</insert> So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.

---

**Jechoniah and Joachim:** <note>original: "Iech. et Ioak. εἷς δὲ ἦν καὶ ὁ αὐτός, διωνυμίᾳ χρώμενος"</note> These two names refer to the same person, who used two different names. Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, writes: <note>original: "Hier Matth 'sciamus igitur Iechoniam priorem...'"</note> "Let us know, therefore, that the first Jechoniah is the same as the one called Joachim; the second, however, is the son, not the father. The first is written with 'k' and 'm', the latter with 'ch' and 'n'. Through the error of scribes and the long passage of time, these became confused among the Greeks and Latins." Looking back at the beginning of his commentary on Daniel, Jerome criticizes Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> for falsely claiming that a generation is missing in Matthew's list. Many other manuscripts <note>original: "mu al plus"</note> including the Harclean and Peshitta Syriac <note>syr^hr, syr^p</note> read: **Joachim; and Joachim (sometimes written Jakim) begat Jechoniah.** The same is confirmed by Irenaeus in his work *Against Heresies* (3, 21, 9): "Joseph is shown to be the son of Joachim and Jechoniah, just as Matthew explains his generation." Epiphanius also suggests <note>original: "ὑπὸ τινῶν ἀμαθῶν"</note> that "ignorant people" caused doubt about the text, as if a passage had been removed during a correction. For those who want to understand the "accurate copies" <note>original: "τὰ ἀκριβῆ τῶν ἀντιγράφων"</note>, he notes that Jechoniah (also called Seloum and Amasias) begat a second Jechoniah (also called Zedekiah and Joachim). It seems to him that in the common text, the words **"and Jechoniah begat Jechoniah"** have fallen out.

**11-12.** Manuscripts E, K, L, U, V, and Π use variant spellings for "deportation" <note>original: "μετοικησιας" or "μετοικισηαν" instead of "μετοικεσίας"</note>. This also occurs in verse 17.

**12. begat:** <note>original: "εγεννησεν"</note> This is the standard reading in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and many others. Codex Vaticanus (B) uses a different tense <note>original: "γεννα*"</note>. | **Salathiel:** Codex Vaticanus and the Old Latin manuscript *k* (and the Curetonian Syriac) spell this *Sealthiel* or *Selathiel*. | **Zerubbabel:** Manuscript Δ spells this *Zorombababel*.

**13.** Codex Vaticanus uses "begat" <note>original: "γεννα"</note> for **begat Abiud**. | Codex Sinaiticus spells the name *Abiout*. | Manuscripts M, V, Π, and the Coptic versions spell the name *Eliakim* with an "i".

**14. Zadok:** <note>original: "σαδωχ"</note> The first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and several Old Latin manuscripts use this spelling ending in "ch." Manuscript Γ reads *Sadak*. | **Achim:** <note>original: "αχειμ"</note> Found in most major manuscripts. Manuscript Δ reads *Achein*. Others read *Achin* or *Achen*. Codex Sinaiticus and others spell it *Achim*. | **Eliud:** Codex Sinaiticus and manuscript E have variant spellings ending in "t" or "ei."

**15.** Variant spellings for **Eliud** and **Matthan**. The common text (ς) uses two 't's in *Matthan*, supported by most manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.

**16. the husband... of whom was born:** Several Old Latin manuscripts (a, g^1, k, q) read: **to whom the virgin Mary, being espoused, bore Jesus.** This is similar to the Curetonian Syriac, Armenian versions, and early church writers like Gaul and the author of the *Opus Imperfectum*. | Manuscript 64 omits the name **Jesus**. | The Old Latin *b* and *d* and the Curetonian Syriac omit the phrase **who is called**.

**17. David:** See note at 1:1. | At the end of the verse, Old Latin manuscripts *b* and *c* and the Ethiopic version add: **"So all the generations from Abraham until the coming of Jesus Christ are 42 generations."**

### 1, 18. ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

**18** Now the birth of Jesus Christ happened in this way. <insert>3. 5</insert> When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. **19** <insert>4. 10</insert> And Joseph her husband, being a just man and not wanting to make a public example of her, intended to divorce her quietly. **20** But while he thought about these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife; for that which is 
<margin>Luke 2:21</margin> conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. **21** and she will bear a son, and you shall call—

---

**18.** Harclean Syriac marginal note: <note>original: "genealogia hucusque, incipit ev. sec. mt"</note> "The genealogy ends here; the Gospel according to Matthew begins." | **Jesus Christ** <note>abbreviated as "ιν χν" in the Greek</note> is supported by Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Codex Ephraemi (C), and many others including the Sahidic and Coptic versions; Codex Vaticanus (B) and others read **Christ Jesus**; Tischendorf and Griesbach read simply **the Christ** based on the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Irenaeus. Irenaeus writes: <note>original: "ceterum potuerat dicere Mt: Iesu vero generatio sic erat..."</note> "Matthew could have said: 'Now the generation of Jesus was thus,' but the Holy Spirit, foreseeing those who would corrupt the truth and guarding against their fraud, says through Matthew: 'Now the generation of the Christ was thus.'" | **Birth** <note>original: γένεσις - "genesis"</note> is supported by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; however, the Textus Receptus <note>the standard printed Greek text of the Reformation era</note> uses a different word for **birth** <note>original: γέννησις - "gennesis"</note>. The Dialogue of Maximus notes: <note>original: "ἡ γένεσις εἶπεν, οὐχὶ ἡ γέννησις... πρῶτον γένεσιν ἄκουσον τοῦ ναοῦ καὶ τότε γέννησιν"</note> "It says *genesis* (origin/existence), not *gennesis* (the act of birth). One 'n', not two. First hear of the *genesis* of the temple, and then the *birth*." | **Betrothed**: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus support the shorter reading; the Textus Receptus adds "for" <note>original: γαρ</note>. 

**19.** **Make a public example**: <note>original: δειγματίσαι - "deigmatisai"</note> Griesbach and others prefer this shorter form. Eusebius explains: <note>original: "εὖ γοῦν καὶ τὸ μὴ θέλων αὐτὴν δειγματίσαι εἰρῆσθαι δοκεῖ..."</note> "The Evangelist seems to have spoken well in saying 'not wanting to *show* her' (deigmatisai); for he did not say 'make a public example of her' (paradeigmatisai), but simply 'to show,' there being a great difference. To *make a public example* suggests exposing a wrongdoer to public disgrace and accusation, whereas *to show* simply means to make manifest." Other manuscripts use the longer word <note>original: παραδειγματίσαι - "paradeigmatisai"</note> which implies "to disgrace." A scholarly note adds: <note>original: "δειγματ. μὲν γάρ ἐστι τὸ ἁπλῶς ἀπολῦσαι, παραδειγμ. δὲ τὸ ἐπὶ κακῷ φανερῶσαι καὶ παραδοῦναι εἰς θάνατον ὡς μοιχαλίδα"</note> "To *show* means simply to release, but to *make a public example* means to expose for a crime and hand over to death as an adulteress."

**20.** Some manuscripts read "thinking" <note>original: ενθυμουμένου</note> as a participle. | **Mary**: Most manuscripts read *Mariam* <note>the Hebrew/Aramaic form</note>, but some like Codex Vaticanus read *Marian* <note>the Hellenized Greek form</note>. | **Is from the Holy Spirit**: The word order varies slightly between "the Holy Spirit is" and "is the Holy Spirit" across different manuscripts like Sinaiticus and the Vulgate.

**21.** **You shall call**: Some versions use slightly different verb endings for "you shall call" (singular vs. plural or future tense variations). | In the phrase **his people**, the Curetonian Syriac <note>an ancient version of the Gospels in the Aramaic dialect of Edessa</note> reads **the world**.

## II.

**1** Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, Magi <note>Wise men or scholar-priests, likely from Persia</note> from the East arrived in Jerusalem, **2** saying, “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and 
<margin>(Numbers 24:17)</margin>
have come to worship him.”

---

**22.** **all**: The Curetonian Syriac <note>a 5th-century manuscript of the Old Syriac Gospels</note>, the Latin translation of Irenaeus (twice), and Epiphanius omit this word. | **by**: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), Bezae (D), and others. The standard received text adds “the” before “Lord”. | **the prophet**: Supported by Eusebius, Irenaeus, and Augustine; however, Codex Bezae (D), some Old Latin versions, and the Curetonian Syriac add the specific name “Isaiah.” | **saying**: Omitted by some versions and Irenaeus.

**23.** **they shall call**: Supported by most major manuscripts including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Codex Bezae (D) and others read “you shall call” (singular), matching the Greek Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> version of Isaiah. | **his**: Omitted in the original hand of Sinaiticus. | **the**: Omitted in Vaticanus due to a scribal error.

**24.** **raised**: Supported by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The standard received text uses a word meaning “awakened.” | **Joseph**: Some manuscripts add the definite article “the Joseph.” | **his wife**: The Sahidic and Coptic versions, and a correction in Sinaiticus, add the name “Mary”; the Curetonian Syriac reads simply “Mary” instead of “his wife.”

**25.** **did not know**: The Vulgate and Augustine use a tense implying a continuing state (“was not knowing”). Codex Bezae and others use a simple past tense (“knew her not”). The Curetonian Syriac adds “and he lived with her chastely until...”. | **until**: Omitted by Vaticanus. | **a son**: Supported by the earliest manuscripts ($\aleph$, B, Z). The standard received text and many later manuscripts read **her firstborn son**, likely influenced by the phrasing in Luke 2:7. Jerome <note>the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> notes that some “most perversely” suspect Mary had other children based on this verse, arguing that “firstborn” simply refers to the child who opens the womb, whether or not siblings follow.

**II. 1.** **Now**: Omitted by Sinaiticus and some others. | **of Judea**: The Vulgate and Syriac versions often read “of Judah.” Jerome notes: “This is an error of the librarians; for we think it was first published by the Evangelist, as we read in the Hebrew itself, as ‘Judah,’ not ‘Judea.’” | **in the days of Herod the king**: Omitted in one branch of the Sinaiticus tradition but restored later. | **Jerusalem**: Variations exist in the Greek spelling between the classical form (*Hierosolyma*) and the more Hebraic form (*Hierousalem*).

**2.** **we saw**: Small variation in Greek spelling between *eidomen* and *idomen*. | **him**: A minor grammatical variation in the case of the pronoun.

...we have come to worship him. **3** When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. **4** And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ <note>original: "ho Christos"; the Anointed One or Messiah</note> was to be born.

<margin>
Micah 5:1
John 7:42

**5** They said to him, “In Bethlehem of Judea; for so it is written by the prophet: **6** ‘And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’” **7** Then Herod, secretly calling the Magi, determined exactly from them the time of the star’s appearance. **8** And sending them to Bethlehem, he said, “Go and search diligently for the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.” **9** After listening to the king, they went their way; and behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. **10** When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. **11** And going into—

---

**3.** **the king Herod**: Found in manuscripts $\aleph$ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), D (Bezae), Z, and others. Other versions like C, E, K, L (the "Majority Text") place "Herod" before "the king." | **all (Jerusalem)**: Some versions add the feminine article "the," while Codex Bezae (D) omits "all."

**4.** **priests**: Codex Delta (Δ) writes "priests" instead of "chief priests." | **of them**: Omitted by some manuscripts (D, Γ, and others).

**5.** **they said**: The spelling *eipan* is found in the oldest manuscripts ($\aleph$, B); the standard *eipon* is in later ones. | **to him**: Omitted in some versions of the Church Father Chrysostom. | **by the prophet**: One manuscript adds "Micah saying," and a Syriac note specifically names "Micah."

**6.** **land of Judah**: While the main text says "land of Judah," Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions say "of Judea." The Vulgate and Jerome use "land of Judah." | **by no means**: Various manuscripts use different Greek negatives (*oudamōs* vs *mē*), but all convey that Bethlehem is "not" the least. | **from you**: Most manuscripts use *ek sou*, but some early ones use *ex ou*. | **for**: Omitted by $\aleph$ (Sinaiticus); some versions add "to me" (*moi*). | **shepherd**: Codex Bezae (D) uses a slightly different verb form meaning "he shall rule" or "govern."

**7.** **determined exactly**: Spelling variation in B (Vaticanus) and D (Bezae).

**8.** **Bethlehem**: Various spellings (Bethleem, Bethleaim, Bithleem) appear across manuscripts. | **he said**: Some ancient Syriac and Latin versions add "to them." | **search diligently**: The word order varies between the oldest manuscripts ($\aleph$, B, C, D) and the later "received" Greek text. | **when**: Different Greek conjunctions (*epan*, *otan*, *ean*) are used across manuscripts to mean "whenever" or "after."

**9.** **the (star)**: Omitted by manuscript L and others. | **saw**: The spelling varies between *eidon* (standard) and *idon* (found in $\aleph$, C, V). | **came to rest**: The oldest manuscripts use *estathē* ("was stood/placed"), while later ones use *estē* ("stood"). | **where the child was**: Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions simply say "over the child."

**10.** **star**: Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$) uses a slightly different grammatical ending (*asteran*).

<term>KATA MAΘΘAION</term> (According to Matthew): The title of the Gospel.
<term>Ἡρῴδης</term> (Herod): Herod the Great, the Roman-appointed King of Judea.
<term>Ἱεροσόλυμα</term> (Jerusalem): The holy city and seat of Herod's power.
<term>Βηθλεὲμ</term> (Bethlehem): A small town south of Jerusalem, the prophesied birthplace of the Messiah.
<term>Ἰουδαίας</term> (Judea): The southern region of ancient Israel.
<term>Ἰσραήλ</term> (Israel): The people or the land of the covenant.
<term>Χριστὸς</term> (Christ): The Greek translation of the Hebrew "Messiah," meaning "Anointed One."
<term>Codex Sinaiticus (א)</term>: A 4th-century Greek Bible, one of the most important witnesses to the text.
<term>Codex Vaticanus (B)</term>: A 4th-century manuscript kept in the Vatican Library.
<term>Codex Ephraemi (C)</term>: A 5th-century "palimpsest" where the biblical text was erased and written over.
<term>Codex Bezae (D)</term>: A 5th-century manuscript featuring both Greek and Latin text, known for its unique readings.
</vocab>

**1** In those days John the Baptist appears, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, **2** saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.” <margin>4:17</margin> **3** For this is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.” <margin>Isaiah 40:3</margin> **4** Now John himself had his garment made of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist; and his food was locusts and wild honey. **5** Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the surrounding region of the Jordan were going out to him, **6** and they were being baptized in the Jordan River by him, confessing their sins. **7** But seeing many...

...of human anointing, yet he obtained the name of "Nazirite" among men, not becoming a Nazirite from the oil called *nazer* <note>original Greek: "ναζὲρ" — referring to a specific type of consecrated oil</note>, but being such by nature, and called a Nazirite by men because he was from Nazareth. <note>The author is finishing a thought from the previous page arguing that Jesus was a Nazirite (consecrated one) by nature rather than by ritual oil.</note> In the text of Matthew itself, he writes *Nazoraios* <note>original: "ναζωραῖος"</note> (whereas it was previously edited as *Naziraios*, just as the Old Latin and Vulgate manuscripts write *nazareus*).

### <term>Critical Apparatus<note>Scholarly notes comparing different ancient versions of the New Testament. The letters and symbols (ℵ, B, C, etc.) represent specific ancient manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus or Codex Vaticanus.</note></term>

**III. 1.** The word **but** (δε) is included in manuscripts ℵ, B, C, U, R, 1, 33, and most others, including the Vulgate and Coptic versions. The Textus Receptus <note>The "Received Text" used for the King James Bible</note> (followed by D, E, K, etc.) omits it. Manuscript B* spells John as *Iōanēs* with one 'n'.

**2. saying** (λεγων): Supported by ℵ, B, and the Sahidic Coptic. The Textus Receptus adds "And" before "saying."

**3. through** (διὰ): Supported by ℵ, B, C, D, and others. The Textus Receptus uses "by" (ὑπὸ). | **saying** (λεγοντος): Omitted by manuscript 360 and some Syriac/Irenaeus versions. | **his** (paths): Some versions (Old Latin, Syriac) add: *"every valley shall be filled and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall become straight and the rough ways smooth, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God"* — taking this expansion from Luke 3:5–6.

**4. the** (before John): Omitted by manuscript D and others. | **was his [food]**: The word order varies between manuscripts. | **locusts and wild honey**: Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note> reports that the Gospel of the Ebionites <note>A Jewish-Christian group who were vegetarians</note> altered this to: *"and his food was wild honey, the taste of which was like manna, like a cake in oil"* (or rather "in honey"). Epiphanius adds this criticism: *"so that they might change the word of truth into a lie and make 'cakes' [enkridas] instead of 'locusts' [akridas]."* <note>A pun in Greek: 'akridas' (locusts) and 'enkridas' (honey-cakes) sound very similar.</note>

**5. Jerusalem**: Some manuscripts (like 1 and Origen) add "all" before Jerusalem.

**6. were being baptized**: Manuscript 33 and Hilary add "all." | **river**: Included in ℵ, B, C, and many others; omitted by the Textus Receptus and the Vulgate. | **by him**: Omitted by the original hand of manuscript ℵ.

<note>The following section contains variants found in ancient Christian writings and lost gospels that differ from the standard Bible text.</note>

In many other [sources], the *Gospel of the Ebionites* <note>original: "Ev. Ebion." — an early Jewish-Christian gospel now lost</note> according to the testimony of Epiphanius reads thus: *And a voice came from heaven saying: "You are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased"; and again: "Today I have begotten you." And again a voice from heaven to him: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And then,* it says, *John falling down before him said: "I beg you, Lord, you baptize me." But he prevented him, saying: "Let it be, for thus it is proper that all things be fulfilled."*

Similarly, Justin <note>Justin Martyr, an early Christian philosopher</note> in his *Dialogue with Trypho* (103): *At the same time as he went up from the river Jordan, the voice spoke to him: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you."* Again in the same place (88): *When John went down to the water, a fire was kindled in the Jordan etc.* In the *Treatise on Not Repeating Baptism* (found in Cyprian's works, edited by Rigaltius, p. 142): *In which book (titled "The Preaching of Paul") you will find Christ confessing his own sin against all the scriptures—likewise, when he was baptized, fire was seen upon the water.* From the *Gospel of the Nazarenes*, Jerome brings these things: *It happened then, when the Lord had ascended from the water, the whole fountain of the Holy Spirit descended and rested upon him and said to him: "My Son, in all the prophets I was waiting for you that you might come and I might rest in you. For you are my rest, you are my firstborn son, who reigns forever."* According to the "Secret" works: *And John indeed baptized him in water, but he baptized John in spirit.*

### <term>Critical Apparatus<note>This list shows how different ancient hand-copied manuscripts (Codices) vary in their wording. Letters like ℵ, B, C, and D refer to specific famous Bibles from the 4th and 5th centuries.</note></term>

**IV. 1.** **Jesus** <note>original Greek: "ο ι̅ς̅"</note>: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Bezae (D), and others. (Codex L reads: **But Jesus was led up**) ... Tischendorf (Ti) reads **Jesus** with Codex Vaticanus (B) and others. | Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and the Syriac versions read: **by the Holy Spirit** <note>original Greek: "υπο του πν."</note> **into the wilderness.**

**2.** **Forty** <note>original Greek: "τεσσερακ."</note>: This spelling occurs twice in the oldest manuscripts (ℵ, B, C, L). Other versions use a slightly different spelling for the number 40. | **And forty** (omitted in manuscript 130) **nights**: Found in ℵ and D (along with the Latin Vulgate and Coptic). Others (B, C, E) swap the order to: **And nights forty**. Manuscript 1 and the Syriac omit the mention of nights entirely, similar to the accounts in Luke and Mark.

**3.** **The tempter, coming to him, said**: Supported by ℵ, B, and the Latin/Coptic/Syriac versions. The older "standard" text (ς) adds the word **to him** earlier: **Coming to him, the tempter said**.

**4.** **But he answering** <note>original: "ℵ^b ο δ αποκρ."</note> | Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin and Syriac copies read: **But Jesus answering** | **The** <note>original Greek: "ο"</note>: Found in ℵ, B, C, D, and the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. Some later manuscripts omit it. | **By** <note>original Greek: "επι"</note>: Found in ℵ, B, and many others. Other editors (Ln, Ti) use **In** <note>original: "εν"</note> based on Codex C and D. | **Coming out of the mouth [of God]**: Omitted in some Old Latin and Syriac versions.

<note>The following notes represent the "critical apparatus," where scholars compare different ancient versions of the Bible to see where they differ.</note>

17. **I have not come, etc.** (also in the *Clementine Homilies* and Ptolemy's *Letter to Flora*): According to the witnesses in the *Dialogue against Marcion* (63), Marcion <note>A famous 2nd-century teacher who rejected the Old Testament</note> corrupted this text. The witness says: "The Judaizers wrote this: 'I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it'; but Christ did not say it this way, for he says: 'I have not come to fulfill the Law but to abolish it.'" Similarly, Isidore (1, 371) records Marcion's version as: "What do you think? That I came to fulfill the Law or the Prophets? I came not to fulfill but to abolish."

18. **For** (Old Latin and Vulgate read "Amen, indeed"): Six other manuscripts, many Old Latin versions, and the Sahidic translation omit this. | **from the Law** (Clementine Homilies, Origen): Manuscripts 13, 124, the Armenian, and the Syriac versions add "and the prophets." The Valentinians <note>A group of early Christian gnostics</note> according to Irenaeus (page 14) omit it in both Greek and Latin. | **shall pass** (second occurrence): Omitted by the original hand of Codex Vaticanus.

19. **If** (Manuscripts D and 33 read "whenever"): Omitted by Codex Bezae (D) and most of the Vulgate and Old Latin. | **Therefore** (Old Latin reads "For"): Omitted by Codex Leningrad, the Armenian version, Cyprian, and Lucifer of Cagliari. | **breaks**: Omitted by Codex Delta. | **this one** (Cyprian and others place this before "teaches"): Omitted by Codex Bezae. | **of heaven** (twice): Manuscript M reads "of God."

20. **For I tell you... kingdom of heaven** (Justin Martyr in *Dialogue with Trypho* 105 writes: "It is written in the memoirs that he [Christ] said these things: 'Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.'"): Omitted by the Old Latin manuscript 'd'. | **Exceeds**: Variant spellings found in Codex L and Codex Delta. | **Your righteousness**: Manuscript group ℵBEKLMV, Justin, and Clement place "your" first; while the "Received Text" used by later editors (like Stephanus) places "righteousness" first.

21. **It was said**: Variant spellings "errethē" or "errēthē" appear between Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae.

22. **With his brother**: Found in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Vulgate. Note that the phrase "without cause" <note>original: "eikē"</note> is missing here. Pseudo-Athanasius notes: "The accurate copies contain only this; for 'without cause' was added later as an insertion." Justin Martyr and Ptolemy also support the shorter reading (e.g., "Whoever is angry is liable to the fire").

### Critical Apparatus
<note>This section compares different ancient hand-copied versions of the text to determine the most likely original wording.</note>

40. **to the one wanting**: Manuscript D reads **the one who wants**; Manuscript Delta reads **the one wanting** (different grammatical case) | **let [him] have** (Origen, Irenaeus): Manuscript D and Basil read **you shall let [him] have** (Latin: *dimittes*) | **to him**: [Manuscript] Sinaiticus (corrector) reads **to this one** | **cloak**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus, 33, and about 10 others, as well as Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions add **your**.

41. **whoever** (Basil: **who**; Chrysostom: **if someone**) **you** (Basil: **if you**, Manuscripts L and Delta omit **you**, Sinaiticus and Delta add **if**) | **will force**: based on Manuscripts B, L, M, S, U, and others; Manuscript D reads **forces**; Sinaiticus, E, G, K, V, and others read **should force** (a slight change in Greek mood) | **two** (Latin versions *f*, Coptic, Syriac, Ethiopic, Gothic, Basil, Chrysostom): Latin versions *d, a, b, e, g1, k* and Chromatius read **two more**, while the Vulgate and others read **another two** or **two others**.

42. **you** (Sinaiticus corrector): Sinaiticus (original hand) reads **to you** | **give**: based on Sinaiticus, B, D, 13, 124, and Clement. The "Received Text" reads **be giving** (a continuous action) based on E, G, K, and others, likely influenced by the parallel in Luke | Manuscript *d* and 4 others read **to the one wanting**; most Latin versions and the Vulgate read **from the one wanting to borrow from you do not be turned away** | **from you**: Manuscripts *d, k, m*, Clement, and Cyprian omit this phrase | **to borrow**: based on Sinaiticus, B, D, etc. (Luke 6:34 uses a different spelling found in A, L, P); other editors (Lachmann, Tischendorf) use a variant spelling found in E, G, K, etc.

43. **it was said**: spelling variant between Manuscripts Sinaiticus, L, S, U and others versus B, D, E, G, K, etc.

44. **your enemies**: based on Sinaiticus, B, 1, 22, 209, several Latin versions, Vulgate, Coptic, and early Church Fathers (Origen, Eusebius, Irenaeus, Cyprian). The "Received Text" adds **bless those who curse you** (found in D, E, K, L, M, etc., and Syriac/Armenian versions), which most scholars believe was moved here from Luke's Gospel | **and pray**: based on Sinaiticus, B, 1, 22, and others. The "Received Text" adds **do good to those who hate you** before this, again matching Luke's version | **those persecuting**: (some versions read **those threatening**) based on Sinaiticus, B, 1, 22, and others. The "Received Text" adds **those who falsely accuse you and** before "persecute you," matching the phrasing in Luke.

45. **heaven**: (Origen, Eusebius): several manuscripts and Church Fathers add the definite article **the** [heavens] | **that**: (Constantine, Chrysostom): many Latin and Syriac versions read **who** (referring to the Father); Eusebius reads **whoever**. | **evil and good**: (Latin versions *b, d, k*)...

### Critical Apparatus
<note>This section lists variations found in different ancient copies of the Bible. Scholars use these to determine the most accurate original wording.</note>

**45.** Versions of this verse appear in the Syriac Peshitta, the Gothic version, and the writings of Athenagoras, Origen, Eusebius, and others.
*Compare also Justin Martyr (Apology 1, 15):* "his sun rise on sinners and righteous and evil," and in his *Dialogue with Trypho (96):* "the sun... rising on ungrateful and righteous and raining on holy and evil." The Naassene fragment reads: "who makes the sun rise on righteous and unrighteous and rains on holy and sinners." Clement of Alexandria (Homily 3, 57) reads similarly: "who makes the sun rise on good and evil and brings rain on righteous and unrighteous." This is also found in Irenaeus, Origen, Tertullian, and Augustine.
| **Manuscript Sinaiticus (original hand):** omits "and sends rain on the righteous and unrighteous." Compare to the citation in Justin Martyr above.

**46. you have:** supported by Manuscript Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the majority of manuscripts. **you will have:** supported by Manuscript Bezae, the Vulgate, and Cyprian.
*Compare also Athenagoras (Embassy 12):* "For if you love, he says, those who love and lend to those who lend to you, what reward will you have?"
| **not even:** Manuscript Sinaiticus (original hand) and the Curetonian Syriac omit this.
| **the same:** supported by Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. Other versions read **this** (Latin Vulgate) or **so** (Manuscript Bezae, Coptic).

**47. brothers:** supported by Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae. **friends:** found in many later manuscripts and the Syriac Peshitta.
| **Gentiles:** supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae. **tax collectors:** found in many later manuscripts and the Gothic version.
| **the same:** supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. Some read **so** or **this same thing**.

**48. as:** supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Origen. **just as:** supported by Manuscript Bezae and the majority of manuscripts.
| **the heavenly [Father]:** supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Vulgate. **in the heavens:** supported by the original hand of Manuscript Bezae and the Curetonian Syriac.

**VI. 1. But:** supported by Sinaiticus and others. Omitted by Manuscript Vaticanus and the Vulgate.
| **righteousness:** supported by the original hand of Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae.

11. **daily**: <note>original: "τ. επιουσιον" (t. epiousion)</note> Chrysostom says: *that is, for the day*; Sahidic: *coming*; Coptic: *of tomorrow*; Peshitta Syriac: *necessary* (*indigence*); Old Latin and various fathers: *daily*; Vulgate: *supersubstantial*. Jerome says: *epiousion* i.e., *principal, excellent, particular*... *Some say, because it is above all "ousiai" (essences), that is, above all substances*... which does not differ much from the sense we explained. He also notes: *What we expressed as "supersubstantial," in Greek is "epiousion," which the Septuagint frequently translates as "periousion" (treasured)*... *in Hebrew "sgolla" (treasure), Symmachus "exaireton" (choice)*... *in the Gospel according to the Hebrews "mahar" (tomorrow) is found*... *we can understand "supersubstantial bread" differently, as that which is above all substances and surpasses all creatures.* Ambrose says: *supersubstantial*... *The Latin called this bread "daily," which the Greeks called "coming," because the Greeks say "the coming day"* <note>original: "τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν ἡμέραν"</note>.

*Victorinus <note>Victorinus Afer, a 4th-century philosopher and convert.</note> (Book 2 against Arius, page 273): "Daily" <note>original Greek: "ἐπιούσ." (epiousion)</note> is named from substance <note>original Latin: "denominatum a substantia"</note>—the Latins, either not understanding this or not being able to express it, put only "daily" <note>original Latin: "quotidianum"</note>—(page 262) for from where is *epiousion* derived if not from substance?—(page 270) consubstantial. ### Critical Apparatus

12. **debts**: Manuscript D reads *debts* <note>original: "οφιλεματα"</note>; manuscripts K and L read *debts* <note>original: "οφεληματ."</note>. | **we have forgiven**: according to manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Dublinensis, and others <note>ℵ* B Z 1, 124, etc.</note>, as well as the Vulgate and Syriac. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa read: "forgive us our debts because we also have forgiven." ... Other manuscripts <note>D E L etc.</note> read **we forgive** <note>original: "αφιομεν" or "αφιεμεν"</note>... matching the version in Luke.

13. **from the evil [one]**: (Editors Griesbach and Scholz). Found in manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae <note>ℵ B D Z</note>. Some manuscripts add "Amen." Many scholarly notes and editions observe: "the phrase 'for yours is' etc. does not appear in some [manuscripts] up to the 'Amen'." A similar note in Codex 36 for Luke 11 adds that while Luke ends at "into temptation," Matthew is found to add "but deliver us from the evil one." 

<note>The following notes discuss the 'Doxology' (For yours is the kingdom...). This famous ending is missing from the oldest Bibles but appeared early in church tradition.</note>

Various ancient versions <note>Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic</note> end at "evil." Gregory of Nyssa <note>4th century Father</note> ends his explanation: "...from the evil one who has gained power in this world, from whom we might be delivered by the grace of Christ, because to him is the power and the glory together with the Father and the Holy Spirit now and forever. Amen." 

Caesarius <note>page 116</note> notes that this is a liturgical formula heard from the priests: "we hear the thanksgiving offered to God by the priests... when they say: the might and the kingdom and the power and the glory of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit..." This matches Euthymius, who calls it a concluding exclamation added by the "divine lights and teachers of the Church." 

Cyril of Jerusalem <note>page 331</note> says: "from the evil one—the evil one is the opposing demon from whom we pray to be delivered. Then after the completion of the prayer you say 'Amen,' sealing the things in this God-taught prayer with the Amen." 

Tertullian and Cyprian respond with a similar clause but essentially end at "deliver us from evil." 

**Addition:** The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by ς</note> adds: **For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.** This is supported by manuscripts E, G, K, L, M, S, U, V, Delta, and Pi, as well as the Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian, and Gothic versions. The Sahidic version reads "for yours is the strength and the power forever and ever, amen," and manuscript 'k' reads "for yours is the virtue forever and ever."

14. **For**: Omitted by Manuscript D and L. | **also to you**: Manuscripts D and Old Latin read "to you also." | **heavenly**: [Text continues...]

**17.** B [reads] "fruit produces good," Δ [reads] "good produces fruit."

<note>The following notes represent a "critical apparatus," which documents differences found between various ancient hand-copied manuscripts of the Bible. Letter symbols like א (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and C (Ephraemi Rescriptus) refer to specific famous parchment books from the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>

**24.** **therefore** <note>original: ουν</note>: Codex Sinaiticus, *a few others*, and some Latin versions omit this word | **of mine** <note>original: μου</note>: Codex L places this *before* **hears**, while *most versions and Church Fathers* place it after **words** | **these** <note>original: τουτους</note>: Codex Vaticanus, *four others*, and several early versions (Old Latin, Coptic, Syriac) omit this; Lachmann places it in brackets [**these**] | **will be likened** <note>original: ομοιωθησεται</note>: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many early manuscripts. However, the *Received Text* <note>The "Textus Receptus," used for the King James Version</note> reads **“I will liken him”** based on later manuscripts (C, E, G, K, etc.) and some Syriac versions | **he built** <note>original: οικοδομησεν</note>: Codex C (original hand) spelling variation | **his house** <note>original: αυτ. τ. οικ.</note>: Order found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Origen; the *Received Text* swaps the order to **the house of him**.

**25.** **came** <note>original: ηλθον</note>: Standard spelling in Sinaiticus, C, E, etc.; the *Received Text* uses an alternative spelling (**ηλθαν**) | **beat against** <note>original: προσεπεσαν</note>: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. The *Received Text* has a slightly different form (**-σον**); a few others read **struck against**, **rushed against**, or **crashed against**.

**26.** **these**: omitted by *a few* Latin, Syriac, and Gothic versions | **will be likened**: Origen reads **is like**; Latin versions use **I will liken him** | **he built**: spelling variation in Codex C | **his house**: Vaticanus and Sinaiticus place "his" first; *most others* and Origen place "house" first | **sand** <note>original: αμμον</note>: Sinaiticus (corrector), Chrysostom, and Theophylact use a more poetic word for **sand** <note>original: ψαμμον</note>.

**27.** **came**: standard form in most; Sinaiticus uses the alternative spelling | Sinaiticus (original hand) omits **and the winds blew** | **struck against** <note>original: προσεκοψαν</note>: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most. A few others, including Basil, read **rushed against** | **great**: A few manuscripts and versions add **exceedingly** <note>original: σφοδρα</note>.

**28.** **finished** <note>original: ετελεσεν</note>: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Origen; the *Received Text* uses a compound form meaning **completed/fully ended** <note>original: συνετελεσεν</note> | **these words**: A few manuscripts and versions add **all** [these words] | Sinaiticus and Eusebius read **the crowds were astonished** (with a slightly different Greek verb form); some manuscripts add **all** [the crowds].

**29.** **their [scribes]**: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and early versions. Codex C and others add **their [scribes] and the Pharisees**; one Old Latin manuscript (k) reads **as the Pharisees and their scribes**.
