### VIII.

> <margin>1—4 Mark 1, 40—44; Luke 5, 12—14</margin> **1** ⁶³.² When he had come down from the mountain, large crowds followed him. **2** And behold, a leper came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.” **3** And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying, “I am willing; be made clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <margin>Leviticus 14, 2</margin> **4** And Jesus said to him, “See that you tell no one; but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
> <margin>5—13 Luke 7, 1—10</margin> **5** ⁶⁴.³ When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion <note>A Roman military officer in command of 100 men.</note> came to him, pleading with him **6** and saying, “Lord, [my] servant...”

---

<note>The text below is the critical apparatus, used by scholars to track differences between ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. Ancient manuscripts often have small variations in spelling or word choice.</note>

*Others* of the same group ²⁷ (Hilary of Poitiers alludes to this); Codex c¹ adds nothing except *“and the Pharisees,”* while Codex b reads *“and their Pharisees”* ... the Received Text <note>The standard printed Greek text used for centuries, abbreviated as ς.</note> omits this. Codices E, L, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Π² and many others, including the Gothic version: compare Mark 1:22 and Luke 5:30.

**VIII. 1.** **when he had come down** <note>original: καταβαντι δε αυτω</note>: Most manuscripts, including the original hand of Sinaiticus (א*), E, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, and Π. Codex k reads *“and following him as he descended.”* ... The corrected Sinaiticus (אᵇ), Vaticanus (B), and Ephraemi Rescriptus (C) use a slightly different grammatical form <note>the genitive absolute: καταβαντος δε αυτου</note>. Old Latin and Vulgate versions also reflect this variation: *“when he had descended”* or *“as he was descending.”*

**2.** **coming near** <note>original: προσελθων</note>: Found in Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and several early versions including the Sahidic, Gothic, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Cyprian and Chrysostom also support this ... **approaching** <note>original: ελθων</note>: Found in Codices C, K, L, S, U, V, X, and most others. Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac versions read *“coming.”*

**3.** Sinaiticus (א*) and others add **his** <note>original: αυτου</note> to **hand** | **touched him**: Found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and early Egyptian versions ... The Received Text (ς) adds **Jesus** <note>original: ο ις</note> before the verb, supported by many later manuscripts and the Vulgate | **immediately**: Omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus | **was cleansed**: There are minor spelling differences between the older manuscripts (B, E, L, X) and the later ones (א, C, K, M).

**4.** **says**: The original Sinaiticus (א*) and Codex k read **said** <note>original: ειπεν / dixit</note> | **to no one**: Some manuscripts add an extra negative for emphasis | **but** <note>original: αλλα</note>: Spelling varies between "alla" and "all" across different manuscript groups | **offer**: There is a minor grammatical variation in the ending of this verb between the oldest manuscripts (B, C) and the later ones | **Moses**: Early manuscripts (א, B, C) use the spelling *Mōysēs*, while others use *Mōsēs*.

**5.** **When he had entered** <note>original: εισελθοντος δε αυτου</note>: Supported by the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C). Origen notes *“when the Lord entered... the centurion approached him.”* Most Old Latin and Vulgate versions read *“but when he had entered.”* Later manuscripts (E, F, K, M, etc.) use a different grammatical case <note>dative: εισελθοντι δε αυτω</note> | **Capernaum**: The spelling *Kapharnaoum* is found in the earliest manuscripts (א, B) and the Egyptian versions, while later manuscripts use *Kapernaoum* | **centurion**: Minor variation in the Greek ending of the title (*-archēs* vs *-archos*).

**6.** **Lord**: Omitted by the original Sinaiticus and the Curetonian Syriac.

*And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. 24 And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was being covered by the waves; but he was sleeping. 25 And they went and woke him, saying: "Lord, save us, we are perishing!" 26 And he says to them: "Why are you afraid, you of little faith?" Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. 27 And the men marveled, saying: "What kind of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?"*

<note>The following section is a "critical apparatus," a scholarly tool that lists differences found in ancient manuscripts of the Bible. Letters like א, B, and C refer to specific ancient books (codices).</note>

**20.** **lay** <note>original Greek: "klinē"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), and others. Other manuscripts read **lays** or **to lay**.
**21.** **disciples** with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B). The Received Text (ς) and many others (including Latin and Syriac versions) add **his** <note>original: "autou"</note>, as seen in other passages like Matthew 14:22.
**22.** **But he** <note>original: "ho de"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ). The Received Text (ς) and editors Lachmann (Ln) and Tischendorf (Ti) add **Jesus**. | **says** with Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Ephraemi. The Received Text (ς) and most others read **said**. | **to him**: Clement of Alexandria quotes this as "the Lord saying to Philip: 'Leave the dead, but you follow me.'"
**23.** **to him**: certain manuscripts and the Syriac read **into the boat**. | **the boat** <note>original: "to ploion"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus and most others. Codex Vaticanus and others omit the word **the** <note>resulting in "into a boat"</note>, similar to the Gospel of Luke.
**24.** Certain manuscripts read **there arose a great [storm]** in a different word order. | **by** <note>original: "hypo"</note>: Codex Vaticanus reads **from** <note>original: "apo"</note>. | **waves**: some Latin and Syriac manuscripts add **for the wind was against them**.
**25.** **And they went** <note>some add "to him"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The Received Text (ς) and most others add **us**. | Codex Delta (Δ) reads **because we are perishing**.
**26.** **to them**: some Latin and Syriac versions add **Jesus**. | **the winds** <note>plural</note>: Some early versions and manuscripts read **the wind** <note>singular</note>, as in Mark and Luke.
**27.** **and** <note>first occurrence</note>: Omitted by editor Lachmann (Ln) based on Codex Ephraemi and several Latin and Syriac versions. | **obey him**: with Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. ---

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus." It lists variations in ancient manuscripts. Scholars use these to determine the most original wording of the Bible. Letters like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and C (Ephraemi) represent specific 4th and 5th-century parchment books.</note>

**28.** **when he came** <note>original: "elthontos autou"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus (corrected hand), Vaticanus, Ephraemi, and several early minuscules (1, 13, 22, 33, etc.) and most Vulgate copies. Codex Sinaiticus (original hand) reads **when they came**. The Received Text (ς) and editor Tischendorf read **to him having come** <note>original: "elthonti auto"</note> with several later codices and Athanasius. | **Gadarenes** <note>original: "gadarenon"</note> (editors Griesbach and Scholz) with Codex Vaticanus, Ephraemi (original hand), and several Syriac versions. Origen <note>An early Church Father, c. 185–254 AD</note> notes: "into the parts of the Gergesenes, as Mark says, or in the borders of the Gergesenes (or rather Gerasenes) as Luke says, or Gadarenes as Matthew says, or Gergesaeans as some copies have." He further comments: "Gerasa is a city of Arabia having neither sea nor lake nearby. The evangelists, men who knew Judea well, would not have said such an obvious and easily refuted falsehood. Since we found 'into the region of the Gadarenes' in a few copies, we must address that too: Gadara is a city of Judea near which famous hot springs happen to be, but there is no lake with cliffs adjacent to it. But Gergesa, from which the Gergesenes come, is an ancient city near the lake now called Tiberias, around which is a cliff adjacent to the lake, from which it is shown that the swine were cast down by the demons. 'Gergesa' is interpreted as 'dwelling of those who have cast out,' perhaps named prophetically for what the citizens of those places did when they begged the Savior to depart from their borders." Almost the same things are written in the scholia <note>ancient marginal notes</note> and catenae <note>commentary chains</note>. Moreover, Origen seems to refer to all three evangelists who recorded this history; certainly, he did not distinguish between them. Editors Griesbach and Lachmann read **Gerasenes** with certain manuscripts mentioned by Origen, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate. The Received Text (ς) reads **Gergesenes** with Codex Sinaiticus and others, which Origen preferred to read despite the evidence of his own manuscripts.

**29.** **Son** <note>original: "huie"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi (original hand), and many early versions including the Coptic and Origen. The Received Text (ς) adds **Jesus** before "Son" with later manuscripts and many Latin and Syriac versions. <note>original: "Iesou"</note> | **to torment us before the time**: Codex Sinaiticus (original hand) reads **to destroy us before the time** <note>original: "emas apolesai"</note>, though the corrected hand returns to **to torment us**.

**30.** **at a distance** <note>original: "makran"</note>: Some Latin versions and the Vulgate read **not far off**. | **feeding**: Some Latin and Coptic versions use a slightly different grammatical form <note>original: "boskomenon"</note>.

...but sinners. Origen (Volume 4, 143): "of the one having come to call not the righteous but sinners." <note>The following section is the "apparatus criticus," where the editor compares different ancient manuscripts to show variations in the text.</note>

**4.** The Textus Receptus <note>the "received text" used for the King James Version</note> reads **the Cananaean** <note>original: "kananitēs"</note> supported by Codices S, E, F, G, K, M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, and most others, as well as the Sahidic and Syriac Peshitta versions and Chrysostom | The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) adds **the** before **Judas** (though a later corrector removed it) | **the** before **Iscariot** (found in the editions of Griesbach and Scholz) is supported by the original hand of Sinaiticus, and Codices B, D, K, M, S, Delta, Pi, and many others... but the Textus Receptus omits it along with the later hand of Sinaiticus and Codices C, E, F, G, L, U, V, X, Gamma, and more than 40 others :: similar to Mark and Luke | **Iscariot**: spelled this way in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most Greek manuscripts, the Vulgate, and Coptic versions; however, Origen notes it as **Judas the son of Simon Iscariot**, while other Latin versions and the Syriac Sinaiticus/Curetonian read **Scariot** or **Scarioth** | **the one who also betrayed [him]**: certain manuscripts and Origen read **who also delivered him up**.

**5.** The third hand of Codex Ephraemi (C³) and many others omit **the twelve** | Codex F reads **having sent [them] out** | **saying** (omitted by Origen and the original hand of Sinaiticus): Codex Bezae (D) and most Old Latin versions add **and** before this word | Codex Delta reverses the phrases: **do not enter... do not go** | **Samaritans**: spelled **Samaritōn** in Sinaiticus, C, and L; but spelled **Samareitōn** in the editions of Lachmann and Tischendorf, and Codices B, E, K, M, U, X, Gamma, and Delta; Codex Bezae and the Vulgate use the Latin form **Samaritanorum**.

**6.** **but go**: Codex Bezae (D) reads **depart** <note>original: "hypagete"</note>.

**7.** **that**: found in almost all manuscripts (Sinaiticus, C, D, E, F, G, etc.); however, Codex Vaticanus (B) omits it. The Sahidic version reads **Repent, for the kingdom has come near.**

**8.** Codex Bezae (D) uses the imperative form **heal!** | **raise the dead**: placed here in the editions of Griesbach, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi (C*), and Bezae (D), along with many Old Latin and Vulgate versions, and the Ethiopic and Persian versions; however, the Textus Receptus places it before **cast out demons**, and other manuscripts like Delta and the Syriac Peshitta place it after. Tischendorf and Scholz omit the phrase entirely based on the later hand of Sinaiticus, C³, E, F, G, K, L, M, and more than 150 others, as well as Eusebius and Basil. Jerome notes: *"He gives them power to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons, so that the greatness of the signs may prove the greatness of the promises."* | Codex Bezae (D) uses the imperative forms **cleanse!**, **cast out!** | Codices G, L, and others read **give!**

**9.** The original hand of Sinaiticus omits **nor silver** | **nor** <note>original: "mēde"</note>: supported by Sinaiticus, B, C, E, and most others; Codex Bezae (D) and L read a different form of **nor** <note>original: "mēte"</note>.

**10.** **no/nor**: various manuscripts (D, Syriac, Coptic) alternate between different Greek forms for "nor" | Codex Bezae (D*) spells **tunics** slightly differently | **staff**: included in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and many others, as well as the Vulgate and Coptic. Eusebius notes that while others allow it, Matthew says he did not permit them a staff, nor a bag, nor sandals, nor two tunics.

**the worker is [worthy] of his food.** <margin>83.2</margin> **11 Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy; and stay there until you depart.** <margin>84.5</margin> **12 As you enter the house, greet it.** **13 And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.** <margin>85.2</margin> **14 And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, as you go out of that house or city, shake the dust off your feet.** <margin>11, 24</margin> **15 Truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment**

<note>The following section is the "apparatus criticus," where the editor, Tischendorf, compares different ancient manuscripts to show variations in the original Greek text.</note>

**10.** <note>Regarding the word for "staff"</note> The editions of Griesbach and Scholz, along with Tischendorf, read **staves** <note>original: "rabdous"</note> supported by Codices C, E, F, G, K, L, M, P, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, and nearly 150 other manuscripts, as well as the Old Latin *a* and *k*, the Syriac Peshitta, and Chrysostom (similarly, the reading in Luke fluctuates). Additionally, the Old Latin *a, b, c, g, h, q* and Hilary (though not *d, f, ff, k* or the Vulgate) add **in your hands** (though *q* omits "your") | **for** <note>original: "gar"</note> is omitted by some manuscripts | **of his food** <note>original: "tēs trophēs"</note> (also found in the Latin translation of Irenaeus): certain manuscripts and many Old Latin versions read **of his reward** <note>original: "tou misthou"</note>, following the wording in Luke 10:7 (Clement's *Homilies* also say: "not considering that the worker is worthy of his reward") | **his** <note>original: "autou"</note> is supported by Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), C, L, and others, along with the Sahidic and Coptic versions; the Textus Receptus adds **is** <note>original: "estin"</note> supported by Codices E, F, G, K, M, P, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, and most others.

**11.** **Into whatever city or village you enter**: Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most others follow this; however, Codex Bezae (D) reads **The city into which you enter...** | **who in it**: some manuscripts swap the order to **in it who** | Codex L omits **is** | **stay**: some manuscripts use the present tense **remain** | **until you depart**: omitted by Ambrose.

**12.** **greet it**: supported by Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many others; however, the original hand of Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae (D), and Codex L add **saying, "Peace to this house"** <note>original: "legontes eirēnē tō oikō toutō"</note> (similarly the Sahidic and others), likely influenced by Luke 10:5.

**13.** **And if**: Codex Bezae (D) omits **and** | **is**: some read **was** | **that house**: read by a few manuscripts | **worthy**: omitted by Codex L | **let [your peace] come**: Tischendorf and others prefer the form *elthatō* based on Codices Sinaiticus and L; the Textus Receptus uses *elthetō* based on Vaticanus and others; Codex Bezae (D) says **it shall be** | **but if it is not worthy**: Codex Bezae (D) uses a slightly different Greek construction for **if not** | **to** <note>original: "pros"</note> is supported by almost all manuscripts (the Latin versions read "to you," having previously said "upon it"); however, Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus use **upon** <note>original: "eph"</note>.

**14.** **whoever etc.**: some versions use the plural **those who do not receive you** | Tischendorf uses one form of **if/ever** <note>original: "ean"</note> while other editors use another <note>original: "an"</note> | **out** <note>original: "exō"</note> is supported by Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae (D), as well as the Vulgate; the Textus Receptus omits it | **of the house or**: Codex Bezae (D) omits | **or of the city**: Sinaiticus reads **the city or village** | **that**: omitted by Codex Bezae (D) and most Old Latin versions | **from** <note>original: "ek"</note> is found in Sinaiticus and the Vulgate; the Textus Receptus omits it (compare Acts 13:51 and Luke 9:5).

**15.** **Truly**: a few manuscripts read **Truly, truly** | **Gomorrah**: the corrected hand of Sinaiticus adds **land of** before it.

25. **you have hidden**: according to **Sinaiticus, Vaticanus**, and **Clement's Homilies** (which quotes: "I praise you, Father... because you have hidden these things from the wise elders and revealed them to suckling infants... do not say he acted impiously against the wise by hiding these things from them")... the **Majority Text** reads **you have hidden away** (a more emphatic form), following **Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae**, and almost all others.

**1** <gloss>114, 2</gloss> At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples were hungry and began to pluck heads of grain and eat. <margin>Deuteronomy 23:25; Exodus 20:10</margin> **2** But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, "Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on a Sabbath." <margin>Verses 3-4: 1 Samuel 21:6</margin> **3** But he said to them, "Have you not read what David did, when he was hungry and those with him? <margin>Exodus 29:33</margin> **4** How he entered into the house of God and they ate the bread of the Presence <term>Bread of the Presence: Also called showbread, these were twelve loaves set out in the Tabernacle or Temple as an offering to God, usually eaten only by priests</term>, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those with him, but only for the priests?" <margin>Numbers 28:9 and following</margin> **5** <gloss>115, 10</gloss> "Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? **6** But I say to you that something greater than the temple is here. <margin>Matthew 9:13; Hosea 6:6</margin> **7** But if you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the guiltless. **8** For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath."

<note>The following notes are part of the "Critical Apparatus," where scholars list differences between ancient manuscripts of the Bible.</note>

**XII. 1.** **went**: Manuscript U and others read **was going** <note>original: "επορεύετο"</note> | **the**: Manuscript D omits | **on the Sabbath**: Most manuscripts including Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Ephraemi (C), and Codex Bezae (D) use the form *sabbasin*... Codex Vaticanus (B) uses *sabbatois* | **heads of grain**: Manuscript D and about 15 others add the article **the heads of grain** (similar to the versions in Luke and Mark). Furthermore, the Curetonian Syriac and Latin manuscript 'c' add **and rubbing them in their hands** (drawn from the account in Luke).

**2.** **seeing**: Found in Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), and most others... but Codices C, D, L, and others add **them** | **they said**: Most ancient manuscripts... the traditional Greek text uses a different spelling of the same word <note>original: "ειπον"</note> | **look**: The Curetonian Syriac reads **why** (drawn from Luke) | **on a Sabbath**: Omitted by Latin manuscript 'k' and the Curetonian Syriac.

**3.** **David**: Variations in spelling between *Daueid*, *Dabid*, and *Dauid* | **when**: Manuscript Γ reads **that** | **he was hungry**: Found in nearly 100 manuscripts... the traditional text adds **himself**, as found in the parallel accounts in Luke and Mark.

**4.** **they ate** (following "he entered"): Found in Codex Sinaiticus (א) and Codex Vaticanus (B)... the traditional text and many others read **he ate** | **which**: A neuter pronoun <note>original: "ὃ"</note> in B and D... but the traditional text uses the masculine/plural **which [loaves]** <note>original: "οὓς"</note> to match "the bread," similar to Mark and Luke | **it was lawful**: Codex Bezae (D) uses a different word order; Origen uses a single-word verb form | **only**: Manuscripts L and Δ read a different form of the word "only."

**5.** Manuscript Γ omits **or** | **on the Sabbath**: Manuscripts C and D and the writings of Cyril add the word **in**.

**6.** **but**: Some Latin and Syriac versions read **for** | **greater**: Most manuscripts (א, B, D, etc.) use the neuter form **something greater** <note>original: "μειζον"</note>, while the traditional text uses the masculine **someone greater** <note>original: "μειζων"</note>.

**7.** **mercy**: Most early manuscripts (א, B, C, D) use the neuter form <note>original: "ελεοσ"</note>... the traditional text uses the masculine form <note>original: "ελεον"</note> | **not**: Manuscript Δ uses a stronger form of "not" | **you would not**: Manuscript Γ reads simply **not**.

**8.** **is**: Most manuscripts... the traditional text reads **is also**.

<note>The following section is the scholarly "apparatus," which compares different ancient versions of the Greek text. The letters and symbols (like ℵ, B, C) refer to specific ancient manuscripts.</note>

*Commonly found in minor manuscripts, the Vulgate, and the Peshitta Syriac (Manuscripts 1, 33, 157 and others add "even on the Sabbath" after "man") :: parallel readings from Luke and Mark*

**9.** **departing from there:** <note>Greek: ekieithen</note> Manuscripts C, E, G, and others, along with some Latin and Syriac versions, add **Jesus**.

**10.** **a man [having a] hand:** <note>Greek: anthr. cheir.</note> Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and several early Latin and Coptic versions (the Curetonian Syriac adds "right" after "having"). .. **a man who was [having] the hand** is found in many other manuscripts (G, K, S, V, X, etc.) | **asked:** some manuscripts use a slightly different verb form | **him:** one manuscript reads "of him" | **to heal:** <note>Greek: therapeusai</note> Supported by Codex Sinaiticus, Bezae (D), and others ... **to heal [ongoing]:** <note>Greek: therapeuein</note> found in many other major manuscripts | **they might accuse:** some manuscripts use a different future-tense spelling. *Regarding this, Jerome (in his commentary on this passage) brings a quote from the Gospel used by the Nazarenes and Ebionites:* <note>The Nazarenes and Ebionites were early Jewish-Christian groups whose specific Gospel is now lost, except for quotes like this.</note>
> This man who has the withered hand is described as a stonemason, praying for help with these words: "I was a stonemason, seeking a living with my hands; I pray you, Jesus, to restore my health to me, so that I do not shamefully beg for food." <note>Jerome’s Latin original: "Homo iste qui aridam habet manum caementarius scribitur..."</note>

**11.** **What man will there be:** Supported by most major manuscripts (ℵ, B, C, E, G, etc.) and the Latin Vulgate ... **What man is there:** found in Codex Bezae (D) and several Old Latin versions ... **Which man:** found in Codex Sinaiticus (original hand), Codex Washingtonianus (L), and others. | **among you:** one manuscript reads "in you" | **man:** omitted in some manuscripts | **will have:** <note>Greek: exei</note> Codex Bezae and others read "has" | **one [sheep]:** omitted in some early Latin and Syriac versions | **if:** omitted in some versions | **falls:** <note>Greek: empesē</note> different manuscripts use slightly different forms of the word for "fall" | **this [sheep]:** omitted in many Latin and Syriac versions | **into:** some manuscripts add the definite article "the" | **will he [not] take hold and:** some versions read "having taken hold" | **it [the sheep]:** moved to after "lift it out" in some versions, omitted in others | **lift it out:** <note>Greek: egerei</note> variations in spelling between different manuscripts.

**12.** **how much [more]:** <note>Greek: posō</note> variations in the grammatical case of the word | **than the sheep:** one manuscript adds "of the" | **Sabbath:** Codex Vaticanus uses a different plural form of the word.

**13.** **your hand:** <note>Greek: sou t. cheira</note> Supported by Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and several others ... **the hand of you:** found in Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others | **stretched it out:** several Latin and Syriac versions add **his hand** | **was restored:** <note>Greek: apekatestathē</note> Supported by the majority of ancient manuscripts ... some use a shorter form **apokatestē** | **healthy:** omitted in some early Syriac and Latin versions | **as the:** one manuscript reads "as if the."

**14.** **But departing:** <note>Greek: exelth. de</note> Codex Bezae and others read "And departing" | **against him:** supported by most major early manuscripts.

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a technical list where scholars compare different ancient versions of the Bible to find the original wording.</note>

27. **and if**: Found in manuscripts D, 1, 33, and others. Manuscript **but if** is found in the Old Latin and most others. | **beelzebub**: see the note for verse 24. | **L** and others write **cast out** (future tense), whereas **L** also uses **will cast out** in verse 26. | **the**: Manuscript **L** and a few others omit the word "the" before "sons." | **your** (used twice): Manuscript Sinaiticus and others read **our**. | **cast out**: Manuscripts **E**, **L**, and many others (including the writings of Church Fathers Cyril and Chrysostom) use a slightly different spelling of the verb. | **will be your judges**: Followed by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many early Latin and Syriac versions. Other manuscripts (including the Byzantine tradition) change the word order to **your judges will be** or **judges of you will be**.

28. **by the Spirit of God I**: This word order is found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many others. The traditional Byzantine text puts **I** before **by the Spirit of God**, as seen in various Latin and Syriac versions.

29. **anyone**: Manuscript Delta and some Latin versions place this word before "can," while **L** omits it entirely. | **enter**: Manuscript Delta and a few others place this after "strong man." | **seize**: Found in Vaticanus and early Egyptian fragments. <note>original Latin note: "The Savior says: he advises to bind and seize the goods as if from a strong man."</note> The traditional text uses **plunder** (a more intense word), which is found in Sinaiticus and the majority of manuscripts. | **binds the strong man**: Manuscript Delta varies the word order to **the strong man binds**. | **plunder**: There is a minor spelling difference in many manuscripts (between *-sē* and *-sei* endings). Some editors (Lachmann and Tischendorf) prefer **will seize** based on a perceived error in manuscript B (Vaticanus).

30. Manuscript Gamma adds a preface: **the Lord said: the one who is not**. | **scatters**: Manuscript Sinaiticus, the Coptic version, and Chrysostom add the word **me** (scatters me), while the Syriac margin notes **scatters for me**.

31. **to people**: Manuscript Vaticanus and Athanasius add **to you** before this phrase. | **but the [blasphemy] of the spirit...**: A group of Latin and Syriac manuscripts omit the very end of this verse. | **will not be forgiven**: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Vulgate agree on this shorter ending. Other manuscripts and Church Fathers like Chrysostom add **to them**, or as in the traditional Byzantine text, **to people**.

32. **whoever** (a variation in the Greek particle *ean* vs *an*): Most early manuscripts use *ean*. | **will be forgiven**: Manuscript Vaticanus (first hand) mistakenly writes **will NOT be forgiven**. | **the Holy Spirit**: Manuscript D reads **the spirit the holy**. | **not be forgiven**: Most manuscripts use the standard negation. Manuscript Vaticanus and the editor Lachmann use a stronger double-negative form (**by no means be forgiven**).

**Verse 15.** "eyes" added | "might hear": some omit | "might understand" <note>original: "συνωσιν"</note> (so also the Received Text of 1550, likewise the 1624 and 1633 editions; afterwards usually edited as "συνιῶσι" [syniosi] by Wetstein as if it were the standard reading) ... many others read "συνιῶσι": so Griesbach and Scholz | "they might turn" <note>original: "επιστρεψωσιν"</note> according to manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others . . . other manuscripts read "they will turn" <note>original: "-ψουσιν"</note> | "I will heal" <note>original: "ιασομαι"</note> according to Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others . . . the Received Text reads "I might heal" <note>original: "-σωμαι"</note> according to manuscripts K, U, X, and Chrysostom.

**Verse 17.** "Truly" according to Sinaiticus and many Old Latin manuscripts, the Armenian and Ethiopic versions, and Hilary (Cyril reads "Truly, truly") ... the Received Text and Lachmann and Tischendorf add "for" <note>original: "γαρ"</note> (mirroring Luke: "For I say to you") based on Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and many others | "and righteous": Vaticanus omits (Clementine Homilies read "many prophets and **kings** [like Luke] longed to see what you see...") | "to see what": others add "you" [see] | "they saw" <note>original: "ιδαν"</note> (manuscript 33 and others read "ιδ.," Vaticanus "ειδ.": so Lachmann and Tischendorf) ... the Received Text reads "ειδον" [eidon] according to several major manuscripts; manuscript Bezae reads "they were not able to see." ...receiving it with joy; 21 but he has no root in himself but is temporary, and when tribulation or persecution occurs because of the word, immediately he falls away <note>original: "σκανδαλίζεται", literally 'is tripped up' or 'stumbled'</note>. 22 And the one sown among the thorns, this is the one hearing the word, and the anxiety of the age and the deception of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful. 23 But the one sown on the good ground, this is the one hearing the word and understanding, who indeed bears fruit and produces, some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.

<note>The following section is the apparatus criticus, comparing various ancient manuscripts and citations from early Church Fathers.</note>

**Verse 30.** Origen <note>original: "Or"</note> and Irenaeus <note>original: "Ir"</note> read: “Bind the weeds in bundles and hand them over to the fire.” Irenaeus’ Latin translation <note>original: "Ir int"</note> reads: “...gather first the weeds and bind the bundles.” See below in Epiphanius. | **“To burn them up”** <note>original: "κατακ. αυτα"</note>: The manuscript Codex Bezae <note>original: "D"</note>, a few others, and most Old Latin manuscripts omit the word “them.” | **“Gather”**: According to many early manuscripts including Codex Sinaiticus <note>original: "א"</note>, Codex Vaticanus <note>original: "B"</note>, and others. The editor Lachmann <note>original: "Ln"</note> uses a slightly different spelling based on Codex Vaticanus and others. The Manichaeans <note>a dualistic religious group</note>, cited in Epiphanius <note>original: "Manich. ap Epiph"</note> (perhaps from the *Gospel of the Hebrews*?), record the parable this way: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man, a householder, who sowed good seed in his field. And while the men slept, an enemy man came and sowed weeds. Then his servants said to him: ‘Did you not sow good seed in the field?’ and he said, ‘Yes.’ ‘From where then did the weeds come?’ and he answering said, ‘An enemy did this.’ And the servants said to him, ‘Do you wish then for us to go and root up the weeds?’ and he said to them, ‘No, lest in rooting up the weeds you root up the wheat as well. But let them be until the time of harvest, and I will say to the harvesters: Collect the weeds and bind them in bundles upon bundles, but the wheat store in the barn, and prepare the weeds to be consumed by unquenchable fire.’”

**31. “He put before”** <note>original: "παρεθηκεν"</note>: Found in most manuscripts. However, Codex Bezae and some others read **“He spoke”** <note>original: "ελαλησεν"</note>. | **“To them”**: One manuscript adds “Jesus.” | **“Is like”**: Some manuscripts use a slightly different Greek verb tense meaning “has been likened to.”

**32. “Of all the”**: Codex Bezae and others omit the word “the.” | **“Has grown”**: Minor spelling variations in various manuscripts. | **“Larger”**: Minor grammatical variations in Codex Bezae and Chrysostom. | **“The”**: Many manuscripts add “all” before “the garden plants,” making it “all the plants,” similar to the Gospel of Mark. | Some manuscripts omit the phrase “come and” before “make their nests.”

**33. “He spoke”**: One manuscript reads “He put before.” | **“To them”**: Many manuscripts including Codex Sinaiticus and others add the word **“saying”** <note>original: "λεγων"</note>. The Syriac Curetonian version <note>original: "syr cu"</note> reads “a wise woman.” | **“Hid”** <note>original: "ενεκρυψ."</note>: Found in most early manuscripts. The Gnostic followers of Valentinus, cited in Irenaeus, use the same word. Some later manuscripts and the scholar Cyril use a simpler word for “hid” <note>original: "εκρυψεν"</note>, similar to the Gospel of Luke.

**34. “Nothing”**: Found in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others, as well as citations in Clement and Origen.

<note>The following notes are part of the "apparatus criticus," a technical record of differences found in ancient handwritten copies of the Bible.</note>

**Verse 34.** ...and he did not <note>original: "ουκ"</note> speak... found in manuscripts Codex Sinaiticus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others <note>The letters ℵ, C, D, E, etc., refer to specific ancient codices</note>, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Curetonian Syriac versions... Origen <note>An early Christian scholar</note>... similar to Mark | He was speaking <note>original: "ελαλει"</note>: found in most manuscripts... but some few have "He spoke" <note>original: "ελαλησεν"</note>.

**Verse 35. Isaiah** <note>original: "ησαιου"</note>: Found in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus <note>ℵ*</note>, and several minuscules <note>small-script manuscripts</note>. Eusebius <note>a church historian</note> notes: "By which prophet were these things said? Was it by the aforementioned Asaph? Some, not understanding this, added 'through Isaiah the prophet' into the Gospel. However, in the accurate copies, the addition of 'Isaiah' is absent, and it is simply stated 'through the prophet.'" Similar comments appear in the commentaries on the Psalms.

Likewise, in the editions of Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century philosopher who critiqued Christianity</note> and some editions mentioned by Jerome <note>the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> (on this passage): *“I have read in some manuscripts—and the diligent reader will perhaps find it himself—in that place where we have placed it and the common edition has it: 'through the prophet saying,' there it is written 'through Isaiah the prophet saying.' Because this was not found in Isaiah at all, I believe it was later removed by prudent men. But it seems to me it was originally published thus: 'what was written through Asaph the prophet saying' <term>Asaph: the person credited with writing Psalm 78, which is the text actually being quoted here</term>—and the first scribe did not understand who Asaph was and thought it was a scribe's error, so he 'corrected' the name to Isaiah, whose name was better known.”*

Jerome says again in his short notes on Psalm 77 <note>Psalm 78 in modern numbering</note>: *"It is said in Matthew: 'These things were done to fulfill what was written in Asaph the prophet.' This is how it is found in all the old manuscripts. (But Jerome did not actually testify to this in his own edition of the Gospel. Does he mean the manuscripts of the Psalms?)"* But ignorant men removed it. Finally, many Gospels even today have it as: *“To fulfill... Isaiah the prophet: I will open...”* Isaiah did not say this, but Asaph did.

Furthermore, that impious Porphyry <note>A common title given to him by Christian writers</note> proposes this very point against us, saying: *"Your evangelist Matthew was so unskillful that he said: 'what was written through Isaiah the prophet: I will open...' It was an error of the scribes to write Isaiah instead of Asaph. For we know that the early church was gathered from unskillful gentiles. Therefore, when they read in the Gospel 'in Asaph the prophet,' the first person who copied the Gospel began to say: 'Who is this Asaph the prophet?' He was not known among the people, and so, while trying to fix an error, he created an error."*

In the same place and in the same manner, Porphyry attributes Matthew 27:9 (naming Jeremiah instead of Zechariah) and Mark 15:25 (the "third hour" instead of the "sixth") to the "error of the scribes." Moreover, the Clementine Homilies confirm the very old reading of **Isaiah**: *“as Isaiah also said: I will open my mouth in parables and utter things hidden from the foundation...”*

**of the world** <note>original: "κοσμου"</note>: Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>19th-century biblical scholars</note> omit this word, following Codex Sinaiticus (corrected), Vaticanus, and most ancient versions like the Vulgate and Syriac. Eusebius, Chrysostom, and Jerome (as seen above) also omit it. | **foundation** <note>original: "καταβολης"</note>: found in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and early versions. Origen notes that since the Gospel uses the word "foundation" plainly, it should be established that this depends on the Gospel text, not the Psalm. | Other manuscripts add **"of the world"** <note>original: "κοσμου"</note> following "foundation," as seen in the Clementine Homilies and Chrysostom. (Note: While the Greek Old Testament <note>LXX</note> says "from the beginning," the phrase "from the foundation of the world" is common in Matthew 25:34, Luke 11:50, and John 17:24, and usually does not vary).

<summary>This page discusses a famous textual error in Matthew 13:35, where a quote from the Psalms is attributed to Isaiah instead of Asaph. It features extensive quotes from Saint Jerome and the critic Porphyry regarding how scribes may have "corrected" the text to a more familiar name.</summary>

36 $^{140. 10}$ Then, leaving the crowds, he went into the house. <note>The following notes represent the "apparatus criticus," a record of how different ancient manuscripts of the Bible vary in their wording.</note>

**36. he went:** <note>original: "ηλθεν"</note> Found in Codex Sinaiticus <note>denoted as ℵ</note> and Origen. Other versions like Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus and certain Latin versions <note>a, b, h, q</note> have “he entered” or “he departed.” | **house:** <note>original: "οικιαν"</note> Found in the major early codices <note>ℵ, B, D</note>, the Vulgate, and various eastern translations. Some manuscripts add “his” <note>“his house”</note>. The standard received text <note>denoted by the symbol ϛ</note> adds “Jesus” <note>written as a 'Nomina Sacra' or sacred shorthand: ο $\overline{ιϛ}$</note>. | **they came:** The editors Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>Ln Ti</note> use a slightly different Greek spelling for “came” <note>-λθαν instead of -λθον</note> based on Codex Vaticanus <note>B</note>. | **explain:** <note>original: "φράσον"</note> Most manuscripts and Origen use this word. However, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus use a different word meaning “clarify” or “make clear” <note>original: "διασαφησον"</note>. The editor Lachmann prefers “clarify.” The note observes that since "explain" is used in Matthew 15:15 without variation, its presence here is debated.

**37. he said:** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note> Found in the primary early manuscripts. The received text adds “to them” <note>original: "αυτοις"</note> based on later manuscripts <note>C, E, F, G, etc.</note> and the Syriac and Armenian versions.

**38. these are the sons:** The manuscript Delta <note>Δ</note> and some Old Latin and Syriac versions omit the word “the.” | **of the evil one:** <note>original: "του πονηρου"</note> Translated in various Latin versions as “the worthless,” “wickedness,” “the unjust,” or “the evil.”

**39. he who sowed:** Manuscript L and a few others use a different phrasing for the sower. | **them:** Omitted by Codex Bezae <note>D</note>. | **is:** <note>original: "εστιν"</note> The position of this word varies in the Greek of Codex Vaticanus and some Latin versions. | **end of the age:** <note>original: "συντέλεια αἰῶνος"</note> Most early manuscripts <note>ℵ, B, D</note> omit the definite article "the" before "age." The received text includes it <note>“the end of *the* age”</note>.

**40. are gathered / is burned:** Codex Bezae <note>D</note> uses plural verbs here <note>“are burned”</note>. Some editors <note>Griesbach, Scholz, Tischendorf</note> use a simpler form of the verb "to burn" <note>καίεται</note> found in later manuscripts and Chrysostom. | **of the age:** The received text adds "this" <note>“the end of *this* age”</note>, but the earliest manuscripts <note>ℵ, B, D</note> simply say “the age.”

**41. will send:** <note>original: "αποστελει"</note> Minor spelling variations exist in some manuscripts <note>one 'l' vs two 'l's in the Greek verb</note>. | **his:** Omitted in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex F. | **those who do lawlessness:** The Syriac versions add “all” before this phrase.

**42. they will throw:** <note>original: "βαλουσιν"</note> Codex Sinaiticus and Bezae use a present-tense spelling <note>“they are throwing”</note>. | **weeping:** One manuscript <note>E</note> contains a spelling error <note>κλαθμοσ instead of κλαυθμοσ</note>.

<note>The following notes are part of the "apparatus criticus," a scholarly record showing where ancient manuscripts differ in their wording. The symbols (like ℵ, B, D) refer to specific famous hand-written Bibles from the 4th century and later.</note>

**43. will shine forth:** <note>original: "εκλαμψουσιν"</note> Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), and many other early manuscripts. Justin Martyr (in his *First Apology* 1, 16) quotes this as: “Then there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when the righteous shine as the sun, but the unrighteous are sent into eternal fire.” | **ears:** <note>original: "ωτα"</note> The earliest manuscripts (ℵ, B) and Old Latin versions stop here. Epiphanius provides a slightly different version of the parable's explanation.

**44. is like:** <note>original: "ομοια"</note> Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Bezae (D), along with Old Latin and Syriac versions. Some manuscripts (B, Origen, and the Armenian version) omit the word "everything." The "Received Text" (ϛ) changes the word order to "sells all that he has."

**45. a man:** <note>original: "ανθρωπω"</note> This word (specifically "unto a man") is found in many versions including Origen and Cyprian. It is omitted in Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B), as well as by Athanasius and Chrysostom.

**46. and having found:** <note>original: "ευρων δε"</note> Found in Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Bezae (D). The "Received Text" (ϛ) uses "who, having found." | **one:** <note>original: "ενα"</note> Omitted by Codex Bezae (D), some Latin versions, and Cyprian. | **sold:** <note>original: "πεπρακεν"</note> Codex Bezae (D) uses a different Greek word for "sold" <note>original: "επωλησεν"</note>. | **everything:** <note>original: "παντα οσα"</note> Manuscripts vary between "everything," "all things," and "whatever."

**47. gathering:** <note>original: "συναγαγουση"</note> A few manuscripts and Origen use a slightly different form of the verb "gathering together."

**48. which, when:** <note>original: "ην οτε"</note> Codex Bezae (D) and many Latin versions (including Ambrose and Augustine) read "but when." | **they drew up:** <note>original: "αναβιβασαντες"</note> Most early manuscripts do not include the word “it” <note>original: "αυτην"</note> after the verb. Later manuscripts (P, S, and the Received Text) add “it.” Chrysostom provides a summary: "which they brought up to the shore, and sitting down and collecting the good ones into a vessel, they threw out the bad ones." | **onto the shore:** <note>original: "επι τ. αιγ."</note> Supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae.

53 And it happened when Jesus had finished these parables, <margin>54-58 Mark 6:1-6</margin> he departed from there. 54 <gloss>141.1</gloss> And coming into his own hometown, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished and said, "From where did this man get this wisdom and these miraculous powers? 55 Is this not the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary..."

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," where scholars note differences between ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. Symbols like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and D (Bezae) represent specific famous manuscripts from the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>

**48. pulled onto the shore:** <note>original: "επεβιβασε τ. αιγιαλ."</note> This phrasing is supported by manuscripts ℵ, 1, and the Old Latin versions $ff^1$ and $g^2$, as well as the Vulgate and the writings of Cyril. The editor Tischendorf (Ti) omits the word "and" <note>original: "και"</note> before this phrase, following manuscript L and others. | **good ones:** <note>original: "καλα"</note> This is the standard reading; however, manuscript "d" uses a word meaning "the best" <note>original: "καλλιστα"</note>, and some Old Latin and Syriac versions use terms for "excellent" or "the best things." | **vessels:** <note>original: "αγγη"</note> Supported by the earliest Bibles (ℵ, B, C). Later manuscripts (marked ϛ) use a more common word for containers or jars <note>original: "αγγεια"</note>. The ancient dictionary-maker Hesychius notes that the rarer form "αγγος" is explained by the more common "αγγειον." | **threw out:** <note>original: "εβαλον"</note> Manuscript ℵ and others use a form suggesting a continuous action ("were throwing out").

**49. of the age:** <note>original: "αιωνοσ"</note> Codex Bezae (D) instead uses "of the world" <note>original: "κοσμου"</note>.

**50. they will throw:** <note>original: "βαλουσιν"</note> Some early copies use a slightly different tense <note>original: "βαλλουσιν"</note>. In manuscript E, the word for weeping is misspelled <note>original: "κλαθμοσ"</note>.

**51. Have you understood:** The "Received Text" (ϛ) and many later manuscripts add the phrase "Jesus says to them" <note>original: "λεγει αυτοισ ο ις"</note> before the question. The earliest authorities (ℵ, B, D) lack this addition. | **Yes:** The majority of later manuscripts add "Lord" <note>original: "κυριε"</note>, but the oldest ones (ℵ, B, D) and early versions simply read "Yes."

**52. And he said:** While most manuscripts use "said" <note>original: "ειπεν"</note>, Codex Vaticanus (B) and Bezae (D) use "says" <note>original: "λεγει"</note>. | **for the kingdom:** <note>original: "τη βασιλεια"</note> There is significant variation here. Some manuscripts (ℵ, B, C) use "for the kingdom" (the dative case), others (D, M) use "in the kingdom" <note>original: "εν τη βασιλεια"</note>, and the "Received Text" (ϛ) uses "into the kingdom" <note>original: "εισ την βασιλειαν"</note>. | **brings out:** Some manuscripts (E, G, L) use a form meaning "he will bring out."

**54. coming:** Manuscript L changes this to "he came" and omits the following "and." | **hometown:** One scribe of manuscript ℵ accidentally wrote "Antipatris" (a specific city name) instead of "hometown." | **were astonished:** <note>original: "εκπλησσεσθ."</note> This is the older spelling found in the earliest codices; later ones (ϛ) use a more modern Greek spelling <note>original: "εκπληττ."</note>. | **this wisdom:** Manuscript D and some ancient translations add the word "all" <note>original: "πασα"</note>, as in "all this wisdom."

**55. the carpenter's:** Some Old Latin and Syriac versions specify "Joseph's" <note>original: "Iosephi"</note> before the word "son." Justin Martyr (in his *Dialogue with Trypho*) refers to Jesus as "the one reputed to be [the son of the carpenter]."

<note>The following notes document minute differences in how ancient scribes wrote these verses. Scholars use these to trace the history of the text.</note>

**to him** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> <margin>v. 15</margin> found in manuscripts CDEFGKLMSUVXΓΔΘΠ and most others, as well as most Old Latin, the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic versions, and the writings of Origen and Chrysostom (though Chrysostom omits "to him") :: see note at 8:21 | **the hour has already passed** [word order variation] with the Received Text, manuscript 1, and Origen ... the editions of Lachmann and Tischendorf read **already passed the hour** with BCDI and nearly all other uncials (Old Latin, Vulgate, etc.) and Chrysostom (Origen elsewhere omits "already") | **therefore** <note>original: "ουν"</note> with the Received Text, manuscripts 1, 238, Coptic, and the margin of the Philoxenian Syriac, and Origen ... Lachmann omits this with BDEFGKLMSUVXΓΔΘΠ and many others (following the style of Mark) | **into the [villages]**: manuscript 33, some others, and the margin of the Philoxenian Syriac and Armenian add **surrounding** [villages] :: following the style of Luke and Mark | **villages**: Codex Sinaiticus and the Greek of Codex Δ read **regions** <note>original: "χωρασ"</note>

**17.** **they say** (Latin manuscripts read "they said" or "they answered"): manuscript z omits this or reads "they said," Old Latin and Vulgate read "they answered" | **we have**: KLUΓΘ and many others read **we might have** [subjunctive mood] | Codex Sinaiticus reads **loaves except five** [reversing the order]

**18.** **he said**: manuscript P adds **to them** | **them here** with Sinaiticus, B, Z, 33 ... the Received Text and Tischendorf read **them here** [different word order] with CEFG KLMPSUVXΓΔΘΠ and nearly all others including many Latin and Syriac versions ... manuscript D, 1, and most Old Latin and Curetonian Syriac omit **here** (manuscripts ff$^1$ and Armenian omit **to me**)

<note>This lower section is the "apparatus criticus," where scholars document differences between ancient manuscripts. The letters and symbols (like א, B, D) refer to specific ancient codices or Bible versions.</note>

**Gennesaret** <note>original: "γεννησαρετ"</note> [spelled thus] according to manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Dublinensis, Zacynthius, and many others; also the Latin manuscript 'f', the Syriac Peshitta, and the Armenian version; likewise Origen... Lachmann and Tischendorf read **Gennesareth** <note>original: "γεννησαρεθ"</note> according to manuscripts E, F, G, K, L, M, and many others, including the Coptic and Ethiopic versions... Codex Bezae and the Vulgate show variants like **Gennasar**.

**35. that** <note>original: "εκεινου"</note>: The corrected Sinaiticus omits this. Old Latin manuscripts 'a', 'b', and 'c' add the phrase **they worshiped him and** <note>original: "adorabant eum et"</note>.

**36. him**: Vaticanus and Origen omit this. | **that**: Certain manuscripts add **all** <note>original: "παν"</note>, as in "that they might touch at least the hem of his garment." | **touched**: Some manuscripts use a different Greek verb form for "touched." | **were made well**: The original hand of Sinaiticus reads "were saved," similar to the wording in Mark's Gospel.

**XV. 1.** Codex Bezae reads **they came forward** <note>original: "προερχονται"</note>; Origen reads **they went away**. | **Jesus**: Nearly all manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) include the name; however, Codex Bezae and the Vulgate read **to him**. | **from**: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus support "from"; the Received Text and Tischendorf read **those from** <note>original: "οι απο"</note>. | **Pharisees and scribes**: Supported by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf reverse the order to **scribes and Pharisees**.

**2. tradition**: Variant spelling in some manuscripts. | **their hands**: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus omit "their," simply saying **the hands**; the Received Text and others add **their** <note>original: "αυτων"</note>.

**3. to them**: Omitted by Codex Bezae and Coptic versions. | **and**: Omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus and Irenaeus.

**4. commanded, saying**: Supported by the majority of manuscripts. However, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae read **said** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note>. Ptolemy (writing around 160 AD) quotes it as: "For God, he [the Savior] says, said: 'Honor your father and your mother, so that it may be well with you.' But you, he says, have said to the elders: 'A gift to God is whatever you might have profited from me'; and you have nullified the law of God through the tradition of your elders." This also appears in Irenaeus and Cyril.

1 And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and testing him, they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. 2 But he answered and said to them: <note>The following section in brackets is missing from some of the earliest and most important manuscripts, suggesting it may have been added later by scribes to harmonize with other Gospels.</note> [“When evening comes, you say: ‘Fair weather, for the sky is red’; 3 and in the morning: ‘Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to discern the face of the sky, but can you not discern the signs of the times?”]

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a technical shorthand used by scholars to track differences between ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts) of the Bible.</note>

**37.** **took up the pieces:** <note>original: "ēran to pe. t. kl."</note> Supported by **Codex Sinaiticus (א), C, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, P, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π** and most other manuscripts, including the Latin versions **f, ff1, k, q**, the Coptic, Armenian, and **Chrysostom**. **39. he went into:** <note>original: "enebē"</note> Supported by **Sinaiticus (א), B, S, 1, 33**, and **D** <note>which uses the present tense "goes into"</note>. **Griesbach** and **Tischendorf** read "he went up into" <note>original: "anebē"</note> based on **C, E, F, G**, and about 100 others. | **Magadan:** Supported by the most ancient manuscripts **Sinaiticus (א), B, D**, and early Syriac and Persian versions. **2. But he answered... to them:** Some versions <note>Syriac, Ethiopic, and various Old Latin manuscripts</note> omit "to them." **"When evening... signs of the times" (v. 3):** This entire passage is included in **C, D, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, Δ, Π**, most other manuscripts, the Vulgate, and many early Church Fathers like **Chrysostom** and **Theophylact**. However, it is **omitted** by the oldest and most important witnesses: **Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), V, X, Γ**, and several others. **St. Jerome** remarked that "this is not found in most manuscripts." **Origen** also seems to have lacked this text in his copies. | **is red:** Supported by **D, K, U, Δ, Π**; while **C, E, F, G** use a slightly different spelling. | **the sky:** **Sinaiticus (א)** adds "and it happens so," similar to the phrasing in **Luke**.

**3. and in the morning... sky:** Omitted by manuscript **F** and some Syriac copies. **the sky:** **Codex D** reads "the air" <note>original: "o aēr"</note>. **now:** <note>original: "men"</note> Included by **D, L, Δ, 1, 33**, the Vulgate, and others. **ς** <note>the Textus Receptus</note> adds the word "Hypocrites!" before this sentence, based on **E, F, G, H, M**.

**7.** <note>This section discusses the phrasing "Woe to the man."</note> Found in the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac versions... <header>ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 18, 15.</header>

*...behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.* 12 <sup>182. 5</sup> <margin>12—14 Luke 15:4—7</margin> *What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go out to search for the one that is wandering? 13 And if he happens to find it, truly I say to you that he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray. 14 In the same way, it is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.* 15 <sup>183. 5</sup> *If your brother sins against you, go and point out the fault to him between you and him alone...*

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record showing how different ancient manuscripts vary in their wording. Letters like ℵ, B, and D represent specific ancient Bibles, while "syr" or "vg" refer to early translations in Syriac or Latin.</note>

**11.** <note>original: ς ἦλθε γὰρ... ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός</note> This verse—"For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost"—is omitted by the earliest manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note> and B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>. Other versions, like the Syriac, connect it to the previous verse. Some manuscripts add "to seek" (ζητησαι) before "to save." The scholar Origen seems not to have recognized this verse here, as he moves directly from verse 10 to verse 14 in his commentary. Most scholars believe this verse was later moved here by scribes from Luke 19:10 to harmonize the two Gospels.

**12. What:** <note>original: τι</note> Codex D, the Old Latin, and Syriac versions add "but" (δε). **leaving and going:** <note>original: αφεις et πορευθεις</note> Many manuscripts use these participles, but Lachmann's edition uses "he will leave" (αφησει) and "and going" (και πορευθεις) based on Codex B. **ninety-nine:** There are minor spelling variations (ενενηκοντ. vs εννενηκ.) across the manuscripts. **on the mountains:** Omitted in the first draft of Sinaiticus (ℵ*) but added by a later corrector. **searches:** Some manuscripts use the future tense "will search" (ζητησει).

**13. he rejoices:** <note>original: χαιρει</note> Some manuscripts use the future "he will rejoice."

**14. before:** <note>original: εμπροσθεν</note> Omitted by Sinaiticus and Origen. **your Father:** <note>original: υμων</note> Found in most manuscripts, including Sinaiticus. However, some early versions (Vaticanus, Sahidic Coptic) read "my Father" (μου). Note that in verse 10, "my Father" is used without variation. **one:** <note>original: εν</note> Found in the oldest Greek manuscripts; later versions often use "one of" (εις).

**15. sins:** <note>original: αμαρτηση</note> There is a debate here: did the original say "sins" or "sins *against you*"? The phrase "against you" (εις σε) is found in many manuscripts and the Vulgate, but is notably absent from the oldest copies like Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B), as well as the writings of Origen and Cyril. **go:** <note>original: υπαγε</note> Omitted in some Syriac versions and by the church father Basil.

**24.** [referring to "the one brought forward"] whenever alluding to "the one brought forward" <note>original: ὁ προσαχθείς</note> :: the word "to bring" <note>original: προσενεγκαι</note> is used frequently by Matthew; but he nowhere uses "to bring near" <note>original: προσαγειν</note> | "one to him" <note>original: εἷς αὐτῷ</note> with manuscripts א* <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note> and B ... the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "to him one" <note>original: αὐτῷ εἷς</note> with manuscripts א corrected, D, 14 uncials, (the Old Latin and Vulgate read "to him one" <note>original: ei unus</note>), Origen, and Chrysostom | "ten thousand" <note>original: μυρίων</note> (also in Origen's heading and Latin translation): א*, the Sahidic and Coptic versions, Origen... some versions read "many" <note>original: πολλων</note> (Juvencus reads "much"), others read "a hundred."

### ...good should I do that I may have eternal life? 17 And he said to him: Why [do you ask] me

<note>This section is a technical "critical apparatus," listing variations found in ancient manuscripts and writings of the early Church Fathers.</note>

Hilary on Matthew ... <note>The siglum ς refers to the "Textus Receptus," the standard printed Greek text for centuries; Gb refers to the scholar Griesbach.</note> add **"good"** <note>original: "agathe"</note> along with <term>Codices C, E, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, Γ, Δ<note>These are medieval Greek manuscripts used to reconstruct the text.</note></term> and most others, as well as several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, all Syriac versions, the Sahidic and Coptic, Basil’s *Ethics*, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Chrysostom. (Hilary’s citation in *On the Trinity* is barely distinguishable from Matthew). See also below for Justin, the Marcosians, etc. | **"good"** <note>referring to "good thing," original: "agathon"</note> (Origen): manuscripts 238, 248, Old Latin *ff²*, the Curetonian Syriac, Sahidic, and Coptic codices, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Chrysostom omit this word. | **"should I do that"**: <term>Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)<note>One of the two oldest and most important Greek Bibles, dating to the 4th century.</note></term>, Codex L, and others; Basil's *Ethics*, Chrysostom, and the Latin Irenaeus read **"having done."** | **"I may have"** with Codices B and D, Origen, and the main text ... whereas the Textus Receptus reads **"I may possess"** with Codices E, F, G, H, and others, Basil, Chrysostom, and Cyril. ... Codex Sinaiticus, Codex L, and others <note>including the Old Latin *e*: "so that I may attain eternal life"</note>, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, and Arabic versions, Origen's commentary, and the Latin Irenaeus <note>"to him who asked him: 'doing what shall I inherit eternal life?' responding thus: 'If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.' To him asking: 'Which?' the Lord again said: 'You shall not commit adultery,' etc."</note> use the word **"I may inherit"** <note>original: "klēronomēsō"</note>, and place it after "eternal life": compare with the accounts in Luke and Mark. Furthermore, see the *Clementine Homilies* (18, 3): "Our teacher said to the Pharisee who asked, 'By doing what shall I inherit eternal life?'—first he said: 'Do not call me good; for the one who is good is one, the Father who is in the heavens.' Immediately after, he says: 'If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.' When the man asked 'Which?', he referred him to the commandments of the Law." Also Justin Martyr's *First Apology* (1, 16): "When someone approached him and said <note>and in his *Dialogue with Trypho* 101</note> 'Good teacher,' he answered saying: 'No one is good except God alone, who made all things.'" Also the Marcosians <note>A Gnostic group</note> according to Irenaeus (1, 20, 2): "To the one who said to him, 'Good teacher,' he confessed the truly good God, saying: 'Why do you call me good? One is good, the Father in the heavens.'" Allusions also appear in the Gnostic Valentinus (quoted by Clement of Alexandria): "Writing to certain people in these very words: 'One is good,'" and the Gnostic Ptolemy in his *Letter to Flora*: "For our Savior declared that there is only one good God, his own Father." In the Latin Origen (this is not in the Greek; perhaps the translator added it?): *“It is written in a certain gospel, which is called 'according to the Hebrews'—He said to him, another of the rich men: 'Master, what good thing doing shall I live?' He said to him: 'Man, do the law and the prophets.' He answered him: 'I have done so.' He said to him: 'Go, sell all that you possess and divide it among the poor, and come, follow me.' But the rich man began to scratch his head, and it did not please him. And the Lord said to him: 'How can you say: I have done the law and the prophets, since it is written in the law: You shall love your neighbor as yourself; and behold, many of your brothers, sons of Abraham, are covered in filth, dying of hunger, while your house is full of many good things, and nothing at all goes out from it to them.' And turning, he said to Simon his disciple who was sitting by him: 'Simon, son of Jonah, it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.'”*

17. **And he [said]**: Codices Σ, Μ, 33, and many others, as well as the Old Latin and Syriac, add **"Jesus."** | **"Why do you ask me concerning the [good]"**: (Codex D and Origen omit "the") according to Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), B, D, L, and others. (Manuscript 251 contains verse 17 as the Textus Receptus does, but after the word "Which?" it proceeds: "But Jesus said to him: Why do you ask me concerning the good? No one is good except... [continuing to] the commandments.") Found in the Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Ethiopic, Coptic, and Armenian.

<note>The following section contains the "critical apparatus," a specialized set of notes used by scholars to track differences between ancient handwritten copies of the Bible.</note>

**23.** **rich person with difficulty** <note>original: "πλουσ. δυσκολ."</note> occurs in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Codex Bezae (D), Codex Dublinensis (Z), and manuscripts 1 and 33. Also found in many other manuscripts, several Old Latin versions (a, b, c, ff¹, g¹, g², n), the Vulgate (vg), the Ethiopic version, Origen, Chromatius, and others... **24.** **And again:** <note>original: "παλιν δε"</note> a few manuscripts and Old Latin versions (e, g¹, g², h, q) and the Vulgate read **And again** <note>original: "και παλιν"</note>; others read simply **Again** | **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> occurs in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Ephraemi, and others, as well as the Sahidic and Coptic versions and both Ethiopic versions... The "Received Text" and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf omit it, following Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and many other uncials <note>Manuscripts written in large capital letters.</note> | **camel** <note>original: "καμηλον"</note> occurs in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, and Bezae (Eusebius notes a similar phrase in Isaiah 60:6 regarding "herds of camels")... some manuscripts read **rope** <note>original: "καμιλον"</note>, and the Old Latin version 'b' uses the Latin term *camillum*. **Scholion (attributed to Origen):** <note>A 'scholion' is an ancient marginal note or commentary.</note> <note>original: "κάμηλον δὲ ὧδε οὐ τὸ ζῶον λέγει, ἀλλὰ τὸ παχὺ σχοινίον, ᾧ δεσμοῦσι τὰς ἀγκύρας οἱ ναῦται."</note> "By 'camel' here he does not mean the animal, but the thick rope with which sailors tie anchors." Theophylact says something similar. **Another scholion:** "Some say 'camel' is the rope of the machine, others say the animal. The first is more certain to the senses, but understand it according to the mind." However, Suidas and the scholia on Aristophanes state: "A *kamēlos* [camel] is the [burden-bearing] animal; a *kamilos* is the thick rope [spelled with an 'i']." | **eye** <note>original: "τρυπηματοσ" - literally 'a hole'</note> occurs in Codex Sinaiticus, Ephraemi, and many others, including Clement of Alexandria and Origen (who, in his work against Celsus, says that Jesus's saying about the camel and the needle-hole was claimed by Celsus to be a corrupted version of a Platonic saying about the impossibility of a very good man also being very rich), Chrysostom, and others... **25.** **And hearing** <note>original: "ακουσ. δε"</note> (the Curetonian Syriac reads "And again hearing"): Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) omits "and" <note>original: "δε"</note>, as do some Old Latin versions | **the disciples** <note>original: "οι μαθητ."</note> occurs in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many others... the "Received Text" adds **his** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> | **were astonished:** <note>original: "εξεπλησσοντο"</note> several Old Latin versions (d, a, b, c, e) and the Curetonian Syriac add **and they were afraid**.

<note>The following section is the "Critical Apparatus," where the editor compares different ancient versions of the Bible. He uses symbols like ℵ (Codex Sinaiticus), B (Codex Vaticanus), and ς (the Textus Receptus/Standard printed Greek text) to show where the wording differs across history.</note>

**21.** **she said** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note> with Codices ℵ, C, D, N, Z, many uncials, various Latin versions, the Vulgate, and the Coptic... but B, the Sahidic, and John of Damascus read **but she said**; other Latin versions read **and she said** or **she said to him** | **Lord** <note>original: "κυριε"</note>: the Curetonian Syriac adds "Lord" | **these** <note>original: "ουτοι"</note> with Codices ℵ, B, D, N, etc... but some manuscripts and Isidore of Pelusium omit this; therefore, Lachmann puts it in brackets [these] | **two** <note>original: "δυο"</note>: some manuscripts omit "two" | **your right hand** <note>original: "δεξιων σου"</note> with ℵ, B, and John of Damascus... but the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf add **your** <note>original: "σου"</note> with Codices C, D, N, etc., and most versions (possibly harmonized from Mark) | **your left** <note>original: "ευωνυμων σου"</note> with ℵ, B, C, N, Z, and most ancient versions... but the Textus Receptus (following editors Griesbach and Scholz) omits **your** following Codices D and several Latin versions | **your kingdom**: the Curetonian Syriac adds **and in your glory** (likely from Mark).

**22.** **but he**: the Textus Receptus reads **but he [answering]** which is considered clumsy here | **said** (supported by many Latin versions and the Vulgate): other versions add **to them**, including the Curetonian Syriac and Sahidic | **to drink**: some versions place this after **the cup** | **to drink** <note>original: "πινειν"</note> with Codices ℵ, C, D, X, and many others: but Codices B and C read **to drink** <note>original: "πιειν"</note>. This is found without the following addition in ℵ, B, D, L, Z, the Vulgate, and many others. However, the Textus Receptus adds **and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with** following several uncials and the Peshitta Syriac (this is likely an early scribal addition imported from the Gospel of Mark 10:38) | **to him**: omitted by Codex D, the Curetonian Syriac, and the Ethiopic.

**23.** **He says** <note>original: "λεγει"</note> with ℵ, B, D, Z, and the Vulgate... but the Textus Receptus reads **And he says** <note>original: "και λεγει"</note> with Codex C and others. However, many manuscripts (including D and Δ) add **Jesus** after **to them** | **you shall drink** <note>original: "πιεσθε"</note> with ℵ, B, D, L, Z, and the earliest versions... but the Textus Receptus adds **and you shall be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with** (again, likely harmonized from the Gospel of Mark) | **and from** <note>original: "και εξ"</note> with ℵ, C, D, Z, and most others... but Codices B, L, and others read **or from** <note>original: "η εξ"</note> (compare Mark) | **left**: most manuscripts read simply "left," but the Textus Receptus adds **my** following later manuscripts and the Sahidic | **this** <note>original: "τουτο"</note> with C, D, and Δ... but the Textus Receptus and Lachmann omit it (as in Mark) following ℵ, B, Z, and the Vulgate. Some Latin versions translate it as **to give to you** | **but for those** <note>original: "αλλ οις"</note>: one minuscule (225) reads **to others** <note>original: "αλλοις"</note>, as do some Latin fathers like Hilary and Augustine (likely influenced by Mark 10:40) | **by** <note>original: "υπο"</note>: Codex L reads "from" <note>original: "απο"</note>, and others read "beside/from" <note>original: "παρα"</note>.

<note>The following long passage in Latin is an "interpolation"—an addition found in several ancient Latin and Syriac manuscripts but absent from the standard Greek text. It resembles a parable found in Luke 14 regarding humility at a banquet.</note>

The following follows in this place in manuscripts a, b, c, d, e, ff¹, ff², g², h, and n (though not in f, g¹, l, m, or q), as well as in the Emmeram, Theodulf, and Curetonian Syriac versions. **"But when you are invited** <note>Manuscript 'd' says 'entering'; 'm', 'g²', and Emmeram say 'But when you have entered'</note> **to a dinner, do not recline** <note>Manuscripts 'ff¹' and 'h' say 'do not sit down'; 'd' says 'should not sit'</note> **in the more prominent places** <note>Manuscripts 'e' and 'ff²' say 'eminent places'; 'g²', Emmeram, and Theodulf say 'superior places'; 'm' says 'honorable places'</note>, **lest perhaps a more distinguished person** <note>Manuscripts 'd', 'm', 'g²', Emmeram, and Theodulf say 'more worthy'; 'e' says 'more honored'</note> **than you should arrive, and the one who invited you to the dinner** <note>Manuscript 'ff¹' says 'who invited you'; 'm' says 'the inviter'; 'd' says 'the inviter of the dinner'</note> **should say to you: 'Move** <note>Manuscript 'e' and the Curetonian Syriac omit 'still'</note> **further down,' and you be put to shame** <note>Manuscripts 'ff¹' and Theodulf say 'and it will be a shame to you'; the Curetonian Syriac adds 'in the sight of those reclining at the table'</note>. **But if you recline in a lower place and there arrives** <note>Manuscript 'g²' and Emmeram say 'comes forward'; 'd' says 'should arrive'</note> **one more humble** <note>Manuscript 'd' says 'lesser'</note> **than you, the one who invited you to the dinner will say to you: 'Move** <note>Manuscript 'd' says 'gather yourself'</note> **up higher'** <note>Manuscripts 'b', 'ff¹', 'h' say 'upward'; 'm' says 'to a superior place'</note>, **and this will be more useful to you** <note>Manuscript 'e' says 'and then you will have glory before those reclining with you'; the Curetonian Syriac says the same</note>." The Peshitta Syriac (marginal note of codex 1) agrees mostly with manuscript 'd', adding this note: <note>original: "Haec quidem in exemplis antiquis..."</note> *“These things are indeed read in ancient copies only in Luke, chapter 53 (Luke 14:7 and following); however, they are found in Greek copies (or rather, in a specific Greek copy?) in this place; therefore, they have also been added here by us.”* Likewise, this is acknowledged by Hilary, Leo, and Juvencus.

**29. As they were going out** <note>original: "εκπορευομενων αυτων"</note> with Codices ℵ, B, C, D, E, K, L, M, N, S, U, V, X, Z, Π, etc.: But Codices F, H, Δ, 33, and others, as well as the Coptic and Armenian versions and Basil, read **As he was going out** <note>original: "εκπορευομενου αυτου"</note>; additionally, the Syriac Scholiast and others read **As Jesus was going out** | **Jericho**: spelled as *Iereicho* in B, C, L, Z... but Tischendorf and Lachmann spell it *Iericho* with Codices ℵ, G, H, K, M, N, S, U, V, X, Γ, and others (also supported by the Sahidic, Coptic, and Gothic versions) | **followed him a large crowd**: (the plural "crowds" is noted in some versions) Codices D, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate read **large crowds followed him**.

**30. behold**: omitted by the Curetonian Syriac | **hearing, etc.**: Codex D and the Vulgate read **they heard that Jesus was passing by, and...** | **have mercy on us**: The word **Lord** <note>original: "κυριε"</note> is absent in Codices ℵ, D, 13, 69, 118, 209, 346, the Old Latin, and the Curetonian Syriac... but Lachmann and Tischendorf add **Lord** with Codices B, L, Z, 124, the Vulgate, and Coptic versions; the Textus Receptus (ς) also adds **Lord** with Codices C, E, G, H, K, M, N, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π, and others.
