<note>The following notes are the "critical apparatus," where scholars list differences between various ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts) of the Bible.</note>

**23.** **when he had come** <note>original: ελθοντος αυτου</note> follows the manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, Bezae, and several others, as well as the scholar Origen. The common received text and Tischendorf follow another group of manuscripts that read **to him as he came** <note>original: ελθοντι... αυτω</note> | **they came**: manuscript 33 uses a slightly different spelling for the verb | **as he was teaching**: this phrase is omitted in several Old Latin manuscripts and the Curetonian Syriac version | **and who**: some Latin versions read **or who** <note>original: η τις</note>, likely following the phrasing in the Gospels of Mark and Luke | **gave**: Codex Θ <note>Koridethi Gospels</note> places this word after "this authority" to match the phrasing in Mark.

**24.** **But** <note>original: δε</note> is included in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most manuscripts, but omitted in the editions of Tischendorf and Lachmann based on several Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac copies | **I will ask**: Codex Bezae and some others use a more intensive form of the verb **I will question** <note>original: επερωτησω</note>, matching Mark’s version | **one thing**: manuscripts differ on the word order, with some placing "one" <note>original: ενα</note> before "thing" <note>original: λογον</note> as seen in Mark and Luke | **which if**: Codex Bezae and its Latin translation omit this, reading instead "if you tell me, then I..."

**25.** **the** <note>second use</note>: The definite article before "John" is found in the oldest manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, but omitted in most later manuscripts | **reasoned**: Manuscript G uses a word meaning **miscalculated** <note>original: παρελογ.</note> | **among** <note>original: παρ</note> is found in most manuscripts, but Lachmann uses **within** <note>original: εν</note> based on the Vaticanus and others.

**26.** **to us**: a few manuscripts read **to you** | **therefore** <note>original: ουν</note>: present in the majority of manuscripts including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, but omitted in others following the style of Mark and Luke | **did you not believe**: some Latin versions use the present tense **do you not believe** | **as a prophet** <note>original: ως προφητ.</note>: the word order varies between manuscripts, with some placing it before and some after "John." St. Augustine’s writings show he translated this freely as "because they held John to be a prophet" | **they hold**: some manuscripts and early translations use the past tense **they held** <note>original: ειχον</note>, again matching the Gospel of Mark.

**27.** **they said** <note>original: ειπαν</note>: the spelling varies slightly across different manuscript traditions | **He also**: some versions including Sinaiticus and various Latin and Syriac copies explicitly name him as **Jesus**.

Reason does not allow that a feigned profession should obtain the merit of perfect truth, as if it were better to have deceived by promising than to have completed everything without a promise. Who would not prefer to be denied what he asks, provided that what he asked is done, rather than having that which was promised not be done? ... Nor can another passage in Origen be used as evidence for it, where he says: "the Gospel thus: 'Have you never read... the stone which they rejected... the cornerstone; everyone who falls... will crush him.'" For although the words "Have you never read" [without "in the scriptures"] seem to depend on Matthew, it is very clear that the whole passage is brought in from Luke, because from the words "into the head of the corner," he continues with Luke alone: "everyone who falls.") Eustathius (who, having copied everything from verse 33 to 43 word for word, ought to have added verse 44, I think, if he had found it in his manuscripts. But he proceeds: "and the parable is related to that in Isaiah") and Irenaeus (who also copied verses 33–43 without adding verse 44). It is also passed over by the Lucianic version. See also Cyril of Alexandria, who, after treating the parable up to "in their seasons" in verse 41, adds: "and to these things Christ says: 'Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of heaven will be taken from you and given to another nation producing its fruits,'" but adds nothing else. On the other hand, the same author [Cyril] in a different collection, after saying "Therefore... its fruits," then added: "and he who falls on..." <note>The editor notes: These words seem entirely taken from Luke, in whose account the speech concludes with this, just as it does with verse 43 in Matthew. A corrector likely adapted Luke’s words freely into Matthew, as often happens with such interpolations, a matter that has been discussed repeatedly.</note>

# XXII.

<margin>Section 221. Eusebian Canon 5</margin> 1 And Jesus answering again spoke in parables to them, saying: <margin>Verses 2–14: compare Luke 14:16–24</margin> 2 “The kingdom of heaven is likened to a human king, who made wedding feasts for his son. 3 And he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding feasts, and they were not willing to come. 4 Again he sent other servants saying: ‘Tell those invited: Behold, my dinner I have prepared, my bulls and the fatted cattle have been slaughtered, and everything is ready; come to the wedding feasts.’ 5 But they, being negligent, went away, one to his own field, and another to his business; 6 and the rest, having seized his [servants]...

---

XXII. 1. **again** <note>original Greek: *palin*</note>: (Manuscript 33, Old Latin g<sup>2</sup>, the Vulgate, Origen [volume 3, page 791], and Chrysostom place this after **said**; it is also transposed differently in several Old Latin and Syriac versions; for instance, the Curetonian Syriac reads "again Jesus answered and said to them in parables"): Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (F) omits it; Codex Basiliensis (E) omits "said to them" | **in parables to them** with Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), Regius (L), and manuscripts 1. 33. 69. 124. 209. g<sup>2</sup>. Vulgate, Origen ... **the majority of manuscripts** <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> read **to them in parables** with Codex Ephraemi (C), Σ, Δ, Π, and 8 other uncials, many other manuscripts, Old Latin ff<sup>2</sup>. q (and most Old Latin, though "again" is placed after "to them"), the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, and the Armenian | **saying**: omitted by Old Latin ff<sup>2</sup>. h l and the Armenian (and the Curetonian Syriac as noted above).

2. **is likened** <note>original: *ōmoiōthē*</note>: Codex Ephraemi (F) and others, as well as John of Damascus, spell it *omoiōthē* | **made** followed by **and** (also in Eusebius): manuscripts 1, Origen (page 791 and 824) read **making** <note>original: *poiōn*</note> without the word "and."

3. **his servants**: Jerome <note>an influential 4th-century scholar and translator</note> on this passage: "and he sent his servant to call those invited." [He notes:] "There is no doubt that [this refers to] Moses"— "but if we read 'servants,' as most copies have it, it must be referred to the prophets." "The servants who were sent the second time are better understood as the prophets than the apostles, provided that 'servant' was written above. But if you read 'servants' in that same place, these second servants are to be understood as the apostles." Compare this with Luke 14:17, from which this reading [the singular 'servant'] likely originated.

4. **he sent**: Codex Regius (L) reads **he sends** <note>present tense</note> | **my** (the first instance): manuscript 1 and Origen omit it | **I have prepared** <note>original: *ētoimaka*</note> (approved by Griesbach) with Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C*, original hand), Bezae (D), and manuscripts 1. 22. 33. ... **the majority of manuscripts** read **I prepared** <note>original: *ētoimasa*</note> with Codex Ephraemi (C<sup>3</sup>, corrected), Σ, Δ, Π, 9 other uncials, Origen, Cyril, Chrysostom, and John of Damascus ... about 10 others read **is prepared**. | **my** (the second instance): Old Latin a, b, e, ff<sup>2</sup> and John of Damascus omit it | **fatted cattle** <note>original: *sitista*</note> (supported by Origen, Cyril, and Chrysostom): Codex Wolfii A (G) and others read **grain-fed** <note>original: *siteuta*</note>. Additionally, several manuscripts and the Syriac and Ethiopic versions add the word **my**.

5. **one** [went]... **and another** [went] <note>using the Greek relative pronouns *hos men... hos de*</note> with Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C*, original), Regius (L), and many others including Origen ... **the majority of manuscripts** read **the one... and the other** <note>using the articles *ho men... ho de*</note> with Codex Ephraemi (C<sup>2</sup>, corrected), Σ, Δ, Π, and others. ... Codex Bezae (D) and several Old Latin manuscripts read **some... and others** <note>plural: *hoi men... hoi de*</note> | **to his** <note>original: *eis ton*</note>: Origen once reads **upon his** <note>original: *epi ton*</note> | **to his** <note>original: *epi tēn*</note> (approved by Griesbach and Schulz) with Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (C, D) and several others ... **the majority of manuscripts** read **into his** <note>original: *eis tēn*</note> | **his** <note>original: *autou*, singular</note>: Codex Bezae (D) and several Latin versions read **their** <note>original: *autōn*, plural</note>.

23 On that day, the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect that denied the resurrection of the dead</note> came to him, saying

---

*to us:* <note>original: "ημιν"</note> found in Old Latin manuscripts (d, a, b, e, ff¹, ff², q) and Cyril of Alexandria's *Glaphyra*; omitted by others | *tax:* <note>original: "κηνσον"</note> omitted by the first hand of Codex Sangallensis (Δ), but the same scribe supplied it before the word "to give."

18. *said:* <note>original: "ειπεν"</note> manuscript 33, the Sahidic Coptic, the Curetonian Syriac, and the Ethiopic versions add **to them**.

20. *and he says:* <note>original: "και λεγει"</note> supported by Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Regius (L), Monacensis (X), Sangallensis (Δ), and Cyprius (Π), along with nine other uncials and nearly all others; the Old Latin (a, c, f, q), Vulgate, and Coptic versions... but Codex Bezae (D) and manuscript 69 read **and he said**; other Old Latin manuscripts (b, e, ff¹, ff², g², h) and the Sahidic Coptic also vary | *Jesus:* <note>original: "ο Ιησούς"</note> <note>These are "Nomina Sacra," or sacred names, which were abbreviated in Greek manuscripts to save space and show reverence.</note> found in Codex Bezae (D), Regius (L), and many others including the Vulgate and Syriac; it is omitted in the Textus Receptus <note>original: ς</note> and by the primary hands of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, following the style of Mark | *this [word] after image:* <note>original: "αυτη post εικων"</note> found in almost all major manuscripts (א, B, C, D, X, Δ, Π, etc.) and the Vulgate (*imago haec*); however, some manuscripts (L, Z, 157) place "this" after "inscription." The Valentinians (according to Clement of Alexandria) and Origen cite it as: **"The Lord did not ask 'whose property is this?' but 'whose image and inscription?'"**

21. *they say:* <note>original: "λεγουσιν"</note> supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and some early versions; the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf add **to him** with the majority of manuscripts (D, L, X, Δ, Π) | *to them:* <note>original: "αυτοις"</note> several Old Latin manuscripts add **Jesus** | *therefore:* <note>original: "ουν"</note> (also found in many Latin and Syriac versions, and cited by Origen and Justin Martyr, who writes: **"They asked him if it was necessary to pay taxes to Caesar, and he answered: 'Tell me, whose image does the coin have?' They said: 'Caesar’s.' And again he answered them: 'Render therefore the things of Caesar to Caesar' etc."**): found in Codex Bezae and several early versions. | *to Caesar:* <note>original: "καισαρι"</note> found in nearly all manuscripts; however, some (D, K, Δ, Π) and Justin Martyr or Origen read **to the Caesar** <note>original: "τω καισαρι"</note> using the definite article; Luke's Gospel shows similar variation.

22. *they went away:* <note>original: "απηλθαν"</note> using the older Greek ending in Vaticanus and Bezae; the Textus Receptus uses the more common ending **-on** <note>original: "-ηλθον"</note> with Sinaiticus and the majority of manuscripts.

...that there is no resurrection, and they questioned him 24 saying: "Teacher, Moses said: If someone dies not having children, his brother shall marry his wife as next of kin <note>This refers to 'Levirate marriage,' an ancient custom where a man was obligated to marry his deceased brother's childless widow to continue the family line.</note> and raise up offspring for his brother. 25 Now there were seven brothers among us; and the first, having married, died, and having no offspring, he left his wife to his brother. 26 Likewise also the second and the third, until the seventh. 27 And finally, after them all, the woman died. 28 In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife of the seven will she be? For they all had her." 29 But Jesus answered and said to them: "You are led astray <note>original: "πλανᾶσθε" — to wander from the truth or be deceived</note>, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. 30 For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels..."

---

<note>The following notes are technical 'textual apparatus,' comparing different ancient hand-written copies of the Bible to find the most original wording.</note>

Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note>... The Received Text <note>The standard Greek text used for centuries, abbreviated as ς</note> and Lachmann <note>A 19th-century biblical scholar</note> read **those who say** <note>original: "οι λεγοντεσ"</note> along with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Vaticanus (B), and many other Greek manuscripts, as well as the Sahidic and Coptic versions. Similarly, the Old Latin and Vulgate versions read **who say** (Codex Bezae reads **saying**; manuscript ff¹ reads **denying**). For **questioned**, Codex Nanianus (U) reads **asked**.

24. **Moses:** The spelling varies between *Mōüsēs* and *Mōsēs* across many manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and the writings of Origen. | **said:** Several Syriac and Coptic versions add **to us**; compare this with the parallel accounts in the Gospels of Mark and Luke. | **shall marry as next of kin:** <note>original: "επιγαμβρευσει"</note> This reading is found in nearly all manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B). However, Lachmann and others add **that** <note>original: "ινα"</note> based on Codex Bezae (D) and the Vulgate (*ut ducat*). | **children:** Some Latin versions read **son** or **sons**. | **his wife:** Codex Bezae (D) omits **his**. | **shall raise up:** Some manuscripts use a more emphatic form of the verb.

25. **now:** <note>original: "δε"</note> Omitted by Codex Bezae (D) and some Latin versions. | **having married:** <note>original: "γημασ"</note> Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Origen. Other manuscripts use a different Greek form for "married" <note>original: "γαμησασ"</note>. | **his wife:** Codex Regius (L) and a few others omit **his**.

26. **likewise:** Codex Nanianus (U) adds **and**. | **until:** One Syriac version reads **and until**.

27. **all:** Omitted by Codex Sangallensis (Δ) and Chrysostom. | **the woman:** Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and others. The Received Text (ς) and Tischendorf read **also the woman** based on Codex Bezae (D) and the Vulgate.

28. **resurrection therefore:** Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B). Some Latin versions read **in the resurrection however**. | **of the seven will she be:** Variant word orders exist in Codex Bezae (D) and the Vulgate. | **all:** Some versions read **seven**. | **her:** A few manuscripts add **as a wife**.

29. **but answering:** Sinaiticus (ℵ) reads **and answering**. | **to them:** Omitted by Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Codex Cyprius (V).

30. **given in marriage:** <note>original: "γαμιζοντ."</note> Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and early fathers like Clement of Alexandria and Origen. Other manuscripts use slightly different forms of the verb <note>original: "εκγαμιζ." or "γαμισκοντ."</note>. It is noted that these specific forms of the verb "to give in marriage" are virtually never found in ancient non-biblical Greek; they appear to be unique to the New Testament's vocabulary.

...of God in heaven they are. 31 But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read that which was spoken to you by God, saying: 32 <margin>* Exodus 3: 6</margin> ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? ---

<note>The following notes are technical 'textual apparatus,' comparing different ancient hand-written copies of the Bible to determine the most accurate original wording.</note>

I partake <note>original: "μεταλαμβάνω"</note>, while the word *to give in marriage* <note>original: "γαμίζω"</note> means *to grant a marriage to someone*. The form *to be given in marriage* <note>original: "γαμισκ."</note> is cited from several places, such as Aristotle, Heraclides, and the *Florilegium* found in Stobaeus and Clement. Furthermore, *to be married out* <note>original: "ἐκγαμηθῆναι"</note> carries an unfavorable sense of marrying outside one's group [as Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> says: “when a virgin is given to another race, as if to those she shouldn't be”]. | **but** <note>original: "αλλ"</note>: Codex Bezae (D) reads the longer form **but** <note>original: "αλλα"</note> | **angels**: Manuscripts 1, 22, and Origen read **the angels**. | **of God** <note>original: "θεου"</note> along with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Regius (L), and others. Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father</note> also uses this. The Received Text <note>The standard Greek text for centuries, abbreviated as ς</note> and Lachmann <note>A 19th-century scholar</note> read **of the God** <note>original: "του θεου"</note> along with several uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>. (In Codex Basiliensis (E), the words **of the God... they are** were written over an erasure, as something was missing.) Other versions like the Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic include "of God," while Lachmann and Griesbach omit it based on Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Bezae (D), and several Old Latin versions :: similar to the Gospel of Mark | **in**: Codex Nanianus (U) and others read **those who are in** | **the heaven** <note>original: "τω ουρ."</note> along with Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Coptic versions. The Received Text (ς) omits **the** <note>original: "τω"</note> along with Bezae (D) and Chrysostom | **they are** <note>original: "εισιν"</note>: certain Latin and Egyptian versions place this after **but** :: similar to the Gospel of Mark.

31. **to you** <note>original: "υμιν"</note>: Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Sangallensis (Δ), and others omit this.

32. **Isaac**: Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Bezae (D) use the spelling **Isak** | **the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob**: Sinaiticus (ℵ) omits the article **the** <note>original: "ο"</note> in both instances (Origen notes: “for it is not written: I am God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, but I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob; and so they recorded it in Matthew, Mark, and Luke”) :: similar fluctuations in the reading are found in Mark | **is God** <note>original: "εστιν θεοσ"</note> (with Sinaiticus and Bezae; Lachmann reads **the God** based on Vaticanus and others): the Received Text (ς) reads **is the God, the God of the dead** based on several later manuscripts, the Syriac, and the Apostolic Constitutions | **God** without the article "the": according to Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Bezae (D), and Eusebius (who wrote: “the Savior taught saying: the God of Abraham... until 'of the living'”). Lachmann reads **the God** <note>original: "ο θεοσ"</note> based on Vaticanus (B) and various Coptic versions. Furthermore, if Origen’s authority stood above the most ancient manuscripts, we should publish it according to the Received Text (ς). For in his writings, having cited the full passage from Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he gives Matthew **the God, the God** <note>original: "ο θεοσ θεοσ"</note>, and Mark and Luke **the God** <note>original: "ο θεοσ"</note>. But against all the most ancient witnesses with which he usually agrees—for the fact that elsewhere he approaches a contrary reading without any Evangelist's name being attached carries little weight—I fear lest the license of scribes has intruded the later Byzantine reading. Certainly, our reading (and Irenaeus's) shares the praise of antiquity with Origen. Yet Origen’s specific reading is commended because it assigns to Matthew a unique wording different from Mark.

When those who knew she had borne a son tried to stop her, Zechariah stood up and told them she was worthy of the virgins' place, as she was still a virgin. Therefore, as if he were acting against the Law by allowing a mother to stand in the virgins' place, the men of that generation killed Zechariah between the temple and the altar.”* ... **Codex Sinaiticus** (corrected), **Manuscript 6**, and **Manuscript 13** omit this, as does Eustathius of Antioch, which seems a particularly suitable place for proving this (see before). An old scholarly note: **he means Zechariah son of Jehoiada <note>original: "Zacharian de ton iōdae"</note>; for he had two names.** Another scholarly note: **it is likely he is now speaking of the father of John.** (More details about his death are told in the same note; see Matthaei’s note on this passage, and also Euthymius and Theophylact. Other traditions are found in the Infancy Gospel of James, chapters 23 and 24. Still others regarding the "Birth of Mary" are reported by Epiphanius.) **Jerome** says on this passage: *“In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes <note>An early Jewish-Christian group</note>, we find 'son of Jehoiada' written instead of 'son of Barachiah.'”*

36. **will come:** following **Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and Regius**, Manuscript 1, 124, several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Irenaeus... **Griesbach** (but later revised), **Scholz** read **that it will come** <note>original: "oti ēxei"</note> with **Codex Ephraemi, Monacensis, Tischendorfianus, Zacynthius, Petropolitanus**, 9 other uncials, and over 150 others, the Syriac, Origen, and Chrysostom | **all these things:** following **Codex Sinaiticus, Ephraemi, Wolfii, Regius, Boreelianus**, and many others, the Vulgate, Coptic, Origen, and Chrysostom... **Lachmann and Tischendorf** read **these things all** <note>original: "panta tauta"</note> with **Codex Vaticanus, Monacensis, Tischendorfianus, Zacynthius, Petropolitanus**, 7 other uncials, and about 60 others, and Irenaeus.

37. **the one** <note>original: "ē"</note> (so also Clement, Origen everywhere, Eusebius, Cyril, etc.): **Codex Sinaiticus** (original hand) omits it | **killing the prophets:** in this order also in Clement, Origen, Eusebius, Basil, Cyril, Irenaeus, Hilary, and the corrected **Codex Sinaiticus**: the original hand of **Sinaiticus** and Origen read **the prophets killing** <note>original: "t. proph. apokt."</note> | **killing:** <note>original: "apokteinousa" (present tense)</note> with **Codex Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius, Monacensis, Petropolitanus**, and many others... **Codex Sinaiticus, Manuscript 33, 69**, and 40 others read **will kill** <note>original: "apoktenousa" (future tense)</note>; Origen and Theodoret read **having killed** <note>original: "apokteinasa" (past tense)</note> | **to her:** <note>original: "pr. autēn"</note> **Codex Bezae** and 2 others read **to you** <note>original: "pr. se"</note>, one manuscript reads **to yourself** <note>original: "pr. seauton"</note> (Latin versions read **to you** <note>original: "ad te"</note>) | **to gather together:** (**Clement and Caesarius** read **to gather** <note>original: "sunag."</note>) also in the corrected **Codex Sinaiticus**.

<note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," a technical record of how different ancient hand-written copies of the Bible vary in their wording. The symbols like ℵ, B, and D represent specific ancient manuscripts.</note>

**Verse 31.** Manuscripts H, X, and a few others, along with the Latin manuscript "h," read "he sends" <note>original: αποστελλει</note> (though H and others accent it as "he will send") | The word "great" is included in ℵ, L, Δ, and many others, including the Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian versions, and is cited by early church fathers like Eusebius, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Chrysostom. | However, Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>19th-century biblical scholars</note> note that "of a voice" <note>original: φωνης</note> is prefixed in manuscripts B, X, Γ, Π, and many others; likewise, the Syriac versions place "voice" before "trumpet." | Additionally, manuscript D and at least ten others, along with the Vulgate and Old Latin versions, prefix "and a voice" <note>original: και φωνης</note> (Scholz notes: "either 'and a voice' should be read or 'voice' should be expelled") | "They will gather together" <note>original: επισυναξουσιν</note> (also in the corrected ℵ): but the original ℵ, a few others, and Hippolytus read "he will gather" <note>original: -αξει</note>, which matches the wording in the Gospel of Mark | "From" <note>original: απ</note> (also in the margin of the Syriac): Manuscripts D, X, and a few others read "away from" <note>original: απο</note> | "Until" <note>original: εως</note> is found in ℵ, D, L, X, and almost all others; Lachmann adds "of the" <note>original: των</note> based on manuscript B and others | "From the ends" <note>original: ακρων</note>: several Latin manuscripts (d, b, c, h, q) add a phrase found in the Gospel of Luke: "When these things begin to take place, look up and raise your heads because your redemption is drawing near."

**Verse 32.** "When already" <note>original: οταν ηδη</note>: Manuscript H erroneously reads "that" <note>original: οτι</note> | "The" <note>original: τα</note>: omitted by the original ℵ and a few others | "Puts out" <note>original: ἐκφύῃ</note>: with this accent in manuscripts B², U, X, and many others; the Latin translates it as "has brought forth," "produces," or "sent out," and the Armenian and Hilary use "has blossomed" | Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use a different accent <note>original: ἐκφυῇ</note> based on E, F, G, and others; Latin versions use "are born" or "sprout" | "You know" <note>original: γινωσκετε</note>: Manuscript D reads "it is known" <note>original: -σκεται</note> | "Near": Manuscript D and others add "is" <note>original: εστιν</note> after the word "summer."

**Verse 33.** "All these things": supported by ℵ, D, H, and many others, including the Syriac and Armenian versions | Lachmann and Tischendorf reverse the order to "these all" based on B, L, and others. Additionally, some Latin manuscripts add "happening" <note>original: γινομενα</note>.

**Verse 34.** "Truly": Manuscript L and ten others add "but" <note>original: δε</note> | "Will not" <note>original: ου μη</note> is supported by ℵ, X, Γ, and many others; Lachmann adds "that" <note>original: οτι</note> to the phrase, matching Mark and Luke, based on B, D, F, and L | "All these things": the order varies between manuscripts, with some reading "these things all" and a few omitting "these" entirely.

**Verse 35.** The original scribe of manuscript ℵ* omitted this entire verse. Since this cannot be explained by *homoioteleuton* <note>a common error where a scribe's eye skips between two identical word endings</note>, and because the parallel passages in the other Gospels use the exact same words, it seems doubtful whether Matthew himself originally included it. However, by the second century, it was already accepted in Matthew, as evidenced by the Old Latin versions.

It is certain from the codices <note>manuscripts</note> and from Origen (who explains this more fully in his interpretation of this passage). Whether Irenaeus read this cannot be said; for in only one place does he allude to words of this kind (Book 5, 35, 2: "Similarly it is said: Earth and heaven will pass away." <note>original Latin: Terra et caelum transiet</note> The singular form "will pass away" is also provided by many of the most ancient witnesses for Luke and Mark) which can be applied with equal right to the accounts in Mark and Luke. The same holds true for Tertullian: see *Against Hermogenes* 34. | **will pass away** <note>singular Greek: παρελευσεται</note> is found in manuscripts B, D, L, and about 30 others, along with the Old Latin (which uses the singular *transiet*). Conversely, the plural **will pass away** <note>original Greek: παρελευσονται</note> is found in ℵ, C, X, and the vast majority of other manuscripts, as well as the Vulgate and other versions.

36. **and hour** <note>original Greek: και ωρασ</note> is found in ℵ, B, D, and over 120 others, as well as Cyril (who precedes it with the words "But immediately etc." from verse 29; likewise, the things that follow match Matthew). ... The variation **and of the hour** <note>original Greek: και τησ ωρασ</note> is found in many other manuscripts and the Syriac version. | **nor the Son** <note>original Greek: ουδε ο υιοσ</note> (some Latin manuscripts add "of man"; others read "but not even the Son") is found in ℵ, B, D, several early numbered manuscripts, the Old Latin, the Syriac, Ethiopic, and Armenian versions, and Irenaeus. Irenaeus writes (in a Latin translation): "And the Lord, the Son of God himself, allowed that only the Father knows the day and hour of judgment itself, clearly saying: 'But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the Son, but the Father alone.' If therefore the Son did not blush to refer the knowledge of that day to the Father... it is therefore necessary to leave this knowledge to God, just as the Lord did regarding the hour and day." <note>This is a significant theological point: early scholars debated whether Jesus, being divine, could actually be "ignorant" of the timing of the end times.</note> It is unlikely Irenaeus would have said this if he had not found these words in Matthew as well as in Mark. Additionally, the word "alone" which he adds is characteristic of Matthew's version. Origen also discusses this at length after providing the text: "And the Savior, according to this passage, joins himself with those who are ignorant of that day and hour. And it is reasonably to be asked how he, who is confident that he knows the Father, saying: 'No one knows the Father except the Son,' etc., knows the Father indeed, but does not know the day and hour of the end? And how did the Father hide this from the Son? But perhaps what he said about not knowing the day and hour of the end, he said before his dispensation <note>his earthly mission or incarnation</note>... Another explanation which is more famous than those already handed down says something else about what is written: 'nor the Son, but the Father alone.' It says, for instance, that the Apostle speaks somewhere about the Savior and about the things to be ordered at the end of the age in this way: 'But when all things shall be subjected to him,' etc." From this lengthy discussion by Origen regarding the words "nor the Son," in which he even brings in the famous explanations of others, it becomes most plain not only that he found those words in his manuscripts, but also that he [ignored...] <note>The text continues on the next page</note>

# 164 24, 37. ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

For as the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son <note>original: τοῦ υἱοῦ [τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] / tou huiou [tou anthropou]; usually completed as "Son of Man"</note>

---

[The phrase is said] to be absent in other manuscripts <note>abbreviation: cdd. = codices</note>. Moreover, against such clear testimony from the commentary of Origen himself, the evidence that Jerome testifies regarding the manuscripts of "Adamantius and Pierius" <note>Adamantius is another name for Origen; Pierius was a 3rd-century scholar in Alexandria</note> is not valid. Chrysostom (on this passage: <note>original: τω μεν ειπειν... / tō men eipein...</note> "by saying: *not even the angels*, he silenced them, so that they might not seek to learn what those [angels] do not know; but by saying: *nor the Son*, he prevents not only learning but even seeking. — How then, if all things were made through him etc., was he ignorant of the day? etc.") Cyril [of Alexandria] in the *Treasury* 800 (see just before; "but concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone." See also the excerpt in Mai 481). Hilary, Ambrose, and the author of the *Opus Imperfectum* also acknowledge [it]... Tischendorf omits [it] along with manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note> corrected, A, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Π and many others, as well as the Old Latin versions g<sup>1</sup> and g<sup>2</sup>, the Vulgate (including the Amiatinus, Gatianus, Maihingensis, Toletanus, Jacobeus, and Erlangensis manuscripts; the Fulda manuscript, which provides a harmony of the Gospels, seems to have it from Mark), Saxon, and the Sahidic-Münter version (Münter testifies to this, not the opposite), the Coptic, both Syriac versions, and other manuscripts according to Jerome (on this passage: "In some Latin manuscripts there is added *nor the Son*, although in Greek and especially the copies of Adamantius and Pierius this is not found added; but because it is read in some, it seems necessary to discuss it. Arius and Eunomius rejoice, as if the teacher were ignorant" <note>Jerome is noting that heretics like Arius used this phrase to argue that Jesus was inferior to God the Father because he lacked knowledge</note> — Nevertheless, after he proved that the passage must be explained differently than the words seem to sound, he continues: "therefore, because we have proved that the Son is not ignorant of the day of consummation, the cause must be given why he is said to be ignorant," from which he seems to distrust the manuscripts that do not have it.) Basil in letter 236 (page 361. "The wording of Matthew is this: *but concerning that day and the hour* [many manuscripts omit "and the hour"] *no one knows, not even the angels of the heavens, but the Father alone.* But that of Mark: *concerning... and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father.* What then is worth noting in these? That Matthew said nothing about the ignorance of the Son; but Mark seems to agree in sense by saying: *except the Father alone.*" Many of these points passed into the ancient scholia <note>marginal explanatory notes</note>.) Didymus the Blind in *On the Trinity* 195 (i.e., book 3, chapter 22, after quoting Mark's words he continues: "For Matthew before him... did not say that the Son was ignorant, but even set forth the form of the end itself to be known thus: *but concerning that day or the hour... the Father alone; for just as etc.*" And he adds more for the sake of explanation, following what Basil wrote in the letter to Amphilochius.) Pseudo-Athanasius in *Disputations* 170 ("in Matthew it is not found: *nor does the Son know that day.* — But Mark alone said: *nor does the Son know the day.*") John of Damascus in *Parallels* 346; Euthymius ("Consider how in Matthew *alone* is placed, but the Son is not mentioned"). Phoebadius 251; Paulinus ("in the ancient gospel books which are kept by us and in the chest of our holy church, the word *of the Son* was by no means found inserted in the same gospel passage."). Furthermore, Ambrose in *On the Faith* 5, 8 seems to deny entirely that *nor the Son* is read in the Gospels; for he says: "The ancient Greek manuscripts do not have *for neither does the Son know*; but it is not surprising if those who interpolated the divine scriptures also falsified this." (Amphilochius in excerpts at Galland 6, 499. On the words *but when he says: nor the Son, except the Father, he does not falsely claim ignorance of the Son, but explains the cause of the knowledge*—this refers to Mark rather than Matthew.) :: From everything that has been cited, it is clear that, at least in the 4th century, in most Greek (and some Latin) manuscripts, the passage of Matthew was written without the words **nor the Son**

<note>The section below is a "critical apparatus." It lists variations in the text found in different ancient manuscripts. Abbreviations like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and D (Bezae) refer to specific famous handwritten Bibles. **29.** **to everyone** <note>original: "παντι"</note> (Origen <note>A 3rd-century scholar</note> cites this freely in several places, and it is not clear whether he is quoting Luke or Matthew): The manuscript D, the Syriac version, and Chrysostom omit this. (The Old Latin, Vulgate, and Origen’s Latin translation read *to every one indeed having*, similar to the Gospel of Luke). (Schulz suggests it should be omitted based on Matthew 13:12 and Luke 19:26) | **will have abundance** <note>original: "περισσευθήσεται"</note> (The manuscripts Sinaiticus and Gamma read "will have abundance"): Manuscript D reads "will abound" | **but from the one not [having]** (Griesbach’s minor variant) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others, including the Old Latin and Vulgate (*but to him who has not - it shall be taken from him*); the Coptic reads *but this one to whom there is not, this which is his they shall take from him* ... but the "Received Text" reads **but from the one not [having]** <note>original: "απο δε του μη"</note> with manuscripts A, C, X, and many others, as in Luke | **what he has**: some manuscripts read "what he seems to have" <note>original: "ο δοκει εχειν"</note> (likely influenced by Luke 8:18) | **from him**: Manuscript C and several others (especially "evangelistaries" or lectionaries used in church services) add: **Saying these things he cried out: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear,"** while others add this same phrase at the end of verse 30.

**30.** **cast out** with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most major manuscripts; manuscript D reads **throw outside** (the Old Latin also reads *throw outside*). The scholar Schulz notes that the *Clementine Homilies* (3,61) reference this: "And let him expect to hear: 'You wicked and slothful servant, you should have put my money with the bankers... cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness.'"

**31.** **But when**: The manuscript Gamma adds "the Lord said," while others omit the word "but." | **angels**: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many early versions (Latin, Coptic, Syriac, etc.) and Church Fathers like Origen, Eusebius, and Cyril. The "Received Text" adds **holy** <note>original: "αγιοι"</note> (holy angels) with manuscript A and others (likely influenced by the prophecy in Zechariah 14:5: *the Lord my God shall come and all the holy ones with him*). | **will sit**: variations in spelling in several manuscripts.

**32.** **will be gathered**: The majority of manuscripts use the plural form "they will be gathered," while manuscript A and others use the singular "it [the nations] will be gathered." | **he will separate** <note>original: "αφορισει"</note>: found in Sinaiticus and others. The "Received Text" uses a slightly different future tense form of the same verb. | **from**: Manuscript D uses a different Greek preposition for "from." | **goats**: Manuscript B uses a slightly different spelling.

<note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," where scholars compare different ancient versions of the Bible to see how the text changed over centuries of hand-copying.</note>

**33. indeed** <note>original: "μεν"</note> (also found in several Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac versions, and cited by early church writers like Hippolytus, Eusebius, and Cyril) : Manuscript D, the Old Latin manuscript *p*, and the early Syriac versions omit this word | **his** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> with manuscripts B, D, I, L, Gamma, Delta, Pi, and the majority of others, as well as the Vulgate and Coptic versions... Manuscripts Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, as well as some early Latin translations, omit this. (Clement of Alexandria, around 200 AD, quotes this as: <term>for the one setting some on the right and others on the left</term>). However, manuscript Sinaiticus (along with Coptic and Syriac versions) adds "his" after the word "left."

**34. blessed** <note>original: "ευλογημενοι"</note> (as found in Clement, Hippolytus, Origen, and many others) : Manuscript Delta uses a slightly different spelling for "blessed" | **for you** <note>original: "υμιν"</note> : A few manuscripts read "for us."

**35. I was thirsty** <note>original: "εδιψησα"</note> (found in Clement, Origen, and the writings of Basil the Great) : Manuscript Delta and the Syriac version add the word "and" before this. On this point, a saying attributed to Christ in Origen’s works can be compared: <term>And Jesus says: for the sake of the sick I was sick, and for the sake of the hungry I was hungry, and for the sake of the thirsty I was thirsty.</term> Also, a similar saying appears in Justin Martyr: <term>Wherefore also our Lord Jesus Christ said: In whatever state I find you, in these also I will judge you.</term> This is also found in Clement and in the works of Nilus: <term>For such as I find you, such a one will I judge you, says the Lord.</term> <note>These are "agrapha"—sayings of Jesus not found in the standard Gospels but preserved by early Christian writers.</note>

**36. you clothed me** : Manuscript Delta originally wrote this (with a spelling error) before the phrase "you welcomed me" | **you came** <note>original: "ηλθατε"</note> (a reading preferred by the scholar Schulz) found in the great early Bibles Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae... A more common later spelling <note>original: "ηλθετε"</note> is found in many other manuscripts and in the printed editions of the Church Fathers. | Manuscript Sinaiticus reads "to me" <note>original: "πρ. εμε"</note> instead of "toward me."

**37. the righteous** : Manuscript Delta omits this | **we saw** : There are minor spelling variations between "we saw" <note>original: "ειδομεν"</note> and "we have seen" <note>original: "ειδαμεν"</note> across the major manuscripts.

**38. and** <note>original: "δε"</note> : Omitted in manuscript Pi, the Sahidic (Egyptian) version, and the works of Cyprian | **we saw** : Manuscript D and Clement place the word "you" before "we saw." | **or naked** : Manuscript D reads "and naked." | **we clothed** : Manuscript D and a few others use a slightly different verb tense.

**39. and when** (found in Cyprian, the Vulgate, and Coptic versions) | **or when** | **we saw** : minor spelling variations | **sick** : Manuscripts B and D use the word for "being ill" <note>original: "ασθενούντα"</note>, while the majority of other manuscripts use the simpler adjective "sick" <note>original: "ασθενη"</note>.

13. **truly** <note>original: αμην (amēn)</note>: The corrected Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sangallensis (Δ), Old Latin (q), and Armenian add **but**; the Syriac versions have **and amen**. This variant likely comes from the parallel in Mark. | **if** <note>original: εαν (ean)</note>: Codex Bezae (D), Codex Regius (L), and a few others, along with Origen and the *Catena* <note>a commentary composed of excerpts from earlier authors</note>, use the shorter form **an** <note>original: αν</note>.

Variants include **Scariotes** (various Old Latin and Syriac manuscripts) and **Carioth** (Old Latin manuscript h).

14. 15. **went** and **said**: Codex Bezae (D) and most Latin and Syriac versions read **he went away and said**. Furthermore, many of these same manuscripts add **to them** <note>original: αυτοισ</note> after "said."

15. **and I** <note>original: και εγω</note>: Most manuscripts support this phrasing, though some of the earliest (including Vaticanus and Sinaiticus) use the contracted form **k'ego** <note>original: καγω</note>. | **for him**: Codex Sangallensis (Δ) reads **for them**. | **thirty**: Sinaiticus and Bezae use the numerical symbol **λ** <note>The Greek letter lambda stands for 30</note>. | **pieces of silver** <note>original: αργυρια (argyria)</note>: Supported by the majority of Greek and Latin manuscripts. However, Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts use the term **staters** <note>original: στατηρασ (stateras); a stater was a specific silver coin</note>. This connects to the Prophecy in Zechariah 11:12: *And they set my wages at thirty pieces of silver.*

16. **betray** <note>original: παραδω (paradō)</note>: Most manuscripts conclude here, but Codex Bezae, some Latin versions, and Coptic manuscripts add **him to them**.

17. Some manuscripts read **the disciples came to him saying to him**. | **saying** (without adding "to him"): Supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and the Coptic. Many later manuscripts add **to him**. | **should we prepare**: Variants exist between the subjunctive **prepare** <note>original: ετοιμασωμεν</note> and the future **will prepare**. <note>A significant note here mentions the "Gospel of the Ebionites" cited by Epiphanius (30, 22), where the Ebionites (a Jewish-Christian sect) altered the text to reflect their vegetarianism. In their version, when the disciples ask where to prepare, Jesus replies: "Have I desired with desire to eat this meat, the Passover, with you?"</note>

18. **and he**: Several manuscripts add **Jesus**. | **said**: Many manuscripts add **to them**. | **go**: One manuscript uses the singular command. | **the teacher says**: Codex Alexandrinus (A) omits this. | **near**: Codex Bezae has a slight spelling variation. | **I will keep/do** <note>original: ποιω (poiō)</note>: Most Latin and Vulgate versions have **I do/keep**; Codex Bezae and some Old Latin versions have the future **I will do/keep** <note>original: ποιησω</note>.

The apparatus provides evidence for various spellings of "Iscariot" and notes a vegetarian alteration of the text in the non-canonical Gospel of the Ebionites.</summary>

**21** <margin>279. 4</margin> And as they were eating, he said: “Truly I say to you, one of you will betray me.” **22** <margin>280. 1</margin> And being greatly distressed, they began to say to him, each one of them: “Is it I, Lord?” **23** <margin>281. 2</margin> And he answered and said: “The one who has dipped his hand in the dish with me, this one will betray me. **24** The Son of Man goes just as it has been written concerning him. <margin>282. 6</margin> But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed; it would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” **25** <margin>283. 10</margin> And Judas, the one betraying him, answered and said: “Is it I, Rabbi?” He says to him: “You have said it.”

---

**19. directed** <note>original: συνέταξεν (synetaxen)</note>: The first hand of Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph^*$), Codex Nanianus (U), and about ten others read **commanded** <note>original: προσεταξεν (prosetaxen)</note>. | **and they prepared the Passover**: The <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>the "received text" used for the King James Version</note> omits this; John Chrysostom <note>an influential 4th-century church father</note> passes over the entire verse.

**20. twelve disciples**: Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$) and Codex Bezae (D) use the numeral **12**. About ten manuscripts, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, and the Ethiopic versions add **his**. This reading is supported by many major codices (A, L, M, Δ, Π, etc.) and ancient versions. The Textus Receptus ($\varsigma$) omits **disciples**, as do codices B, D, F, and others. In Mark 14:17, the reading **with the twelve** is consistent across sources.

**21. said**: Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$) reads **says**. | **Truly**: The Vulgate adds **but**.

**22. to him**: Omitted by Codex Bezae (D) and several others, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, and Origen. | **each one**: Supported by the major Greek codices $\aleph$, B, C, L, and Z. Some (D, M) add **of them** <note>original: αυτων (autōn)</note>. The Textus Receptus ($\varsigma$) reads **each of them**, supported by codices A, Γ, Δ, and Π.

**23. the one who dipped**: Codex Bezae (D) uses the present tense **the one dipping**, following the phrasing in Mark. | **with me his hand in the dish**: Supported by $\aleph$, A, B, L, Z and others. There are minor variations in word order (e.g., placing "with me" after "the dish") in the Syriac and Coptic versions. The Textus Receptus ($\varsigma$) places **the hand** at the end of the phrase.

**24. indeed** <note>original: μεν (men)</note>: Codex Bezae (D), Codex Zacynthius (Z), and Chrysostom add **therefore** <note>original: ουν (oun)</note>. | **concerning him**: Codex Alexandrinus (A) reads **concerning himself**. | **better**: Codex Bezae (D) adds **because of this** <note>original: δια τουτο (dia touto)</note>. | **if not**: A few manuscripts read **or not**. | **born**: A similar phrase can be found in Clement of Rome’s letter to the Corinthians (Chapter 46): "Remember the words of Jesus our Lord... Woe to that man; it would have been better for him if he had not been born, than that he should cause one of my elect to stumble."

**25. Judas**: Codex Bezae (D) and a few others add the article, **the Judas**. | **Rabbi**: $\aleph$, A, B, D, and others use the spelling **Rabbei** <note>original: ραββει</note>; the Textus Receptus and many later manuscripts use **Rabbi** <note>original: ραββι</note>. | **He says to him**: Several manuscripts, including Sinaiticus ($\aleph$) and the Old Latin versions, add **Jesus**.

**26. as they were eating** <note>original: εσθι. δε αυτ.</note>: (so also in several Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate <note>the standard 4th-century Latin Bible</note>): Codex Bezae (D) and others read **but as they were eating**. | **Jesus** <note>original: <term>ις</term>, a sacred abbreviation for 'Iesous'</note>: Codex Bezae places this before "taking," while Manuscript Delta (Δ) omits it entirely. | **bread** <note>original: αρτον</note>: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Ephraemi (C), and others. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> and many others read **of the *new* covenant** <note>adding 'new' (kainēs) to match the wording in Luke and 1 Corinthians</note>. | **for** <note>original: περι, 'concerning' or 'on behalf of'</note>: Codex Bezae and the church father John Chrysostom read **on behalf of** <note>original: υπερ</note>. | **is poured out**: There is a minor spelling difference in the Greek verb between the oldest manuscripts and the later majority.

<note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record comparing different ancient handwritten versions of the New Testament. The letters (א, A, B, etc.) represent famous ancient manuscripts.</note>

**38.** "to them" <note>original: autois</note> without addition, with [manuscripts] א, A, B, C (original hand), D, I, L, 1, 33, 69, and almost many others; the Old Latin <note>it</note> versions b, c, ff¹·², g¹·², l, q; the Vulgate <note>vg</note>; the Syriac <note>syrsch</note>; Sahidic and Coptic; Armenian; Ethiopic; and Chrysostom... **39.** "Going forward" <note>original: proselthōn</note> (Griesbach and Scholz approve; Schulz considers it along with Matthew 21:28, 28:2, 9, 18, and says "going ahead" <note>original: proerchomenos</note> is unheard of in Matthew) with א, A, C, D, I, L, Gamma, Delta, Pi (second hand), eight uncials, 1, 33, 69, and about 100 others; the Peshitta Syriac; and most editions of Chrysostom... The Received Text <note>ς</note>, Lachmann <note>Ln</note>, and Tischendorf <note>Ti</note> read "going ahead" <note>original: proelthōn</note> with B, M, I (original hand), and many others, likewise the Old Latin and Vulgate (reading "progressus"), Origen, and Hilary, and as it appears in Sahidic and Coptic. | "Father" <note>original: pater</note> with L, Delta, 1, 209, and ten others; the Old Latin manuscript 'a'; the Amiatinus Vulgate; and Justin Martyr (who says: "he prayed saying: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me, and after this praying he says: not as I will, but as you wish"); the Valentinians according to Irenaeus ("in saying: Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me"); Origen twice (who says: "Matthew recorded the Lord saying," adding also the passages from Luke and Mark); likewise in Origen's work against Celsus ("O Father, if this cup can pass away"); also in Eusbeius, Athanasius, Pseudo-Athanasius, Didymus the Blind ("the reading found in Matthew"), Cyril, Basil (four times), Chrysostom, Cyprian (twice), Hilary (twice), Jerome (though not in this specific place), and Augustine (though not in his *De Consensu Evangelistarum*). :: So remarkable an authority of the Church Fathers supports the weight of Codex L, which so often alone, or nearly alone, confirms manuscripts א and B... The Received Text <note>ς</note> and Lachmann <note>Ln</note> add "my" <note>original: mou</note> with א, A, B, C, D, I, Gamma, Pi, nine uncials, and most others; the Old Latin (except 'a'); the Vulgate (except the Amiatinus; though g¹·² and most others read "my Father," whereas in verse 42 the Latin versions do not fluctuate between "Father" and "my Father"); Sahidic, Coptic, both Syriac versions, Armenian, Ethiopic, Hilary (three times), most of Ambrose, Jerome (at this place), and Augustine. 46. **let us go**: The <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>A 16th-century printed edition of the Greek New Testament</note> along with five other manuscripts, the Old Latin version 'a', the Armenian version, and Chrysostom add the word "from here" | **betrays** (also in the corrected <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>; this reading does not fluctuate in the Gospel of Mark): the original hand of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> uses a slightly different verb form for "betraying."

47. **and while**: (Found also in various Old Latin versions, Origen, and Hilary): <term>Codex Bezae</term> reads "but while," while others including several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, and Lucifer of Cagliari read simply "while." | **elders**: The <term>Codex Delta</term> and a few others include the definite article "the" before "elders."

48. **the one I kiss**: Found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term>, and many others, including Origen and Eusebius... The scholar Lachmann reads a slightly different Greek particle for "whomever" based on <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, <term>Codex Bezae</term>, and others.

49. **said**: The Coptic and Ethiopic versions, as well as Eusebius, add "to him" | **Rabbi**: Spelled as "rhabbei" in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, and others... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and scholar Lachmann spell it "rhabbi" following <term>Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> and the majority of manuscripts. See also the note at verse 25.

50. **but Jesus said to him**: (Found in various versions and Origen): <term>Codex Bezae</term>, the Vulgate, and others read "But Jesus said..." or simply "Jesus said to him" | **friend**: In some versions like the Syriac and Latin, this word is placed after "why are you here?" | **why**: (Supported by scholars Griesbach and Scholz) along with <term>Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae</term>, and others... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> uses a slightly different relative pronoun meaning "for what [purpose]."

51. **with Jesus**: <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> reads "with him" | **striking... cut off**: (Supported by the Vulgate and Origen): <term>Codex Bezae</term> and many Old Latin or Syriac versions read "he struck... and cut off."

52. **then**: Omitted by some manuscripts; the Coptic/Ethiopic version reads "but he says" | **your sword**: Supported by <term>Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae</term>, Origen, and many Church Fathers... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and scholar Tischendorf reverse the order to "sword of yours," while some Syriac and Coptic versions omit "your" entirely | **by the sword**: There is a minor spelling difference in the Greek word for "sword" between the early <term>Codices</term> and the majority of later manuscripts | **will perish**: Found in the primary early manuscripts including <term>Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus</term>, as well as Origen and Chrysostom (four times). However, a large number of later manuscripts, the Syriac, and the Ethiopic versions read "will die" (an alternative reading noted by scholar Griesbach).

53. **do you think**: A few manuscripts and the Syriac margin read "does it seem to you?" | <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> has a slight spelling variation for the word "I can."

**Schulz** with **Codex Sinaiticus (א)**, **B**, **L**, 33. 102. and various ancient versions (Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, Persian, Arabic) and Origen ... **Textus Receptus (ς)**, **Lachmann**, and **Tischendorf** read **"to Pontius Pilate"** <note>original: "ποντιω πιλατω"</note> with **Codex Alexandrinus (A)**, **C**, **X**, and almost all others including the Vulgate and Gothic versions. **Origen** (in his commentary) writes: <note>original Latin: "utrum autem etiam nomina utraque praesidis..."</note> "Whether both names of the governor have some reason suitable to the dispensation of the Lord Savior is not easy to answer with a definitive opinion. # 27, 7. ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

<margin>Deuteronomy 23, 19</margin> ...taking the pieces of silver, they said: "It is not lawful to put them into the **treasury** <note>original: "korbanan," a term derived from the Hebrew word for an offering dedicated to God</note>, since it is the price of blood." **7** And after taking counsel, they bought with them the **potter's field** as a burial place for strangers. <margin>Acts 1, 19</margin> **8** Therefore that field has been called the **Field of Blood** until this day. **9** Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying:

*not by hanging but he lived on...* <note>This fragmentary note likely refers to a tradition, mentioned by early writers like Papias, suggesting Judas survived the hanging or suffered a different fate.</note> — this is more clearly recorded <unclear>l</unclear>

<margin>n BL 33.</margin> **6. they said** <note>original: "eipan"</note> with **Codex Sinaiticus (א)**, **Codex Alexandrinus (A)**, **Codex Vaticanus (B²)**, **Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C)**, **L**, **Γ**, **Δ**, **Π**, and thirteen other uncials <note>large-lettered parchment manuscripts</note> and almost all others as seen in **Chrysostom** | **treasury** <note>original: "korbanan"</note> with **א**, **A**, **B²**, **C**, **L**, **Γ**, **Δ**, **Π**, and six other uncials, many others, the Peshitta Syriac, and the Armenian. 
<margin>Same as Chrysostom</margin> The same in **Chrysostom**; likewise "corbanan" in the **Codex Amiatinus**, **Fulda**, **Forojuliensis**, **Ingolstadt**, **Emmaram**, and **Hilary of Poitiers**. Other versions like **Cyril of Jerusalem**, **Augustine**, and various Latin copies read **"korbonan"** or **"corbonam"**; some Sahidic, Coptic, and Gothic versions read **"corban."** — <note>note: "korban," also "corban" in other Latin and Ethiopic copies.</note>
<margin>c ff². in place</margin> **7. And taking counsel**: Some versions and the *Acts of Pilate* read "But taking counsel" or "And they took counsel."
**8. that field**: The Itala <note>Old Latin</note> (except for manuscript f), the Vulgate, and **Origen** add **"Acheldemach"** <note>original: "acheldemach," the Aramaic name for the Field of Blood</note> (found in manuscripts b, c, g, l, and others) or "Aceldama" (found in q, the San-Gallensis, and others) which means... <note>this addition comes from Acts 1:19</note>.
<margin>Jeremiah thus: g and 5 others (4 in Scrivener) until the</margin> **9. then** (supported by **A**, **C**, **F**, and others) | **Jeremiah** (supported by **A**, **C¹**, and others, **Chrysostom**, **Origen**, **Codex Sinaiticus**, **Codex Vaticanus**, **Codex Ephraemi**, **L**, **X**, and almost all others including the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian. <margin>Origen</margin> One manuscript (22) and the margin of the Harclean Syriac read **"Zechariah,"** while manuscript "l" reads **"Isaiah."** 

Regarding this, **Origen** writes: "Among the things that are written, it is not found that Jeremiah prophesied this anywhere in his books, whether those read in the churches or those cited among the Jews; but if anyone can know, let him show where it is written: I suspect there is either an error in the writing and **Jeremiah** was put for **Zechariah**, or there is some **secret writing** <note>apocrypha</note> of Jeremiah in which it is written. Such a text, however, is found in the prophet Zechariah. — But if anyone says this and thinks he is offended, let him see if perhaps this is prophesied in some secret book of Jeremiah, knowing that even the Apostle [Paul] brings forward certain secret writings, as when he says: *What eye has not seen nor ear heard*; for this is found in no regular book except in the **Secrets of Elijah the Prophet**. Likewise, what he says: *As Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses*, is not found in the public scriptures but in a secret book titled *The Book of Jannes and Mambres*. For this reason, some dared to reject the Epistle to Timothy as having text from a secret source, but they could not. As for the First Epistle to the Corinthians, I have never heard of anyone rejecting it as spurious for this reason." 

Likewise, **Eusebius** notes: "You will observe, since these things are not found in the prophecy of Jeremiah, one must either suspect they were removed from it by some tampering, or that a scribal error occurred..."

->*“And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, whom”*<-

...to have occurred among those who have somewhat carelessly produced copies of the sacred Gospels, some person having erred and placed "Jeremiah" instead of "Zechariah." <note>original Greek: "...νεναι των αμελεστερον τα των ιερων ευαγγελιων αντιγραφα πεποιημενων σφαλέντος τινος και αντι μεν του ζαχαριου ιερεμιαν τεθεικοτοσ." This is a fragment of a Greek commentary suggesting scribal error.</note> Likewise **Augustine** in *The Harmony of the Evangelists* 3,29: “If anyone is troubled by the fact that this testimony is not found in the writings of the prophet Jeremiah, and therefore thinks that the credibility of the Evangelist [Matthew] is to be diminished in some way, he should first know that not all manuscripts of the Gospels include the phrase ‘spoken through Jeremiah,’ but only ‘through the prophet.’ We could say, then, that those manuscripts are rather to be believed which do not have the name of Jeremiah; for this was said through the prophet, but it was Zechariah. Hence it is thought that the manuscripts containing the name of Jeremiah are faulty, because they ought to have either Zechariah’s name or no name at all, as some do, but only ‘through the prophet speaking,’ who is certainly understood to be Zechariah. But let whoever wishes use that defense; as for me, the reason why it does not please me is this: because more manuscripts have the name of Jeremiah, and those who have more carefully considered the Gospel in Greek copies report that they found it so in the ancient Greek ones. There was no reason why this name should be added to create a mistake; however, there was certainly a reason why it would be removed from some manuscripts—that a bold lack of skill did this, since it was troubled by the question of why this testimony was not found in Jeremiah. What, then, is to be understood, except that this was done by the more secret counsel of God’s providence, by which the minds of the Evangelists were governed? For it could happen that while Matthew was writing the Gospel, the name ‘Jeremiah’ occurred to him instead of ‘Zechariah,’ as often happens. He would nevertheless have corrected this without any doubt, at least if warned by others who could read this while he was still living in the flesh, unless he thought that to his memory—which was ruled by the Holy Spirit—the name of another prophet had occurred for a reason; namely, because the Lord determined it should be written thus. As for why the Lord so determined it, that first very useful reason should be easily considered: that it was thus suggested that all the holy prophets spoke with one Spirit and stand in a marvelous agreement with each other... Since therefore the things said through Jeremiah belong as much to Jeremiah as to Zechariah, and the things said through Zechariah belong as much to Jeremiah as to Zechariah, what need was there for Matthew to correct it, when he had reread the name of one occurring to him for the other written by himself...?” Likewise **Jerome** <note>original: "Hier," short for Hieronymus</note> on this passage: “This testimony is not found in Jeremiah; but in Zechariah, who is almost the last of the twelve prophets, a certain similarity is reported, and although the sense does not differ much, yet both the order and the words are different. I recently read in a certain Hebrew volume, which a Hebrew man of the **Nazarene sect** <note>An early Jewish-Christian group that maintained Jewish law while accepting Jesus as Messiah</note> offered to me, an **apocryphon** <note>A non-canonical or "hidden" religious text</note> of Jeremiah, in which I found these things written word for word. But yet it seems to me that the testimony was rather taken from Zechariah in the common manner of the Evangelists and Apostles, who, having set aside the order of words, bring forth only the sense from the Old Testament as an example.” Again, in his *Short Treatise on Psalm 77* regarding the passage in Matthew 13:35, after the words “while he would correct an error, he would make an error” (see above, page 75), he continues thus: “Let us say something similar also in another place in the Gospel according to Matthew, when Judas returned the thirty pieces of silver... ‘As it is written,’ he says, ‘in Jeremiah the prophet.’ This is written in Matthew. We have searched in Jeremiah the prophet...”

<note>The following technical notes compare different ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts) of the New Testament to show where the wording varies.</note>

**29.** **Placed:** <note>original Greek: periethek.</note> The scholar Chrysostom and the Acts of Pilate use a word meaning "placed around"; manuscripts 1, 69, 124 and twelve others use a simpler word for "placed" <note>original: ethekan</note>. | **On the head:** <note>original: epi tēs kephalēs</note> The Sinai and Vatican manuscripts, along with others, use this phrasing... while some versions use a slightly different grammatical case for "the head" <note>original: tē kephalē</note>. | **In his right hand:** <note>original: en tē dexia</note> This reading is found in the Sinai, Alexandrian, Vatican, and Bezae manuscripts, as well as the Latin Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic versions... however, other ancient sources say **upon the right hand** <note>original: epi tēn dexian</note>. | **They mocked:** <note>original: enepaixan</note> This past tense is found in the Sinai, Vatican, and Regius manuscripts... while other versions use a form suggesting repeated action ("they were mocking"). | **The King:** <note>original: ho basileus</note> Most manuscripts use this form... but the scholar Lachmann follows the Vatican manuscript which uses the direct address **O King** <note>original: basileu</note>.

**31.** **Mocked him:** Most manuscripts say "him" in the dative case <note>autō</note>, while a few use the accusative case <note>auton</note>. | **Stripped him of the cloak and dressed him:** <note>original: ekdysantes... enedysan</note> The Sinai and Regius manuscripts use participles ("having stripped... they dressed")... whereas the scholar Tischendorf and others use two direct verbs ("they stripped and they dressed"), matching the phrasing in the Gospel of Mark. | **And led him away:** The original hand of Codex Bezae and the Coptic version omit the word "and."

**32.** **Found:** <note>original: euron</note> Most manuscripts use this spelling, though a few use a slightly different Greek spelling for the same word <note>ēuron</note>. | **Cyrenian:** <note>original: Kyrēnaion</note> Codex Bezae (D) adds the phrase **coming to meet him** <note>original: eis apantēsin autou</note>, a detail also found in many Old Latin manuscripts. | **Compelled:** <note>original: ēggareusan</note> There are several minor spelling variations of this verb (using 'n' or 'k' sounds) across different ancient copies.

**33.** **Coming:** <note>original: elthontes</note> A few manuscripts add **the soldiers** <note>original: hoi stratiōtai</note> as the ones who arrived. | **Place:** The Vatican manuscript specifies **the** place. | **Golgotha:** Ancient manuscripts show many ways of spelling this Aramaic name, including *Golgotha*, *Golgaltha*, or *Golgothan*. | **Which is:** <note>original: ho</note> Most major manuscripts (Sinai, Vatican, etc.) use the neuter "which," while some others use the masculine form <note>hos</note>. | **Called Place of a Skull:** <note>original: kranion topos legomenos</note> There are many variations in word order here; some manuscripts use the word for "translated" <note>original: methermēneuomenon</note> instead of "called."

### called, 34 <gloss>333. 4</gloss> they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; <margin>(Psalm 69:21)</margin> and after tasting it, he was not willing to drink. 35 <gloss>334. 1</gloss> And after they crucified him, they divided his clothes by casting lots, 36 and sitting down, they kept watch over him there. 37 <gloss>335. 1</gloss> And they placed above his head the charge against him, written: This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.

<note>The following technical notes compare different ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts) of the New Testament to show where the wording varies. Scholars use these codes—like ℵ (Sinaiticus) or B (Vaticanus)—to identify specific ancient books.</note>

34. **they gave:** <term>υ</term> and *edōkan* <note>original Greek: εδωκαν</note>. (Formerly "and coming," <note>original Latin: et venientes</note>). Compare the Old Latin versions (except manuscript f, which has "and coming - they gave") and the Vulgate: "and they came - and gave" | **to drink** <note>original Greek: piein</note> appears twice (Sinaiticus has *pin*) in the original hand of Sinaiticus and the Bezae manuscript ... the scholars Lachmann and Tischendorf read "to drink" <note>original: πιειν</note> with the corrected Sinaiticus, the Alexandrian, Vatican, and almost all other manuscripts <term>apparently</term> (also published in Origen, volume 1, page 703) ... the Latin, Coptic, and Armenian versions omit it in the first instance | **wine** <note>original: oinon</note> (Griesbach's second edition) with Sinaiticus, Vatican, Bezae, and several others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac versions, Armenian, Ethiopic, and various Church Fathers ... Origen notes: "According to Matthew, Jesus, receiving vinegar mixed with gall, tasted it and would not drink; but according to Mark, when wine mixed with myrrh was given to him, he did not receive it." In the Psalms it is written: "and they gave gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." Compare Mark 15:23 and John 19:29 | **he was willing** <note>original: ēthelēsen</note> with the original Sinaiticus, Vatican, Bezae, and others (the Latin and Vulgate read "he would not"). 35. **casting** <note>original: balontes</note> with Sinaiticus, Alexandrian, and about thirty others, and Eusebius ... (A note in some Syriac manuscripts says: "this passage from the prophet is not found in two [or three] Greek manuscripts nor in the old Syriac"). ... However, the Majority Text (supported by Griesbach and Scholz, though questioned by Schulz) adds the long phrase: **that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet: "They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots."** This is found in manuscript Delta and a few others, and some later Latin and Syriac versions. It is likely brought over from the text of John 19:24. Jerome notes that while these words were sometimes published in Matthew, he thinks they were not originally there because they appear in the Psalm he had just cited.

36. **there** <note>original: ekei</note>: omitted by manuscript 229, most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, and Eusebius.

<header>ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 27, 50. 203</header>

<margin>
50 — 54
Luke 23:44 — 49
Mark 15:37 — 39
</margin>

**50** <margin>343. 1</margin> **And Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, yielded up his** <note>The sentence concludes on the following page with "spirit" or "breath."</note>

---

<note>The following notes discuss a famous "interpolation"—a passage added by later scribes—where a soldier pierces Jesus's side while he is still alive, based on a similar event in John 19:34.</note>

...already by then the gospel writing of Matthew had been expanded by a tradition concerning the piercing of Jesus’s living body. The same sense can be understood from Barnabas 7 <note>The "Epistle of Barnabas," an early Christian writing</note>: <note>original: "ουχ ουτος εστιν ον ποτε ημεις εσταυρωσαμεν, εξουθενησαντες και κατακεντησαντες και εμπαιξαντες"</note> “Is this not he whom we once crucified, despising and piercing and mocking him?” But these things are indeed written too freely. Eusebius <note>in his *Canons*, a cross-reference system for the Gospels</note> (for he places John 19:31 through 37 in the tenth canon, which contains things unique to each Gospel; furthermore, in 10.8, he asserts that the prophetic saying <note>original: "ωσει υδωρ εξεχυθην"</note> “I was poured out like water” [Psalm 22:14] was fulfilled by those things which “John” recorded about the soldier piercing Jesus’s side). 

Hilary, Jerome, Augustine... Codices ℵ, B, C, L, U, Γ and several others <note>these are major ancient Greek manuscripts</note> add: **but another, taking a spear, pierced his side, and** (Codex U adds: **immediately**) **there came out water and blood** (Codex U reads: **blood and water**): compare John 19:34. 

The same is also witnessed by Chrysostom <note>an influential early Church Father</note> (for having quoted the text of the words freely, as he does so often elsewhere: <note>original: "ετερος δε προσελθων λογχη αυτου την πλευραν ενυξε"</note> “but another, approaching, pierced his side with a spear,” he adds: “What could be more lawless than these men, what more beastly? They who extended their madness to such a point as to insult even a dead—it appears he does not mean this in a literal sense—body? But you, look with me at how he used their lawless acts for our salvation. For after the blow, the springs of our salvation gushed out from there. And Jesus, crying with a loud voice, yielded up his spirit.”) 

Cyril according to Severus of Antioch (see below); a note in manuscript 72 <note>original: "οτι εις το καθ ιστοριαν ευαγγελιον διοδωρου και τατιανου και αλλων διαφορων αγιων πατερων τουτο προσκειται"</note> (“that this is added in the historical Gospel of Diodorus and Tatian and other various holy fathers—Chrysostom also says this. When Matthew, therefore, indicated that he was stabbed by the soldier with a spear in the side before his death, and thus died after being pierced, but John said he was pierced with the spear after he had finished, there is no conflict in what was said; for both reported the truth. For while Matthew, as one making his account very quickly in his writing, mentioned even the stabbing that occurred after death and mixed it into his writing, John reported the precise knowledge of this: that the body received the stabbing after death.” These words, starting from “When Matthew, therefore,” are also read in a note in manuscript 238 which is attributed to Severus; the earlier parts regarding the Gospels of Diodorus and Tatian have not been found elsewhere.) 

Several writers mentioned in Severus of Antioch (compare Assemani, *Bibliotheca Orientalis* II, 81, where it is read: “Petrus the Younger [died 591] brings forward from Letter 26 of Book 9, which Severus [died 539] wrote after his exile to Thomas, Bishop of Germanicia: ‘Regarding the fact that the side of our Lord and God Jesus Christ was struck by a soldier with a lance after he gave up his spirit, and from it blood and water miraculously flowed out, the divine evangelist John wrote, of which fact no one else makes mention. Some, however, openly doing violence to Matthew’s Gospel, thrust in there that which is against the evangelist’s mind, namely to show that Christ’s side was first struck by a soldier’s lance while he was still living, before he had given up his spirit. This matter was discussed with great zeal when my insignificance was in the royal city [Constantinople] on account of Macedonius, formerly archbishop of that same city. Therefore, the Gospel of Matthew was produced in the midst, which had been magnificently transcribed and was kept with the highest veneration in the royal chapel, and which they say was found in a city on the island of Cyprus along with Saint Barnabas during the reign of Zeno; and when it was opened, it was discovered...’”)
