> The addition of this story concerning the soldier and the spear does not appear in this manuscript at all. He adds that none of the ancient commentators mention this matter except for Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> and Cyril of Alexandria, into whose commentaries this addition crept. [(It is well known that Cyril’s commentary on Matthew has perished.)] Furthermore, the opinion—arising from that reading of the Gospel of Matthew—that Jesus’s side was opened with a spear while he was still alive was condemned by Pope Clement V at the Council of Vienne in the year 1311, teaching that John <note>referring to the Gospel of John 19:34, where the piercing happens after death</note> maintained the correct order of events.

**50. again** <note>original: "παλιν"</note> (also Origen, Eusebius, Cyril): [Manuscripts] F, L, and about 10 others omit this word (Origen notes that if he cried out "again," it proves he gave up his life voluntarily).

**51. the curtain of the temple**: compare Jerome on this passage: *“In the Gospel [of the Hebrews], which we have often mentioned, we read that the lintel <term>lintel: the horizontal beam above a door</term> of the temple, of immense size, was broken and divided. See also the letter to Damasus, where regarding the words of Isaiah 6:4 about the lintel being moved and the house filled with smoke, he adds: ‘Some claim the lintel was moved at that time when the temple curtain was torn.’ Again, in the letter to Hedibia, he says: ‘In the Gospel written in Hebrew letters, we read not that the curtain was torn, but that the lintel of the temple of wondrous size collapsed.’”* | **into two** <note>original: "εις δυο"</note> (Codex Bezae adds "parts," as do the Old Latin and Vulgate versions). This phrase appears after the word "bottom" in Codices Vaticanus and Ephraemi Rescriptus, and the Coptic and Ethiopic versions; however, the common text and most other manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, etc.) place it after "was torn" (similar to the Gospel of Mark). | **from above** <note>original: "ανωθεν"</note> (supported by Codex Sinaiticus and Origen); the common text and many others add "from" before it (as in Mark). | **until**: Codex Boreelianus reads "into the."

**52.** Codex Sinaiticus omits **and the tombs were opened.** | **tombs** <note>original: "μνημεια"</note> (supported by Origen, Eusebius, and Cyril): Codex Tischendorfianus reads "sepulchers." | **were opened**: supported by the vast majority of ancient manuscripts including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; a few others use a slightly different Greek spelling for "opened." | **were raised**: supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others; the common text uses a singular form, "was raised," found in Codex Alexandrinus and many later manuscripts.

**53. out of the tombs**: omitted in some Syriac, Arabic, and Persian versions. | **after his resurrection** (a few manuscripts read "after *their* resurrection"): omitted in some Syriac versions. | **they entered**: (supported by Origen; Codex Bezae and the Vulgate read "they came"): Codex Sinaiticus omits this word along with the following "and." | **appeared**: Codex Bezae uses "were shown" or "appeared."

<note>The following are historical debates about the identity of "Mary the mother of James":</note>
Compare here the commentary of **Chrysostom**: "Who were these women? His mother; for he calls her the mother of James, etc." 
**Hesychius of Jerusalem** <note>A 5th-century priest and exegete</note> in a collection of commentaries: "Since mention of many Marys is found in the Gospels, we ought to know that there are three in total—for we believe that Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the other Mary named by the Evangelists, is the Mother of God <note>The Virgin Mary</note> and no other." 
On the contrary, **Origen** states: "But among the most prominent was Mary the mother of James and Joseph, or, as Mark says, the mother of James the Less and Joseph." 
Likewise, **Eusebius**: "We find four Marys in total present at the Savior’s passion with the other women. First, the Mother of God, the mother of the Savior himself; second, her sister Mary..."

<header>28, 20. ACCORDING TO MATTHEW</header>

[...of the] Spirit, **20** teaching them to observe all things as many as I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all the days until the completion of the age.

---

20. **I am with you** <note>original: "μεθ υμ. ειμι" (meth hym. eimi)</note> along with manuscripts A, B, Γ, Δ, Π, nine other uncials <note>manuscripts written in large capital letters</note>, and almost all others seen; also the Old Latin, the Vulgate, Origen (in multiple citations), the Apostolic Constitutions, Eusebius, Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, Cyril, and others... manuscripts א <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, D, and Origen (in two citations) read **I am with you** <note>original: "ειμ. με. υμ." (eimi meth hym.) — a slight change in word order</note>. | **age** <note>original: "αιωνος" (aiōnos)</note> without addition, along with א, A*, B, D, and various minuscules <note>later manuscripts written in cursive</note>, the Old Latin, the Vulgate (in most editions), the Coptic, and Armenian versions, as well as Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, and Cyril. ... The majority of manuscripts (represented by the symbol ς) add **Amen** <note>original: "αμην"</note> along with manuscripts A (corrected), Γ, Δ, Π, and many others, including certain versions of the Vulgate and Syriac.

---

### Subscriptions <note>Scribal notes added at the end of the book</note>:
The manuscripts א, F, and M have no closing note at all (manuscripts C and L are missing this section). ... Manuscript B simply reads **According to Matthew** <note>original: "κατα μαθθαιον"</note>. ... Manuscripts Δ, E, H, K, U, V, and others read **The Gospel According to Matthew**. Manuscript *n* reads **The Gospel according to Matthew**, while various Latin manuscripts like *ff^1* and the Vulgate read **The Gospel according to Matthew is finished** <note>original: "explicit evangelium secundum mattheum"</note>. 

Manuscript D reads **The Gospel according to Matthew is finished; the Gospel according to John begins**. Many Latin manuscripts follow this same pattern, indicating that in their collection, John followed Matthew. For example, manuscript *gat* adds "likewise" and *mm* states **the Gospel of Jesus Christ now begins**. Other Latin manuscripts like *b, e, f,* and *q* note that Matthew is finished and **the Gospel according to John begins**. 

Later cursive manuscripts often add more elaborate titles such as **The end of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew**. Manuscript Γ adds a personal note: **The beloved Lord's Matthew the Evangelist was completed in the month of August.** 

Furthermore, several manuscripts (G, H, K, S, and others) add the number of **lines** <note>term: "stichoi" — a way of measuring the length of a scroll for payment or reference</note>: manuscripts H and K count 2,700 lines, while others count 2,600, 2,500, or 2,514. Some also count **words** <note>original: "ρηματα" (rhēmata)</note>, **chapters** <note>original: "κεφαλαια" (kephalaia)</note> (360), or **titles** <note>original: "τιτλους" (titlous)</note> (68). 

The "Ammonian Sections" <note>an early system of dividing the Gospels into numbered sections for comparison</note> are numbered up to 355. In the famous Codex Vaticanus (B), the Gospel of Matthew is divided into 170 chapters. 

Over time, these closing notes grew with historical traditions. For instance, manuscript K notes: **The Gospel according to Matthew was published by him in Jerusalem eight years after the Ascension of Christ.** Manuscript 126 adds that it was written **in the Hebrew language** (other manuscripts say **in the Hebrew dialect**). Some manuscripts even add who translated it into Greek: manuscript 5 and others claim it was **translated by John**, while manuscript 53 suggests **by James, the brother of the Lord**, and manuscript 293 suggests it was later translated **by Bartholomew**.

<summary>This page concludes the Gospel of Matthew with the promise of Christ's presence and provides an extensive scholarly comparison of how different ancient manuscripts ended the book, including various titles and historical traditions about Matthew's Hebrew origins.</summary>

[The Gospel] of the all-praiseworthy apostle was translated into the Greek language—as some say, by **John the Theologian** <note>John the Apostle, often called "the Theologian" in the Eastern tradition</note>, and these individuals have indeed spoken the truth. *Schaaf’s Syriac edition* <note>original: "Syrsch"</note>: **The holy Gospel of the preaching of Matthew is finished, which he preached in Hebrew in the region of Palestine.** Likewise, the *Syriac Peshitta* <note>original: "syrP"</note>: **The holy Gospel of Matthew the Evangelist is finished, which he spoke in Hebrew in Palestine.** The *Ethiopic version* <note>original: "AethP"</note>: **The Gospel of Matthew is finished. ## ACCORDING TO MARK

### CHAPTER 1

1 <note>1.2</note> The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, 2 as it is writ-

---

*According to Mark* <note>original: "κατ. μαρκ."</note> with Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Boreelianus... [scholarly editions of] Griesbach, Scholz, Lachmann, Tischendorf. *The Gospel according to Mark* with Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, Codex Seidelianus I, Codex Seidelianus II, Codex Cyprius, Codex Regius, Codex Campianus, Codex Nanianus, Codex Monacensis, Codex Tischendorfianus IV, Codex Sangallensis, Codex Petropolitanus, and many others (Codex Guelferbytanus A adds a supplement, but it is preceded by "The chapters of the Gospel according to Mark"; Minuscule 69: *From the Gospel according to Mark*; Minuscule 258: *Gospels* [but for Matthew "Gospel"] *according to Mark*). ... The [Textus Receptus] <note>The "Received Text," the standard printed Greek text of the 16th-19th centuries, denoted by the symbol ς</note> *The Gospel according to Mark* (The Textus Receptus adds "Holy" with many minuscules, but the Elzevir edition omits it with most minuscules).

1. **Jesus Christ** <note>original: "ι̅υ̅ χ̅υ̅" — abbreviated "Nomina Sacra" for Iesou Christou</note> without addition <note>referring to the omission of "Son of God" in some early sources</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Minuscule 28, Minuscule 255, and **Irenaeus** (page 191) ("Matthew indeed proclaims his human birth saying: *The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham*—but Mark made the beginning from the prophetic spirit coming upon men from on high, saying: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet*, showing the winged image of the gospel." The Latin translation of Irenaeus says: "He made the beginning: Beginning, saying, of the gospel just as it is written" etc.; the translator therefore omits the name "Jesus Christ" itself, agreeing with a note in Codices 237, 238, and 259, where the words of Irenaeus are repeated without mentioning his name: "Mark the Evangelist from the..." until "...showing." Similarly, **Epiphanius** (page 427) says: "The beginning of the gospel, as it is written in..." etc.) **Origen** (Volume 1, page 389) ("But also one of the evangelists, Mark, says: *The beginning of our gospel, Jesus Christ; as it is written in Isaiah the prophet*..." through "...before you.") (Volume 4, page 15, twice) ("For the same Mark says: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet, Behold...* until *his paths.*" A few words before, a little more freely: "As Mark says: *The beginning of the gospel of Christ Jesus.*") (Volume 4, page 125) ("In Mark it is recorded thus as the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ according to the writing of Isaiah: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet*... until *his paths.*") Likewise the Latin Origen (Volume 4, page 464) ("'Set apart,' he says, 'for the gospel of God.' In other places of scripture they say it is the gospel of Christ, just as Mark the Evangelist writes: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet.* But because Christ is the Word, and in the beginning was the Word and the Word was with God and the Word was God, it is one and the same thing to say 'the gospel of God' and 'the gospel of Christ,' or because the Lord himself speaks—therefore the gospel of the Father is also the gospel of the Son.") **Basil** in *Against Eunomius* (page 250) ("Matthew was the narrator of the birth according to the flesh, as he himself says: *The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David* [the codex adds 'son of Abraham']; but...")

...written in Isaiah the prophet: "Behold, I send my messenger"

---

**Mark made the beginning of the Gospel from the preaching of John**, saying: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness...'" whereas Luke [begins differently], etc. <note>original: "μαρκος αρχην του ευαγγ. το ιωαννου πεποιηκε κηρυγμα..." — Titus of Bostra, writing against the Manichaeans</note> (from Gallandi's collection, volume 329: "But if Mark says: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet,' and Matthew says: 'The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,' and while one..." etc.) **Serapion** <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Thmuis</note> against the Manichaeans (page 25): ("The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as written in Isaiah the prophet.") **Cyril of Jerusalem** (page 42): ("For John was the leader—the end of the prophets; for 'all the prophets and the law were until John.' But he was the first-fruits of the Gospel events; for he says, 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ,' and the rest: 'John was in the wilderness baptizing.'") (**Severian**, *The Six Seals*, page 566; see below). **Victorinus of Pettau** on the Apocalypse (from Gallandi, volume 55: "Mark the evangelist, thus beginning: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the wilderness,' has the likeness of a lion. However, it seems that the addition was inserted into this place somewhat inappropriately. It would certainly be foolish and contrary to the whole history of the sacred text to say that such a thing was removed by those of little faith rather than inserted by those with a misguided piety... **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** <note>Scholars who edited major Greek New Testaments in the 19th century</note> add **"Son of God"** <note>original: "υιου θεου"</note> with the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, and Codices Vaticanus, Bezae, and Regius. (**Severian**, *The Six Seals*, page 566: "Again the blessed Mark, immersing himself in the Gospel and being emboldened by those who were previously trained, speaks of the 'Son of God,' but immediately contracted the word and shortened the thought—saying: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold I send... before you.' He therefore clearly recognizes the addition 'Son of God,' but did not display it in the text itself, as it was certainly published.") Catena of Oxford, Catena of Possinus; likewise the **Textus Receptus** <note>The standard printed text of the era, denoted by the symbol ς</note> "Son of God" with Codices Alexandrinus, Boreelianus, Seidelianus, and many others. <note>This section is a "critical apparatus," a dense scholarly shorthand used to compare different ancient versions of the Bible to find the original wording. The letters like א, B, and D represent specific ancient manuscripts.</note>

**Titus of Bostra** (against the Manichaeans, page 250), **Serapion of Thmuis** (page 25), **Severian** (page 566)... [The reading "the prophets"] is supported by **Lachmann** <note>A 19th-century biblical critic</note> as it appears in **Codex Alexandrinus (A)**, **Codex Ephraemi (C)**, **Codex Bezae (D)**, **Codex Regius (L)**, and many others, including the Greek version of **Irenaeus** and **Origen**. | [The reading "in Isaiah the prophet"] is supported by <term>Codex Sinaiticus (א)</term> <note>One of the oldest and most complete Bibles, found in a monastery in the 1800s</note>, <term>Codex Vaticanus (B)</term>, **Codex Bezae (D)**, and the **Vulgate** <note>The standard Latin Bible</note>. (In some cases, like Codex 1, the text is a "conflation" or a mix of both readings: "in the prophets, in Isaiah the prophet"). This reading is also found in the Syriac and Coptic versions. 

**Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar from Alexandria</note> notes (4,126): <note>original: "οτι ο μαρκ. δυο προφητειας..."</note> "Because Mark brought together two prophecies spoken in different places by two prophets into one, he wrote: 'as it is written in...'" **Porphyry** <note>A philosopher who criticized Christianity</note> is cited by **Jerome** in his commentary on Matthew 3:3: "We, however, think the name of Isaiah was added by a scribe's error, which we can prove in other places, or certainly one body was formed from different testimonies of the scriptures." (See also Jerome's commentary on Malachi 3:1, noting the evangelist joined two testimonies under one prophet's name).

**Eusebius of Caesarea** <note>The "Father of Church History"</note> (quoted in the scholia of various manuscripts): <note>original: "τουτο προφητικον μαλαχιου εστιν..."</note> "This is a prophecy of Malachi, not Isaiah. It is therefore a scribe's error, as Eusebius says in his work *To Marinus* concerning the apparent dissonance in the Gospels." Other witnesses include **Augustine**, who notes in *The Harmony of the Gospels* (2,25): "Mark and Luke also agree that this testimony of Isaiah is about John."

The reading "in the prophets" is found in **Codex Alexandrinus (A)** and many later manuscripts, as well as the Syriac and Armenian versions. **Theophylact** <note>An 11th-century commentator</note> and some versions of **Irenaeus** also support this, likely to correct the historical "error" of attributing a Malachi quote to Isaiah.

Regarding the word **"I"** (Greek: *egō*): **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** omit it, following <term>Codex Vaticanus (B)</term> and <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term>, along with several old Latin and Syriac versions. However, it is present in <term>Codex Sinaiticus (א)</term>, **Codex Alexandrinus (A)**, and almost all other manuscripts. **Jerome** includes it in his letters and commentaries. **Origen** (2,403) notes: "Those scouts who are sent [into Jericho] before the face of Jesus can also be thought of as the angels of God..."

("as it is written: Behold, I send" etc.) **Jerome** <note>A 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> once (on Matthew 3:3) and others (though **Tertullian** in *Against the Jews*, chapter 9, attributes this rather to Malachi) :: the reading of the liturgical books fluctuates; the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> according to Codex Alexandrinus (A) and most others have the word "I" added, but it is not found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus (א)</term> or <term>Codex Vaticanus (B)</term>. | "I send" [present tense]: Codex Sinaiticus and a few others (see **Origen** 3,769) read "I will send" [future tense]. | The phrase "your way" appears without any addition in א, B, D, K, L, P, Π and many Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions. **Origen** (4,15 and 126) notes: <note>original: "την δ ομοιαν επιτομην πεποιηται..."</note> "Mark made a similar summary... for he did not include the phrase 'before you'." 3. **"In the wilderness: prepare..."** etc: It has long been observed that the Gospel writers followed the punctuation of the Septuagint in this manner (which Origen and others also recognize). It is different in the original Hebrew of the prophet Isaiah, where "in the wilderness" and "in the desert" (according to the interpretation of **Symmachus**) correspond to each other before the command to "make straight." (**Tregelles** <note>A 19th-century textual critic</note> published his version according to the Hebrew standard.) | **"His"** [paths] is found in א, A, B, L, P, Γ, Δ, Π and almost all others, including the Vulgate and Coptic. **Origen** (4,126) notes: <note>original: "ο μεν γαρ προφητης φησιν..."</note> "For the prophet says, 'Prepare... the paths of our God,' but Mark says, 'Prepare... his paths'." **Jerome** also notes that while the Septuagint translated "of our God," Mark and Luke said "his." | Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions read "of our God." Furthermore, the Latin manuscript **c** <note>Codex Colbertinus</note> has these additions (taken from Luke 3:5–6 and Isaiah 40:4–5):

"Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and all crooked things shall be made straight, and the rough ways into a plain: and the glory of the Lord shall be seen, and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God, for the Lord has spoken. The voice of one saying: Cry out. And he said: What shall I cry? <note>The following technical notes compare different ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts) of the New Testament. Scholars use these to determine the most likely original wording.</note>

5. **went out** <note>original: "εξεπορευετο" - singular verb</note> is found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus (א)</term>, **Codex Alexandrinus (A)**, **Codex Vaticanus (B)**, **Codex Bezae (D)**, and others, as well as several Latin versions (where it is translated as *veniebat*, "he was coming"). **Griesbach** <note>An 18th-century biblical critic</note> also notes this. | **they went out** <note>original: "εξεπορευοντο" - plural verb</note> is found in E, F, H, L, and over 50 other manuscripts, as well as Gothic and Coptic versions. | <term>the</term> <note>original: "η̈"</note>: Omitted by **Sinaiticus**, M, and a few others. | **the** [before "inhabitants"]: Omitted by **Bezae** and some Syriac margins. | **Jerusalemites** [spelling variant]: Found in א, A, B, D; other versions like **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** use the spelling *Hierosolymitai*. | **all** [at this position]: Found in א, B, D, L, and most early versions (Latin, Coptic, Armenian, etc.), as well as in the writings of **Origen** and **Eusebius**. In the <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>original: "ς" — the "Received Text" used for the King James Version</note>, "all" is placed after "baptized" following manuscripts like P, Γ, and Π. | **and were baptized**: א and some others omit "and." | **by him in the Jordan River**: Found in א, B, L, and most Latin/Vulgate versions. The **Textus Receptus** and **Lachmann** place "by him" after "river," following A, D, and others. | **the river**: Omitted by D and several Old Latin versions.

6. **And John was** <note>original: "και ην"</note>: Found in א, B, L, and the Vulgate. The **Textus Receptus** reads "Now John was" <note>original: "ην δε"</note>, following A, D, and others, likely harmonizing with the Gospel of Matthew. | **John** <note>spelled with one 'n' or two</note>: א, B, L, and P include the article "the." **Lachmann** and the **Textus Receptus** omit the article "the," following A and D. | **hair**: **Codex Bezae (D)** reads "skin" <note>original: "δερρην"</note>; one Latin version reads "pelt" <note>original: "pellem"</note>. | **camel**: Some manuscripts (G) use a spelling variant <note>original: "καμιλου"</note> which can sometimes mean "rope." | **and a leather belt around his waist**: This entire phrase is omitted by **Bezae** and some Old Latin versions. | **ate** <note>original: "εσθων"</note>: Found in א, B, and L. The **Textus Receptus** and **Lachmann** use a different form of the verb "eating" <note>original: "εσθιων"</note> found in almost all other manuscripts. | One ancient Latin version places the entirety of verse 6 after verse 8.

The manuscripts a, b, c, ff$^2$, g$^1$, and the Munich fragment (but not f, ff$^1$, g$^2$, or the Vulgate) and Ambrose omit the section regarding the sandals. ...and the Spirit like a dove descending into him. <margin>2 Peter 1:17</margin> 11 And a voice came from the heavens: "You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased."

<margin>12 and following; Matthew 4:1 and following; Luke 4:1 and following</margin> 12 And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness. 13 And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan, and he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him.

<note>The following notes represent the "apparatus criticus," a record of variations found in ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. Scholars use these to determine the most likely original wording.</note>

**10.** The variations for "opened" or "to be opened" come from the accounts in Matthew and Luke | The word **as** <note>original: "ωσ"</note> is found in manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Parisinus, and most others (including the Syriac)... whereas the Received Text (edited by Stephanus and Sz) uses **as if** <note>original: "ωσει"</note> with manuscript M and many others. | The word **descending** <note>original: "καταβαῖνον"</note> is found in the major uncials (Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.) and most versions... but manuscript Sinaiticus and several others add the phrase **and remaining** <note>original: "και μενον"</note> (this is missing in Mark and Luke and likely originated from the Gospel of John). | The phrase **into him** <note>original: "εισ αυτον"</note> is found in Vaticanus, Bezae, and some Old Latin manuscripts... the Received Text uses **upon him** <note>original: "επ αυτον"</note> (matching the wording in Matthew, Luke, and John) found in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and many others; some Latin versions use "upon him" or "in him."

**11.** The word **voice** <note>original: "φωνη"</note> appears alone in the original hand of Sinaiticus and Bezae... but the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **there was** <note>original: "εγενετο"</note> following Sinaiticus (corrected hand), Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and almost all others including the Vulgate and Syriac; manuscript 28 and others suggest the voice **was heard**. | The phrase **in you** <note>original: "εν σοι"</note> is supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the majority of ancient versions... the Received Text uses **in whom** <note>original: "εν ω"</note> following Alexandrinus and many others; this matches Matthew’s phrasing, whereas Luke uses **in you**. This variation is also noted in the Gospel of the Ebionites. | The word **I am well pleased** <note>original: "ευδοκησα"</note> is found in the earliest manuscripts, though a later hand in manuscript Bezae and several others uses a slightly different spelling of the same verb.

**12.** The word **immediately** <note>original: "ευθυς"</note> is found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most manuscripts... Lachmann uses a longer form of the same word <note>original: "ευθεωσ"</note> found in Alexandrinus and Bezae. | The Spirit: Manuscript Bezae adds **Holy** <note>original: "το αγιον"</note>. | The phrasing **drives him out** <note>original: "αυτον εκβαλλει"</note> is the standard order in Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus... though Bezae and a few others reverse the word order.

**13.** The phrase **in the wilderness** appears without the word **there** <note>original: "εκει"</note> in the primary manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, etc.)... the Received Text includes **there in the wilderness** (defended by the scholar Schulz) based on many later manuscripts. | The spelling of **forty** <note>original: "τεσσερακ."</note> varies slightly between manuscripts. <note>The following scholarly notes compare different ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. These notations help scholars determine the most accurate original wording by looking at variations across centuries of transcriptions.</note>

**17. become**: This word <note>original: "γενεσθαι"</note> is omitted by manuscripts 1, 13, 28, 69, 118, 209, and ten others, as well as the Old Latin (b), the Peshitta Syriac, Ethiopic, and Persian versions; this omission makes the text match the parallel verse in Matthew. | **fishers**: There is a spelling variation between the editors <note>Lachmann and Tischendorf</note> regarding the Greek word for "fishers" <note>original: "αλιεισ"</note>; see the note at verse 16.

**18. immediately**: The shorter form <note>original: "ευθυσ"</note> is found in manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), L, and 33. The Received Text (ς), Lachmann, and Tischendorf use the longer form <note>original: "ευθεωσ"</note> found in Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Bezae (D), and twelve other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>. | **the nets**: The phrase "their nets" is found in the Received Text and Tischendorf based on many manuscripts, while the simpler "the nets" is supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Vulgate. Manuscript Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions read "all things" <note>original: "παντα"</note> instead. | **followed**: Manuscript Vaticanus (B) uses a tense that implies they "began following" or "kept following" <note>original: "ηκολουθουν"</note>, while others use the standard "followed."

**19. going on**: Manuscript Bezae (D) uses a slightly different verb for "going forward." The word "from there" <note>original: "εκειθεν"</note> is omitted by Vaticanus, Bezae, and several early versions, though the Received Text and Lachmann include it; Sinaiticus omits the word "little" but includes "from there," similar to the Gospel of Matthew. | **saw**: Variations in spelling for "saw" <note>original: "ειδεν" vs "ιδεν"</note> exist across major manuscripts. | **Zebedee**: Manuscript Gamma (Γ) and others use a double 'd' in the name <note>original: "ζεβεδδαιου"</note>. | **the nets**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others read "the nets," while later manuscripts and the Syriac version add "**their** nets" to match Matthew.

**20. immediately**: Again, manuscripts Sinaiticus and Vaticanus use one form of "immediately" <note>original: "ευθυσ"</note>, while the Received Text and others use another <note>original: "ευθεωσ"</note>. Manuscript Delta (Δ) and others place the word earlier in the sentence. | **went away after him**: Manuscript Bezae (D), the Old Latin, and the Vulgate read "followed him."

**21. they enter**: Several manuscripts (1, 6, 22, etc.) and Origen <note>An early Christian scholar, c. 184–253 AD</note> use the singular "he enters" <note>original: "εισπορευεται"</note>. Other versions use the past tense "they entered." | **Capernaum**: Spelled "Capharnaum" <note>original: "καφαρναουμ"</note> in the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae); the Received Text spells it "Capernaum" <note>original: "καπερναουμ"</note>. | **on the Sabbath**: Most manuscripts read "on the Sabbath," but a few (C, G, 433) read "**in** the Sabbath." | **he was teaching**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus and L place this verb after "Sabbath," while the Received Text and Lachmann place it after "synagogue." Some versions (Bezae, Vulgate, Syriac) add that he was teaching "**them**" or "**the people**." | **the synagogue**: Several manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, etc.) do not include the word "entering" <note>original: "εισελθων"</note>, simply saying "he taught into the synagogue." The Received Text and Lachmann include "entering."

# 224 ACCORDING TO MARK 1, 26.

"Come out of him!" **26** And the unclean spirit, having convulsed him and cried out with a loud voice, came out of him. **27** And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying: "What is this? A new teaching with authority! He even commands the unclean spirits, and they obey him." **28** And his fame spread immediately everywhere into the whole surrounding region of Galilee.

---

<note>The following notes represent the "critical apparatus," a record of variations found in the oldest surviving hand-written copies of the Bible. Scholars use these symbols (like B for Codex Vaticanus or א for Codex Sinaiticus) to determine the most likely original wording.</note>

**out of him**: <note>original: "εξ αυτου"</note> (Manuscript D and several others read "out of the man" <note>original: "εκ του ανθρωπου"</note>; see also notes on manuscripts "ab" and "de"): Codex Damascus, Manuscripts 33, 433, and nearly 15 others. A parallel reading in the Damascus text reads "from him" <note>original: "απ' αυτου"</note>, likewise in Old Latin versions "a" and "b" (which read "from the man" <note>original: "ab homine"</note>) and "c," "f," and "g¹." (Other Latin versions "b," "d," "e," "ff²," and "q" read "from the man" <note>original: "de homine"</note>). This is as in Luke <note>to whom Origen also refers, volume 2, page 333</note>. Furthermore, manuscripts d, 8pe, and several Old Latin and Ethiopic versions add **unclean spirit** <note>original: "πνευμα ακαθαρτον"</note>; compare with Mark 5:8.

**26. and having convulsed etc**: <note>original: "και σπαραξαν"</note> Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions read: "and the unclean spirit went out and having convulsed him and having cried with a loud voice, he went out from him." | **the unclean spirit**: Codex B (Vaticanus) and Manuscript 102 omit the word **spirit**. | **cried out**: <note>original: "φωνησαν"</note> Supported by Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), L, 33, and Origen. Other editions like those of Lachmann read "crying out" <note>original: "κραξαν"</note> (as in Mark 9:26) following Manuscripts A, C, D, and the majority of others. | **out of**: <note>original: "εξ"</note> Supported by the majority of uncials. Griesbach and Lachmann read "from" <note>original: "απ"</note> following Manuscripts C, D, and others.

**27. they were amazed**: <note>original: "εθαμβηθησαν"</note> Manuscript D and Origen read a slightly different form of the word for "amazed" <note>original: "εθαμβησαν"</note>. | **all**: <note>original: "απαντεσ"</note> Supported by Sinaiticus (א) and Vaticanus (B); others read "everybody" <note>original: "παντεσ"</note>. | **questioned**: <note>original: "συζητεῖν"</note> Supported by the oldest manuscripts. | **themselves**: <note>original: "αυτουσ"</note> Supported by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and some Latin versions (which use the phrase "they were inquiring"). Other editions follow the majority of manuscripts which read "among themselves" <note>original: "προσ εαυτουσ"</note> or "with one another" (as in the parallel passage in Luke). | **saying**: <note>original: "λεγοντασ"</note> Manuscripts א, B, D, and others use this form; a few others use "they were saying" <note>original: "λεγοντεσ"</note>. | **what is this**: <note>original: "τι εστιν τουτο"</note> Omitted by Manuscript D and several Old Latin versions. | **a new teaching with authority**: <note>original: "διδαχη καινη κατ εξουσιαν"</note> This is a point of much debate regarding punctuation. Some versions read it as a question: "What is this new doctrine with authority?" or "What is this? A new teaching! With authority he commands..." Lachmann punctuates it as "new; with authority." The oldest manuscripts (א, B, L) support the reading "a new teaching with authority," while later manuscripts and versions (like the Syriac and Vulgate) add the word "this" <note>original: "αυτη"</note> to make it "What is this new teaching?" or "What is this new teaching of his?"

**28. and spread**: <note>original: "και εξηλθ."</note> Supported by the oldest manuscripts (א, B, C, D, L); others read "but there went out" <note>original: "εξηλθ. δε"</note>. | **immediately**: <note>original: "ευθυσ"</note> Omitted by some early versions and manuscripts like 1, 28, and 33. | **everywhere**: <note>original: "πανταχου"</note> Supported by the major early manuscripts.

**7.** *why*: manuscript B reads *that*. | *thus*: with א, B, D, E, G, H, L, M, U, Γ, Δ, Π and many others ... the Textus Receptus (ς) uses a slightly different spelling of *thus* with A, C, K, N and many others ... about 20 others and the Syriac and Persian omit it. | *speaks; he blasphemes* with א, B, D, L and Old Latin 'a', 'f', 'ff<sup>1.2</sup>', 'g<sup>1.2</sup>' and the Vulgate ('c' reads *speaks blaspheming*; 'b' and 'q' read *nothing but blasphemy here* or *why does this one blaspheme*) ... the Textus Receptus (ς) reads *speaks blasphemies* with A, C, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials and nearly all others (though a few read *blasphemy* in the singular); Old Latin 'e' reads *speaks blasphemy*; Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Gothic also use *blasphemies*, just as in the Gospel of Luke where the reading does not vary. | Codex Bezae (D) reads *the sins*. | *one* (Old Latin 'a' reads *one*, other Old Latin and Vulgate read *alone*): the Greek text of Codex Bezae (D) omits it.

**8.** *immediately* <note>original: "euthus"</note> with א, B, L, 33 ... the Textus Receptus (ς) uses a longer form of *immediately* <note>original: "eutheos"</note> with A, C, Γ, Δ, Θ<sup>f</sup>, Π and most others ... Codex Bezae (D) and several others including Old Latin 'a', 'b', 'c' and the Armenian omit it, as do Matthew and Luke in their versions. | *Jesus*: Codex Sinaiticus (א) and others omit this. | *his* [spirit] (also in 'f', 'g<sup>1</sup>', the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and others; 'g<sup>2</sup>' reads *holy* instead of *his*): Codex Bezae (D) and many Old Latin versions ('a', 'b', 'c', 'e', 'q') and one Coptic version omit it. | *that they were thus* with א, A, C, D, L, Γ, Δ, Θ<sup>f</sup>, Π and nearly all others, including 'f', 'g<sup>2</sup>', Vulgate, Coptic, and one Syriac (the other Syriac reads *why*) ... Lachmann (Ln) omits *thus* with B and 102, as do Old Latin 'a' and 'g<sup>1</sup>'. | *reasoning* <note>original: "dialogizontai"</note> with א, B, D, G, L, 1, and the Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions ... # ACCORDING TO MARK 2, 17.

the scribes of the Pharisees. ---

The Coptic editions <note>Sahidic and Bohairic versions</note> read: "the scribes and the Pharisees." And seeing (the Latin manuscript *b* reads: "and they saw," but poorly omits "they were saying") — this reading is found in manuscripts Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Regius (L), Codex Sangallensis (Δ), and minuscules 33 and the Coptic. It also seems to be in the Washington Manuscript (W), but the writing between "and" <note>Greek: kai</note> and "of the Pharisees" <note>Greek: tōn Pharisaiōn</note> has perished. ... The editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read: "and the scribes and the Pharisees" (manuscript 3pe adds the article "the"; manuscript 124 uses "of the Pharisees" instead of "and the Pharisees"). "Seeing" (Lachmann brackets "and") is found in Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Ephraemi (C), Codex Cyprius (Γ), Codex Petropolitanus (Π), nine other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and most others, including many Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, the Syriac, Armenian, and Gothic. Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note> (following the phrase "and they followed him") reads: "and the scribes and the Pharisees, and they saw" (followed by "and they said"). This confirms the grouping of the subjects which we have edited from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.

| "that he was eating" <note>Greek: hoti ēsthien</note> | with Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, Codex Regius, and the Latin manuscripts *c, ff¹, g¹*, the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic. |

"Tax collectors and sinners" with Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, the corrected Codex Regius, and almost all others. ... Lachmann and Tischendorf read "sinners and tax collectors" (Codex Vaticanus, Bezae, and 33 add the article "the") with manuscripts B, D, L, 33, 2pe, and several Old Latin and Coptic versions. (Note: Mark seems to have written the same thing in both places here). ... Manuscripts 28, 69, and others omit "and sinners." | "Why" <note>Greek: hoti</note> with Codex Vaticanus, Regius, and others. ... The Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf also use "Why" <note>Greek: hoti</note> with Codex Alexandrinus and others. (The scholar Scholz notes: "Mark did not say 'ti hoti' <note>Why is it that</note>, but Luke often did"). ... Codex Sinaiticus and Bezae use "For what reason" <note>Greek: dia ti</note>. "Tax collectors and sinners" (Codex Vaticanus adds "the") with almost all manuscripts and versions. ... Lachmann and Tischendorf read "sinners and the tax collectors" (Tischendorf omits "the") with Codex Bezae, Latin *a*, and Ethiopic. Augustine in his *Harmony of the Gospels* (2,61), citing the text of both Matthew and Mark, adds: "Therefore, what this one [Mark] added, 'and drinks,' was omitted by Matthew." ... Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others omit "and drinks" (similar to Matthew); hence Lachmann puts it in brackets. Additionally, many manuscripts and the Coptic and Ethiopic versions add "your teacher" <note>Greek: ho didaskalos hymōn</note> — likely brought in from the Gospel of Matthew.

# ACCORDING TO MARK 2, 22.

[...no one] sews a patch of unshrunk cloth <note>original: "agnaphou" — cloth that has not yet been processed or shrunk by a fuller</note> on an old garment; otherwise, the new patch pulls away from the old, and a worse tear results. 
22 And no one puts new wine into old wineskins <note>original: "askous" — leather bags used for fermentation</note>; otherwise, the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins.

---

[The following section is the "critical apparatus," a scholar’s map of how different ancient manuscripts of the Bible vary in their wording.]

**[patch]** <note>original: "rakkous"</note> with manuscripts ADFGHMΓΠ and many others | **unshrunk** <note>original: "agnaphou"</note> (a few others read: *aknaph.*): manuscripts EFGLA and a few others -*phous* | **sews upon** <note>original: "epiraptei"</note> with manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, B*, C, E, F, G, H, L, V, Π and many others ... Lachmann <note>a 19th-century biblical editor</note> reads *epirraptei* with B², K, M, U, Γ and the vast majority ... Codex Bezae (D) reads **sews together upon** <note>original: "epissynraptei"</note> | **on an old garment** with ℵ, B, C, D, L, 33 ... the Textus Receptus <note>the standard printed text of the era</note> reads **to an old garment** <note>using a different grammatical case</note> as in Matthew, with A, Γ, Δ, Π and almost all others | **not**: manuscripts κ, Δ, Π*, 28, 33 and about 20 others read **not indeed** <note>original: "mēge"</note> :: as in Luke | **takes away**: or **shall take away** | **the patch from it** (Vaticanus [B] reads: **from itself**) with ℵ, B, L and a few others, also Latin manuscript *l* (**it takes away from it the quantity of the new patch**), the Syriac Peshitta (?) ... Manuscripts D, 13, 28, 69, 124 and various old Latin versions and the Vulgate (Syriac according to White: **otherwise it takes away the new supplement from the old**) (Coptic: **the new patch takes away the supplement of the old**) nothing but **the patch** but they continue (likewise the Syriac and Armenian, following **its patch**) **the new from the old** ... the Textus Receptus reads **its patch** (Griesbach suggests **its** was a conjecture based on Codex D) with many others :: as in Matthew | **new**: or **common** <note>The Greek words "kainon" (new) and "koinon" (common) sounded similar and were often confused by scribes</note> | **and a worse tear results**: Manuscript L omits this.

**22.** **old**: Latin manuscripts a, b, c add **but into new [skins]** | **not**: manuscripts C, L, M² and a few others read **not indeed** :: as in Matthew and Luke | **will burst** <note>original: "rhēxei"</note> with ℵ, B, C, D, L, 33 and others, including Latin manuscripts b, ff, g, i, q (which restores "it breaks" from "it will break") and the Vulgate (Codex Vercellensis [a] reads: **the skins will be burst by the wine**) ... the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read **bursts** <note>present tense</note> with A, Γ, Δ, Π and almost all others, including the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions :: the reading **will burst** may seem brought in from Luke; yet even in Luke the reading fluctuates between **will burst** and **bursts**, and in our current passage **bursts** should seem more fitting because of what follows. It should be added that the same manuscripts ℵ, B, C, D, L correctly preserve **the wine** without adding **the new**, which was taken from Luke. Hence, the reading **will burst** found in the most ancient witnesses is often unfairly dismissed by editors because of the parallel passage in Matthew. | **the wine** with ℵ, B, C*, D, L and many others, including the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian ... the Textus Receptus adds **the new [wine]** with A, C², Γ, Δ, Π and the majority, including the Gothic version :: from Luke | **is lost** (L reads: **is poured out**) **and the skins** with B, L, 102 and Coptic (**and the wine is lost with the skins**); similarly Codex Bezae (D) and old Latin manuscripts **and the skins will be lost** ... the Textus Receptus and Lachmann read **is poured out and the skins are lost** with ℵ, A, C, Γ, Δ, Π and the majority, including the Vulgate and Syriac | **and the skins** without further addition with D and several old Latin manuscripts ... ℵ* and B add nothing except **but new wine into new skins** (in this way the addition from Luke began to be written here); likewise the Textus Receptus and Lachmann read **but new wine must be put into new skins** (certain versions omit "must be put," i.e., "they put" as in Matthew) with ℵ, A, C, L and almost all others. Furthermore, several other manuscripts and the Saxon version add even more.

# 3, 27. ACCORDING TO MARK

...is divided, and he cannot stand, but has an end. **27** But no one can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his house. **28** <gloss>34.2</gloss> Truly I say to you, that all sins will be forgiven the sons of men, and whatever blasphemies they may utter; **29** but whoever blasphemes against

---

**is divided** | **has been divided and not**: read with manuscripts ℵ*, C*, Δ and others, and the Latin versions <note>original: "hi Latini dispertitus est et non"</note>; also read as **is divided against himself and not** <note>original: "divisus est super se et non"</note> in some Latin copies, and **is divided against his kingdom and not** <note>original: "dividitur super regnum eius et non"</note> in others. Similarly, certain versions do not connect the words **is divided** or **has been divided** to what came before, although they do not add the word **and** after the verb for dividing. Manuscript D reads **has been divided against himself—not**; other Latin versions read **is divided against his kingdom, not**. The editors Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **and has been divided, not** with manuscripts A, C, Γ, Π, and nine other uncials <note>large-lettered parchment manuscripts</note> and almost all others, including the Syriac, Coptic, and Gothic versions. Manuscripts ℵ, B, and L read **and was divided**, but ℵ adds or retains **and** here. (It seems these readings were adapted to match the phrasing in verses 24 and 25; our reading is less likely to have been copied from Matthew 12:26.) | **to stand**: with ℵ, B, C, L... while Stephanus and Lachmann read a different form of **to stand** <note>original: "stathēnai" instead of "stēnai"</note> with A, D, Γ, Π, and almost all others. Additionally, manuscript D and several Latin versions add **his kingdom**. | **an end**: manuscript D reads **the end**.

**27. but**: with ℵ, B, C, L, Δ and many numbered manuscripts, the Coptic, Armenian, and part of the Syriac versions. Other versions read **but no one** or **and**. Stephanus and Lachmann omit the word with A, D, and many others. | **no one can**: with ℵ, B, C, Δ, and a few others (the Coptic reads **there is no power for anyone**)... other editors read **no one is able** with A, D, L, and over 120 other manuscripts. | **entering the house of the strong man, to plunder his goods**: with ℵ, B, C, L, Δ, 33, 102, and the Coptic and Syriac versions (the latter two read **to enter into the house of the strong man and**). Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **to plunder the goods of the strong man, entering into his house** with A, Γ, Π, and most others. (Manuscript D and others omit **his**, while some reorder the sequence of entering and plundering). | **he will plunder**: with ℵ, B, C, H, L, M, S, Δ and many others... while some editors use a slightly different future tense spelling <note>original: "diarpasē" vs "diarpasei"</note> found in A, E, F, G, and about 100 others.

**28. to the sons of men the sins**: (Manuscript Δ and others simply say **to men**) with ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, Δ, and about 10 others, along with the Vulgate and Coptic. Stephanus reads **the sins to the sons of men** with E, G, H, K, and most others, including the Syriac and Gothic. (One Latin version reads **every sin is forgiven the sons of men**; others vary the order of **sins** and **blasphemies**.) | **and the**: with ℵ, A, B, C, E, F, G, H, L, Δ and about 25 others... Stephanus omits **the** with D, K, M, S, and the vast majority. | **whatever**: with ℵ, B, D, E, G, H, and about 10 others... Stephanus reads a slightly different form of **whatever** with A, C, F, K, L, and most others. | **may**: with ℵ, A, D, E, G, H, K, and most others... Tischendorf uses an alternative Greek word for **may** with B, C, F, L, Δ, and a few others. | **they may utter**: omitted in several Latin versions and the writings of Cyprian and Ambrosiaster.

**29. but whoever**: (Latin versions read **he however who**): Manuscript D reads **but if anyone**. | **blasphemes**: a few manuscripts use a future tense **will blaspheme**. | **against**: (first occurrence): found in most Greek and Latin versions.

**they were saying** (ελεγον): <note>Refers to verse 22 or 30 from the previous section</note> Found in manuscripts 22, 124, 238, 299, 433, and about 100 others, as well as several Old Latin versions (a, b, c, f, ff², l, q), the Syriac Peshitta, the Gothic, and the Old Church Slavonic. | The common text (ς) <note>original: "Textus Receptus"</note> omits this, along with the great fourth-century codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Ephraemi (C), as well as others (G, K, Δ, Π). **33. and answering them, he says** (και αποκριθεις αυτοις λεγει): Found in ℵ, B, C, L, and Δ, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac Peshitta. The Old Latin versions (c, g¹, ff², q) read "who responding said to them," while version 'e' reads "but he responding said to them." | The editors Griesbach and Lachmann, following the common text (ς), read **and he answered them saying** (και απεκριθη αυτοις λεγων) with manuscripts A, D, Γ, Π, and most others. | **and my** (και οι): Found in ℵ, B, C, G, L, U, V, and Δ, as well as most Old Latin versions and the Coptic. **34. Verse omitted:** This entire verse is omitted in manuscripts 235, 271, and 14 others due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>a scribe's error where the eye skips from one line to another because they end with the same word, in this case "my brothers"</note>. | **and** (και): Found in almost all manuscripts. | **in a circle** (κυκλω): This word is placed here in ℵ, B, C, L, and Δ. Griesbach and Lachmann read a different form of "Behold" (ιδου, as in Matthew) with manuscripts A, D, G, K, and others.

**35. Whoever** (ος αν): Found in B, several Old Latin versions, and the Coptic. # ACCORDING TO MARK 4, 4. 247

a very large crowd gathered to him, so that he got into a boat and sat out on the sea; and the whole crowd was by the sea on the land. **2** And he taught them many things in parables, and said to them in his teaching: "**3** Listen! Behold, the sower went out to sow. **4** And it happened that as he sowed, some fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up <note>The Greek text on this page ends mid-sentence at 'ate up'; the apparatus discusses the object 'it' which follows on the next page.</note>

---

**[gathered]** (ται <note>original: "συνάγεται" - is gathered</note>): Found in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), Regius (L), and Dublinensis (Δ), along with minuscules 13, 28, 69, and 124. (Manuscripts 1, 209 read "come together" <note>original: "συνέρχεται"</note>). | The common text (ς) reads **was gathered** (συνήχθη) with Codex Bezae (D), Codex Petropolitanus (Π), nine other uncials, and the majority of others; the Latin versions likewise read "was gathered" (it, vg), as does the Syriac Peshitta and Origen (Latin translation). | Manuscript A and about ten others read **they were gathered** (συνήχθησαν), as do the Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Gothic versions (though these latter versions follow with "the crowds" in the plural). Compare with Matthew's account. | **crowd** (ὄχλος): Codex Bezae (Latin side) reads "the people" (d: *o laos*). | **very great** (πλεῖστος): Found in ℵ, B, C, L, and A. | The common text (ς) and editors Lachmann (Ln) and Tischendorf (Ti) read **great** or **many** (πολύς) with Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Bezae (D), Π, and almost all other uncials (the Latin and Vulgate read "a large or great crowd"). | **boat** (πλοῖον): Found in ℵ, B, C, K, L, M, and about 15 others, as well as the Gothic version. | The common text (ς) and editors Ln and Ti read **the boat** (τὸ πλοῖον) with A, the second corrector of B, D, and the majority of other uncials, as well as the Coptic versions. | **having entered** (ἐμβάντα): Found here in ℵ, B, C, D, L, U, and Δ, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Armenian, and Theophylact. | The common text (ς) and Ti place this after "so that he" with Codex A, Π, and most others, including the Gothic and Syriac Peshitta. (The Latin Origen reads "so that he entered into a ship and sat in the sea"). | **to sit** (καθῆσθαι): Some manuscripts (M) have slight spelling variations (καθῆσαι or καθῆσται). | **in the sea** (ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ): Supported by the Vulgate and Latin Origen. Variations include: "across the sea" (Codex Bezae), "beside the sea," "near the shore," or "at the shore" in various Old Latin versions. | **by the sea on the land** (πρὸς τὴν θάλασσαν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς): The Latin versions show several variations here, such as "around the sea upon the land" or "on the shore." | **they were** (ἦσαν): Found in ℵ, B, C, L, A, and minuscule 33. | The common text (ς) and Ln read **it was** (ἦν) with A, D, and the majority of others, reflecting the singular "crowd."

**2. many things** (πολλά): Codex Bezae reads "in many [parables]." Some minuscules and Latin versions replace "many things" with **saying** (λεγων / *dicens*). | **to them** (αὐτοῖς): Omitted by Codex L and the Syriac, as well as some Latin versions which omit the entire phrase "in his teaching."

**3. Listen!** (ἀκούετε): Some manuscripts use a different form of the command "Hear!" (ἀκούσατε), and a few omit it entirely. | **to sow** (σπεῖραι): Found in the original hand of ℵ and B, and most Latin versions. | The common text (ς) and Ti read **for the sowing** (τοῦ σπείρειν) with the majority of uncials. **4. it happened** (ἐγένετο): Omitted by Codex D, F, and some Latin and Syriac versions. | **sowing** (σπείρειν): Codex D uses a different verb form (σπεῖραι). | **came** (ἦλθεν): Found in ℵ, A, B, C, L, and most others. Codex D and some others use plural forms ("they came"). | **the birds** (τὰ πετεινά): Supported by a vast number of manuscripts and versions. | The common text (ς) adds **of the heaven** (τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) (following the parallel in Luke) with Codex D, G, M, and the Vulgate. | **ate up** (κατέφαγεν): A few manuscripts use different grammatical endings. | **it** (αὐτό): A few manuscripts read "him" or "them."

# 4, 5. ACCORDING TO MARK

it. **5** And other seed fell on the rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up because it had no depth of soil; **6** and when the sun rose, it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered away. **7** And other seed fell among the thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no fruit. **8** And other seeds fell into the good soil, and yielded fruit, springing up and increasing, and bore thirty and sixty and <note>The text ends here mid-sentence; the yield of "a hundred" follows on the next page.</note>

---

**5. and other** <note>original: "και αλλο"</note>: (The plural form "and others" <note>original: "καὶ ἄλλα"</note> appears in Codex Bezae [D], minuscule 33, and a few others) found with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), Regius (L), and others ... The common text (ς) reads **but other** <note>original: "ἄλλο δὲ"</note> with Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Petropolitanus (Π), eight other uncials, and the majority of manuscripts. | **fell**: Codex Bezae (D) uses the plural form "they fell." | **on the rocky ground**: Found with ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, Π, and the majority of manuscripts, including the Vulgate (vg) and some Old Latin versions (it). ... ℵ, D, and others read **on the rocky places** (plural), as do several Latin versions. | **where**: Found in most manuscripts ... Codex Vaticanus (B) reads **and where**; Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions read **and because**, often omitting the phrase "because it had no depth of soil." | **immediately** <note>original: "ευθυς"</note>: Found in ℵ, B, C, D, L, Δ ... The common text (ς) reads **straightway** <note>original: "ευθεως"</note> with A, Π, and the majority of manuscripts. | **sprang up**: Some minuscules (1, 13, 28, etc.) read **sprouted** <note>original: "εξεβλαστησεν"</note>. | **depth of soil**: Found in most manuscripts ... Lachmann’s edition reads **depth of the soil** following Codex Vaticanus (B).

**6. and when the sun rose**: (Approved by scholar Scholz) found with ℵ, B, C, D, L, Δ, the Vulgate, and others ... The common text (ς) reads **but after the sun had risen** <note>original: "ἡλίου δὲ ἀνατείλαντος" - a genitive absolute construction similar to Matthew's account</note> with Codex Alexandrinus (A), Π, and the majority of manuscripts. | **it was scorched**: Found in ℵ, A, C, D, L, Π and most others ... Codex Vaticanus (B) and Bezae (D) use the plural **they were scorched**, matching the plural "they withered" found in those same manuscripts (as also seen in Matthew’s Gospel).

**7. other**: Several manuscripts and the Old Latin version (e) use the plural **others**, followed by "they yielded." | **into** <note>original: "εις"</note>: Found in ℵ, A, B, D, L, Π and most manuscripts ... Codex Ephraemi (C) and others read **upon** <note>original: "επι"</note>, matching Matthew's account. | **choked**: Minuscule 33 and others use a slightly different compound verb for "choked out" <note>original: "απεπνιξαν"</note>.

**8. others** <note>original: "αλλα"</note>: Found in ℵ, B, C, L, and various minuscules ... The common text (ς) and editors Lachmann (Ln) and Tischendorf (Ti) read the singular **other** <note>original: "αλλο"</note> with A, Δ, Π, and the majority of others. | **into the** <note>original: "εις την"</note>: Some minuscules and the Syriac versions read **upon the** <note>original: "επι την"</note>. | **yielded**: One manuscript reads the plural "they yielded." | **increasing**: Found in A, C, D, L, Δ ... ℵ and B use a slightly different grammatical ending (neuter plural). The common text (ς) uses an active form "increasing itself." <note>The editor notes that the intransitive use of "increase" is common in the New Testament, as in Matthew 6:28 or Luke 1:80.</note> | **bore** <note>original: "εφερεν"</note>: Found in A, B, L, Π and most others ... Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Ephraemi (C) read the plural **they bore**. | **unto** <note>original: "εις"</note>: This preposition is used three times in ℵ, Δ, B, and L ... The common text (ς) and Lachmann (Ln) use **in** <note>original: "εν"</note> with Codex Bezae (D) and most Latin versions. <note>The editor suggests "in" may have been adapted to match the phrasing "one [thirty], another [sixty]" found in Matthew.</note>

# ACCORDING TO MARK 4, 12.

[thirty and sixty and] a hundred. 9 And he said: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
<margin>10—20 Matthew 13, 10—23; Luke 8, 9—15</margin>
10 And when he was alone, those who were around him along with the twelve asked him about the parables. 11 And he said to them: "To you the mystery of the kingdom of God has been given;
<margin>37. 1</margin>
but to those outside, everything happens in parables, 12 so that 'seeing they may see and not perceive, and
<margin>Isaiah 6, 9 etc.</margin>
hearing they may hear and not understand, lest they should turn back and [be forgiven].'"

---

From where the word "into" <note>original: "εἰς"</note> was introduced one can hardly say. | **thirty, sixty, a hundred**: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Codex Bezae (D), as is their custom, use Greek numerals <note>original: "λ̄ ξ̄ ρ̄"</note>. Likewise, manuscript "i" and others read 30, 60, 100 in Roman numerals.

9. **he said**: Found in ℵ, Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Ephraemi (C), Codex Regius (L), and many others ... The common text (ς) adds **to them** with the margin of Codex Basiliensis (M) and a few others | **he who has**: Found in ℵ, B, C, D ... The common text (ς) reads **the one having** (following the style of Matthew and Luke) with A, L, and almost all others | **let him hear**: D and several Old Latin versions (a, b, ff², g¹, ²) and the Syriac Peshitta add **and let the one who understands understand**.

10. **and when**: Found in ℵ, B, C, D, L ... The common text (ς) reads **but when** with Codex Petropolitanus (Π) and the vast majority of manuscripts including Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions | **they asked**: Found in ℵ, C, and also A, B, and others in a slightly different form ... The common text (ς) uses a different past tense ("they questioned") with the majority of manuscripts | **those who were around him with the twelve**: (This entire phrase is omitted in L and one other) ... D and several Old Latin versions read **his disciples** instead | **the parables**: Found in ℵ, B, C, L, and the best Vulgate manuscripts ... D and many Old Latin versions read **what this parable was** (mirroring Luke) ... The common text (ς) reads **the parable** (singular) with A and the majority of manuscripts.

11. **he said**: D reads **he says**, and several Latin versions read **he dicit** (he says) or **he ait** (he said) | **the mystery has been given**: Found in ℵ, B, C, L ... The common text (ς) reads **it has been given to know the mystery** with the majority of manuscripts (mirroring Matthew and Luke) | **to those outside**: (Codex Δ omits "to those") ... One manuscript reads **to those from outside** | **everything**: Found in ℵ, D, K, Π ... The common text (ς) reads **all these things** with A, B, C, L, and the majority ... Omitted in some Old Latin manuscripts | **happens**: D and several Old Latin versions read **is said** or **is spoken**.

12. **they may see**: Found in ℵ, A, B, C, D, and the majority ... Several manuscripts and the scholar Origen add a "not" before this word, though some of these then omit the following phrase "and not perceive" | **they may hear**: (Some manuscripts omit this phrase) ... The common text (ς) uses a slightly different future-leaning tense of the verb | **they may understand**: Found in ℵ, A, B, C, D, and the majority ... Differing forms appear in D, L, and others.

# 4, 13. ACCORDING TO MARK

[lest they should] be forgiven. 13 And he says to them: "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?" <margin>38. 2</margin> 14 The sower sows the word. 15 And these are the ones by the path where the word is sown; and when they hear, immediately Satan comes and carries away the word that was sown in them. 16 And these likewise are those sown on the rocky places, who when they hear the word immediately receive it with joy, 17 and they have no root in themselves but are temporary; then when tribulation or persecution happens because of the word, they immediately fall away <note>The Greek word "skandalizontai" implies being tripped up or stumbling in faith.</note>. 18 And others are those sown among the thorns; these are the ones who [hear] the [word...]

<margin>understand |</margin> **be forgiven** according to <note>The letter "c." stands for "cum," meaning "with" or "according to."</note> Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Bezae (D), Regius (L), and others. # ACCORDING TO MARK 4, 20.

[having] heard the word, 19 and the cares of the world <note>The Greek "aiōnos" can mean "age," "world," or "lifetime."</note> and the deceitfulness of wealth and the desires for other things entering in choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful. 20 And those are the ones

---

(= Griesbach) **these are** according to manuscripts A, the second corrector of C, Π, and nine other uncials, minuscules 33, and most others, as well as the Old Latin versions f and q, both Syriac versions, the Ethiopic, and the Gothic...
Manuscripts 1, 13, 28, 69, 124, and many others in the Armenian version **omit** this; **the ones who are**: manuscript Δ (but not the Latin version δ) and five others omit **the ones** |
**in** according to ℵ, C, A, and the Coptic... Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **into** (:: but note that in Matthew and Luke the reading is essentially the same without fluctuation; likewise it appeared as **into** in verse 7 above) according to manuscripts A, B, D, L, Π, nine other uncials, and nearly all others |
**these are** according to ℵ, B, the original hand of C, D, L, Δ, 1, 13, 28, 69, 124, and many others including most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Armenian (both Syriac versions? The Peshitta reads "but those who are sown among thorns, those are they who hear the word"; the Philoxenian version edited by White reads "and these are they who are sown among thorns, who hear the word")... Manuscripts A, the second corrector of C, Π, nine other uncials, 33, and most others, as well as the Old Latin f and q, the Gothic, and Ethiopic **omit** this (it is also omitted in the 1633 edition) :: it follows that the double occurrence of **these are** is found in no uncial codex and hardly any other documents except perhaps a few | **having heard** (Griesbach's variant) according to ℵ (though it places it before "the word," as does the Coptic), B, C, D, L, Δ, 13, 69, 124, 346, and five others, the Coptic, and the Peshitta... Griesbach and Lachmann read **hearing** with A, Π, nine other uncials, and most others including the Old Latin and Vulgate (*those who hear* in Latin) the Philoxenian Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Gothic (:: Matthew uses **hearing**, Luke uses **having heard**)

19. **and the cares** (D* reads **cares-is**) etc: the Vulgate reads *and the hardships of the world and the deception of riches and the desires about other things entering in choke [it];* likewise the Old Latin ff¹, g², (and likely l). *Surprisingly, many Old Latin manuscripts vary here:* g¹ reads *and the anxieties of livelihood and the errors of the world and the deception of riches and the remaining desires occurring together choke [it];* f reads *and through the anxieties of this world and the enticements of riches and the other desires entering in choke [it];* ff², d, e, and q read *and the anxieties* (q: *anxiety*, d: *anxiety*, e begins from the later parts of the word) *of livelihood* (e: *of life*) *and the delights* (e: *pleasures*, d and q: *errors*) *of the world* (e: *of the age*) *advancing together* (q, d: *entering together*, ff²: only *advancing*, e: *accompanying*) *choke [it]* (q: *choak*); c reads *and conquered by anxieties and estranged by the delights of the world they choke [it],* b reads *and through the anxieties of life and going together in the error of the world they choke [it],* i reads *and because of the anxiety of livelihood and the errors of the world kindling together they choke [it].* | **world** (The Greek D and Latin c use **life**; see the Old Latin versions **livelihood, conquered, life** above) according to ℵ, B, C, D, L, Δ, 1, 102, and six others, and Old Latin b, c, e, ff¹, ff², g¹, g², i, q, the Vulgate, and Armenian... Griesbach adds **this** according to A, Π, nine other uncials, most others, f, the Coptic, both Syriac versions, the Ethiopic, and Gothic | **and the deceit** (Δ reads **love**, δ reads **deception or love**) **of wealth**: D and the Armenian read **and the deceptions of the world**, likewise see above for e, ff², q, g¹, c, i (f) | **and the desires about other things**: D, 1, a (in Blanchini's edition the letters *li* remain, in Iricus's edition *di*: hence it likely read either *mundi* [of the world] like c, d, ff², i, q, or *saeculi* [of the age] like b, e. Since the word *together* follows immediately, these should be applied not to **of the world** but to **of the world** [replacing **wealth**]) b, c, ff², i, q, and the Armenian **omit** this | **choke** (A, B, D spell it **choak**) according to ℵ, A, B (original hand), C, D, E, L, Δ... Griesbach and Lachmann read **choke** [different spelling] according to the second hand of B, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, Π, and many others. Furthermore, the original hand of ℵ reads: *chokes the word and the desires about other things entering in* (from which writing, which has much probability, it may depend that several Old Latin manuscripts omit **and the desires about other things**), the first corrector of ℵ adds **they choke the word**, the previous words having not been deleted, seemingly through carelessness. | **becomes unfruitful**: d, 124, b, c, e, ff¹, ff², g¹, i, q (but not f or g²) and several Vulgate manuscripts (but not the standard Vulgate, am, fu, ing, and others) and the Coptic read **they become unfruitful**.

20. **those** (Scholz notes: *"Appropriate for Mark, compare 7:15; 12:7 with other passages"*) according to ℵ, B, C, L, Δ, and the Peshitta... Griesbach and Lachmann read **these** according to A, D, Π, nine other uncials, and nearly all others (the Old Latin and Vulgate read *hi* [these], likewise the Coptic)

# ACCORDING TO MARK 4, 29.

...for whoever has, to him it shall be given; and he who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away from him.

**Verse 24.** [With the measure you] measure, it will be measured to you and more will be added to you, (manuscript 33 and others omit "to you") with manuscripts א <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, B, C, L, Δ, Π, eight other uncials, and most others; also Latin versions c, f, ff², g², i, q, the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac (both versions), Ethiopic, and Gothic. **Verse 26.** "he said": manuscript c* adds "that" | "as" (manuscripts 13, 28, 69, 124, 2pe, and others read "just as") with א, B, D (Greek text), L, Δ, 13, 28, 33, 69, 118, 124, 2pe, and about 5 others; also the Toledo manuscript and Coptic (reading "in the manner of a man who casts"), also manuscript 1 ("as a man when..."), and the Received Text ("as when a man sends") ... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "as if" with A, C, Θᵇ, Π, nine other uncials, and most others; most Old Latin, the Vulgate ("just as if"), Gothic (also Syriac versions, etc.) | "should cast (the) seed": manuscript D reads "seed should cast".

**Verse 27.** "should sleep" with א, A, B, C, D, G, K, L, M, S, V, Θᵇ, Π, and most others (Δ reads "to sleep") ... <note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," where the editor, Tischendorf, lists variations found in ancient hand-copied manuscripts.</note>

**1.** <note>continued from previous page</note> **he came:** <note>original: "ēlthen"</note> according to Griesbach's edition, with manuscripts C, G, L, M, Δ, and about 30 others, the Coptic (Wilkins and Schwartze editions), the Syriac (Peshitta and Philoxenian), the Armenian; furthermore, manuscript G and a few others (including lectionaries) add **Jesus** | **of the sea:** <note>original: "tēs thalassēs"</note> (Old Latin manuscripts *c, g2*, and likely *ff1, g1*, and the Vulgate read "across the strait of the sea," while manuscripts *b, f, l,* and *e* omit "of the sea" and read "across the sea"): manuscript D in Greek reads "to the place across and into the region"; manuscripts 13, 69, and others read "beyond" or "further" | **of the Gerasenes:** <note>original: "gerasēnōn"</note> according to Griesbach, with manuscripts א (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), D, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate... but the standard received text reads **of the Gadarenes** <note>original: "gadarēnōn"</note> with manuscripts A, C, Π, eight other uncials, and a vast majority of others, including the Syriac and Gothic... while manuscripts L, U, Δ, 1, 28, 33, 118, and about 20 others, along with the Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic read **of the Gergesenes** <note>original: "gergesēnōn"</note>. Likewise, Epiphanius <note>a 4th-century bishop</note> says "as Mark says," and see the notes on Matthew 8:28; also Theophylact <note>an 11th-century commentator</note> on this passage says: "**The more accurate of the copies have 'into the region of the Gergesenes.'**" Furthermore, see Origen's <note>a 3rd-century scholar</note> commentary on Matthew 8:28. The notes found in various commentary chains (catenae) from Oxford and Moscow also depend on Origen. In the Oxford catena, it reads as follows:

<note>The following is a long scholarly argument from antiquity regarding geography.</note>
"Neither 'of the Gadarenes' nor 'of the Gerasenes' is found in the accurate copies, but 'of the Gergesenes.' For **Gadara** is a city of Judea, near which are the famous hot springs, but there is no lake with cliffs adjacent to it, nor a sea. And **Gerasa** is a city of Arabia, having neither sea nor lake nearby. The Evangelists, being men who carefully knew the regions of Judea, would not have spoken such an obvious and easily disproved falsehood. **Gergesa**, therefore, is the place from which the Gergesenes come; it is an ancient city near what is now called the Lake of Tiberias <note>The Sea of Galilee</note>, near which there is a cliff hanging over the lake, from which it is shown that the swine were cast down by the demons. 'Gergesa' is interpreted as '**the dwelling of those who have been cast out**,' being named perhaps prophetically for what the citizens of that country did to the Savior, when they begged him to depart from their borders."

These things Origen says in the sixth volume of his *Explanations of the Gospel according to John*. Augustine, in his *Harmony of the Evangelists*, does not touch upon this difference in the text; the Latin manuscripts among all three Evangelists maintain **Gerasenes**, but he does not add the name of the region.

**2. when he had gone out:** <note>original: "exelthontos autou"</note> (Scholz <note>an editor</note> notes: "This is the better reading, see Mark 6:54 and 11:12; also see Luke 8:27") with manuscripts א, B, C, L, Δ, 1, 13, 33, 69, and about 10 others, including the Coptic and Syriac... but the standard received text reads **as he was going out** <note>original: "exelthonti autō"</note> with manuscripts A, Π, 9 other uncials, and most others, including the Vulgate and Gothic... while manuscript D and some Old Latin manuscripts read **as they were going out** <note>original: "exelthontōn autōn"</note> | **immediately:** <note>original: "euthys"</note> with א, C, L, Δ... the standard text reads **immediately** <note>original: "eutheōs" - a slightly different Greek form</note> with A, D, Π, and nearly all others... Lachmann's edition omits it (following Matthew and Luke) with several Old Latin manuscripts and the Syriac | **met:** <note>original: "hypēntēsen"</note> with א, B, C, D, G, L, Δ and about 20 others... the standard text reads **met** <note>original: "apēntēsen" - a different Greek prefix</note> with A, Π, and 8 other uncials | **a man out of the tombs:** <note>original: "ek tōn mnēm. anthrōpos"</note> (so also the Vulgate and Coptic): manuscripts D, and several Old Latin, Armenian, and Gothic versions read **a man from the tombs** <note>reversing the word order</note>.

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of variations found in different ancient handwritten copies of the New Testament.</note>

**feeding** <note>original: "boskomenē"</note>: found in manuscripts א <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, C, A, L, and Δ. However, a few others read **of those feeding** <note>original: "boskomenōn"</note>, similar to the Gospel of Luke.

14. **and those who were feeding**: found in א, A, B, C, D, L, M, and Δ. The "Received Text" reads **but those feeding** <note>original: "oi de boskontes"</note>, matching the wording in Matthew. | **them** <note>referring to the pigs</note>: found in א, B, C, D, L, and the earliest versions. 21. **And having come** (manuscript d adds "but"): manuscripts 2pe, a, b, c, ff² read **but having come** (c, ff²: "but when an opportune day had happened"; b: "but an opportune day being made"; a: "but on an opportune day") | **when** (Lachmann edited this as "the"): manuscripts D, a, b, f, q, and the Vulgate omit. 34 And coming out, he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them, because they were like sheep not having a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things. 35 <gloss>Reference number 64. 1</gloss> And when it was already a late hour, his disciples approached him and were saying that, "This place is desolate, and it is already a late hour; 36 dismiss them, so that going away into the surrounding fields and villages they may buy themselves something <note>The Greek text here is "ti," meaning "something," which implies "something to eat."</note>

---

<note>The following notes compare different ancient handwritten versions of the Bible to show where they disagree on specific words.</note>

(*Codex Petropolitanus* reads: "they came") **to him** (Manuscript 28 reads: "to him" <note>original: "autō"</note>) (*Old Latin manuscripts b, ff², and i read: "and they gathered there"; manuscript c: "and they ran together there"*), *likewise* 1. **and they came there** (*omitting* "there" *after* "ran together") *and so* Griesbach <note>Johann Jakob Griesbach, an 18th-century biblical critic</note>, manuscript a reads *and they came* ... 209. 240. 244. Euthymius <note>A 12th-century monk and commentator</note> *omits all these words after* "they ran together there" ...
