[The text below is the "critical apparatus," where scholars list differences between early copies of the Bible. Ancient manuscripts are referred to by letters like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), or D (Bezae).]

...with A, L, Γ, Δ, Π, nine other <term>uncials</term><note>Uncials are early Greek manuscripts written in all capital letters.</note>, and almost all others, and Origen (but manuscript 33, a few others, the Old Latin version *a*, the version *l*, and Origen omit the second instance) :: the word for "looking up" in Luke does not vary | Sinaiticus reads "by hundreds and by fifties," Bezae reads "by 100 and by 50."

41. **the** (omitted by manuscript D) **five** etc: Origen <note>An early Christian scholar, c. 184–253 AD.</note> says: "Again – in these very words the three evangelists say that taking the five loaves and the two fish, looking up to heaven, he gave a blessing." | **gave a blessing**: Manuscripts L, Δ, 28, 262, and others read "gave a blessing" <note>Using a slightly different Greek verb form</note>. | **broke** (L reads "divided") **and kept giving** (:: same as in Luke): Sinaiticus and others read "having broken, he gave" (the corrector of Sinaiticus wrote "and he kept giving," but by oversight did not change "having broken"); manuscript 33 (following Matthew) reads "having broken, he gave the loaves to the disciples" | **the** (manuscripts D, *b*, and *c* add "five") **loaves**: Latin version *q* omits this | **to the disciples**: with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, Δ, 33, 102, Coptic, and Armenian... The Received Text and Lachmann read a different form of the verb "set before" with manuscripts A, D, and others (see notes at 3:12; 6:8 and 12) | **them**: Manuscript D reads "in front of them," similarly the Old Latin and Vulgate read "before them"... manuscript M reads "to the crowd" :: see Mark and Luke, also Mark 8:6 and Matthew 15:36 | **two**: Sinaiticus and Bezae use the numeral symbol for "2" | **divided** (the Received Text and a few others read "and divided," some read "divided among," others read "set before"): manuscript Γ reads "to divide."

42. **all and were satisfied**: Manuscripts 1 and 209 read "and were satisfied all."

43. **of fragments** (thus in Sinaiticus and several others; Vaticanus, L, and Δ read "the fragments"; manuscript 1 omits) **twelve** (Sinaiticus and Bezae use the numeral symbol for 12) **baskets full**: with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, Δ, 1, and others... 44. **were**: Manuscript M and 111 omit this | **the** (manuscript M adds "five") **loaves**: with A, B, L, Γ, Δ, Π, and most others including Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions... <note>The following section is a "critical apparatus," a technical list comparing how different ancient handwritten copies (manuscripts) of the Bible differ in their wording.</note>

49. **Manuscripts D, Γ, and others** read **seeing** <note>original: "ειδοντες"</note> | **walking on the sea** <note>original: "επι τ. θαλ. περιπατ."</note> follows this order in Manuscripts ℵ, B, L, Δ, 33, and the scribal hand of manuscript c (:: the same order appears in Matthew, but there it refers to the "waves") ... the editors **Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf** read **walking on the sea** <note>original: "περιπ. επι τ. θαλ."</note> (:: but this order appears in both verse 48 and in John and does not vary) along with Manuscripts A, D, X, Γ, Π, nine <term>uncials</term><note>Early Greek manuscripts written in capital letters.</note>, and most others, as well as the Old Latin, the Vulgate, Coptic, both Syriac versions, Armenian, and Ethiopic | **that it is a ghost** <note>original: "οτι φαντ. εστ."</note> with Manuscripts ℵ, B, L, Δ, 33 (:: in Matthew, this is preceded by the word "saying") ... the editors **Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf** read **to be a ghost** <note>original: "φαντασμα ειναι"</note> with Manuscripts A, D, X, Γ, Π, nine uncials, and most others, including the Latin (the Latin versions read: "they thought it was a ghost") and Armenian.

**21.** **sexual immoralities** <note>original Greek: "πορνειαι"</note> (The manuscripts Codex Sinaiticus [א], Codex Alexandrinus [A], and others use a slightly different spelling) **thefts, murders** (verse 22) **adulteries** according to Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus [B], Codex Ephraemi [L], and the Coptic and Ethiopic versions; similarly Codex Bezae [D] reads "sexual immorality, thefts, adulteries, murder," likewise the Old Latin manuscripts (a, b, c, d, i, q) have "adultery, thefts, sexual immorality, murder," and the Gothic version has "sexual immorality, adultery, murder, theft." Griesbach and Tischendorf favor the spelling **Syraphoenician** <note>original: "συραφοινικισσα"</note> based on Codex Vaticanus [B] and over 100 other manuscripts. | **he might cast out** <note>original: "εκβαλη"</note> according to the majority of manuscripts, though some use a future tense spelling; the Received Text [ς] and Tischendorf use a double-consonant spelling <note>original: "εκβαλλη"</note>. | **out of** <note>original: "εκ"</note>: manuscripts 1, 13, and others omit this phrase.

**27. And he said** <note>original: "και ελεγεν"</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus [א], Codex Vaticanus [B], and the Coptic; Codex Bezae [D] reads "and he says"; the Syriac Peshitta reads "and Jesus said." The Received Text [ς] reads **But Jesus said** <note>original: "ο δε ις ειπεν"</note> with Codex Alexandrinus [A] and the majority of manuscripts. | **to her**: omitted in manuscripts 1, 28, and some Latin. | **it is good** <note>original: "εστ. καλ."</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus [א], Codex Vaticanus [B], and the Vulgate; the Received Text [ς] reverses the word order to **good it is**. | **to throw to the little dogs** <note>original: "τ. κυν. βαλ."</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus [א] and Codex Vaticanus [B]; the Received Text [ς] and Lachmann read **to throw to the little dogs** <note>original: "βαλ. τ. κυν."</note>, matching the phrasing in the Gospel of Matthew.

**28. and says to him**: several Old Latin manuscripts read "saying to him" or "she responded and said to him." | **yes** <note>original: "ναι"</note>: omitted in Codex Bezae [D] and some Latin and Armenian versions. | **even** <note>original: "και"</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus [א], Codex Vaticanus [B], and the Coptic; the Received Text [ς], Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **for even** <note>original: "και γαρ"</note>, again matching Matthew; Codex Bezae [D] and some Latin read **but even**. | **eat** <note>original: "εσθιουσιν"</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus [א], Codex Vaticanus [B], and more than 12 others.

**eat** <note>original: "εσθιει"</note> (as in Matthew): The Received Text <note>symbol ς; the standard printed Greek text of the era</note> reads this along with Codex Alexandrinus [A], Codex Vaticanus [N], and nine other uncial <note>capital letter</note> manuscripts and most others. | **crumbs** <note>original: "ψιχιων"</note>: Codex Bezae [D] reads **fragments/scraps** <note>original: "ψιχων"</note>. | **children** <note>original: "παιδιων"</note>: Some manuscripts read **little children**. **VIII. 1. in those** <note>original: "εν εκειναις"</note>: Manuscripts D, 28, and several Old Latin versions (a, b, c, ff², i, q) add **but/and** <note>original: "δε"</note>. | **again a large** <note>original: "παλιν πολλου"</note>: Supported by Griesbach and manuscripts ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), D, G, L, M, N, Δ, and many others, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, and Armenian versions. Tischendorf [Ti] reads **a vast** <note>original: "παμπολλου"</note> following manuscripts A, E, F, H, K, S, U, V, Wᵈ, and most others. Note: the word for "vast" or "very great" <note>original: "παμπολυς"</note> is frequent in classical Greek but is not found in the Septuagint [the Greek Old Testament] nor in the New Testament except in this place. | **being** <note>original: "οντος"</note>: Manuscript Wᵈ reads **having gathered** <note>original: "συναχθεντοσ"</note>. | **having** <note>original: "εχοντων"</note>: Manuscripts D and 2ᵖᵉ add **them** <note>original: "αυτων"</note>. | **having called** <note>original: "προσκαλεσαμενοσ"</note>: Found in ℵ, A, B, D, K, L, M, N, Wᵈ, Δ, Π, and many others. Additionally, manuscript Δ adds **again** <note>original: "παλιν"</note>.

**2. upon the crowd**: Most manuscripts read this. Codex L and others read **upon this crowd**. Manuscript D reads **on this crowd** <note>using the genitive case "επι του οχλου τουτου"</note>. | **three days**: Supported by ℵ, A, L, N, Wᵈ, Γ, Π, and most others. The Received Text [ς], Lachmann [Ln], and Tischendorf [Ti] read **hungry** <note>original plural spelling: "νηστεισ"</note> following A, B, D, L, N, Wᵈ, and most others. | **to** <note>original: "εισ"</note>: A few manuscripts (13, 28, 69, etc.) add **the** <note>original: "τον"</note>. | **their** <note>original: "αυτων"</note>: Omitted by manuscript D and some Latin versions. | **and if... will faint**: Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions (a, b, ff², i, q) read **and to dismiss them hungry to [their] home I am not willing, lest they faint**, which appears to be influenced by the parallel passage in Matthew 15:32. | **and some**: Supported by ℵ, B, L, Δ, and several others. Manuscript D reads **because also some**. The Received Text [ς] reads **for some** <note>original: "τινεσ γαρ"</note> following A, N, Wᵈ, and most others. | **of them**: Found in D and many others.

<header>ACCORDING TO MARK 8, 8.</header>

...have come from far away. 4 And his disciples answered him: "How will anyone be able to satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?" 5 And he asked them: "How many loaves do you have?" They said: "Seven." 6 And he directed the crowd to recline on the ground. And taking the seven loaves, having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before them; and they served them to the crowd. 7 They also had a few small fish; and having blessed them, he set them before them. 8 And they ate and <note>The text continues on the next page.</note>

---

**8:3. from them** <note>original: "εξ αυτ."</note>: Found in manuscript q and the Vulgate. | **from** <note>original: "απο"</note>: Supported by the major codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and Regius, along with various minuscule manuscripts and Latin versions which read "from a distance" or "from far off." The standard Byzantine text <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> and Lachmann omit this. | **have come** <note>original: "ηκασιν"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and several other early manuscripts. Some versions read **they are** <note>original: "εισιν"</note> or **have arrived** <note>original: "ηκουσιν"</note>, while the Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions generally translate this as "they came."

**4. to him**: Omitted by Codex Sinaiticus and the Old Latin manuscript ff²*. | **that whence** <note>original: "οτι ποθεν"</note>: Found in Vaticanus and others. Sinaiticus reads **and they said, "Whence..."** <note>original: "και ειπαν ποθεν"</note>. The standard text and Lachmann read simply **whence** <note>original: "ποθεν"</note>. | **will be able** <note>original: "δυνησεται"</note>: Variant spelling found in manuscript 69 and others. | **here** <note>original: "ωδε"</note>: Placed in various positions in different manuscripts; omitted by Codex Bezae and several Old Latin versions. | **of loaves** <note>original: "αρτων"</note>: Some manuscripts use the singular **bread** <note>original: "αρτον"</note>. | **in the wilderness** <note>original: "επ ερημιας"</note>: Most major manuscripts use this phrasing, though some use a slightly different grammatical case <note>original: "επ ερημιαις"</note>.

**5. he asked** <note>original: "ηρωτα"</note>: Found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. The standard text and Lachmann use a more emphatic form, **he questioned** <note>original: "επηρωτα"</note>. The Latin versions vary between "he was asking" and "he asked." | **loaves do you have**: The order of these words varies in Sinaiticus, Bezae, and the Latin versions. | **they said** <note>original: "ειπαν"</note>: Preferred by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; the standard text uses a different spelling <note>original: "ειπον"</note>. Some versions add **to him** <note>original: "αυτω"</note>.

**6. he directed** <note>original: "παραγγελλει"</note>: Present tense in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Regius. <term>Origen</term> <note>a 3rd-century scholar</note> notes this specific wording in his commentary, observing that while other accounts use "commands" <note>original: "κελευει"</note> or "ordered" <note>original: "επεταξε"</note>, here Mark uses the word for "directs" or "charges." The standard text uses the past tense **he directed** <note>original: "παρηγγειλε"</note>. | **having given thanks** <note>original: "ευχαριστησας"</note>: Found in most major manuscripts. Some versions add **and** before the word. | **to set before them** <note>original: "παρατιθωσιν"</note>: A present-tense verb form; some manuscripts use the future/aorist form.

**7. they had** <note>original: "ειχαν"</note>: An older form of the verb found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus. | **having blessed**: Manuscript Bezae and some Latin versions replace this with **having given thanks** <note>original: "ευχαριστησας"</note>. | **them** <note>original: "αυτα"</note>: Placed after "blessed" in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, but before it in others. The standard text omits the word entirely. | **he set before** <note>original: "παρεθηκεν"</note>: Found in the original hand of Sinaiticus. The standard text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **he said** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note>, with some Latin versions adding that he **ordered** <note>original: "iussit"</note> them to be served.

*(he said)* **to set before** <note>original: "παραθειναι" (paratheinai)</note> (so the Textus Receptus <note>indicated by ς</note> with the main text of Codex G, and manuscripts N, U, V, X, Pi, and many others; likewise manuscripts E, F, H, K, S, and the corrected W, and many others; also both the Syriac versions, the Gothic, Coptic, and Armenian; Tischendorf reads **to be setting before** <note>original: "παρατιθεναι" (paratithenai)</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, M-marginal, Delta, and a few others; Lachmann reads **to be set before** <note>original: "παρατεθηναι" (paratethenai)</note> with Alexandrinus and a few others, and also the Old Latin and Vulgate which read "apponi"; manuscript 33 and the Coptic read **set ye before**). **and them** <note>original: "και αυτα" (kai auta)</note> (with manuscripts A, E, F, G, H, K, the main text of M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Pi, and the vast majority; also the Peshitta Syriac, Gothic, and Coptic; manuscript v and about 10 others, along with the Scholia Syriac, read **them**; Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, L, and Delta read **and these things** placed before the verb; Codex Bezae reads **and them** placed before "he dismissed"; manuscripts M-marginal, N, the corrected W, and several minuscules, along with most Old Latin versions and the Vulgate, omit the phrase entirely—hence Griesbach marks it for omission; however, M-marginal and a lectionary read **to the crowd** <note>compare Matthew 14:16</note>, and N reads **to them**, while the Coptic reads **before them**) :: *compare John 6:11*

8. **and they ate** <note>original: "και εφαγ."</note> (with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, D, L, Delta, and minuscules 1, 28, 33, 40, 124, 2pe, and the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, and Peshitta Syriac... the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read **But they ate** <note>original: "εφαγον δε"</note> with Alexandrinus, N, the corrected W, X, Gamma, Pi, and nine other uncials, along with the majority of manuscripts, the Gothic, and the Philoxenian Syriac. Additionally, Sinaiticus and possibly manuscript 282 add **all**, as do manuscripts K, M, Pi, and about 20 others after "satisfied" :: *compare Matthew 15:37; also Mark 6:42 and parallel passages*) | **leftovers** <note>original: "περισσευματα" (perisseumata)</note> (with manuscripts A, B, L, N, the corrected W, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, nine other uncials, and nearly all others... the corrected Sinaiticus and Coptic read **the leftovers**, Codex Bezae and 2pe read **the leftover of the...**, and 33 reads **having abounded**) | **of fragments** (manuscript 33 reads **fragments**; Delta omits it) | **seven** (Codex Bezae uses the symbol "ζ"; manuscripts D, L, 2pe, and manuscript q of the Old Latin place "seven" after "baskets") | **baskets** <note>original: "σπυριδασ" (spyridas), referring to large flexible hampers</note> (with Alexandrinus-corrected, Vaticanus, C, L, N, the corrected W, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, and nearly all others... Lachmann reads **baskets** <note>original: "σφυριδασ" (sphyridas), a variant spelling</note> based on Sinaiticus, the original hand of Alexandrinus, and Codex Bezae (D). Note that Codex Bezae alone maintains this spelling in 8:20 and Matthew 15:37; it is also found in Matthew 16:10, Acts 9:25, and elsewhere. However, it seemed inconsistent to print one spelling in this verse and another in verse 20. Furthermore, manuscripts 13, 33, 69, and about 10 others add **full** :: *likely from Matthew*).

9. **Now they were** <note>original: "ησαν δε"</note> (Griesbach marks this as a variant) (with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, Delta, 33, and several lectionaries and the Coptic... the Textus Receptus and Lachmann add **those who had eaten** <note>original: "οι φαγοντες"</note> with Alexandrinus, C, D, N, the corrected W, X, Gamma, Pi, nine other uncials, and the majority, including Latin, Gothic, and Syriac versions :: *as in Mark 6:44*) | **about** <note>original: "ως" (hos)</note> (manuscript M and 10 others read "as if"; Sinaiticus and Coptic omit it :: *as in Matthew*) | **four thousand**: (Manuscripts G, Delta, and several Old Latin manuscripts add **men** <note>original: "ανδρεσ"</note> :: *as in Mark 6:44*).

10. **immediately** <note>original: "ευθυς" (euthys)</note> (with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, L, Delta, and minuscules 1, 13, 28, 69, 253, 346... the Textus Receptus reads **straightway** <note>original: "ευθεωσ"</note> with Alexandrinus, N, W-corrected, X, Gamma, Pi, and the vast majority. Its position in the sentence varies: placed here in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, E, F, G, H, L, S, V, X, Gamma, Delta, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Armenian... but placed after "having stepped in" in A, K, M, N, U, W-corrected, Pi, 1, 69, 124, etc., and Syriac/Gothic... Codex Bezae and some Old Latin omit it) | **having stepped in** (Codex Bezae reads **he went up**, 2pe reads **he stepped in** and then both add **and came**; similarly some Old Latin versions read "he ascended and came"): Codex Vaticanus adds **himself**, as does Lachmann [in brackets]; some Old Latin manuscripts add "Jesus himself ascended") | **the** boat: (omitted by L, 1, 28, 33, 69, 124, 209, and the Gothic) | **he came**: (Sinaiticus and L add **Jesus**) | **the regions** <note>original: "μερη" (mere)</note>: (Codex Bezae reads "the borders" <note>original: "ορια" (oria)</note>, as do some Latin and Armenian versions... manuscript N reads "the mountains" <note>original: "ορη" (ore)*</note>) | **Dalmanutha** (Vaticanus spells it **Dalmanountha**): so read the main Greek text and several Latin manuscripts, the Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic. Codex Bezae (original) reads **Melegada**, the corrected Bezae reads **Magada**, others read **Mageda**, **Magidan**, or **Magedan**. *Compare Augustine, On the Harmony of the Evangelists 2, 3:* "Mark—mentions the same thing as Matthew, except that Matthew did not say Dalmanutha, which is read in some codices, but Magedan. However, it is not to be doubted that it is the same place under both names. For most codices, even according to Mark, have only Magedan." Jerome also notes...

11. **Hebrew reference 3, 250:** <note>original: "μαγεδαν ο χς επεδημησεν, ως ο ματθαιος· και ο μαρκος δε της μεγαιδαν μνημονευει· και εστι νυν η μαγαιδανη περι την γερασαν"</note> Christ visited Magedan, as Matthew says; and Mark also mentions Magedan; and it is now called Magaidane (or Megaidane) near Gerasa... Manuscripts 1, 13, 69, 209, 271, 347, and the Coptic <note>Middle Egyptian</note> read **Magdala**; the Gothic reads **Magdalan**. **Scholion 238:** <note>A scholarly note found in the margins of ancient manuscripts</note> And Matthew said Magdala, but Mark said Dalmanutha. There is no disagreement here; for the one named the town, while the other recorded the regions far from the city; for Magdala and Dalmanutha are neighboring places.

11. **and they came out** <note>original: "και εξηλθον"</note> (some variants use different Greek endings for the verb): Manuscripts 33 and 252 omit the definite article; others place **the Pharisees** after **they began** | **to argue with him** <note>original: "συζητειν αυτω"</note> with <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (ℵ), <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (B), and many others... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> (ς) reads **to argue** with other manuscripts | **to argue with him**: Codex D reads **to argue together with him**, while the <term>Old Latin</term> and <term>Vulgate</term> read **to dispute with him** | **seeking from him**: Manuscript Delta omits this | **a sign**: Codex D reads **the sign**, another reads **what sign** before the word "from" | **from** (manuscripts 13, 69, 346 read **out of**): Sinaiticus and the Old Latin prefix this with the word **to see**

12. **sighing deeply** <note>original: "αναστεναξας"</note>: Sinaiticus and ten others read simply **sighing** | **his** (manuscripts A and L read **of himself**): Codex D and several others omit this | **he says**: Manuscript Gamma and a few others read **he said**, as does the Old Latin | **Why**: Manuscript c and Origen read **Because** | **seeks a sign** with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others, as well as the Old Latin and the majority of Vulgate editions... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads **seeks after a sign** (similar to the wording in Matthew) with many other manuscripts and Origen | **to you**: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and others include this, but Vaticanus and L omit it | **if** <note>The Greek "ει" (if) here functions as a strong Hebrew-style negation: "if a sign is given... [then let me be cursed]," meaning "no sign will be given."</term> (Origen notes: "if—that is to say, it shall not be given"): Manuscript Delta and others read **not** | **this**: Several manuscripts read **the same**

13. **leaving**: Sinaiticus reads **leaving behind** (matching the wording in Matthew) | **again having stepped in** with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> flips the order to **having stepped in again** with many other manuscripts... others omit **again**. Furthermore, the phrase **again having stepped in** appears without addition in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others... but the <term>Textus Receptus</term> adds **into the boat** with many manuscripts, while others read **into a boat**; the Old Latin and Vulgate vary between **into the ship** or **having ascended the ship**.

14. **they forgot**: Codex Bezae (D) and others add **the disciples**, while some read **his disciples** (following Matthew's wording) | **to take loaves of bread**: Manuscripts 13, 69, and the Vulgate reverse this to **loaves of bread to take** | **and except for one loaf they did not have etc.**: Various Latin versions read **and they did not have except one loaf**... Codex D reads **if they did not have one loaf**, while others read **they were not having except one loaf**; some Old Latin versions specify they had the loaf **with them in the ship**.

<header>8:15. ACCORDING TO MARK</header>

...they had with themselves in the boat. 15 <sup>79.2</sup> And he strictly ordered them, saying: “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” 16 <sup>80.6</sup> And they were reasoning with one another, saying, “It is because we have no bread.” 17 And knowing this, he says to them: “Why do you reason that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Is your heart still hardened? 18 Having eyes, do you not see? And—

---

<term>Verse 14 (continued)</term>: <note>Latin: "plius habebant nisi unum panem quem secum habeb. in nave"</note> They had nothing more except one loaf which they had with them in the boat. Found in manuscripts 1, 13, 28, 69, 209, 346. The manuscript 2pe reads <note>original: "ενα μονον αρτ. εχοντες"</note> “having only one loaf.” Manuscript 69 reverses the order to “having loaves.” For the word “with,” manuscript D uses a variant spelling <note>original: "μετ"</note> before the word “themselves.”

15. **strictly ordered**: <note>original: "διεστέλλετο"</note> Manuscripts E, F, 13, 28, 69, 131, 346, and a few others use the tense <note>original: "διεστείλατο"</note> “he ordered,” while manuscript Δ uses <note>original: "ενετείλατο"</note> “he commanded.” Likewise, the Old Latin versions a, b, c, f, ff², i, and q use the term “he commanded,” as opposed to the Latin Vulgate and others which use “he was commanding.” | **Watch out**: Manuscript c, along with 13, 28, 69, 124, 8pe, and various Latin and Coptic versions, add the word **and** <note>original: "και"</note> before “beware”; this was followed by the editor Lachmann. However, manuscripts D, 1, 2, 118, 209, 2pe, and several Old Latin versions omit it. Manuscript Δ omits the word **beware** <note>original: "βλεπετε"</note>, while a note above the word “watch out” suggests it could mean “see” or “beware.” | **and**: Manuscripts G, Δ, 1, 28, 69, 124, 209, 346 add the word **from** <note>original: "απο"</note> after “and.” | **Herod**: Manuscripts G, 1, 13, 28, 69, 118, 209, 251, 346, 2pe, along with the Old Latin i and the Armenian version, read <note>original: "των ηρωδιανων"</note> **the Herodians**.

16. **they were reasoning**: <note>Latin: "c dicebant"</note> The Old Latin c reads “they were saying.” Codex Sinaiticus (א) uses a slightly different verb form for reasoning. | **with one another**: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and Bezae (D). The <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>symbolized by ς</note> and many other manuscripts add **saying** <note>original: "λεγοντες"</note>, matching the phrasing in the Gospel of Matthew. | **we have**: Supported by many uncials and versions. However, the editors Lachmann and Tischendorf use **they have** <note>original: "εχουσιν"</note>, following Codex Vaticanus (B) and others. The Coptic version reads “there was no bread for them,” and some Old Latin versions use “they did not have.”

17. **And knowing**: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and the Coptic. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> and editor Lachmann add **Jesus** <note>original: "ο ι̅ς̅"</note>. | **reason**: Most manuscripts support this. However, manuscripts D, U, and several others add **in your hearts** <note>original: "εν ταις καρδιαις υμων"</note>, likely influenced by other passages in Mark or Luke. Additionally, a group of manuscripts (13, 28, 61, etc.) add **O you of little faith** <note>original: "ολιγοπιστοι"</note> from the Gospel of Matthew. A marginal note in the Syriac version mentions that “in your hearts, O you of little faith” was not found in two Greek copies nor in the ancient Syriac. | **you have**: Manuscript Δ and others read “we have.” | **nor understand**: Omitted by manuscripts 1 and 209. | **hardened**: Supported by the earliest manuscripts. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Tischendorf add the word **still** <note>original: "ετι"</note>. | **you have your heart hardened**: <note>Latin: "caecatum habetis cor vestrum"</note> “you have your heart blinded.” Manuscripts D and 2pe read “your heart is hardened,” while various Old Latin versions read “your heart is/hearts are blunted.”

18. **The symbols ς Gb Sz Ti**: <note>These represent various scholarly editors like Griesbach, Scholz, and Tischendorf</note>. They debate the punctuation—whether to end with “do you not see?” and “do you not hear?” or continue to “and do you not remember?”

<header>ACCORDING TO MARK 8, 21. 297</header>

Having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember? 19 When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments did you take up? They say to him, "Twelve." 20 And when the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of fragments did you take up? And they say, "Seven." 21 And he said to them: "Do you not yet understand?"

---

**...remember?** <note>original: "μνημονεύετε;"</note> In the editions of Lachmann <note>a 19th-century biblical scholar</note>, the text reads "Do you see? — Do you hear? — Do you remember, when..." This variation is found in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), the Coptic versions, and Peter of Alexandria. **omit and**: The word "and" is omitted in several sources. Instead of "and do you not remember," Codex Bezae (D) reads "neither do you remember." Codex Sinaiticus and other manuscripts (2pe) read "do you not yet perceive, neither do you remember."

19. **when**: <note>original: "ὅτε"</note> Several manuscripts (including 28 and 60) and Old Latin versions (b, c, ff², i, k) omit this word. Other manuscripts (13, 69, 346) change the order to "the loaves which I broke." It appears that Codex Bezae intended the same, as the Latin parallel (d) reads: <note>original: "nec meministis quando de V panibus quos fregi"</note> "nor did you remember when [I dealt] with the five loaves which I broke." | **the five thousand**: Some manuscripts (Δ, and Old Latin a, b, c, ff², g¹, g², l, q) add the word **men** <note>original: "ανθρωπους"</note>. | **and how many**: Found in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Codex Bezae, and many others. Scholarly editors like Lachmann and Tischendorf use simply "how many," following Codex Vaticanus (B) and the majority of ancient copies. | **baskets full of fragments**: There is a variation in word order here. The Majority Text <note>the standard Byzantine text type</note> places "full" after "baskets," while older manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus place "full of fragments" together. A few manuscripts (13, 69, etc.) and some Old Latin versions omit the word "full" entirely.

20. **and when**: <note>original: "ὅτε καὶ"</note> Found in Codex Sinaiticus and several Latin versions. Other major editions (Lachmann, Tischendorf) use "but when," following Codex Alexandrinus (A) and most other uncials <note>manuscripts written in all-capital letters</note>. Codex Vaticanus and others use only "when." | **the seven**: Several manuscripts (including Sinaiticus and Ephraemi Rescriptus) add the word **loaves** <note>original: "αρτους"</note> for clarity, similar to the Gospel of Matthew. | **the four thousand**: Some manuscripts (Δ, c, q) add the word **men**. | **how many large baskets full of fragments**: <term>large baskets</term> <note>original: "σπυρίδων"</note> — the Greek distinguishes these flexible hampers from the sturdy baskets <note>original: "κοφίνους"</note> used in the first miracle. Codex Bezae and some Latin versions use slightly different phrasing for "how many baskets of fragments." | **and they say**: Most early manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) include this. However, the Majority Text and Lachmann's edition read "but they said," following Codex Alexandrinus and the bulk of later manuscripts. Tischendorf adds the word **to him** <note>original: "αυτω"</note>, though it is omitted in Sinaiticus and the Syriac versions.

21. **And he said**: <note>original: "καὶ ἔλεγεν"</note> Found in the vast majority of manuscripts including Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus. A few (Codex Bezae and some Old Latin) use "And he says." | **not yet**: <note>original: "οὔπω"</note> Found in Sinaiticus and several others. Lachmann's edition reads "How [is it that] you do not yet [understand]?" following Codex Alexandrinus and many others. The Majority Text reads simply "How [is it that] you do not [understand]?", likely influenced by the parallel passage in Matthew. | **understand**: <note>original: "συνίετε"</note> Found in most manuscripts. Codex Vaticanus and Codex Bezae use the word "perceive" <note>original: "νοειτε"</note>, again mirroring the language of the Gospel of Matthew.

<summary>This page records the textual variations of Jesus's questions to his disciples about the two miraculous feedings, highlighting his frustration with their lack of spiritual insight. The critical apparatus compares ancient Greek uncials and Latin versions to determine the most authentic wording of his rebuke.</summary>

<header>8, 22. ACCORDING TO MARK</header>

## 22 <margin>81.10</margin> And they come to Bethsaida. And they bring a blind man to him, and they entreat him that he might touch him. 23 And taking the blind man’s hand, he led him out of the village; and having spit on his eyes, and having laid his hands upon him, he asked him if he saw anything. 24 And looking up, he said: "I see men, for I see them walking like trees." 25 Then again he placed his hands upon his eyes, and he saw clearly <note>The Greek verb *dieblepsen* implies a restoration of full, penetrating sight.</note>

---

22. **they come**: <note>original: "ερχονται"</note> This plural form is supported by the major manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Bezae (D), and others. Latin versions vary between the present "they come" (*veniunt*) and the perfect "they came" (*venerunt*). The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> uses the singular "he comes" <note>original: "ερχεται"</note> based on the Alexandrinus (A) and other later manuscripts. | **Bethsaida**: <note>original: "βηθσαιδαν"</note> Spellings vary between *Bethsaidan* and *Bethsaida*. Interestingly, Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions read **Bethany** <note>original: "βηθανιαν"</note> instead. | **a blind man**: Manuscript Δ <note>Codex Sangallensis</note> adds "who was demon-possessed."

23. **taking the hand**: <note>original: "επιλαβ. της χειρος"</note> Codex Bezae (D) uses a slightly different Greek phrasing for "grasping the hand." | **of the blind man**: Manuscripts 1, 2pe, and 3pe read "his hand"; others combine them to say "the hand of the blind man himself." | **he led him out**: <note>original: "εξηνεγκεν"</note> Versions vary on the specific verb for leading out. Latin manuscripts use a variety of terms: *duxit* (led), *eduxit* (led out), *produxit* (brought forth), or *eicit* (cast out). | **having laid**: <note>original: "επιθεις"</note> Several manuscripts (including 1, 13, 69) and Old Latin versions add "and" before this action, making it a sequence of events: "and he spit... and he laid." | **upon him**: <note>original: "αυτω"</note> Some manuscripts (A, K, Δ) read "his [hands]" <note>original: "αυτου"</note> while others, like the Coptic and Peshitta Syriac, include both "on him" and "his hands." | **he asked**: <note>original: "επηρωτα"</note> Codex Bezae (D) uses the present tense "he asks." | **if he sees [anything]**: <note>original: "βλεπει"</note> Supported by most manuscripts. However, Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and Codex Bezae (D) read "Do you see anything?" <note>original: "Τι βλεπεις"</note> as a direct question.

24. **he said**: <note>original: "ελεγεν"</note> Supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. Some (like C) use the simple past "he said" (*eipen*), while others (D, N) use the present "he says" (*legei*). | **for I see [men] walking like trees**: <note>original: "οτι ως δενδρ. ορω περιπατ."</note> This phrasing is found in the oldest majuscules (א, A, B, C, L). However, Griesbach and Scholz’s editions, following other manuscripts and the Vulgate, omit the words "for" and "I see," resulting in the simpler: "men walking like trees."

25. **Then**: <note>original: "ειτα"</note> Found in the Vulgate, Coptic, and several Old Latin versions. It is replaced by "And" in others, or omitted entirely in the Syriac and Armenian versions. | **he placed**: <note>original: "επεθηκεν"</note> Most manuscripts use this form, though Vaticanus (B) and Regius (L) use a simpler form of the verb "to place" (*ethēken*). | **hands**: Sinaiticus (א) and the Coptic versions add "his." | **and he saw clearly**: <note>original: "και διεβλεψεν"</note> This specific reading is in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. There is significant variation here: Codex Bezae (D) and the Vulgate read "and he began to look up" (*et coepit videre*); the Textus Receptus (ς) and Lachmann read "and he made him look up" <note>original: "και εποιησεν αυτον αναβλεψαι"</note>; the Armenian version says "and he opened [his eyes] and saw." Griesbach marks this final section as doubtful.

<summary>This page covers the healing of the blind man at Bethsaida (Mark 8:22-25), notable for being the only miracle in the Gospels that occurs in two stages. The critical apparatus documents the high level of variation in early manuscripts regarding the specific wording of the man's recovery.</summary>

and he was restored, and began to see everything clearly. 26 And he sent him to his home, saying: "Do not even enter the village."

<margin>
27-30

**25. he was restored**: <note>original: "απεκατεστη"</note> (Manuscript B reads <note>original: "απōκ."</note>) found in manuscripts א, B, C, L, Δ, and a few others... (varying the word order).

**28. they spoke**: <note>original: "ειπαν"</note> with א, B, C, L, Δ, and Coptic/Syriac versions... the Textus Receptus and Lachmann read "they answered" <note>original: "απεκριθησαν"</note> with A, D, N, X, Γ, Π, and almost all others. Additionally, the phrase **saying to him** <note>original: "αυτω λεγοντες"</note> is supported by א, B, C, D, L, Δ, and several minuscules and Latin versions.

The if') 'you can believe'; all things" (the 1624/1633 editions have: 'believe, all things'), etc.; Lachmann reads: "to him: The 'if you can believe,' all things are possible to the one who believes."

**25.** **And seeing** in א, A, B, C, L, N, Γ, Δ, Π, nine uncials, and nearly all others, Coptic, Gothic, both Syriac versions, etc.; manuscript d and Old Latin (and when he saw; but f reads "but when he had seen") and the Vulgate read "and when he saw" | **the crowd** in א, A, L, M, S, X, Δ, Π, 28, 33, 69, 124, and about 50 others, plus Armenian... the Received Text and Lachmann read "a crowd" with B, C, D, N, Γ, seven uncials, and most others (1 and 118 add "a large crowd") | **saying**: Manuscript D reads "having said" | **to it**: manuscripts 235, 2pe and a few others, and Old Latin a and q omit this | **the mute and deaf spirit** in א, B, C*, D, L, Δ, 1, 33, 73, 118, 2pe, Old Latin, and Vulgate (a, f, ff², i, l, q and the Vulgate read: "deaf and mute spirit," which manuscript a places after "I command you"; c and k read "mute and deaf spirit," b reads "deaf unclean spirit," Coptic and Armenian also agree (Didymus the Blind in *On the Trinity* 3,21: "the mute," he says, "and deaf demon, I command you, come out") ... the Received Text reads "the spirit, the mute and deaf" with A, C³, N, X, Γ, Π, nine uncials, most others, Gothic, and Syriac versions ("deaf spirit who does not speak") and Ethiopic | **I**: א* and 33 and the Vulgate (Codex Gat) omit this | **command you** in א, B, C, L, Δ, 33, ff², k, the Clementine Vulgate and a few manuscripts, Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic... the Received Text and Lachmann read "you command" <note>changing word order</note> with A, D, N, Γ, Π, nine uncials, most others, Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, Armenian, and Didymus | **out of** <note>Greek: "ex"</note> in א, A, B, C³, D, L, N, Γ, Π, and nine uncials, most others, and Gothic... Lachmann reads "away from" <note>Greek: "ap"</note> with C*, Δ and six others, as well as the Old Latin and Vulgate.

**25.** *enter*: Manuscripts E, L, X, Γ, and a few others use a different spelling of the Greek verb. *Compare the writings of John Chrysostom* <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> <sup>6,555</sup>: "The Master did not say: 'I charge you, mute and deaf demon,' but 'I command you—come out of him.'" *Again indeed* <sup>8,26</sup>: "I say to you, the demon, the deaf and mute, come out of him"; *likewise* <sup>441</sup>: "I say to you, the demon, come out of him."

**26.** **crying out and convulsing**: The masculine form of these words is found in manuscripts א, B, C (original hand), D, L, (Δ)... while the Received Text <note>ς, the standard 16th-century Greek text</note> uses the neuter form <note>matching the gender of the word 'spirit'</note> with manuscripts A, C (third corrector), N, X, Γ, Π, nine other uncials, and many others | **greatly**: Manuscript Δ and others place "greatly" before "and convulsing" | **convulsing**: The word appears without the object "him" in the original hand of Sinaiticus (א) and various Latin versions... the Received Text adds "him" with manuscripts A, C, N, X, Γ, Π, nine uncials, and most ancient versions (Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic) | **it came out**: Manuscript D and a few others add "from him" | **like**: Manuscript D uses a slightly different word for "as if" | **the many**: Found in manuscripts א, A, B, L, Δ... the Received Text omits the word "the" | **said**: One manuscript reads "saying."

**27.** **his hand**: Found in manuscripts א, B, D, L, Δ, 1, 13, and many others, as well as the Vulgate and Coptic... the Received Text and Tischendorf read "him by the hand" with manuscripts A, C, N, X, Γ, Π, and many others.

**28.** **when he had entered**: Found in manuscripts א, B, C, D, L, Δ, and many others... the Received Text and Tischendorf use a different grammatical form of "having entered" with manuscripts A, N, X, Γ, Π, and most others | **house**: A few manuscripts and Coptic versions add the word "the" before "house" :: *compare note at Mark 7:17* | **privately before 'asked him'**: Found in א, B, C (original hand), D, L, Δ, and the Vulgate... the Received Text places it after "asked him" with manuscripts A, C (third corrector), N, X, Γ, and others; some manuscripts read "they approached him privately and asked him, saying" :: *compare Matthew's account* | **asked**: Some manuscripts use the past tense "they questioned" or "they asked" | **Why** <note>Greek: 'hoti'</note>: Found in א, B, C, L, N, X, Γ, Δ, and many others... but manuscripts A, D, K, Π, and over 30 others use a different word for "why" <note>Greek: 'dia ti'</note>. One manuscript notes: *The word 'that' (hoti) is used instead of 'why' (dia ti); for so Matthew spoke; or 'questioned him' instead of 'they were saying to him'; for there are many such unusual usages in Mark.* | **able**: A few manuscripts use a slightly different spelling | **cast out**: Several manuscripts use a different accentuation here | **it**: A few manuscripts change the gender to "him."

**29.** **to them**: Some versions add "Jesus" | **by nothing... can come out**: One manuscript reads "is not able to come out," and another reads "does not go out" :: *compare Matthew* | **by prayer**: Found in the original hand of Sinaiticus (א), and some Old Latin manuscripts... the Received Text and Lachmann add **and fasting** with the corrected Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and almost all other manuscripts and versions, though the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions vary in how they emphasize "fasting."

*...and fasting.* <note>original: "και προσευχ."</note> <note>This note refers back to verse 29 on the previous page</note> Some manuscripts have this. (:: Similarly, in 1 Corinthians 7:5, the phrase "to fasting" was added to "to prayer" by a later hand. **30.** **from there also** <note>original: "κακειθεν"</note> with manuscripts א, B, D, L, Δ ... the Received Text <note>ς, the standard 16th-century Greek text</note> reads **and from there** <note>original: "και εκειθεν"</note> with A, C, N, X, Γ, Π, nine other uncials <note>large-letter parchment manuscripts</note>, and almost all others | **passed through** with א, A, B (corrected), C, L, N, X, Γ, Δ, nine other uncials, and nearly all, likewise the Latin versions reading *praetergrediebantur* <note>passed by</note> or *transiebant* <note>passed through</note> (including the Vulgate, and various Old Latin manuscripts), the Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian ... but manuscripts B (original hand), D (Greek text), and some Old Latin and Gothic versions read **were going**. | **know** <note>original: "γνοι"</note> with א, B, C, D, L ... the Received Text reads the variant spelling <note>original: "γνω"</note> with A, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π, and nearly all others.

**32.** **to ask:** some manuscripts read a simpler form of the verb "to ask."

**33.** **they came** (manuscript D reads "they entered") with א, B, D, and various minuscules <note>later manuscripts written in small cursive script</note> and the Vulgate and Syriac ... the Received Text reads **he came** with A, C, L, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π, and many others (:: Note: An <term>ecclesiastical reading</term> <note>a passage used in church liturgy</note> begins here, hence the name "Jesus" is added in various places) | **Caphar-naoum** <note>original: "καφαρναουμ"</note> with א, B, D, and most Latin and Coptic versions ... the Received Text reads **Caper-naoum** with A, C, L, N, X, Γ, Π, and most others | **were you discussing**: some manuscripts use a different past tense; manuscript Δ uses an infinitive; the Received Text adds **among yourselves** <note>original: "προς εαυτους"</note> with A, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π, and most others, but manuscripts א, B, C, D, L, and the Vulgate omit it.

**Verse 41.** It seems it was omitted due to redundancy <note>original: "vdtr propter pleonasmum omissum esse"</note>; if someone had introduced the word **mine**, I think they would have ejected the phrase **because you are Christ’s** <note>original: "oti chu este"</note>. ---

Manuscripts b, c, ff², i, k read **where there is**; manuscript 238 adds **into the unquenchable fire** (Sinaiticus reads **unquenchable**) along with the original and corrected hands of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and many others; likewise the Old Latin manuscripts d and r read **of the fire**; the Clementine Vulgate and Syriac Peshitta read **of the unquenchable fire**; manuscripts q and others read **unquenchable fire**... but Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others omit this, which Griesbach also notes.

44. The Textus Receptus <note>The standard Greek text used for centuries, often abbreviated as ς</note> and Lachmann include the phrase **where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched** following manuscripts such as Alexandrinus, Bezae, and many others, including most Old Latin versions and the Vulgate; the Syriac and Gothic versions also include it. Augustine, in *The Harmony of the Evangelists* (4.7) and *The City of God* (21.9), noted that the author was not reluctant to repeat these same words three times in one place. Irenaeus also writes (Against Heresies 165): **but the unjust and those who do not do works of righteousness he will send into the eternal fire, where their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished** <note>original: "iniustos autem et qui non faciunt opera iustitiae mittet in ignem aeternum, ubi vermis eorum non morietur et ignis non exstinguetur"</note>, though it is not entirely clear if he is relying specifically on this verse. We have omitted it following the earliest manuscripts like Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Ephraemi Rescriptus, as well as the Coptic and Armenian versions.

45. **And if**: Manuscript Bezae reads **And whenever** | **causes to stumble**: found in most major manuscripts; slight spelling variations appear in Sinaiticus and others | **it** (manuscript Δ reads **her**): the Coptic and Armenian versions add **cast it from you**, likely influenced by Matthew | **it is better**: found in the earliest manuscripts; Lachmann adds **for** in brackets based on manuscript Alexandrinus and others | **for you to enter**: standard reading, though many manuscripts vary the word order or use the dative form of **you**; some omit the word entirely | **into life**: some versions add **eternal**, though the earliest manuscripts do not. **Lame**: Manuscript Bezae and several Latin versions place this word before **to enter**. Additionally, for **lame**, Codex Sinaiticus reads **crippled or lame**, again showing influence from Matthew | **to be thrown** (some manuscripts read **to go away**): Sinaiticus places this after **into Gehenna** | **into Gehenna**: Most early manuscripts provide this without further addition; however, some manuscripts add **of fire**, and others (including the Textus Receptus) add **into the unquenchable fire**.

46. The Textus Receptus and Lachmann include the refrain **where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched** with the same supporting manuscripts as in verse 44. We have omitted it here for the same reasons as in verse 44.

47. **And if your eye causes you to stumble**: Manuscript Bezae reads **And if your eye is causing you to stumble**. Variations in the placement of the word **for you** occur between the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and the later Byzantine tradition | **with one eye**: translated in Latin as **with one eye** or **having one eye**.

<note>The following notes are the "critical apparatus," where scholars list differences between ancient copies of the Bible. Letters and symbols like ℵ, B, and D represent specific ancient leather books (codices).</note>

**17.** **kneeling**: Manuscripts D, 28, 69, 124, and 346 read "falling on his knees." <note>original: "γονυπετων"</note> Compare also the church father Clement of Alexandria, who says (regarding Mark): "for he says that [the man] ran up and falling on his knees entreated him, and that Jesus, looking at him, loved him." | **him** (the first instance): omitted by several Old Latin manuscripts, the Coptic, Syriac, Gothic, Armenian versions, and Clement. | **asked him**: Manuscripts 13, 69, 121, 124, and others add **saying**. | **what**: Clement adds **good**, as it appears in the Gospel of Matthew.

Even the oldest Greek translations of the Old Testament vary in this same way. | **Do not steal**: Omitted in manuscript 300 and some Old Latin copies. | **bear false witness**: Manuscript D uses a slightly different Greek spelling. | **do not defraud**: The Old Latin and Vulgate translate this as "do not do fraud"; other early versions translate it as "do not deny." ***

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," where the editor compares different versions of the Greek text found in ancient manuscripts.</note>

**he says to them** <note>original: "ait illis"</note>: Manuscript c reads “to them again he says,” and manuscript q omits **answering** <note>original: "αποκρίθ." / "apokrith."</note> and reads “again he says to them.” So too does Clement of Alexandria. | **But again Jesus | says**: Manuscript Δ and a few others read **said**. | **children** <note>original: "τεκνα" / "tekna"</note>: Found in manuscripts ℵ, B, C, D, F, H, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ and many others. The scholar Lachmann <note>Ln</note> reads **little children** <note>original: "τεκνια" / "teknia"</note> following manuscripts A, N, and several others, as well as Clement. The Latin versions <note>it, vg</note> also use **little children** <note>original: "filioli"</note>. (Note: the form "little children" is used more often than "children" in the New Testament, especially in 1 John and John 13:33; however, the Latin translator, who rarely sides with manuscript A against the others, likely did not read "little children" here.) | **it is difficult**: Manuscript ℵ originally had a misspelling. This reading appears without any added phrases in manuscripts ℵ, B, Δ, and others. The scholar Stephanus <note>ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add the phrase **for those who trust in** <note>original: "τους πεποιθοτας επι" / "tous pepoithotas epi"</note> **riches** <note>original: "χρημασιν" / "chrēmasin"</note>. This addition is found in many manuscripts including A, C, D, N, X, and the Syriac, Gothic, and Armenian versions. Similarly, some Latin manuscripts add **who have money** or **those trusting in them**, while others like manuscript c mention nothing but **the rich man**. The Ethiopic version reads **for those who have wealth**. (Note: It seemed unsafe to desert the most ancient authorities we usually follow here. Such an addition clearly seemed necessary to later scribes, as they used three different ways to insert it; yet the sentence flows correctly even if nothing is added.) | **to enter**: Manuscripts 69, 124, and 346 place this earlier in the sentence.

**25. Clement of Alexandria** <note>Clem</note> **reads this way**: “Easier through the perforation of a needle a camel will enter than a rich man into the kingdom of God.” Similarly, those who place this verse between verses 23 and 24, such as Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note>, read: “Quicker a camel will pass through the perforation of a needle than a rich man into the kingdom of God” (though the Latin translation of D reads “it is easier for a camel...”). Manuscript a reads: “Easier a camel will enter through the hole of a needle...” | **easier** <note>original: "ευκοπωτερον" / "eukopōteron"</note>: Manuscript A adds **but**, others add **for**. | **camel**: One manuscript <note>bscr</note> and the Palestinian Syriac version <note>syrᵖ</note> transcribe the Greek word using Syriac letters. See similar notes in Matthew and Luke. | **the** <note>article</note>: Found twice in manuscripts B, E, G, H, etc. Some scholars <note>Griesbach and Lachmann</note> omit the first or second instance of the article “the” based on manuscripts ℵ, C, D, F, etc. (Note: At both positions, the reading fluctuates across the Gospels of Matthew and Luke.) | **eye** <note>original: "τρυμαλιασ" / "trymalias"</note>: Manuscript ℵ originally read **hole** <note>original: "τρηματος" / "trēmatos"</note>; others read **perforation** <note>original: "τρυπηματος" / "trypēmatos"</note>. | **needle** <note>original: "ραφιδοσ" / "rhaphidos"</note>: Some manuscripts and Clement use a different word for needle <note>original: "βελονησ" / "belonēs"</note>, as found in Luke. | **to pass through**: Found in B, C, D, K, and many Latin and Syriac versions. However, manuscripts ℵ, A, N, X, and others read **to enter**, as does the scholar Stephanus. (Note: It is extremely difficult to say which of the three Evangelists originally wrote "pass through" since the evidence is similar for all three. It is possible none of them wrote it and it was introduced by later editors; however, we preferred to keep it in Mark as the witnesses suggested.)

Most manuscripts include **the** <note>original: "τω" / "tō"</note> before **God**. | **for all things are possible** <note>original: "πάντα γὰρ δυνατὰ" / "panta gar dynata"</note>: Most manuscripts add **is** <note>original: "εστιν" / "estin"</note>. Manuscript B and others omit **the** before **God**. Some versions (like the Old Latin and Ethiopic) vary the phrasing to "but with God all things are possible" or "with the Lord everything is possible." A few manuscripts omit the entire phrase **for all things are possible with God**, likely trying to match the shorter versions in Matthew and Luke.

28. **began** <note>original: "ηρξατο" / "ērxato"</note>: Found in ℵ, A, B, C and others. The *Textus Receptus* reads **And Peter began** following manuscript D and others. Other manuscripts read **But Peter began**, **Then Peter began**, or simply **Peter began**. | **Peter began to say to him**: Variants include "Peter says to him," or "to him Peter began to say." | **followed** <note>original: "ηκολουθηκαμεν" / "ēkolouthēkamen"</note>: Found in B, C, D. The *Textus Receptus* uses a different Greek tense <note>original: "ηκολουθησαμεν" / "ēkolouthēsamen"</note> following ℵ and others, likely to match Matthew and Luke. | **you** <note>original: "σοι" / "soi"</note>: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) reads **your**. Some manuscripts and the Old Latin add **what then will there be for us?** <note>original: "τι αρα εσται ημιν" / "ti ara estai hēmin"</note>, taking the phrase directly from Matthew 19:27.

29. **Jesus said** <note>original: "εφη ο ις" / "ephē o is"</note>: Found in ℵ, B, Δ. Other editors (Griesbach, Lachmann) read **Jesus answering said** <note>original: "αποκριθεις ο ις ειπεν" / "apokritheis o is eipen"</note> following manuscripts A, M, S, and others, as well as the Latin and Syriac versions.

# 10, 41. ACCORDING TO MARK

<margin>
Verses 41—45

Parallel to Luke 22, 25—27

41 <gloss>Section 114, subsection 2</gloss> And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant with James and John. 42 And Jesus called them to him and said to them: "You know that those who are recognized as rulers of the Gentiles <note>The non-Jewish nations</note> lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. 43 But it is not so among you; but whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, 44 and whoever among you wishes to become—

<note>The following section is the 'critical apparatus,' where the editor compares different ancient versions of the Bible to identify changes made by scribes over centuries.</note>

[...to be given] **to those for whom it has been prepared**): Codex Sinaiticus (א) in its original hand and later corrections, minuscules 1, 209, and five others, the Old Latin 'a', and the margin of the Syriac Philoxenian add "by my Father" <note>original: "υπο του πατρος μου"</note> (likely imported from the Gospel of Matthew). On the contrary, the Catena of Moscow 204 and Oxford 386 state: "whence even Mark has not said 'by my Father'."

**43.** **So**: variant spellings of the Greek word for "so" <note>original: "ουτως" vs "ουτω"</note> appear across various manuscripts. | **But**: (also in Latin, Coptic, Gothic, and Syriac versions): Codex Bezae and several Old Latin versions omit this (following Matthew). | **it is**: (editor Tischendorf prefers this) supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and several others... The Received Text and others flip the order to **to become among you great**. Codex Bezae reads **to be great among you**, while many Old Latin and other versions use similar variations of "to be" or "to become." | **shall be**: supported by most major manuscripts... Codex Sinaiticus, C, X, and others read **let him be** <note>original: "εστω"</note> (a command rather than a future statement). The editor believes **let him be** should be rejected here because it is unlikely Mark would use the command form in this verse but the future form in the next; the command form was likely added by a scribe to match the Gospel of Matthew. | **your servant**: supported by almost all major uncials and versions... the Received Text flips the order to **servant of you**.

<note>The following notes are technical comparisons of how this passage appears in different ancient manuscripts. Biblical scholars use these to determine the most original wording of the New Testament.</note>

**Verse 406.** a few others including Old Latin and the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> place "to say" after "have mercy on me, Jesus, son of David." Manuscript 'k' reads: "Son of David, have mercy on me, Jesus."

Origen notes that Jesus did not call him himself, as in Matthew's version, but commanded him to be called. | "**And they call the blind man, saying to him**": Manuscript D and several Old Latin versions read "**but they say to the blind man**." | "**Take heart**": several manuscripts use variations meaning "being encouraged." | "**get up**": variations in the Greek spelling between <note>εγειρε</note> and <note>εγειραι</note> or <note>εγειρου</note>.

**Verse 50.** "**throwing off**": one manuscript reads "**putting on**." | "**jumped up**" <note>original: αναπηδησας</note> is supported by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads "**rising up**" <note>original: αναστας</note>. **Verse 51.** "**Jesus said to him**": supported by the major early codices. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads "**Jesus says to him**." | "**for you**" <note>original: σοι</note> before "**what do you want**": supported by Vaticanus and others. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> places it after "**to do**." | "**Rabbouni**" <note>original: ραββουνι</note>: there are many spelling variations of this Aramaic word across manuscripts (Rabboni, Rabbonei, Rabouni). **52. And Jesus** <note>original Greek: ο δε ῑς</note>: This reading is found in Codex Sinaiticus, the Vulgate, and almost all other ancient versions. | **said** <note>original Greek: ειπεν; Latin: dixit</note>: Some manuscripts use "says" <note>Greek: λεγει; Latin: ait</note>. | **immediately** <note>original: ευθυσ</note>: Found in the oldest manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. **XI. 1. When they approach** <note>original: οτε εγγιζουσιν</note>: The Latin versions vary between "when they were approaching" <note>cum adpropinquarent</note> and "when they had approached" <note>cum adpropinquassent</note>. Most early manuscripts use the Greek-style *Hierosolyma*, while some later ones use the Semitic-style *Hierousalem*. | **and to Bethany** <note>original: και εισ βηθανιαν</note>: There is significant variation here. Others use the past tense "**he sent**" <note>απεστειλεν</note>.

**2. and he says** <note>original: και λεγει</note>: This is the reading in several Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate <note>Latin: *ait* or *dicit*</note>, and the scholar Origen. | Some manuscripts (such as Codex Bezae) read "and he said" <note>original: και ειπεν</note>, while others use "saying" <note>original: λεγων</note>. | **opposite** <note>original: κατεναντι</note>: A few manuscripts use a slightly different Greek word for "opposite" <note>original: απεναντι</note>. | **opposite you**: This phrase is missing in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus <note>$\aleph$</note> but was added by a later corrector. It is possible these words were imported from the parallel accounts in Matthew and Luke. | **immediately** <note>original: ευθυσ</note>: Found in the primary early manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.). The Textus Receptus <note>$\varsigma$ — the traditional "Received Text" used for the King James Bible</note> and the editor Lachmann use a different form of the word <note>original: ευθεωσ</note> based on the majority of later manuscripts. | **into it** <note>original: εισ αυτην</note>: Found in Origen, the Vulgate, and Coptic versions; however, many Old Latin manuscripts omit this. | **no one among men has ever yet** <note>original: ουδεισ ανθρωπων ουπω</note>: There are many variations here. The earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) include "yet" <note>original: ουπω or πωποτε</note>. The Vulgate translates this as "no man yet of men" <note>Latin: *nemo adhuc hominum*</note>. Some later manuscripts and the scholar Tischendorf omit the word "yet." Origen notes that according to Mark and Luke, the colt was "tied, upon which no man has sat." | **untie it and bring** <note>original: λυσατε αυτον και φερετε</note>: This is the reading of the oldest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and the early versions (Latin, Vulgate, Coptic). | Other versions (the Textus Receptus and Codex Bezae) read "having untied it, lead it" <note>original: λυσαντεσ... αγαγετε</note>, which matches the wording found in Matthew and Luke.

**3. if**: Some manuscripts use a different Greek form for "if" <note>original: αν instead of εαν</note>. | **says to you**: Codex Delta reverses the order to "to you says." | **Why are you doing this?** <note>original: τι ποιειτε τουτο</note>: This is the standard reading in the oldest manuscripts and the Coptic/Gothic versions. The Latin versions read "What do you do this?" <note>Latin: *quid hoc facitis*</note>. | Some manuscripts (Codex Bezae and others) read "Why do you untie the colt?" <note>original: τι λυετε τον πωλον</note>, which mirrors the wording in Luke. | **say** <note>original: ειπατε</note>: The oldest manuscripts omit the word "that" <note>original: οτι</note> before the quote. The Textus Receptus and several editors include "that," matching the style of Matthew and Luke. | **immediately** <note>original: ευθυσ</note>: Found in the earliest manuscripts; later ones use a different form <note>original: ευθεωσ</note>. | **sends** <note>original: αποστελλει</note>: Found in the majority of early manuscripts and the Gothic and Syriac versions. | The Textus Receptus and some later manuscripts use the future tense "will send" <note>original: αποστελει</note>, similar to the Gospel of Matthew. | **back/again** <note>original: παλιν</note>: Found in the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae) and Origen. However, the Textus Receptus and editors like Tischendorf omit it. The editor Schulz notes that "again" is very characteristic of Mark’s writing style and should not be quickly dismissed.

The Textus Receptus <note>$\varsigma$</note> and Lachmann read **they brought** <note>original: ηγαγον</note> (similar to Matthew and Luke) with Alexandrinus <note>A</note> and most others. | **they throw** <note>original: επιβαλλουσιν</note> with Sinaiticus <note>$\aleph$</note>, Vaticanus <note>B</note>, and Bezae <note>D</note>... The Textus Receptus <note>$\varsigma$</note> reads **they threw** <note>original: επεβαλον</note> with Alexandrinus <note>A</note> and the majority of manuscripts. | **their garments** <note>original: τα ιματ. αυτων</note> (also found in the Vulgate and most versions; manuscript d reads "his"): Omitted by some Old Latin and Armenian manuscripts. | **he sat** <note>original: εκαθισεν</note>: Some manuscripts use **he sits** <note>original: καθιζει</note>... Sinaiticus and others read **they sat** <note>original: εκαθισαν</note>. | **upon it** <note>original: επ αυτον</note> with Sinaiticus <note>$\aleph$</note>, Vaticanus <note>B</note>, and Bezae <note>D</note>... The Textus Receptus <note>$\varsigma$</note> reads a slightly different Greek form for **upon it** <note>original: επ αυτω</note> with Alexandrinus <note>A</note> and many others. Most Latin versions read **upon him** <note>Latin: super eum</note>. Origen omits the text from "and he sat" to the next verse.

8. **and many** <note>original: και πολλοι</note> with Sinaiticus <note>$\aleph$</note>, Vaticanus <note>B</note>, and early versions... The Textus Receptus <note>$\varsigma$</note> and Lachmann read **but many** <note>original: πολλ. δε</note> with Alexandrinus <note>A</note> and others.

onto the road, while others cut leafy branches from the fields. 9 <margin>119. 1</margin> And those leading the way and those following were shouting: "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! 10 Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest heaven!"

8. <note>Regarding "their garments" in verse 8</note> 8 uncial manuscripts <note>large-lettered Greek manuscripts</note> and nearly all others, as it seems, including the Latin, Sahidic Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Gothic versions | **their garments** <note>original: τα ιματια αυτων</note>: The manuscript L (and the manuscript "i" in Blanchini's edition, though likely by error) omits **their**; manuscript B uses **their own** <note>original: εαυτων</note>, and manuscript $\aleph$ <note>Sinaiticus</note> uses **his**. | **they spread** <note>original: εστρωσαν</note> (as in Matthew): manuscripts d, 1, 28, 63, 91, 209, 241, 299, and 2$^{pe}$ use the imperfect tense **they were spreading** <note>original: εστρωννυον</note> (similar to Luke); likewise the Latin manuscripts a, b, c, ff$^2$, i, k and the Syriac; on the other hand, the Latin manuscripts f, l, g, the Vulgate, Armenian, and Gothic use **they spread**. | **into the road** <note>original: εις την οδον</note> according to manuscripts $\aleph$, B, C, D, L, X, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, 6 uncials, and many others; whereas manuscripts A, K, M, N, $\Pi$, and about 20 others, along with Latin and Armenian versions, read **in the road** <note>original: εν τη οδω</note> (similar to Matthew and Luke). | **but others**: manuscripts $\Pi$*, 1, 299, about 10 others, and the Syriac omit **but** <note>original: δε</note>. | **leafy branches** <note>original: στιβαδ. / στουβαδ.</note>: manuscripts $\aleph$, B, D, E, G, H, K, L, M, U, $\Delta$, $\Pi$, and about 30 others, along with Origen, use the spelling *stibadas*; whereas manuscripts A, C, S, V, X, $\Gamma$, and many others use *stoibadas*. Note that the ancient scholar Eustathius derives *stibas* from the word for "treading," calling it a **cheap and trampled-down bed** <note>original: ευτελη και καταπεπατημενην στρωμνην</note>; however, the lexicographer Zonaras states: **a "stoibas" is a bed for luxury or soft living** <note>original: η στρωμνη η τρυφης θρυψις</note>, from the word for "piling up." | **having cut from the fields** <note>original: κοψαντες εκ των αγρων</note>: manuscripts $\aleph$, B, L, $\Delta$, and the Sahidic Coptic (which reads *in the fields*). Other Coptic versions add **and they spread them in the road**. Origen, in one passage, writes: **others cut branches from the fields and spread them in the road**; elsewhere he contrasts this with Matthew's "branches cut from trees." The Ethiopic version translates this as: **and many were spreading leaves they had cut; and there were those who spread their clothes in the road.** The common "Received Text" used for centuries reads **they were cutting branches from the trees and spreading them in the road** (similar to Matthew), supported by manuscripts A, D, N, X, $\Gamma$, $\Pi$, and 8 uncials.

9. **and those leading** <note>original: και οι προαγ.</note>: manuscript $\Gamma$ adds **but**, and the Sahidic Coptic omits "and." | **were shouting**: manuscripts $\aleph$, B, C, L, $\Delta$, and several others provide this without additions; the "Received Text" adds **saying** <note>original: λεγοντες</note>, supported by manuscripts A, D, N, X, $\Gamma$, $\Pi$, and many others (following the phrasing in Matthew). | **Hosanna**: manuscript L spells it *Hosana*; manuscript D and some Latin versions omit it entirely. Conversely, some manuscripts add **in the highest** or **in the heights**. | **he who comes**: manuscript "x" omits this.

10. **Blessed** <note>original: ευλογημενη</note>: Supported by $\aleph$, B, C, L, and most others. Manuscripts A, D, K, M, and $\Pi$ add **and** <note>original: και</note> before it. | **coming**: omitted by several manuscripts, including the Latin manuscript "k". | **kingdom**: Supported by $\aleph$, B, C, D, L and many others; the "Received Text" adds **in the name of the Lord** <note>original: εν ονοματι κυριου</note> (similar to the previous verse), supported by manuscripts A, N, X, $\Gamma$, and $\Pi$.

*to see if perhaps he would find anything on it; and when he came to it, he found nothing except*

---

...the phrase "and blessed is the coming kingdom in the name of the Lord, of our father David" is excellently stated; for in many places the prophets said that the kingdom according to our Lord <note>abbreviated as "ιν χν" for Iesoun Christon</note> Jesus Christ would come in the name of David, etc. Likewise, Euthymius <note>a 12th-century commentator</note> explicitly on Matthew 21:9 | **David**: <note>original: δαυειδ</note> the standard text <note>represented by the symbol ς</note> reads *Dabid*; Griesbach and Scholz read *Dauid*; see the note at Matthew 1:1 | **Hosanna**: (Codex Bezae <note>D*</note> reads *ossanna*; see the note at verse 9): manuscripts 1, 91, 118, 209, 299 add "peace in heaven and glory in the highest" <note>likely imported from Luke’s Gospel</note>; the Armenian version omits "Hosanna in the highest"; manuscript 251 and the Peshitta Syriac <note>syr$^P$</note> add this note before "Hosanna": "This is not found in all Greek copies, nor in that of Mar Xenaias; however, we found it in some accurate ones, as we believe."

11. **he entered** (The Old Latin manuscript g$^1$ and the Vulgate read *he entered*; manuscript q reads *he went in*; manuscript k reads *they entered*): Codex Bezae <note>D</note> reads **having entered**, as do Old Latin manuscripts a, b, c, f, ff$^2$, g$^2$, and i, reading *when he had entered* (or *had entered* collectively) | **into Jerusalem** (Griesbach marks this as probable): following the earliest manuscripts $\aleph$, B, C, D, L, $\Delta$, and others; the standard text <note>ς</note> adds **Jesus** along with Codex Alexandrinus <note>A</note> and many others, as do the Gothic, Syriac, and Armenian versions | **temple**: The margin of Codex $\Delta$ reads **sanctuary** <note>original: ναον</note> | **and (second instance)**: found in the Greek side of Codex Bezae, Old Latin a and b, the Syriac, and Armenian | **into the** following manuscripts $\aleph$, B, C, L, M, $\Delta$, and others; the standard text <note>ς</note> reads **and into the temple** following Codex Alexandrinus, Bezae, and many others | **temple**: The margin of Codex $\Delta$ reads **sanctuary** | **and (second instance)**: omitted in the Greek side of Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts (manuscript "a" reads *having entered - looking around*; others read *when he had entered, he looked around*. Conversely, the Vulgate reads *he entered - and having looked around at all things*) | **late**: following $\aleph$, C, L, and $\Delta$ (which adds **but**); the standard text and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read **of evening** <note>original: οψιας</note> following A, B, D, and the vast majority of manuscripts | Codex Bezae <note>D*</note> reads **being** <note>feminine plural variant</note> | **the** (omitted by Codex Bezae and others) **hour** (some manuscripts read **day**): omitted by Codex Vaticanus <note>B</note>. Manuscripts 40 and 72 (manuscripts with commentary) add in the margin: **"the Jews being unworthy, in other copies."** | **he went out**: Codex Sinaiticus <note>$\aleph$</note> reads **and he went out** | **twelve** (so in most Latin and the Vulgate): Codex Bezae and others add **disciples** (some add **his disciples**)

12. **as they were leaving** (some manuscripts omit **they**): Codex Bezae reads **having gone out** <note>singular</note>, as does Codex $\Gamma$. Similarly, several Old Latin manuscripts read *when he had gone out* or *when he was going out*, as does the Syriac (though others read *when they had gone out* or *when they were going out*) | **from Bethany**: omitted in manuscripts 1 and 299 | The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus <note>$\aleph$*</note> omits **he was hungry** (later added by a corrector).

13. **a fig tree**: supported by most major manuscripts and the Vulgate (Codex Bezae and others place this after **from a distance**) ... Codex Sinaiticus and others add the word **one** <note>original: μιαν, implying "a single fig tree"</note>, likely from Matthew's account | **from** (Griesbach and Scholz consider this probable): following $\aleph$, A, B, C, D, and others; the standard text <note>ς</note> omits it with the majority of later manuscripts | **if perhaps he would find anything**: (different Greek spellings for "find" appear in various manuscripts); the Vulgate reads *if by chance he might find anything*; Codex Bezae and others read **to see if there is anything**.

<note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," where scholars compare different ancient copies of the Bible to find variations in the text.</note>

**[Verse 14-15 variants]**: The Sahidic and Ethiopic versions and manuscript 126 omit "where..." | The word "but" <note>original: αλλ</note> is supported by manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and others... The Old Latin manuscript g1, the Vulgate, and several Coptic and Syriac versions follow Lachmann <note>a scholar known for early critical editions</note> in reading "tell us therefore" <note>original Latin: "dic nobis ergo"</note> (though some manuscripts read "they said"). **15.** "But he": Manuscripts D, G, and several others (including Latin and Armenian versions) add the name "Jesus" <note>original: ις</note> :: compare with Matthew | "Seeing" <note>original: ιδων</note> is found in Sinaiticus and D... while the editions of Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "knowing" <note>original: ειδωσ</note> following most major manuscripts (Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.). <note>This highlights a subtle difference between Jesus "seeing" their trickery vs. "knowing" it intuitively.</note> | "Test me": Several manuscripts (N, F, G) and the Syriac and Armenian versions add "you hypocrites" :: from the Gospel of Matthew | "Denarius": Manuscripts E, K, L and others use a different spelling <note>original: διν.</note>. **37. himself:** found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and several others, as well as various Old Latin, Sahidic, and Coptic versions. **39. front seats:** several manuscripts show slight spelling variations in the Greek word for "front seats" or "places of honor."

**40. who devour:** Sinaiticus and others use one spelling <note>original: "katesthiontes"</note>, while Vaticanus uses a slightly different form. Codex Bezae and others use a different verb form <note>original: "katesthiousin"</note> | **the [houses] and of the [widows]:** Codex Bezae and one other omit these articles | **widows:** Codex Bezae and several others add *and orphans* | **and:** Omitted by Codex Bezae and many Latin and Syriac versions | **for a pretext... long [prayers]:** Various manuscripts use different Greek and Latin forms for "pretext" or "guise," with some Latin versions reading *under the cover of long prayer* or *by occasion of long prayers*.
