<header>13, 3. ACCORDING TO MARK</header>

[thrown] down. **3** <gloss>138. 2</gloss> And as he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, *Peter* and *James* and *John* and *Andrew* asked him privately: **4** “Tell us, when will these things be? And what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” **5** And *Jesus* began to say to them: “See that no one leads you astray. **6** For many—”

---

<note>The following notes represent the "apparatus criticus," a record of how different ancient hand-written copies (manuscripts) of the Bible differ from one another.</note>

<note>Refers to the end of verse 2</note> Not wavering <note>original: "non fluct"</note>, compare also the Gospel of Luke. Found in Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), Sangallensis (G), and several other ancient Greek manuscripts and early Latin versions. The Armenian version transposes some words. Some Latin versions (manuscripts 'e' and 'k') say **in the temple**, and manuscript 'c' says **in this temple**. Similarly, the church father Cyprian (in *Testimonies* 1, 15) says: *In the Gospel the Lord says: there shall not be left in the temple stone upon stone which shall not be dissolved, and: After three days another shall be raised without hands.* | **upon a stone** <note>original: "επι λιθον"</note>: found in most major manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Some older scholarly editions (Lachmann and Tischendorf) use a slightly different grammatical case <note>original: "επι λιθω"</note> based on other manuscripts. | **which shall not be thrown down**: found in the majority of manuscripts. A few manuscripts use a slightly different future tense form. 
Furthermore, Codex Bezae (D) and several Old Latin manuscripts (a, b, c, ff2, etc.) and Cyprian add the phrase: **and after three days another shall be raised without hands**, <note>original: "και δια τριων ημερων αλλος αναστησεται ανευ χειρων"</note> mirroring the Latin: *and after three days another will be raised without hands* (variants of this phrase appear in several Latin manuscripts, some using "after three days," others "in three days," or "on the third day"). This likely refers to the "temple of his body" mentioned in Mark 14:58 and John 2:19.

**3.** **And as he was sitting**: Manuscript L omits the word **and**; a few others use **but** or **therefore**. | **of the temple**: Manuscript 'k' mistakenly writes **of the mountain**. | **he was asking** <note>original: "επηρωτα"</note>: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. The scholarly edition by Lachmann and many later manuscripts use the plural **they were asking** <note>original: "επηρωτων"</note>. | **privately**: Codex Sinaiticus has a slight spelling variation; two other manuscripts omit this word entirely. | **Peter**: Some manuscripts include the definite article (**the** Peter), while others, followed by Lachmann and Tischendorf, omit it. | **James and John**: A few manuscripts swap the order to **John and James**. | **John**: Codex Vaticanus and the original hand of Sinaiticus spell this with only one 'n' in the Greek <note>original: "ιωανης"</note>.

**4.** **Tell** (plural): Found in the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae). The common medieval text (Textus Receptus) uses the singular **Tell** <note>original: "ειπε"</note>. | **these things will be**: One manuscript writes **these things are**. | **when** <note>original: "οταν"</note>: A few manuscripts use a different Greek word for **when** <note>original: "οτε"</note>. | **is about to** <note>original: "μελλη"</note>: Most manuscripts use this form, though Tischendorf chose a slightly different spelling <note>original: "μελλει"</note> based on Codex Bezae and others. | **all these things are about to be accomplished**: There is significant variation in word order here between the oldest Greek manuscripts and various Latin, Coptic, and Syriac translations. Some manuscripts omit the word **all** <note>original: "παντα"</note>.

**5.** **And Jesus**: Found in the oldest manuscripts. The common medieval text (Textus Receptus) adds the word **answering** <note>original: "αποκριθεισ"</note>, resulting in **And Jesus answering them began to say**. This addition is found in many later manuscripts and some Latin versions. | **began to say to them**: This reading is well-supported by the oldest Greek and Latin sources.

<note>The following notes represent the "critical apparatus," where scholars compare different ancient copies of the Bible. Letters like A, B, and D refer to specific famous manuscripts, such as Codex Vaticanus or Codex Bezae.</note>

The Latin versions (l, q, Vulgate), Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac (Peshitta), and Ethiopic... the "Received Text" <note>original: "ς"</note> includes **to them he began to say** <note>original: "αυτ. ηρξ. λεγ."</note> with manuscripts A, E, F, H, K, M (original hand), S, V, X, Gamma, Pi and many others; likewise **he began to say** but with **to them** placed between **answering** and **Jesus** in manuscript G and a few others; likewise manuscripts M (corrected), Delta, 69, 124, 157, 346, and the 2nd Petropolitanus have **he began to say to them**... **6. many**: with Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), and Ephraemi Rescriptus (L) (recorded by Blanchini, but not by Alter), Ethiopic, and Persian versions... the "Received Text" <note>original: "ς"</note> and the editor Lachmann add **for** <note>original: "γαρ"</note> with manuscripts A, D, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, nine other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note> and almost all others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian versions. :: But this is how it appears in both Matthew and Luke; Mark, however, is fond of writing without such conjunctions, as evidenced by many examples where editors often substituted what seemed most fitting from parallel passages (see notes on 3:35; 4:28; 9:24; 10:27, 28, 39; 11:23; 12:6, 24, 29, 31, 36, 37). | **in** <note>original: "επι"</note> (Old Latin and Vulgate: *in*): Manuscript G has **in** <note>original: "εν"</note>. | **my name**: Latin manuscript 'k' adds **false prophets**. | **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> (so also 'a', 'i', 'l', and the Vulgate): Manuscripts D, 33, and a few others, along with 'b', 'c', 'ff2', 'g2', 'k', 'q', and 'gat', omit it. :: As in Matthew. | **I am**: Manuscripts 13, 28, 61, 69, 124, 346, and 5 others, with 'b', 'c', 'g2', 'l', 'gat', the Saxon version, Sahidic, Coptic, and Armenian add **the Christ**. :: As in Matthew.

**7. you hear** <note>original: "ακουσητε"</note>: with $\aleph$, A, D, L, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, 9 uncials, and almost all others (manuscript 69 has a different spelling). ... <note>The following section is the "apparatus criticus," a scholarly shorthand used to compare different ancient handwritten copies of the Bible to find the original wording.</note>

*...Armenian version... 17 <insert>161.4</insert> And when evening had come, he comes with the twelve. 18 And as they were reclining and eating, Jesus said: "Truly I say to you that one of you will betray me, the one who eats with me." 19 <insert>162.1</insert> They began to be grieved and to say to him one by one: "Surely not I?" 20 <insert>163.2</insert>

<note>The following section is the "Apparatus Criticus," a technical record of differences found in ancient hand-copied manuscripts. Scholars use these notes to determine the most likely original wording of the Bible.</note>

In the written copy it reads: **a large upper room, furnished, swept, and ready; there prepare for us** <note>original Latin: "exscriptum legitur ανωγεον μεγα εστρωμμενον σεσαρωμενον ετοιμον· εκει ετοιμασατε"</note> | **ready** <note>original: "etoimon"</note> appears with manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), B, C, D, L, M, P, X, Γ, Π, eight other uncials <note>Uncials are manuscripts written in all capital letters on parchment.</note> and many others, as well as the Old Latin, Syriac, and Coptic versions. . . Griesbach and Lachmann <note>Famous 18th and 19th-century biblical scholars.</note> include **ready** in brackets :: as in Luke | **and there** <note>original: "kakei"</note> with Sinaiticus, D, and others, or **and in that place** <note>original: "kai ekei"</note> in B, C, L. . . whereas other editions follow manuscripts A and P, simply reading **there** <note>original: "ekei"</note>, similar to Luke.

**16.** **the disciples** without the word "his" <note>original: "autou"</note> with Sinaiticus, B, L, and Δ. . . most other manuscripts (A, C, D, P) and versions (Latin, Syriac) include **his disciples** | The Greek text of Codex Bezae (dGr) repeats the words **and his disciples went out**; the Latin side (d) reads: **and his disciples went away and his disciples came and he came into the city and they did just as...** | Sinaiticus (א*) omits **and they came** | **they found** (Δ reads "they were found"; manuscript k omits "and they found"): manuscripts D and several Old Latin versions read **they did**.

**17.** **and [when it was] evening** (also in k and Coptic): manuscripts D and various Latin versions read **but [when it was] evening** <note>original Latin: "opsia de"</note> :: as in Matthew | **twelve**: some Latin manuscripts add **disciples** or **his disciples**.

**18.** **Jesus said** <note>original: "ho Iesous eipen"</note> with Sinaiticus, B, C, L . . . others (A, P, Δ) read **said Jesus** <note>original: "eipen ho Iesous"</note>, which is a more common word order in such passages; others like Codex Bezae (D) read **Jesus says**, while the Vulgate and others read **Jesus said to them**. | **the one who eats** with Sinaiticus, A, C, D, L, P etc: manuscript B reads **of those eating** <note>original: "ton esthionton"</note>, which the scholar Schulz called "a good reading," and the Coptic versions are similar.

**19.** **they began** <note>original: "erxanto"</note> with Sinaiticus, B, L, Coptic, and Origen (who notes that Mark says "they began to be grieved") . . . whereas most other manuscripts (A, D, P) read **but they began** <note>original: "hoi de erxanto"</note> :: here again, Mark’s use of "asyndeton" <note>A Greek term for a style where sentences are not joined by connecting words like "but" or "and," creating a more direct, clipped tone.</note> is noticeable | **to him**: omitted by Sinaiticus and several Latin versions | **one by one** <note>original: "eis kata eis"</note> with Sinaiticus, B, L, Δ . . . others read **one by one** with a slightly different spelling <note>original: "eis kath eis"</note>. The scholar Beza proposed a change to "and then," but ancient writers like Plutarch and Eusebius use the "one by one" phrasing found here. . . manuscript c reads **each one** :: from Matthew. The Latin versions use various words for "one by one" or "singly." | **Surely not I?**: Manuscript A adds **am I, Rabbi?**, as do others and the Coptic version <note>This addition brings Mark's text into alignment with Matthew's account.</note>. Furthermore, after "I?", many manuscripts (A, D, W, etc.) and the Syriac add **and another [said], "Surely not I?"** We have omitted this along with Sinaiticus, B, C, L, and the Vulgate, as scholars like Griesbach and Schulz agree that after "one by one," this addition is unnecessary.

**20.** **And he** (Griesbach, likely Scholz) with manuscripts אBCDL [and various Old Latin and Syriac versions] ... the Received Text <note>The "Received Text" or *Textus Receptus* refers to the standard Greek printed text used for centuries, though modern scholars often prefer older manuscripts.</note> adds **having answered** (as in Matthew, where the reading does not vary) with manuscripts APW and almost all others, along with the Palestinian Syriac and others | **said**: manuscript D reads **says**, likewise manuscript k reads **he says**, while others [a c d f etc.] and the Vulgate read **he said** | **one of the twelve**: manuscripts m and k omit this | **one of** with אBCL ... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **one from among** with ADPW and many others (the Latin versions say "one from" or "of" the twelve, but the Latin cannot render the Greek 'one of' in any other way) | **the one dipping**: manuscript D reads **the one being dipped** | **with me** with אBCDPW and almost all seen versions, including the Coptic and Syriac. ### ACCORDING TO MARK 14, 30. 375

<margin>Zechariah 13:7</margin>
*"for it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered."* 28 <gloss>Section 169. Canon 6</gloss> *"But after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee."* 29 <gloss>Section 170. Canon 1</gloss> *And Peter said to him: "Even if all* <margin>29 and following; Luke 22:33; John 13:36 and following</margin>
*fall away, yet I will not."* 30 *And Jesus says to him: "Truly I say to you that today, this very night, before the rooster* <margin>Mark 14:72</margin>

---

<note>This section is the "critical apparatus," a technical list comparing different ancient manuscripts of the Bible.</note>

The Syriac (Curetonian and Philoxenian), Armenian, and Ethiopic versions; likewise some add **in me** <note>original: "en emoi"</note> without **in this night** in manuscript G, three other manuscripts, and Latin versions a, f, i, k, l; likewise **in this night** without **in me** in five or more manuscripts, including various Vulgate versions (Amiatinus, Emmeramus, Fuldensis, etc.), and the Saxon and Bede's versions | **for (Delta adds 'behold') it is written**: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and manuscript k read **for it is written** [with the word 'for' in a different position] | **the sheep** before **will be scattered** with manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), B, C, D, L, 13, 69, 115, 127, 346, 2pe, and versions i, k, q, Sahidic, and Armenian... The Received Text <note>The standard printed Greek text used for centuries.</note> and Lachmann place **the sheep** after **will be scattered** with manuscripts A, N, Wb, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, nine other uncials, most others, and Latin/Syriac versions :: but it is thus also in Matthew and the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> (see below) | **will be scattered** [plural: *diaskorpisthesontai*] with Sinaiticus (ℵ), A, B, C, D, F, G, K, L, M, Lambda, and many others... The Received Text reads **will be scattered** [singular: *diaskorpisthesetai*] with E, H, M, S, U, V, Wb, X, Gamma, Pi, and most others :: similarly the reading in Matthew fluctuates. Furthermore, after **the sheep will be scattered**, E, F, K, M, Pi, and twenty others along with Latin versions a and c add **of the flock** <note>original: "tēs poimnēs"</note> (from Matthew and the Septuagint). The Septuagint according to manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B) reads: *Strike the shepherds and draw out the sheep*; according to Alexandrinus (A) and the corrected Sinaiticus (ℵᶜ): *strike the shepherd and the sheep of the flock will be scattered* (ℵᶜ omits 'of the flock'). It is also helpful to compare Eusebius [Eusecl 1, 30] where the prophet wrote: *strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered*, but the evangelist wrote: *strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered*. Apply these notes to the study of Matthew.

**28. But after**: manuscript c reads **and after**, about 15 others read **but after** [using the particle *de*].

**29. said to him** (also ff², Sahidic; manuscripts c, k, and Armenian read **responded and said to him**): manuscript D reads **says to him**, while a, d, f, g¹, i, l, q, and the Vulgate read **said to him** or **to that one**... manuscripts 1, 13, 69, 124, 209, 346, 2pe, and Sahidic read **answering, he says** | **Even if** with manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), B, C, G, L, 1, 13, 69, and a few others and Armenian... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **And if** [Greek: *kai ei*] (D reads **and if** [Greek: *kai ean*], 2pe reads **even if** [Greek: *kan*]) with A, D, E, F, H, K, M, N, S, U, V, Wb, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, most others, Coptic, and Syriac. Likewise Latin versions a, c, f, ff², g¹, i, k, l, q, and Vulgate read **and if**... some others and Sahidic/Ethiopic simply read **if** | **will fall away** (D reads **might fall away**; Latin versions use the future or perfect tense): manuscripts E, G, U, 1, 108, 127, and eight others, and the edited Vulgate and Armenian manuscripts add **in you** <note>original: "en soi"</note> :: from Matthew | **yet I will not**: manuscript D reads **but I will not fall away** [using a double negative], while others and the Ethiopic read **but I will not be caused to stumble**.

**30. Jesus**: Sinaiticus (ℵ) omits | **you**: with A, B, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, N, S, U, V, Wb, X, Gamma, Pi, most others, and versions c, k, g¹, g², Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic... The Received Text omits (matching Matthew) with Sinaiticus (ℵ), C, D, Delta, and many others and versions a, f, ff¹, i, l, q | **today**: with Sinaiticus (ℵ), A, B, C, L, N, Wb, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, eight other uncials, and almost all versions: D, Sigma, 2pe, and versions a, f, ff², i, q, and Armenian omit (matching Matthew) | **this very night**: with Sinaiticus (ℵ), B, C, D, and versions a, f, ff², i, k, q... The Received Text reads **in this night** with A, N, Wb, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, eight uncials, most others, and versions c, g¹, g², l, and Vulgate... | **before**: Sinaiticus (ℵ), D, 69, 238, 2pe, and a few others omit the particle **that** [Greek: *ē*] | **twice**: with A, B, C², L, N, Wb, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, nine other uncials, most others, and versions f, g¹, g², l, q, Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac; but some versions place **twice** after **crowed**... manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), C*, D, 238, and versions a, c, ff², i, k, and others omit it (matching the accounts in Matthew, Luke, and John).

<note>The following notes are a "critical apparatus," used by scholars to track differences between the oldest surviving hand-written copies (manuscripts) of the New Testament.</note>

30. **you will deny me** <note>original: "me aparnese"</note>: (Manuscripts Sinaiticus, 99, 124 read "denying") with Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and a few others, and Old Latin versions a, c, ff$^2$, g$^{1.2}$, i, k, l, q, and the Vulgate... The Received Text reads **he said** <note>original: "elege"</note> with A, C, N, W$^b$, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, nearly all uncials, Latin a ("he was saying"), and the Sahidic, Coptic, and both Syriac versions. **33.** **Peter** <note>original: τον πετρον</note> (thus Manuscript Sinaiticus): the original hand of Sinaiticus and a few others omit the article "the" :: in the parallel passage in Matthew, the article does not fluctuate | **James** <note>original: ιακωβον</note> with Manuscripts Sinaiticus, C, D, E, F, G, H, M, N, S, U, V, W$^b$, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi and many others... the Received Text (as used by editors Griesbach and Scholz) reads **the James** with Manuscripts A, B, K, L, Pi and many others | **John** (Manuscript B reads "Johanni") with Manuscripts Sinaiticus, C, D, E, F, G, H, L, M, N, S, U, V, W$^b$, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi and many others... <note>The following section is the "apparatus criticus," a scholarly shorthand used to compare different ancient manuscripts. Abbreviations like "ℵ" refer to Codex Sinaiticus, "B" to Codex Vaticanus, and "vg" to the Latin Vulgate.</note>

"Take this cup from me" <note>original: παρενεγκε το ποτ. του. απ εμ.</note>. Likewise [in Origen's writings] *but less accurately*: "Father, if it be possible, take this cup from me; nevertheless not what, etc." ... Manuscripts DN and Origen read "this cup from me" (likewise Origen elsewhere *freely* reads "Father, if it be possible, take this cup from me"), Manuscripts K, M, Pi and some others, along with the Syriac and Ethiopic versions, read "from me this cup" (Manuscript c reads *this chalice*) ... The Received Text and editor Tischendorf read "the cup from me this" <note>original: το ποτη. απ εμου τουτο</note> with Manuscripts E, F, H, S, V, W$^b$ and many others | **but**: Manuscript Sinaiticus (ℵ) reads "nevertheless but" <note>original: πλην αλλ</note> (Origen reads "nevertheless") :: *compare with the Gospels of Matthew and Luke* | **not what** (the Latin versions read *non quod* or *quod non*): Manuscript D and 70 read "not" <note>original: ουχ</note>, others read "not yet," others "not as" <note>original: ουχ ως</note> | **I will**: Manuscript a reads *I say* <note>original: dico</note> | **but what**: Manuscript D and others read "but that which" or "but if anything," others "but as not" (Manuscript L and others read "to you"): Manuscripts D, a, c, f, and various ancient versions (Sahidic, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic) add **you will**.

**37.** **and says**: Manuscript A *omits* "and" | **to Peter**: Manuscript A *omits* the article "the" <note>In Greek, names often have the word "the" before them</note> | **could you [singular]**: (Manuscript Delta reads "could you [plural]") : Manuscripts D, 1, 69, 124, 209, 346 and others read **could you [plural]** <note>original: ισχυσατε</note> :: *this likely comes from the parallel in Matthew* | **to watch**: (Manuscripts 61 and c read "to keep awake"): Manuscripts F, 44, 64 and others *add* **with me** :: *this also likely comes from Matthew*.

**38.** **pray**: This is the spelling in Manuscripts B and w$^b$ | **so that not**: Manuscript D *omits* "so that" (Latin versions read *ut non* or *lest*) | **you [plural] enter**: (this matches Manuscript Sinaiticus, B, 346, and others, as well as early Church fathers like Cyprian) ... The Received Text and editor Lachmann read **you [plural] might enter into** <note>original: εισελθητε</note> (:: *as in Matthew and Luke*) with Manuscripts A, C, D, L, N and almost all others. In Matthew and Luke, no Greek manuscript uses "enter" <note>original: ελθητε</note> without the "into" prefix, though some Latin versions vary.

**39.** **he prayed**: Manuscripts 13, 69, and 346 read "he made a vow/prayed" <note>original: ηυξατο</note> | **saying the same word**: Manuscripts D, a, c, ff$^2$, and k *omit* this.

**40.** **returning he found them again**: (Some sources like the Sahidic and Sinaiticus move the word "again" to different spots in the sentence; others omit it): This word order follows Manuscripts A, C, N, W$^b$ and the Syriac/Armenian versions ... Editor Lachmann reads **returning he came and found them** (:: *matching Matthew*) following Manuscripts Sinaiticus, B, and L. Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions omit "again" | **their eyes**: (:: *matching Mark’s usual style; here the same order is found in Matthew*) with Manuscripts Sinaiticus, B, C, L, and Delta ... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **the eyes of them** with Manuscripts A, D, N and most others | **were very heavy** <note>original: καταβαρυνομενοι</note>: found in Manuscripts A, B, K, L, N, and others; Manuscript D reads "were burdened"; the original hand of Sinaiticus reads "had been burdened"; others read simply "were heavy" ... The Received Text reads "were heavy" <note>original: βεβαρημενοι</note> (:: *borrowed from Matthew*) with Manuscripts C, E, F, G, H, and many others | **answer him**: (word order varies between "to him answer" and "answer him"): found in Manuscripts Sinaiticus, A, B, C, D, L and many others ... the Received Text swaps the order with Manuscripts E, F, G, H and many more ... some versions omit "him" entirely.

<note>The following notes represent the "apparatus criticus," where the editor, Tischendorf, compares different ancient versions of the Bible to find the most accurate original text.</note>

**41.** **hereafter** <note>original: το λοιπον</note> with Manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and many others. The editors Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **hereafter** <note>original: λοιπον</note> without the article, following Manuscripts A, C, D, and about 160 others | **take your rest**: Manuscript D spells this slightly differently. The scholar Schulthess suggests that in both Mark and Matthew, this should be punctuated as a question <note>e.g., "Are you still sleeping and resting?"</note>, as seen in Manuscript F and a few others | **it is enough** <note>original: απεχει</note>: The Latin Vulgate translates this as *sufficit* (it is enough). This reading is confirmed by Saint Augustine, who noted that in Mark’s account, the phrase follows "take your rest" to mean "it is enough that you have rested." A few manuscripts add "the end" <note>original: το τελοσ</note> | **the hour has come**: Manuscript D reads "it is enough, the end and the hour [have come]," while some Old Latin versions (d, q) read "the end and the hour are sufficient." Other Latin versions read "the end is present, the hour has come." The Syriac versions read "the end has drawn near and the hour has come." After the phrase "sleep now," the Old Latin Manuscript k continues: "behold, he who betrays me has drawn near. And after a little while he woke them and said, 'Now is the hour, behold the Son of Man is delivered into the hands of sinners; rise, let us go,'" etc. | **the** [hands] with Manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and most others. > kissed him fervently. **46** But they laid their hands 

---

<note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," a specialized system used by scholars to compare different ancient versions of the New Testament to determine the most likely original wording.</note>

**43.** **from** <note>original: παρα</note>: Found in the Old Latin and Syriac versions, and the writings of Origen. Some manuscripts like Codex Bezae (D) use a different Greek word for "from" <note>original: απο</note>. | **the scribes**: Many ancient sources including Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B) include the word "the" before scribes, while others like Codex Alexandrinus (A) omit it. | **the elders**: A large group of manuscripts including the "majority text" used in later centuries include the word "the" here, though earlier versions like the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) and several others omit it. Origen once quoted this as "from the scribes and the Pharisees and elders."

**44.** **had given** <note>original: δεδωκει</note>: The Latin versions use the past perfect tense "had given" <note>original: dederat</note>, though the Greek Manuscript D uses "gave" <note>original: εδωκεν</note>, matching the wording in the Gospel of Matthew. | **a signal** <note>original: συσσημον</note>: This specific word for "signal" or "conspicuous sign" is found in the earliest manuscripts like Sinaiticus (ℵ). A few other manuscripts use the more common word for **sign** <note>original: σημειον</note>, again matching Matthew's phrasing. An ancient commentary by Victor of Antioch notes that "signal" here simply means "sign." | **lead him away** <note>original: απαγετε</note>: There is a slight spelling variation between "lead away" <note>original: απαγετε</note> and "lead away" <note>original: απαγαγετε</note>. The Latin and Syriac versions generally agree on "lead" or "bring him," and several manuscripts add the word **him** at the end of the phrase.

**45.** **arriving** <note>original: ελθων</note>: Omitted in Codex Bezae (D) and several Latin and Syriac versions. | **immediately**: The earliest manuscripts like Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B) use the shorter Greek form <note>original: ευθυς</note>, while later manuscripts use the longer form <note>original: ευθεωσ</note>. | **said to him**: Some manuscripts swap the order to "to him he says," while others omit "to him" entirely. | **Rabbi**: In the earliest manuscripts, Judas says "Rabbi" once. However, many later manuscripts (and the Syriac and Gothic versions) have him saying "Rabbi, Rabbi" twice. Some versions, influenced by the Gospel of Matthew, replace "Rabbi" with **Greetings, Rabbi** <note>original: χαιρε ραββι</note>. There are also minor spelling differences in how "Rabbi" is written in Greek (ending in -ei vs -i).

**46.** **laid hands**: The earliest manuscripts (ℵ and B) use a specific Greek form for "laid" <note>original: επεβαλαν</note>, while nearly all others use a more standard form <note>original: επεβαλον</note>. There is also considerable variation in the word order: some say **laid hands on him**, some say **laid their hands on him**, and others say **laid hands upon him**.

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of how different ancient handwritten copies of the Bible vary in their wording. Symbols like ℵ, B, C, and D refer to major ancient Greek manuscripts.</note>

**51.** **over his naked body** <note>original: επι γυμνου</note> (The Latin Vulgate reads *super nudo* [over a naked man]; other Latin versions read *supra nudum* [over a naked man], *supra nudum corpus* [over a naked body], *sicut erat nudus* [just as he was naked], or *nuditatis* [of nakedness]): Manuscripts 13, 69, 346, and 2pe read "naked"... The scholar Lachmann reads **the blasphemy** <note>original: "την βλασφημιαν" (accusative case)</note> (imitating Matthew) with manuscripts A, D, G, 1, 13, 2ᵖᵉ, and about 5 others. Furthermore, manuscripts D, G, I, N, and about 10 others, along with q, the Gatarianus, and the Gothic and Ethiopic versions add "his," as do 13, 61, 69, 346, 124, 2ᵖᵉ, and the Sahidic (which reads "the blasphemy which he spoke") and the Syriac Peshitta ("behold, from his own mouth you have heard the blasphemy"); the Philoxenian Syriac and Armenian versions add "from" (124 and 2ᵖᵉ read "his from the") **his mouth** :: compare with Luke | **it seems**: <note>original: "φαίνεται"</note> Manuscripts D, N, 28, and 2ᵖᵉ read "it thinks/seems" <note>original: "δοκει"</note> imitating Matthew | **and they all**: <note>original: "οι δε παντεσ"</note> (the Old Latin l and the Vulgate read "who all"): manuscript D reads "but all," manuscripts c, d, k read "all however"... 1, 13, 69, 2ᵖᵉ, and a few others along with a, f, ff², q read "and all" | **him**: <note>original: "αυτον"</note> the original hand of manuscript D reads "to him" | **to be deserving**: <note>original: "ενοχον ειναι"</note> with ℵ, B, L, Δ, 33, l, q, and the Gothic... The Textus Receptus and Lachmann read **deserving to be** with A, E, G, H, K, M, N, S, U, V, Wᵇ, Γ, Π and many others, as well as a, c, f, k, and the Vulgate (all of which read "him [k: that one] to be guilty of death") and the Armenian... Manuscript D and ff² omit "to be."

65. **to spit**: <note>original: "εμπτυειν"</note> (also in ℵ, A, B, C etc.): D and Δ write it as "enptyuein" | **on him**: <note>original: "αυτω"</note> Manuscripts D, a, f, the Gothic, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac Peshitta, and Armenian read "on his face" :: compare Matthew | **and to cover his face**: manuscripts D, a, and f omit this :: compare Matthew | **his face**: <note>original: "αυτου το πρ."</note> according to ℵ, B, C, L, U, Δ, 33, 108, 127... The Textus Receptus and Lachmann read **the face of him** <note>original: "το προσωπ. αυτου"</note> with A, I, N, Wᵇ, X, Γ, Π, and 7 other uncials (manuscript f has a gap from verse 54 onward) and most others, including (as is the Latin custom) c, ff², k, l, q, and the Vulgate | **to strike with fists**: <note>original: "κολαφίζειν"</note> (also in f, l, q, and the Vulgate): manuscripts D, a, c, k read **they were striking with fists**. Thus manuscript c: "and some began to mock him, and they spat on him, and veiling his face they were striking him with fists, and the servants said to him etc"; k: "and some began to spit on him, and veiling his face they were making him bright [likely a scribal error for striking], and some of the servants said to him etc"; a: "and some began to spit in his face and were striking him with fists" (omitting the rest; for it continues: "And while Peter was") | **to say**: <note>original: "λεγειν"</note> Manuscripts D, 2ᵖᵉ, c, k, and the Gothic read "they were saying" | **to him (the second time)**: Manuscript I, 1, 13, 69, the Syriac Peshitta, and Armenian omit this | **Prophesy**: Manuscript G, 1, 118 add "now," while Fʷ and a few others including c, f, k add "to us" (and the Toledo manuscript adds "to us, O Christ"), manuscripts I, U, X, Δ, 13, 33, 69, 108, 124, 127, 2ᵖᵉ, about 20 others, the Gatarianus, Sahidic, Coptic, Philoxenian Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic add "to us (13, 69 and others read 'now', some Coptic manuscripts omit, the Philoxenian Syriac has it with an asterisk) Christ (the Coptic places this after 'you', about 10 others omit it) who is it that struck (Δ: sent, δ: sent) you" :: imitating Matthew and Luke. Regarding Matthew's words: "then they spat... until... who struck you" (Matthew 26:67-68), Augustine in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* 3, 20 notes: "Mark also says this; he mentions as well that they veiled his face. Luke also testifies to these things." | **the officers**: Manuscript D omits this, as do those who connect the verb "to say" to this subject (see above) c and k (the Ethiopic omits "and the officers" through "took") | **him**: Manuscript D and q place this after the verb (manuscripts f, ff², q read "and the ministers with will [f: gladly] with slaps were beating him [q: beating him]") | **took**: <note>original: "ελαβον"</note> with ℵ, B, C, I, K, L, N, S, V, Γ, Δ, Π and about 10 others; meanwhile D, G, 1, 13, 69, 2ᵖᵉ, about 10 others, the Coptic and Philoxenian Syriac read "were taking" <note>original: "ελαμβανον"</note>... The Textus Receptus reads "struck" <note>original: "εβαλλον"</note> with manuscript H and many others, also E, M, U, Wᵇ, X, 33, 157, and more than 25 others.

after **seeing him** <note>original: "ιδουσα αυτον"</note> *together with* manuscripts A, I, N, X, Γ, Π, seven other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and many others (157. 245. *place it before* **him**); the Gothic and Philoxenian Syriac versions (which read "and that girl saw him again") ... manuscripts B and M, 50, and the Sahidic, Coptic, and Ethiopic versions *omit this.* With individual words transposed in manuscript D, 2pe, and the Old Latin versions c, f, k, l, q, the Vulgate, and Eusebius in his *Demonstratio Evangelica*—"but the servant girl, seeing him again" (manuscript k *omits* "again"); manuscript a reads "and when the girl had seen him again" | **the** <note>original: "η"</note> (omitted in manuscript esc^r) **servant girl**: the Coptic (Wilkins and Diez editions) read "**another**" (and seeing him, another girl; whereas the Coptic [Schwab edition] and others read "and the servant girl, seeing him"; the Sahidic reads "but the servant girl, when she had seen him") :: *compare with* Matthew | **began to say**: manuscripts b, Sahidic, Coptic, and Ethiopic read "**said**" (:: in Matthew it reads "**says**") | **those standing by** <note>original: "παρεστωσιν"</note> *together with* ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, C, I, K, L, Δ, Π*, and ten others, and Eusebius... the Textus Receptus and Lachmann edition read **standing near** <note>original: "παρεστηκοσιν"</note> *together with* A, D, N, X, Γ, Π² and many others | **that** (omitted by Eusebius) **this man**: manuscripts 13, 59, 69, 106, 124, 251, 346, the Old Latin a, c, ff², the Syriac (Schaf edition), Armenian, and Ethiopic read "**that this man also**," manuscript D reads "**that he also**"

70. **he denied** <note>original: "ηρνειτο," imperfect tense implying repeated action</note> *together with* ℵ, A, B, C, *etc.* :: Manuscripts F, G, M, N, X, Δ, and many others, as well as Eusebius, read **he denied** <note>original: "ηρνησατο," aorist tense implying a single completed action</note>, *likewise in the Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic (but Diez edition reads "was denying"), Philoxenian Syriac, and Gothic* (:: *as in* Matthew); *also* manuscript D, *but it has the words clumsily transposed* between "but again the servant girl seeing him" *and* "and he began" | **and after** (Sahidic reads "**but after**"): ℵ* and Coptic (Diez) *omit* **and** | **those standing by** (Manuscript D reads "**standing near**"): Manuscript G and 1 read "**those standing around**" | **they said** (*dicebant* in Old Latin a, d, l, and Vulgate): Manuscripts L and 17 read "**they spoke**," Old Latin c, ff², and q read "**they said**"; k reads "**they say**" | **to Peter**: Manuscript D and Old Latin a *omit* | **truly**: Manuscript m *adds* "**and you**," a omits **truly** and reads "**and you are of them**" | **for you are also a Galilean** (*these words are omitted in 73, 131, 142*, Old Latin a, and Gothic) *without the addition according to* ℵ, B, C, D, L, 1, 118, 209, 2pe, and Old Latin a, c, ff², g¹, k, l, and the Sahidic, Coptic, Eusebius, and Augustine (*"Now truly that which Matthew asserts was said to Peter himself: 'Truly you also are one of them, for your speech makes you manifest'; just as John asserts it was said to the same Peter: 'Did I not see you...'; Mark however says they spoke among themselves concerning Peter: 'Truly he is of them, for he is also a Galilean'; just as etc."*) ... The Textus Receptus (but Griesbach *thinks* Schulz is right that "and your speech resembles it" is foreign to Mark) *adds* **and your speech resembles it** <note>original: "και η λαλια σου ομοιαζει"</note> (Δ *omits* "and"; ℵ reads "makes it clear"; 33 reads "clearly resembles you," though the letters are rewritten; the Ethiopic expresses "makes you manifest") *together with* A, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π and many others, as well as Old Latin q, Gothic, both Syriac versions, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Euthymius (on Matthew 26:73) :: *this clearly flowed in from Matthew; the word "resembles" belongs to a commentator.*

71. **and to swear** <note>original: "και ομνυναι"</note> *together with* B, E, H, L, S, U, V, X, Γ and nearly 80 others ... The Textus Receptus (= Griesbach, *but again* Griesbach') reads **and to swear** <note>original: "και ομνυειν"</note> (:: *as in* Matthew) *together with* ℵ, A, C, G, K, M, N, Δ, Π and very many others, as well as Eusebius ... Manuscript D and Old Latin a and q read "**and to say**" (a reads "**saying**"), Armenian reads "**and to swear and to say**" | **this man whom you speak of** (Old Latin a reads "this man whom you say," d, ff², l, q, and the Vulgate read "that one whom you say," c reads "that one whom you say [singular]"): ℵ *omits* (:: *as in* Matthew), k *omits* "**whom you speak of**," manuscript D, K, N and five others *omit* **this man**.

72. **and immediately** (Manuscripts D, G, and Eusebius read the Greek synonym *eutheōs*: *so* Griesbach and Scholz) *together with* ℵ, B, L, 2pe, D, G, 13, 69, 124, 346, and 10 others, as well as Eusebius, *likewise the Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac [Schaf], Armenian, and Ethiopic* ... The Textus Receptus (= Griesbach and Scholz) *omits* **immediately** *together with* A, C, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π and many others, as well as the Sahidic, Coptic, Philoxenian Syriac, and Gothic | **for the second time** (*and Eusebius*): ℵ, L, and Old Latin c *omit* (:: in Matthew it is "**immediately**" *without* "for the second time"). *Compare also the note at verse 68.*

<note>The following notes are the "Apparatus Criticus," which scholars use to compare different ancient versions of the New Testament. The letters and symbols refer to specific ancient manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) or Codex Vaticanus (B).</note>

72. **remembered**: manuscripts G, 1, 13, 69, 209 read "**having remembered**". *From these* **and** *following are not omitted except in* 1, 209. | **the word as** *together with* ℵ, A, B, C, L, Δ and 8 others; the Sahidic, Coptic, and Gothic versions (according to the Griesbach and Scholz editions) ... **the word that** *with* D, N, X, Γ, Π, 7 uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and about 130 others; likewise the Old Latin versions read "**he remembered — the word which**" (manuscript q reads "called to mind," manuscript l reads "recalled") ... the Peshitta Syriac reads "**the word of the speech of Jesus saying to him**," but the margin of the Harclean Syriac reads "**the word of the speech which Jesus had spoken to him**" ... the standard received text reads "**the word of which**" *with* m, 69, and a few others (the Vulgate reads "recalled — the word which"). XV. 1. **immediately** *with* ℵ, B, C, L, A ... the standard received text and Lachmann read "**immediately**" (longer form) *with* A, D, N, X, Γ, Π, 8 uncials, and almost all others ... the Old Latin a and c, Sahidic, and Ethiopic *omit this* | **in the morning** *with* ℵ, B, C, D, L, 46, and Old Latin a ("at first light"), ff², k ("from the morning"), l, q, the Vulgate, c ("but when morning was made"), Sahidic, Coptic, and Origen ... the standard received text and Tischendorf read "**at the morning**" *with* A, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials, and almost all others including the Armenian, Gothic, and Philoxenian Syriac | **having prepared** *with* ℵ, C, L ... the standard received text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "**having made**" *with* A, B, N, X, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials, and many others including the Vulgate, Coptic, Armenian, and Gothic; likewise manuscript D, 5 others, and Old Latin a, c, ff², k, q, and the Sahidic, both Syriac, Ethiopic, and Origen read "**they made**" (*followed by* **and** *before* **bound**) | **elders then scribes** (also Origen): manuscript c, 47, and the Sahidic read **scribes then elders** | **the** *before* **scribes** *with* ℵ, D, 1, 2pe, Sahidic, Coptic, and Origen ... the standard received text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf *omit it with* B, L, N, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials, and most others | **led Him away** *with* ℵ, A, B, L, N, Γ, Δ, Π, 7 uncials, most others, and Armenian (and likely Sahidic and Coptic) ... C, D, G, N, 1, 124, 2pe, 5 others, and Origen read "**they led**" (a different Greek verb), likewise the Old Latin, Vulgate, both Syriac, Gothic, and Ethiopic versions :: *likely following Matthew* (see also Mark 14, 53). Furthermore, manuscript d, and Old Latin a, c, ff², k, q, and Origen *add* "**into the courtyard**" (k reads "into the praetorium" :: as in John, "into the praetorium") | **to Pilate** *with* ℵ, A, B, D ... the standard received text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "**to Pilate**" (variant spelling) *with* C, L, N, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials, and almost all others. This is without the article "**the**" in ℵ, B, C, D, L, A, 1, and others; whereas the standard received text *adds* "**the**" *with* A, N, Γ, Π, 8 uncials, and most others.

<note>The following notes are the "Apparatus Criticus," a technical record of variations found in ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. Letters like ℵ, B, or D refer to specific ancient manuscripts.</note>

**2.** Manuscript *a*, *ff²*, *l*, *q*, and the Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible</note> add <term>saying</term>: as in Matthew and Luke | **But he** (Manuscript *N* and a few others add <term>Jesus</term>): Manuscript *D*, *a*, and the Ethiopic version read **and** | **says to him** (I did not follow the word after **to him** in manuscript *c*, but it entirely seems to be <term>says</term>) with manuscripts *Sinaiticus*, *Vaticanus*, *Ephraemi*, *Bezae*, and the Coptic and Armenian versions (Manuscripts 1, 127, 209, 258 read **says to him**; the Latin *l* and Vulgate read **he said to him**; manuscript *2pe* only has <term>says</term>; likewise *c* [omitting **answering**], *ff²*, and *q* have only **he said**) ... The Received Text and Lachmann read **said to him** with *Alexandrinus*, *N*, *X*, *Γ*, *Δ*, *Π*, 8 other uncials <note>manuscripts written in all capital letters</note>, and most others; manuscript *d* (manuscript *k* reads **he said** omitting **to him**) and the Syriac, Gothic, and Ethiopic versions ... *a* reads **he responded to him**, the Sahidic reads **he responded to him saying**

**3. were accusing** (also in Origen volume 4, page 387): the Greek manuscript *ℸ* reads **they accuse** | **many things** without addition with manuscripts *Sinaiticus*, *Alexandrinus*, *Vaticanus*, *C*, *D*, *X* (certain from the spacing), *Γ*, *Π*, 7 other uncials, many others, and several Latin and Coptic versions ... *N*, *U*, *Δ*, and manuscripts 13, 33, 69, 124, 131, and about 40 others, along with *a*, *c*, Syriac, Armenian, and Origen add **but he answered nothing** :: compare Luke 23, 9 and Matthew 27, 12

**4. Pilate** with *Sinaiticus*, *Alexandrinus*, *Vaticanus*, *D* ... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf spell it <term>Pilatos</term> as in verse 1. | **again**: *C*, *D*, *k*, *q*, and the Coptic and Ethiopic place this after **questioned him** (*ff²* reads **Again Pilate questioned** etc.) ... *U* and manuscripts 127, 131, 238 and a few others omit it :: as in Matthew 27, 13 | **he questioned** with *Vaticanus*, *U*, and manuscripts 13, 33, 69, 124, 2pe, and several Latin and Syriac versions ... The Received Text and Lachmann read **he asked** with *Sinaiticus*, *Alexandrinus*, *C*, *D*, *N*, *X*, *Γ*, *Δ*, *Π*, 7 other uncials, and most others (:: scribes so often changed the imperfect <note>a tense indicating ongoing action in the past</note> of this very word in Mark to the aorist <note>a tense indicating a single completed action</note>; compare Mark 5:9, 9:11, 10:2. Conversely, the aorist does not usually fluctuate in Mark or others) | **him** without **saying** with the original hand of *Sinaiticus*, and manuscripts 1, 209, 2pe, *a*, and the Sahidic (:: and this is entirely out of Mark’s usage to write **to question** without **saying**, as in 5:9, 8:5, etc. Neither Matthew nor Luke do this. Hence, they <term>everywhere</term> supplied **saying**, as in 9:21, 10:17. Where it was truly added by the author, it does not fluctuate: 8:27, 9:11) ... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **saying** with the corrected *Sinaiticus*, *Alexandrinus*, *Vaticanus*, *C*, *D*, and many others | **nothing**: *Vaticanus* (first hand) omits (added by second hand); one manuscript writes **nothing he answered**, omitting the word **not** | **see**: *Δ* reads **let him see** (or **behold**?) | **they accuse** with *Sinaiticus*, *Vaticanus*, *C*, *D*, and manuscript 1, likewise the Latin and Coptic (the Latin translates as **they testify against you** or similar, compare Matthew 26:62, Mark 14:60) ... The Received Text reads **they testify against** (:: from Matthew) with most other uncials and versions.

**5. he answered**: *G* and manuscripts 1, 13, 69, and a few others use a different Greek form for **he answered** | **Pilate**: The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf spell it **Pilatos** as in verses 1, 2, 4.

**6. the feast**: *D* adds the word **the** | **he used to release**: manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 346 read **the governor was accustomed to release** (:: from Matthew), likewise the Latin versions read **he was accustomed to release** or **was used to releasing**, and the Syriac (but he was accustomed at every feast to loosen) | **whom they requested** with the original *Sinaiticus*, *Alexandrinus*, and *Vaticanus* ... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **whomever they requested** with the corrected *Sinaiticus*, *C*, *N*, *X*, *Γ*, *Π*, and most others. This fits the sense of "whomever they had asked" in the Latin versions; conversely, "whom they demanded" in manuscript *k* seems to look to the reading **whom they requested**. The Coptic and Syriac do not express "whomever" but simply "whom."

[manuscript 15 adds] **casting** <note>original: *balontes*</note> (but the letter *mu* is written like a *kappa* in **casting**) | **who [should take] what** (manuscript 13 and others read **takes**) also in manuscripts c, l, the Vulgate, and Augustine’s *Consensus of the Evangelists* 3, 39: Manuscript D, 157. Manuscript z once, ff2, and Blanchinus's edition (omitting "and... upon them"), while manuscripts k and n omit it (:: as in Matthew).

**25. and** <note>original: *de*</note>: manuscript f, the Coptic versions, and Peter's third edition omit this | **the third hour** (manuscripts D and Γ) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others, including the Old Latin and Vulgate. However, manuscripts A, C, K, and a few others read **hour third**. Manuscripts k, a Syriac version, and the Ethiopic read **the sixth hour**, as does Jerome, who in his commentary on Psalm 77 attributes the reading "third" instead of "sixth" to a "scribal error": <note>original: *Error scriptorum fuit; et in Mc hora sexta scriptum fuit, sed multi episemum Graecum Ϛ (i. e. ekte) putaverunt esse Γ (i. e. trite).*</note> "It was a scribal error; in Mark it was written 'sixth hour,' but many thought the Greek symbol Ϛ (representing six) was Γ (representing three)." Compare what we transcribed from Jerome regarding Matthew 13:35. Compare the *Acts of Pilate* B, page 283: "The soldiers took his clothes and divided them among themselves, and they clothed him in a red cloak, and they led him up and nailed him to the cross at the sixth hour of the day." The Moscow Catena <note>A collection of ancient commentaries</note> 2, 105 says: "Some say that Mark, mentioning the decision of the people, said he was crucified at the third hour by the people. For it was the third hour when the Jewish people condemned him to be crucified. But others mentioned the sixth hour, in which, receiving the sentence from Pilate, he was crucified by the soldiers." Similar remarks are found in the Oxford Catena 438. These views seem to depend on Augustine's *Consensus of the Evangelists* 3, 40: "It is understood therefore that it was the third hour when the Jews cried out for the Lord to be crucified... and it is most truly shown that they crucified him then when they cried out; especially because they did not want it to seem that they had done this." | **and** (manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 346 read **when**) **they crucified** (also in c, l, the Vulgate, and Augustine): Manuscript D, ff2, k, and n read **and they kept watch over him** (:: a reading that is strongly recommended by comparison with Matthew 27:36, where after "casting lots" it continues: "and sitting down they kept watch over him there").

**26. and the [inscription] was** (Codex Delta omits "the"): Manuscript D reads **but [the inscription] was**, while d, k, and the Sahidic read **now there was** | **the king**: Codex Bezae (D) and the Gothic (likewise the Syriac according to their language) add **this is**, while manuscript c adds **Jesus** (manuscript 33 adds **this** after "of the Jews"):: compare Matthew and Luke.

**27. they crucify**: Codex Delta reads **they crucify with him**, omitting "with him [later]"... Manuscripts B, C, d, ff2, k, and n (but not l or the Vulgate) and the Gothic and Syriac read **they crucified** (the Coptic and Sahidic could be interpreted as either present or past tense)... Codex Bezae reads **are crucified** (followed by "two rebels," but the ending was corrected) | **one** etc.: manuscript c reads **one on the right named Zoathan and another on the left named Chammatha** (this same manuscript, and it alone, in Matthew uses the names Zoatham and Camma. See also the names **Gestas** and **Dysmas/Demas** in the *Acts of Pilate* A page 231 and B page 264) | **of him**: Manuscripts C, D, 1, and others omit this (:: as in Matthew).

**28.** The Stephen’s 1550 edition <note>indicated by the symbol Ϛ</note> and Lachmann include this verse: **And the scripture was fulfilled which says: "And he was counted with the lawless"** (:: compare Luke 22:37 and Isaiah 53:12) with manuscripts E, F, G, H, K, L, and M.

Pseudo-Hippolytus in *On the Antichrist*, page 37 (Gud. edition), scarcely alludes to this: <note>original: "οσ επουρανιων και επιγειων και καταχθονιων βασιλευς – αποδεδεικται · – καταχθονιων δε οτι και εν νεκροις κατελογισθη, ευαγγελιζομενος τας των αγιων ψυχας δια θανατου τον θανατον νικων"</note> "who has been shown to be king of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and of things under the earth because he was also numbered among the dead, preaching the good news to the souls of the saints, conquering death through death," unless perhaps these should be compared with the Eutychian saying found in Vigilius, book 4 *Against Eutyches*. For Vigilius writes in book 1: <note>original: "Quod enim ibi (in evglio) legitur de Christo, quando inter duos latrones crucifixus est, ex prophetae testimonio dicentis: Et inter iniquos deputatus est, tu dixisti: Et inter mortuos deputatus est."</note> *“For what is read there (in the Gospel) concerning Christ, when he was crucified between two thieves, from the testimony of the prophet saying: 'And he was reckoned among the wicked,' you said: 'And he was reckoned among the dead.'”* Truly, the words of Origen in *Against Celsus* 1, 420 seem wrongly applied to the reading of Mark: <note>original: "ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖός φησιν ὅτι δύναιτο ἄν τις ὁμοίως ἀναισχυντῶν και περὶ λῃστοῦ και ἀνδροφόνου κολασθέντος εἰπεῖν ὅτι οὗτός γε οὐχὶ λῃστὴς ἀλλὰ θεὸς ἦν· προεῖπε γὰρ τοῖς συλλῃσταῖς ὅτι πείσεται τοιαῦτα οἷα δὴ πέπονθε. – καὶ ταῦτα λέγομεν ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγ. προειρῆσθαί πως· ἐπεὶ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη ὁ θεὸς παρὰ τοῖς ἀνόμοις, λῃστὴν μᾶλλον – βουλομένοις ἀπολυθῆναι, τὸν δὲ ιν σταυρῶσαι, καὶ σταυρώσασιν αὐτὸν μεταξὺ λῃστῶν δύο."</note> “The Jew in Celsus’s work says that someone might similarly be so shameless as to say of a thief and a murderer who had been punished, that this man was not a thief but a god; for he foretold to his fellow-thieves that he would suffer such things as he indeed suffered. — And we say that these things were somehow foretold in the Gospels; since God was 'reckoned with the lawless' by the lawless, who preferred a thief to be released, and to crucify Jesus, and having crucified him between two thieves.” These things refer rather to Luke... but we have omitted the verse [v. 28] (<term>Griesbach</term> and <term>Schulz</term> state, "it is not in Mark’s style; the author of the gloss seems to have taken the citation formula from John and the passage from Luke") along with manuscripts <term>Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus (original and 3rd hand), Bezae, and X</term>, and about 45 others (including about 20 lectionaries), manuscript <term>k</term>, the Sahidic, and the Slavonic; likewise the Eusebian Canon, as it seems. For in some older manuscripts that contain the verse itself, such as <term>M</term>, from <term>And with him</term> in verse 27 until <term>was reckoned</term>, it is marked as section <term>215</term> with the addition of canon <term>1</term> (which contains what is common to all 4 Gospels), followed from <term>and those passing by</term> by section <term>216</term> with canon <term>6</term>, which contains what is in both Matthew and Mark. If this is correct, neither Ammonius nor Eusebius read verse 28; otherwise, they would have given it its own number, which it actually has in other manuscripts, both Greek [already in <term>P</term>] and Latin. The authority of Codex <term>M</term> in this matter is increased because, like those that do not have the verse, <term>Alexandrinus</term> and <term>Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> agree in the Ammonian numbers, and Codex <term>Λ</term> also in the Eusebian ones, from which <term>Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> abstains. Furthermore, the same Codex <term>M</term> proves that in Luke the Ammonian-Eusebian numbers were altered by a different hand, in which, contrary to custom, between numbers <term>276</term> and <term>278</term>, the very one in question, <term>277</term>, with its own canon [<term>10?</term> <term>8?</term>], is missing. In most manuscripts, however, section 277 of Luke has the Eusebian canon 8 assigned to it, which contains what is common to Luke and Mark. The indices of the canons we possess follow this same method. Compare the one we have prefixed to our own edition.

36. **δραμ. δε** (but running) (found in the <term>Old Latin manuscripts</term> l, vg, g<sup>1 · 2 ·</sup>): found in manuscripts d, 1, and 2pe (see below for 13, 69, 124, 346), as well as c, ff<sup>2 ·</sup>, k, n, and the <term>Ethiopic version</term> as **και δραμ.** (and running) (similar to the Gospel of Matthew) | **τισ** (someone) with <term>Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (L), and Δ</term>, and the <term>Ethiopic</term>... the <term>Received Text</term> <note>original: ς</note> and editors Lachmann (Ln) and Tischendorf (Ti) read **εισ** (one) (similar to Matthew’s "one of them") with <term>Codices Alexandrinus (A), Ephraemi (C), Bezae (D), P, Γ, Π</term>, <term>nine other uncials</term>, and <term>almost all other manuscripts</term>, including the <term>Latin Vulgate</term> (which has *unus*) and the <term>Gothic version</term> | **και γεμισασ** (and filling) with ℵ, A, C, D, P, Γ, Π, <term>nine uncials</term>, and <term>almost all others</term>, as well as <term>Old Latin k</term> (*and he ran, one [man], and filled*), l, and apparently n, the <term>Vulgate</term>, the <term>Syriac (Peshitta)</term>, <term>Gothic</term>, <term>Armenian</term>, and <term>Ethiopic</term>... manuscripts B, L, and c (ff<sup>2 ·</sup> reads *and running, one [man] filled*) and the <term>Coptic</term> (<term>Syriac Philoxenian</term> reads *when one had run, he filled*) omit the "and" before **γεμισασ** | **γεμισασ:** manuscript D and 2pe use **πλησασ** (having filled) | **δ σφογγον** (the sponge) | **περιθεισ** (having put it around) (manuscript D has **επιθεισ**, having put it on) without the word "and" <note>original: τε (te)</note> in ℵ, B, D<sup>Greek</sup>, L, 33, 67, 2pe, <term>Coptic</term>, and <term>Gothic</term>... the <term>Received Text</term> and Tischendorf add "and" with A, C, P, X, Γ, Δ, Π, <term>eight uncials</term>, and <term>most others</term>; k reads *and filled - and placing it upon*; c reads *filling - he placed*; ff<sup>2 ·</sup> reads *filled and wrapped around*; i reads *the sponge being filled with vinegar he placed*; n reads [*and fil*] *ling the sponge* [*with vinegar*] [*pl*] *acing it*, as the space seems to require; **9—20. That these verses were not written by Mark is proved by suitable arguments.**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;First, they are omitted by Codices ℵ (Sinaiticus) and B (Vaticanus), the Latin manuscript k, ancient Armenian manuscripts, and some Ethiopic and Arabic versions (see later where k and certain Ethiopic manuscripts end the Gospel of Mark here). They are marked with an asterisk (indicating doubt) in manuscripts 137 and 138.

Furthermore, manuscript 274 notes this in the margin at verse 7 in uncial letters, as does the Harclean Syriac at the words "for they were afraid." # 16, 9—20. ACCORDING TO MARK

With [these things] applied, he seems to make an end of the Gospel, having these added: <note>original: "φερετε που και ταυτα"</note> **Somewhere these are also found:** ♰ **And they reported briefly all that had been commanded to those around Peter; and after these things, Jesus himself sent out through them, from the east even unto the west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation** ♰ **of eternal salvation.** ♰ After these things, again with signs placed between, he continues: <note>original: "εστιν δε και ταυτα φερομενα μετα το εφοβουντο γαρ"</note> **And these things are also circulating after "for they were afraid":** ♰ **Now after he rose** etc.

The same is given in the margin of Codex 274 from **And all** to **salvation**, except that it has **easts** <note>plural</note>, omits the sign after **proclamation**, and adds **amen** to **salvation**. Codex k <note>An important Old Latin manuscript from the 4th or 5th century</note> reads thus: *“But all things, whatever had been commanded, they briefly explained to those who were with the boy <note>The translator notes: "correct to 'Peter'"</note>; after these things Jesus himself appeared, and from the east even unto... unto the east <note>The translator notes: "correct to 'west'"</note> he sent through them the holy and incorruptible [preaching] <note>Below is supplied "of the preaching," but under the ending "-onis" it seems the word "preaching" [praedicationem] is hidden</note> of eternal salvation. Amen.”*
Likewise the Ethiopic version: *“And when they had finished saying all that he commanded Peter and his companions, and after the Lord Jesus had appeared to them from the rising of the sun unto its setting, he sent them out so that they might preach the holy Gospel, which is not corrupted, unto eternal salvation.”* Likewise the Harclean Syriac version in the margin at **for they were afraid**: these are also added in some places (they seem to be rendered by these words which are read in Codex L: **somewhere these are also found**): *“But all things which had been commanded to those who were with Peter they reported briefly; but afterward Jesus himself from the east even unto the west published through them the sacred and incorruptible proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.”*

3) The <term>scholia</term> <note>Scholia are ancient marginal notes or comments written by scribes in the margins of manuscripts to provide explanations or textual variants.</note> of very many manuscripts testify that in the older and (as many add) more accurate copies, the Gospel of Mark had its end at verse 9 <note>Though the note says verse 9, it refers to the point where the disputed ending begins after verse 8.</note>. Thus, so that out of about 30 manuscripts we may see three for certain, Codex 22 has: **for they were afraid.** ♰ **THE END: In some of the copies the Evangelist is completed up to here; but in many these are also circulating: Now after he rose etc.** Likewise Codex 1: **In some of the copies the Evangelist is completed up to here; even to the point where Eusebius the son of Pamphilus <note>A 4th-century church historian</note> finished his canons; but in many—** as before. Likewise Codex 20: **From here to the end it is not found in some of the copies; but in the ancient ones all are placed without omission.** It is pleasing to add to these what Matthaei <note>Christian Friedrich von Matthaei, an 18th-century biblical scholar</note> praised from three manuscripts (239, 259, 237) in his 1785 work on the Epistles to the Thessalonians and Timothy, written as a note to John 21:12. It is of such a kind that it excludes the final part of the Gospel of Mark, which is under inquiry. The final words of that scholium are: **so that from this it appears that there were seven appearances of our Savior Jesus Christ to the disciples after the resurrection: one in Matthew, three in John, and three likewise in Luke.** Therefore, Mark is completely passed over.

4) Added to these are the testimonies of the Fathers: Severian, Hesychius of Jerusalem, Victor, and Euthymius, and truly the most weighty of all, Eusebius and Jerome. For to Severian these words are ascribed in the excerpts of Codex Coislinianus 23 (10th century), and likewise in Gallandi’s collection 11, 226: **In the more accurate copies <note>original: "εν μεν ουν τοις ακριβεστεροις αντιγραφοις"</note> the Gospel according to Mark has its end at "for they were afraid"; but in some, these are added: "Now after he rose..."**

<meta>This page continues the scholarly investigation into the "Longer Ending" of the Gospel of Mark (verses 9–20). The previous page discussed how some manuscripts transition from verse 8 to the "Shorter Ending." This page provides evidence from the Church Fathers—including Gregory of Nyssa, Eusebius, and Jerome—regarding the absence of these verses in the oldest and most "accurate" Greek manuscripts.</meta>

# ACCORDING TO MARK 16, 9—20.

The very same words are found in the *Second Oration on the Resurrection*, which they published among the works of **Gregory of Nyssa** <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian</note> (see volume 2, page 841); more recently, however, scholars have preferred to ascribe this work to **Hesychius of Jerusalem** <note>A 5th-century priest and exegete</note>. Hesychius, furthermore, in his *Questions* (Question 52), writes: <note>original: "μαρκος μεν εν επιτομω τα μεχρι του ενος αγγελου διελθων τον λογον κατεπαυσεν."</note> **"Mark, having gone through the events in a summary up to the one angel, brought his account to a close."** These words are also attributed to **Victor** <note>Victor of Antioch, a 5th-century commentator</note> in the <term>catenae</term> <note>A "chain" of interpretations from various Church Fathers written in the margins of Bibles</note> of both the Moscow and Possevin manuscripts (though the name is not added in the Oxford manuscript), from which parts (starting from **"among most [copies]"**) have passed into the <term>scholia</term> <note>Explanatory notes or comments</note>. They read as follows:

**"Since in some of the copies, [the passage beginning] 'Now after he rose' etc., is added to the Gospel according to Mark, and since this seems to disagree with what was said by Matthew, we shall say—as one might—that the ending of Mark circulating in some [manuscripts] is <term>spurious</term> <note>original: "νενοθευται" (corrupted or not genuine)</note>. However, lest we seem to resort to an easy escape, we shall read it thus: 'Now after he rose,' and then, placing a <term>sub-distinction</term> <note>a type of punctuation or pause</note>, we add: 'early on the first day' etc. In most copies, these subsequent verses in the Gospel according to Mark are not present; for some have considered them to be spurious. But we, having found them in many accurate copies according to the Palestinian Gospel of Mark, have—as the truth requires—included the Lord’s Resurrection which follows it, after the words 'for they were afraid.'"** (Compare also the *Library of the Fathers* at Lyon, volume 4, page 414: "But because in certain copies of the Gospel of Mark it is held: *Surgens autem Iesus* [Now after Jesus rose], etc.")

Again, **Euthymius** <note>Euthymius Zigabenus, a 12th-century monk and scholar</note> notes at verse 16:8: **"Some of the interpreters say that the Gospel according to Mark is completed here; and that what follows is a later addition. But it is necessary to interpret this as well, as it in no way harms the truth."**

**Eusebius** <note>The 4th-century "Father of Church History"</note> in his *Questions to Marinus*, when the question was proposed: **"How is it that in Matthew the Savior appears to have risen 'late on the Sabbath,' but in Mark 'early on the first day of the week'?"** responded:

**"The solution to this would be twofold. For the one who rejects the section itself—the passage stating this—would say that it is not found in all the copies of the Gospel according to Mark. At any rate, the accurate copies define the end of the history according to Mark at the words of the young man seen by the women, who said to them: 'Do not be afraid; you seek Jesus <note>original: "ιν̅" (a nomen sacrum or sacred abbreviation for Jesus)</note> the Nazarene,' and the rest, to which he adds: 'And having heard, they fled and said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.' For in this [verse], in almost all the copies of the Gospel according to Mark, the end is defined. The things that follow are found rarely in some, but not in all, and they would be superfluous, especially if they contain a contradiction to the testimony of the other evangelists. This, then, is what someone might say who is declining and entirely removing a superfluous question."**

Furthermore, the same Eusebius is said to have written in a note in the Moscow <term>catena</term> (perhaps by Victor?): **"According to Mark, after the resurrection, he is not said to have appeared to the disciples."** Finally, **Jerome** <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> in his *Letter to Hedibia* (Letter 120, Question 3) writes the following:

**"Either we do not accept the testimony of Mark, which is contained in few manuscripts—almost all Greek books lacking this chapter at the end—especially since it seems to tell things different from and contrary to the other evangelists: or we must respond that both [Matthew and Mark] told the truth."** Again, the same Jerome writes in *Against the Pelagians*: **"In certain, and especially in Greek codices <note>handwritten books</note> according to Mark, at the end of his Gospe[l]—"**

It highlights the early conflict between the different endings of Mark and how scholars attempted to reconcile perceived contradictions between the Gospels.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical evidence regarding the "Longer Ending" of Mark (16:9–20), moving from the testimony of Church Fathers to the evidence found in ancient numbering systems and manuscript margins. It specifically examines the "Ammonian Sections" and "Eusebian Canons"—early systems used to divide and cross-reference the Gospels.</meta>

# 16, 9—20. ACCORDING TO MARK

*...of the Gospel it is written: Afterward when the eleven had sat down - - they did not believe. (This is found in Vallarsi, Volume II, page 759. See later regarding verse 14.)*

5) The final verses are recognized neither by the sections of **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius of Alexandria, a 3rd-century scholar who divided the Gospels into numbered sections for easier comparison</note> nor by the canons of **Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century system of ten tables (canons) used to find parallel passages between different Gospels</note>. Indeed, many of the most important manuscripts, both Greek and Latin, do not have the Ammonian and Eusebian numbers placed beyond verse 8 or 9; others show that these numbers were supplied by later hands, often written only partially or in such a way that the section is noted without its corresponding canon or with the wrong canon. 

Thus, manuscripts **A** and **U** have the last numbers (232, canon 2) at verse 6; **Codex Sinaiticus** (ℵ), **L**, and **S** have 233, canon 2 at verse 8. This notation seems to belong to Ammonius and Eusebius themselves, a fact further confirmed by the testimonies of **Epiphanius** and **Caesarius**. Manuscript **r** has 232, canon 2 at verse 6, and 233 and 234 at verses 8 and 9, but both without a canon number. Similarly, manuscript **π** has 232, canon 2 at verse 6; 233, canon 2 at verse 8; and 234, canon 8 at verse 9. Manuscript **Δ** has 233, canon 2 at verse 8; and 234, canon 10 at verse 13. Similar patterns appear in manuscripts 127, 129, 132, 133, 134, 137, 169, 186, 188, 195, 371, and many others. Many others add only about four numbers after 233, canon 2, as seen in Tischendorf's second edition: 234, canon 2 at verse 9; 235, canon 8 at verse 12; 236 without canon at verse 13; and 237 without canon at verse 15. Likewise in Tischendorf's fourth edition: 234, canon 8 at verse 9; 235 and 236 without canons at verses 10 and 12. 

A full supplement of numbers—though the canon references are partly missing—is found in manuscripts **C, E, K,** and **V**, in which number 241 is placed at verse 20 (with **E** adding canon 2), and in **H** and **M**, where 240 is noted at verse 19. In manuscript **μ**, no canon is added to numbers 235 (236, canon 10), 237, 238, 239, and 240. Among the Latin manuscripts, the **Codex Amiatinus** <note>The earliest surviving complete manuscript of the Latin Vulgate Bible, dating to the early 8th century</note> is especially noteworthy; it has the final numbers 233, canon 2 placed at verse 8, exactly like the Greek manuscripts **ℵ, L,** and **S**. Furthermore, in the index of the canons, the sections for Mark do not proceed beyond number 233. Elsewhere, the number of sections fluctuates in the same way as the marginal notations of the manuscripts. 

Our conclusion—that Ammonius and Eusebius recognized no section beyond 233, canon 2 (at verse 9)—is fully confirmed by **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century bishop of Salamis</note> (in *Ancoratus* 50: <note>original: "τεσσαρα εισιν ευαγγελια κεφαλαιων 1162"</note> **"There are four gospels consisting of 1,162 chapters"**) and **Caesarius** <note>The brother of Gregory of Nazianzus</note> (in *Dialogue* 1, 39: <note>original: "τεσσαρα ημιν υπαρχει ευαγγελια κεφαλαιων 1162"</note> **"We have four gospels consisting of 1,162 chapters"**). Since they state the total sum of chapters in the four Gospels is 1,162, they cannot assign more than 233 to Mark (as Matthew has 355, Luke 342, and John 232).

These testimonies are corroborated by other arguments, such as the fact that when compared with the preceding verses, the words in verse 9—**"from whom he had cast out [seven demons]"**—are added somewhat awkwardly; likewise, many individual features in this passage differ from Mark’s usual style. (Regarding how differently the ancients read verses 15 and 20, see what follows.)

The weight of such a cumulative body of evidence is by no means diminished by the fact that **Irenaeus** <note>A 2nd-century bishop and theologian who is one of the earliest witnesses to the longer ending</note> already knew the addition in question. As we believe we have sufficiently proven in the Prolegomena, the vast majority of the most significant changes and <term>interpolations</term> <note>Additions or alterations made to a text by later scribes</note> in the apostolic text occurred not after Irenaeus, but *before* his time. Nor is it a valid counter-argument that the ancients noted a "disagreement" between these verses and the other Gospels; it is utterly incredible—and proven by nothing—that such a disagreement would have led anyone to mutilate the book of Mark so miserably, and with such widespread success.

The author also addresses the testimony of Irenaeus, suggesting the "Longer Ending" was added very early in the text's history, before the late 2nd century.</summary>

### ACCORDING TO MARK 16, 11.

...can be shown by example. Since these things are so, those who persist in trying to sell as apostolic what we are so clearly taught is foreign to Mark seem to oppose a sound piety toward the sacred text. <note>The author is arguing that the "Longer Ending" (Mark 16:9-20) was not written by Mark himself, and that insisting it is "apostolic" (original) goes against careful study of the Bible.</note>

Therefore, among the Church Fathers who recognize these verses, the most ancient is **Irenaeus**, who, as his translator certainly testifies in *Against Heresies* III, 10, 6, cites verse 16:19. To these are added **Hippolytus** in *On Charisms*, where 16:17–18 are praised; the **Apostolic Constitutions** (VIII, 1, 1 have the same as Hippolytus, plus 16:16; and VI, 15, 3); **Caesarius** in *Dialogue* 4, 193 (verse 16:16); and **Jacob of Nisibis** 1, 13 (verses 16:16–18). On the other hand, scholars have in vain appealed to **Clement of Rome** and **Clement of Alexandria**, or to **Ammonius** and **Tatian** in their Gospel harmonies (for what remains of those works has almost nothing in common with Ammonius or Tatian), or to **Celsus** as quoted in **Origen** (who use these words of Celsus: <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century critic of Christianity; Origen wrote a famous defense against him.</note> *“Who saw this [that a dead man rose and showed the marks of his punishment]? A frantic woman, as you say, and if anyone else etc.”* <note>original: "τισ τουτο [οτι νεκρος ανεστη και τα σημεια της κολασεως εδειξεν] ειδε ; γυνη παροιστρος, ως φατε, και ει τις αλλος etc."</note>). The testimony of **Justin [Martyr]** has a little more probability, who in his *First Apology* (1, 45) seems to allude to verse 20 with the words *“from Jerusalem his apostles, having gone out, preached everywhere.”* <note>original: "ου απο Ιερουσαλημ οι αποστολοι αυτου εξελθοντες πανταχου εκηρυξαν"</note> That he also says Christ *“has ascended into the heavens”* <note>original: "ανεληλυθοτα εισ τους ουρανους"</note> carries less weight. Furthermore, based on manuscripts and versions, these witnesses contain the verses: **Manuscripts A, C, D, E, F, G, W^H** (from verse 14 onwards), **K** (for L see above), **M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π** and almost all others; the **Old Latin** versions **c, ff^2, g^1, g^2, l, n, q**; the **Vulgate**; the **Coptic** (also from the Sahidic manuscript *kw* verse 20 is cited, but it differs considerably from the standard text, see later); the **Gothic** (which fails from verse 12); the **Curetonian Syriac** (begins again at verse 17); the **Peshitta** and **Philoxenian Syriac**; the **Harklean Syriac**; the **Armenian** editions (though the ancient manuscripts that contain them preface these verses with a new title, “Gospel according to Mark”); and the **Ethiopic** editions.

The Textus Receptus (ς) and Lachmann (Ln) <note>Two major scholarly versions of the Greek New Testament</note> present the text thus:

9 *Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.* 10 *She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept.* 11 *And they, when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her—* <margin>Luke 24, 10 ff.</margin>

---

**9.** **“Now when he rose”** (*anastas de*) (also in ancient Latin manuscripts **a, n, q**, the **Vulgate**, and **Saxon**; **l** omits “now/but” (*de*); **c** apparently reads “And rising” (*kai anast.*)): **Manuscripts F, W, 13, 28, 69, 124**, and more than 40 others, plus **Old Latin c, ff^2, g^1, g^2**, the **Sixtine Vulgate**, and others add **“Jesus”** (*ho Is*); (but manuscript **69** and others, especially the Lectionaries, omit “now/but” (*de*)) | **“on the first”** (*prōtē*) (Manuscripts **238, 435**, and others read “of the first” (*prōtou*); **28** and others read “on the first” (*prōtēs*)): **Eusebius** reads “on the one” (*tē mia*) | **“day of the week”** (*sabbatou*): **Manuscripts Κ, Π, 1**, and about 60 others, the **Coptic** (manuscript *dz* and *petr^3*), **Eusebius**, and **Pseudo-Nyssa** read “of the weeks” (*sabbatōn*) | **“he appeared first”** (*ephanē prōton*) (**Eusebius** places “first” after “Mary”; the **Armenian** and **Eusebius** omit “first”): **Codex Bezae (D)** reads “he manifested himself to the first [witnesses]” (*ephanerōsen prōtois*) (the Latin side of **D** is missing after verse 6, as already noted) | **“Mary”** (*maria*): **Old Latin c** reads “Mariam” | **“the”** (*tē*): **Codex Bezae (D)** omits | **“from”** (*aph*) with **Manuscripts A, C (corrector), E, G, K, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π** and almost all others, and **Eusebius**... **Lachmann** reads “from” (*par*) with **Codex Ephraemi (C*), Codex Bezae (D), Codex Regius (L)**, and manuscript **33**.

**10.** **“She”** (*ekeinē*) (so in **n** and the **Vulgate**): **Lachmann** adds **“but”** (*de*) with **Old Latin c**, and a few others (**e, ff^2, g^2, l, q** read “but she”) | **“having gone”** (*poreutheisa*) (**a, n**, and **Vulgate** read “going”; **c, ff^2** read “running ahead”): **Manuscripts Κ, Π** and 6 others read “having departed”; **n** reads “she went and”; **Jerome** reads “going away”... **l** reads “seeing” | **“to those”** (*tois*): **Codex Bezae (D)** reads “to those very ones” (Old Latin and Vulgate read “to these” or “to those” or “to them who”) | **“who had been with him etc.”**: **Harklean Syriac** (similarly the **Armenian**) reads “to those who were mourning and weeping with her.”

**11.** **“And they”** (*kakeinoi*) with **Manuscripts A, C (corrector), D (first hand), X, Γ, Δ, Π**, six other uncials, and most others; **l, n**, the **Vulgate**, both **Syriac** versions, **Armenian, Ethiopic, Gothic**, and **Jerome** (“and they”)... **Old Latin c**, **Codex Bezae (corrector)**, **ff^2, q**, and **Coptic** read **“But they”** (*ekeinoi de*); **Codex Regius (L)** and **Codex Nanianus (U)**, and manuscript **127** read simply “they” (*ekeinoi*) | **“been seen by her”** (*ethe. hyp autēs*): **Manuscript Δ** reverses the order to “by her been seen.”
