### 16, 12. ACCORDING TO MARK

<margin>Luke 24, 13 and following</margin> ...they disbelieved. 12 After these things, he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking, while they were going into the countryside. 13 And those men went away and reported it to the rest; but they did not believe them either.

<margin>[Matthew 28, 16–17; Luke 24, 42–43 and 25]</margin> 14 Later, he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen. 15 And he said to them: "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to every—"

<margin>Matthew 28, 19–20; Luke 24, 47–48</margin>

---

**11.** **disbelieved** (The *Codex Fuldensis*, the Saxon version, and Jerome add *him*): Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae, a 5th-century manuscript famous for unique readings.</note> reads: *and they did not believe her* (others read: *him*).

**12.** **after however**: Manuscript D adds *and* at the beginning | **walking**: Manuscript 1 <note>A 12th-century minuscule manuscript.</note> omits this.

**13.** **to those**: Manuscripts L, ff², and the Armenian version read *those men*.

**14.** **later**: Found in manuscripts C, E, G, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π and many others, as well as the Vulgate. Lachmann <note>Karl Lachmann, a pioneering 19th-century textual critic.</note> adds *but* based on Manuscript A and others | **to them** (*to those eleven* in the Old Latin and Vulgate): Manuscript L and others omit this | **unbelief**: Manuscripts C, D, G, K, L, M, S, U, Γ, Π read this; others read a variation meaning *refusal to believe* | **risen** (Manuscripts E, H, K, M read a slightly different spelling; manuscript x omits it): Supported by C, D, E, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, Γ, Π and the Vulgate. Lachmann adds *from the dead* based on Manuscripts A, C, X, Δ and others | **they did not believe**: The Old Latin manuscript *o* reads: *because they did not believe those who told them they had seen him risen*; similar readings are found in manuscripts *mt* and *q*. 

**The Freer Logion:** <note>A famous "long" addition to verse 14 found in only one Greek manuscript (Codex Washingtonianus) but mentioned by St. Jerome.</note>
After verse 14, we learn from **Jerome** that a unique addition was once found. He writes in *Against the Pelagians* 2, 15: "In certain copies, and especially in Greek codices, at the end of the Gospel of Mark, it is written: *Afterwards, when the eleven had sat down to eat, Jesus appeared to them and rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart—for they did not believe. And they defended themselves, saying: 'This age of iniquity and unbelief is under the substance of Satan, which does not allow the true power of God to be grasped through unclean spirits. Therefore, reveal your righteousness now.'*"

**15—19.** Regarding these verses, compare the *Acts of Pilate* <note>An apocryphal text also known as the Gospel of Nicodemus.</note> XIV, pages 242–243: *They explained—that we saw Jesus and his disciples sitting on the mountain called Mamilch, and he was saying to his disciples: "Go into all the world and preach to all creation (some add: my gospel); he who believes and is baptized will be saved, but he who disbelieves will be condemned. And these signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak in new languages, they will pick up snakes (some add: in their hands), and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick and they will recover." While Jesus was still speaking to his disciples, we saw him taken up into heaven.* (For other variations in the manuscripts, see my edition.)

**15.** **to them**: Manuscript D reads *toward them*. Additionally, manuscript *o* and *mt* add *Jesus* | **all** (manuscripts *c* and *q* place this before "world"): Omitted by Manuscript D and the Coptic version | **proclaim**: Manuscript D adds *and*.

### ACCORDING TO MARK 16, 20.

...to all creation. 16 The one who believes and is baptized will be saved, but the one who does not believe will be condemned. 17 And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak in new tongues; 18 they will pick up snakes, and even if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover. 19 So then the Lord, after speaking to them,
<margin>Luke 24, 50 and following;<br/>Acts 1, 9</margin>
was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God. 20 And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the accompanying signs.

---

(but following *go*) <note>original: "sed praegresso ite"</note> manuscripts c, q, and Ambrose (against *going—preach* <note>original: "euntes—praedicate"</note> found in l, o, the Vulgate, and Augustine's *Harmony of the Gospels* 3,76); Coptic, Syriac (Peshitta), and Ethiopic versions.

**16.** **the one** (manuscript q, Ambrose once, and *The Calling of All Nations* read *and he who*; likewise three Latin manuscripts in the *Acts of Pilate*; manuscript c reads *but he who*) **who believes**: The supplement to Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae, a 5th-century manuscript.</note> and others prefix *that* (likewise manuscript E in the *Acts of Pilate*) | **and is baptized**: Manuscripts L and Δ read *and the one being baptized*.

**17.** **these [signs] will accompany** (Manuscript Δ reads *will follow*): so also in the *Apostolic Constitutions* 8, 1, 1 (likewise Hippolytus <note>A 3rd-century Christian theologian.</note> in *On Charisms* 245): Manuscripts C* and L read *will follow these*; Lachmann <note>Karl Lachmann, a 19th-century textual critic.</note> reads *will accompany these* along with Manuscripts A, C², and 33. | **in**: Lachmann reads *upon* | **they will cast out**: Manuscript D (supplement) reads *they are casting out* (likewise B, C, and G in the *Acts of Pilate*) | **they will speak**: Manuscript D (supplement) reads a different future form | **new**: the *Apostolic Constitutions* (and Hippolytus) and Jacob of Nisibis <note>A 4th-century Syriac bishop.</note> place this before *they will speak*; manuscripts c*, L, Δ, Coptic, and Armenian omit it.

**18.** **snakes**: Manuscripts C*, C², L, M (margin), X, Δ (Greek), 1, 22, 33, and others, the Coptic, Armenian, and some Syriac versions prefix **and in [their] hands** (Coptic and Curetonian Syriac add *their*); likewise manuscript c and the Venetian manuscript in the *Acts of Pilate* | **they will pick up**: Manuscript o reads *they will not fear* <note>original: "non timebunt"</note> | **they drink**: Manuscript D (supplement) has a spelling variation | **not**: manuscript c* reads *nothing* | **them**: Manuscript Δ reads *to them* | **harm**: supported by A, C, D (supplement), E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π and many others, as well as Hippolytus. The Textus Receptus <note>The standard Greek text of the 16th century.</note> (along with Griesbach and Scholz) reads a different form of *harm* found in some minuscules and the *Apostolic Constitutions*. Jacob of Nisibis omits *they will pick up snakes* through *it will harm them*, but quotes the whole passage freely: "And again the Lord says to them: This sign will be for the believers: they will speak in new tongues, they will cast out demons, and they will lay their hands on the sick and they will recover."

**19.** **then** (also in the Greek Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Church Father.</note> found in Cramer's catena): manuscripts c, ff², g¹, l, o, q, and the Vulgate read *and indeed the Lord* (omitting *then*); the Latin Irenaeus reads *and indeed the Lord*. Similarly the Curetonian Syriac and Ethiopic versions... C*, L, 90, and the Armenian omit it | **Lord**: with A, C³, D (supplement), E, G, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Π, and many others, including Irenaeus. C*, K, L, Δ, 1, 22, 33, and others, as well as the Vulgate and Coptic, read **Lord Jesus** (manuscript o reads *Lord Jesus Christ*); Manuscript H and a few others read only **Jesus** | **was taken up**: as Lachmann reads with A, C, D (supplement); the Textus Receptus uses a different spelling found in the rest... manuscripts 36 and 40 read *was carried up*; manuscript 68 reads *was taken up and carried up* | **heaven**: manuscripts 13, 69, 124, and 346 read *the heavens* | manuscripts E, H, K, L and many others use a variant for **sat** | **at the right hand** (also in the Greek Irenaeus): C, Δ and a few others read *in the right hand*; Latin manuscripts c, o, q read *to the right hand* | **of God**: manuscripts 1 and the Coptic read *of the Father* (Ethiopic reads *of the Lord or of God his Father*).

**20.** **through**: omitted by Manuscript L | **signs** without **Amen**: as in the Textus Receptus, Griesbach, Scholz, and Lachmann, with A, C², 1, 33, and many others; the Vulgate and Curetonian Syriac also omit *Amen*.

### Subscriptions. ACCORDING TO MARK

... others add "Amen" <note>original: "ἀμὴν"</note> along with manuscripts C*, D (supplement), E, F, G, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Π (supplement), and many others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, and Ethiopic versions. The entire verse is preserved in the Sahidic version <note>Codex Askew, the final leaf of the manuscript containing the *Pistis Sophia*; it appeared to the scholar Woide to be taken from another book, as it contains only this verse</note> which presents it as follows:

> *They went out in threes into the four regions of heaven and preached the gospel in the whole world, with Christ working with them by the word of confirmation with the signs following them and miracles. And in this way the kingdom of God became known <note>or "was made known"</note> in all the earth and in the whole world of Israel for a testimony to all these nations that exist from the rising of the sun to its setting.*

**Subscriptions:** "According to Mark" <note>original: "κατὰ μάρκον"</note> in Manuscript B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>... "The Gospel according to Mark" <note>original: "εὐαγγέλιον κατὰ μάρκον"</note> in manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, C, E, H, K, L, U, Γ, Δ... "The Gospel according to Mark is finished; the Acts of the Apostles begins" <note>original: "εὐαγγέλιον κατὰ μάρκον ἐτελέσθη ἄρχεται πρᾶξις ἀποστόλων"</note> in the supplement to Manuscript D... in many others, "The End of the [Holy] Gospel according to Mark" <note>original: "τέλος τοῦ κατὰ μάρκον [ἁγίου] εὐαγγελίου"</note>... in the Amiatinus manuscript, "It ends" <note>original: "explicit"</note> (it has no subscription in Matthew); in many Vulgate manuscripts and the Curetonian Syriac, "The Gospel according to Mark ends"; in manuscript g, "The Gospel according to Mark ends; the introduction to the Gospel according to Luke begins"; in manuscript k, "The Gospel according to Mark ends; starts according to Matthew, successfully" <note>original: "feliciciter" (sic)</note>; in manuscript q, "Gospel according to Mark, happily ended, Amen" <note>original: "ἐπιληκητ φελικιτερ ἀμεν"</note>... manuscript Π (supplement) has no subscription. 

Furthermore, manuscripts G, H, K, S, and many others have the number of **verses** <note>original: "στίχοι"</note> noted: G, H, S, and others note 1,600; k and others note 1,700 (also the Ethiopic version notes 1,700 words); others note 1,606; others 2,000; others 1,550; and so on. Likewise, a few also note **words** <note>original: "ῥήματα"</note>: many note 1,675; others 1,676; others 1,000; and **chapters** <note>original: "κεφάλαια"</note>: many note 241; others differ; compare the notes above for verses 9–20, where the number of chapters written in the margins is referenced. It seems that Ammonius and Eusebius did not count more than 233 <note>σλγ'</note>, as explained previously. They also count **titles** <note>original: "τίτλους"</note>: 48. In Manuscript B <note>Vaticanus</note>, the Gospel of Mark has 62 sections. 

Examples of the **additions** with which the subscriptions were gradually enlarged include: Manuscripts G, S, and many others: "The Gospel according to Mark (G adds 'Holy') was published ten (or twelve) years after the Ascension of Christ (G adds 'the Lord')." In a few, it is added: "It was written in Latin in Rome" (likewise manuscripts 160 and 161; elsewhere it is claimed it was written in Egypt). Manuscript 293 reads: "It was written by the hand of Saint Mark himself in Old Rome ten years after the Ascension of Christ our God, and was published by Peter, the chief of the apostles, for the faithful brothers in Rome." Others add after "Ascension": "It was dictated (or related) by Peter." Likewise, elsewhere it is added: "It was delivered to Mark the Evangelist and was preached in Alexandria and all its surrounding region." A manuscript from the library of Sainte-Geneviève states: "It was written in Rome by him in the likeness of a calf" <note>The calf is the traditional symbol for Mark among the four living creatures of Revelation</note> (the same manuscript says of Matthew: "it is in human form"). 

Manuscripts Δ, 20, 262, and 300 read: "Gospel according to Mark: written and compared likewise from the corrected copies in 1,508 <note>αφη'</note> (or 1,506) verses and 237 chapters." That "likewise" refers to what was written at the end of the Gospel of Matthew in manuscripts Δ, 262, and 300: "Gospel according to Matthew: written and compared from the ancient copies in Jerusalem, those kept on the Holy Mountain." Similarly, manuscript 2pe at the end of Mark: "Written and compared likewise from the ancient Jerusalem copies." The Scholars' Syriac <note>Syr-Sch</note>: *Finished is the holy Gospel of the preaching of Mark, who spoke and preached in Latin in Rome.* The Philoxenian Syriac: *Finished is the holy Gospel of Mark, which he spoke in Latin in Rome.* The Roman Ethiopic: *And finished is the Gospel of Mark, and its words are 1,700.*

# 1, 3. ACCORDING TO LUKE

<margin>Acts 1:1</margin>
...delivered to us, those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, 3 it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely from the beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent <term>Theophilus</term><note>Theophilus: Likely a high-ranking Roman official or a symbolic name meaning "Friend of God."</note>, 4 so that you may know the certainty concerning the things about which you have been instructed.

5 In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zechariah, of the <term>priestly division of Abijah</term><note>Abijah: One of the twenty-four groups of priests established by King David to serve in the Temple.</note>; and he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. 6 And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and requirements of the Lord. 7 And they had no—

->### 416 1:27. ACCORDING TO LUKE<-

27 to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary. 28 And coming in to her, the angel said, "Greetings, favored one, the Lord is with you." 29 But she was troubled at the saying, and began to consider what kind of [greeting] this might be—

Acts 10:38 agrees <note>original: "accedit"</note>—it must be established that Luke wrote **Nazareth** <note>original: "Nazareth"</note>, not **Nazaret**, except that the witnesses suggest he used the form **Nazara** in 4:16. For it is incredible that the same writer fluctuated between the endings **-eth** and **-et**. Moreover, editions of the Church Fathers fluctuate similarly; however, **Nazareth** prevails.

Additionally, a few sources add **and blessed is the fruit of your womb** (also from verse 42). 29. **but she** (one manuscript may read **she was**) without addition: with Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and several ancient versions... the Received Text and Lachmann add **when she saw him** with the majority of manuscripts and the Vulgate; others add **when she heard** or **when she knew**. <note>This section contains the "Critical Apparatus"—a technical list of differences found in ancient manuscripts of the Bible.</note>

Many manuscripts <note>original: "pler"</note>, including witnesses e, f, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, Ethiopic, and John of Damascus <note>original: "Dam"</note> (though the Sahidic, Coptic, and Damascus omit the word **his** <note>original: "autou"</note>) and Augustine... instead of the phrase **at the saying**, they place it after the word **troubled**. Manuscripts a, b, ff2, g1, l, q, the Gothic version <note>original: "go"</note>, and Ambrose's commentary on Luke read **at his entrance** <note>original: "in introitu eius"</note>... manuscript c* clearly omits these words | **was troubled**: Manuscripts D, 44, 76, and others read **was greatly troubled** | **was considering**: Manuscripts D, 28, 73, and the Armenian version add **within herself** <note>original: "en eautē"</note>, as does the Gothic (she thought to herself), and other manuscripts add **saying within herself** | **what kind of... this greeting might be**: (Manuscript D reads **what kind of thing this might be**): the Latin witnesses e and the Vulgate suggest **what kind of greeting that was**; others like a, b, and l suggest **that he had blessed her thus**; while others like f, g1, and the Gothic read **what kind of greeting this was and that he had blessed her thus** (even the "Codex tested by Arduino" which reads **because he blessed her thus** <note>original: "oti outōs eulogēsen autēn"</note> seems to be of Latin rather than Greek origin).

30\. **And he said**: Some manuscripts read **But he said** or simply **He said** | **the angel to her**: Most manuscripts follow this order, but others <note>including the Gothic and Cyprian</note> read **the angel addressed her** | **Mary**: Manuscript D uses the form **Maria** (the Vulgate and Latin Fathers also consistently use **Maria**) | **with God**: One manuscript reads **from God**... Origen reads **in the presence of the Lord**.

31\. **you will conceive**: <note>Tischendorf notes a spelling variation between -mps- and -ps-</note>. Likewise, editors of Origen’s commentary on Luke note: "Blessed Mary is found to prophesy, as we find in several copies. as in manuscripts **A, E, K, L**, where the same mark is used to distinguish after the word "mighty" and after "his"—it is not sufficiently clear which reading should prevail. ## II.

<margin>Acts 5:37</margin> 1 And it happened in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the inhabited world should be registered.

---

**before the face** <note>original: "pro prosōpō"</note> with manuscripts A, C, D, L, O (variants a, b, d, e, f), R, W, Γ, Δ, Λ, nine other uncials, and almost all others; also the Old Latin and Vulgate versions (<gloss>for they have "before the face"</gloss>), Origen, the Chronicon Paschale, and the Latin translation of Irenaeus... The manuscripts Sinaiticus (א) and Vaticanus (B), along with Origen, use the word **before** <note>original: "enōpion"</note>. (I do not know whether "before" is preferred simply because "before the face" might be seen as an adaptation of the words of the prophet Malachi, which the evangelists often copied. Even Origen, when explaining this passage, brings in the words of the prophet.)

77. **their** <note>original: "autōn"</note> (Some manuscripts like 130 and 2 read "his") with א, B, D, L, O, W, Γ, Δ, Λ, seven other uncials, and the great majority of others, including the Old Latin and Vulgate (specifically the manuscripts Amianitnus, Fulda, Ingolstadt, and others). Also the Gothic, Coptic, both Syriac versions, the Armenian, and Ethiopic, as well as Irenaeus and the Chronicon Paschale... Manuscripts A, C, M, O (variants a, b, d, f), R, U, and several others read **our** <note>original: "hēmōn"</note>... A few other manuscripts omit the word entirely.

78. **through the tender mercy of our God**: Manuscript F omits this. | **has visited** <note>original: "epeskepsato"</note> with א (corrected), C, D, R, W, Γ, Δ, Ξ, nine other uncials, and almost all others; also the Old Latin and Vulgate (<gloss>these read "visited," though "will visit" is often written the same way in ancient codices</gloss>), the Peshitta Syriac, the Armenian, Ethiopic, Irenaeus, the Chronicon Paschale, and Gregory of Nyssa... Manuscripts א (original hand), B, and L read **will visit** <note>original: "episkepsetai"</note>, as do the Coptic, the Curetonian Syriac, and the Zohrab Armenian edition.

79. **to shine** <note>original: "epiphanai"</note>: Manuscript L reads "to have shone," while others use the past tense "shone." Irenaeus's Latin version reads: <gloss>"the rising sun from on high has looked upon us and appeared to those who were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death"</gloss>; he continues: <gloss>"and he directed our feet into the way of peace."</gloss> Similarly, the Chronicon Paschale reads "will shine." Additionally, manuscript D adds the word **light**. | Manuscript Λ uses a variant spelling for **to guide**.

80. **grew**: Manuscript D uses a slightly different verb form for "was growing." | **the [deserts]**: A few versions read "in those" rather than "in the."

II, 1. **And** <note>original: "de"</note> (Also found in Eusebius and the Chronicon Paschale): Omitted by manuscripts Δ, Σ, and a few others. | **Augustus**: Manuscripts א, C, Δ, and others use the spelling "Agoustou" (omitting the 'u'). | **to be registered**: A few manuscripts and Eusebius use the form "to have been registered." | One manuscript (e) omits the entire section from "all the world" to the beginning of verse 3. Compare this with the *Protevangelium of James* (17, 1), where we have edited it as follows: <gloss>"And a decree came from Augustus the King that all those in Bethlehem of Judea should be registered"</gloss> (Manuscript D says "all those in Jerusalem," and others say "all who are in Judea," while others say "all the inhabited world").

2 **This census took place first while Quirinius was governor of Syria.** 3 **And all went to be registered, each to his own city.** 4 **And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David,** 5 **to be registered with Mary, who was betrothed to him, being pregnant.**

2. **this** <note>original: "hautē"</note> (The word "this" appears as <term>hautē</term> in manuscripts <term>E, G, K, M, S, Δ</term> and others; in manuscript <term>Γ</term> it is written similarly; in <term>L</term> the accent is omitted as is often the case; the Old Latin and Vulgate versions use "haec" [this], never "ipsa" [the same]) without the article "the" <note>original: "hē"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus (<term>ℵ</term>) (The original scribe of Sinaiticus wrote "this census," though it was later adjusted) and in manuscripts <term>B</term> and <term>D</term> (which read "this took place as the first census"). It is also found in manuscript 131 and the writings of Eusebius... but the traditional Received Text <note>represented by the symbol ς</note> and Tischendorf add "the" <note>original: "hē"</note> based on the corrected Sinaiticus, and manuscripts <term>A, C, L, Γ, Δ, Λ</term>, nine other uncials <note>capital-letter parchment manuscripts</note>, and most others, including the Sahidic and Coptic versions and several passages in Eusebius | **took place first** with the original Sinaiticus and <term>D</term> (which reads "the census took place first") and Origen (who writes: "this was the first description by the governor of Syria, Cyrinus")... However, the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **first took place** with the corrected Sinaiticus and <term>A, B, C, L, R, Γ, Δ, Λ</term>, nine uncials and most others (the Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, Coptic, and both Syriac versions render "first" <note>original: "prōtē"</note> as "prima"). The Old Latin manuscript *a* reads "this was the first profession made by the governor"; manuscript *b* reads "this first profession was made by the governor," omitting "took place." Otherwise, the term "profession" <note>meaning a public registration</note> is supported by several Old Latin manuscripts and Ambrose (who says, "this first profession took place — while Cyrinus was governor of Syria this first profession was made"), while "description" <note>or census</note> is found in the Vulgate, Origen, and Augustine | **governing** (Eusebius uses a slightly different verb form): manuscript <term>Δ</term> has a spelling error | **of Syria**: the Harclean Syriac version omits this | **Quirinius** with the corrected Sinaiticus and <term>D, L, R, Γ, Δ, Λ</term>, eight uncials, most others, and Justin Martyr (in his *Dialogue* and *Apology*), and Eusebius; the Latin manuscript *d* spells it "Cyrenio," *g1* "Cyreno," and the Gothic "Cyrenaeo"... The Old Latin and Vulgate mostly use "Cyrino," from which Lachmann edited his text as "Cyrinus." Compare here Justin Martyr (who notes: "the census then taking place in Judea for the first time under Quirinius") and his statement that "Christ was born 150 years ago under Quirinius," and "he was born in Bethlehem, as you can learn from the census records made under Quirinius, our first procurator in Judea." Chrysostom also notes: "hence it is clear he was born during the first census."

<note>This section compares different ancient copies of the Bible to see where they differ in wording.</note>

... **having come from Nazareth, where he lived, to Bethlehem, where he was from, to be registered** <note>original: "lēlythei apo nazaret... eis bēthleem... apograpsasthai"</note>) found in Eusebius and Stephanus (though in this location they put the word for "registration" before "to the city") and also in Cyril of Jerusalem and the *Chronicon Paschale*... The scholar Lachmann reads **to be registered** <note>original: "apographesthai"</note> along with the original Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, and minuscules 33 and 10 others, and Chrysostom | **with** <note>original: "syn"</note>: Manuscripts A, E, U, V, and Γ use a slightly different spelling <note>original: "sym"</note> | **Mary** <note>original: "Mariam"</note> (also in Eusebius, Chrysostom, and the *Chronicon*): Codex Bezae, an Oxford manuscript of Eusebius, and Stephanus use the shorter form **Maria** | **betrothed** <note>original: "emnēsteumenē"</note> with the original Sinaiticus, B, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, L, and Zacynthius... but the Received Text <note>symbol: ς</note> uses **having been betrothed** <note>original: "memnēsteumenē"</note> with corrected Sinaiticus, later corrections of B and C, Codex Bezae, and nine other uncials and almost all others | **to him** <note>original: "autō"</note> without the word **wife** <note>original: "gynaiki"</note> along with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, L, Zacynthius, and several early Latin and Syriac versions... the Received Text and Tischendorf add **to him as wife** with Codex Alexandrinus, Γ, Δ, Λ, nine other uncials, and most others, including the Vulgate (Latin) and several church fathers. It is not entirely clear whether Cyril of Jerusalem read it this way; he writes: "What does the Scripture say? He went up with his betrothed wife being pregnant. For she was pregnant; it did not say 'with his wife,' but with 'his betrothed.'" <note>It is not unlikely that the word "wife" was influenced by the phrasing in Matthew 1:20 and 24.</note> Furthermore, compare the *Protevangelium of James* 19, 1: "I said: She who is betrothed to me. And he said to me: Is she not your wife? And I said to her: It is Mary... she is not my wife, but she has conceived from the Holy Spirit." | **pregnant** <note>original: "enkyō"</note>: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and others; Vaticanus and others use a slightly different spelling <note>original: "engyō"</note>.

6. **While they were** <note>original: "egeneto de... autous"</note> (Chrysostom uses "And it happened"; early Latin versions use "when they were") **there**: also in Eusebius, Amphilochius, Cyril, and the *Chronicon*... Codex Bezae reads **while they arrived** | **were completed** <note>original: "eplēsthēsan"</note> (Eusebius, Amphilochius, Chrysostom, *Chronicon*): Codex Bezae reads **were finished** <note>original: "etelesthēsan"</note>.

Compare also Justin Martyr: "Mary had brought forth the Christ and had placed Him in a manger." The *Protevangelium* 22, 2 says: "She took the child and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and placed him in the manger (some copies add: of the oxen)." | **because** <note>original: "dioti"</note>: manuscript F uses **that** <note>original: "hoti"</note>.

<note>The following notes discuss the scholarly evidence for different versions of the "Gloria" hymn and the subsequent verses, comparing ancient Greek manuscripts and the writings of Church Fathers.</note>

...the creator; they glorified him with these words, who sent from heaven his kindness of salvation to his creation, that is, to men <note>original Latin: "plasmati h. e. hominibus"</note>") Origen in the Latin translation, volume 3, page 946, three times. (And explicitly: "If it were written: *peace on earth*, and the sentence ended there, a question would rightly arise. But now, in what has been added—that is, what is said after 'peace': *In people of good will*—he solves the question. For the peace which the Lord does not give upon the earth is not the peace of good will.") It appears from these words that Origen truly defended the reading **of good will** <note>original: *eudokias*, the genitive form</note>, not the reading **good will** <note>original: *eudokia*, the nominative form</note> as it is now found three times in Greek in his works. Athanasius in Latin volume 2, page 541; Augustine in *The Harmony of the Gospels* 2, 17; and almost all other Latin sources... the reading **good will** <note>original: *eudokia*</note> is supported by the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, the third corrector of Codex Vaticanus, and manuscripts L, P, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, along with 8 other uncials <note>Uncials are ancient manuscripts written in all capital letters.</note> (Manuscript F is missing here, but it is notable etc. others do not put a punctuation mark before "among men") and almost all others seen (likewise in the Ancient Hymn and the Ode), the Coptic, both Syriac versions, Armenian, and Ethiopic (Origen volume 1, 374; volume 2, 714; and volume 4, 15 but see above); Gregory Thaumaturgus 6; Eusebius in *The Proof of the Gospel* pages 163 and 342; Basil volume 2, 602; Cyril volume 5, 593; Epiphanius 1047; *Apostolic Constitutions* 7, 47; Jacob of Nisibis 9, 4; Chrysostom volume 2, 537; Theodotus of Ancyra 446; Proclus 629, and others.

**15.** **the angels went away from them into heaven** <note>original: "ap autōn eis ton ouranon oi angeloi"</note> (Codex Sinaiticus first hand omits, added by a corrector) with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, L, P, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, and 8 other uncials, and most others; the Coptic and Gothic versions (Origen volume 4, 15 "and having said these things, the angels depart from the shepherds into heaven"). Eusebius in *The Proof of the Gospel* 342: Codex Bezae (D) reads **the angels from them into heaven**; minuscules 13, 28, 33, 69, and others, along with several Old Latin versions and the Vulgate and Syriac versions, and the Armenian; Origen in Latin translation volume 3, 947 reads **the angels from them into heaven**; others omit **into heaven**... Manuscript Γ reads **the angels from heaven away from them**. | **the shepherds** <note>original: "oi poimenes"</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, Ξ, and others, several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, and Armenian; Eusebius, Origen in Latin, and Augustine... the editors Stephanus and Tischendorf add **and the men**, Lachmann puts **[and the men]** in brackets, following manuscripts Alexandrinus, Bezae, P, Γ, Δ, Λ, and many others, as well as the Gothic and Philoxenian Syriac and Ethiopic versions. | **they were speaking to one another** <note>original: "elaloun pr. allēlous"</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and several Old Latin versions; Augustine and the Vulgate ("they were speaking to one another"), but Sinaiticus adds **saying**, and some Old Latin versions read **and they said**... the editors Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **they said** <note>original: "eipon" or "eipan"</note> with manuscripts Alexandrinus, Bezae, L, P, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, and almost all others, as well as Eusebius and Origen's Latin translation. | **one another**: manuscript 69 and a few others read **themselves**. | **now** <note>original: "dē"</note>: Stephanus omits. | **even to** <note>original: "heōs"</note> (Manuscript Λ reads "in" according to Tregelles): manuscripts P, 245, and 258 add **into**; some Latin versions read "as far as into" or "unto," while one omits it. | **let us see** <note>original: "idōmen"</note>: manuscript Δ and others have spelling variations like "eidomen." | **which has happened** <note>original: "gegonos"</note>: Codex Bezae and others have spelling variations; Eusebius reads **having happened** <note>original: "genomenon"</note>. | **made known**: Manuscript Γ and others have a spelling variation. | **to us**: Manuscript Γ omits.

**16.** **they went** <note>original: "ēlthan"</note> with manuscripts Vaticanus (first hand), L, and Ξ... the editors Stephanus and Lachmann read **they went** <note>original: "ēlthon"</note> with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and most others. | **in haste** <note>original: "speusantes"</note> (also Eusebius): Codex Bezae and minuscule 61 read **hurrying** <note>original: "speudontes"</note>... Manuscript Ξ reads **having believed**. | **they found** <note>original: "aneuran"</note> with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus... the editors Stephanus and Lachmann read **they found** <note>original: "aneuron"</note> with various uncials... other manuscripts like Bezae and Eusebius use a simpler word for **found** <note>original: "euron"</note>. | **and** <note>original: "te"</note>: Codex Bezae and Eusebius omit, nor is it expressed in the Vulgate, Coptic, or Syriac. | **Mary** <note>original: "Mariam"</note>: Codex Bezae and others spell it **Marian**. | **the**: omitted by some manuscripts and the Gothic and Armenian versions.

**17.** **and** <note>original: "de"</note>: Manuscript Ξ omits. | **they made known** <note>original: "egnōrisan"</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, Ξ, and others, and Eusebius... the editors Stephanus and Tischendorf read **they made known abroad** <note>original: "diegnōrisan"</note> with manuscripts Alexandrinus, P, Γ, Δ, Λ, and most others.

<note>The following apparatus criticus (scholarly notes) documents small variations in the wording of these verses found in different ancient handwritten copies of the Bible.</note>

17\. **of this** <note>original Greek: *toutou*</note>: Omitted by manuscripts D, Lambda, 1, and several others, including some Old Latin versions and the Coptic and Armenian translations.

18\. **those (omitting "the") who heard** <note>original: *hoi akousantes*</note>: Manuscript D and others read "those who are hearing" <note>original: *hoi akouontes*</note>; Latin versions *d* and *e* read "who were hearing"; version *q* reads "who were present." | **wondered**: Manuscript D and others use a tense suggesting they "remained in wonder" <note>original: *ethaumazon*</note>.

19\. **Mary** <note>original: *Maria*</note>: Spelled "Maria" in the oldest manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The Textus Receptus <note>the standard printed Greek text used for centuries</note> spells it "Mariam" based on later manuscripts. | **all** (omitted by one manuscript) **kept**: Various manuscripts change the word order to "kept all." | **these**: Omitted by manuscript B and others. | **pondering** <note>original: *sumballousa*</note>: Spelling varies between "sumballousa" and "sumbalousa" <note>a difference of a single 'l'</note> across many ancient copies. | **her**: Most early manuscripts use "her" <note>original: *autes*</note>, while a few use the more emphatic "her own" <note>original: *eautes*</note>.

20\. **returned** <note>original: *upestrepsan*</note>: Almost all major capital-letter manuscripts <note>uncials</note> agree on this word, though the Textus Receptus uses a slightly different word for "returned" <note>original: *epestrepsan*</note>. | **saw** <note>original: *idon*</note>: This specific spelling of "saw" appears in many major manuscripts; though it looks slightly different from the standard form <note>original: *eidon*</note>, Tischendorf argues it should be kept because the evidence for it is so strong. | **as**: Manuscript G adds "and." | **was told**: One manuscript uses the plural "were told." | **to them**: The Harclean Syriac version adds the phrase "by the angels."

21\. **and when**: A quote from Amphilochius reads "and it happened when." | **were fulfilled**: Some manuscripts use "were completed" or "were finished." Latin translations vary between "were filled," "were completed," and "were perfected." | **days**: Several manuscripts add the article "the" before "days," and manuscript D adds "the" before "eight." | **of**: One manuscript changes "of the circumcising" to "they came to circumcise the child." | **him** <note>original: *auton*</note>: Found in almost all the earliest manuscripts and early Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions. However, the Textus Receptus and several other manuscripts replace "him" with **the child** <note>original: *to paidion*</note>. Origen refers to this passage as "the days of his circumcision." | **and**: Omitted by some manuscripts and Origen. | **was called** <note>original: *eklethe*</note>: Manuscript D uses the word "was named."

<note>The following notes compare different ancient handwritten versions of these verses. Scholars use these to determine the most original wording.</note>

**it was named** <note>original: "nominatum est"</note> | **the [name] called** <note>original: "to klethen"</note> (it was called <note>original: "vocatum"</note> - in most Latin and Vulgate versions): manuscript Sinaiticus reads **the [name] spoken**, and Latin version *e* reads **which had been said**. | **conceived** <note>original: "syllempthenai"</note>: spelled various ways in the major uncial manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.). | **him** <note>original: "auton"</note> (manuscript Sinaiticus): some versions read **her**. | **in the womb**: Manuscript D reads **in the mother's womb**.

**22. were fulfilled** <note>original: "eplesthesan"</note>: Some versions like Sinaiticus and Cyril of Jerusalem read "were completed" <note>original: "eplerothesan"</note>. | **their** <note>original: "auton"</note>: This is the most common reading in manuscripts like Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus. However, it creates a theological question: who needs "purification"? Origen <note>an early church father, c. 185–253 AD</note> noted: <note>original: "propter purgationem, inquit, eorum..."</note> "Because of their purification, it says. Whose [purification]? If it were written 'because of her purification,' meaning Mary who had given birth, no question would arise... but now in saying 'the days of their purification,' it does not seem to signify one person, but two or more." | Other versions read **his** <note>original: "autou"</note> or **her** <note>original: "autes"</note>. Pseudo-Athanasius wrote: "For when, it says, the days of her purification were fulfilled... this concerns the infant; and the sacrifice... this concerns the Virgin and her betrothed." | **Moses** <note>original: "moseos"</note>: Manuscript D and others use a slightly different spelling. | **him**: Manuscript Chron. 381 and Cyril of Jerusalem specify **Jesus** to clarify that he was being presented. | **to present**: Irenaeus uses a Latin word meaning **to stand by**.

**23. law**: Manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus use the simple word "law," while others add the article "the." | **opening**: Some manuscripts use a different Greek spelling for the word "opening."

**24. in the law**: Manuscript Delta reads **to the law**. | **young [pigeons]**: Two different Greek spellings exist here—*nossous* and *neossous*. An ancient scholar, Phrynichus, noted that *neossous* was the more "ancient" or classical way to write it.

<header>2, 25. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

**25** And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. **26** And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. **27** And he came by the Spirit into the temple; and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, **28** he took him into his arms and blessed

---

**25.** **And behold** <note>original: "idou"</note> (also in Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, and Armenian): omitted by Manuscript D, Sinaitic Syriac, and Ethiopic; the Gothic version uses "then" instead of "and behold" (as it also does in Matthew 9:18 and elsewhere). | **there was a man** [variation in word order]: the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and several Latin versions read it this way (the Peshitta Syriac reads **but there was a certain man**) ... the standard traditional text <note>often called the "Textus Receptus"</note> and the editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read **a man was** [in a different order] based on many other uncial manuscripts... one late manuscript (number 243) omits **was**. | Manuscript Sinaiticus reads **whose name was his**. | **Simeon** (also in Old Latin and several Vulgate editions): some manuscripts spell it **Simeon** <note>original: "Simeon"</note> here and in verse 34. | **devout** <note>original: "eulabes"</note> (supported by the most significant uncials including Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae, and the Latin versions which use "God-fearing" or "fearing"): cited by Pseudo-Athanasius (asking "But how was he devout? By fearing the face of the Lord") ... but some manuscripts and the margin of the Philoxenian Syriac read **pious** <note>original: "eusebes"</note>. | **of Israel**: some manuscripts and the writings of Didymus the Blind read **to Israel**. | **was [the Holy Spirit]**: omitted by some early manuscripts; the order **Holy was** is found in the oldest uncials ... while the traditional text reads **was Holy**, supported by Manuscript D, the Latin, Syriac, and Gothic versions.

**26.** **And it had been revealed to him** <note>original: "kai en auto kechrematismenon"</note> (as found in Didymus and Cyril of Jerusalem; Latin versions read **and an answer was given to him** or **he had received an answer**): Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions read **but he had been revealed**, or **but he had received an answer**; one Latin version (e) reads **for he had received an answer**. | **by** <note>original: "hypo"</note>: Manuscript L reads **from** <note>original: "apo"</note>. | **before** <note>original: "prin e an"</note>: some manuscripts omit the particle "an" ... the traditional text and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf omit "an" based on several uncials. Latin versions generally read **unless first** or **before that** ... Sinaiticus and Didymus read **until**. | **he should see** <note>original: "ide"</note>: some later manuscripts and Cyril of Jerusalem read the infinitive **to see** <note>original: "idein"</note>. | **of the Lord**: one uncial (Lambda) and some Coptic versions read **the Lord** (the Jerusalem Syriac reads **the Christ and Lord** <note>original: "ton <term>chn</term> kai kyrion"</note>).

"into Jerusalem" <note>original: "eis ierosolyma"</note> with manuscripts A, C, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials <term>early manuscripts written in capital letters</term>, and many others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions | "festival": manuscripts D and X, and several Latin versions add "of the unleavened bread."

The <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads "and among acquaintances." Manuscript Sinaiticus and others omit "and acquaintances." (Compare the *Gospel of Thomas*: "they sought him among their relatives, and not finding him, they were greatly grieved, and returned again into the city seeking him.")

**45.** "finding" (manuscript D reads "finding him"): some manuscripts omit the word "him." | "searching" (intensive form): supported by many early manuscripts and the Vulgate. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> uses the simpler "seeking." (Compare the *Gospel of Thomas* reference in verse 44).

It highlights a significant textual shift where later manuscripts changed "his parents" to "Joseph and his mother" to protect the doctrine of the Virgin Birth.</summary>

Likewise in the Gospel of Thomas <note>an early non-biblical gospel</note> in the same place; for it continues after "seeking him": "and after the third day they found him in the temple sitting in the midst of the teachers and hearing the law and questioning them." | "after" <note>original: "meta"</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, 1, 33, 131. ... the "Received Text" <note>the standard Greek text used for centuries, often abbreviated as ς</note> and Lachmann read "after" <note>original: "meth"</note> with manuscripts A, C, D, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials <term>early manuscripts written in capital letters</term> and most others | "in the temple": manuscript D (corrected) and manuscript 254 place this after "sitting," a few others omit it | "sitting" <note>original: "kathezomenon"</note> (Gregory Thaumaturgus and Theophanes read "sitting in the midst of teachers"): manuscripts D, 1, 118 read "seated" <note>original: "kathēmenon"</note>, omitted by manuscript G | Manuscripts A, L, U read "in the midst" as one word | "and hearing": also in the Ethiopic, Syriac, and others, and Origen's Latin translation: manuscript D, five others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, and Coptic omit "and" | "hearing them and asking them": various Latin versions and the Vulgate read "hearing them and questioning them"; Origen's Latin reads "hearing and questioning them."

# 440 ACCORDING TO LUKE 3, 1.

### III.

1 <sup>6. 3</sup> **Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip**

---

<note>The following notes continue the evidence for Luke 2:52: "And Jesus increased in wisdom..."</note> Manuscripts A and Π, eight other uncials <term>early manuscripts written in capital letters</term>, and almost all other witnesses, the Old Latin manuscripts f, ff², and g¹, the Vulgate <note>the standard 4th-century Latin Bible</note>, the Gothic version, the Peshitta Syriac, the Armenian (possibly), Origen (in multiple locations), Athanasius, Cyril’s commentary on John and his work on the Trinity, Epiphanius, and Augustine. It is also found in the Gospel of Thomas. On the other hand, manuscripts D and L, several Old Latin versions, the Coptic, and the Curetonian Syriac <note>an early Syriac translation</note> provide variations. Origen in his Greek text writes: "Therefore he progressed in age, he progressed in wisdom, he progressed in grace..." but this is followed immediately by the words we have already noted. Origen's Latin translation reads: "for so it is reported because Jesus progressed in age and wisdom before God and men." Other citations are found in Epiphanius, Cyril’s work against Nestorius, and Amphilochius (who explains: "he progressed then according to age as his body grew according to nature, in wisdom because of... grace," though this is not in the main heading). Also cited by Gregory of Nyssa, Theodoret, and Victorinus (though Jerome notes that "Origen and Victorinus did not feel very differently from each other—because he progressed in age and wisdom and grace before God and men"). | *before God* <note>original: "para theō"</note>: The corrected Sinaiticus <note>a famous 4th-century Bible</note> reads this, while the original hand of Sinaiticus wrote "of God" but continued "and men." | *men*: Manuscript D adds "before" <note>original: "para"</note> before "men."

III. 1. **and** <note>original: "de"</note>: Clement of Alexandria writes: "and in the fifteenth year under Tiberius Caesar the word of the Lord came upon John the son of Zechariah." This word is found in the corrected Sinaiticus, and manuscripts H, K, X, 28, 124, and more than twenty others, as well as the Tolatene manuscript of the Vulgate, the Armenian, Origen’s Latin translation, and Eusebius. It is omitted in some. | **fifteenth**: Manuscript L uses a slightly different spelling for "fifteenth" <note>original: "pentedekatō"</note>. | **reign of Tiberius Caesar**: Manuscript x adds "Augustus." | **governor**: Eusebius uses this term; however, manuscript D, other passages in Eusebius, and the Paschal Chronicle use the term "procurator" <note>original: "epitropeuontos"</note>. Likewise, the Old Latin and Vulgate use the Latin term for "governor" or "procurator." **Pilate**: Manuscripts A, B (original hand), and D spell it one way; while the corrected Sinaiticus, the third hand of Vaticanus, C, L, and almost all other uncials spell it "Pilatos." Editors Lachmann and Tischendorf prefer the latter. **of Judea**: Omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus, but supplied by a later corrector. | **and tetrarch**: Eusebius and the Paschal Chronicle read "and while they were tetrarchs, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias." | **tetrarch**: <note>The editor notes a specific spelling variant here.</note> The spelling with a double 'a' <note>original: "tetraarchountos"</note> is found three times in the original hand and first corrector of Sinaiticus and the Coptic. The Sinaiticus maintains this form everywhere, including Luke 9:7. This form also appears in manuscript L for Luke 9:7, and in several other places. There is little doubt that this unusual form was placed there by the sacred writers themselves, but was cast out by most later scribes. Therefore, it seemed to us that it should be restored everywhere in this edition. Other editors like Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use the more common spelling "tetrarchountos" based on the corrected Sinaiticus, A, B, D, L, and others. | **and tetrarch of Galilee**: These words were omitted by the Greek text of manuscript D by error; a verse was lost in the Greek column, and subsequently, at the end of the page and the beginning of the next, "tetrarch of Iturea" was written twice. | **of Galilee, Herod**: Manuscripts Δ, K, and Π swap the order to "Herod of Galilee." | **Iturea**: This spelling is found in the Coptic and others. Some manuscripts (L, Δ) use a slightly different vowel. One Coptic version and Peter of Alexandria read "Idumea" <note>a region to the south</note>, and a marginal note in Vaticanus reads "the hill country." | The original hand of Sinaiticus omitted the text from "Iturea" down to "Lysanias," but it was supplied by a later corrector. | **and of Trachonitis**: The corrected Sinaiticus reads this; the original Vaticanus has a slightly different spelling. A later hand in Sinaiticus and other manuscripts (69, 48) write "and of Tetrachonitis." | **Abilene**: Spelled this way in most manuscripts including Sinaiticus, A, E, G, H, K, L, S, U, X, Γ, Λ, Π, the Old Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Eusebius. Manuscripts Δ and B use a variant spelling <note>original: "Abeilēnēs"</note>.

The editor argues for restoring an "unusual" spelling of the word 'tetrarch' which he believes was the original wording of the author.</summary>

# 441 ACCORDING TO LUKE 3, 2.

...being tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias being tetrarch of Abilene, **2** during the high priesthood of Annas

---

Gothic *abeileni* ... Majority Text, manuscripts M, V, Δ, and many others, Old Latin c, g <sup>1. 2.</sup>, l, the Vulgate, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac (also in the Greek margin), the *Chronicon* 392 *Abilene* (Latin: *abilinae*). Manuscript D² <note>a later corrector of the 5th-century Codex Bezae</note> reads *Abilene*... The original hand of D reads *Abilliane*, and similarly in Old Latin manuscripts a, b, e, f, ff² *Abilianae* (manuscript *e* reads *Abilineae*, *ff²* reads *Ablianae*), *d* reads *Abillianetis* ... Ethiopic *Sabilanes*. | In Manuscript L, "of Abilene" (the letter η is supplied above the line); the remaining three syllables of the word "being tetrarch" <note>Greek: τετραρχουντοσ</note> were written above the line by the original scribe. 

Concerning the beginning of the Gospel of Marcion <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century figure who created a shortened version of Luke, removing Jewish elements</note>, Tertullian writes in *Against Marcion* 4, 7: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, he puts him forward" (The Paris and Franeker editions read "God" <note>Latin: deum</note> instead of "him"). Previously, in 4, 6, he states that Marcion established that there is another Christ who, in the times of Tiberius, was revealed by a God previously unknown, having "descended into the city of Galilee, Capernaum." Similarly, Epiphanius (42, 11) notes: "at the beginning, having cut out everything Luke recorded from the start—he jumped away and set this as the beginning of the gospel: 'In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar,' and so on." Compare also *Dialogue* 1, 823: "When did the Good One (or rather 'the Good God') descend to save humanity? As the Gospel contains, that it was during the time of Tiberius Caesar, in the times of Pilate." Again in 1, 869: "As they say, having descended in the time of Tiberius (the 'Unknown God' can be supplied from earlier), he appeared in Capernaum." Furthermore, see Tertullian in the same work: "finally, it is unworthy that... while the Christ of God descending from his heaven found no proclaimer." Also the Latin translation of Irenaeus 106: "saying that Jesus, coming from that Father who is above the God who made the world, into Judea in the times of Pontius Pilate the governor, who was the procurator of Tiberius Caesar, was manifested in human form to those who were in Judea, dissolving the prophets and the law and all the works of that God who made the world." Also Hippolytus 7, 31: "Marcion altogether rejected the birth of our Savior, considering it to be absurd—but without a birth, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, having come down from above... he taught in the synagogues." Regarding the title of Marcion's Gospel, see Tertullian 4, 2: "Marcion, to be sure, ascribes no author to his gospel"; compare with *Dialogue* 1, 829: "Not Peter, but Christ wrote the Gospel." That Marcion passed over the subsequent verses until 4:16–30 (which he placed after 4:31–39) is testified by Epiphanius and others. 

Concerning the beginning of the Gospel of the Ebionites <note>A Jewish-Christian group that used a version of Matthew's Gospel</note>—which is added to supplement Matthew 3:1—Epiphanius (30, 13) recorded this: "The beginning of the gospel among them holds that: 'It came to pass in the days of Herod, king of Judea, John came baptizing a baptism of repentance in the Jordan river, who was said to be of the lineage of Aaron the priest, son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, and everyone went out to him.' And after saying many things, he adds that: 'When the people were baptized, Jesus also came and was baptized by John.'" (The things that follow are ascribed to Matthew 3:16.) Again in 30, 14: "For having cut off the genealogies found in Matthew, they begin to make the start, as we said before, saying: 'It came to pass,' he says, 'in the days of Herod, king of Judea, during the high priesthood of Caiaphas, a certain man came, John by name, baptizing [in the Jordan] river,' and so on."

**2.** The word "during" <note>original: επι (epi)</note> is supported by the Majority Text and uncial manuscripts A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, Χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others, Eusebius's *Demonstratio Evangelica* 365 and 398, and Theodoret 2, 1247.

### 3, 17. ACCORDING TO LUKE 446

...than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. 17 <note>The number 11.5 likely refers to a cross-reference or section marker in the original manuscript.</note> His winnowing fan <note>The 'ptyon' was a wooden shovel or fork used to toss threshed grain into the air; the wind would blow the lighter 'chaff' away while the heavier 'wheat' fell back to the floor.</note> is in his hand to thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his storehouse, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.

---

**I baptize you** <note>original: vos baptizo</note>: The Vulgate, Syriac Peshitta, Ethiopic, and Origen (four times, page 132); likewise **baptize you with water** <note>original: βαπτ. υμ. υδατ.</note> (specified as "in water" once in the Latin Origen) [manuscript] f, Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and the scholars' Gothic, Latin Origen (three times, page 961)... Manuscripts D, 1, 13, 69, 131, 124, Latin *e*, and Ambrose on Luke (twice, page 77) read **baptize you in water** <note>original: υμας βαπτιζ. εν υδατι</note>. Eusebius (page 428) reads **you with water baptize** <note>original: υμας υδατ. βαπτ.</note>. Latin manuscripts *a, b, c, q*, the *Liber Comicus*, Gothic, and Ambrose on Luke (twice, page 79) read **I baptize you** (manuscript *q* and the *Liber Comicus* add "in") **with water**. Furthermore, manuscripts C, D, and Latin manuscripts *a, b, c, e, ff*<sup>2</sup>, *g*<sup>1</sup>, *l, q*, the *Gatarian*, and the *Liber Comicus*, and Ambrose on Luke (twice, page 77) (but not manuscript *f* or the Vulgate) and the margin of the Syriac Peshitta (in the Assemani codex) **add**: **unto repentance** <note>original: εις μετανοιαν</note> (manuscript *e* reads "into the water of repentance"): this is not present in Origen (four times, page 132 and 133, who notes: "Matthew alone added this 'unto repentance'") nor in the Latin Origen (three times, page 961) or Eusebius (page 428). | **But he comes** <note>original: ερχεται δε</note> (manuscript *v* omits "but") and Origen (four times, page 132) and Eusebius (page 428): manuscript D, Latin *l*, and the Latin Origen (three times, page 961) read **But the one coming** <note>original: ο δε ερχομενος</note> (compare to Matthew). | **The** (omitted by D) **one stronger than I** (manuscript *c* reads "than me"): manuscript D and Latin *l* **add**: **is**... Manuscript L and six others, and Eusebius **add**: **after me** <note>original: οπισω μου</note> (the Latin Origen reads "he who comes after me"; the Syriac scholars' edition reads "but he comes after me"). | **Worthy** <note>original: ικανος</note>: Manuscripts M, 13, 69, 124, and the *xser* **add**: **stooping down** <note>original: κυψας</note>. Conversely, Origen (four times, page 135) notes: "Let not the phrase 'without stooping down' be left unexamined, as it is similarly spoken by Luke and John." Likewise, Augustine in *Harmony of the Gospels* (2, 26): "regarding the sandals, this differs from Luke because he [Mark] added 'stooping down'." | **Of the sandals** <note>original: των υποδηματων</note> (Origen, page 136: "let us further discuss the sandals named thus by the three Evangelists, comparing those to the one named in the singular by the disciple John"): manuscript D, the Coptic, and Syriac Peshitta read **of the sandal** (singular). Clement (page 679): "I am not, he says, worthy to untie the strap of the Lord's sandal," conforming to John. Even more freely (page 241): "confessing he is not worthy to untie the strap of the Lord's sandals." Furthermore, the phrase **to untie the strap of the sandals** is rendered by Latin manuscripts *a, b, ff*<sup>2</sup>, *l, q*, Armenian, and Ambrose on Luke (page 80) as **to carry the sandals**, likewise Eusebius (page 428): "of whom I am not worthy **to carry the sandals**" <note>original: τα υποδηματα βαστασαι</note>. | **His** (also in *c, e, f*, Vulgate, Origen page 132): manuscript Lambda reads **their**... manuscripts D, *a, b, ff*<sup>2</sup>, *l, q*, and Armenian (and Eusebius, see above) **omit**. | **He** <note>original: αυτος</note> (supplied by the corrector of Codex Sinaiticus): omitted by the original scribe of Codex Sinaiticus. | **Holy**: Manuscripts 63, 64, and Tertullian *On Baptism* (page 10) (he himself professes—to dip in repentance alone, but one would come soon who would dip in spirit and fire), and Augustine *Harmony of the Gospels* (2, 26) **omit**. (Augustine notes: regarding baptism, this [differs] from both because [Mark] did not say "and fire," but only "in the Holy Spirit." For just as Matthew did, so also Luke spoke, and in the same order: "He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire," except that Luke did not add "Holy," as Matthew said). Compare also Heracleon? in Clement’s *Excerpts* (page 25/985): "John says that I indeed baptize you with water, but there comes after me the one baptizing in spirit and fire."

17. **To thoroughly cleanse** <note>original: διακαθαραι - an infinitive</note> with the original scribe of Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Latin *a* (to purge the area), *e* (that he might emundate the area), Coptic, Armenian, and the Latin translation of Irenaeus (page 17) (to emundate). **22. upon** <note>original: επ</note>: manuscript D reads "into" <note>original: εισ</note>; likewise most Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate read *in ipsum* ("into him"), though manuscript 'f' reads *super ipsum* ("upon him") | **from** <note>original: εξ</note>: manuscript Δ reads "away from" <note>original: απ</note>; manuscript D reads "out of the" <note>original: εκ του</note> | **there was [a voice]** <note>original: γενεσθαι</note>: without any addition (according to Griesbach's second preference) along with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and L, as well as several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Ambrose's commentary on Luke (2.83). However, the Majority Text (ς) adds "saying" <note>original: λεγουσαν</note> along with manuscripts A, X, Γ, Δ, Π, and eight other uncials, and many others, including various versions; manuscripts Λ, 13, 69, 262 and a few others read "saying to him" :: compare with Matthew and the Gospel of the Ebionites according to Epiphanius (138) | **in you** <note>original: εν σοι</note>: manuscript 'x' and some others, as well as the Coptic and Gothic versions and Eusebius (page 270), read "in whom" <note>original: εν ω</note> :: as in Matthew. On the contrary, Augustine in *The Harmony of the Evangelists* (2.31) notes: <note>original: "quod alius (Mt) dicit: in quo mihi complacui, alius (Mc): in te complacui, alius (Lc): in te complacuit mihi"</note> "what one (Matthew) says: 'in whom I am well pleased,' another (Mark): 'in you I am well pleased,' and another (Luke): 'in you it has pleased me'" | **I am well pleased** <note>original: ευδοκησα</note> with Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and many other manuscripts and Eusebius; the Majority Text (ς) uses a different spelling <note>original: ηυδοκ.</note> with A, E, G, H, and others. Instead of **"You are my [beloved Son; in you I am well pleased]"**, manuscripts D and several Old Latin versions read: **"You are my Son; today I have begotten you."** <note>This is a famous variant that quotes Psalm 2:7.</note> The same reading is attested by Augustine (2.31): "Indeed, that which some manuscripts have according to Luke—that the voice sounded with what is written in the Psalm: *You are my Son, today I have begotten you*—although it is said not to be found in the older Greek manuscripts, yet if it can be confirmed by some trustworthy copies, what else is to be understood than that both were heard from heaven in whatever order of words?" Likewise Juvencus (1.364): "He addresses Christ, washed by the waves and anointed by the breath: 'I testify to you, son, today through joys as having been begotten of me,' etc." See other Latin testimonies in Sabatier. But compare also what we transcribed for Matthew from the Gospel of the Ebionites, as well as Justin's *Dialogue with Trypho* (88 and 103). Furthermore, compare Clement (page 113): "For immediately when the Lord was baptized, a voice from the heavens echoed as a witness of the Beloved: 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you.'" Likewise Methodius (719).

**23. and Jesus himself was** <note>original: και αυτος ην ις</note> ("Jesus" without the definite article "the" with ℵ, B, L, U, X, 33 and others; against the Majority Text and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf who include "the" <note>original: ο</note> with A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and others) with ℵ, A, B, E, and others; likewise manuscripts 13, 124, 346, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, and Armenian versions read **and Jesus himself was** (*et ipse Iesus erat*) ... manuscript D and Hippolytus, Athanasius, and Epiphanius (432) read **but he was** <note>original: ην δε</note> (Hippolytus adds "the") Jesus (Epiphanius 439: "that Jesus was," 746: "that he himself was the Jesus." Compare also Clement 407: "and Jesus was coming to the baptism being about thirty years old"), the Coptic and Irenaeus read "But Jesus was," the Peshitta reads "but Jesus himself was" | **beginning [his ministry] being about** <note>original: αρχομ. ωσει</note> (Hippolytus and Epiphanius read "about" <note>original: ωσ</note>) **thirty years** with ℵ, B, L, X, and several others, the Vulgate, Hippolytus, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Epiphanius, and Ambrose (Irenaeus: "as if beginning thirty years of age, when he came to the baptism"); likewise 13, 69, 346 and Epiphanius read "beginning to be about thirty" ... the Majority Text and Lachmann read **about thirty years [old] beginning** <note>original: ωσει ετων τριακ. αρχομενος</note> (some manuscripts add "being") with A, D, Γ, Δ, and others | **being the son (as was supposed)** with ℵ, B, L, 1, and others, the Old Latin (*filius ut existimabatur*), Origen, and Africanus (as cited in Eusebius's *Church History* 1.7.4: "who was the son, as was supposed, for he adds this also, 'of Joseph'"), Eusebius, Athanasius, and Epiphanius ... the Majority Text reads **being (as was supposed) the son** with A, X, Γ, Δ, Π, and others, and manuscript 'f' (*sicut extimabatur filius*).

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 3:24.

->[thirty years old], being a son, as was supposed, of Joseph, [son] of Heli, **24** of Matthat, of Levi, of Melchi, of Jannai, of Joseph<-

---

*Supplement to verse 20:* <note>original: Ad v. 20 supple</note> ... the Majority Text <note>original: ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "and he shut up" <note>original: και κατεκλει</note> along with Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Codex Bezae (L), and many other uncials <note>term: uncials (early manuscripts written in large capital letters)</note>, as well as nearly all Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, both the Peshitta and Harclean Syriac, the Gothic, and others.

The Vulgate reads "as he was thought to be the son" <note>original: ut putabatur filius</note>; so also the Coptic, the Palestinian Syriac, the Armenian, and the Ethiopic (though the *Chronicle* 457 omits "being" <note>original: ων</note>) ... Codex Bezae (D) reads "as he was supposed to be a son" <note>original: ωσ ενομειζετο ειναι υιοσ</note>; similarly, various Old Latin manuscripts read "it was thought he was the son," "he seemed to be the son," or "he was seen and said to be the son." Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke (3.1), and the Syriac Scholion read "and he was estimated [to be] a son." | **Joseph** <note>original: ιωσηφ</note>: written without the definite article in Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and many others, including Origen and Epiphanius ... Tischendorf reads "of the Joseph" <note>original: του ιωσηφ</note> with Codex Basiliensis (H) and others, including Africanus (as quoted in Eusebius's *Church History*), Athanasius, and Cyril of Alexandria ("even if he was a son, as was supposed, of Joseph"). | **of Heli... to Nathan (v. 31)**: In Codex Bezae (D), the genealogy from Matthew (from verse 16 back to verse 10) is transferred into Luke's account as follows: "of Jacob, of Matthan, of Eleazar, of Eliud, of Jachin, of Zadok, of Azor, of Eliakim, of Abiud, of Zerubbabel, of Shealtiel, of Jeconiah, of Joachim, of Eliakim, of Josiah, of Amon, of Manasseh, of Hezekiah, of Ahaz, of Jotham, of Uzziah, of Amaziah, of Joash, of Ahaziah, of Joram, of Jehoshaphat, of Asaph, of Abijah, of Rehoboam, of Solomon." <note>This indicates that the scribe of Codex Bezae preferred Matthew's royal lineage over Luke's version.</note> In Codex Basiliensis (E) and many others, the order of individual names was disturbed because scribes made errors while copying from columns. For this reason, in Codex E (folios 165–166), to restore the correct order, one must read starting from "of Heli" (to which "of Jacob" is incorrectly added) and "of Matthat," then jump to the first three names of the second column, then return to "Joseph" in the first column and proceed to "Matthat." From there, one must move to the fourth name of the second column, "of Levi," all the way to "Terah." Then follows the first column from "Nahor" to "Noah," and from there "Lamech" to "of God." | **Heli** <note>original: ηλει</note>: spelled this way in Codex Basiliensis (E), Cyprius (S), and Δ, as well as most Old Latin and Vulgate manuscripts (*Heli*); other manuscripts and versions spell it *Eli* or *Heli*.

**24. Matthat** <note>original: μαθθαθ</note>: spelled this way in Codex Sinaiticus (א) (Codex Bezae reads *Matthan*, as noted before). Compare also verse 29 (we have printed "Mattheos" <note>original: μαθθαιοσ</note> throughout, though we rely on no other witnesses than א, B, and D) ... The Majority Text and Lachmann read *Matthat* <note>original: ματθατ</note> with many uncials, the Coptic, Vulgate, and Gothic ... other manuscripts read *Matthan* or *Mathan*. Furthermore, Old Latin versions show variants like *Matthei*, *Mattheae*, *Mathi*, or *Matthiae*; the Armenian reads *Matathia* and the Ethiopic *Mati*. Moreover, Africanus (in Eusebius's *History*) omits "of Matthat, of Levi" (stating that "according to Luke, similarly, the third from the end is Melchi, whose son was Heli, the father of Joseph"); neither Eusebius nor Ambrose (3.15) include them ("Luke described Joseph as the son of Heli, and Heli as the son of Melchi"). The Latin translation of Irenaeus seems to agree because of the number of generations he counts: "Luke shows that the genealogy, which is from the generation of our Lord to Adam, has seventy-two generations." Regarding **Matthat**, compare also Augustine in *Questions on Deuteronomy* (3.573): "according to Matthew, Matthan is the grandfather of Joseph, but according to Luke, it is not Matthan but Matthat. If anyone thinks there is such a similarity in the name that a mistake of one letter was made by the writers—what will he say about their fathers? For according to Luke, Matthat was the son of Levi, but according to Matthew, Matthan was begotten of Eleazar, etc." | **Levi** <note>original: λευει</note>: spelled this way in א and B (corrected from *Heli*).

## IV.

<margin>
Verses 1–13: Matthew 4:1–11; Mark 1:12 and following
</margin>
**1** But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness **2** for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing in those days, and when they were finished, he was hungry.

---

**Mahalaleel** <note>original: Μελελεὴλ</note>: variants include *malaleel* (manuscript ff²), *malelel* (a, l*), *maleel* (tol), *malleel* (g²), *malehel* (q), *malelehec* (e), or omitted entirely. | **Cainan** <note>original: Καϊνὰμ</note>: spelled with an 'm' in manuscripts ℵ <note>term: ℵ (Codex Sinaiticus, a 4th-century Greek manuscript)</note>, L, ff², and the Coptic (Sahidic) version. The Majority Text <note>term: ς (The "Received Text" or standard Greek text used for centuries)</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf <note>term: 19th-century biblical scholars and editors</note> read **Cainan** <note>original: καϊναν</note> ending with 'n' according to manuscripts A, B <note>term: Codex Vaticanus</note>, D, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all others; similarly in the Latin versions. Manuscript d reads *ainan*, and b reads *aenan*.

**38.** **Seth**: Manuscript A reads *Shem* <note>original: σημ</note>. | **Of God**: The Harleian manuscript <note>A 9th-century manuscript in the British Library</note> adds in slightly smaller letters: "75 generations." ... **Basil** <note>Basil the Great, a 4th-century bishop</note> writes: "Count then the genealogies from Adam until the presence of Christ, and you will find according to the genealogy of Luke that the Lord was born in the 77th succession." (See this passage in Mai's *Scriptionum veterum nova collectio*, Vol. IX, page 663). The same number of 77 is cited by Gregory of Nazianzus (in his sermon on Pentecost) and Gregory of Nyssa (in his 2nd Oration on Genesis 1:26) according to Wetstein. This is supported by the works of Chrysostom and Augustine. (Elsewhere, Augustine in *Sermons on the Lord* counts 43 generations from the Lord back to David.) Additionally, marginal notes in manuscripts 34 and 37 state: "It should be known that the accurate copies contain the number of 77 names from the Lord and including Adam himself." Regarding the calculation of Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century church father</note>, see the note for verse 24. Syriac manuscripts, according to Dionysius bar Salibi, count 56 generations from Abraham to Christ (Jacob of Sarug says 57), which, when others are added, totals 76, though he notes Nazianzus says 77.

**Chapter IV. 1.** **Full of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: πλήρης πνεύματος ἁγίου</note>: Manuscript Fʷ adds "being" <note>original: ων</note>. This reading is supported by ℵ, B, D, E, F, K, L, Ξ, Π, several cursives <note>term: cursives (manuscripts written in a running, lowercase hand)</note>, the Vulgate, Syriac, Sahidic, and Coptic versions, as well as Basil and Origen. The Majority Text (ς) places "full" after "Holy Spirit" following manuscripts A, G, H, M, S, and others. | **In the Spirit** <note>original: εν τω πνευματι</note>: Some Latin manuscripts (a, c) read "by the Spirit" <note>original: a spiritu</note>, while others (e, f, l, q, etc.) read "in the Spirit" <note>original: in spiritu</note>. | **In the wilderness** <note>original: εν τη ερημω</note>: Supported by ℵ, B, D, L, and several Latin and Coptic versions. The Majority Text (ς) reads **into the wilderness** <note>original: εισ την ερημον</note>, matching the wording in Matthew and Mark, supported by A, E, G, H, K, M, and others.

**2.** **Forty** <note>original: τεσσερακοντ.</note>: This spelling is found in ℵ, A, B, L, and Δ. The Majority Text and Lachmann use the alternative spelling *tessarakont* <note>original: τεσσαρακ.</note>. Additionally, some versions (the Ethiopic and several Greek cursives) add "and forty nights," likely harmonizing the text with the Gospel of Matthew. | **By** <note>original: υπο</note>: Manuscript Δ reads "away from" <note>original: απο</note>. | **The Devil** <note>original: διαβολου</note>: Manuscript D and others read **Satan** <note>original: σατανα</note>. | **And he ate nothing**: Some manuscripts (W, Λ, and others) add "nor did he drink." | **When they were finished**: The Majority Text adds "afterward" <note>original: υστερον</note>, but ℵ, B, D, L, and the earliest versions (Latin, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian) omit it.

# 4, 3. ACCORDING TO LUKE 454
