---

**afterward** <note>original: ὕστερον</note>: (as in Matthew, where the text does not vary) found in manuscripts A, E, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, W^b, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all others, as well as the Latin manuscripts f, ff², q, the Gothic version, both Syriac versions, the later Coptic (Dz), and Cyril [of Alexandria] (p. 151): "the forty days of the fast having been spent, afterward he was hungry."

**3. And [the devil] said to him** <note>original: εἶπεν δὲ αὐτῷ</note>: according to manuscripts ℵ <note>term: ℵ (Codex Sinaiticus, 4th century)</note>, B <note>term: Codex Vaticanus</note>, D, L, 1, 33, 67, 130 (Greek text), most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate (which simply says *dixit illi*), and Coptic (the Sahidic version says "the devil said to him" without the word "and"), and Ambrose (on Luke, 1339). ... The Received Text <note>term: ς (the "Stephens" or standard Greek text of the 16th century)</note> reads **And the devil said to him** <note>original: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ</note> according to A, W^b, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials <note>term: uncials (manuscripts written in all capital letters)</note>, and almost all others (Manuscript 157 reads "And he also said to him"), along with Latin manuscripts e, q, the Gothic, both Syriac versions, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Theodoret. | **to this stone** [until] **become** <note>original: τῷ λίθῳ ... γένηται</note>: (some read "from stones... become loaves"): Manuscript D, the evangeliary 31, and the Toledo manuscript read "that these stones may become loaves of bread" (mirroring the wording in Matthew).

**4. And [Jesus] answered**: Manuscripts 13 and 69 read "But he answered"; 130 (Greek), Sahidic, and Syriac read simply "answered"; D reads "And answering." | **to him**: (Manuscripts 13, 69, 76, 346, Sahidic, and Coptic read "him" in the dative case; 130 (Greek) omits it) **Jesus** (Δ omits the definite article "the") according to ℵ, B, L, Δ, 13, 33, 69, 130 (Greek), the Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, and Ethiopic; the Syriac version adds "Jesus responded and said to him"; D after "And answering" continues "Jesus said"; the Toledo manuscript reads "And answering him, Jesus said..." ... The Received Text reads **Jesus** (Manuscript 1, 124, and about 25 others read "the Jesus") **to him** according to A, E, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, W^b, Γ, Δ, Π, and almost all others, the Gothic, Peshitta Syriac, and Armenian. Additionally, the Received Text adds **saying** <note>original: λέγων</note> according to A, E, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, W^b, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all others, and Latin manuscripts c, e, f, g², (likewise "and he said" in a, b, ff², g¹, l, q; see the Syriac above), Peshitta Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Gothic ... we have omitted it following ℵ, B, L, 13, 33, 130 (Greek), and a few others, the Vulgate, Sahidic, and Coptic | **that** <note>original: ὅτι</note>: (Origen 3, 967, from a Greek fragment: "For he answers as if regarding a man and says that not by bread alone shall man live"): D, Tischendorf, 69, 124, 246, and about 10 others omit it, mirroring Matthew. | **the man** <note>original: ὁ ἄνθρωπος</note>: according to ℵ, A, B, D, E, G, L, V, W^b, Δ, Π², and very many others, Sahidic and Coptic ... Griesbach <note>term: J.J. Griesbach, an 18th-century textual critic</note> omits the article "the" following F, H, K, M, S, U, Γ, Δ, Π*, and more than 70 others, the Gothic, and Origen; compare Matthew where the reading similarly fluctuates. Furthermore, we have published this without the following additions according to ℵ, B, L, Sahidic, and Coptic ... The Received Text and Lachmann add **but by every word** <note>original: ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ παντὶ ῥήματι</note> (Manuscript D reads "in", as do the Latin versions: "in bread alone and in every word." See also Matthew) **of God** (Manuscript 20, the Dz Coptic, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Theophylact add "proceeding through the mouth [of God]") according to A, D, W^b, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and eight other uncials, and almost all others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, both Syriac versions, Gothic, and Armenian; these additions are likely imported from the Gospel of Matthew.

**5—8. These verses** are placed after verse 12 in Latin manuscripts b, c, f, g¹, l, q (the Latin manuscripts known to Faber Stapulensis) and Ambrose (on Luke, 1340), following the order of Matthew; but not in a (see note on v. 5), e, ff², or the Vulgate.

**5. [The following section is the critical apparatus, where scholars compare different ancient copies of the Bible to find the most original wording.]

38. **from** <note>original: απο</note> (an edition by Griesbach approved by Schulz) with manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Bezae (D), and several others... but the "Received Text" <note>original: ς; the standard printed Greek Bible for centuries</note> and the editor Lachmann <note>original: Ln</note> read **out of** <note>original: εκ</note> (noting that the reading in the Gospel of Mark does not fluctuate here) along with many later manuscripts and the Gothic version; likewise **from** <note>original Latin: de; which often expresses the Greek "ex"</note> is found in the Old Latin and the Vulgate | **he entered**: Manuscripts D and Π and about 20 others read **he came** (compare Mark)... others add the name **Jesus** | **Simon's**: Certain Old Latin versions and Ambrose's commentary on Luke add **and Andrew's** (following the account in Mark) | **But the mother-in-law** <note>original: πενθερα δε</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, B, D, and the vast majority... some read **But the mother-in-law** with a different word order <note>original: η δε πενθερα or η πενθ. δε</note> (Note: a few manuscripts skip from the first mention of "Simon" to the second "Simon" due to a copying error) | **the**: manuscript x omits this | **Simon's**: the Syriac Peshitta reads "of Peter" | **suffering**: Manuscript D reads **possessed by** <note>original: κατεχομενη; translated in the Latin versions as "detinebatur" or "tenebat"</note>

39. **standing**: Manuscript D reads **having stood** | **And immediately** <note>original: παραχρ. δε</note> with most manuscripts and versions... others read **and immediately** <note>original: και παραχρ.</note> or simply **immediately**; Manuscript D reads **so that having risen she served them**. Cyril of Alexandria joins "immediately" with the preceding words: "and immediately, he says, the fever left her." | After **left her**, manuscript ℵ and some Latin versions add **the fever** (following Matthew's account) | Manuscript Δ reads **having risen** (masculine form)

40. **setting** <note>original: δυνοντοσ</note>: some manuscripts read "having set" <note>original: δυναντοσ or δυντοσ</note>; the Latin versions vary between "at the setting" and "when it had set" | **all** <note>original: παντεσ</note>: manuscripts B and C use a more emphatic form meaning "every single one" <note>original: απαντεσ</note> | **as many as** <note>original: οσοι</note>: some versions read simply **those who** <note>original: οι</note> | Manuscript D uses a different spelling for "they had" | **various**: some manuscripts use a slightly different form of the word | **they brought**: Manuscripts D and the Armenian version read **they were carrying** (following Mark) | **of them**: omitted by Manuscript D and a few others | **his hands**: some Latin versions read "his hand" (singular); most manuscripts read **laying on his hands** <note>original: τασ χειρ. επιτιθεισ</note> but the "Received Text" uses a different grammatical form for "having laid on" | **he healed**: manuscripts B and D use a tense suggesting Jesus was healing them one by one <note>original: εθεραπευεν; the imperfect tense</note> while the "Received Text" and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf use a form suggesting the completed act of healing <note>original: εθεραπευσεν</note>

41. **they were coming out** <note>original: εξηρχοντο; plural</note>: used in manuscripts ℵ and C; the "Received Text" and most editors use the singular form <note>original: εξηρχετο; common in Greek when the subject is neuter plural like "demons"</note> | **from**: omitted by manuscript ℵ and a few others | **shouting**: supported by most major manuscripts.

the Son of God. And rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew him to be the Christ.

**42** When day came, departing, he went into a deserted place, and the crowds were searching for him; and they came to him, and they were holding him back from departing from them. **43** But he said to them, "It is necessary for me to preach the good news <note>original: ευαγγελίσασθαί; literally, 'to evangelize' or 'bring good tidings'</note> of the kingdom of God to the other cities also, because for this I was sent." **44** And he was preaching in the synagogues of Galilee.

***

[The following section is the critical apparatus, where scholars compare different ancient copies of the Bible to find the most original wording.]

**41.** **more than 50** <note>original: plus⁵⁰</note> sources, including **Origen** (volume 4, page 171)... **crying out** <note>original: κράζοντα; Greek varies between singular and plural endings</note> with manuscripts **Sinaiticus (א)**, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Ephraemi Rescriptus (C)**, **F**, **K**, **L**, **M**, **R**, **S**, **X**, **Λ**, **Ξ**, **Π**, and many others (most **Old Latin** versions and the **Vulgate** read "shouting" or "crying out," as does **Victorinus**) | **and saying**: Manuscript **L** omits | **that** <note>original: οτι; often used to introduce a direct quote</note>: Omitted by most **Old Latin** versions | **the Son of God** without the title **the Christ** <note>original: ο χς</note> is supported by manuscripts **א**, **B**, **C**, **D**, **F**, **L**, **R**, **X**, **Ξ**, several numbered minuscules, the **Old Latin**, **Vulgate**, **Coptic**, **Armenian**, **Arabic**, **Origen**, and **Tertullian** in his work *Against Marcion* (which records: "they went out shouting: You are the Son of God")... but the **Received Text** <note>original: ς; the standard printed Greek Bible for centuries</note> adds **the Christ** following manuscripts **Δ**, **Q**, **Γ**, and many others, as well as the **Gothic**, **Syriac**, and **Ethiopic** versions (compare the similar phrasing in Matthew 16:16 and John 6:69) | **that he was the Christ** <note>original: τον χν αυτ. ειναι</note>: Manuscripts **D** and **69** vary the word order; some Latin versions read "that he was Christ himself" or "that Jesus himself was Christ."

**42.** **day**: One Latin version adds "the" | **he went**: Some sources read **he was going** <note>original: επορευετο; implying a continuous action</note>, supported by the **Vulgate** and several Latin manuscripts (though others read **he departed**) | **deserted**: A few manuscripts read **another** | **place**: Omitted in the original hand of **Sinaiticus (א)** | **searching for**: Manuscripts **א**, **A**, **B**, **C**, **D**, and over 115 others use a more intensive Greek verb <note>original: επεζητουν</note> meaning "to seek out diligently," while the **Received Text (ς)** uses the simpler verb **searching** <note>original: εζητουν</note> | **holding back**: Manuscript **D** uses a variant meaning "detaining."

**43.** **But he**: Some **Syriac** versions add the name **Jesus** | **to the other cities**: Manuscript **D** and some Latin versions read **into the other cities** | **it is necessary for me** <note>original: με δει</note>: The word order varies; the editor **Lachmann** and manuscript **B** place "necessary" before "me," as do the **Old Latin**, **Vulgate**, and **Syriac** | **the kingdom**: The original hand of **Sinaiticus (א)** reads **the gospel** <note>original: το ευαγγελιον</note> | **because for this**: Manuscript **D** adds "for" | **for this** <note>original: επι τουτο</note> is supported by **א**, **B**, **L**, and several others; however, the **Received Text (ς)** reads **unto this** <note>original: εισ τουτο</note> following **A**, **C**, **D**, and the majority of manuscripts (matching the wording in Mark's Gospel) | **I was sent**: Supported by **א**, **B**, **C**, **D**, and others; the **Received Text (ς)** uses a different tense <note>original: απεσταλμαι; 'I have been sent'</note> common in later manuscripts.

**44.** **into the synagogues**: Supported by **א**, **B**, **D**, and **Q**; the **Received Text (ς)** and **Lachmann** read **in the synagogues**, matching the majority of manuscripts | **of Galilee**: Supported by **A**, **D**, **X**, and the majority of versions including the **Vulgate** and **Gothic**; however, manuscripts **א**, **B**, **C**, **L**, **Q**, **R**, and some **Coptic** and **Syriac** versions read **of Judea** <note>original: τησ ιουδαιασ; this is a famous variant, as Judea usually refers to the southern region, though it was sometimes used for all of Palestine</note>.

[The following section is the critical apparatus, where scholars compare different ancient copies of the Bible to find the most original wording.]

**V, 1.** **while the crowd pressed upon him** <note>original: εν τω τ. οχλ. επικεισθ. αυτω</note> (supported by the corrected **Codex Sinaiticus [אᶜ]**): the **Textus Receptus [ς]** reads "while the crowd was gathered together," <note>original: εν τω συναχθηναι τ. οχλ.</note> likewise the **Coptic** <note>original: cop</note> reads *when the crowds were gathered to him* | **and heard** <note>original: και ακουειν</note> with manuscripts **Sinaiticus [א]**, **Alexandrinus [A]**, **Vaticanus [B]**, **Codex Bezae [D]**, and others; manuscript **c** reads *it happened moreover when the crowds rushed upon him, and they heard—and he himself etc.* Similarly found in the **Sahidic Coptic** and **Armenian** versions... the **Textus Receptus [ς]** and **Lachmann [Ln]** read "to hear" <note>original: του ακουειν</note> with manuscripts **Ephraemi [C]**, **D**, **Q**, and many others, including the **Vulgate** and **Syriac** | **and he was standing** <note>original: και αυτος ην εστως</note> (Manuscripts **C**, **F**, **G**, **H**, **X** add "Jesus"): Manuscript **D** reads *while he was standing*, likewise the **Old Latin [e]** *when he himself stood* | **lake** <note>original: λιμνην</note> (Corrected **Sinaiticus [אᶜ]**): the original **Sinaiticus [א*]** omits this | **Gennesaret** <note>original: γεννησαρετ</note> with **א**, **A**, **B**, **C**, **G**, **Q**, and most others; however, other manuscripts read **Gessaret**, **Gennesareth**, or **Gennesar** (as in some **Latin** and **Syriac** versions).

**2.** **and** (omitted by a few **Old Latin** sources): Manuscript **Γ** reads "but" | **saw** <note>original: ιδεν</note> with manuscripts **A**, **C**, **D**, **K**, **L**, **Q**... while the **Textus Receptus [ς]** and **Lachmann [Ln]** use a different spelling <note>original: ειδε</note> found in **א**, **B**, **E**, **F**, etc. | **small boats** <note>original: πλοιαρια</note> with **A**, **C**, **L**, **Q**, and others; also *naviculas* (little boats) in **Latin** sources... the **Textus Receptus [ς]** and **Lachmann [Ln]** read "boats" <note>original: πλοια</note> with **א**, **B**, **D**, and most others | **fishermen** <note>original: αλεεις</note> with **א**, **A**, **C**, **L**, **Q**... the **Textus Receptus [ς]**, **Lachmann [Ln]**, and **Tischendorf [Ti]** use the spelling **αλιεις** with **B**, **D**, **R**, **X**, and almost all others | **from them** <note>original: απ αυτων</note> placed here by **Sinaiticus**, **Vaticanus**, and **Codex Bezae** (*from which the fishermen having gone out*)... the **Textus Receptus [ς]** and **Lachmann [Ln]** place it after "having stepped out" with **A**, **C**, **Q**, and many others (the **Coptic** reads *having entered into them*) | **washed** <note>original: επλυναν</note> with **א**, **L**, **X**... or "were washing" <note>original: επλυνον</note> with **B**, **D**. The **Textus Receptus [ς]** and **Tischendorf [Ti]** read "washed thoroughly" <note>original: απεπλυναν</note> with **A**, **C**, **R**, and most others. All **Latin** versions read *lavabant* (were washing), which seems to correspond better to the reading **επλυνον** | **the nets**: a few manuscripts and the **Syriac** and **Coptic** versions add "their" <note>original: αυτων</note>.

**3.** **stepping into** <note>original: εμβας</note>: one manuscript adds "Jesus" | **of the boats** <note>original: των πλοιων</note>: Manuscript **D** and **Old Latin** versions read "of the boat" (singular). The **Syriac** version translates freely: *And one of them was Simon Peter’s, and Jesus ascended, sat in it etc.* | **Simon’s** <note>original: σιμωνος</note> with **א**, **B**, **D**, **L**... the **Textus Receptus [ς]** adds "the" <note>original: του</note> before Simon | **to put out** <note>original: επαναγαγειν</note>: Manuscript **D**, some **Latin**, and **Syriac** versions place this before the phrase "from the land" | **a little** <note>original: ολιγον</note> (omitted by the **Armenian**): Manuscript **d** reads *just a little bit* | **and sitting down** <note>original: καθισας δε</note> with **א**, **B**, **L**, **Q**, and **Coptic**... the **Textus Receptus [ς]** and **Lachmann [Ln]** read "and having sat down" <note>original: και καθισας</note> with **A**, **C**, **D**, **R**, and most other manuscripts and versions.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Luke 6:1, specifically focusing on the philological and theological debate surrounding the enigmatic term "second-first Sabbath" (deuteroprōton sabbaton). # 476 6, 1. ACCORDING TO LUKE

**...him through the grainfields, and his disciples were plucking the ears of grain**

---

...to occur in a cycle from that time until now, recurring every seven days; this is the first [Sabbath]. But the "second Sabbath" is that defined by the Law. — And observe that it is called the "second Sabbath" after the "first Sabbath." This is the holy day of the sheep <note>Referring to the day the Passover lamb was sacrificed</note>, sanctified as a Sabbath, whether it falls on a Sunday, a Monday, or a Tuesday. When it recurs again in a seven-day cycle, it is called the "second-first" <note>original: "deuteroprōton"</note>.

Item Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and counter-heretical writer</note> 158 (writing on the Ebionites): "It was the second-first Sabbath, as the Gospel has it. For the Law defined various Sabbaths: the one recurring weekly is the natural Sabbath, but others are due to the falling of the New Moons according to the lunar cycle and the subsequent festivals, such as the Days of Tabernacles <note>original: "skēnopēgias"</note> and the Days of Passover, when they sacrifice the sheep and thereafter eat unleavened bread. Furthermore, [there are the days] when they fast the one fast of the year called the 'Great Fast' <note>Yom Kippur</note>, and the other which they call the 'Small Fast.' Whenever these days fall—whether on a Monday, a Tuesday, or a Wednesday—they are also defined as a Sabbath for them. Therefore, after the day of Unleavened Bread had occurred and been defined as a day of Sabbath, on the natural Sabbath following the day of Unleavened Bread (which was itself reckoned as a Sabbath), they were found passing through the grainfields—showing that the bond defined by the Sabbath has been loosed, now that the 'Great Sabbath' has come, that is, <term>Christ</term> <note>original: "chu," an abbreviation for Christou</note>, etc." 

The *Chronicon Paschale* <note>A 7th-century Christian chronicle of the world</note> 396 (Bonn edition; Paris edition 211): "He calls 'Sabbath' not only the <term>14th</term> <note>original: "id'"</note> of the first lunar month if it happens to fall on a Saturday, but also the <term>15th</term> <note>original: "ie'"</note> of the first lunar month, which is the first day of Unleavened Bread, even if it falls on the first day of the week [Sunday]; and also the <term>21st</term> <note>original: "ka'"</note> of the same month, which is the seventh day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the seventh day of the week. This Passover, it seems to me, the divine Evangelist Luke intended to show when he says: 'It happened on the second-first Sabbath that <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "in," an abbreviation for Iēsoun</note> and his disciples passed through the grainfields, and the disciples plucking the ears of grain were eating.' He calls this Sabbath 'second-first' not only because it was the seventh day on which the first day of Unleavened Bread was found, but also because from that day they count the <term>50</term> <note>original: "n'"</note> days and celebrate the feast which the divine Law calls the 'Feast of Weeks' <note>Pentecost</note>. Since there were seven Sabbaths in this year of Pentecost—starting from a Sabbath and being completed on a Sabbath—it was the first Sabbath of the seven Sabbaths and yet the last [in the sequence] of the whole count. For these reasons, wishing to show the Lord passing through the grainfields with his disciples during this Passover, the Evangelist said that on the second-first Sabbath <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "is," abbreviation for Iēsous</note> and his disciples were passing through the grainfields." 

John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople famous for his preaching</note>, Homily 40 on Matthew: "When there is a double rest, both of the Sabbath of the Lord and of another festival following it." Similarly, Scholia <note>ancient marginal notes</note> 237: "When after the rest of the Sabbath another festival follows in succession." 

Isidore of Pelusium <note>An 5th-century abbot and prolific letter writer</note>, Epistles 3, 110: "It is called 'second-first' because it was second in respect to the Passover, but first in respect to the Unleavened Bread. For having sacrificed the Passover in the evening, they celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread on the following day, which they also called 'second-first.'" Adding a further explanation, he continues: "If it is called a Sabbath, do not wonder; [for the Jews called all their feasts Sabbaths]..."

<summary>This page provides a scholarly commentary on Luke 6:1, offering multiple historical interpretations of the rare term "second-first Sabbath" by citing early Church Fathers like Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Isidore. The consensus among these sources is that the term refers to a liturgical overlap where a major Jewish feast (like Passover or the start of the harvest count) coincided with the weekly seventh-day Sabbath.</summary>

## and they ate, rubbing them in their hands. 2 But some of the Pharisees said:

---

...for they call every feast a Sabbath, etc. (The same notes are found written in manuscripts 339 scholia, 255 scholia, and 256 scholia). Theophylact <note>An 11th-century archbishop and influential Bible commentator</note> on this passage: "Often a festival fell on a Friday <note>original: 'paraskeuē,' the Day of Preparation</note>, and they called the Friday a 'Sabbath' because of the festival; then they named the actual Sabbath 'second-first' <note>original: 'deuteroprōton'</note>, as being the second one following another festival and Sabbath." Euthymius <note>Euthymius Zigabenus, a 12th-century monk and scholar</note> on this passage: "This Sabbath was called 'second-first' as being the second from Passover, but the first of the days of Unleavened Bread." Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> on Luke 1362: "'Second-first,' he did not say 'first-second,' for 'second-first' is written. For that which excels ought to be preferred. 'Second' because the first preceded it according to the Law, in which even punishment is prescribed if anyone works; but 'first' because that Sabbath was dissolved by the Law which was first: and this became first which was established second." Compare also pseudo-Athanasius 47 (p. 936). (One may moreover compare Eustathius, *Life of Eutychius*, no. 95: "until the seventh hour of the second-first Lord's day," that is, the first Sunday after Passover; likewise "second-tenth" in Jerome's commentary on Ezekiel 45; and "second-last" <note>original: 'deutereschatos'</note> in Heliodorus, cited in *Ancient Surgeons*, p. 94. Relevant here also is Clement, *Miscellanies* 6, 5, citing the *Preaching of Peter*: "if the moon does not appear, they do not observe the Sabbath called the first," etc.) ..... <note>The following symbols refer to ancient manuscripts that omit the word "second-first"</note> Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Regius (L), and manuscripts 1, 22, 33, 69, 118, 157, 209. Furthermore, neither Matthew nor Mark added anything similar. | **to pass through:** manuscript c, x, and a few others [read] "to go." | **him:** manuscript 33 omits it, Codex Bezae (D) places it before "on the Sabbath." | **through** without **the** <note>the Greek definite article 'tōn'</note> according to Sinaiticus, A, B, L, Δ, Λ, Π, 1, and more than 10 others ... the Textus Receptus adds "the" (conforming it to Matthew and Mark) with Sinaiticus (corrected), C, D, E, H, K, M, R, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, and many others, including Chronicon 346 (see before), the Coptic, and Armenian. | **and his disciples were plucking:** Codex Bezae (D) [reads] "but his disciples began to pluck," manuscript b "and his disciples had begun to pluck," manuscript e "but his disciples were plucking" :: compare the parallel passages. | **the ears of grain** in this place with Sinaiticus, A, C (corrected), X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others ... but B, C (original), L, R [place it] after **they ate** | **and they ate:** manuscripts a and q place this after **hands** ("rubbing with their hands and they ate" in a, "crushing with their hands and they were eating" in q) ... **2.** **said** (manuscript x [reads] a different form of "said"; the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac Peshitta [read] "were saying", compare Codex Bezae) without **to them** according to Sinaiticus, B, C (original), L, X, 1, 118, 131, 157, 209, and manuscripts a, c, e, and Coptic ... the Textus Receptus adds "to them," as does Lachmann [in brackets] with A, C (corrected), R, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and most others ... Codex Bezae (D) [reads] "they were saying to him" :: as in Mark | **Why are you doing, etc.:** Codex Bezae (D) [reads] "See what your disciples are doing on the Sabbaths, which is not lawful" :: these have been conformed to the wording in Mark | **not:** Sinaiticus (original) [uses a different Greek spelling for 'not'] | **to do** (L and Syriac Peshitta [place it] after "Sabbaths") according to Sinaiticus, A, C, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, q, Coptic, Syriac, Ethiopic ... ## "Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?" <margin>1 Samuel 21:6</margin> 3 And Jesus answering them said, "Have you not even read this, what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him? 4 how he entered into the house of God and took the bread of the Presence <note>original: 'tous artous tēs protheseōs'—these were twelve loaves of 'showbread' set out in the Tabernacle</note> and ate, and gave also to those with him, which it is not law-

---

-ful. | "on the Sabbath" <note>original: 'tois sabbasin'</note> (The Latin manuscripts *a, b, c, e, f, l* place the word *sabbatis* after "why are you doing," but manuscript *q* does not; manuscript *ff²* reads "what are you doing on the Sabbath that is not lawful") with manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, D <note>Codex Bezae</note>, L, R, U, and minuscules 1, 22, 69, 124, 131, 440, and a few others, most Old Latin, and Armenian... 3. "and answering": Codex Bezae reads "but answering" | "Jesus said to them" <note>original: 'ho iēsous pros autous eipen'</note> with Sinaiticus and L, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Peshitta Syriac; the same reading, but with "to them" placed after "said" (manuscript D reads "was saying" instead of "said"), is found in manuscripts A, C, D, K, M, R, X, Π, very many others, the Harklean Syriac, and the Ethiopic (though the Ethiopic omits "Jesus"). (Manuscript *q* and the Palestinian Syriac read "Jesus answered and said to them"). In manuscript 33 and a few others, "Jesus" is placed after "toward them." The Received Text reads "Jesus said toward them" with manuscripts B, C, E, H, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, and most others; Latin *a, b, g¹, l* read "Jesus said to them." (Notes: phrases like "to them" usually follow the word "said"; likewise "Jesus" is often repositioned). | "not even" <note>original: 'oude'</note>: Manuscripts D, H, and L read "never" <note>original: 'oudepote'</note>; additionally, H, L, and the Armenian omit "this" <note>original: 'touto'</note>, following the wording in Mark. | "David" <note>original: 'Daueid'</note>: see the note at Matthew 1:1. | "when" <note>original: 'hopote'—noting that this specific word is found only here in the New Testament</note> with manuscripts A, E, H, K, M, R, S, U, V, Γ, Λ, Π and most others. Lachmann omits this with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others, as "those being" is not present in the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark.

<term>Apparatus Criticus</term> <note>The following section lists variations in ancient manuscripts. Scholars use these to determine the most likely original wording of the New Testament.</note>

**10.** The Jerusalem Syriac version does not express "them." For "all of them," manuscripts D, X, and others add "in anger." Furthermore, various Old Latin versions include "in anger" <note>original Latin: 'in ira'</note>, "being angry" <note>original Latin: 'iratus'</note>, or "and looking around at all of them, being in anger" <note>original Latin: 'et circumspiciens omnes illos esse in ira'</note>. These additions are found in several early Latin and Syriac versions but not in the standard Vulgate or Coptic versions. | **"He said"** <note>original Latin: 'dixit'</note>: Manuscript D uses "He says." | **"To him"**: Found in many major manuscripts (A, B, E, etc.). However, the <term>Received Text</term> <note>The 'Textus Receptus', the standard printed Greek text since the 16th century, marked here as ς</note> reads **"to the man"** <note>original Greek: 'tō anthrōpō'</note>, supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and others. | **"And he did [so]"**: Manuscript D and the Vulgate read **"And"**. | **"He did"**: Some versions add "thus" <note>original Greek: 'outōs'</note>. Others, including Codex Sinaiticus and the Vulgate, read **"he stretched it out"** <note>original Greek: 'exeteinen'</note>. | **"Was restored"**: Various spellings of the Greek word occur across manuscripts. | **"His hand"**: Many manuscripts (ℵ, A, B, D, etc.) omit the word **"healthy"** <note>original Greek: 'ugiēs'</note>, though the Received Text includes it, likely following the wording in the Gospel of Matthew. Similarly, the phrase **"as the other [one]"** is omitted by ℵ, B, and L, but included in the Received Text and other versions. I conclude <note>original Latin: 'statuo'</note> that these additions flowed into the text from Matthew. At the end of this verse, Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note> adds the text from verse 5: **"And he said to them that the Son of Man is Lord also of the sabbath."**

**11. "discussed"**: Some manuscripts use "spoke" or "conferred." | **"with one another"**: A few versions add "saying." | **"what they might do"**: Manuscript D reads **"how they might destroy him"**. | **"to Jesus"**: One manuscript reads "to him."

**12. "in those [days]"**: Manuscript D and the Vulgate read **"in these [days]"**. | **"that he went out"**: Most major manuscripts (ℵ, A, B, D) support this phrasing, which is a common construction in Luke. | **"to the mountain"**: Some Syriac versions add "Jesus" as the subject here. | **"to pray"**: Manuscript D reads **"and to pray"**. | **"in [prayer]"**: The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) reads "upon" <note>original Greek: 'epi'</note> instead of "in" <note>original Greek: 'en'</note>. | **"to God"**: Cited by Origen, Cyprian, and Ambrose.

<term>Apparatus Criticus</term> <note>This section compares different ancient copies of the New Testament to show where they disagree. Scholars use these notes to trace how the text was copied and changed over centuries.</note>

**13.** **called to him** <note>original Greek: 'prosephōnēsen'</note>: Manuscript D and others read "called" <note>original Greek: 'ephōnēsen'</note>. | **the disciples**: Some manuscripts use a different grammatical case <note>original Greek: 'tois mathētais'</note>. | **from** <note>original Greek: 'ap'</note>: Several manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate use "out of" <note>original Greek: 'ex'</note>. | **named**: Manuscript D and five others read "called" <note>original Greek: 'ekalesen'</note>.

**14.** **Simon**: Manuscript D adds "first" <note>original Greek: 'prōton'</note>, likely following the phrasing in Matthew. | **whom he also named Peter**: Manuscript D and the Armenian version use a different verb for "nicknamed" or "gave the name" <note>original Greek: 'epōnomasen'</note>. | **and James**: There is significant variation here. Many major manuscripts (like $\aleph$ and B) <note>$\aleph$ refers to Codex Sinaiticus, B to Codex Vaticanus, the two oldest complete Greek Bibles from the 4th century</note> include "and" <note>original: 'kai'</note> between every name. Others omit the "and," grouping the names in pairs as seen in Matthew. | **John**: Manuscript D adds "his brother, whom he nicknamed Boanerges, which is, Sons of Thunder" <note>original: 'boanērges ho estin huioi brontēs'</note>, borrowing this detail from the Gospel of Mark. | **and Philip**: Again, older manuscripts tend to include "and," while later ones omit it.

**15.** **and** <note>before Matthew</note>: Included in the oldest manuscripts ($\aleph$, B, D, L) but omitted in later Byzantine-style texts. | **Matthew**: Spelled with a double 'th' <note>original: 'Maththaion'</note> in the oldest manuscripts, but with a single 't' <note>original: 'Matthaion'</note> in later ones. | **Thomas**: Manuscript D adds "who is called the Twin" <note>original Greek: 'ton epikaloumenon didumon'</note>, a detail taken from the Gospel of John. | **and James**: Variations in the inclusion of "and" continue here. | **Alphaeus**: Some manuscripts include the article "the [son] of" <note>original: 'ton tou'</note> while the oldest ones simply say "of Alphaeus."

**16.** **and** <note>before Judas</note>: Included in the oldest manuscripts but omitted in many later versions. | **Iscariot**: There are many spelling variations for this name in the ancient manuscripts, including "Iscarioth," "Scarioth," and "Iscarioten." Some versions (like certain Old Latin copies) omit the name entirely here. The apparatus notes that the variations often reflect whether a scribe was influenced by the phrasing in Mark or Matthew.

<term>Anglo-Saxon version</term> reads **the prophets** (manuscripts 243. reads **the** and **the**). <term>Epiphanius</term> <note>A 4th-century bishop and hunter of heresies.</note> 324 says: "if he mentions prophets, he does not deny prophets" etc.; this likely refers to verse 23. On the other hand, <term>Tertullian</term> <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD.</note> in *Against Marcion* writes: "But it is as much his part to reproach false prophets who were praised or blessed by their fathers as it is to reproach prophets who were vexed and rejected" etc. | **their fathers** [οι πατερ. αυτων] (manuscripts 69. 142* 251. and the Latin translation of <term>Irenaeus</term> read **your**): <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> <note>One of the oldest and most important Greek Bible manuscripts, dated to the 4th century.</note> omits.

**28. those who curse you** [καταρ. υμασ] with <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term>, and many others (roughly 60). <term>Clement of Alexandria</term> <note>A prominent teacher in the early church, c. 150–215 AD.</note> 605: "Love your enemies, it says, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you etc.," also on page 307 — "he commands to bless even those who curse us." <term>Origen</term> and <term>Eusebius</term> also agree, as do the Old Latin manuscripts *a, b, ff², g¹, l, q* ... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> (following Griesbach and Scholz) and Tischendorf read **to those who curse you** [κατ. υμιν] with manuscripts E, H, L, S, U, V, Δ, Λ and many others (also the Vulgate and <term>Ambrose</term> read **curse you** [maledic. vobis]). <term>Justin Martyr</term> <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher and apologist.</note> in *First Apology* 1, 15: "But I say to you: pray for your enemies and love those who hate you and bless those who curse you and pray for those who mistreat you." <term>Origen</term> 1, 772: "reading: bless those who curse you." | **pray** [προσευχεσθε] with <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and most others, including the Peshitta (Syriac), Armenian, and Gothic versions... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads **and pray** [και προσευχ.] with a few late manuscripts and some Latin versions (see <term>Justin Martyr</term> above; in *Dialogue with Trypho* 8, 12, he says "our Lord, being good, says: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you," which refers to Matthew) and <term>Tertullian's</term> *Against Marcion* 1, 15. | **for** [περι] with <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and L... Lachmann reads **for** [υπερ] with A, D, P, R and many others. (Wetstein and Griesbach did not notice this variant). <term>Clement</term> 307: "He commands to love enemies and to bless those who curse us and pray for those who mistreat us." <term>Eusebius</term> in his *Commentary on Psalms* 21: "the: pray for those who mistreat" and on page 137: "of the one who commanded his disciples: pray for those who mistreat and do wrong to them" and on page 699: "pray for those who mistreat and persecute you" (cf. Matthew). Note: the word for "for" [υπερ] does not fluctuate in Matthew. In Luke, [περι] is also used in Acts 8:15. Paul uses both frequently, but in Colossians 1:3 [περι] was changed to [υπερ] by some, though not in 1:9. | Manuscripts A, L, X, and others have spelling variations of **mistreating** [επερεαζοντ.]. | **you** [υμασ]: Manuscript Δ reads **your** [υμων]. Additionally, manuscript 69 adds **and those who persecute you**, likely influenced by Matthew.

**29. unto the** [εισ την] with the original hand of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Bezae</term>, and <term>Clement</term> (who accurately quotes "to the one who strikes" all the way to "the other"). <term>Origen</term> and the Vulgate also read **on the cheek** [in maxillam]... the <term>Textus Receptus</term>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **upon the** [επι την] with the corrected <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and almost all others. (*Note*) | **the tunic** <note>original: "ton chitona"</note>: Manuscripts A and Γ, and a few others including the Coptic and Syriac versions, add **your** <note>original: "sou"</note>. ... **If you do good** <note>original: "Ti agathopoieite"</note>: supported by manuscripts D, H, M, P, S, Γ, Δ, Λ, the minuscule 33, and nine others (and no doubt many more). |
**to you** <note>original: "hymin"</note>: Manuscript "c" omits this; manuscripts "d," "a," and the Syriac Peshitta place it after **what credit** (the Syriac Peshitta reads: "what grace is to you"). |
**it is credit** <note>original: "charis estin"</note> (so in manuscript "q"): Manuscript P and "b" read "it will be grace"; "c" reads "which is grace"; "e" omits the phrase "for if you do good to those who do good to you"; "ff²" reads "it will be grace." | The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible.</note>, Coptic, Ethiopic, and Harklean Syriac read **credit is** (the Syriac Peshitta reads "what is your grace"). |
**and** <note>original: "kai"</note> without the word **for** <note>original: "gar"</note>: supported by Codex Sinaiticus <note>A 4th-century Greek manuscript, one of the most important in existence.</note>, Codex Vaticanus, Λ, and the Ethiopic version... while the editions of Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **for** with manuscripts A, D, L, P, R, Ξ, and almost all other uncials <note>Ancient manuscripts written in all-capital letters.</note>. Notably, Codex Sinaiticus skips from **for even** to the later phrase **sinners lend to sinners** <note>A common scribal error where the eye jumps between similar words.</note>. |
**the** <note>original: "oi"</note>: Omitted by Manuscript A and a few others. |
**the same** <note>original: "to auto"</note>: Omitted by Λ and manuscript 262. Manuscript "e" and the Syriac Peshitta read "that very thing"; d, a, and the Vulgate read **this** <note>original Latin: "hoc"</note>; while others (130, b, c, f, q) read **these things**.

34. **and if**: Manuscript D reads "and whenever"; manuscript "e" reads "but if." |
**lend** <note>original: "dani-" or "danei-"</note>: The spelling varies between ancient manuscripts (a common vowel shift in Greek called itacism). |
**you lend** <note>original: "danisēte"</note>: supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and manuscript 157; also the Latin versions "b," "f," "ff²," "vg" (if you give a loan) and "e" or Tertullian <note>An early Christian author, c. 155–220 AD.</note> (if you lend at interest). |
The edition of Stephanus reads "daneizēte" (present tense) with several other manuscripts. Compare also Justin’s *First Apology* <note>An early defense of Christianity written around 150 AD.</note> 1, 15: "For if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what new thing do you do? Even the tax collectors do this." |
**from whom**: Manuscripts Γ and Ξ use a slightly different Greek form. |
**to receive** <note>original: "labein"</note>: supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. The editions of Stephanus and Lachmann read **to receive back** <note>original: "apolabein"</note> with manuscripts A, D, E, H, and most others. |
**what credit is that to you**: The word order varies across Latin manuscripts; some read "grace also to you" or "to you is grace." |
**and** <note>the second occurrence</note>: Omitted by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Coptic. Others add **for** <note>original: "gar"</note>. |
**sinners** <note>without "the"</note>: supported by most major uncials including A, B, D, E. |
**to sinners**: Manuscript Λ omits this. |
**an equal amount** <note>original: "ta isa"</note>: supported by the Vulgate and others, but omitted by several early Latin manuscripts (d, a, b, c, e).

35. **But** <note>original: "plēn"</note>: Manuscript "u" and the Latin "e" add "I say to you," similar to the wording in the Gospel of Matthew. |
**lend**: Spelling varies as noted in verse 34. |
**despairing of no one** <note>original: "mēdena apelpizontes"</note>: supported by Codex Sinaiticus and the Syriac versions (interpreting it as "not cutting off the hope of any person"). |
However, the editions of Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **despairing of nothing** <note>original: "mēden"</note> with manuscripts A, B, L, R, and many others. The Latin manuscripts vary: some say "despairing of nothing," others say "hoping for nothing in return," and others simply "not hoping." |
**despairing**: Manuscripts א, A, B, L, and R use one Greek spelling, while Tischendorf follows a slightly different spelling found in D and P.

[your re]ward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked. 
<margin>Matthew 5:48</margin>
36 Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. 
<margin>Matthew 7:1–2</margin>

<margin>Mark 4:24</margin>

35. **great** <note>original: "polys"</note>: Codex Sinaiticus <note>A 4th-century Greek manuscript, abbreviated as ℵ</note>, Codex Alexandrinus (A), and two other manuscripts. Manuscripts "c," "a," "l," the Saxon version, and Ambrose (in his commentary on Tobit) add **in heaven** <note>original: "en tois ouranois"</note>; see verse 23 and Matthew 5:12. Based on this, the scholar Lachmann includes "in the heavens" in brackets. | **of the Most High** <note>original: "hypsistou"</note>: Found in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and many others. The "Received Text" <note>The standard printed Greek Bible since the 16th century, abbreviated as ς</note> adds the article **the** <note>original: "tou"</note> based on many later minuscule manuscripts and Basil. | **kind** <note>original: "chrēstos"</note>: Codex Sinaiticus and three other manuscripts read **Christ** <note>original: "christos," likely a scribal spelling error as the words sounded similar</note>. | **the ungrateful and the wicked**: A few manuscripts and the Armenian version swap the order to "the wicked and the ungrateful."

36. **Be** <note>original: "ginesthe"</note>: The word **therefore** <note>original: "oun"</note> is omitted in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many early versions (Old Latin, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic) and early writers like Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Athanasius, and Cyril. <note>Origen notes the command: "Be merciful... and: Be perfect."</note> Justin Martyr also omits it. However, the Received Text and Tischendorf add **therefore** based on Codex Alexandrinus and many later manuscripts, the Vulgate, and Syriac versions. <note>The translator notes: "In such a matter, the testimonies of the Church Fathers are of slight importance; even if they faithfully preserve such particles elsewhere, they often neglect them here."</note> | **just as** <note>original: "kathōs"</note>: Clement, Athanasius, and Chrysostom sometimes use a different word for "as" <note>original: "hōs"</note>. Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus omit the word **also** <note>original: "kai"</note> following "just as," while the Received Text and many others include it. | **your Father**: Many sources add **the heavenly [Father]** or **who is in the heavens**, including Justin Martyr, Clement, and Chrysostom.

37. **and** (the first instance): Omitted by Codex Bezae, the Vulgate, and several others to match the phrasing in the Gospel of Matthew. | **and you will not be judged**: Most manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) use the double negative for emphasis <note>original: "ou mē"</note>, but Lachmann uses **lest you be judged** <note>original: "hina mē"</note> to match Matthew, following Codex Alexandrinus and the Old Latin. | **and do not condemn**: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus include **and**, while the Received Text and others omit it. | **condemn**: Some manuscripts use slightly different verb endings. Codex Vaticanus reads **judge** <note>original: "dikazete"</note> instead of "condemn." | **and you will not**: Again, some versions substitute **lest** <note>original: "hina mē"</note>.

38. **good** <note>original: "kalon"</note>: A few manuscripts and the Syriac Peshitta add the word **and** before this. | **pressed down**: Codex Sinaiticus has a slight spelling variation. Some manuscripts and Origen place **shaken together** before "pressed down." A few versions omit "shaken together" entirely.

<header>6, 39. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

[they will give] into your lap; for with the measure you use, it will be measured 
<margin>Matthew 15:14</margin> back to you. 39 <gloss>57.5</gloss> And he also told them a parable: "Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? 
<margin>Matthew 10:24; John 13:16, 15:20</margin> 40 <gloss>58.3</gloss> A disciple is not above his teacher; 
<margin>41 and following; Matthew 7:3-5</margin> but everyone, when fully trained, will be like his teacher. 41 <gloss>59.5</gloss> Why [do you see the speck...]

---

38. **will give into your lap** <note>original: "sousin eis ton kolpon hymōn"</note>: The Received Text <note>The standard printed Greek Bible used for centuries, abbreviated as ς</note> adds **and** <note>original: "kai"</note> based on Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Ephraemi (C), and many others. | **shaken together** <note>original: "sesaleumenon"</note>: Read without the word "and" in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and various Latin and Coptic versions. The Received Text adds "and" here as well. | **running over** <note>original: "hyperekchynnomenon"</note>: Spelled with a double 'n' in several major manuscripts; other manuscripts use a single 'n'. | **lap**: Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note> uses a slightly different spelling. | **your**: Manuscript L reads **to you**. | **for with the measure** <note>original: "hō gar metrō"</note>: This phrasing is found in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The Old Latin versions vary, with some saying "for with what sort of measure" and others "for with the same measure." Origen <note>An early Christian scholar, c. 185–253 AD</note> and Eusebius use this wording. The Received Text reads **For with the same measure with which** <note>original: "tō gar autō metrō hō"</note>, which is supported by the majority of later manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate. | **it will be measured back** <note>original: "antimetrethēsetai"</note>: Found in most manuscripts. However, some early versions and Polycarp <note>An early bishop and martyr, c. 69–155 AD</note> simply use the word **measured**. Polycarp quotes the Lord's teaching: "Remembering what the Lord said in his teaching: judge not, that you be not judged; forgive, and you will be forgiven; be merciful, that you may receive mercy; with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you; and that blessed are the poor and those persecuted for righteousness' sake..."

39. **he said**: Some manuscripts (D and others) read **he was saying** <note>original: "elegen"</note>, and the Latin versions reflect this. | **also** <note>original: "de kai"</note>: This is present in the oldest manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; the Received Text omits the "also." | **Can...** <note>original: "mēti"</note>: A Greek particle suggesting a question that expects a "no" answer. | **fall into** <note>original: "empesountai"</note>: Most older manuscripts use this form (meaning "fall into"). The Received Text uses a simpler form of "fall" <note>original: "pesountai"</note>, similar to the wording in the Gospel of Matthew.

40. **the teacher**: Several early manuscripts (ℵ, B, D) read simply "the teacher" without adding **his**. The Received Text adds **his** <note>original: "autou"</note> based on later manuscripts and the Coptic and Syriac versions. | **fully trained** <note>original: "katērtismenos"</note>: Some manuscripts omit the "but" <note>original: "de"</note> that follows this word. | **will be** <note>original: "estai"</note>: While most versions say "will be," some manuscripts and the *Apostolic Constitutions* <note>A 4th-century collection of Christian precepts</note> read **let him be** <note>original: "estō"</note>. Some Latin versions add a conditional phrase: "if he is [fully trained]."

<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 6, 44.</header>

...but why do you see the speck <note>Greek: *karphos*, referring to a small piece of straw or wood</note> in the eye of your brother, but the log <note>Greek: *dokon*, a large wooden beam</note> in your own eye you do not perceive? 42 How can you say to your brother: "Brother, let me remove the speck in your eye," while you yourself do not see the log in your own eye? Hypocrite, first remove the log from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck in the eye of your brother. 43 <margin>Matthew 7:16 and following; 12:33</margin> For there is no good tree producing rotten fruit, nor again a rotten tree producing good fruit. 44 For each [tree is known by its own fruit...]

---

[...the phrase "that it be"] in the edited Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> and some manuscripts (such as those from Perugia and the Gatarianus manuscript), likewise "that it be" in manuscripts *b* and *ff²*. On the other hand, manuscripts such as *e, am, for, ing, tol,* and *lrint* continue with "just as," etc.

41. **the second "the"** <note>original: "to"</note> (found as "tō" in manuscripts E, X, Γ, Λ, Π and others; likewise in Γ, Λ and others in verse 42 in two places): Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note> and a few others omit it; nor do the Old Latin versions express it (except manuscript *e*, which reads "the straw which is"), nor the Vulgate or Coptic versions | **but the log in your own eye**: Manuscripts P, 13, 69, 124, 346 read "your" <note>original: "sō"</note> rather than "own" <note>original: "idiō"</note>; manuscripts D and several Latin/Vulgate versions also read "in your eye" following the wording in Matthew's Gospel.

42. **how** <note>original: "pōs"</note> (Scholz recommends this due to parallel passages) along with Codex Vaticanus (B) and Latin manuscripts *e* and *ff²*. ... **but how** <note>original: "pōs de"</note> in manuscript 251 and some Latin versions; **and how** <note>original: "kai pōs"</note> in various Vulgate manuscripts; **or how** <note>original: "ē pōs"</note> according to Lachmann <note>Ln</note> and the Received Text <note>ς</note> along with Codices A, C, D, E, H, K, L, M, P, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ and almost all other manuscripts, Latin versions, the edited Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Gothic versions (Note: while "or how" is the standard reading in Matthew and does not vary there, it is certain that many elements from Matthew were used to change this passage in Luke; therefore, the reading that differs from Matthew is preferred. The variations "but how" and "and how" seem to have arisen from the simplicity of the reading in Codex Vaticanus, confirmed by Latin evidence) | **brother**: Manuscript D, 157, and several Old Latin versions omit this word, following Matthew's version | **the [speck] in your eye**: Manuscript D, 33, and many Latin, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions read **out of your eye** <note>original: "ek/apo tou ophthalmou sou"</note> following Matthew | **while you yourself... do not see**: Manuscript 13, 69, 124 read "not seeing" <note>original: "mē blepōn"</note>; Codex Γ reads "not looking at" <note>original: "ouk emblepōn" </note>. Manuscripts D and several Old Latin versions read: **and behold the log in your own eye lies beneath** <note>original: "hypokeitai"</note> (Old Latin manuscript *i* has "is in your eye") | **the log**: Latin manuscript *c* omits the word "the" | **to remove** placed after "your brother" following Codex B and others. ... Manuscript L and 1 place it after "the speck"... The Received Text and Lachmann place it after **you will see clearly** (Note: in Matthew this reading does not fluctuate; the same reasoning applies here as was stated for the word "how" above) following Codices א, A, C, D, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and many others | **the [speck] in the eye**: Manuscript D, the Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions read **out of the eye**, following Matthew.

43. **for... not** <note>original: "ou gar"</note> (also in Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Gothic, and Philoxenian Syriac): Manuscript D, Old Latin *a*, the Sinaitic Syriac, and Ethiopic versions read simply **not**. (Clement of Alexandria's quote "For a good tree is not - good fruit" proves nothing here). Manuscript 346 reads **nor** | **rotten fruit** (also in Clement and Tertullian, who in *Against Marcion* writes "likewise a good tree may not bring forth evil fruit," though elsewhere he interprets the "bad tree" as the Creator): Many Latin and Syriac versions read the plural **rotten fruits**, and conversely **good fruits** instead of "good fruit," following the phrasing in Matthew | **nor again** <note>original: "oude palin"</note> according to Codices א, B, L, Ξ and others, and the Coptic and Armenian versions. (Clement uses "nor indeed"). The Received Text omits the word **again** to match the stable reading in Matthew; Lachmann puts it in brackets. It is found in many major manuscripts (A, C, D, etc.) and versions. Compare the *Dialogue against the Marcionites* 820 and 821, which says: "The Gospel says: a rotten tree cannot bear good fruits."

<page-num>492</page-num>
<header>6, 45. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

<margin>Matthew 12: 34-35</margin> ...for [each] tree is known by its own fruit.⁶¹∙⁵ For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor do they pick a bunch of grapes from a bramble bush. 45 ⁶²∙⁵ The good person out of the good treasure of the heart brings forth what is good, and the evil person out of the evil [treasure] brings forth what is evil; for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.

---

...nor for a good tree to bear bad fruits (a little later: to bring forth). Likewise, Marcion <note>A 2nd-century teacher later declared a heretic, who produced an edited version of Luke</note> in Hippolytus <note>A 3rd-century Christian writer</note> 10, 19 they use it thus, saying: "a good tree cannot make evil fruits." Likewise Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop</note> 45 [regarding Marcion] "saying thus—there is no good tree which makes bad fruit, nor a bad tree which makes good fruit."

44. **for** <note>original: "gar"</note> (The manuscript Γ reads **but** <note>original: "de"</note>): Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note>, Γ (according to Tregelles), and 7 other manuscripts, along with Old Latin versions *a, b, c, e, ff², l, q* and the Toledo manuscript omit this; however, Latin versions *f, g¹, g²,* and the Vulgate do not omit it | **of [its] own fruit** <note>original: "idiou karpou"</note> (omitted by manuscript *v* and 5 others): Manuscript D reads **of its fruit** <note>original: "karpou autou"</note>, likewise the Old Latin and Vulgate read *by its fruit* <note>original: "fructu suo"</note> | **from thorns they gather figs** <note>original: "ex akanthōn syllegousin syka"</note> (Sinaiticus spells "gather" as *synlegousin*; Latin versions *f, g¹, g²,* and the Vulgate read *from thorns they collect figs*): manuscripts *a, b, c, d, ff², l, q* read (with *c* specifically using "collect") *from thorns figs* (manuscript *b* reads *grapes*), the Greek of manuscript D reads *they select from thorns figs*, manuscript *e* reads *for from thorns figs are not read* <note>meaning "picked"</note> (it continues *nor from the bramble are grapes harvested. Similarly* the Gothic version: *for figs are not collected from thorns, nor are grapes trodden from the bramble.*) | **figs**: manuscript 28 reads **roses** | **bramble** <note>original: "batou"</note> (thus in the corrected Sinaiticus; the original Sinaiticus read **sprout** <note>original: "blastou"</note>): Manuscripts U, 49, and several others read **brambles** (plural) | **a bunch of grapes** <note>original: "staphylyn"</note> (manuscript κ reads "of a bunch"): Manuscripts L, 13, 69, 346, Latin *c, e*, Coptic, both Syriac versions, and the Gothic version read **bunches of grapes** (plural) | **grapes they harvest** <note>original: "staphylēn trygōsin"</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others... the Received Text <note>The standard printed Greek text of the era, marked with "ς"</note> and Lachmann read **harvest grapes** (reversed order) with manuscripts A, E, H, and many others, including the Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic (*they harvest grapes from the bramble*), Gothic, Armenian, and Ethiopic.

45. **of the heart** <note>original: "tēs kardias"</note> with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus... the Greek of Bezae reads **of his heart**, likewise the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **of his heart** with manuscripts A, L, X, and almost all others including the Latin and Vulgate; the Dialogue against the Marcionites omits it | **brings forth** <note>original: "propherei"</note> in two places: Manuscript L, Γ, and others read **offers/presents** <note>original: "prospherei"</note>, even in the second instance in manuscript *v* | **the good** (Manuscript D omits "the"): Origen and manuscript 565 read **good things** (plural), and the Dialogue reads **good things** | **and the evil [person]**: (Griesbach considers this probable) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, and several Latin manuscripts, the Coptic, and Arabic; however, the Received Text adds **man/person** <note>original: "anthrōpos"</note>, and Lachmann puts **[person]** in brackets following many other manuscripts and the Vulgate, Syriac, and Gothic, similar to the phrasing in Matthew | **out of the evil**: (Griesbach) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others; some Latin and Coptic manuscripts add **treasure**, and the Received Text adds **treasure of his heart**, and Lachmann puts **[treasure of his heart]** in brackets following many others and the Vulgate, Syriac, and Gothic; the word "treasure" was added from the earlier part of the verse, and "of his heart" was likewise adopted from the preceding phrases | **abundance** <note>original: "perisseumatos"</note> without the article "the" with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many others... the Received Text adds **the** with manuscript C and many others, as in Matthew | **heart** <note>original: "kardias"</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others... the Received Text adds **the** following many other manuscripts, as in Matthew | **speaks** <note>original: "lalei"</note> in this position with manuscripts A, Bezae, Vaticanus, and many others... but Lachmann places it at the end of the verse following Sinaiticus, the Latin versions, Vulgate, and Coptic, as in Matthew | **his mouth**: Latin manuscript *e* reads **evil** ("out of the abundance of the heart he speaks evil," so that these words depend on those that precede) | **his** <note>original: "autou"</note>: Manuscript C and about 20 others, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac omit this, as in Matthew; hence Griesbach marked it for possible omission.

<page-num>493</page-num>
<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 6, 49.</header>

<margin>46 63. 3</margin> **46** Why do you call me, "Lord, Lord," and do not do what I say? <margin>Matthew 7, 21</margin>
<margin>47 64. 5</margin> **47** Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and <margin>47-49 Matthew 7, 24-27</margin>
does them, I will show you what he is like. **48** He is like
a man building a house, who dug and went deep and laid
a foundation on the rock; and when a flood occurred,
the river burst against that house, and was not strong enough to shake it because
it was well built. **49** But the one who hears and does not do [them]
is like a man who built a house on the ground without
a foundation, against which the river burst, and immediately it collapsed, and the
ruin <note>original: "rhēgma," meaning a breach or fracture</note> of that house was great.

---

46. **but me** <note>original: "de me"</note> (The standard text reads **why but call me** <note>original: "ti de kal. me"</note>): Manuscript Δ reads **me but**. | **you call** <note>original: "kaleite"</note> (also in Basil's *Rules* 491): Manuscript D, 28. Clement <note>early Christian teacher from Alexandria</note> 583, 901, and 943 (in all three places he cites the whole verse as **why do you say to me** <note>original: "ti me legete"</note> until "I say") uses **you say** <note>original: "legete"</note>, as do manuscripts κ, 259, and z-scr which uses **you speak** <note>original: "laleite"</note>. Similarly, the Latin versions *d*, Irenaeus 1282 and 302, Origen 4, 494, and Gaudentius use **you say to me** <note>original: "mihi dicitis"</note> ("Why do you say to me: Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say" in Irenaeus 282; the same with "to you" added in Irenaeus 302 and Gaudentius; Origen has "but why do you say to me" etc. See also Tertullian's *Against Marcion* 4, 17: "why do you call [others: call ye]: Lord, Lord," and shortly after: "and do not do what I say") | **the things which** <note>original: "ha"</note> (also in Latin Irenaeus twice, Clement three times, Latin Origen, Tertullian's *Against Marcion*, and Basil's *Rules*): Latin versions *b, e, g* and the Syriac-Peshitta read **that which** <note>original: "ho"</note>.

47. **everyone** <note>original: "pas"</note>: Manuscript Δ reads **and** <note>original: "kai"</note> | **of the words** <note>original: "tōn logōn"</note> (Manuscript κ* and others read **the word** in singular, without changing "them," but a few others change it to "it"): Manuscripts C, F, W, M, X and 10 others read **the words** (Latin versions *x, b, q* and a Syriac manuscript add **these**) :: as in Matthew. Furthermore, Manuscript ℵ* <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note> reads **my of the words my** (corrected in ℵc) and | **is like** <note>original: "estin homoios"</note> (Manuscript Δ reads **you are like** <note>original: "este" instead of "estin"</note>): Manuscripts 69, 346, and most Old Latin versions (except *a, e*) and the Vulgate read **like is**.

48. **who** <note>original: "hos"</note>: Manuscript Δ, y-scr, 3pe and others along with the Syriac-Peshitta add **and** | **flood** <note>original: "plēmmyrēs"</note> according to ℵ, B*, L, Ξ, 33. . . . Lachmann <note>a 19th-century textual critic</note> reads **floods** <note>original: "plēmmyras"</note> with Manuscripts D, E, H, S, 2, V and a few others (Δ reads *plēnmyras*) along with A, B³, C, D, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and nearly all others | **burst against** <note>original: "proserēxen"</note> according to ℵ*, B*, D, L . . . Lachmann reads the variant spelling **proserrēxen** with ℵc, A, B³, C, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π and most others | **the river**: omitted by Manuscript Γ | **because it was well built** <note>original: "dia to kalōs oikodomēsthai"</note> (B³ and 33 read "oikodomeisthai," likewise 157) according to ℵ, B, L, Ξ, 33, 157, Coptic (the Coptic-Sahidic version recently added "upon the rock") and the margin of the Syriac-Philoxenian (Ethiopic reads "because it was built on the rock and was well built") . . . the standard text and Lachmann read **for it had been founded upon the rock** <note>original: "tethemeliōto gar epi tēn petran"</note> (Manuscripts F, W read "it was founded") with A, C, D, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, most other uncials, Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac-Peshitta :: but in this way [it matches] the reading in Matthew which does not vary.

49. **having built** <note>original: "oikodomēsanti"</note> with ℵ, A, B, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π and nearly all others, both Syriac versions, and Coptic . . . Lachmann reads **building** <note>original: "oikodomounti"</note> with manuscript *c*, 13, 69, 346, c-scr and a few others. Likewise (which hardly forces us to conclude that the translators found "building," just as the Latin versions *d* and *δ* maintain) **building** in the Old Latin and Vulgate | **a house**: Manuscript U and 10 others read **the house** | **against which the river...** <note>original: "hē pr. ho potamos"</note>: Latin versions *f, g²*, Vulgate read **into which the river dashed** . . . *a, b, ff², g¹, l, q* read **the river struck that house**, *c* reads **the river beat against that house**, *e* reads **the river beat**, and *d* along with Manuscript D omit **against which** | **burst against** <note>original: "proserēxen"</note> (Manuscript D reads **crashed together** <note>original: "synerēxen"</note>) with B*, D, L . . . the standard text and Lachmann read **proserrēxen** with ℵ, A, B³, C, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π and nearly all | **immediately** <note>original: "euthys"</note> with ℵ, B, C, L, Ξ, 33, y-scr and about 10 others . . . the standard text and Lachmann read **straightway** <note>original: "eutheōs"</note> with A, E, H, K, M, R, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and most others . . . Manuscript D and Latin *a, c* omit this :: as in Matthew | **collapsed** <note>original: "synepesen"</note> (Latin "concidit" in *b, d, e, l, q* and the Toledo manuscript) with ℵ, B, D, L, R, Ξ, 1, 13, 33, 69, 124, y-scr and 10 others, plus Latin *b, e, l, q* and Toledo . . . the standard text and Lachmann read **fell** <note>original: "epesen"</note> (Latin "cecidit" in *a, c, f, ff²*).

### VII.

<margin>Matthew 7, 28</margin>
**1** ^{65.3} After he had finished all his words in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum.

<margin>2-10 Matthew 8, 5-13</margin>
**2** A certain centurion’s slave, who was highly valued by him, was ill and about to die. **3** When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his slave. **4** And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, "He is worthy to have you [do this] for him..."

---

*g*^{1. 2.} *the Vulgate*) *with* manuscripts A, C, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and seven other uncials <note>manuscripts written in all capital letters</note>, and many more Old Latin versions and the Vulgate :: *as in Matthew* | **the ruin** <note>original: "to rhēgma," referring to the collapsed house from the previous verse</note> (Manuscript E* and others read "the word"): Γ 131, 435, and ten others *omit* "the." *Compare Origen* <note>an early Christian scholar</note> 1, 307: "For great indeed is the fall that comes with denial, or, as Luke says, great was the ruin of the house built without a foundation."

**VII, 1.** **After** <note>original: "epeidē"</note> *with* manuscripts A, B, C*, Χ, Π and several others, as well as several Latin versions... but others add "and"... others read "after but" <note>original: "epei de"</note> *with* the corrected Sinaiticus (א), E, H, L, and most others, including Coptic and Gothic versions... Manuscript D (Codex Bezae) and some Old Latin versions read **and it happened when** <note>original: "kai egeneto hote"</note>. | **he finished** <note>original: "eplērōsen"</note> (Latin versions: "he fulfilled"): Manuscript D reads **he completed** <note>original: "etelesen"</note>. | **all** (Sinaiticus and others omit) **his words** ("his": some manuscripts substitute "these," while many Old Latin versions omit it): Manuscript D reads **these words**. | **in the hearing of the people**: Manuscript D reads **speaking**, while one Latin version reads **which he was speaking to the people**. | **he entered** (Manuscript D: **he went**): Some manuscripts and the Syriac version *add* **Jesus**. | **Capernaum** <note>original: "Kapharnaoum"</note> *with* Sinaiticus, B, C, D, and the Coptic versions ... most others read **Kapernaoum** <note>standardized spelling in some traditions</note> with A, C, E, and others.

**2.** **slave** <note>original: "doulos"</note>: A later correction in Manuscript D reads **child** or **servant** <note>original: "pais"</note>, similar to the wording in Matthew. | **was ill**: omitted in the original hand of Sinaiticus. | **was about to** <note>original: "ēmell."</note> *with* Sinaiticus, A, B, C, D, and most others ... some others use an alternate spelling <note>original: "emell."</note>. | **valued** <note>original: "entimos"</note>: Manuscript D uses **honored** <note>original: "timios"</note>.

**3.** **and having heard** <note>original: "akousas de"</note>: Manuscript D, the Vulgate, and some Syriac versions read **and when he heard**. | **to him**: omitted in Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions. | **asking**: Sinaiticus uses a slightly different Greek grammatical form. | **that** <note>original: "hopōs"</note>: Sinaiticus adds **he himself**. | **he might save**: some manuscripts use an alternate spelling for the verb.

**4.** **having come**: some manuscripts use a different Greek spelling. | **to Jesus**: some manuscripts read "to him," and Manuscript D and others omit it, proceeding directly to "they were asking Jesus." | **they were asking** <note>original: "ērōtōn"</note> *with* Sinaiticus, D, and others ... many editors (Lachmann, Tischendorf) prefer **they entreated** <note>original: "parekaloun"</note> following manuscripts B, C, R, and many others. | **saying** *with* Sinaiticus, B, C, D, and most versions: Manuscripts A, C, and others *add* **to him**. | **for whom** <note>original: "hō"</note>: Manuscript Γ and others use a different case for the relative pronoun.

4. **you will grant** <note>original: "parexē"</note> (Griesbach's second edition) with manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, B, C, D, E, H, L, R, X, Δ, Ξ, Π, nearly 20 others... but the Received Text <note>the standard 16th-century Greek text</note> reads **you shall grant** <note>original: "parexei"</note> with G, K, M, S, U, V, Γ, Λ and many others.

5. **synagogue**: Manuscript R and the Coptic version add "our" | **built**: The Received Text and manuscript D read it with a slightly different spelling of the initial vowel.

6. **And Jesus went with them** (found in Latin versions b, f, ff², g¹, ², and the Vulgate): Manuscripts D, a, c, e, and l read **And Jesus then went** (c reads "therefore," e reads "and so") **with them** | **now** (one manuscript reads "still"): omitted in the Peshitta Syriac (but not in the Philoxenian or Harclean Syriac), Armenian, and Ethiopic versions | **his**: Manuscript D places this after "being far from" | **not**: the Harclean Syriac omits this | **from the house** <note>original: "tēs oikias"</note> with ℵ, D, 1, 13, 69, 124, 346, and others... but the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **away from the house** <note>original: "apo t. oik."</note> with A, B, C, L, R, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π, eight other uncials, and most others | **sent**: manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 346 read "sent away"... manuscripts 1, 131 read "having sent" followed by "he said." (Note: in the book of Acts this spelling is used almost everywhere, though the alternative form has been introduced by many in several places)... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **centurion** <note>original: "hekatontarchos," a different Greek suffix</note> with ℵ, A, C, D, R, Ξ, and most others... D omits "the centurion" entirely | **saying** without addition in ℵ*, b, q, and the Vulgate... but the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **to him** with ℵ corrected, A, B, C, D, L, R, and most others; likewise 69 and the Gothic add "to him" | some manuscripts spell **trouble** with a single 'l' | **I am worthy** (Scholz notes this matches the Received Text in Matthew 8, 8) with ℵ, B, and several Latin and Syriac versions... but the Received Text and Lachmann read **worthy I am** with A, C, D, E, G, H, K, L, M, R, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π, and almost all others including most Latin, the Vulgate, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, and Ethiopic :: likely adapted from Matthew 8, 8. Griesbach's second edition reads **my under the roof** (as in Matthew) with ℵ, C, D, L, M, R, X, Γ, Ξ, and about 40 others.

7. **therefore I did not even count myself worthy to come to you**: Manuscripts D, 63, 240, 244, and several Old Latin versions omit this :: likely following Matthew's account | **but** <note>original: "alla"</note> with A, B, C, E, G, L, R, Δ... but ℵ, D, K, M, S, U, V, Γ, Λ, Π, and many others use the shortened form **but** <note>original: "all"</note> | **say**: manuscripts 13, 69, 90, 124, 346, and the Harclean Syriac add **only** :: from Matthew | **the word** <note>original: "logō," in the dative case, meaning 'by a word'</note> (and most Latin and the Vulgate: "speak in a word"): Γ, 69, 300, and about 10 others read **the word** <note>original: "logon," in the accusative case</note> | **let him be healed** <note>original: "iathētō," an imperative</note> with B and L... but the Received Text and Lachmann read **he shall be healed** <note>original: "iathēsetai," a future statement</note> (as in Matthew where there is no variation) with ℵ, A, C, D, R, and almost all others.

8. **under**: D, F, and a few others use the shortened form | **set**: manuscripts 33, 69, 242, 50 :: compare Matthew | **under myself**: Γ, 13, 69 read a slightly different possessive form.

...soldiers, and I say to this one: Go, and he goes; and to another: Come, and he comes; and to my servant: Do this, and he does it. **9** When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd following him, he said: "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith." <margin>66,5</margin> **10** And those who had been sent, returning to the house, found the servant in good health.
