8. **go**: <note>original: "poreuthēti"</note> found in manuscripts D, X, and 209. Others read **go** <note>original: "poreuou"</note>. Compare here the Valentinians <note>A Gnostic sect</note> as cited in Irenaeus (Book 1, chapter 7, section 4): "and that he himself (that is, the Creator) is the centurion in the Gospel, saying to the Savior: 'For I too have soldiers and servants under my own authority, and whatever I command, they do.'" Compare also the *Clementine Homilies* (9, 21): "saying to this one: Come, and he comes; and to another: Go, and he goes, etc."

9. **these things Jesus**: Manuscript 157 and the Peshitta Syriac read **Jesus these things**. | **at him**: (found in the Gothic, both Syriac, and Harclean versions): omitted in manuscripts D, R, X, 5 others, most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, a Syriac codex, and Armenian; this omission matches the version in the Gospel of Matthew. | **to the crowd following him he said**: Manuscript D reads **he said to the crowd following** (manuscript 'e' adds "him"); likewise the Coptic, both Syriac, Harclean, and Ethiopic versions. | **I say**: Manuscripts D, X, 69, 124, 346, 5 others, most Old Latin manuscripts (except b and q), the Vulgate, Gothic, and the margin of the Coptic version add **Truly** <note>original: "amēn"</note>, following Matthew. | **I say to you**: Manuscripts A, U, about 15 others, the Peshitta Syriac, and Peter of Alexandria's Harclean Syriac (as well as the Coptic and Armenian) add **that**... Epiphanius, writing on Marcion (page 312), reads **But I say to you** (though on page 324, Scholion 7, he omits "but"). | **not even** <note>original: "oude"</note> (found in ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, B, C, K, L, M, R, X, Γ, Π and many others): Manuscript D reads **never** <note>original: "oudepote"</note>... E, F, G, H, S, U, V, Δ, Λ and about 70 others read **neither** <note>original: "oute"</note> (noted as likely by Griesbach and recommended by Scholz). | **in Israel**: Latin manuscripts d and e place this after **found**. Epiphanius on Marcion (pages 312 and 324) reads: **such faith not even in Israel have I found** (page 324 uses a slightly different spelling for "found"). Epiphanius himself continues (page 324, Refutation 7) "if not even in Israel such faith he found as in etc." Compare also Tertullian against Marcion (Book 4, chapter 18): "he declared that he had not found such faith even in Israel." For the phrase **not even in [Israel]... found**, Old Latin manuscripts a, b, c, ff², g¹, l, q, and the Ethiopic version read: **in no one have I found such great faith in Israel**; likewise Ambrose on Luke (page 1376), but he adds: "but if according to the Greeks: 'Not even in Israel such faith have I found.'"

10. **to the house those sent**: this word order is found in ℵ, B, D, F, K, L, X, Π and about 15 others, Latin versions a, b, c, e, Coptic, Harclean Syriac, and Ethiopic (manuscript 'd' also adds "the servants")... the Received Text and Tischendorf read **those sent to the house** with manuscripts A, C, E, G, H, M, R, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, many others, and Latin versions f, ff², g², l, the Vulgate, Gothic, both Syriacs, and Armenian. Latin manuscripts a, g¹, and q omit "to the house." | **the servant**: found in ℵ, B, L, 1, 157, 209, Latin versions a, b, c, ff², g¹, l, q, Coptic, and Harclean Syriac... the Received Text and Tischendorf read **the servant who had been sick** with manuscripts A, C (D omits "servant"), E, F, G, H, K, M, R, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, many others, Latin versions f, g² (likely), the Vulgate, Gothic, both Syriacs, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Compare also Matthew.

11. **it happened**: omitted in manuscript D, Latin version 'e', and Ethiopic. | **on [the next]**: omitted in manuscript D, Latin versions 'c' and 'e'. The phrase **on the next [day]** <note>original: "en tē hexēs"</note> is found in the original hand of ℵ, C, D, K, M, S, Π, very many others, Latin versions 'c' and 'f', Gothic, Coptic, both Syriacs, Armenian, and Ethiopic... but the corrected hand of ℵ, A, B, E, F, G, H, L, R, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, about 70 others, Latin versions a, b, ff², g¹, l, q, and the Vulgate read **on the [following]** <note>original: "en tō hexēs"</note> (Griesbach marks this as likely but Scholz rejects it). <note>Note: in Luke 8:1 "on the following" uses the masculine/neuter article without variation; in 9:37 it is specifically "on the next day"; and the phrase "on the next" appears three times in the Acts of the Apostles.</note> | **he went**: <note>original: "eporeuthē"</note> found in ℵ, B, R, 13, 69, 346... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **he was going** <note>original: "eporeueto"</note> with A, C, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others; likewise the Latin versions and Vulgate read "he went." Furthermore, the corrected Received Text and manuscripts U, X, Δ, 69, 127, 131, 262, and some others add "Jesus." | **called**: omitted in the original hand of ℵ, but added by a later corrector. | **Nain**: found in ℵ, A, B, C, D, F, H, K, L, M, R, S, U, V, X, Δ, Π, many others, and Latin versions a, ff², q, Coptic, and both Syriacs... manuscripts E, G, Γ, Δ and some others read **Naein**; manuscripts 1, 209, and a few others read **Naeim**... Latin versions b, c, f, g¹, ², l, and the Vulgate read **Naim**... Latin versions 'e' and the original hand of 'l' read **Caphar-** <note>Presumably Capharnaum, a scribal error from the previous scene</note>.

**Nain** <note>original: "naum"</note> | **to him** <note>original: "autō"</note> is found in manuscripts <term>א</term> <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B, C, D, L, and many others... but omitted in manuscripts A, R, U, X, and about 15 others. |

**a large crowd**: several manuscripts add **of the city**.

**12.** **as he drew near** <note>original: "hōs de ēngisen"</note> (manuscript 69 and a few others use a slightly different verb form): The Vulgate and some Latin versions agree; however, Codex D and several Old Latin versions read **and it happened as he was drawing near**. | **and behold**: Omitted in Codex D, the Ethiopic, and several Latin and Syriac versions. | **a dead man** <note>original: "tethnēkōs"</note> (Cyril of Alexandria places this after "only son," and manuscript 122 uses a different word for "dead"): Omitted in manuscript A and others, hence Lachmann brackets it. | **only son** <note>original: "monogenēs huios"</note> found in <term>א</term>, B, L, X... while the standard received text and Tischendorf read **son only**, supported by A, C, D, E, and most other versions. Compare Luke 8:42 and John 1:18. | **and she was a widow**: Codex D reads **being a widow**. | **and she was** <note>original: "kai autē ēn"</note> (also in the received text) is found in <term>א</term>, B, C, L, and most Latin and Syriac versions... whereas Tischendorf and others omit **was** <note>original: "ēn"</note> based on manuscripts A, E, F, G, and many others. Furthermore, we have written **she** <note>original: "autē"</note> as it appears in most manuscripts and versions. | **a large crowd of the city**: Codex D reads **a large crowd from the city**, while others read **a considerable crowd of the city**. | **was with her**: found in <term>א</term>, B, L, and the Coptic and Armenian versions... whereas the received text and Tischendorf omit **was** <note>original: "ēn"</note> following A, C, E, F, and most others... Codex D reads **had come together with her**, and another Latin version reads **was following her**.

**13.** **and seeing**: Codex D and the Syriac read **but seeing**. | **her**: Omitted in Codex D and the Syriac. | **the Lord**: Codex D and several others read **Jesus**; the Gothic and Ethiopic read **the Lord Jesus**. | **had compassion**: <note>original: "esplagchnisthē"</note> misspelled in manuscript F. | **upon her** <note>original: "ep' autēn"</note> (using the accusative case) is found in <term>א</term>, K, R, U, and about 30 others... whereas the received text and Tischendorf use **upon her** <note>original: "ep' autē"</note> (using the dative case), found in A, B, C, D, L and most others. Compare Matthew 6:34 where the cases are similarly substituted in various manuscripts.

**14.** **bier** <note>original: "sorou"</note>: A few manuscripts spell this as "heap" <note>original: "sōrou"</note>. | Codex D and some Latin versions repeat the address: **Young man, young man**. | **to you** <note>original: "soi"</note>: manuscripts E, G, H read the subject **you** <note>original: "sy"</note>.

**15.** **sat up** <note>original: "anekathisen"</note>: most Latin versions translate this as **sat up** or **sat back**. | Manuscript B reads **sat**.

**another** <note>original: "allon"</note> with manuscripts A, D, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and nine other uncials <note>capital-letter manuscripts</note>, most other manuscripts, and Origen (who writes: "having sent two of the disciples, he asked: 'Are you the one,' etc."; and likewise: "because of this he said: 'Are you the one,' etc." It is not clear whether he is citing this verse or verse 20; but it seems he drew from Luke rather than Matthew.) ... manuscripts <term>א</term> <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B, L, R, X, Ξ, 33, and fifteen others, and Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> read **a different one** <note>original: "heteron"</note> :: as in Matthew, where the reading does not fluctuate. 25. **and luxury** <note>original: "kai tryphē"</note> [living]: omitted by manuscripts c, g¹, l, Ambrose's commentary on Luke <note>Ambluc</note>, the Harclean Syriac <note>syrʰʳ</note>, and an Ethiopic manuscript <note>aethᶜᵒᵈ</note>. It is doubtful in Tertullian, where it appears as: "the precursor—indeed greater than all born of women," and a little later: "who could be greater than such a prophet." ... Griesbach and other editors omit it with manuscripts <term>א</term>, B, K, L, M, X, Π, and about 25 others, as well as several Old Latin, Coptic, and Origen ("because of [the phrase]: 'no one among those born of women is greater than John'", and "that which was said concerning John").

<note>This section compares different ancient manuscripts to see how the wording of verse 28 varies.</note>
**...no one among those born of women is greater than John the Baptist** <note>original Greek: "meizōn en gennēt. gyn. iōannou tou bapt. oudeis estin"</note>, and <note>referencing Origen's works</note> volume 2, page 495: **John, than whom no one was greater among those born of women according to the testimony of our Savior who says: "Among those born of women, no one is greater than John the Baptist"** :: but the omission <note>of the word "prophet"</note> seems to have flowed entirely from the Gospel of Matthew; in the phrase **no one** <note>original Latin: "nemo"</note>, the word **prophet** <note>original Greek: "prophētēs"</note> is added | **of John** <note>manuscripts B, D spell it "Iōanou"</note> without the addition <note>of "the Baptist"</note> (Griesbach's minor edition) with manuscripts Codex Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note>, Vaticanus <note>B</note>, Regius <note>L</note>, and Zacynthius <note>Ξ</note>, various minuscules, the Coptic, the Harclean Syriac, the Armenian, and Origen (this also seems to be the case in Tertullian's *Against Marcion*, since in treating our passage extensively he nowhere adds "the Baptist" to "John") ... but the Lachmann edition adds **the Baptist** <note>original: "tou baptistou"</note> (Codex Δ omits "the") with manuscripts A, D, and the majority of others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac versions :: but in Matthew, the reading does not fluctuate | **there is no one** <note>original: "oudeis estin"</note>: omitted by manuscript "m" through carelessness | **but the one** <note>original: "ho de"</note> (manuscripts "a" and "i" read "and he"; "b", "ff²", "l", and "q" read "for he"): manuscript D reads **because the one** <note>original: "hoti ho"</note> | **least** <note>original: "mikroteros"</note>: manuscript D adds **of him**.

29. **the people when they heard** (manuscript 7ᵖᵉ and "a" read **having heard**) **and the tax collectors**: manuscripts "m", 71, and gˢᶜʳ read **the crowd and the tax collectors, having heard**. Compare also Chrysostom, volume 2, page 440: **the tax collectors and the crowd acknowledged God's justice, etc.** | **acknowledged justice** <note>original: "edikaiōsan"</note>: manuscript D reads **will acknowledge justice**; manuscript "d" <note>the Latin side of D</note> reads **he will justify** | Manuscripts B, D, and "d" spell it **John** <note>original: "Iōanou"</note>.

30. **and the**: manuscript D omits "the" | **for themselves** <note>original: "eis heautous"</note> (Cyril reads "in themselves"; manuscript g² reads "in himself"): manuscripts Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note>, D, and Cyril omit this. | **by him** <note>original: "hyp' autou"</note>: manuscripts "a", "b", "c", "e", "ff²", and "l" omit this.

31. **To what then** <note>original: "tini oun"</note> (Manuscript Fᵂ and a few Coptic versions omit "then"; Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note> has "but"): found in manuscripts Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note>, A, B, D, E, F, W, and nearly 150 others, including the Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac. However, Codex Zacynthius <note>Ξ</note> (having brought these words into the text from the margin) prefixes these words: **He no longer said [these things] to them, but to the disciples...** Griesbach and Scholz editions prefix **And the Lord said** <note>original: "eipe de ho kyrios"</note> with minuscules and the Vulgate (likewise, many Lectionaries have at the beginning of this section: **The Lord said:**) | **and what** <note>original: "kai tini"</note>: Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note> reads **and who** <note>original: "kai tines"</note>.

32. **to children**: manuscript D prefixes **to the** | **in the marketplace**: Manuscript Fᵂ and Δ read **in the marketplaces**, as in Matthew | **saying** <note>original: "legontes"</note> (from which reading all the others are to be explained) with manuscripts D, L, 13, 69, and several Old Latin manuscripts (which read **sitting in the marketplace and speaking to one another, saying**; others read **calling to one another**). Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note> and Vaticanus <note>B</note> read **which says** <note>original: "ha legei"</note>; others read **who say**. Lachmann and the majority reading is **and they say** with manuscripts A, P, X, and the majority.

and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not weep. 33 For John the Baptist has come neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, "He has a demon." 34 The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, "Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" 35 And wisdom is justified by all her children.

<note>This apparatus compares the Greek text above with many ancient versions. Symbols like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and D (Bezae) refer to famous 4th and 5th-century parchment bibles.</note>

**32.** Manuscripts d, g<sup>1. 2.</sup> and the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> read: **sitting in the marketplace and speaking to one another and saying** | Manuscripts ℵ, A, and many others read: **we played the flute** | Manuscript L, X, and others read: **you danced** | The word **wail** <note>original: "ethrēnēs."</note> appears without the word **to you** in manuscripts ℵ, B, D, L, Ξ, and several others, including the Coptic and Armenian versions. The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by ϛ, the traditional 16th-century Greek text</note> and the editors Lachmann and Tischendorf **add** the word **to you** based on manuscripts A, E, G, H, and the majority of others, as well as several Latin versions and the Syriac | The word **you wept** (spelled *-sete* in E) appears in some manuscripts; however, manuscripts 13, 69, 346 and Basil’s commentary on the Psalms read **you beat your breasts** <note>original: "ekopsasthe"</note>, which matches the wording in the Gospel of Matthew.

33. **For** <note>original: "gar"</note> (the Latin manuscript *l* reads **but**): Manuscripts F<sup>w</sup>, 150, and seven others, along with the Armenian version, omit this word. Origen <note>An early Church Father, c. 184–253 AD</note> writes: "The Savior says: John the Baptist has come neither eating nor drinking, and you say: He has a demon," which seems to be quoted from Luke rather than Matthew | **John** (Origen uses "the John"): Manuscripts B and D spell it **Iōanēs** | The word **neither** <note>original: "mē"</note> according to ℵ, B, Ξ, 157 and **nor** <note>original: "mēde"</note> according to ℵ and 157; also Latin manuscript *f* (**not eating bread nor drinking wine**) and Orosius | The Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use a different form of **neither/nor** <note>original: "mēte... mēte"</note> based on manuscripts A, D, L, P, X, and almost all others. In Matthew, this phrasing does not vary | **eating** <note>original: "esthiōn"</note> in this verse and the next is supported by ℵ, A, L, P, and others; however, Lachmann and Tischendorf use a shorter spelling <note>original: "esthōn"</note> in this verse based on B and D | The word **bread** after **eating** and **wine** after **drinking** are found in ℵ, B, L, Ξ, 157, the Vulgate, and others. The Textus Receptus places **bread** *before* **eating** and **wine** *before* **drinking** based on the majority of manuscripts. Manuscripts D, 1, 13, 69, and several others omit **bread** and **wine** entirely (making it match Matthew); however, since the sentence starts again with "eating," it is unlikely "bread" was originally missing | **you say**: A few manuscripts read **they say**, again matching Matthew. Eusebius <note>early church historian</note> also quotes this from memory, not following Matthew or Luke exactly.

34. **has come**: ℵ reads **came**, as in Matthew | For the spellings of **eating**, see the notes above | The word **friend** is placed *before* **tax collectors** in the vast majority of ancient manuscripts including ℵ, A, B, D, and the Vulgate. The Textus Receptus (following the editors Griesbach and Scholz) places it *after* **tax collectors**, matching Matthew. Clement of Alexandria <note>c. 150–215 AD</note> clearly quotes the version from Matthew: "For the Son of Man came, and they say: look, a gluttonous man and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors."

35. **was justified**: The original hand of manuscript B reads **is justified** | The word **all** (manuscript Γ uses a slightly different form for "all") is placed *after* **her children** in the majority of manuscripts (A, E, G, H, etc.) and the Coptic and Syriac versions. Lachmann and Tischendorf place **all** *before* **children** following ℵ, B, 69, 157, and the Vulgate. However, manuscripts ℵ<sup>c</sup>, D, L, and others omit the word **all** entirely (matching the Gospel of Matthew).

<header>7, 36. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

36 **36** One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him; and entering the house of the Pharisee, he reclined at the table. **37** And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that he was reclining at the table in the house of the Pharisee, brought an alabaster jar of ointment, **38** and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and with the hair...

---

<note>The following notes compare the Greek text above with dozens of ancient sources. Symbols like ℵ, B, and D refer to primary parchment manuscripts from the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>

Ambrose <note>Bishop of Milan, 4th century</note> explicitly maintains the opposite, see below. | **children**: <note>original: "teknōn"</note> Codex Sinaiticus reads **works** <note>original: "ergōn"</note> (the same reading we adopted in the Gospel of Matthew). Ambrose testifies to the same regarding the Greek manuscripts in his commentary on Luke. For he has these words concerning the phrase "by all her children": "Well said 'by all,' because justice is preserved toward all, so that there may be an acceptance of the faithful and a rejection of the faithless. Whence most Greeks have it thus: *wisdom is justified by all her works*, because it is the work of justice to preserve the measure toward the merit of each one."

**36.** **asked**: <note>original: "ērōta"</note> Manuscript D, several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, and some Syriac versions read **he asked** <note>original: "ērōtēsen," using a different tense</note>. The Curetonian Syriac reads: "And a certain Pharisee came asking him," etc. | **him a certain [one]**: Manuscript D, the Vulgate, and others change the word order to **a certain [one] him** | **of the Pharisees**: A few manuscripts read **of the Jews**; others add **the Lord Jesus** <note>original: "ton Iēisoun"</note> | **the house**: <note>original: "ton oikon"</note> Manuscripts ℵ, B, D, L, and several others use the masculine form for "house," while the Received Text <note>indicated by ϛ</note> and many others use the feminine form <note>original: "tēn oikian"</note> | **he reclined**: <note>original: "kateklithē"</note> Manuscripts ℵ, B, D, and L support this; the original hand of Sinaiticus read **he was reclining**; the Received Text uses a different verb for reclining <note>original: "aneklithē"</note> supported by the majority of later manuscripts.

**37.** **who was**: <note>original: "hētis ēn"</note> This phrase is placed here by ℵ, B, L, the Vulgate, and Ambrose. Others place it after **in the city**. Manuscripts D and the Ethiopic version omit it entirely | **and [knowing]**: Manuscripts ℵ, A, B, and many others include the word **and** before **knowing**; however, manuscripts D, E, G, and the Vulgate omit it | **knowing**: <note>original: "epignousa"</note> Manuscript D uses a simpler form of the verb "to know" <note>original: "gnousa"</note> | **is reclining**: <note>original: "katakeitai"</note> Supported by ℵ, A, B, D, and others. The Received Text uses a variant for reclining <note>original: "anakeitai"</note> | **alabaster jar of ointment**: Manuscript D reverses the order to **of ointment an alabaster jar**.

**38.** **behind**: <note>original: "opisō"</note> Placed after **standing** in manuscripts ℵ, B, D, and L, as well as the Vulgate and most versions. The Received Text <note>representing the editors Griesbach and Scholz</note> places it after **at his feet** | **his**: Some manuscripts and the Syriac read **of Jesus** <note>original: "tou Iēisou"</note>. Note the citation in Epiphanius: "And the woman, the sinner, standing behind at his feet, wet his feet with tears and anointed and kissed them." | **weeping**: Omitted in some Latin versions and the Vulgate | **with tears**: <note>original: "tois dakrusin"</note> Placed before **she began to wet** in ℵ, B, D, and L.

...with the hair of her head she wiped them, and she kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. **39** When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he spoke within himself, saying: “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner.” **40** And answering, Jesus said to him: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he says: “Teacher, speak.” **41** “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender; one owed five hundred denarii <note>A denarius was a silver coin typically representing a day's wage for a laborer.</note>, and the other fifty. **42** Since they did not have the means to pay him back, he freely forgave them both. Which...”

---

<note>The following notes are part of the critical apparatus, a scholarly tool that lists every variation found in ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. Letters like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and D (Bezae) represent specific famous manuscripts.</note>

**38.** <note>The text continues from the previous page regarding the phrase "after his feet"</note> The Textus Receptus <note>The "Received Text" used for the King James Version</note> and Tischendorf read this after "his feet" along with manuscripts A, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine other uncials <note>Manuscripts written in all capital letters</note>, and almost all others including the Gothic, Peshitta Syriac, Ethiopic, and Amphilochius. | **she began to wash**: <note>original: "ērx. brechein"</note> (Found in manuscripts f, g², and likely the Vulgate, Coptic, and both the Palestinian and Harklean Syriac): Manuscript D reads **she washed**, likewise "he was watering" in Old Latin versions b, ff², l, q; "he was irrigating" in version a; "he was moistening" in version e; "he washed" in version c and the Latin Origen; likewise in the Curetonian Syriac and Ethiopic. | **with the hair [plural]**: <note>original: "tais"</note> Manuscript A reads **with the hair [singular]** <note>original: "tois"</note>. | **hair**: <note>original: "thrixin"</note> spelled as in ℵ, A, B, E, G, K, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ etc.; Lachmann reads **hair** <note>original: "thrixi"</note> with D, M, U, Π, etc. | **she wiped**: <note>original: "exemaxen"</note> as found in ℵ*, A, D, L, X, and minuscules <note>Manuscripts written in cursive</note> 33, 106, 157, and Coptic. Lachmann and Tischendorf read **she was wiping** <note>original: "exemassen"</note> (though E*, H*, Δ, Π* and some others read "exemasen") with ℵ corrected, B, Ρ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine uncials, most other minuscules, and most Old Latin (though version e omits everything from "and with the hair" to "kissed his feet"), the Vulgate, all Syriac versions, and the Latin Origen.

**39.** **the one who invited him**: (also found in Latin Origen and Amphilochius): Manuscript D and version e read **at whose house he was reclining**; the Jerusalem Syriac omits this. | **saying**: manuscripts D, X, and minuscules 69, 106, and others, as well as version e, the Harklean Syriac, Armenian, Amphilochius, Latin Origen, and Augustine (twice) omit this. | **if**: this word is dropped in G, H, and a few others. | **prophet**: written as in ℵ, A, D, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine uncials, and almost all others. Manuscripts B and Ξ read **the prophet**. | Manuscript D spells the word for "what kind" as *podapē*. This same spelling appears in D at Mark 13:1 and Luke 1:29 (Matthew 8:27 has a gap here). | **who touches**: manuscript d (Greek), Origen, and several others read **the one touching**.

**40.** **he said to him**: (The Textus Receptus places "Jesus" before "said"). Manuscript 33 reads **to him he said**; manuscript x and a few others read **said to him**; version f and the Gothic read **said to Peter**; version e reads **to Peter he said to him**; version c reads **said to Simon (continuing: Simon)**. | **he says**: <note>original: "phēsin"</note> placed after "Teacher, speak" by ℵ, B, I, L, Ξ, and minuscules 1, 131. The Textus Receptus and Lachmann place it after "but he" with Ρ, Χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine uncials, most others, and the Old Latin and Vulgate (b, f, q, etc. read "but he said"; c and e read "he however said"; l reads "and he said"; a reads "who said"); also the Gothic and Peshitta Syriac; likewise A, D, and others, the Coptic, and Ethiopic read **he spoke** (the Curetonian and Sahidic Syriac read "he said to him"; other Syriac codices read "he however said"; the Jerusalem Syriac reads "and he said").

**41.** **two**: as found in ℵ, A, B, I, L, Ρ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π, nine uncials, and most others, as well as Old Latin versions a, l, q, and the Vulgate; likewise it appears so in ff², g¹, g². Manuscript D, the Sahidic Coptic, the margin of the Harklean Syriac, and the Ethiopic add **but he said** (Ethiopic adds "to him"); the Armenian reads "and he says"; the Harklean Syriac text and version c read "he says to him"; the Jerusalem Syriac reads "he said to him"; manuscript x reads "but Jesus said"; versions b, c, f read "therefore Jesus said"; version e reads "and Jesus says"; the Curetonian and Sahidic Syriac read "Jesus said to him"; the Bohairic Coptic reads "answering Jesus said to him." | **debtors**: <note>original: "chreopheilet."</note> found in ℵ, A, B, D, E, F, G, H, K, I, corrected L, M, P, S, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π, etc. The Textus Receptus reads **debtors** with a different spelling <note>original: "chreōph."</note> in L and many others. Furthermore, the ending is spelled *-philetai* in ℵ, A, B, D, L, P, Δ, Ξ; but B, E, F, G, H, I, K, M, S, U, X, Γ, Λ, Π and many others use *-pheiletai*. | **moneylender**: <note>original: "danistē"</note> found in ℵ, A, B, D, I, L, P, Δ, Λ, Ξ. The Textus Receptus and Lachmann read the spelling **moneylender** <note>original: "daneistē"</note> with B, E, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, X, Π and many others (manuscript r omits the first letters). Compare note at Luke 6:34. Also Origen: "there were two debtors to a man who was a moneylender; one owed," etc. Amphilochius reads "to a certain man" instead of "to a moneylender." | **owed**: Manuscript L and minuscules 69 and a few others use this form. | **fifty**: (Supported by Origen, Amphilochius, and John of Damascus): Manuscript D, minuscule 69, and versions a, c, and several Syriac versions add **denarii** before or after the number.

**42.** **they not having**: without the word "but" (as noted by Griesbach) in B, D, L, P, Ξ, and several minuscules, as well as Old Latin versions a, ff², g², l, the Vulgate, Origen, Amphilochius, Augustine, and an anonymous work on the lapsed. The Textus Receptus adds **but** with ℵ, A, I, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine uncials, and most others, as well as Old Latin versions b, f, g¹, q, the Gothic, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, and Armenian.

<header>7, 43. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

> Therefore, which of them will love him more? **43** Simon answered and said: "I suppose the one to whom he forgave more." And he said to him: "You have judged correctly." **44** And turning toward the woman, he said to Simon: "Do you see this woman? I entered your house, and you gave me no water for my feet; but she has wetted my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. **45** You gave me no kiss; but she, from the time I entered, has not ceased kissing my <note>The sentence continues onto the next page, ending with "feet."</note>

---

<note>The following technical notes compare different ancient versions of the New Testament. Scholars use these symbols to identify which manuscripts contain specific wordings.</note>

**Ethiopic version**, **Ambrose on Tobias 619**; likewise in manuscripts **c, e**, the **Curetonian Syriac**, and the **Sinaitic Syriac**; and since they did not have [the means to pay], **Amphilochius 484** (twice) and **John of Damascus 1, 601** read "since they did not have." | **of them** <note>original: "autōn"</note> (first instance): **Origen**, **Amphilochius 484** (three times): **8pe**, **al³**, **scri al**, and a few others including **John of Damascus 1, 601** omit this word. | **of them** (second instance): **Manuscripts D, I, 69, 157, 262**, and various Old Latin versions (**a, b, c, ff², g¹, ², l, q**), the **Vulgate** (but not the **Toledo manuscript**), the **Armenian**, and **Ethiopic** versions, and **Ambrose** omit this. | **more** <note>original: "pleion"</note>: (**Manuscript D** reads "pleon," **F** and **zscr** read "pleiona," and **D** with a few others and Latin versions place it after "will love him," having "will love him more") without the preceding word "said" in **Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)**, **Codex Vaticanus (B)**, **Codex Bezae (D)**, **Codex Regius (L)**, **Codex Zacynthius (Ξ)**, and others. **Tischendorf** <note>The editor of this Greek text</note> prefixes "said" (but **Manuscript A** reads "upon," making it "upon more") following **Manuscripts A, E, F, G, H, I, K, M, P, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π** and most others, including the **Gothic** and **Peshitta Syriac** (which adds "to me"). The **Harklean Syriac** adds "tell me" at the end of the verse; the **Armenian** adds "tell" before "who." Compare also the **anonymous author on Novatian 373** who wrote: "And he asked: Which of them loves him more?" | **will love him**: following **Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)**, **Codex Vaticanus (B)**, **Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C)**, and others. The **Textus Receptus** reads "him will love" following many uncials <note>Manuscripts written in capital letters</note>.

**43. Simon answered**: (regarding "Simon" and "the Simon" see below) without the conjunction "and" or "but" in **Codex Vaticanus (B)**, **Codex Bezae (D)**, **Codex Regius (L)**, and others; likewise the **Armenian** "Simon says," the **Curetonian Syriac** "Simon said to him," the **Peshitta Syriac** "Simon answered and said"; the **Ethiopic** "And Simon answered him." The **Textus Receptus** reads "but Simon answering," and **Lachmann** reads "but [Simon] answering" with **Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)** and many others. | **Simon without the article**: <note>In Greek, names often have "the" before them; "the Simon" vs "Simon."</note> following **Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)** and **Vaticanus (B)**. The **Textus Receptus**, **Lachmann**, and **Tischendorf** include the article "the Simon" following most other manuscripts. | **more**: **Manuscript D** spells this "pleon." | **and he**: **Manuscripts m, 157**, and a few others add "Jesus"; likewise the **Curetonian** and **Sinaitic Syriac** say "Jesus said to him."

Other Latin manuscripts read "to my feet," "on my feet," or "in my feet." The **Textus Receptus** and **Lachmann** read "upon my feet" following many manuscripts. | **hair**: without additions in **Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)**, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Bezae (D)**, and others. The **Textus Receptus** adds "of her head" following many later manuscripts and the **Curetonian Syriac**.

**45. a kiss to me**: **Manuscripts Δ, 184, 262**, and **346** add "of love." | **I entered**: (found in most Latin and Syriac versions). Several manuscripts including **L**, **13**, and **69** use a different verb form.

49. **those reclining at table:** Manuscript I adds "with him" | **among themselves:** Manuscript Delta (Δ) reads "among them" | **Who is this:** This phrasing is found in manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), B, L, X, Gamma (Γ), Delta (Δ), Lambda (Λ), Pi (Π), nine other capital-letter manuscripts, and most others (though manuscript 131 omits "is"). The early Christian writer Tertullian notes: "that wealthy women adhered to Christ, who also ministered to him from their resources," etc. | **for them:** This is the reading preferred by editors Griesbach and Scholz, found in manuscripts B, D, E, F, G, H, K, S, U, V, and nearly 190 others, as well as several Latin versions.

...hear, Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, etc. ... Manuscript D reads: *those who follow*. **13.** **on the rock** <note>original: "επι την πετραν"</note> according to manuscripts Sinaiticus (original hand), D, F, W, X, and Origen (quoting Luke) ... Manuscript D and others use a slightly different spelling | **of testing**: Codex Sinaiticus has a slight spelling variation | **fall away**: the Curetonian Syriac translates this as *are offended* or *stumble* :: as in parallel passages.

**14.** **fell**: Manuscript Delta and others read **fell into** (others read **fell out**) | **having heard** (found in Latin manuscripts e, f, ff², g¹, the Vulgate, and Syriac): manuscripts 33, 131, and others read **hearing** (*those who are hearing*). Furthermore, several manuscripts and versions add (either before or after) **the word** | **by cares and wealth** (Origen): Manuscript D and others read **by the cares of wealth**; Latin manuscript 'l' reads *by the anxieties of the age and of riches* | **pleasures**: Manuscript A and others add the preposition *by* | **are choked**: (Manuscripts A, B, D spell this with a slight vowel variation) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others ... the editions of Stephens and Lachmann use the standard spelling found in the majority of manuscripts.

**19** $^{82.2}$ And his mother and his brothers came to him, and they were not able to meet with him because of the crowd. **20** And it was reported to him, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside wanting to see you." **21** But answering, he said to them: "My mother and my brothers are these: those who hear the word of God and do it."

---

**19. came** <note>original Greek singular: "παρεγενετο"</note>: found in manuscripts B, D, X, 50, 71, and Coptic versions... the editions of Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use the plural **came** <note>original: "παρεγενοντο"</note> following manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), A, L, and many others, including the Old Latin and Vulgate; a similar situation occurs in Mark, where we preferred the singular "he comes" over "they come." | **his mother** <note>original: "η μητ. αυτου"</note>: found in Sinaiticus, D, and several others, as well as Coptic and Syriac versions, and the writings of Epiphanius (who twice notes: "he did not have 'his mother and his brothers,' but only 'your mother and your brothers'") ... the editions of Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf omit **his** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> based on manuscripts A, B, L, and many others, including most Latin and Syriac versions. | **his brothers**: the Curetonian Syriac adds *and they were standing outside*. | **were able** <note>original: "ηδυναντο"</note>: found in Sinaiticus, A, B, D, and many others; some others use the spelling *ηδυνοντο* or *εδυναντ*.

**20. And it was reported** <note>original: "απηγγ. δε"</note>: found in Sinaiticus, B, D, L, X, and others including Old Latin versions (with some Latin manuscripts reading "it was therefore announced to him") and Coptic... the editions of Stephanus and Tischendorf read **And it was reported** <note>original: "και απ."</note> based on A and the majority of manuscripts, as well as the Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac. | **reported** <note>original: "απηγγελη"</note>: some manuscripts use a different spelling; the Coptic and certain Syriac versions use the plural "they told." | **to him** <note>original: "αυτω"</note> without additions: found in Sinaiticus, B, D, L, and many Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions (Basil of Caesarea also quotes it this way) ... the editions of Stephanus and Tischendorf add **by those saying** <note>original: "λεγοντων"</note> based on A, X, and the majority of manuscripts, plus the Syriac and Armenian. | **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note>: found in Sinaiticus, D, L, X, many Latin and Syriac versions, and the Gothic... the editions of Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf omit it based on A, B, and the majority of manuscripts. | **your** <note>first instance</note>: omitted by Sinaiticus. | **standing outside**: Manuscript D and some Latin versions, as well as Basil and Tertullian (who writes in *Against Marcion* 4, 19: "it could not have been announced to him that his mother and brothers stood outside, seeking to see him"), use the order **outside standing**. | **wanting to see you**: found in Sinaiticus, A, L, X, and almost all others (Eusebius quotes: "someone said to him: behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside wanting to see you") ... B reads **wanting you to see** <note>reversing the word order</note> ... most Latin and Syriac versions read *wishing to see you* ... Manuscript D reads **seeking you** <note>original: "ζητουντες σε"</note>.

**21. answering**: omitted by some manuscripts and the Armenian version. | **to them**: Lachmann (by error) uses the dative *them* following Manuscript D and others. | **mother**: Manuscripts D, X, and others add the article **the** before "mother" and "brothers." Tertullian adds before "My mother etc." the phrase *who is my mother and who are my brothers?* Similarly, Tertullian notes in *On the Flesh of Christ* section 7 that the heretic Apelles and his followers "wish to deny that God himself was born because he said: 'who is my mother and who are my brothers?'" | **my** <note>second instance</note>: omitted by a few manuscripts and Latin versions. | **of God**: omitted by Sinaiticus. | **hearing**: Sinaiticus uses a different Greek tense <note>aorist vs present participle</note>. | **doing**: without the word **it** <note>original: "αυτον"</note> in Sinaiticus, A, B, D, L, the Latin, Vulgate, and others ... the edition of Stephanus adds **it** following many later manuscripts and the Coptic. Tertullian (*Against Marcion* 4, 19) adds the word *my* to "words."

<note>The following notes document variations found in ancient manuscripts for the text above.</note>

**49. [the teacher]** <note>original: "διδάσκαλον"</note> supported by manuscripts such as the Sahidic and Coptic versions, and the Harclean Syriac... The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add "to him" <note>original: "αυτω"</note> along with Codices A, C, D, P, R, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others; as well as most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Gothic, Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and John of Damascus. (Compare Mark 5:35 where Codex D adds "to him" after "saying"). | **your daughter:** <note>original: "η θυγ. σου"</note> Codex Sinaiticus <note>א</note> and some Old Latin versions read "the daughter of you." | **any longer:** <note>original: "μηκετι"</note> supported by Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus <note>B</note>, and D, the Sahidic, and the Peshitta Syriac. The Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read simply "not" <note>original: "μη"</note> with Codices A, C, L, P, R, X, and almost all others, as well as the Vulgate <note>"noli"</note> and Coptic. (Compare Luke 7:6 "do not trouble yourself"; in Mark 5:35 the phrase "why still trouble" likely did not influence this). | **trouble:** <note>original: "σκυλλε"</note> Many manuscripts and John of Damascus read "vex" <note>original: "σκυλε"</note>. | **the teacher:** (the Vulgate and others read this): Codices 1 and 131, most Old Latin, and the Vulgate (except manuscript mm) read "him" <note>original: "αυτον"</note>; Ambrose reads "Jesus." Ambrose <note>in his commentary on Luke</note> cites the text freely: *“The servants came, he said, saying to the ruler: Do not trouble him, your daughter is dead.”*

**50. hearing:** Manuscript U omits this. Codex D, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate add "the word" or "the speech" <note>original Latin: "audiens sermonem" or "audito hoc verbo"</note> as found in Mark. | **answered:** Manuscript Sinaiticus <note>אᶜ</note> reads this. However, the original hand of Sinaiticus <note>א*</note>, along with many Old Latin versions, the Sahidic, Curetonian Syriac, and Ethiopic, read "said" <note>original: "ειπεν"</note>. | **to him:** The Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, and Ethiopic clarify this as "to the father of the girl." | **to him [without addition]:** supported by Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, X, Δ, Ξ, and versions like the Sahidic and Vulgate. The Textus Receptus adds "saying" <note>original: "λεγων"</note> with Codices A, C, D, P, R, and many others, as well as the Coptic <note>"responding, he said"</note> and Armenian. | **believe:** <note>original: "πιστευσον"</note> supported by Codices B, L, and Ξ. The Textus Receptus and Lachmann read a different form of "believe" <note>original: "πιστευε"</note> which matches the steady reading in Mark, found in Codices Sinaiticus, A, C, D, R, X, and almost all others. | **will be saved:** <note>original: "σωθησεται"</note> The Old Latin and Vulgate use "will be saved" or "will be safe." The Sahidic and Syriac versions use "will live." The Curetonian Syriac adds "your daughter."

**51. when he came:** (similar to Matthew and Mark) supported by Codices Sinaiticus, A, B, C, E, F, H, K, L, and many others, as well as the Vulgate and Syriac. The Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read "when he entered" <note>original: "εισελθων"</note> with Codex D, V, and several others. | **but/and:** <note>original: "δε"</note> found in most; omitted by Codex Δ. | **did not permit etc.:** Codex Sinaiticus reads "he permitted no one to enter with him." | **anyone... with him:** Codices B, C, D, L, X, 33, and 69, along with the Sahidic, Coptic, and Ethiopic. The Textus Receptus reads "no one" <note>original: "ουδενα"</note> with Codices A, C, E, H, K, M, and many others (matching the wording in Mark). | **John and James:** Codices B, D, E, F, H, K, M, and others, including many Old Latin versions. The Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **James and John** (the standard order in Mark) supported by Sinaiticus, A, L, S, X, and the Vulgate, Coptic, and Ethiopic. See also Irenaeus <note>Against Heresies, Book 1</note>: *“For he permitted no one, he says, to enter except Peter and James and the father and mother of the girl.”* These words were preceded by a Gnostic opinion: *“But the Lord, entering fifth, raised the dead girl.”* It follows that the Gnostics read this passage without mentioning John; for in order to achieve the number five <note>the Pentad</note>, which they greatly delighted in, they counted the Lord himself in the fifth place. | **of the child:** <note>original: "της παιδος"</note> Codex D reads "of the girl" <note>original: "του κορασιου"</note>.

<note>The following notes document variations found in ancient manuscripts for the text above. Scholars use these to determine the most authentic original reading.</note>

**52. But he:** <note>original: "ο δε"</note> Manuscripts R, 33, 282, and others, as well as the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac (but not the Philoxenian or Harclean versions) and the Ethiopic add "Jesus" <note>original: "ι̅ς̅"</note> | **not:** <note>original: "ουκ"</note> (compare Mark, though the connection is slightly different) supported by Codices A, E, H, K, M, R, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Π, and many others, as well as Old Latin versions *b* and *e*, the Vulgate (including the Amiatinus, Fuldensis, Forojuliensis, and Toletanus codices), the margin of the Peshitta Syriac, and Origen (who writes "concerning whom he said: she has not died but sleeps") and Ambrose. Griesbach and Lachmann read "for not" <note>original: "ου γαρ"</note> (compare Matthew) supported by Codices Sinaiticus <note>א</note>, Vaticanus <note>B</note>, C, D, F, L, X, Δ, and about 25 others, several Old Latin versions, the Sahidic and Coptic, and the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac versions. | **died:** <note>original: "απεθανεν"</note> Codices F, L, M, X, and various numbered manuscripts, the Vulgate (though not all copies), Sahidic, Coptic, and various Syriac versions add "the girl" <note>original: "το κορασιον"</note> (influenced by Matthew 9:24). Furthermore, Augustine notes in *The Harmony of the Evangelists* 2, 68: "As for the fact that some codices have according to Matthew: 'For the woman is not dead but sleeps,' while Mark and Luke testify she was a twelve-year-old girl, you should understand that Matthew spoke according to Hebrew custom," etc.

**53. they laughed at:** <note>original: "κατεγελων"</note> Codex D reads a different verb form <note>original: "-γελουν"</note> | **knowing:** <note>original: "ειδοτες"</note> Codex Sinaiticus reads "seeing" <note>original: "ιδοντεσ"</note>.

**54. but he:** <note>original: "αυτοσ δε"</note> without additions (favored by Griesbach and Schuman) in Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, D, L, X, etc., and the Vulgate. The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> adds "putting them all out" <note>original: "εκβαλων εξω παντασ"</note> based on parallel passages in other Gospels. | **hand:** <note>original: "χεροσ"</note> in Codex Δ | **saying:** <note>original: "λεγων"</note> omitted by manuscripts 1, 118, 131, 209. | **arise:** <note>original: "εγειρου"</note> supported by the majority of manuscripts (A, E, H, K, etc.). This specific Greek form is used here; Lachmann prefers a different spelling <note>original: "εγειρε"</note> found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, D, X. Additionally, Epiphanius records the command as "Child, stand up" <note>original: "η παισ αναστηθι"</note>.

**55. returned:** <note>original: "επεστρεψεν"</note> Codex D uses a similar word meaning "returned back" <note>original: "υπεστρ."</note> | **and she stood up immediately:** <note>original: "και ανεστη παραχρημα"</note> omitted by the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus. | **directed:** <note>original: "διεταξεν"</note> Codex D reads "commanded" <note>original: "επέταξεν"</note> | **to be given to her:** The word order varies between "to her be given" and "be given to her" across various manuscripts.

**56. and they were amazed:** <note>original: "και εξεστ."</note> Latin version *a* reads "they were stunned," version *e* reads "they marveled." Codex D and others show slight variations in phrasing regarding the parents. | **he charged:** <note>original: "παρηγγειλεν"</note> Codex D has a slight variation in the conjunction.

**IX, 1.** The Textus Receptus <note>ς</note> has the first verse in three places. | **having called together:** <note>original: "Συγκαλεσάμενος"</note> variations in spelling <note>original: "συνκ."</note> occur in Sinaiticus, D, and R.

<note>The following notes provide a "critical apparatus"—a scholarly record of how different ancient copies of the Bible vary in their wording for these verses.</note>

1. **Called together** <note>original: "συγκ."</note> as found in <term>ABCLΓΔΛΞΠ</term> <note>These letters refer to major parchment manuscripts from the 4th to 9th centuries, known as Uncials.</note> and 8 other uncials etc.; **but** <note>original: "δε"</note> (found in the 3rd corrector of Codex C, the margin of H, and others; the Curetonian Syriac omits "but"): the 3rd corrector of Codex C, Codex F, the margin of H, and several others (likewise in Gospel lectionaries), the Sixtine Vulgate, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, and the Harclean version <note>original: "Et tunc ille domin. Iesus convocavit"</note> <note>translated: "And then the Lord Jesus called together"</note> add **Jesus** <note>original: "ο ις"</note> | **the twelve** <note>original: "τους δωδεκα"</note> (Codex D writes this as the numeral **12** <note>original: "ιβ'"</note>) with <term>ABDKMRSVΓΔΠ</term> and nearly 100 other manuscripts, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, and the <term>Dialogue</term> <note>reference 828</note> (reading: "I read from the Gospel: 'having called together the twelve he gave them' until 'to heal'") ... Stephens' 1550 text (Griesbach and Scholz editions) and Lachmann (by error regarding Codex B) add *his disciples* <note>original: "μαθητας αυτου"</note> (as in Matthew) with the 3rd corrector of C, E, F, H, U, and many others, as well as Old Latin versions b, ff², g¹, l, q ... Codices Sinaiticus <note>א</note>, C (original hand), L, X, Δ, Ξ and several others, the Vulgate, Coptic, and various Eastern versions add *apostles* <note>original: "αποστολους"</note> | **gave:** Codex Sinaiticus <note>א</note> reads *has given* <note>original: "δεδωκεν"</note> | **power to them:** Codex Vaticanus <note>B</note> and the Coptic (though not the Sahidic dialect) read *their power* <note>original: "δυν. αυτ."</note> | **authority:** Codex c incorrectly writes the word as <note>original: "εξουσιασιν"</note> | **all the demons:** Codex D reads *every demon* <note>original: "πασαν δαιμονιον"</note> (corrected by a second hand to *all*); the Curetonian Syriac reads *all spirits and demons* | **diseases:** Codex E spells this with a double 's' <note>original: "νοσσους"</note>

2. **to heal** <note>original: "ιασθαι"</note> (Codex F and manuscript 226 read *to have healed*) without addition, as in Codex B, the Curetonian Syriac, and the <term>Dialogue</term> <note>reference 828</note> (see above, the entire passage is quoted there) ... Griesbach and Lachmann add *the sick* <note>original: "τους ασθενεις"</note> with Codices Sinaiticus <note>א</note>, A, D, L, Ξ and others; likewise Stephens' 1550 text adds *those being ill* <note>original: "τους ασθενουντας"</note> with C, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and many others; manuscript 407 and the Gothic version add *all*, while lectionary 20 has *those being diseased*; Old Latin version f has *all infirmities*; most Old Latin and Vulgate versions have *the infirm* or *the sick* <note>original: "infirmos, aegrotos"</note>, as do the Sahidic, Coptic, and various Syriac versions.

3. **the:** <note>original: "την"</note> Codices C, X, Δ and others omit this, similar to the Gospel of Mark | **staff** with Codices Sinaiticus <note>א</note>, B, C, D, E, F, L, M, Ξ (Codex X reads *little staff* <note>original: "ραβδιον"</note>), many Latin and Coptic versions, and <term>Eusebius on Luke</term> <note>reference 169</note> (writing: "According to Matthew, he forbade them the possession of gold and silver—but according to the others [Mark and Luke] and the same Matthew, not permitting them neither staff nor bag etc.") <term>Tertullian against Marcion</term> <note>4.24</note> ("Christ, moreover, did not prescribe for the disciples to carry a staff on the journey," but it is questioned whether Tertullian wrote *staff* or *bag*; for based on the context of the 70 apostles, *bag* seems more likely) <term>Cyril of Alexandria on Luke</term> <note>230</note> <term>Augustine on the Harmony of the Gospels</term> <note>2.71</note> ("it is also often asked how Matthew and Luke recorded that the Lord said they should not carry a staff, when Mark says: 'except a staff only'" etc.) ... Stephens' text reads *staves* <note>original: "ραβδους"</note> with Codex A and others, following Matthew | **bag:** Old Latin versions a, b, c, e, ff², g¹, l, q add *nor sandals* <note>original: "neque calciamenta"</note> following Matthew | **each** <note>original: "ανα"</note> with Codices A, C, D and many others and the Peshitta Syriac ... Codices Sinaiticus <note>א</note>, B, C, F, L, Ξ and others omit it, as do the Vulgate and Coptic | **to have** <note>original: "εχειν"</note>: Codices Sinaiticus <note>א</note>, F, W, L and others read *you (plural) have* <note>original: "εχετε"</note>; the Sahidic version reads *nor let there be upon you*; Codex Sinaiticus (original hand) omits it.

4. **whatever:** <note>original: "ην"</note> several manuscripts add the particle <note>original: "αν"</note> | **house:** several manuscripts and the Peshitta Syriac read *city or house*, comparing it to Matthew | **stay:** Codex Sinaiticus <note>א</note> uses a different spelling for *remain* <note>original: "μινατε"</note> | **and from there:** Codex D uses a contracted form; several manuscripts and the Vulgate add *not*. Similarly, Old Latin version f and the Coptic read *until you go out* for *and from there go out*; the Ethiopic reads *and do not go out from there until you have gone out*.

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," where the editor, Tischendorf, lists differences found in ancient manuscripts for the verses above.</note>

5. **if** <note>original: "αν"</note> with <term>Codices ℵ, A, B, D, K, L, U, Λ, Π</term> and many others... but the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read a different form of **if** <note>original: "εαν"</note> with <term>C, E, F, H, M, S, V, X, Γ, Δ, Ξ</term> and nearly 70 others. | **receive** <note>original: "δεχωνται"</note> (Griesbach's edition) with <term>ℵ, A, B, C (original hand), K, L, M, U, Ξ, Π</term> and about 15 others... the Textus Receptus reads **dexōntai** <note>another grammatical form of 'receive'</note> with <term>C (third hand), D, E, F, S, V, X, Δ</term> and most others (the Latin and Vulgate translate this as "they have received") :: compare with parallel passages; likewise in <term>H, Γ, Δ</term> and about 20 others which read **dexontai** <note>future tense: "they will receive"</note>. | **you**: the Sahidic Coptic version adds "nor heard your words" :: likely from parallel passages in other Gospels. | **from** <note>original: "απο"</note> with <term>A, B, C, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π</term> and 8 other uncials and most others... <term>ℵ, D</term> and others read **out of** <note>original: "εκ"</note>, likewise the Latin and Vulgate use *de* (:: Matthew uses *exō* "outside," which was substituted with "out of" or omitted entirely). Furthermore, manuscripts 69, 124, and 346 read "from that house or from that city," and manuscript 33 reads "from that city or village" :: compare Matthew 10:14 and 11. | **and the dust** <note>original: "και τ. κονιορτ."</note> with <term>A, C (third hand), E, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term> and the vast majority, as well as Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac versions, and Ambrose... <term>ℵ, B, C (original hand), D, L, X, Ξ</term> and manuscripts 1, 33, 124, and some Latin versions omit **and**; hence Lachmann puts "and" in brackets :: but since it appears in Matthew and Mark without variation, it is much more likely it was omitted here based on those parallels than added here from Luke 10:11. It seems altogether that Luke wrote "and" in both locations—the second of which he alone contains. | **from** <note>original: "απο"</note> (manuscripts L and 33 add "the"): <term>D, U</term> and 15 others, as well as the Vulgate (which reads "the dust of your feet"), the Sahidic, Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and Armenian omit it :: compare Matthew. Other Latin versions read: "dust from your feet" or "your dust from your feet." | **shake off** <note>original: "αποτινασσετε"</note> with <term>ℵ, B, 1, 131, 157</term>... the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **apotinaxate** <note>an imperative form: "Shake it off!"</note> with <term>A, B, C, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π</term> and most others; <term>Codex D</term> reads **ekteinaxate** <note>"shake out"</note>. <term>Codex D</term> and some Latin versions place "the dust" before "and" :: following parallel passages. | **against them** <note>original: "επ αυτουσ"</note> with <term>ℵ (corrected), A, B, C, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π</term> and most others, including the Latin and Vulgate (reading *super* or *supra* "upon/against them")... <term>ℵ (later corrector) and X</term> read **ep autois** <note>a different Greek case for "them"</note>... <term>ℵ (original hand)</term> and others read simply **autois** <note>"to them"</note> :: as in Mark. Tertullian, in *Against Marcion* 4.21, paraphrases: 
> "He orders them to shake the dust from their feet against those by whom they had not been received, and he commands this to be done as a testimony."

6. **And departing**: the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac (but not the Harclean or Persian) add "the apostles" (Curetonian adds "his"). | **they went through**: <term>Codex Λ</term> adds "from that city." | **through the villages**: (some manuscripts omit "the") **villages** (manuscript *x* reads "cities," Sahidic and Armenian read "cities and villages," several Latin and Syriac versions read "towns and cities"): <term>Codex D</term> reads "according to cities they went" (and the Latin *d* reads "they passed through the surrounding cities"), Old Latin *e* reads "they passed through the towns."

7. **heard**: <term>Codex D</term> reads "having heard." | **the** <note>article</note>: <term>Codex Δ</term> omits. | **tetrarch** <note>original: "τετραάρχης"</note> with <term>ℵ</term> (manuscript *a* omits "the tetrarch") and others. Compare Matthew 14:1, where <term>ℵ, C, Z, Δ</term> and Luke 3:1 and 19 use this spelling... the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use an alternative spelling **tetrarchēs** <note>original: "τετραρχ."</note> with <term>A, B, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term> and almost all others. | **the things happening** <note>original: "τα γινομενα"</note> (some read "the things having happened," others "whatever things were done") without the addition of "by him" with <term>ℵ, B, C (original hand), D, L, Ξ, 69, 157</term> and Latin and Syriac versions... the Textus Receptus (but with Griesbach doubting) adds **by him** <note>original: "υπ αυτου"</note>, and Lachmann puts it in brackets, following <term>A, C (third hand), E, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term> and most versions. | **all**: (found in Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic versions).

<note>The following notes are part of the critical apparatus, comparing different ancient manuscript versions of the text above.</note>

**7.** **the things happening** <note>original: "τα γινομ."</note>: <term>Codex D</term> and others place this before the verb; this is not the case in the Sahidic, Peshitta Syriac, Armenian, or Gothic versions; <term>Manuscript 157</term> reads "all things" <note>original: "απαντ."</note> | **and he was perplexed**: <term>Codex d</term> <note>the Latin side of Codex Bezae</note> reads "he was in doubt" <note>original: "ηπορειτο"</note> | **John**: <term>Codex B</term> (but not <term>Codex D</term>) spells it with a double 'n' <note>original: "ιωαννησ"</note> | **had been raised** <note>original: "ηγερθη"</note>: found in <term>Codices ℵ, B, C, L, Ξ</term> and about 10 others... but the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Tischendorf read "has been raised" <note>original: "εγηγερται"</note> with <term>Codices E, H, X, Γ</term> and several others :: similar to the phrasing in Mark ... <term>Codex D</term> places "rose" <note>original: "ανεστη"</note> after "from the dead" <note>original: "νεκρων"</note>, following the same order as the Old Latin versions <term>c, e, a</term> ("he rose from the dead") | **from** <note>original: "εκ"</note>: <term>Codex ℵ</term> and 6 others read "from the" <note>original: "εκ των"</note>; <term>Manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 346</term> and a few others read "away from the" <note>original: "απο των"</note>.

**8.** **by some**: <term>Manuscript 69</term> reads "others" | **Elijah** <note>original: "ηλειασ"</note>: found in <term>Codices ℵ, B, D</term>... the <term>Textus Receptus</term>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "Elias" <note>original: "ηλιασ"</note> with <term>Codices A, C, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π</term> and almost all other manuscripts | **others**: <term>Codices L, Ξ, and Manuscript 157</term> read "by some" | **but** <note>original: "δε"</note>: <term>Codex Ξ</term> omits this | **one** <note>original: "τισ"</note>: (commended by Schulz) found in <term>Codices ℵ, B, C, L, X, Δ, Ξ</term>, the Gothic and Armenian versions, and Tertullian ("some one of the ancient prophets") ... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Lachmann read "one" <note>original: "εισ"</note> with <term>Codices A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term> and many others, as well as the Vulgate and Syriac versions :: see Matthew 16:14 and Mark 8:28 "one of the prophets," where the text does not vary, nor does the "one" in Mark 6:15 vary, except where <term>Manuscript 33</term> introduced the text of Luke ... <term>Codices D, 69, 346</term> and several Latin/Syriac versions omit this | **rose** <note>original: "ανεστη"</note> (Curetonian Syriac adds "from the dead"): <term>Codex D</term> reads "rose up" <note>original: "ηνεστη"</note> ... <term>Codex Γ</term> and others read "is" <note>original: "εστιν"</note>.

**9.** **And he said** <note>original: "ειπεν δε"</note>: found in <term>Codices ℵ, B, C, D, L, X, Ξ</term>, the Old Latin and Sahidic versions ... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads "And he said" <note>original: "και ειπ."</note> with <term>Codices A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term>, the Vulgate, and Syriac | **Herod**: found in <term>Codices ℵ, A, C, D, E, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term> and most others ... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads "the Herod" <note>adding the definite article "ο"</note> with <term>Codices B, L, X, Ξ</term> and a few others (similar to variations in Mark and Matthew) | **John**: <term>Codices C and D</term> prefix "that" <note>original: "οτι"</note>, as do the Sahidic and Coptic | **I hear** <note>original: "ακουω"</note>: found in <term>Codices ℵ, B, C, L, Ξ</term> and several Latin and Coptic versions ... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> prefixes "I" <note>original: "εγω"</note> with <term>Codices A, C, D, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π</term>, the Vulgate, and others; likewise, several versions add it after "hear" | **such things** <note>original: "τοιαυτα"</note>: <term>Codices D, F, L, X, Ξ</term> and several others read "these things" <note>original: "ταυτα"</note> | **see him**: <term>Codex D</term> and several Latin and Gothic versions read "him to see."

**10.** **to him**: <term>Manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 346</term> and the Peshitta Syriac read "to Jesus" <note>using the abbreviation "ι̅ω̅"</note> | **all that** <note>original: "οσα"</note>: <term>Codex ℵ</term> and Coptic versions read "what" <note>original: "α"</note> :: compare Mark "all things that" | **they had done**: <term>Codex A</term> adds "and all that they had taught" :: from Mark | **withdrew** <note>original: "υπεχωρησεν"</note>: found in <term>Codices ℵ, A, B, C, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π</term>... <term>Codex D</term> and a few others read "departed" <note>original: "ανεχωρ."</note> | **a city called** <note>original: "πολιν καλουμενην"</note>: found in <term>Codices ℵ, C, A, B, L, X, Ξ</term> and the Coptic versions; similarly <term>Codex D</term> reads "a village called" <note>original: "κωμην"</note> ... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Lachmann read "a deserted place" <note>original: "τοπον ερημον"</note>... **19.** Manuscripts B and D read **John** | **Elijah** <note>original: "ηλειαν"</note> as found in manuscripts B and D (and in verses 8 and 30, and Codex Sinaiticus); <note>original: "cf inprimis..."</note> compare especially to 4:25-26 where the spelling with "ei" is supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc., against the spelling with "i" in other versions... **20.** **who do you say that I am?**: The *Dialogue* <note>A 4th-century Christian text, the Dialogue on the True Faith in God.</note> reads only “who?” | **and Peter answering**: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Coptic versions; whereas Stephanus and Lachmann read **but Peter answering** with manuscripts Alexandrinus, Bezae, and the majority of others. Additionally, several Latin versions and the Syriac read **answering Simon Peter** or **Simon Cephas answered**, adding the name Simon | **the Christ of God**: Manuscript D and some Latin versions add “the Son,” and Origen’s commentary reads “the Son” instead of “the Christ.” The Vulgate and other versions read **you are the Christ the Son of God**. <note>original: "tu es christus filius dei"</note> Compare Origen 3, 533: “For he is called blessed in Matthew not just for saying ‘You are the Christ,’ but with the addition ‘the Son of the living God.’ Those who recorded it, Mark and Luke, wrote that Peter said ‘You are the Christ’ and did not add what is in Matthew... and thus did not record the blessing given to him.” Similarly, Cyril of Alexandria notes: “He says ‘The Christ of God,’ for he does not simply say he is Christ, but rather the Christ of God.”

**21.** **commanded**: manuscripts 28, 209, and the Peshitta Syriac add **them** | **to tell** <note>original: "λεγειν"</note>: supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. **22.** **saying**: Epiphanius’s work against Marcion reads **speaking** (omitting the word “that” which follows) | **that, etc.**: The original hand of Sinaiticus reads “that it is necessary for the Son of Man” | **by**: Manuscript D and others use a different Greek preposition for “by” <note>original: "υπο" instead of "απο"</note> | **the elders and chief priests**: Several manuscripts and Origen’s commentary reverse the order to “the chief priests and the elders” | **and scribes**: The Curetonian Syriac and Tertullian’s work against Marcion place this **before** “the chief priests.”

Origen <note>An early Christian scholar, vol 2, page 496</note> omits | **on the third day** <note>original: "τη τριτ. ημερα"</note> (The Latin versions, Sahidic, Coptic, both Syriac versions, Gothic, Armenian, and Ethiopic read "on the third day" <note>original: "tertia die"</note>): Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note>, several Old Latin manuscripts, the *Dialogue*, and Epiphanius read **after three days** <note>original: "μεθ’ ημερας τρεις"</note> (The Latin manuscripts read *post tres dies* or *post triduum*) :: This matches the phrasing in the Gospel of Mark | **to be raised** <note>original: "εγερθηναι"</note> (likewise in Matthew) is supported by the manuscripts Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), and many others, including Epiphanius in his *Refutations* ... The editors Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf prefer **to rise** <note>original: "αναστηναι"</note> (likewise in Mark) based on manuscripts Alexandrinus (A), Codex Bezae (D), and others. See also Justin Martyr <note>2nd-century writer</note> who says: "He himself saying that the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand, and that he must suffer many things from the scribes and Pharisees and be crucified and on the third day rise again." Additionally, see Gregory Thaumaturgus: "saying: it is necessary for the Son of Man to suffer many things and be killed and on the third day rise from the dead." Compare also Luke 24:7 and 24:46.

**23.** **to all**: The Curetonian Syriac <note>A very old Syriac translation</note> omits this | **to come** <note>original: "ερχεσθαι"</note> is supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae... The "Received Text" <note>the standard Greek text used for centuries</note> reads a different form of **to come** <note>original: "ελθειν"</note> (likely from Matthew) supported by later manuscripts | **let him deny** <note>original: "αρνησασθω"</note> is found in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus ... The "Received Text" uses a stronger form **let him utterly deny** <note>original: "απαρνησασθω"</note> | **and take up his cross**: Omitted by Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts (Griesbach and Scholz note this is also present in Matthew and Mark) | **daily** <note>original: "καθ’ ημεραν"</note>: This word is found in many major manuscripts including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and ancient versions like the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac. Jerome <note>the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> notes in his *Letter to Principia* that it is found in "ancient copies," and in his commentary on Matthew, he says "in another Gospel it is written: *He who does not take up his cross daily*." See also Chrysostom <note>a famous 4th-century preacher</note>... The editors Griesbach, Scholz, and Lachmann omit the word based on later manuscripts and some Old Latin versions. Chrysostom’s commentary mentions being "ready for slaughter and a daily death," which suggests he might have read "daily" in his copy, though it is not entirely clear which text he was quoting from. It seems more likely the word was accidentally omitted in some copies than added in from 1 Corinthians 15:31 | Manuscript K and others read **let him follow** <note>original: "ακολουθητω"</note>.

**24.** **whoever** <note>original: "εαν"</note> is supported by Sinaiticus and many others... while Lachmann uses **whoever** <note>original: "αν"</note> based on Alexandrinus and Vaticanus | **desires** <note>original: "θελη"</note>: Some manuscripts use a slightly different grammatical form <note>original: "θελει"</note> | **his life** <note>the first instance</note>: Origen reads "his own" <note>original: "την εαυτου"</note>, omitting the word "life/soul" in the manuscript | **will lose** <note>original: "απολεσει"</note>: Some manuscripts use a different future form | **his life** <note>the second instance</note>: Manuscripts F and W place the words in a different order.

### 534 ACCORDING TO LUKE 9, 25

for my sake, this one will save it. 25 For what does it benefit a man if he gains the whole world, but loses or forfeits himself? 26 For whoever is ashamed of me and my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. 27 But I tell you truly, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.

<note>The following technical notes compare different ancient manuscripts of these verses to determine the most original wording.</note>

24. **this one** <note>original: "ουτος"</note> (also found in the Old Latin manuscripts *b, e, g1, q*, the Coptic, both Syriac versions, and Origen vol. 2, p. 282) : Manuscripts 63, 116, 253 read **he** <note>original: "αυτος"</note> (Scholz noted this is "not foreign to Luke's usage") ... manuscripts 56, the Old Latin *a, c, f, ff2, g2* (apparently), *l*, the Vulgate, Gothic, Sahidic, Curetonian Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Tertullian in *Against Marcion* 4, 21 omit the word.

25. **for** <note>original: "γαρ"</note> : omitted in manuscript Sinaiticus ($\aleph$) | **man is profited** <note>original: "ωφελειται ανθρωπος"</note> (Manuscripts $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ spell it differently): Manuscripts Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), and Ephraemi Rescriptus (C) read **it profits a man** <note>original: "ωφελει ανθρωπος"</note> (Manuscript D originally had "man" in the accusative case). The Latin versions: *what does it profit* <note>original: "quid prode est"</note> (manuscripts *c* and *f* read *prodest*) *a man* in manuscripts *a, b, c, d, e, f, l*; *what does a man profit* <note>original: "quid proficit homo"</note> in *ff2, g1, g2,* and the Vulgate | **having gained and having lost or having been forfeited**: Manuscript D reads **to gain and to lose or to be forfeited** (A later hand in D corrected this to **if he should gain... and should lose or be forfeited**). The Latin versions: *if he should gain - and lose or* (or *but* in *ff2*) *suffer detriment* in *b, f, ff2, g1, q,* and the Vulgate; *if he should have made a gain - and lose or cause damage* in *e*; *to gain - to lose or make a loss* <note>original: "iacturam"</note> in *a* and *c*; *to gain - to lose and suffer a loss* in *d*; *to make a gain - to lose* (omitting the rest) in Cyprian p. 323 ... the Curetonian Syriac and Ethiopic omit (as Cyprian does) **or having been forfeited**.

26. **whenever** <note>original: "αν"</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), and others ... Manuscripts C, L, M, and many others use a different form of the word <note>original: "εαν"</note> | **me** (also Origen vol. 1, p. 296): Manuscript D and Origen vol. 1, p. 298 use the emphatic form **me** <note>original: "εμε"</note>. Additionally, the Curetonian Syriac adds **before men** | **and**: The Gothic version uses **or** | **my words** <note>original: "τουσ εμουσ λογουσ"</note> (matching the parallel in Mark) with nearly all manuscripts including Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), etc. ... Manuscript D, Old Latin *a, e, l,* the Curetonian Syriac, and Origen omit the word **words** (though Origen elsewhere includes a passage about not being ashamed of him or his words, and later mentions Jesus enduring the cross and his followers despising shame) | **his [glory] and**: Manuscript *cant* (the Latin side of Codex Bezae), the Curetonian Syriac, and the scholia omit this; likewise Eusebius in *To Lucianus* p. 172 (who writes: "that he will be ashamed of the one who was ashamed of him, when he comes in the glory of the Father, to which he immediately joins the saying: there are some of those standing here") | **of the Father** (also Origen and Eusebius): Manuscript D, several others, Sahidic, Coptic, and various Syriac and Ethiopic versions add **his** | **angels**: The Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic versions add **his**.

27. **truly** <note>original: "αληθωσ"</note>: Several manuscripts add **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note>; others place punctuation after "truly," and the Old Latin *a, b, c,* Vulgate, Gothic, Coptic, and Syriac versions join the words similarly ("but I say to you truly:"). Manuscript D reads **that truly**, while other major manuscripts and Origen join "truly" with the following word "there are" | **here** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> (literally "of him/there") with manuscripts Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), and others... but the standard text <note>term: Textus Receptus</note> and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf use **here** <note>original: "ωδε"</note> (following Matthew and Mark) supported by Alexandrinus (A), Codex Bezae (D), and the majority of manuscripts | **standing** <note>original: "εστηκοτων"</note> with $\aleph$, B, and others ... while editors Griesbach, Scholz, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use a different Greek form for **standing** <note>original: "εστωτων"</note> supported by manuscripts A, C, D, and over 100 others (the first form is used in Mark, the second in Matthew) | **who** <note>original: "οι"</note>: Manuscript Alexandrinus and others read **whoever** <note>original: "οιτινεσ"</note> following the other Gospels | **will [not] taste** <note>original: "γευσωνται"</note> (subjunctive) with most manuscripts ... the standard text uses the future tense **will taste** <note>original: "γευσονται"</note> with manuscript G and others, omitting the "not."

Earlier in chapter 22, Tertullian wrote: "you allow him to be seen with Moses and Elijah in the retreat of the mountain, where—"

[...the] destroyer had arrived." Shortly after: "now even if their presence was necessary, they would not certainly be shown in conversation—which is a sign of familiarity—nor in a fellowship of brilliance," <note>original: "nec in consortio claritatis"</note> from which it becomes probable that the word **were talking together** <note>original: "συνελάλουν"</note> was also accepted by Marcion. # ACCORDING TO LUKE 9, 36. 537

...let us make three shelters, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah—not knowing what he was saying. 34 While he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them; and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. 35 <margin>2 Peter 1:17</margin> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying: "This is my Son, the Chosen One; listen to him." 36 When the voice had finished, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
