**Manuscript Variations for Verse 33**

The Latin manuscript *ff²* omits the start of the verse | **Master** <note>original: "epistata"</note>: Manuscript *x* and manuscript 157 read **Teacher** <note>original: "didaskale"</note> | **here** <note>original: "hōde"</note>: The third corrector of Codex Claromontanus and about 10 other manuscripts add the word **always** <note>original: "pantote"</note> (compare with 1 Thessalonians 4:17) | **and** <note>original: "kai"</note>: Manuscript *x* uses an abbreviation, about 20 others and the Sahidic Coptic omit it; Manuscript *ff²* reads **if you wish** <note>original: "si vis"</note>, while the Coptic and another version read **and if you wish**. Tertullian (against Marcion 4, 22), Codex Sinaiticus, and a few others read **and we will make** ... Manuscript D (Bezae) reads **do you want me to make** <note>original: "theleis poiēsō"</note>, similar to the wording in Matthew | **three shelters** <note>original: "skēnas treis"</note>: This order is found in most major uncials including Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Ephraemi Rescriptus, as well as the Vulgate and several Syriac versions ... however, manuscripts D, K, L, and many others read **three shelters** in the reverse order <note>original: "treis skēnas"</note> | **one for you**: Sinaiticus and the Curetonian Syriac read **for you one** | **Moses**: Spelled **Mōyseĩ** in the oldest manuscripts like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus ... but spelled **Mōsẽ** in Codex Alexandrinus and the Received Text | **one** (the second instance, before Moses): Most uncials place it before the name ... but the Received Text and Sinaiticus place it after the name | **one** (the third instance, before Elijah): Manuscripts 1 and 131 and the Curetonian Syriac place it after the name | **Elijah**: Spelled **Ēleia** in Vaticanus and Bezae ... but Tischendorf and Lachmann prefer **Ēlia** as found in Sinaiticus and most others | **what he says**: Manuscript D reads **the things he says**, and a few others read **what he was saying**.

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 34**

34. **saying**: A few manuscripts read **speaking** | **overshadowed**: Found in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus ... while the Received Text and most others use a different tense of the same verb | **as they entered**: Found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Coptic versions; the Vulgate and some Latin versions read **as those men were entering** ... while the Received Text and others read **as those (Moses and Elijah) entered**; the Syriac versions vary, with one stating **when they saw them entering the cloud they feared**, and another **they feared when they saw Moses and Elijah entering the cloud**.

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 35**

35. **came** <note>original: "egeneto"</note>: Manuscript *d* reads **came down**, and the Curetonian Syriac reads **was heard** ... omitted by one manuscript | **saying**: Omitted by several Latin manuscripts | **my Son**: One manuscript reads **my Son the...** | **the Chosen One** <note>original: "ho eklelegmenos"</note>: Scholars Griesbach and Schulz note this is typical of Luke’s style (compare 2:15, 23:35). It is found in the oldest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and the Sahidic Coptic and some Latin versions ... but the Received Text and Lachmann read **the Beloved** <note>original: "ho agapētos"</note>, following the wording in Matthew and Mark, supported by Codex Alexandrinus and the Vulgate. Additionally, Codex Bezae and about 20 others add **in whom I am well pleased**, clearly borrowed from the account in Matthew | **listen to him**: Manuscript D and some Latin versions reverse the word order to **to him listen**.

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 36**

36. **voice**: One manuscript reads **cloud** ... another adds **this** | **Jesus**: The Received Text adds the definite article **the Jesus**, while the older uncials omit it | **and they**: Manuscript D and some Coptic versions read **but they** | **nothing**: Omitted by a few minor manuscripts | **they had seen**: <note>The entry ends abruptly here, likely continuing on the next page.</note>

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 9, 37. 538

<margin>
37–43
Matthew 17, 14–23
Mark 9, 14–29
</margin>

37 **99. 2** It happened on the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, that a large crowd met him. 38 And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, saying: "Teacher, I beg you, look upon my son, for he is my only child, 39 and behold, a spirit seizes him and he suddenly cries out; it convulses him with foaming at the mouth, and it scarcely leaves him, crushing him. 40 And..."

---

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 36 (Continued)**

**they had seen** <note>original: "heōrakan"</note>: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), and others. Tischendorf prefers the form **they had seen** <note>original: "heōra-"</note> based on Ephraemi Rescriptus (C) and several others. The Latin Vulgate translates this as **they had seen** <note>original: "viderant"</note>, while some older Latin versions use **they saw** <note>original: "viderunt"</note>. The Ethiopic version adds **and what they had heard**.

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 37**

**the next day** <note>original: "tē hexēs hēmera"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. The Latin manuscript *f* reads **that day** <note>original: "illa"</note>; the Sahidic Coptic reads **the same day**; the Curetonian Syriac reads **that day again**. Some manuscripts (C, E, G, etc.) add the word **in** <note>original: "en"</note> before "the next day." Manuscript D (Bezae) and several Old Latin versions read **during the day** <note>original: "dia tēs hēmeras" / "per diem"</note>. | **when they had come down** <note>original: "katelthontōn autōn"</note>: Manuscript D reads **when he had come down** <note>original: "katelthonta auton"</note> in the singular. | **from** <note>original: "apo"</note>: Manuscript Γ reads **out of** <note>original: "ek"</note>. | **met him** <note>original: "synēntēsen autō"</note>: Some versions (Latin and Syriac) read **met them**, though this is not found in the parallel in Matthew. Manuscript D reads **a large crowd came together to him**.

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 38**

**behold**: Omitted by some Syriac versions. | **cried out** <note>original: "eboēsen"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae. The scholar Scholz notes that the compound form **shouted out** <note>original: "anaboan"</note> is not typical for Luke, who uses the simple form five times and a different compound in Acts. However, many other manuscripts (A, R, etc.) use the compound **shouted out** <note>original: "aneboēsen"</note>. The Latin versions use **exclaimed** <note>original: "exclamavit"</note>. | **look upon** <note>original: "epiblepsai"</note>: Most manuscripts use this infinitive form (meaning "to look upon"), while Sinaiticus and others use the command **look!** <note>original: "epiblepson"</note>. Latin versions use **look/regard** <note>original: "respice"</note> or **attend** <note>original: "adtende"</note>. Syriac versions translate this as **have mercy**. | **he is to me** <note>original: "moi estin"</note>: Variations exist in the order of these words (e.g., "is to me" vs "to me is").

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 39**

**behold**: Omitted by Sinaiticus and some Syriac versions. | **and behold a spirit seizes him and suddenly he cries out**: Manuscript D and the Old Latin *e* read **for a spirit suddenly seizes him** <note>original: "arripit enim illum spiritus"</note>. | **cries out**: The Syriac and Ethiopic versions read **throws him down**, which aligns somewhat with the description in manuscript D. | **and convulses** <note>original: "kai sparassei"</note>: Sinaiticus reads **and dashes down** <note>original: "kai rhessei"</note>. Other Latin and Syriac versions add **and he grinds his teeth and is torn** (comparing this to the description in Mark). | **him** (second occurrence): Omitted by Bezae and some Latin versions. | **scarcely** <note>original: "mogis"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and others. Manuscripts B and R use the variant spelling **hardly** <note>original: "molis"</note>, which Scholz argues is the more correct Lukan form. | **crushing** <note>original: "syntribon"</note>: Manuscript D and Latin version *e* change this to a verb, **and it crushes him**, while omitting the phrase "scarcely leaves him."

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 9, 43.

I begged your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.” 41 And Jesus answered and said: “O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and endure you? Bring your son here.” 42 And as he was yet coming, the demon threw him down and convulsed him; but Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, and healed the child and gave him back to his father. 43 <gloss>100. 8</gloss> And they were all amazed at the <margin>43–45 Mark 9, 30–32 Matthew 17, 22 and following</margin> majesty of God.

<gloss>101. 2</gloss> While everyone was wondering at all the things he was doing, he said

---

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 40**

**disciples** <note>original: "mathētōn"</note>: Omitted in manuscript L* | **cast out** <note>original: "ekbalōsin"</note>: Found in Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and many others. The standard text used by editors Griesbach and Scholz reads a different spelling <note>original: "ekballōsin"</note> found in a few minuscules. Manuscript D (Bezae) uses **deliver from** <note>original: "apallaxōsin"</note>. The Curetonian Syriac phrases this freely as **and they were not able to heal him and cast it out** for the phrase starting from **to [cast out]... to the end** | **it** <note>original: "auto"</note>: Manuscript D and about ten others read **him** <note>original: "auton"</note> (The Old Latin and Vulgate use **him** <note>original: "illum"</note> because they previously mentioned the **spirit**) | **they could not** <note>original: "ēdynēthēsan"</note>: Some manuscripts use a different Greek spelling for "could"; manuscript C reads **they were not strong enough** <note>original: "ischysan"</note> (similar to the Gospel of Mark). Compare this with the writings of the church father Epiphanius: **I begged your disciples. And it says after: they could not cast it out, and [Jesus said] to them: O faithless generation, how long shall I endure you?**

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 41**

**And answering [Jesus]** <note>original: "apokritheis de"</note>: These words are omitted in the original hand of manuscript C; the manuscript *am** omits **and** <note>original: "de"</note> | **faithless** <note>original: "apistos"</note>: Manuscript D uses the vocative form **O faithless one** | **and perverse**: Omitted in the writings of Epiphanius and Tertullian | A few manuscripts (28, 69, 346) read **I shall be and I shall endure** | **be with you** <note>original: "esomai pros hymas"</note>: Most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, and Tertullian read **be among you** <note>original: "ero apud vos"</note>. Sinaiticus reads **be with you** <note>original: "meth' hymōn esomai"</note>; others (sah, cop, syr) also read **be with you** (Note: Mark uses "with/toward," Matthew uses "with/among") | **and** (before **endure**): Many manuscripts (syr, arm, etc.) use **until** <note>original: "heōs"</note> or **and until** (similar to Mark). Tertullian reads **how long shall I be among you** omitting **and endure you**. Epiphanius reads **how long shall I endure you** omitting **how long shall I be among you** | **Bring** (Manuscript D uses **Bring forward**): Sinaiticus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and others add **to me** <note>original: "moi"</note>, likely following Matthew | **here** <note>original: "hōde"</note>: Positioned here in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. Griesbach and Scholz place it after **your son** following Alexandrinus and many others (similar to Matthew). Manuscript D and some Latin versions omit it entirely (similar to Mark).

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 42**

**And while [he was] yet**: Found in Latin and Syriac versions (one Latin version reads **but when he approached**, omitting **yet**) | **coming** <note>original: "proserchomenou"</note>: The original hand of Sinaiticus reads **praying** <note>original: "proseuch-"</note> | **convulsed** <note>original: "synesparaxen"</note>: Manuscript D and others read **disturbed** <note>original: "synetaraxen"</note>. Several versions (Coptic, Syriac, etc.) add **him** <note>original: "auton"</note> | **the unclean spirit**: Manuscript D reverses the order to **the spirit unclean** | **healed... and gave him back**: Manuscript D reads **he let him go and gave back the child** <note>original: "aphēken auton kai apedōken ton paida"</note>.

**Manuscript Variations for Verse 43**

**And everyone was amazed**: Manuscript D and some Latin versions swap the order to **And all were amazed**. The Syriac versions read **all were wondering** or **and all wondered** | Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Bezae, and others use a different spelling for **majesty** <note>original: "megaliotēti"</note>, unlike Alexandrinus and Vaticanus | **While everyone [was wondering]**: Sinaiticus and some Latin versions read **Therefore everyone...**; others read **And while all...** | **at all [the things]**: Manuscript U omits **all** | **he was doing** <note>original: "epoiei"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others. The standard text of Griesbach reads the past tense **he did** <note>original: "epoiēsen"</note> following many later manuscripts. Also, the name **Jesus** is omitted here in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.

# 9, 44. ACCORDING TO LUKE

to his disciples: 44 “Let these words sink into your ears; for the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” 45 But they did not understand this saying, and it was hidden from them so that they might not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

<margin>
46—48
Mark 9, 33—37
Matthew 18, 1—15
</margin>
46 <gloss>102. 2</gloss> An argument arose among them as to which of them might be the greatest. 47 But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their heart, took a child and stood him by his side, 48 and

---

**1.** <note>This long note discusses variations in how verse 43 ends and verse 44 begins across different ancient copies.</note> Manuscripts 131, 157, 209, and several Old Latin copies <note>original: "mscr a b c e ff2. g1. g2."</note>, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and Armenian versions... The editor Lachmann <note>original: "Ln"</note> (by error) adds **Jesus** <note>original: "ho Iēsous"</note> along with Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and many others. Furthermore, after the phrase **was doing**, several Old Latin and Gothic versions add: **Peter said to him: Lord, why** <note>original: "quare"</note> **were we not able to cast it out? To whom he said: because this kind is cast out by prayer and fasting.** <note>This is a famous variant where some manuscripts include a question from Peter that usually appears in the Gospels of Matthew or Mark.</note> Compare parallel passages. | **said**: Codex Washingtonianus (W) adds **but**, as do several Latin and Gothic copies. | **his** <note>original: "autou"</note>: Omitted by Codex Washingtonianus and one Latin copy.

**44. into the ears**: Several Old Latin copies read **in the ears**; the Vulgate and others read **in the hearts**. | **delivered**: Manuscript 69 has a slight spelling variation. | **men**: Some manuscripts (76, 106, 251, and the Syriac) add **sinful** <note>original: "hamartōlōn"</note> **men**.

**45. hidden**: Manuscripts use different Greek words for "hidden" <note>original: "parakekalymmenon" vs "parakekrymenon"</note>. | **from**: Various manuscripts use different prepositions for "from" or "by" <note>original: "apo, hypo, epi, para"</note>. | **perceive**: Some copies use a slightly different verb form. | **ask**: Most major manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) use the standard word for "ask" <note>original: "erōtēsai"</note>, but Lachmann and others use a more intense form **ask thoroughly** <note>original: "eperōtēsai"</note> based on Codex Bezae (D) and others. | **him**: The placement of the word "him" varies in several manuscripts, and is omitted in Codex Bezae and some Latin copies. | **this saying**: Omitted in one manuscript.

**46. an argument arose**: Codex Bezae (D) omits this entire sentence. | **which**: A few manuscripts omit the article "the" <note>original: "to"</note> before "which." The ancient scholar Origen <note>original: "Or"</note> noted that in Luke, the argument did not "rise up" into the disciples but rather "entered" into them.

**47. knowing** <note>original: "eidōs"</note>: Found in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and others. Other versions use **recognizing** <note>original: "gnous"</note> or **seeing** <note>original: "idōn"</note>. Origen comments that Jesus was **seeing the reasonings of their hearts with his own eyes**. The reading "knowing" is preferred here because it matches Jesus's insight described elsewhere in Luke (5:22 and 6:8). | **the heart**: Its position in the sentence varies in Codex Bezae; it is omitted in some Syriac and Latin versions. | **child**: Minor spelling variation in some major manuscripts <note>original: "paidion" vs "paidion"</note>. | **him**: Variation in gender or omitted entirely in some Latin versions. | **by his side**: Codex Bezae reads **towards himself**; the Ethiopic version reads **before them**.

said to them: “Whoever receives this child in my name, receives me; and whoever receives me, receives the one who sent me; for the least among you all, he is great.”

**48.** **to them** <note>original: "αυτοισ"</note> (found in manuscripts f, g1, g2, the Vulgate, both Syriac versions, etc.): Omitted by Codex Bezae (D), manuscript 157, and Old Latin a, b, c, e, ff2, l, q, and the Curetonian Syriac | **whoever** <note>original: "οσ εαν"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and many others... Lachmann <note>original: "Ln"</note> reads **whoever** <note>original: "οσ αν"</note> based on D, L, Ξ, and others | **receives** <note>original: "δεξηται"</note>: Manuscript X spells it differently | **this child** <note>original: "τουτ. το παιδ."</note> (also Origen): D, 1, 209, and some Old Latin (though manuscript 'a' omits the section from "whoever receives" to "receives me; and") and the Vulgate and Syriac. Cyril of Alexandria fluctuates in the word order | **whoever receives me... receives**: Omitted by manuscript d and 71 (retaining only "and the one who sent me") | **whoever** <note>original: "αν"</note> with B, K, L, U, Ξ, 33, 69, etc. ... while the Majority Text and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read **whoever** <note>original: "εαν"</note> with A, C, E, F, etc. ... ℵ omits | **receives** <note>original: "δεξηται"</note>: ℵ, X, and 69 read **is receiving** <note>original: "δέχεται"</note> | **all** <note>original: "πασιν"</note> (also Origen and Cyprian): Omitted by the Majority Text, Curetonian Syriac, and some Cyprian citations | **being** <note>original: "υπαρχων"</note> (also Cyprian): Omitted by manuscript d, b, and some Cyprian citations; the Curetonian Syriac adds *as this child* | **is** <note>original: "εστιν"</note> (Griesbach's secondary reading) with ℵ, B, C, L, X, Ξ, 1, 33, and about 10 others, most Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Coptic (Curetonian Syriac does not express the verb). Origen adds: *we have read in other places: and he shall be great*. The Majority Text reads **will be** <note>original: "εσται"</note> with A, D, and many others, including various Latin and Syriac versions and Cyprian. Compare this with the parallel in Mark.

**49.** **And John answered** <note>original: "αποκρίθ. δε"</note> (Curetonian Syriac reads *and he answered*): Manuscript c omits **and** <note>original: "δε"</note> | **John** <note>original: "ο ιωανν."</note> (B and D spell the name slightly differently) with ℵ, A, C, E, F, and the majority... Lachmann and Tischendorf omit the article **the** <note>original: "ο"</note> based on B, D, 28, 69, 346, etc. | **Master** <note>original: "επιστατα"</note> (also manuscript c): L, Ξ, and some Syriac and Coptic sources read **Teacher** <note>original: "διδασκαλε"</note>, likely influenced by the parallel in Mark | **we saw** <note>original: "ειδομεν"</note> with ℵ, B, C, D, etc. ... other manuscripts use slightly different Greek spellings (idomen or idamen) | **in the** [name] <note>original: "επι τω"</note> with A, C, D, etc. ... ℵ, B, L, X, and several others, as well as the Coptic, Vulgate, and Old Latin, read **in the** [name] <note>original: "εν τω"</note>, which is the certain reading in the parallel passage of Mark | **casting out** <note>original: "εκβαλλοντα"</note>: minor spelling variations in V and Δ | **demons** <note>original: "δαιμονια"</note> with ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, X, etc. ... the Majority Text reads **the demons** <note>original: "τα δαιμ."</note> | **we forbade** <note>original: "εκωλυσαμεν"</note> with A, C, D, X, and almost all versions... ℵ, B, L, Ξ, and some Old Latin read **we were forbidding** <note>original: "εκωλυομεν"</note>. The first reading (forbade) is better supported here, as Mark clearly wrote "were forbidding." However, since "were forbidding" has strong support in Luke as well, it is hard to define which one the author originally wrote. It should be noted that in this same verse, many witnesses seem to have borrowed "in" <note>original: "en"</note> from Mark instead of "on" <note>original: "epi"</note>. | **with us** <note>original: "μεθ ημων"</note> (see Phrynichus's Epitome): Some manuscripts read **to us** <note>original: "ημιν"</note> (as in Mark); the Curetonian Syriac reads *with us after you*. Manuscripts Δ and δ confuse this, reading *he follows with us is* (is following with us).

**50.** **But said** <note>original: "ειπ. δε"</note> with ℵ, B, C, D, L, X, Ξ, and several others, as well as some Latin, Syriac, and Coptic versions... the Majority Text and Tischendorf read **And said** <note>original: "και ειπ."</note> with A and many others. | **to him** <note>original: "προσ αυ-"</note>

**ton** <note>original: "τον"</note>: [Found in manuscripts] 13. 61mg 69. 235. 254. and others, the Vulgate, Syriac, Ethiopic. Omitted by Codex Bezae (D), Old Latin e, and others | **Jesus** <note>original: "ις"</note> without the article "the" with Sinaiticus* and Vaticanus... The Majority Text and Lachmann read **set firmly** <note>original: "εστηριξε"</note> | **to** <note>original: "εισ"</note>: Manuscript A reads **in**.

Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read **as** <note>original: "ωσ"</note> :: but "as" seems too much like a later correction | **him** <note>original: "αυτω"</note>: Manuscript Gamma reads **himself**.

### ACCORDING TO LUKE 9, 56.

his face was set toward Jerusalem. 54 And when the disciples James and John saw this, they said: "Lord, do you want us to bid fire to come down from heaven and consume them?" 55 But having turned, he rebuked them. 56 And they went to another village.

---

**53. going** <note>original: "πορευομενον"</note> (Old Latin manuscript *a* "tending," *c* "proceeding," *d* "going," Jerome "walking"): manuscripts *b, f, l, q*, the Vulgate, and Ambrose’s commentary on Luke read **of [him] going** <note>original: "euntis"</note>; manuscript *e* reads **to [them] going** <note>original: "euntibus"</note>.

**54.** Manuscript Γ and others read **seeing** <note>original: "ειδοντες"</note> | **the disciples** without the word **his** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> in agreement with <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (ℵ), <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (B), and manuscripts 1, 118, 131, 157, the Old Latin *e*, Armenian, and a homily by Antiochus (Cyril of Alexandria’s homily reads: "and indeed, being stung by this, the disciples approached and spoke") ... the <term>Received Text</term> (ς), Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **his** with Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Ephraemi (C), Codex Bezae (D), and many others, most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, and Ethiopic | Codex Vaticanus (B) and Codex Bezae (D) spell **John** <note>original: "ιωαννης"</note> with one 'n' | **they said** <note>original: "ειπαν"</note> with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and others ... the Received Text and Lachmann read **they said** <note>original: "ειπον"</note> with most other manuscripts. Additionally, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac add **to him** | **should we say** <note>original: "ειπωμεν"</note>: some manuscripts read **let us say**, while the Old Latin and Vulgate read **we say** | **from heaven** <note>original: "απο του ουρανου"</note> found in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc. ... but others read **out of heaven** <note>original: "εκ του ουρανου"</note> or simply **from heaven**. Additionally, Old Latin manuscripts *a, b, c, l, q* add **upon them**, and manuscript *e* adds **to them** | **and consume them** (omitted in manuscript *l*) without further addition, agreeing with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Cyril of Alexandria (who quotes: "and consume them; but the Savior turned to them again and said: leave them; or do you not know that I can call upon my Father and he will provide for me etc.") ... the Received Text and Lachmann add **as also Elijah did** <note>referencing 2 Kings 1:10, 12</note> based on Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi, Codex Bezae, and most other manuscripts, many Old Latin versions, Syriac, Gothic, Ethiopic, and the writings of Basil and Chrysostom (who notes: "when they said: let us bid fire — and they remembered Elijah etc."). Augustine also recognizes this in his *Sermon on the Mount*. However, it is not certain this was read by <term>Tertullian</term> (Against Marcion 4, 23). For as he compares "Christ loving the little ones" with the "Creator" who "sent bears upon the boys, avenging Elisha the prophet," so a little later he writes: "the Creator represents the plague of fires at Elijah's request against that false prophet. I recognize the severity of the Judge; on the contrary, [I recognize] the leniency of Christ rebuking the disciples who were intending that same punishment upon that Samaritan village. Let the heretic also recognize that this leniency of Christ was promised by that same most severe Judge: He shall not strive, he says, nor shall his voice be heard in the streets" etc. John Mill (pp. 418-419) says it is not so clear these were read by Tertullian. "It is more likely that the example of Elijah, noted by him and others, gave occasion for this interpolation in this place." See the following verse regarding Clement in Macarius's *Chrysocephalus*.

**55. but having turned** (so in *d* and *e*; *c* reads "and so having turned"; others "and having turned"): manuscripts K, Π, and others add **Jesus** | **he rebuked them** without addition <note>referring to the famous omitted phrase "You do not know what kind of spirit you are of"</note> according to Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and many others, the Vulgate, Coptic, and Ethiopic. Jerome says: "he rebukes them because they did not remember his doctrine and the evangelical goodness in which he said—"

<header>9, 57. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

<margin>57-60 Matthew 8, 19-22</margin>

# 57 <sup>105. 5</sup> **And as they were going on the road, someone said to**

[The manuscript notes continue:] assigning Matthew 5:30 and Luke 6:35) <note>original: "catoxon"</note> (see below) ... the <term>Received Text</term> (ς) adds **"and he said: you do not know of what spirit you are"** <note>original: "και ειπεν· ουκ οιδατε οιου πνευματος εστε υμεις"</note> (Found in <term>Codex Bezae</term> [D] and others, plus 10 <term>minuscules</term> <note>handwritten copies from the middle ages</note>, Chrysostom, and Antiochus). This phrase appears with or without the word **"you"** <note>original: "υμεις"</note> in various manuscripts including <term>Codices</term> F, K, M, U, Γ, Λ, and several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, and the Gothic version. It is also found in the writings of Didymus (who seems to reference it here: "you do not know of what spirit the Son of Man is"), Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in a letter to Demophilus: "we will not accept your zealot-like impulses, even if you were to repeat the examples of Phinehas and Elijah ten thousand times. For Jesus, hearing such things, was not pleased with the disciples who did not share in his gentle and good spirit." It is also found in Ambrose’s commentary on Luke ("fire from heaven? Jesus answered: You know not," etc. The words **"as also Elijah did"** are thus omitted here). Furthermore, Clement [of Alexandria] as witnessed by Macarius Chrysocephalus seems to recognize it. See Clement's fragment in Macarius, oration 8 on Matthew chapter 8, etc. However, it seems doubtful to me whether the final words of that passage are actually excerpted from Clement: "And for this reason the Lord spoke to the apostles when they suggested punishing with fire those who did not receive them, following Elijah's example: 'You do not know,' he says, 'of what spirit you are.'"

**56. And they went** etc. <note>original: "και επορευθ."</note>. The words **"for the [Son of Man]"** etc. are not placed before this in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (א), <term>Vaticanus</term> (B), <term>Alexandrinus</term> (A), and many other major <term>uncials</term> <note>manuscripts written in all capital letters</note>, nor in various Latin and Coptic versions, or the works of Basil ... the <term>Received Text</term> (ς) adds **"For the Son of Man did not come to destroy the souls of men but to save them"** <note>original: "ο γαρ υιος του ανθρωπου ουκ ηλθε ψυχας ανθρωπων απολεσαι αλλα σωσαι"</note> (cf. similar sayings in Luke 19:10 and Matthew 18:11) with various manuscripts (F, K, M, U, Γ, Λ, Π), Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Armenian, Gothic, and Ethiopic versions, as well as Cyprian (in his 64th letter) and Ambrose. As for the words **"as also Elijah did"**, I would hardly say anyone deleted them to excuse the apostles; it is quite clear why someone might add them. Indeed, the same interpolator is responsible for the words following **"having turned, he rebuked them,"** by which that "rebuke" is not made harsher but is softened. Finally, it is highly significant that the third addition, **"For the Son [of Man]"** etc., must derive from the same hand and cannot be considered counterfeit on its own; for it fits the argument and its authority is closely tied to the previous phrases in question. It cannot be doubted that by the second century, this entire interpolation was commonly circulated in manuscripts, as shown by the authority of the witnesses, especially the Latin and Syriac ones. | **And they went** <note>original: "και επορευθησαν"</note> (manuscript 71 and a few others read "went" in a different form) **to another village** <note>original: "εις ετερ. κωμην"</note> (manuscript Λ reads "city," then corrected it to "village"): omitted by the original scribe of Λ and a few others.

**57. And** <note>original: "και"</note> (Griesbach marks this as likely an addition) according to <term>Codices</term> Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), and others, as well as Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. <term>Codex Bezae</term> (D) and others read **"And it happened"** <note>original: "και εγενετο"</note> ... the <term>Received Text</term> (ς) and Lachmann read **"And it happened"** <note>original: "εγενετο δε"</note> with Codices Alexandrinus (A), Cyprius (K), and many others, as well as the Vulgate and Gothic versions. One manuscript gives the beginning of the reading as: **"At that time it happened, as Jesus was going,"** which is also found in the margins of manuscript M <note>indicating it was used for church readings</note> (cf. note at Luke 8:42) | **as they were going** <note>original: "πορευομενων"</note> (Manuscript E reads "as he was going" but keeps "them") **they...**

<summary>This page analyzes the textual variants of Luke 9:56-57, specifically debating whether Jesus's famous rebuke "You do not know of what spirit you are" was part of the original Gospel or a later addition by scribes. The author concludes that while these famous lines appear in many ancient translations and early church writings, they are likely early interpolations not found in the oldest Greek manuscripts.</summary>

> 3. **behold**: found without the word **I** in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and some Old Latin: the <term>Received Text</term> adds **I** (**behold, I send**) matching the phrasing in Matthew | **lambs**: some manuscripts read **sheep** (likely changed by ancient scribes to match the wording in Matthew) | **in the midst**: some manuscripts use a slightly different Greek spelling for the prepositional phrase.

> 4. **Carry**: one manuscript uses a different verb tense | **money bag**: the major manuscripts use the spelling *ballantion*: the <term>Received Text</term> uses *balantion* with one "l" | **nor (second instance)**: some manuscripts and the Vulgate use a slightly different negative particle (*mēte* instead of *mē*) | **nor (third instance)**: found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others: the <term>Received Text</term> and others use a stronger negative (*mēde*): Clement of Alexandria reads **sandal** (singular) | **no one**: found in Sinaiticus: Tertullian, writing *Against Marcion* 4, 24, quotes it as: "greet no one, he said, on the road." He could have omitted the "and," but he often quotes such passages together.

...woe to you, Bethsaida; because if in Tyre and Sidon the miracles <note>original: "δυνάμεις" - literally "powers," a common term for miracles in the New Testament</note> that were performed in you had occurred, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. 14 But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you. 15 And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades <note>The realm of the dead</note>. 16 <gloss>Section 116. 1</gloss> He who hears you <margin>Matthew 10, 40; John 13, 20</margin>

**[Textual Commentary and Manuscript Variants]**

Regarding the name **Chorazin** <note>original: "χοραζιν"</note>: the Gothic version, the Textus Receptus <note>The "Received Text" used for the King James Bible</note>, and editors Griesbach, Scholz, and Lachmann read "Chorazin" with <term>Codices U and Δ</term> and many others, including Coptic versions. The Textus Receptus also uses the spelling **Chōrazin** <note>original: "χώραζιν"</note> with manuscripts 127, 157, and many others, as well as the Sahidic Coptic and Peter of Alexandria (this is also in the 1779 edition by Caesarius, which we used for Matthew, though it is unclear if it depends on Matthew or Luke here). <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> reads "Chorozain," as do several Old Latin versions (a, b, f) and the Vulgate; others (d, i, l, q) read "Chorozain" or "Corazain." ... Manuscript 'e' reads **Capernaum**. | **Bethsaida**: the spelling varies; manuscripts C, f, i, and the Vulgate use "Bethsaida." <term>Codex Vaticanus (B)</term> originally had "Beths.," <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> "Bedsaida," and various Latin versions use "Bedsaida" or "Betsaida." Most manuscripts (A, B, C, D, L, etc.) end the name with "-da," while several others (1, 28, 69, etc.) use **Bethsaidan**, a form we restored in the Gospel of Matthew. | **were performed**: the word <note>original: "εγενηθησαν"</note> is found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus (א)</term>, Vaticanus, and others, while the Textus Receptus and most other manuscripts use a slightly different form <note>original: "εγενοντο"</note>. | **in sackcloth and ashes**: in the phrase "in cinere et cilicio" <note>Latin for "in ashes and haircloth"</note>, <term>Codex F</term> omits "and ashes." | **sitting**: the masculine form <note>original: "καθημενοι"</note> is found in the oldest manuscripts (א, A, B, C, F, L, etc.); however, the Textus Receptus and a vast majority of later manuscripts use the feminine form <note>original: "καθημεναι"</note>. Manuscripts 68, 108, and some Syriac versions omit this, similar to the parallel passage in Matthew.

**14. in the judgment**: (found in the Vulgate and several Greek manuscripts). Manuscripts 13, 69, and 346, along with the Gothic and Syriac versions, read **in the day of judgment** <note>original: "εν ημερα κρισεως"</note>. <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> and others omit the phrase. | **than for you**: <term>Codex L</term> omits "than," while <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> reads "than for us."

**15. Capernaum**: spelled "Capharnaum" in the oldest Greek manuscripts (א, B, C, D) and most Latin versions. The Textus Receptus and later manuscripts (A, L, etc.) use the more common "Capernaum." | **will [you] be exalted**: the phrasing here is debated. The oldest manuscripts (א, B, D, L) and early Latin and Syriac versions suggest a question: "Will you be exalted?" <note>original: "μη... υψωθηση"</note>. However, the Textus Receptus and many others (A, C, R, etc.) read it as a statement: "You who were exalted to heaven" <note>original: "η... υψωθεισα"</note>. Note that in <term>Codex Vaticanus (B)</term>, the scribe initially made an error but corrected it. | **heaven**: most ancient manuscripts (א, B, C, D) omit the definite article "the," while later ones add it. | **Hades**: similar to "heaven," the oldest manuscripts omit the definite article "the." | **will be brought down**: the verb <note>original: "καταβιβασθηση"</note> is found in almost all major Greek and Latin manuscripts. However, <term>Codices Vaticanus (B) and Bezae (D)</term>, along with the Syriac and Ethiopic versions, use a word meaning **will go down** <note>original: "καταβηση"</note>. This matches the reading we published for Matthew. If "will go down" is to be accepted in either place, it is undoubtedly more certain in Matthew.

**16. he who hears you**: <term>Codex Alexandrinus (A)</term> and several others, including the Vulgate and Syriac, reverse the order to "of you he who hears." An early correction in Codex A even reads "he who hears me [hears] you."

**[Critical Apparatus: Manuscript Variants]**

16. **hears**: Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> (page 81) adds *and him who sent me*; the manuscript w<sup>a</sup>, the interpolated letters of Ignatius, and Cyprian (page 122) add: *and he who hears me hears* (Ignatius reads *does not hear me but*) *the one who sent me* (Ignatius adds *the Father*). | **and he who rejects you**: the Old Latin <note>Early Latin translations prior to the Vulgate</note> (except manuscript 'a'), the Vulgate: *and he who despises you*... the interpolated Ignatius, the Apostolic Constitutions (2, 20, 1), and Eusebius read: *he who rejects you*. | **rejects me**: Manuscript Δ reads *me* <note>original: "με"</note>; manuscripts 'a' and 'b' add *and him who sent me*. | **and he who [rejects me]**: Manuscripts L and Ξ, Apostolic Constitutions, and likewise Eusebius (page 484) read: *He said to his disciples: he who rejects you rejects me, and you are not wronged; and he who rejects me, rejects me* (manuscript w<sup>a</sup> reads *rejects me*), *rejects the one who sent* (Ignatius: *the one having sent*) *me and*. Manuscripts c, f, m, q, the Vulgate, Eusebius, the Latin translation of Origen (4, 625), and Cyprian (page 81) read: *nothing except "and him who sent me"* (similarly therefore to manuscripts 'a' and 'b', except that these have other additions... Manuscripts D, a, b, and i read: *and he who hears me hears the one who sent me*... The margin of manuscript E, manuscripts 13, 124, 346, the Curetonian Syriac, the Peshitta, and the Harclean Syriac, the Armenian, and the Ethiopic furthermore add: *and he who hears me* (manuscript Σ: *hears me*) *hears the one who sent me*. Compare also Justin Martyr (Apology 1, 63): *as our Lord himself said: he who hears me hears the one who sent me*; and (Apology 1, 16): *for whoever hears me and does what I say, hears the one who sent me*. Likewise the Apostolic Constitutions (8, 46, 1, the same in Hippolytus page 85 and Lagarde): *For he who hears you, says the Lord, hears me, and he who hears me hears the one who sent me; and he who rejects you rejects me, and he who rejects me rejects the one who sent me.*

17. **the seventy**: <note>A famous textual variant: did Jesus send 70 or 72 disciples?</note> See the note at 10, 1. To those witnesses are added in this place manuscripts m, w<sup>a</sup>, i, and the Curetonian Syriac... Manuscripts B, D, a, c, e, g, l, the Vulgate, the margin of the Peshitta, the Armenian, and the Persian versions add **two** <note>original: "δυο"</note> (manuscript 'a' also reads *two*); hence editor Lachmann brackets [two]. <note>The following notes are part of a "critical apparatus," where scholars compare different ancient versions of the Bible to find the original wording.</note>

All these things rather depend on the Gospel of Matthew <note>original: "a Mt pendere"</note>. Furthermore, in the Latin translation of Irenaeus [it reads] *I confess*: Epiphanius in his work against Marcion (313 and 329) reads **I give thanks to you** <note>original: "ευχαριστω σοι"</note> (also in the Refutation 22: **He gives thanks to the Lord of heaven** <note>original: "ευχαριστει κυριω του ουρανου"</note>), likewise Tertullian in his work against Marcion (4, 25) reads *I give thanks and I confess*. Compare Origen (1, 221): "The voice of our Lord saying 'I confess to you' is an example of thanksgiving... to infants; for 'I confess' is the same as 'I give thanks'." | **Father, Lord** <note>original: "πατερ κυριε"</note> (also found in the Marcosians <note>a Gnostic group</note> and Origen in the places mentioned, likewise Eusebius (704) whom the final words prove to have drawn from Luke: **who the son is, who the father is**): [Found in manuscripts] c, e, ff², i, and the Forojuliensis (but not in the Amiatinus, Sangallensis, or Toletanus) as *Lord Father*; Clement (117) has *Father, God*... manuscript f, Epiphanius (against Marcion 313 and 329), and Tertullian (against Marcion 4, 25) omit **Father** (Epiphanius (329) says "it did not even have 'Father.' But he is refuted, for further down it had: 'Yes, Father.' Likewise in Refutation 22: 'Even if you ignore the word Father so that you do not show him to be his Father, Marcion, etc., having forgotten, O Marcion, the phrase 'Yes, Father'") | **of heaven** <note>The Marcosians read "of the heavens"</note> **and of the earth**: Epiphanius and Tertullian omit **and of the earth** | **wise and understanding**: Manuscript D reverses this to *understanding and wise*; manuscript e reads only *by the wise* | **yes, Father**: The Marcosians read *O, my Father* | manuscript wᵃ reads *so* | **was the good pleasure** <note>original: "εγενετ. ευδοκια"</note> [found in] Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others, as well as the Gothic, Coptic, and all Syriac versions... [Editors] Lachmann and Tischendorf read **the good pleasure was** <note>original: "ευδοκ. εγεν."</note> based on Codices Vaticanus and Regius. It is difficult to say whether Matthew or Luke wrote it this way. We published "the good pleasure was" in Matthew; therefore, "was the good pleasure" was preferable in Luke. Compare also the *Clementine Homilies* (8, 6): "Our Lord himself says: I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise elders and revealed them to **nursing infants** <note>original: "νηπιοις θηλαζουσιν"</note>." Likewise (18, 15): "And Simon said: Accuse your teacher for saying: I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, that those things which were hidden from the wise, you revealed to nursing infants. And Peter said: The word was not spoken that way... for our Lord did not actually say 'those things which were hidden,' but rather 'you revealed them to nursing infants.' To say 'you have hidden' implies they were once known to them... do not say he acted impiously by hiding them from the wise."

**22.** **And turning** (manuscript wᵃ reads "But turning") **to the disciples** (manuscript C² and others add **his**) **he said** (so read the editions of Stephens and Sz; and by error from Codex Vaticanus, Lachmann) with manuscripts A, C, E, G, and many others... but omitted by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. These words are missing in Matthew and no one added them; furthermore, the same words appear in the next verse (with the addition "privately," which was not introduced in our passage), which caused them to be removed here.

**22. to me were handed over** <note>original: "μοι παρεδοθη"</note> found in manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, W, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, seven other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note> and many others (and some manuscripts read "have been handed over to me" <note>original: "μοι παραδεδοται"</note>, as does Justin Martyr in *Dialogue with Trypho* 100: "And in the Gospel it is also written that he said: All things..." etc.). The Textus Receptus <note>original: "ς"; the standard Greek text used for centuries</note> reads "were handed over to me" following Griesbach and Scholz with a few minuscule <note>handwritten cursive</note> manuscripts and the Syriac (Curetonian and others), Armenian, Ethiopic, and Pseudo-Eusebius 704. | **by** <note>original: "υπο"</note>: Codex Bezae (D) reads **from** <note>original: "απο"</note>. | **of mine** <note>original: "μου"</note>: Omitted by manuscripts d, a, c, l, and the Amiatinus, Forojuliensis, and several other Latin versions; also the Armenian and Pseudo-Eusebius. (Tertullian in *Against Marcion* 4, 25 says, "He says all things were handed to him by the Father"). It is also omitted in Justin’s *Dialogue* 100 and by the Marcosians according to Irenaeus. | **knows** <note>original: "γινωσκει"</note> (also Pseudo-Eusebius): Compare with Westcott & Hort, Codex Δ, and about 25 others (and Basil, though he mixes Matthew and Luke in his writing) which read **fully knows** <note>original: "επιγινωσκει"</note>, as in Matthew (see the notes there). | **who the son is... except the father... and who the father is... except the son**: Manuscript 'a' contains only this: *who the father is except the son*. | **to whom** <note>original: "ω"</note> (manuscripts W, X, Γ, etc. read "ο"): **ever** <note>original: "εαν"</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, C, E, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Ξ, Π and most others, including Pseudo-Eusebius. Compare Methodius (mixing Luke and Matthew): "For he says, blessed are your eyes—those seeing what you see. To him who did not make me at all?" Scholarly notes observe that while Matthew mentions the Father in heaven, Luke, preaching the greater kingdom of God, remains silent about the phrase "in heaven." The majority of manuscripts (Alexandrinus, Bezae, etc.) and the Vulgate add **Our Father who is in heaven**, likely harmonizing Luke's text with the more famous version in Matthew. Origen clarifies that even if Luke’s version of the request "teach us to pray" is used, the prayer taught is to the Father, saying "Our Father who is in heaven," though he acknowledges this depends on Matthew's tradition.

# 11, 2. ACCORDING TO LUKE

-> Father, hallowed be your name; let your kingdom come. <-

**hallowed be the** <note>original Greek: ἁγιασθήτω το</note>: Manuscripts D, K, and U omit the word **the** | **your** <note>original: σου</note>: Manuscript D adds **upon us** | **let it come** <note>original: ελθατω</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus and Ephraemi Rescriptus <note>ℵC</note>... <term>Lachmann</term> reads **let it come** <note>original: ελθετω</note> with manuscripts Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius, and others (also found in the works of Origen). | **your kingdom** <note>original: η βασιλ. σου</note>: <term>Griesbach</term> reads **the kingdom of you** <note>original: σου η βασ.</note> with the Greek-Latin manuscript Bezae and manuscript 57. Furthermore, compare **Gregory of Nyssa** (in *On the Lord's Prayer*, Oration 3), where he notes regarding the phrase "let your kingdom come": "Or as the same meaning is more clearly interpreted for us by Luke, he who asks for the kingdom to come calls for the aid of the Holy Spirit. For thus it says in that Gospel: Instead of 'let your kingdom come,' it says, **'let your Holy Spirit come upon us and cleanse us.'**" (*He also confirms this later: "For Luke speaks of the Holy Spirit, while Matthew named it the kingdom," etc.*) To the testimony of Gregory is added **Maximus the Confessor** (on Matthew 6:10): "What Matthew says here as 'kingdom,' another of the Evangelists elsewhere has called the 'Holy Spirit,' saying: **'let your Holy Spirit come and cleanse us.'**" (Later: "let your kingdom come, that is, the Holy Spirit.") A trace of this same reading was sought in **Tertullian** (*Against Marcion* 4, 26), where after the words: "To whom shall I say 'Father'?" — "*To him who generated me by making and instructing me?*" — he continues: "*From whom should I ask for the Holy Spirit?*" But these words rather correspond to the phrase: **hallowed be your name**. For after intervening remarks: "*By whom is the worldly spirit not provided? Or by him by whom even the angels are made spirits, and whose Spirit in the beginning was borne over the waters?*" he continues: "*Should I hope for his kingdom to come, whom I have never heard of as the King of Glory? Or in whose hand are even the hearts of kings? Who will give me daily bread?*" It seems, therefore, that **Marcion** <note>A 2nd-century teacher often accused of altering the Gospels</note> had something similar for "hallowed be," etc., like that which was placed in Nyssa's text for "let it come," etc. | After **your kingdom**, we have omitted **your will be done**, etc., following manuscripts Vaticanus, Regius, 1, 22, 130, and the Latin manuscript 346, ff², the Vulgate (except for certain editions like the Perusinus and Harleianus), the Curetonian Syriac, Armenian, and **Origen** (who notes: "but Luke's version is thus," see above) and elsewhere (regarding "your will be done, as in heaven and on earth," he says: "Luke, having passed over these things after 'let your kingdom come,' placed 'our bread,' etc. Therefore, let us examine the words we set forth as lying only in Matthew," etc.). See also **Tertullian** (*Against Marcion* 4, 26, where after "His kingdom," he proceeds immediately to "daily bread") and **Augustine** (in the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 116): "*The Evangelist Luke, however, in the Lord’s Prayer, has included not seven but five petitions; nor does he truly disagree with Matthew, but by his very brevity he warns how those seven are to be understood. For the name of God is hallowed in the spirit, but the kingdom of God is to come in the resurrection of the flesh. Luke, showing that the third petition is in a way a repetition of the two above it, makes it understood by leaving it out. Then he adds three others: concerning daily bread, the forgiveness of sins, and the avoiding of temptation. But that which Matthew placed at the end: 'But deliver us from evil,' Luke did not include, so that we might understand it belongs to that which was said above concerning temptation.*") ... <term>Lachmann</term> adds **your will be done as** (manuscripts b, e, l omit 'as') **in heaven and on the** (omitted by some versions of Sinaiticus and others) **earth** (but Lachmann places "as in heaven and on earth" in brackets) with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Bezae, and many others.

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 11, 4.

3 **Give us each day our daily bread;** 4 **and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us; and lead us not into temptation.**

---

<note>Manuscripts</note> Toledo, Saxon, and Syriac (Schaaf edition), as well as the Peshitta, Coptic, and Ethiopic; likewise omitting "as in heaven also on earth" are the Latin manuscripts a, Harley, the Vulgate (codex Mosquensis).

**3. our** <note>original: ημων</note>: **Marcion** <note>a 2nd-century teacher often accused of altering texts</note>, as witnessed by **Origen** in the Mazarin MS catena, reads **your** <note>original: σου</note> (see Origen, Huet edition, in the final additions, p. 130: "But since the followers of Marcion have the text thus: 'Give us **your** daily bread each day,' let us challenge them—since they flee from allegory and spiritual interpretation—who is this 'bread of God'?") | **the** <note>original: τον</note> (omitted by manuscript Delta) **daily** <note>original: επιουσιον / epiousion</note>: compare **Cyril of Alexandria** (Commentary on Luke, 265): "Some say it is the bread that is to come and be given in the age to come—but if this were true—why do they add: 'Give us each day'? For through these words one can see that they make a request for daily food, clearly as those who possess nothing; 'daily' [epiousion] should be understood as 'sufficient,' etc." See also the preceding remarks there: "They turn the saying into spiritual contemplation, and indeed they say they ask for bread, not earthly, not physical, but rather that which comes down from above and out of heaven," etc. Likewise **Origen** (vol 1, p. 245): "First, one must know that the word **epiousion** is used by none of the Greeks, neither the scholars nor in the common speech of ordinary people, but it seems to have been coined by the Evangelists." He then compares it to the word **periousion** <note>meaning 'special' or 'chosen'</note> and says: "And it seems to me both words are formed from **ousia** <note>substance or essence</note>, the one signifying the bread contributing to our substance," etc. Furthermore, see the notes on Matthew | **give** <note>original: διδου / didou</note> (Manuscript G reads **giving**) also found in Origen: supported by manuscripts Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note>, Bezae <note>D</note>, 2, 28, 71, 106, 300, and more than 10 others. Cyril of Alexandria reads **give** <note>original: δοσ / dos — an alternative Greek form</note> (as in Matthew). **Origen** distinguishes them accurately: "since it does not say: 'Give us our daily bread **today**,' but 'Give us our daily bread **each day**.'" | **the** <note>original: το</note> (omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus and some Origen manuscripts) **each day** <note>original: καθ ημεραν</note> also found in several Latin and Syriac versions, the Coptic, and Origen... Manuscripts Bezae, 2, 28, 71, 106, 300, and several Latin manuscripts (a, b, c, e, f) and the Syriac read **today** <note>original: σημερον</note> (as in Matthew).

**4. the sins** <note>original: τασ αμαρτιασ</note> also in Latin manuscripts (a, f, l, q), the Vulgate, Origen frequently, Cyril, and Tertullian (Against Marcion 4, 26). **Origen** notes: "And forgive us our **debts** <note>original: οφειληματα / opheilemata</note>, as... to our debtors; or as Luke says: 'And forgive us our **sins**, for even we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us'": Manuscripts 1, 118, 209 read **the transgressions** <note>original: τα αμαρτηματα</note>... Manuscript Bezae and several Latin versions read **the debts** (following Matthew) | **for even we ourselves** <note>original: και γαρ αυτοι</note> (Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Latin a, g, Vulgate): the original hand of Sinaiticus and others read **as even they** <note>original: ως και αυτοι</note>, while **Clement** reads **for even we** <note>original: και γαρ ημεισ</note>; other Latin and Syriac manuscripts read **as even we** (following Matthew) | **we forgive** <note>original: αφιομεν / aphiomen</note> with many manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.)... others read **we forgive** <note>original: αφιεμεν / aphiemen — a different spelling</note> with manuscripts F, L, M, and others. The Coptic and Origen read **we have forgiven** <note>original: αφηκαμεν</note> (following Matthew) | **to everyone indebted to us** <note>original: παντι οφειλοντι ημιν</note>: Manuscripts L, X, 33 and 10 others add "the." Several Latin and Coptic manuscripts read **to our debtors** (following Matthew) | **into temptation** <note>original: εισ πειρασμ.</note> without any further addition <note>such as "but deliver us from evil"</note> according to manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and several others.

### 11, 5. ACCORDING TO LUKE

> 5 <gloss>124. 10</gloss> **And he said to them: Which of you shall have a friend, and will go to him at midnight and say to him: Friend, lend me three loaves, 6 since a friend of mine has arrived from a journey to me and I have nothing to set before him. 7 And that one from within answering might say: Do not cause me trouble; already the door has been closed, and my children are with me in bed; I am not able to get up and give** <note>to you</note>

---

<note>The following notes discuss the omission of "but deliver us from evil" in Luke, which is present in Matthew.</note>

Armenian version; **Origen**, volume 1, pages 227, 256, 265 (page 256: "but the phrase: 'but deliver us etc.' is kept silent <note>original: σεσιωπηται / sesiopetai</note> in Luke," and page 265: "It seems to me that Luke, through the words 'lead us not into temptation etc.', has effectively taught also the 'deliver us from the evil one.' ### ACCORDING TO LUKE 11, 11.

to you. 8 I tell you, even if he will not get up and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence <note>original: ἀναιδίαν / anaidian — literally "shamelessness" or "boldness"</note>, he will get up and give him whatever he needs. 9 <margin>9-13 Matthew 7:7-11</margin> And I say to you: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. 10 For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks, it will be opened. 11 What father among you will his son ask for bread—

---

<note>This horizontal line separates the biblical text from the apparatus criticus, which lists differences found in ancient hand-copied manuscripts.</note>

*et P aeth om* <note>The Ethiopic version and others omit "and"</note> | **into the bed** (*Latin manuscript i: "into the bed-chamber," l: "into the bed"*): Manuscripts D, 57, and several Old Latin versions (b, c, f, ff², g¹, g², m, q) as well as the Vulgate and Sahidic Coptic. Compare **Clement of Alexandria** (*Theodotus* 979): "these are the children already resting together in the bed." | **with me**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), b, l, q, and Sahidic place this after "into the bed" | **they are**: Manuscript D reads "it is" | **not**: Manuscript Sinaiticus (א) reads "and not"

**8.** **I tell you** *likewise*. Latin versions b, f, g¹, q (manuscripts a and e are missing text here). *For perus* <note>Referring to a specific edition or manuscript group</note>: c, ff², i, l, m, and the Vulgate (including manuscripts *am, em, tol*) and the Armenian version add "and" (c and Armenian use "but") "that man, if he should persevere in knocking" | **even if** (the Curetonian Syriac and Sahidic omit "even"): Manuscript D omits | **his friend** with manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), B, C, L, X, and others, as well as the Vulgate. **Origen**, **Basil**, and **Chrysostom** support this. Other manuscripts (E, F, G, H, etc.) place "friend" before "his." Manuscript D reads "him his friend." | **yet because of** (simply rendered as "on account of" in b, d, l; the Vulgate uses "yet on account of impropriety," f uses "nevertheless on account of impropriety"): Manuscript Sinaiticus (א), c, and Chrysostom read "but because of." Other Latin versions use "but on account of" or "on account of impropriety indeed." | **persistence** <note>original: ἀναιδίαν / anaidian</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), C, D, E, K, L, R, X and others. Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>19th-century biblical scholars</note> prefer the spelling *anaideian* with manuscripts A, B, F, G, H, and others. | **will give to him** also in Origen, Basil, Chrysostom, and Macarius. Manuscript D, the Syriac, and Origen (in another volume) omit "to him." | **as many as** with manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), A, B, C, K, M, R and Latin versions a, b, f, ff², i, l, m, q (which use "how many"). The Vulgate uses "as many as" or "how many." Griesbach <note>another scholar</note> reads "as much as" with manuscripts D, E, F, G, H, and others.

**9.** **given to you**: Manuscript Δ omits "to you" | **seek and you will find**: the Curetonian Syriac omits; similarly, in verse 10, the Sahidic omits "and the one seeking finds" | **you will find**: Manuscript Λ and others use a slightly different Greek verb form | **it will be opened** <note>original: ἀνοιχθήσεται / anoichthesetai</note> with manuscripts D, E, F, G, H, and others. **10.** **it will be opened** (Griesbach) with manuscripts A, E, F, G, H, and others. Other manuscripts use *anoigesetai*. Manuscripts B and D use *anoigetai* ("it is opened"). In the Gospel of Matthew, the form *anoigesetai* is firmly established; hence, there is little doubt that this form was imported from Matthew into the text of Luke.

**11.** **Which [father]** with manuscripts A, B, C, R and others, as well as several Latin versions. **Epiphanius** quotes this as: "For which father among you will a son ask for a fish, and instead of a fish will he give him a snake, or instead of an egg a scorpion?" Similarly in the *Dialogues* (if anyone, he says, among you his son shall ask for bread—or if he shall ask for a fish, will he not give him a snake... etc.). The *Clementine Homilies* seem to depend on Matthew here. Among Latin versions, f reads: "which father indeed among you if a son asks for bread," while others read "from which father among you will a son ask..." Manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), D, L, X, and the Vulgate read "Who."

### 11, 12. ACCORDING TO LUKE

...him, will he give him a stone? Or also a fish, will he give him a snake instead of a fish? **12** Or also if he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion? **13** If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

---

<note>This section provides a technical breakdown of how different ancient manuscripts record the words above. The letters (ℵ, A, B, C, etc.) refer to primary Greek codices like the Codex Sinaiticus or Codex Vaticanus.</note>

**your** [children] <note>original: υμων / hymōn</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others, including the *Dialogue against the Marcionites*, Origen, and Epiphanius... likewise the Old Latin and Vulgate... Or also**: omitted by some Old Latin versions, the Sahidic Coptic, and Origen | **will he give** (third person singular): variant spellings exist in several manuscripts | **or also** <note>original: η και / ē kai</note>: found in most major codices, though some versions like the Vulgate simply use "or," and the Standard Received Text uses "if also." | **a fish**: some versions add "if your son asks" | **not instead of** <note>original: μη αντι / mē anti</note>: found in most versions, though some omit "instead of." | **will give to him**: the word order varies between manuscript B (Vaticanus) and the Standard Received Text.

**12.** **This verse**: Manuscript 'c' places this before the "fish" section of verse 11; it is omitted by some minor Greek manuscripts | **or also**: found in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; the Standard Received Text reads "or if also" | **he will ask**: found in the majority of ancient codices, though some use a slightly different grammatical form | **an egg**: placed before "he will ask" in some manuscripts | **not**: found in almost all manuscripts except Vaticanus and the Sahidic Coptic | **will he give him a scorpion**: manuscript D (Bezae) and some Latin versions use a different word order or the word "proffer."

**13.** **being** <note>original: υπαρχοντεσ / hyparchontes</note>: with manuscripts A, B, C, and many others, as cited by Antiochus. However, manuscripts Sinaiticus, D, and others use a simpler word for **being** <note>original: οντεσ / ontes</note>, similar to the wording in the Gospel of Matthew | **gifts** <note>original: δοματα / domata</note>: placed before **good** in the oldest and most numerous manuscripts; the Standard Received Text reverses the order to **good gifts** <note>original: αγαθα δοματ. / agatha domata</note> matching the Vulgate and some citations by Clement of Alexandria. Origen uses this passage quite freely, sometimes referring to "the Father of mercies" or "good gift from heaven." | **your**: manuscript K reads "our" | **the Father**: with most major manuscripts and the Coptic and Syriac versions. Lachmann <note>A 19th-century editor</note> adds **your** [Father] to match the Gospel of Matthew, following manuscript C and others.

### ACCORDING TO LUKE 11, 15.

**14** <margin>14 following;<br/>Mt 9:32–34;<br/>12:22 following;<br/>Mk 3:22</margin> And he was casting out a demon, and it was mute; and it happened that when the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled. **15** But some of them said: By Beelzebul <note>A name used for the "prince of demons," often associated with the Philistine god Baal-Zebub.</note>...

---

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a technical record showing where ancient manuscripts differ in their wording. The symbols like ℵ (Sinaiticus) and B (Vaticanus) represent the world's oldest surviving Bibles.</note>

**your Father** <note>original: ημ.</note>) found in manuscripts b, c, i, l, q, the Vulgate, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions; also cited by Epiphanius and Cyril of Alexandria. | **the Father from heaven** <note>original: ο εξ ουρανου</note>: found in manuscripts ℵ (Sinaiticus), L, X, and others. Several Latin and Coptic versions omit the definite article "the." Epiphanius reads "the heavenly one." | **the Holy Spirit** <note>original: πνευμ. αγιον</note>: This reading is found in manuscript f and the Vulgate. However, other manuscripts (L, various Syriac versions) read **the good Spirit** <note>original: πνευμ. αγαθον</note>. Still others, including the Old Latin and citations from Ambrose, read **a good gift** <note>original: αγαθον δομα</note> (the Armenian reads "good gifts" and the Ethiopic "the good gift of the Holy Spirit"). Origen also notes that God will give "the good gift" of "complete purification" to those who ask with their whole soul.

Ambrose, in the passage cited above, writes:
> *We observe that the Holy Spirit is good by the judgment of the Lord and the testimony of the evangelists, since one (Matthew) named "good things" instead of the Holy Spirit, while the other (Luke) named the "Holy Spirit" instead of "good things"—nor is it a mistake that some manuscripts also have, according to Luke: "How much more will your Father from heaven give a good gift to those who ask him."*

**14. And he was** [casting out]: Manuscript F adds "Jesus." **And it was** [mute]: This phrase is included in many major manuscripts (A, C, R, X) and the Vulgate, but is omitted by the oldest manuscripts like ℵ (Sinaiticus), B, and L. 
The manuscript 'd' <note>Codex Bezae</note> reads: "But while he was saying these things, they brought to him a mute demoniac." The Old Latin 'c' is similar: "When he had said these things, they offered him a certain demoniac, deaf and mute. And it happened while he was casting out the demon, the man himself was mute." Manuscript 'f' reads: "But when he had said these things, they led to him a demoniac. And he cast out the demon, and it was mute." | **It happened that** [when the demon had gone out]: The word **had gone out** <note>original: εξελθοντος</note> is supported by ℵ (Sinaiticus), B, R, and others. However, the editor Lachmann <note>Ln</note> prefers **had been cast out** <note>original: εκβληθεντος</note> based on manuscripts A, C, L, and X. | **the mute man spoke and the crowds marveled**: Codex Bezae (D) reads: "and when he had cast it out, everyone marveled." The Latin versions vary slightly in whether the crowds "were stunned," "marveled," or "were in admiration."

**15. But some**: Manuscripts 'd', 'c', and the Curetonian Syriac read "And some." | **of them**: Some Old Latin versions and the Syriac add "of the Pharisees." | **said**: The editor Tischendorf <note>Ti</note> notes a spelling variant <note>ειπαν vs ειπον</note>. Though manuscript B (Vaticanus) is often cited for the "a" spelling, Tischendorf argues the physical spacing in the manuscript better fits the "o" spelling. | **Beelzebul**: This spelling <note>Βεελζεβοὺλ</note> is found in the majority of manuscripts (A, C, D, E, etc.). However, the two oldest and most important manuscripts, ℵ (Sinaiticus) and B (Vaticanus), spell it **Beezebul** <note>Βεεζεβουλ</note>.

<summary>This page records the beginning of the "Beelzebul Controversy" in Luke 11, where Jesus heals a mute man. The scholarly notes detail significant variations in ancient manuscripts regarding whether God gives the "Holy Spirit" or "good gifts."</summary>
<keywords>Luke 11, mute demoniac, Holy Spirit, good gifts, Beelzebul, Beezebul, textual variants, Ambrose, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus</keywords>

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 11, 38. 573

...therefore, [watch] lest the light that is in you be darkness. 36 If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be entirely full of light, as when the lamp illumines you with its rays.

<margin>135. 5</margin> 37 While he was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine <note>The Greek term 'aristese' refers to the first meal of the day, often translated as breakfast or a midday meal.</note> with him; so he went in and reclined at the table. 38 But the Pharisee, seeing this, was amazed that he did not first wash <note>literally: "baptize himself"</note> before the meal.

---

35. **"watch therefore" etc:** In place of these words, and omitting the following verse, manuscripts D, a, b, e, ff², and i <note>These represent the Codex Bezae and several Old Latin versions.</note> have (similar to Matthew): *if then the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness* (the Latin versions read: *si ergo lumen quod in te est tenebrae sunt, tenebrae quantae*). Augustine recognizes the same reading in his *Questions on the Gospels*. The Curetonian Syriac adds the same after verse 35. Manuscripts 57, 239, and 433 omit the verse entirely; Griesbach marks it for possible omission.

36. **This verse** (as already noted) is omitted by manuscripts D, a, b, e, ff², i, and the Curetonian Syriac; hence Griesbach marks it for omission. | **full of light** (Sinaiticus* reads: *dark*): manuscript x adds *is* | **having** according to manuscripts Sinaiticus, A, B, C, E, K, L, S, U, V, Π and many others: manuscripts G, H, M, X, Γ, Δ, and 33. use a different grammatical form [masculine instead of neuter] | **any part** according to Sinaiticus, E, H, S, U, V, Δ, Λ and many others... Lachmann and Tischendorf read **part any** following A, B, G, K, M, X, Π and about 20 others... C, L, and Γ omit **any** | **the lamp** (Sinaiticus corrected): Sinaiticus* omits | **with its rays**: manuscript b adds *in* before this | **illumines**: manuscripts E, X, Γ and a few others use a slightly different verb ending | **you**: manuscript x omits this. Manuscript q translates the whole verse as: *if therefore your body, not having a bright lamp, is dark; how much more when the lamp shines does it enlighten you.* Similarly (though corrupted), manuscript f adds at verse 36: *for if the body which is in you has no shining lamp, it is dark to you; but how much more shall your shining lamp shine for you.*

37. **While he was speaking... a Pharisee:** Manuscript D reads: *a certain Pharisee begged him that [he would dine]*. The Curetonian Syriac and Saxon versions are similar (*and a certain Pharisee begged him*). | **speaking**: Lachmann adds *him* following A, and manuscripts 1, 69, 118, 124, 131, 346 and about 10 others add *these things*. The Latin versions c, e, f, ff², g¹, i and the Vulgate read: *and when he spoke these things* (f: *these things speaking*), while the Vulgate omits *these things*; b and q read: *but in that time when he was speaking* (b adds *himself*); a reads: *but while he was speaking* | **asked** according to Sinaiticus, A, B, M, 69, 71, 248 and others (Griesbach and Scholz did not note this) and manuscript e (*requested*)... the Received Text <note>original: ς</note> and most others read *was asking* | **a Pharisee** according to Sinaiticus, B, L, 1, 13, 69, 118, 131, 157... the Received Text and Lachmann read **a certain Pharisee** following A, C, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and most other manuscripts, including the Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, and Armenian; also manuscript D, the Greek manuscript 130, and Latin versions a, c, f, ff², i, the Vulgate, and Ethiopic read *a certain Pharisee*. | **with him** (c and f read *at his house*, e reads *with him*, Vulgate reads *at his own house*): D reads *with him* [using a different preposition], as do b, d, q, while ff² and i read *with that man*, and a reads *with himself*. | **he went in and reclined**: manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 346 read: *and having entered into the house of the Pharisee, he sat down.*

38. **seeing, was amazed that** (Manuscript 300 and a few others place *amazed* after *seeing*; also f, the Peshitta and Philoxenian Syriac, and Coptic): Manuscript D, 251, most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, and the Latin of 130 read: **he began to debate within himself saying why** (251: *that*), manuscript d reads: *he began to think in himself saying why*, b, ff², i, q, and the Vulgate read: *he began to think/ponder within himself saying why*, c: *he began to dispute with himself saying why*, e: *he began to ponder at his house saying why*, a: *he began to reconsider within himself saying why*. Similarly, the Curetonian Syriac: *he began to say in himself why*. Compare also Tertullian's *Against Marcion* (4, 27): *The Pharisee who had invited him to dinner was considering within himself why he had not been dipped <note>Latin: "tinctus," implying a ritual bath</note> before reclining.*

39. **the Lord:** Manuscripts including the cursive 'u' and others, as well as the Peshitta Syriac, read *Jesus* (the Ethiopic reads *Lord Jesus*). | **the Pharisees:** Manuscript D and the Old Latin 'b' add *hypocrites*. | **the** [before dish]: Manuscript Λ reads *of the*. | **but the inside:** Manuscripts 'u' and 'y' read *but those inside*.

41. **the things within** (Manuscript L reads *the things being*): The Old Latin manuscripts 'b', 'd', and 'q' read *the things which are*; the Vulgate reads *that which remains*; the Old Latin 'f' reads *from these things which you have*; Tertullian reads *what you have*. | **all things:** Manuscripts L, X, Γ, and others read *every thing*. | **are for you:** Manuscript 'b', 'f', and the Vulgate read *are to you* (manuscript 'c' reads *to you all things are clean*; 'e' reads *to you clean all things*).
