->### 11, 49. ACCORDING TO LUKE<-

...of yours, because they indeed killed them, and you build [their tombs].
<margin>49 141.5 Matthew 23:34–36</margin> **49** For this reason also the Wisdom of God said: "I will send to them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute," **50** so that the blood of all the prophets shed from the foundation of the world may be required of this generation,
<margin>Genesis 4:8; 2 Chronicles 24:21</margin> **51** from the blood of Abel <note>Abel is presented here as the first martyr of the Hebrew Bible</note> to the blood of Zechariah <note>referring to Zechariah son of Jehoiada, whose death in the Temple court is recorded in 2 Chronicles</note> who perished between the altar and the sanctuary; yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
<margin>52 142.5 Matthew 23:13</margin> **52** Woe to you experts in the law <term>legal experts: 'nomikoi', scholars of the Mosaic Law</term>, for you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered.

---

**48.** **to consent** (from "and it does not please you" <note>original Latin: "e non placere vobis"</note>), likewise manuscripts a, b, q, and Lucifer of Cagliari <note>original Latin: "Lcif"</note> (in the same place) **not consenting**... manuscripts 57, 61, 69, 124, the Vulgate, and Armenian: **that you consent** | **that they etc.**: Curetonian Syriac: **and you are the sons of those murderers**; compare Matthew | **you build** (from "you boast" <note>original Latin: "e gloriamini"</note>) with manuscripts ℵ, B, D, L, a, b, e, i, l ... the Received Text <note>symbolized by ς</note> (but Griesbach <note>Gb</note> marks as doubtful) adds **their tombs**, Lachmann <note>Ln</note> puts **[their tombs]** in brackets with A, C, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 other uncials, and almost all others, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic; likewise manuscripts 1, 131, 157, 209, and Chrysostom (volume 7, page 806), and Lucifer: **their graves** (Chrysostom uses a different Greek word for **graves**); likewise 13, 69, 124, 346 place **their graves** before **you build**.

**49.** **and** (omitted by A, Curetonian Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian) **the Wisdom of God** (omitted by the Peshitta Syriac edition) **said**: omitted by D, b, and Lucifer | **I will send** (manuscript X: I will send): D, b, q, and Lucifer read **I am sending** | **and from [them]**: A, K, U, Π, and 10 others, as well as the Curetonian and both Syriac versions, omit **and** | **they will kill**: manuscript ℵ* <note>the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus</note> reads **they are killing** | **they will persecute** (manuscript 69 reads **they will drive out**) with A, D, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 other uncials, and most others (this specific word is found only here and in 1 Thessalonians 2:15) ... ℵ, B, C, L, X, and 12 others read **they will pursue**; compare Matthew. Furthermore, Marcion <note>as recorded by Epiphanius and Tertullian</note> omits verses 49 through 51. (Epiphanius on Marcion 313 and 333: "He did not have: 'Therefore the wisdom of God said, I will send to them prophets,' and concerning the blood of Zechariah and Abel and the prophets, 'that it will be required of this generation.'")

**50.** **it may be required**: ℵ (corrected), L, and 5 others, and the margin of the Philoxenian Syriac read **it may be avenged** | **the blood of all** (omitted by 258, 2pe, and others; Lachmann omits; Δ omits the following word): Lucifer reads **all blood** | **shed** <note>original Greek: "εκχυννομενον"</note> with ℵ, A, C, D, E, G, L, U, Λ, Π, and others ... the Received Text reads a variant spelling with one 'n' with H, K, M, S, V, X, Γ, Δ, and many others ... B, 33, 69 read **having been shed** | **from** second occurrence (thus f, Vulgate; e omits **from this generation**, likewise 69 leaves a blank space): D, a, b, c, i, l, q, Curetonian Syriac, and Lucifer read **until** (Schulz says "not ineptly"), manuscript dscr reads **up to**.

**51.** **from** without the article "the" (Griesbach indicates) with ℵ, B, C, D, L, X, 1, 33 ... the Received Text adds **the** (following Matthew) with A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 other uncials, and most others | **Abel** (also Lucifer): K, M, Π, and about 30 others, and many Syriac versions add **the righteous** (following Matthew) | **until** without the article "the" with ℵ, B, D, L, X, 1, 33 ... the Received Text adds **the** (following Matthew) with A, C, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 other uncials, and most others | **Zechariah** (also Lucifer): D, 73, 251, Coptic, and Curetonian Syriac add **son of Barachiah** (following Matthew) | **who perished between** (also Lucifer): D, a, and Ethiopic read **whom they murdered in the middle of** (compare Matthew) | **sanctuary** <note>original: "οικου", literally house</note> (most old Latin and Lucifer read **shrine**): D and 2 others read **temple** | **yes**: manuscript Γ and a few others read **and** | **I tell you**: 69, 124, e, and both Syriac versions add **that**.

Manuscripts a, b, c, e, q, the Curetonian Syriac, and Armenian: **you hid** (Latin b, e, q: *absconditis* <note>meaning "you have hidden"</note>), Ethiopic: **you took and you hid**. | **the key**: Codex Bezae (D): **the keys**. | **themselves** (found in Latin e, f, the Vulgate, and Origen in two places): Codex Bezae, manuscripts 22, 69, 124, 157, 346, Latin a, b, c, i, l, q, Ethiopic, the Latin translation of Origen, and Ambrose: **and themselves**; manuscript M and 5 others: **for themselves**. | **you entered** (Griesbach's preferred reading) with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus (corrected), Ephraemi Rescriptus (corrected), Bezae, and others... The Textus Receptus: **you have entered** (Manuscript Delta: **you came upon**) with several later manuscripts and Origen. | **those entering** (also in Origen): Codex Bezae: **those going in**. | **you hindered**: manuscript G and Latin c (which also has "you enter"), and Armenian: **you are hindering**.

**53.** **and as he was going out from there** with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Codex Zacynthius, manuscript 33, Coptic, and the Peshitta Syriac marginal note... manuscript 69 has nothing but **and**... The Textus Receptus and Lachmann: **While he was saying these things** (manuscript 48 adds "Jesus", Codex Bezae and a few others omit "these things", manuscript 13 adds "all these things") **to them** with Alexandrinus, Codex Cyprius, and many others, the Vulgate, and various Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. But Codex Bezae, Codex Zacynthius, and manuscript 157 have a gap here; Latin a, b, c, e, f, i, l, q, the Curetonian Syriac, and Ethiopic add **before all the people** (Latin i: "in the presence of the crowd"), and manuscript 254 with Armenian add further: **they were put to shame, and**. Similarly, the Peshitta Syriac marginal note: **he said these things to them before all the people, and they were put to shame; and**. | **the scribes and** (manuscript 243 omits this) **the Pharisees**: Codex Bezae and several Latin versions: **the Pharisees and the lawyers**, Latin a: **both scribes and also doctors of the law**, manuscripts 1, 118, 239, and the Peshitta Syriac marginal note: **the lawyers and the Pharisees**. | **to press hard** (manuscripts 1, 131, and 5 others add "him") with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and many others... manuscript c: **to hold against**, manuscript H and 30 others: **to hold together**, others: **to endure**, **to rebuke**, or simply **to have**. Latin versions: **to regard him severely** (c, e, i), **to regard him badly** (b, d, q), **to bear it heavily** (l), **to insist severely** (Vulgate), **to behave badly** (a), **to be saddened** (f). The Harklean Syriac: **to bear it with difficulty** (adding "and they were angry"); the Curetonian Syriac: **began to be borne with difficulty by the scribes and Pharisees**; the Peshitta Syriac: **to oppose him**. | **to provoke him to speak** <term>apostomatizein: literally "to speak from the mouth," here meaning to interrogate or trap into speaking</term> (some manuscripts read "to silence" or "to muzzle"), the Vulgate: **to overwhelm his mouth**, Latin a: **to threaten him**: Codex Bezae and 69: **to dispute with him**, Latin b, d, i, l, q: **to engage with him**, Latin c and e: **to confer with him**, Latin f: **to argue with him**. | **about many things** (manuscripts 157 and Latin f connect this with what follows): omitted in manuscripts 17, 115, 258, 433.

**54.** **lying in wait** without any addition with Sinaiticus, Codex Zacynthius, and the Coptic: The Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **him** with Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and many others, the Vulgate, and Syriac... Codex Bezae and most Old Latin versions omit it entirely. Furthermore, we have written this without "and seeking" or "seeking" following Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others... Griesbach, Scholz, and Lachmann add **seeking** with Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, and others, while the Textus Receptus adds **and seeking** with the Vulgate and others. | **to catch something out of his mouth** (Latin f: "to take something out of his mouth," Vulgate: "to catch something [various manuscripts: some thing] from his mouth"): Codex Bezae: **to find some opportunity against him**, similarly the Old Latin versions: **to find some occasion** (a, b, e, q) **from** (a: "from," i: "in") **him** (c, e, l omit "from him"), likewise the Curetonian Syriac... all these were marked as doubtful by Griesbach. After **his mouth**, we have added nothing, following Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Coptic.

## XII.

<margin>Matthew 16, 6</margin> 1. In these circumstances, when the crowds had gathered by the tens of thousands, so that they trampled one another, he began to speak to his disciples first: <margin>144.2</margin> "Watch yourselves for the <term>leaven<note>A metaphor for a small influence that spreads through and transforms a whole batch of dough; here, Jesus uses it to describe the spreading influence of Pharisaic hypocrisy.</note></term> of the Pharisees, which <margin>8, 17 Mark 4, 22 Matthew 10, 26 ff</margin> is hypocrisy. 2 <margin>145.5</margin> For nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, and nothing is hidden that will not be known. 3 Therefore, whatever you said in the darkness will be heard in the light, and what you spoke into the ear in the inner rooms will be proclaimed upon the rooftops. <margin>4—9 Matthew 10, 28—33</margin> 4 And I say to you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill—

<note>The following section contains technical notes regarding variations found in ancient manuscripts of the New Testament.</note>

Ethiopic ... [end of verse 54] (but Griesbach's second edition notes) Lachmann adds **so that they might accuse** (Manuscripts A, X, Delta, and 69: **they will accuse**) **him** along with Manuscripts A, C, D, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, almost all uncials, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, the Peshitta Syriac, and the Armenian; likewise Manuscript D, f, and the Curetonian Syriac: **so that they might find [occasion] to accuse him** <note>Latin f: *ut occasionem invenirent accusare eum*</note> :: compare Matthew 12, 10 and Mark 3, 2.

**Chapter XII. 1.** **In these circumstances... of the crowd**: Manuscript d: **while many crowds were standing around in a circle**, likewise most Old Latin and Vulgate: **with many crowds standing around**; d: **with many crowds of those standing around**; e: **when a large crowd had surrounded him**; a: **a large crowd... containing themselves in the circuit?**; the Philoxenian Syriac margin: **with many tens of thousands gathered in a circle** | **so that they trampled one another** (Old Latin and Vulgate: **that they trampled each other** <note>Latin: *ut se invicem conculcarent*</note>): Manuscript d: **so that they suffocated each other** <note>Greek: *ὥστε ἀλλήλους συνπνίγειν*; Latin d: *ut alterutros suffocarent*</note> | **he began**: Gamma and 69 add **but** | **his**: Manuscript D, a, i, l, q omit this word | **first**: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and many others connect this word with the preceding phrase [i.e., "he said to his disciples first"]; but Manuscripts G, L, Delta, and many others, along with versions c, f, i, l, q, and the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, connect it with what follows [i.e., "first of all, watch yourselves"]; manuscripts B, M, U, Gamma, and others, as well as versions a and e, have no punctuation before or after it; manuscript b and the Vulgate omit it; likewise Tertullian (*Against Marcion* 4, 28: "Beware, he said to the disciples, of the leaven of the Pharisees" etc.) and Lucifer of Cagliari | **yourselves** (Manuscript L and a few others: **them**)... manuscripts 253, 435, and Epiphanius (where he says: "Watch out for") omit this | **of the Pharisees**: (also Epiphanius, Tertullian, and Lucifer): Manuscripts B, L, and version e place this after **hypocrisy**.

**2.** **But**: found in Manuscripts A, B, C, L, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, almost all uncials, b, c, e, f, i, l, q, Coptic, and Syriac... Manuscript D, a, Curetonian Syriac, and Armenian have **for**... **4.** **my [friends]**: (also Origen, Epiphanius's quotes of Marcion, and Tertullian, though the latter says "to my [friends]").

Furthermore, 225, 245, **a, e,** Coptic, **Curetonian Syriac, Epiphanius, Tertullian,** and **Lucifer** place the word **not** <note>original: ουκ (ouk)</note> before the phrase *against the [Spirit]*; **G, Lambda,** and others (including Latin **a, b, ff², i, l, q**) and **Epiphanius** add *to him*; likewise **D, c, e,** and the **Ethiopic** (and **Lucifer**) add *to him neither in this age nor in the one to come* (:: *from Matthew*)

<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 12, 15.</header>

Whenever they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not worry how or what you will say in your defense, or what you should say; 12 for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what it is necessary to say.
13 And someone from the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” 14 But he said to him, “Man, who appointed me a judge or an arbitrator over you?” 15 And he said to them, “See and guard yourselves from all—

---

11. **bring in** <note>original: εισφερωσιν (eispherōsin)</note>: Scholars like Schulz mark this as "good." It is found in the major manuscripts **Sinaiticus (א)**, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Leopoldinus (L)**, and others, as well as the **Vulgate** (using the word *inducent*, "they will lead in"). In contrast, the **Received Text** and editor **Lachmann** use **bring before** <note>original: προσφερωσιν (prosphpherōsin)</note> based on manuscript **Alexandrinus (A)** and most later Greek manuscripts. | **upon** <note>original: επι (epi)</note>: Found in most manuscripts; however, some (like **Sinaiticus** and the **Clementine** edition) use **into** <note>original: εις (eis)</note>. It appears that scribes who preferred the word "into" changed the preposition to match, while those who preferred "upon" substituted "bring before." | **do not worry** <note>original: μεριμνησητε (merimnēsēte)</note>: Supported by the oldest manuscripts. The **Received Text** uses **do not be anxious** <note>original: μεριμνατε (merimnate)</note>. This reflects a parallel with the Gospel of Matthew, whereas the wording in Mark is slightly different (**pre-meditate**). | **how or what** <note>original: πως η τι (pōs ē ti)</note>: Found in almost all witnesses. However, **Codex Bezae (D)** and several Old Latin versions omit "or what." The **Sahidic Coptic** version rearranges it to "what you say, [and] how you defend."

12. **will teach**: A few manuscripts use a slightly different grammatical form of the same verb. | **in that very hour**: Omitted by some early fathers like **Clement** and **Origen**, perhaps for brevity, but present in the major ancient Bibles and **Tertullian**.

13. **to him** <note>original: αυτω (autō)</note>: Placed after "from the crowd" in **Sinaiticus** and **Vaticanus**, but placed before "from" in most other manuscripts. The **Curetonian Syriac** version expands the request to "the land and the inheritance."

14. **judge** <note>original: κριτην (kritēn)</note>: Supported by the oldest Greek manuscripts and the **Sahidic Coptic**. The **Received Text** uses **magistrate/arbitrator** <note>original: δικαστην (dikastēn)</note>. It is highly likely that this later reading "flowed" into the text from the Book of Acts 7:27 (quoting Exodus 2:14), where the same phrase "Who appointed you a ruler and a judge over us?" appears. | **over you** <note>original: εφ υμας (eph hymas)</note>: Most read "over you" (plural), though the original hand of **Sinaiticus** wrote "over us."

15. **to them**: The **Syriac** versions specify "to the crowds" or "to the disciples." | **and guard yourselves**: Omitted by some Syriac and Coptic versions.

**Verse 15.** (unless you give your heart): **Manuscript 157** reads "guard yourselves." | **from all** <note>original: πασησ (pasēs)</note> (Supported by Griesbach's second edition) with manuscripts **Sinaiticus (א)**, **Alexandrinus (A)**, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Bezae (D)**, **Cyprius (K)**, **Regius (L)**, **Monacensis (M)**, **Borgianus (Q)**, **Rossanensis (R)**, **Zacynthius (Ξ)**, **Freer (W)**, **Π**, and about 40 others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and both the Armenian and Ethiopic versions. Clement of Alexandria notes: "because one's life is not in the abundance of his possessions..." Manuscripts E, G, H, etc., read "the life to him." **Manuscript Bezae (D)** and the Curetonian Syriac omit "his." | **is** <note>original: εστιν (estin)</note>: **Manuscript Bezae (D)** and the Old Latin version place this before "the life"; other manuscripts place it before "in the abundance," and others after "his possessions." **Manuscripts R and Π** (where it was erased in both places) and **157** omit the word entirely. | **to him** <note>original: αυτω (autō)</note> is supported by **Sinaiticus (א)**, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Bezae (D)**, etc. The **Received Text** reads "his" <note>original: αυτου (autou)</note> with **Alexandrinus (A)** and many others.

Some use a double-N spelling <note>original: γεννηματα (gennēmata)</note>. The Vulgate translates this as "the things that have been born to me," while others translate it as "my fruits." However, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Regius (L)**, and **Freer (W)** read **the wheat** <note>original: τον σιτον (ton siton)</note> instead. | **my** (second instance): Found in almost all manuscripts including **Sinaiticus (א)** and **Alexandrinus (A)**. It is omitted by **Vaticanus (B)**, **Regius (L)**, and others. | **and** (Armenian adds "all") **my goods**: Supported by most manuscripts including **Sinaiticus (א)** and **Vaticanus (B)**. Matthew) Athanasius¹, 663 | *body*: Tischendorf, Westcott and Hort, and about 30 others, along with manuscript 'a', the Sahidic and Coptic (Egyptian) versions, the Peshitta Syriac, the Ethiopic version, and Clement of Alexandria page 231 (but not page 579 nor Athanasius) add **your** <note>original: "υμων"</note> (likely influenced by the similar passage in Matthew); hence Lachmann <note>A 19th-century biblical scholar.</note> includes **[your]** in brackets.

ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus, a 4th-century manuscript</note>, A, P, Q, T, W, O, I, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and the majority of others, including Latin versions f and g2, the Vulgate, Sahidic and Coptic, and the Curetonian and both Syriac versions, and the Ethiopic...

42. **And he said** <note>original: και ειπεν (kai eipen)</note> according to ℵ, B, D, L, and manuscripts 1, 13, 33, 69, 118, 124, 131, 346, and Latin l, the Coptic, and the Ethiopic... Latin manuscript i, the Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and the scholars read this without the conjunction <note>i.e., just "He said"</note>, but Latin i, the Curetonian Syriac, and the scholars add "to him"...
Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>influential 19th-century editors</note> read **But he said** <note>original: ειπ. δε (eipen de)</note> with A, P, Q, R, T, W, O, I, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight uncials, the majority of others, most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Philoxenian Syriac, and Armenian | **is** <note>original: εστιν (estin)</note> also in Origen: Manuscripts A, K, Π, and six others (four according to Scrivener) read **shall be** <note>original: εσται (estai)</note> (Irenaeus's Latin interpretation reads: "Who then will be the faithful manager, good and wise, whom the lord prefers over his family to give them food in time," which appears to be a mixture of Matthew and Luke). Referring quite freely to this are Origen and Eusebius [in his commentary on Psalm 50], who write: "As in: who is the faithful and wise steward?" | **steward** <note>original: οικονομοσ (oikonomos)</note> (supported by the corrector of ℵ): the original hand of ℵ reads **servant** <note>original: δουλοσ (doulos)</note>, as does Latin manuscript c: "who then is the faithful servant, the wise and good manager?" :: compare with the parallel in Matthew | **the wise** <note>original: ο φρονιμοσ (ho phronimos)</note> (according to Griesbach): supported by B, D, E, G, H, K, P, Q, S, T, W, O, I, X, V, Δ, Λ and many others, as well as the Sahidic, the margin of the Philoxenian Syriac, and the Ethiopic (see Latin c above; Latin e reads "prudent and good")... **and wise** <note>original: και φρονιμοσ (kai phronimos)</note> according to ℵ, A, L, M, U, X, Γ and many others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and its scholars, and the text of the Armenian and Origen. Furthermore, D, manuscript 157, and two lectionaries add **the good** <note>original: ο αγαθοσ (ho agathos)</note>, as do Latin versions c and e and the Curetonian Syriac (the Ethiopic reads "good, faithful, and prudent"); compare also the Latin of Irenaeus above | **he will set** <note>original: καταστησει (katastēsei)</note> (Manuscript L has a spelling variant, M has "he set") also in the corrector of ℵ and Origen; "he will appoint" in Latin f, i, the Vulgate, Ambrose, and Augustine... The original hand of ℵ, along with T, W, O, I, (the Sahidic?), manuscript 124, and Latin b, c, d, e, ff2, l, q, and the Vulgate read **he set** <note>original: κατεστησεν (katestēsen)</note>, meaning "he appointed" (Irenaeus's Latin translation uses "prefers," see above) :: compare with Matthew | **the** (omitted by L) **lord**: manuscripts 235, 435, and others, the Sahidic, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Origen add **his** <note>original: αυτου (autou)</note> | **of the household staff**: Manuscript D reads **the household staff** [in the accusative case]... Manuscripts 1 and 124 and Origen read **of the domestic servants**, while manuscript 131 and Origen elsewhere read **of the house** | **to** <note>original: του (tou)</note> with ℵ, A, B, P, R, T, W, O, I, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight uncials, the majority of others, Origen, and once in the Oxford Catena on 1 Corinthians... Lachmann omits this with D, L, Q, X, two lectionaries, Origen, and the Oxford Catena (note: there is similar fluctuation in the text of Matthew) | **to give** <note>original: διδοναι (didonai)</note> (supported by the corrector of ℵ; the original hand of ℵ and others read "to distribute," a few others read "to have given"): manuscript 69, a few others, and most Latin and Coptic versions, the Curetonian Syriac, and the Ethiopic add **to them**, while manuscript e, Origen, and the Oxford Catena twice add **to his fellow servants** :: compare with Matthew | **the food allowance** with ℵ, A, L, P, Q, R, T, W, O, I, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all others including the Sahidic, Coptic, and Origen... B and D and manuscript 69 omit **the**.

43. **He will find**: Manuscript D adds **him** | **doing so** with A, B, D, P, R, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, the majority of others, the Curetonian Syriac, Sahidic, Coptic, etc... ℵ, L, T, W, O, I, X, and manuscripts 33, 69, 157, 346, and several others, including the Old Latin and Vulgate, read **so doing** :: as in Matthew.

44. **Truly**: Manuscript D, a few others, and the Latin translation of manuscript 130 read **Amen** :: from Matthew; Latin version e omits **truly I say to you**.

# 590 12, 45. ACCORDING TO LUKE

[all his] possessions he will set him. 45 But if that servant says in his heart: "My master is delaying his coming," and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk; 46 the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect and at an hour when he does not know, and will cut him in two <note>original: διχοτομήσει (dichotomēsei); a severe punishment literally meaning to be cut in two, often interpreted as being scourged or separated from the master's house</note>, and will assign his place with the unfaithful. 47 And that servant who knew the will of his master and did not prepare or act according to his will shall be beaten with many [lashes];

---

44. **his** <note>original: αυτου (autou)</note>: Found in manuscripts **M, P, T**, and others. Manuscript 157 and others read **to him** <note>original: αυτω (autō)</note>. The Latin version **c** reads "what are his," and version **e** reads "what are for him."

45. **the servant**: Found in manuscripts **M, X**, and several others, including the Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic versions. Irenaeus and Origen (in his 3rd volume) read "if that evil servant grows [bold] to say..." <note>The translator notes this phrasing seems to depend on the version of this story found in the Gospel of Matthew</note>. The *Dialogue against the Marcionites* (vol. 811) says "that the master of the evil servant will come on the day etc." which also seems to follow Matthew rather than Luke. | **in his heart**: Manuscript Λ omits this "through carelessness" <note>Latin: per incuriam</note>, though it keeps the word "his." Caesarius (vol. 98) reads it freely as "but if that servant says in himself," following Matthew more than Luke in the following sections. | **my master**: Found in **Sinaiticus (ℵ)**, **Vaticanus (B)**, **Ephraemi Rescriptus (C)**, and most others. Some versions (like the 1st volume of Origen) put "master" before "my." It is noted that "my master" likely transferred here from the Gospel of Matthew. | **to come**: Manuscripts **K, M, P** and others use a different Greek word for "to come" <note>original: ελθειν (elthein) instead of ερχεσθαι (erchesthai)</note>, likely influenced by Matthew. | **to beat the servants**: Manuscript **D** simply has "to beat." Origen reads "his fellow-servants and the girls," with Syriac and Ethiopic versions adding "of his master," again following Matthew's phrasing. | **to eat etc.**: Manuscript **D** (the Greek text) uses the forms "eating and drinking and being drunk." Latin version **e** reads "eating and drinking and he shall be inebriated."

46. **of that servant**: Found in Matthew as well. Origen and Irenaeus follow this, but Manuscript **D** and the Latin version of Irenaeus (vol. 282) read "his [master]." | **unfaithful**: Found in most major sources. However, Manuscript **X** and others read **hypocrites** <note>original: υποκριτων (hypokritōn)</note>, which is the word used in Matthew. Eusebius (vol. 182) notes: "The faithful one—and the one opposite to him—receiving his lot and portion with the hypocrites or the unfaithful, whose end is weeping and gnashing [of teeth]." Origen's Latin translation (vol. 3, 879) notes that they will be placed "with hypocrites and infidels." | **will assign**: Manuscript **D**, along with Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac versions, places this verb before the phrase "with the [unfaithful]."

47. **of his master**: Found in **Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D)**, and many others. Some later editions (like Tischendorf) use a slightly different form of "his" <note>original: εαυτου (heautou) vs αυτου (autou)</note> based on later manuscripts and church fathers like Basil and Cyril. | **and not having prepared or**: The word "or" is found in **Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B)** and others. Other editors use "neither" <note>original: μηδε (mēde)</note> based on Codex Alexandrinus (A) and the Vulgate. The Sahidic version reads "not preparing or not doing." Manuscript **D**, Origen, and several others omit "prepared or," reading simply "and not having done." Irenaeus's Latin version reads "who knows the will of the master and does not do it." Cyprian and several Syriac and Old Latin versions read only "and not having prepared," omitting "or having done."

# 591 12, 52. ACCORDING TO LUKE

...prepared <note>original: ravit; likely part of "paravit"</note> (manuscript **b** reads "shall have prepared" <note>original: paraverit</note>), versions **c, e, l, q** and Cyprian read "and did not obey" <note>original: non paruerit</note> (version **c** "he obeyed") ... manuscript **g²** omits all these things | **many**: manuscript Δ, the *Dialogue against the Marcionites* (Antioch 1011 and 1055) read "much" <note>original: πολλα (polla)</note>. Likewise the *Dialogue* (volume 5, page 48) reads "few" (The Antiochian text does not add the following verse).

48 But the one who did not know, yet did things worthy of blows, shall be beaten with few [lashes]. To everyone to whom much was given, much will be sought from him, and to whom they committed much, they will ask all the more from him. 49 <gloss>160.5</gloss> I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! 50 But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is completed! <margin>51-53 Matthew 10, 34 following</margin> 51 Do you think that I came to give peace on the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. 52 For from now on there will be five in one [house]...

---

48. **but** <note>original: δε (de)</note> (the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac read "for" <note>original: enim</note>): the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (**א***) [corrected by the scribe "a"], the Coptic (Lower Egypt), and Peter of Alexandria omit this. | **was given**: Codex Bezae (**D**) reads "they gave." | **much will be sought from him**: The Greek manuscripts 1, 64, 131, 209 and others read this. The Latin Codex Bezae (**d**) reads "they will seek more from him," likewise the Latin **ff²** and the Ethiopic read "they will seek much from him." Compare also the *Pistis Sophia*: "because for everyone to whom they entrusted more, they will seek more from him." | **more**: Codex Bezae (**D**) reads "greater/more" <note>original: πλεον (pleon)</note>. | **they will ask**: Manuscripts **D, U**, and about thirty others, the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Macarius, and Basil read "they will demand" <note>original: απαιτησουσιν (apaitēsousin)</note>. Compare also Justin Martyr (*First Apology* 1, 17): "To whom God gave more, more will also be demanded from him"; Clement of Alexandria: "to whom more was given, this one will also have more demanded"; Epiphanius: "to whom more is given, they will demand more from him." Regarding the earlier part of the verse, Cyril of Alexandria (*Adoration in Spirit and Truth*) says: "for to whom they committed much, they will seek much from him."

49. **fire**: The Latin manuscripts **x, b, e, ff², g¹, l** add "Do you not know that [I came to cast fire]." | **upon** <note>original: επι (epi)</note>: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus (**א**), Vaticanus (**B**), and many others, including Clement, Origen, Archelaus, Eusebius, Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, and Cyril. Some manuscripts (including **D, E, G**) and the text of Tischendorf read **into** <note>original: εις (eis)</note>. The Latin versions and Tertullian read "in terram" (into/upon the earth). | **was kindled**: One manuscript reads "was brought up" <note>original: ανηχθη (anēchthē)</note>. See also *Pistis Sophia*.

50. **but** <note>original: δε (de)</note>: Found in most Latin and Syriac versions and Origen. It is omitted by Codex Regius (**L**) and several others, as well as the Sahidic Coptic and Ethiopic versions. | **how**: Origen (vol. 1) reads "what" <note>original: τι (ti)</note>. | **until**: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others support this reading. Some other manuscripts read "where" <note>original: ου (ou)</note>. | **is completed**: A correction in Codex Sinaiticus reads "is finished together" <note>original: συντελ (syntel.)</note>. Compare here Irenaeus (writing about the Marcosians <note>A Gnostic sect</note>): "And this is what he says: 'and I have another baptism to be baptized with, and I strongly hasten toward it.'" Also Epiphanius (writing about the Arians): "He says 'I have a cup to drink, and how I hasten until I drink it; and I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I wish it were already baptized.'"

51. **to give**: Codex Bezae (**D**) and some Syriac versions read "to make." Other Latin versions and the *Pistis Sophia* read "to send" <note>original: mittere</note>. | **but rather**: Codex Bezae and the Coptic versions read simply "but."

52. **five**: Codex Bezae and some Latin versions place this word later in the sentence. | **in one house**: Supported by Codex Sinaiticus, Bezae, and others.

# 592 12, 53. ACCORDING TO LUKE

<margin>Micah 7:6</margin> ...divided in a house, three against two and two against three. 53 They will be divided: father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.

<margin>54 — 56 Matthew 16:2 following</margin> 54 <gloss>161.5</gloss> And he said also to the crowds: "When you see a cloud rising in the west, immediately you say that a shower is coming, and it happens so; 55 and when the south wind is blowing, you say that there will be scorching heat..."

Manuscripts **L, c, e, ff², blan**, the Curetonian Syriac, and Hilary (page 659) ... the Textus Receptus <note>original: ς</note> and Tischendorf read "in one house" <note>original: εν οικω ενι</note> with Codex Sinaiticus (**א**), Codex Washingtonianus (**W**), and most other uncials and versions including the Vulgate and Syriac | **divided** <note>original: διαμεμερισμενοι</note> (Manuscripts **L, T, W** and others read a slightly different form <note>original: διαμερ.</note>): Codex Bezae (**D**) places this after "three," while version **c** and the *Pistis Sophia* omit it | Codex Sinaiticus (**א**) originally omitted "they will be" <note>original: εσοντ.</note> up to the word "divided," but it was added by a later corrector | **three to three**: Codex **H** omits this | **against** <note>original: επι</note> (used twice): Codex Bezae uses "in" <note>original: εν</note>, as do most Old Latin versions and the Vulgate (Hilary reads "in two and over three"; version **f** reads "against two and against three") | **two**: Manuscripts **L, U** and others use the form *dusin* or *dusini*.

53. **they will be divided** <note>original: διαμερισθησονται</note> according to Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and many others, including the Vulgate and Coptic versions (Manuscripts **D, L, U** place a punctuation mark after this, whereas Sinaiticus and Vaticanus do not) ... the Textus Receptus <note>original: ς</note> (placing a point after "three") reads "he/it will be divided" <note>original: διαμερισθησεται</note> (singular) with Codex Alexandrinus and most other manuscripts | **against son**: Griesbach <note>original: Gb</note> notes a variant; Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others read this ... but the Textus Receptus and Lachmann <note>original: Ln</note> read "upon son" <note>original: εφ υιω</note> with Codex Alexandrinus and others (Manuscripts 253, 259 place "against son" before "father") | **against father**: Versions **d, b, c, e, i, l, q** and Ambrose add "his" <note>original: αυτου</note> | **against daughter**: according to Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae; or **against the daughter** according to Tischendorf and others ... the Textus Receptus reads "upon daughter" <note>original: επι θυγατρι</note> | **against mother**: according to Sinaiticus and others; or **against the mother** according to Lachmann and Tischendorf with Codex Vaticanus and Bezae ... the Textus Receptus reads "upon mother" <note>original: επι μητρι</note> | **against the daughter-in-law** without adding "her": according to the original hand of Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae ... but the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add "her" <note>original: αυτησ</note> with most other manuscripts and versions | **the mother-in-law** without "her": according to the same group of early manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) ... but the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add "her" with the majority.

54. **you see**: Manuscript Λ reads a different form of "see" | **a cloud**: according to Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and others ... the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read "the cloud" <note>original: την νεφελ.</note> | **in** <note>original: επι</note>: according to Sinaiticus and Vaticanus ... the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "from" <note>original: απο</note> the west (most Latin versions read "from the setting sun" or "from the west") | **immediately**: Manuscripts 253, 259, and the Curetonian Syriac omit this | **that** <note>original: οτι</note>: present in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and most uncials and versions ... Lachmann puts it in brackets, and the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf omit it along with Codex Bezae and several Latin versions | **thus/so**: found in almost all uncials ... the Textus Receptus reads a slightly different form of the word "thus."

55. **blowing**: Codex Bezae uses a word for "sailing" or "navigating" <note>original: πλεοντα</note> by mistake | **that** <note>original: οτι</note>: present in most manuscripts ... but omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and others.

# 593 ACCORDING TO LUKE 12, 59.
### 38

...will be, and it happens. 56 Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and the sky; but why do you not interpret this time? 57 And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
<margin>162.5</margin> <margin>58 see Matthew 5, 25 following</margin> 58 For as you go with your adversary to a magistrate, make an effort on the way to be settled with him, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. 59 I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the very last <term>lepton</term> <note>A "lepton" was the smallest denomination of Greek copper coin in circulation; often translated as a "mite" or "cent."</note>.

---

**will be** <note>original: εσται</note> (Codex Bezae reads <note>original: εσεται</note>): Codex Sinaiticus <note>original: ℵ*</note> (manuscript **a** reads <note>original: εστ.</note>), manuscript 157. | **comes** | **happens**: manuscripts 69. 124. 157. 209. 254. 346. Armenian and Ethiopic versions add **thus** <note>original: ουτως</note> (69 reads -τος); likewise, Latin versions **b, c, e, f, g², i, l, q**, the Gatarianus manuscript, and others prefix this.

56. **the**: manuscripts **d, yscr**, and a few others; versions **b, q**, and the Sahidic Coptic add **indeed** <note>original: μεν; as in Matthew</note> | **of the earth and the sky**: found in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Regius, Sangallensis, and many others, including the Vulgate and Syriac versions (In Codex Sangallensis, "of the sky" was written at the start of the line before "of the earth and" was prefixed. It seems both were written by the original scribe) ... A corrected hand in Sinaiticus, along with Codices Bezae, Cyprius, Paris, and others, as well as the Vulgate and several Syriac versions and Tertullian, read **of the sky and the earth** | **but... this time**: (Codex Regius omits "but," Codex Vaticanus places "but" after "time"): Codex Bezae and 157 read **nonetheless this time**, while Latin versions **c** and **e** read **but truly that time**; version **l** reads **but the signs of the times**, and the Curetonian Syriac reads **this time and its signs** | **why**: omitted by Codex Bezae and Latin versions **c, e, i**, and the Curetonian Syriac | **not interpret**: supported by Codices Alexandrinus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and almost all others ... Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Regius, and others read **you do not know how** <note>original: ουκ οιδατε</note> **to interpret**. Additionally, manuscript **x** omits the phrase from "but" until "interpret" (it seems the scribe agreed with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus but skipped the text due to the similar ending of the words).

57. **And why**: omitted by Codex Bezae, Latin **b**, and the Curetonian Syriac.

58. **For**: omitted by manuscript 235, the Curetonian Syriac, and the Armenian version | **your**: omitted by Codex Sinaiticus | **the**: Codex Bezae reads "this" | **to be settled** <note>original: απηλλαχθαι</note> (also in Origen and Basil): Codices Alexandrinus and Sangallensis read "to be released" <note>original: απαλλαχθ.</note> ... Codex Bezae reads a different form of "to be set free" <note>original: απαλλαγηναι</note>. Compare Clement: "Walking with the adversary, try to be set free as a friend" | **from** <note>original: απ</note>: omitted by Codex Vaticanus and Basil (also Origen: "unless someone is found having made the effort to be settled with the adversary") | **drag you**: (The Vulgate reads "draw you to," but other versions read "before" instead of "to"): Codex Bezae and several Latin versions read **condemn** <note>original: κατακρεινη</note> ... other Latin versions read **hand over** (most continue with "you before the judge") :: compare Matthew (Irenaeus has the first part from Luke and the latter from Matthew, as does Origen) | **hand you over**: (Codex Bezae and 157 read "hand over you"): found in Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and others ... the Textus Receptus <note>original: ς</note> reads "might hand you over" with Codices Regius, Monacensis, and most others :: compare Matthew | **officer**: Codex Alexandrinus reads "parktori" <note>a spelling error</note>, others read "praktori" | **you**: Codex Bezae and others place this after the verb "throw" | **throw**: supported by Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others ... other editors read a different form of "might throw" <note>original: βαλη or βαλλη</note> with Codices Alexandrinus, Regius, and others; some read "is throwing," and the Old Latin reads "puts" or "might put."

59. **I tell**: Codex Regius and some Syriac versions prefix **Truly** <note>original: αμην</note> :: as in Matthew.

**7** And he spoke to those who were invited a parable, observing <note>original: ἐπέχων; literally "holding onto" or "noticing"</note> how they were choosing the places of honor <note>original: πρωτοκλισίας; the most prestigious reclining spots at a table</note>, saying to them: **8** “When you are invited by someone to wedding feasts, do not recline in the place of honor, lest one more honorable than you has been invited by him, **9** and the one who invited both you and him, coming, will say to you: ‘Give this man the place,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the last place. **10** But when you are invited, going, recline in the last place, so that when he who has invited [you] comes—

**6. and they were not able to answer back:** Manuscripts ℵ, L, 1, 131, 209, and a few others read "to answer" <note>original: αποκρίθ.</note>. Manuscript D and minuscule 47 read: "But they were silent." The Old Latin manuscript *e* reads: "but they were able to respond nothing." Furthermore, the Textus Receptus <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> and the editions of Lachmann and Tischendorf add "him" <note>original: αυτω</note> along with manuscripts A, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and most others, as well as several Latin versions (including the Vulgate), the Sahidic and Coptic, the Curetonian and other Syriac versions, the Armenian, and the Ethiopic... we did not add it, following manuscripts ℵ, B, D, L, 1, 118, 124, 131, 157, 209 (though among these, 1, 118, 131 read "before him" <note>πρ. αυτον</note> instead of "to these things" <note>πρ. ταυτ.</note>), and Old Latin manuscripts *e* and *l*.

**7. and he spoke:** Manuscripts D and *a* (and likely several others) as well as the Vulgate and Armenian versions add "and." Manuscript variants of "places of honor" <note>original: πρωτοκλησιας</note> and "recline" <note>original: κατακληθης</note> appear in manuscripts A, E, H, K, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, and others. | **observing how they were choosing the places of honor:** The Curetonian Syriac reads "and they were choosing the first reclining places." | **saying to them:** Omitted in Old Latin *e*, the Peshitta Syriac, manuscripts 1, 131, 209, and the Coptic.

**8. invited by someone:** This is the reading of Old Latin *b* and *f*, the Vulgate, and several Syriac versions. Manuscript D, Old Latin *e* ("when you all are invited"), the Vulgate, and Clement of Alexandria (writing "when you are invited to weddings, do not recline in the place of honor") omit "by someone." | **to wedding feasts:** Manuscript D and a few others read "wedding" in the singular; the Armenian adds "or to a banquet." This phrase is omitted by Old Latin *b*, the Sahidic, and a Syriac marginal note. In a homily by Antiochus, it is written: "when you are invited to a meal <note>original: αριστον</note>." | **has been invited by him:** Manuscript D reads "will come"; the Curetonian Syriac reads "will be there." Manuscript ℵ and L omit "by," while several Old Latin versions and the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic omit the entire phrase "by him."

**9. you will begin:** Manuscript Λ reads "he will begin." Manuscript D and Old Latin *e* read "you will be" (and then you will be—holding the place). | **with:** Manuscript ℵ and many others use one form <note>μετα</note>, while the Textus Receptus and others use a slightly different spelling <note>μετ</note> before a vowel. | **the:** Omitted by the original hand of Manuscript D.

**10. you are invited:** A few manuscripts read "you have been invited." | **going:** Omitted by manuscript D, Old Latin *e*, and Clement of Alexandria. | **recline:** Griesbach and Scholz use one spelling <note>αναπεσε</note> which Schulz thought was a "writing error" for another <note>αναπεσαι</note>. It is found in manuscripts ℵ, A, B, E, H, and about 100 others. Griesbach also notes another variation <note>αναπεσαι</note> in B, G, L, M, and others. The Textus Receptus uses another form <note>αναπεσον</note> found in a few minuscules. Since in the New Testament the verb "to fall" <note>πεσειν</note> and its compounds are used very often, but the middle form <note>πεσασθαι</note> is never used, the spelling "recline" <note>αναπεσαι</note> should be considered only a spelling variation from the other <note>αναπεσε</note>, just as "ai" and "e" are placed interchangeably in countless places in the most ancient manuscripts. The same reasoning applies to Luke 17:7.

This is found without the word **all** <note>original: παντα</note> in the original Sinaiticus (ℵ*), B, L, R, and several Latin versions (which read "it is now ready")... The "Received Text" and Tischendorf add **all** (making it "all things are ready"), while Lachmann puts **[all]** in brackets, found in corrected Sinaiticus (ℵᵃ), A, P, X, and many others, including the Vulgate and various Syriac and Armenian versions; D and several others place it before "ready"; Eusebius also recognizes this reading ("they were invited to the banquet that brings all things ready").

**18.** **all to excuse themselves** <note>original: παντες παραιτεισθ.</note>: This reading is found with the manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), Regius (L), Boreelianus (R), and Monacensis (X), as well as manuscript 1, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, and the Syriac Peshitta (though the Syriac Curetonian omits **all**). The "Received Text" <note>the standard printed text of the time</note> and Tischendorf's earlier editions place **excuse themselves** before **all** with manuscripts A, P, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, and eight other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, most others, the Gothic, the Harklean Syriac, and Basil of Caesarea's work *On Baptism*. | **the first** <note>original: ο πρωτοσ</note>: Manuscripts P, c, and e add "and" before this; Lachmann <note>a famous 19th-century editor</note> puts **[and]** in brackets. | **to him** <note>original: αυτω</note>: Omitted by manuscripts D, 1, 118, 209, and several Old Latin versions, the Gothic, Coptic, and Armenian versions, and Basil. | **I must** <note>original: εχω αναγκην</note>: This word order is supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus, and others. **19.** **I ask you, have me excused**: Manuscript e omits this. For he wishes this to happen through grace, as he confesses himself unworthy through his own merits. He does not add what he had said in that reflection: 'Make me like one of your hired hands.' For when he had no bread, he desired to be even a laborer; but after the father's kiss, he now most nobly disdains this."</note>... <margin>Matthew 5, 32; 19, 9; Mark 10, 11 and following</margin>
**18** $^{195. 2}$ "Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery." **19** $^{196. 10}$ "There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and..."

<note>The following notes are part of the critical apparatus, used by scholars to track variations in ancient manuscripts of the New Testament. The symbols (like א, B, D) represent specific ancient codices/books.</note>

**14. all:** Several manuscripts place this word before "these things" (seen in the Vulgate and Peshitta Syriac). Manuscripts D and others omit "all" entirely. | **the Pharisees:** Found in Codex Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and others. The Textus Receptus (indicated by ϛ) and editors like Lachmann and Tischendorf read "also the Pharisees," following Codex Alexandrinus (A) and the majority of later manuscripts. | **and:** Omitted by a few manuscripts (245, 253, etc.).

**15. to them:** Codex Γ reads "towards them." | **among humans:** Codex Vaticanus (B) reads "to a human" (singular). | **before God:** Codex Vaticanus reads "before the Lord." Others read "beside God." We have printed the text without the word "is" following the oldest manuscripts (א, A, B, etc.), though the Majority Text (ϛ) and others add "is" <note>original Greek: *estin*</note>.

**16. until:** Using the word *mechri* according to the earliest manuscripts (א, B, L, etc.). The Majority Text (ϛ) uses *heōs*, likely influenced by the parallel wording in the Gospel of Matthew. | **John:** One manuscript (sah) reads "reached until John." Codex D adds "prophesied" <note>original Greek: *eprophēteusan*</note>, again following Matthew's phrasing. | **is preached:** Manuscript Λ uses a plural form. | **and everyone is forcing their way into it:** Omitted by the first hand of Sinaiticus (א), but added by a later corrector with the addition: "and the violent seize it" (following Matthew 11).

**17. stroke of a letter:** Different spellings of the word *keraia* <note>original: *keraian*, *kerean*, or *kairean*</note> appear across manuscripts. Codex Vaticanus and others place this word before "one."

**18. commits adultery (first instance):** Some manuscripts use a different Greek verb for "commits adultery" <note>original: *moichatai* instead of *moicheuei*</note>, mirroring Matthew. | **and he who:** The Majority Text (ϛ) reads "and everyone who." | **divorced from her husband:** Omitted by Codex D and some versions. | **commits adultery (second instance):** A few manuscripts change the verb form as they did earlier. References are also found in early Christian writers like Justin Martyr (1st Apology) and Theophilus of Antioch.

**19. a man:** Some manuscripts (d, bodl) and margin notes in others add an introductory phrase: "And he spoke also another parable," or "The Lord spoke this parable."

<note>The following notes compare different ancient versions of the Bible to see how the wording changed over centuries of hand-copying.</note>

[*it is profitable* <note>original Latin: "expedit"</note>]. Furthermore, Manuscript D (Greek) adds *but* <note>original: "de"</note> | *if etc.* (following manuscripts *e, f,* and the Vulgate): Manuscripts *a, b, c, i, ff^2, l, q* read "that he should not have been born, or (manuscript *i* adds *if*) a stone etc." (Compare Matthew 26, 24). However, the <term>Received Text</term> <note>the standard printed Greek text of the era, marked ς</note> and the scholar Lachmann read "should lose" <note>subjunctive: "απολεση"</note> based on **B, D, E,** and most others. Some Greek and Gothic manuscripts use the present tense "is taken" (matching Matthew). | **will be left**: Some manuscripts use the present tense "is left" (matching Matthew).

**35.** The original hand of **ℵ**, manuscript **209**, and some Vulgate copies omit this verse entirely. | **there will be two**: This order is in **ℵ, A, B, D,** and many others. The Received Text uses "two will be." Some Latin versions omit "there will be" entirely. | **together**: (The Curetonian Syriac and Ethiopic add "at the mill"): The original hand of **ℵ** and Maximus of Turin read "in the mill" <note>original: "εν τω μυλωνι"</note>, likely influenced by the phrasing in Matthew. | **the one... the other**: There are minor variations in the Greek articles used here ("the one" vs "one") between the major manuscripts like **ℵ, B,** and the Received Text.

**36.** This verse is included in the Received Text and Scholz's edition as: "Two will be in the field; the one will be taken and the other will be left." It is found in manuscripts **D, U,** and many Latin and Syriac versions. However, we have not included it in the main text (nor did Griesbach) because it is missing from **ℵ, A, B, L, Q,** and the vast majority of ancient manuscripts. Optatus <note>a 4th-century bishop</note> notes: "Indeed, Luke the Evangelist explains concerning two in a bed and two at the mill; but the present passage of Matthew is concerning two in the field." This suggests the verse was moved from Matthew into later copies of Luke.

## XVIII.

**1** <margin>214. 10</margin> Then he spoke a parable to them about the necessity for them to always pray and not to lose heart, **2** saying, "In a certain city there was a certain judge who did not fear God and did not respect—"

"and concerning the two at the mill. For where Luke placed two in a bed, there Matthew placed two in a field. From which we are given to understand that the evangelists intended both the 'bed' and the 'field' to mean the same thing." Maximus of Turin <note>Maximus of Turin was a 5th-century bishop known for his sermons.</note> (for after he explained the words *there will be two in a bed* etc., he continues: "let us see what remains. For the divine sentence says: *There will be two women grinding in the mill-house, one taken and one left.*" He treats nothing truly beyond this.)

37. <term>and answering</term> <note>original: και αποκριθεντεσ</note> found in manuscripts **a, e, f, ff².** 1: **c, i,** and the **Vulgate** <note>the standard 4th-century Latin Bible</note> omit <term>and</term>; **b, g¹, q** read *but responding*; the **Curetonian Syriac** <note>an ancient 5th-century translation</note> omits <term>and answering</term>. | <term>they say to him</term> <note>original: λεγουσιν αυτω</note>, *they say to him* in **g¹, Vulgate**: **a, b, e, f, ff², i, l, q, mt** read *they said to him*; **c** reads *to him they said* ... —coming. **3** Now there was a widow in that city, and she kept coming to him, saying: "Vindicate me against my adversary." **4** And for a time he was unwilling; but after these things he said within himself: "Even if I neither fear God nor respect man, **5** at least because this widow causes me trouble, I will vindicate her, so that she may not wear me out by her continual coming." <note>Literally "give me a black eye," a metaphor for wearing someone down or ruining their reputation.</note> **6** And the Lord said: "Hear what the unrighteous judge says; **7** and will not God bring about the vindication of—"

3. <term>Now a widow</term> <note>original: χηρα δε</note> (found in the "Received Text," and editions by Griesbach and Scholz) supported by almost all <term>uncials</term> <note>early manuscripts written in large capital letters</note> (except for manuscript Λ), many others, the Gothic version, the Peshitta Syriac, the Ethiopic version of Basil, and writers like Chrysostom and John of Damascus ... the "Received Text" adds <term>a certain</term> <note>original: τισ</note> with manuscript Λ and many others, most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, Coptic, Curetonian Syriac, and Hippolytus’s *Treatise on Christ and Antichrist*.

From the Latin versions, **a, c, d, f, i,** and the Vulgate read *thump me* <note>original: suggillet me</note>, **e** reads *be more annoying to me*, **l** reads *cause me ill-will*; **b, ff², q** read *constrain me*. Compare Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* under the word *hypōpiazō* ("to beat someone black and blue," "to batter someone’s ears") and *hypopiezō* ("to suppress"). Also compare the Suda <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>. In the manuscripts, these three spellings are often confused. Compare also 1 Corinthians 9:27.

and the scholia <note>ancient explanatory notes found in margins</note> and the Ethiopic version read **two men** <note>original: δυο ανθρ.</note> | **the one** <note>original: ο εις</note> with manuscripts א (Sinaiticus), A, L, Q, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, most uncials <note>early capital-letter manuscripts</note>, and nearly all others, the Sahidic and Coptic versions, the Armenian version, Origen, and Basil ... **14.** **went down** <note>original: κατέβη</note> with manuscripts א (Sinaiticus), A, B, D, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, most uncials <note>early capital-letter manuscripts</note>, the Vulgate, Ethiopic, Basil, and Cyril ... Manuscripts K, Q, Π, and many others, as well as the Old Latin *a*, the Syriac Curetonian, and the Harclean versions, add **that** <note>original: οτι</note> before this word; hence Lachmann includes **[that]** | **to his house** <note>original: εις τον οικ. αυτου</note> (Manuscript B and L read **his own**): omitted by manuscript D and the Sahidic version | **rather than that one** <note>original: η γαρ εκεινοσ</note> (supported by Griesbach and Scholz) with manuscripts A, P, Q, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, and 150 others, the Gothic ("than indeed that one"), and the Peshitta Syriac (which renders it accurately). This is also the reading in Basil and Cyril ... The Textus Receptus (Stephanus, Griesbach, Scholz) reads **than that one** <note>original: η εκεινοσ</note> with many minuscules <note>later cursive manuscripts</note>, the Armenian version, and the commentaries of Theophylact ("instead of: more than that one") and Euthymius ("more than that one, namely, not that one") ... Lachmann reads **beside that one** <note>original: παρ εκεινον</note> with manuscripts א, B, L, and minuscules 1, 22, 94, 209, as well as the Sahidic and Coptic versions and Origen ("rather than him, he goes down to his house justified"). Manuscript D reads **more than** <note>original: μαλλον παρ</note> ("more besides that Pharisee," with the Syriac and Persian versions and Latin versions adding "the Pharisee"). The Latin versions read: *a* "beyond that Pharisee," the Vulgate "from that one" (some adding "more from" or "Pharisee"), while others read "more than that Pharisee" ... minuscule 157 and Basil read **than indeed that one**, while Dorotheus reads **above that one** (Note: "for than" <note>original: η γαρ</note> is spoken unusually but does not seem to be inconsistent with Greek usage; see examples of "for" <note>original: γαρ</note> used similarly in Stephanus's Thesaurus) | **himself** <note>original: εαυτον</note> (the first instance): manuscript D reads **him** | **but the one** <note>original: ο δε</note> with א, B, D (Greek), I, L, P, Q, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, and most others, including the Gothic, Sahidic, Coptic, and Peshitta Syriac ... Lachmann reads **and the one** <note>original: και ο</note> (as in Luke 14:11 and Matthew 23:12) with manuscript A, some Latin versions, the Vulgate, the Curetonian and Harclean Syriac, Ethiopic, and Origen.

**15.** **even** <note>original: και</note> also in Latin versions *c, e, f, i, q*, the Vulgate, Curetonian Syriac, and Armenian ... omitted by manuscript D, the Gothic, Coptic, and some Syriac versions | **the** <note>original: τα</note>: omitted by D and minuscules 1, 13, 69, 118, 131, 247, and Origen | **infants** <note>original: βρεφη</note>: Origen notes, "While Matthew says 'children' <note>original: παιδια</note> were brought to Jesus, and Mark also, Luke says they brought 'even infants.'" He later adds: "The intention of those bringing the children was, according to Matthew, that he might lay hands on them, according to Mark, that he might touch them, and according to Luke—who says they were infants—that he might touch them" ... Manuscript D reads **children** | **them** (Manuscript B initially omitted this, later added) **might touch** with manuscripts א, A, B, D, L, Q, Γ, Δ, Λ, most uncials, the Latin and Vulgate versions, and Origen ... some read **he might touch them** (reversing the word order, as in Mark) | **but when they saw** <note>original: ιδοντεσ δε</note> (so in *a, d, e*; others read "which when they saw"): some minuscules and the Syriac read **and when they saw** | **the disciples**: some minuscules, the Syriac, and Ethiopic add **his** | **were rebuking** <note>original: επετιμων</note> with א, B, D, G, L, and several minuscules, and the Latin, Vulgate, and Coptic versions ... the Textus Receptus reads **rebuked** <note>original: επετιμησαν</note> (aorist tense) with manuscripts A, I, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, and many others | **them** <note>original: αυτοισ</note>: manuscript Δ and Γ read "these ones" <note>original: αυτουσ</note>.

**16.** **called** <note>original: προσεκαλεσατο</note> (manuscript D and others use a slightly different verb form) **them saying** with א, B, L, and the Latin version *a*...

Tertullian, *Against Marcion* book 4, chapter 36: <note>original: "Tertmarc 36"</note> "asked by a certain man: 'Best teacher, what doing shall I possess eternal life?' he [Jesus] demanded whether he knew, that is, performed, the commandments of the Creator." <note>original: "interrogatus ab illo quodam: Praeceptor optime, quid faciens vitam aeternam possidebo? de praeceptis creatoris an ea sciret, id est faceret, expostulavit."</note> "And when he had affirmed that he had observed all the most important ones from his youth, he [Jesus] said, 'one thing is lacking to you,'" etc. <note>original: "Cumque ille principaliora quaeque affirmasset observasse se ab adolescentia, unum, inquit, tibi deest"</note> Furthermore, compare the things read in Macarius Chrysocephalus cited from Origen on Luke (Origen, volume 3, page 980): <note>original: "Or3, 980"</note> "he sends [him] back to the law so that he might gather commandments from there," etc. <note>original: "επι τον νομον αναπεμπει ιν εκειθεν συναγη εντολας"</note> at any rate, he bears witness to the one who received [the commandments], from Deuteronomy the 'you shall love the Lord' etc., and from Leviticus 'your neighbor as yourself.' Cyril of Alexandria (380): 
> "the 'camel' is not the animal, but the thick rope used on ships." <note>original: "καμηλον ου το ζωον, αλλα το εν τοις πλοιοις παχυ σχοινιον"</note> 
Similarly, see the scholarly notes on Matthew. Theophylact on this passage: 
> "it is entirely impossible for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, whether you understand 'camel' as the animal itself or as a certain thick nautical rope." <note>original: "αδυνατον γαρ παντως καμηλον δια τρυπηματος βελονης χωρησαι, ειτε το ζωον αυτο νοησεις καμηλον, ειτε σχοινον τινα ναυτικην παχειαν."</note> 
Ambrose on Luke, page 1489: 
> "the camel therefore is understood as a type of the Gentile people, whom that lion, seeking whom he may devour, burdened with a treasure of prophetic appearances, drives into the desert." <note>original: "camelus ergo in typo populus gentilis accipitur, quem leo ille quaerens quem devoret onustum thesauro propheticis agitat speciebus in desertum."</note> 
| **opening:** <note>original: "τρηματος"</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, D, 49 ... L, R, 157, 242, and others [read] **perforation** <note>original: "τρυπηματος"</note> (the word used in our edition of Matthew) ... the Textus Receptus [reads] **eyelet** <note>original: "τρυμαλιας"</note> (the word used in our edition of Mark) with A, P, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, nine uncials, and most others. Latin versions everywhere use "foramen" (manuscript 'e' uses "cavernam") **of a needle.** | **of a needle:** <note>original: "βελονης"</note> (Griesbach's preferred reading) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, D, L, 1, 13, 69, 124, 157, 209, 251, 346. (Compare also Clement of Alexandria, page 440: 
> "one must therefore believe much more in the Scripture saying that a camel will pass through the eye of a needle sooner than a rich man will study philosophy") <note>original: "πιστεον ουν πολλω μαλλον τη γραφη λεγουση θαττον καμηλον δια τρυπηματος βελονης διελευσεσθαι η πλουσιον φιλοσοφειν"</note> 
... the Textus Receptus [reads] **needle** <note>original: "ραφιδος"</note> (as in Matthew and Mark) with A, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, nine uncials, and most others. | **to enter** (first instance) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, eight uncials, and by far the majority, including the Coptic and Syriac versions ... A, D, M, P, and over 20 others, as well as most Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Armenian versions [read] **to pass through** <note>original: "διελθειν"</note> (the word used in our edition of Mark; see also Matthew). | **to enter** (second instance): manuscripts 'd', 'b', 'c', 'f', 'g', Vulgate, Coptic, and Harklean Syriac place this before "into the kingdom..." ... 'a', 'e', and others do not express it; manuscript 'l' omits the entire verse 25.
**26. they said:** <note>original: "ειπαν"</note> with Sinaiticus and R ... the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf [read] **they said** <note>original: "ειπον"</note> with A, B, D, L, X, and nearly all others. | **those** <note>original: "οι"</note>

# 18, 27. ACCORDING TO LUKE #

27 But he said: "The things that are impossible with men are possible with God."

<margin>
28—30
Matthew 19:27—29
Mark 10:28—30
</margin>
28 Then Peter said: "Behold, we have left our own possessions and followed you." 29 <gloss>221.2</gloss> And he said to them: "Truly I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God, 30 who will not receive back..."

---

**those who heard** <note>original: "ακουσαντεσ"</note> (manuscripts 'd' and 'g1' <note>Latin: *qui audierunt*</note>): Greek manuscript D, L, 118, 131, 209, 254. **those hearing** <note>original: "οι ακουοντεσ"</note>, likewise in most of the Old Latin and the Vulgate <note>Latin: *qui audiebant*</note>, and manuscript 'l' <note>Latin: *audientes*</note>.

27. **But he:** <note>original: "ο δε"</note> Lambda, 124, 251, Scrivener's manuscripts 'i' and 'y', and a few others, and the Peshitta Syriac add **Jesus** <note>original abbreviated: "ι̅ς̅"</note>; likewise also (though manuscript 'b' and the Matthew parallel omit it) **Jesus said to them** <note>Latin: *ait illis Iesus*</note> in 'b', 'c', 'f', 'ff2', 'i', 'l', the Matthew parallel, and the Ethiopic version. | **impossible with men** <note>original: "αδυνατ. παρ. ανθρωποισ"</note> (Also found in the Latin translation of Irenaeus, pages 127, 254, and 299; and Tertullian in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, 57. Justin Martyr's *Apology* 1, 19 also points here, though we noted it under Matthew): manuscript 69, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac (but not the Palestinian or Harklean), and Theophylact volume 2, page 13 [read] **with men [things are] impossible** <note>original: "παρ. ανθρ. αδυν."</note>. | **the** <note>original: "τω"</note> [before "God"] is included with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, L, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, and most others, including the Coptic... Lachmann omits it along with Bezae (D), P, 157, Scrivener's 'f', Justin Martyr, and Theophylact (compare parallel passages). | **is** <note>original: "εστιν"</note> [placed] in this position with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, 1, 28, 118, 131, 157, 209, and a few others, including Old Latin 'a' and 'e', and Jerome’s commentary on Pelagius (also the Curetonian, Peshitta, and Palestinian Syriac)... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς; the "received text" used for early English Bibles</note> places it after **possible** <note>original: "δυνατα"</note> with Delta, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, nine other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and most others, including Old Latin 'b, c, f, ff2, i, l, q', the Vulgate (though the Old Latin and Vulgate also have **which things are impossible with men** <note>Latin: *quae inpossibilia sunt ap. homines*</note> before it), the Gothic, Coptic, Harklean Syriac, and the Latin translation of Irenaeus on pages 127 and 299 (but page 254 and Tertullian omit the word **is/are** <note>Latin: *sunt*</note> in both places).

28. **Peter** <note>original: "πετρ."</note> with Alexandrinus, P, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, eight other uncials, and by far the majority of others (though manuscript 21 only in Scrivener)... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς</note> and Lachmann read **the Peter** <note>original: "ο πετρ."</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, R, U, X, and many others (Note: though the reading in Matthew and Mark is quite unstable, in Luke both usages occur). | **having left** <note>original: "αφεντεσ"</note> (placed after **our own** <note>original: "τα ιδια"</note> in Bezae, 1, 118, 131, 209). **our own** <note>original: "τα ιδια"</note> (manuscripts 1, 13, 69, 118, 131, 209, 346, and Old Latin a, c, e, l, q add **all** <note>original: "παντα"</note> before it) with the corrected Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, 157, 1, 13, 69, 118, 131, 209, 346, the Coptic, the margin of the Harklean Syriac, Armenian, and most Old Latin (manuscripts 'i' and 'ff2' [read] **having left our things** <note>Latin: *relictis rebus nostris*</note> [though the second omits "our"], 'a', 'l', and Armenian read **having left all our things** <note>Latin: *relictis omnibus nostris*</note>, 'c' and 'q' read **having left all things** <note>Latin: *relictis omnib. rebus nostris*</note>; 'b' reads **having left our nets** <note>Latin: *relictis retibus nostris*</note>; 'e' reads **we sent away all our things** <note>Latin: *remisimus omnia nostra*</note>, and the Curetonian Syriac is similar)... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς</note> [reads] **we have left all and [followed]** <note>original: "αφηκαμεν παντα και"</note> (as in Matthew and Mark) with the original hand of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, nine other uncials, and most others, including manuscript 'f', the Vulgate (f, the Vulgate, Ambrose’s commentary on Luke, and Augustine [read] **we have dismissed all things and** <note>Latin: *dimisimus omnia et*</note>), the Gothic, Peshitta, and the text of the Harklean Syriac, and the Ethiopic. | **we followed you:** <note>original: "ηκολουθησαμεν σοι"</note> (manuscript R uses the ending **-kamen**, as in Mark). The corrected Sinaiticus, X, Old Latin 'c', Scrivener’s 'e', and 'l' add (from Matthew): **what then will there be for us?** <note>original: "τι αρα εσται ημιν"</note>.

29. **But he:** <note>original: "ο δε"</note> the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac and the Ethiopic add **Jesus** (the Ethiopic reads: **and the Lord Jesus said to his disciples** <note>Latin: *et dixit domin. Ies. discipulis suis*</note>). | **Truly I say to you** <note>original: "αμην λε. υμιν"</note> without the word **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> with the original hand of Sinaiticus, Bezae, Delta, 131, Old Latin 'a, b, c, e, ff2' (and apparently g1 and g2), 'i, l, q', the Vulgate, and Cyprian page 310... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> with the corrected Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, L, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, eight other uncials, and most others, including 'f', and Jerome’s commentary on Jovinian (Note: Mark omits it, but Delta adds it similarly; whereas in Matthew the word "that" does not vary). | **house:** <note>original: "οικιαν"</note> manuscripts D, H, 69, 49 (Gospel lectionary), and a few others, along with the Peshitta Syriac, Armenian, and Persian versions [read] **houses** <note>original: "οικιασ"</note> (as in Matthew). | **or wife or brothers or parents** <note>original: "η γυναικ. η αδελφ. η γον."</note> in this order with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, and the Coptic... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς</note> and Lachmann read **or parents or brothers... or wife** <note>original: "η γον. η αδελφ... η γυναικ."</note> (see Bezae, X, Delta, etc., below) with Alexandrinus, Bezae, P, R, other uncials, and apparently all others, including the Old Latin, Vulgate, and other Syriac versions (Note: "wife" is missing in Matthew and Mark, but many witnesses inserted it before "children"). Furthermore, after **or brothers**, manuscripts Bezae, X, Delta, and seven others, along with Cyprian page 91 (though not on pages 185, 273, or 310), add **or sisters** <note>original: "η αδελφασ"</note>, as in Matthew and Mark. | **or children:** <note>original: "η τεκνα"</note> manuscript Bezae (D) adds **in this time** <note>original: "εν τω καιρω τουτω"</note> (from the following verse). | **for the sake of** <note>term: eneken, a preposition indicating purpose</note> [using the spelling <note>original: "εινεκεν"</note>] with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (no one uses this spelling in Matthew or Mark)... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf [use the spelling] **eneken** <note>original: "ενεκεν"</note> with Alexandrinus, Bezae, L, P, R, the other uncials, and all others (except U and a few others who have **eneka** <note>original: "ενεκα"</note>).

30. **who [shall] not [receive]** <note>original: "οσ ουχι μη"</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, 1, 124, 209... The Textus Receptus <note>symbol: ς</note> and Lachmann read **who [shall] not** <note>original: "οσ ου μη"</note> with Alexandrinus, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, eight other uncials, and most others... manuscript Bezae and the Armenian read **unless he receives** <note>original: "εαν μη"</note> (from Mark); likewise Old Latin 'b, c, e, i, l' read **unless he receives** <note>Latin: *nisi ut recipiat*</note> (with 'e' having "you receive" and 'i' having "you all receive"); on the other hand, 'a, ff2, q' read **who does not receive** <note>Latin: *qui non recipiat*</note> (with 'a' having "will not receive"), while 'f', the Vulgate, Cyprian, and others follow the standard reading.
