# ACCORDING TO LUKE 18, 33 #

...many times more in this time, and in the age to come, eternal life.

<margin>
31—34
Matthew 20, 17—19
Mark 10, 32—34
</margin>

31 <gloss>222.2</gloss> Then taking the twelve aside, he said to them: "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all the things written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. 32 For he will be handed over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spat upon, 33 and after scourging him, they will kill him, and—"

---

**and not receive** <note>Latin: *et non recipiat*; variant: *tollet/tolliet*</note> | **receive** <note>original: "απολαβη"</note> found in manuscripts ℵ, A, L, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, 7 uncials, and many others... B, D, M, and 10 others, and the Armenian version have **take** <note>original: "λαβη"</note> (mirroring Mark and Matthew). | **many times more** <note>original: "πολλαπλασιονα"</note> (as in manuscript 'f' and the Vulgate; and 'g1', 'g2'): D, and Old Latin manuscripts 'a', 'b', 'c', 'e', 'ff2', 'i', 'l', 'q', the Peshitta Syriac margin, and Cyprian (pages 91, 185, 273, 310) read **seven times more** <note>original: "επταπλασιονα"</note>. Jerome <note>the 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate</note> argues against this; after he mentions Jovinian's words "how the Lord promises in another Gospel *a hundredfold* <note>Latin: *centies*</note> and in another *sevenfold* <note>Latin: *septies*</note> to the apostles for leaving children and wives," Jerome states: "—lest he exult in a lie—let him know that in Matthew and Mark a hundredfold was promised to the apostles who had left everything, but in the Gospel of Luke 'much more' <note>original: "πολυ πλειονα"</note>, and in absolutely no Gospel is 'seven' written for 'one hundred,' and he [Jovinian] is held guilty of either forgery or ignorance." | **in this time:** manuscript Chi adds **now** <note>original: "νυν"</note> (matching Mark). | **the [age] to come eternal life** (manuscript 'e' reads: *he will follow eternal life*, likewise the Curetonian Syriac): 'a', 'b', 'c', 'ff2', 'g2', 'i', and 'l' add **will possess** <note>Latin: *possidebit*</note> (though not 'f', 'g1', 'q', or the Vulgate).

**31—34.** Epiphanius on Marcion <note>an early Christian writer documenting a "shorter" version of Luke used by the heretic Marcion</note> (pages 315 and 340): "He cut out <note>original: "παρεκοψε"</note> this: 'Taking the twelve, he said: Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things written in the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled; for he will be handed over... and be killed, and on the third day he will be raised <note>original: "εγερθησεται"</note>.' He cut all of these out."

**31.** **but:** 'c', 'f', 'ff2', 'i', 'l', 'q', and the Vulgate add **Jesus** (not 'a', 'b', or 'e'). | **twelve** (manuscript D uses the numeral 12 <note>original: "ιβ'"</note>, Origen reads "twelve" <note>original: "δεκαδυο"</note>): E, 'a', 'b', 'f', 'ff2', and 'i' add **disciples** <note>original: "μαθητας"</note> (but not 'c', 'e', 'l', 'q', or the Vulgate). | **to them** <note>original: "πρ. αυτους"</note> also in 'a', 'b', 'e', 'q', and Origen: 'd', 'c', 'f', 'ff2', 'i', 'l', and the Vulgate read "to them" in a different case <note>original: "αυτοις"</note>. | **we are going up:** manuscript 'r', 69, and a few others use a slightly different verb form. | **Jerusalem:** spelled *Hierousalem* in ℵ, B, D, L, R, Scrivener's 'y', 'e', the Gothic, Coptic, and Origen... Lachmann's edition uses the Greek-style *Hierosolyma* (following the standard text of Matthew and Mark) with A, P, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, 8 uncials, and most others, including Old Latin and the Vulgate. | **will be fulfilled:** 60, Scrivener's 'y' and 'z', 10 others, and Origen read "will be completed" <note>original: "τελειωθησεται"</note>. | **to the Son:** D, 13, 69, 124, 346, 6 others, and Epiphanius's Marcion (see above) read **concerning the Son** <note>original: "περι του υιου"</note> (the scholar Schulz calls this "well-read"), likewise Delta (omitting "concerning"), and the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian.

**32.** **For he will be handed over:** manuscript D reads "because he will be handed over" <note>original: "οτι παραδοθ."</note>. | **will be mocked:** A, D, E, P (but not ℵ, B, L, R, and the rest) use a different spelling of the word. | **and will be insulted** (the Peshitta Syriac moves this to after "scourging" in verse 33, reading: *and they will scourge him and they will treat him with ignominy*): ℵ, A, P, R, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, 8 uncials, the Coptic, Gothic, and Curetonian/Peshitta Syriac, and Ethiopic; manuscripts 130 (Greek and Latin), 'f', 'vg', and Armenian read "and will be scourged," likewise 'c' but placed after "spat upon"... D, L, 11 others, 'a', 'b', 'e', 'ff2', 'i', 'q', the Peshitta, and the Zohrab Armenian omit it (following Matthew and Mark who do not have it); manuscript 'l' reads the whole verse: *he will be handed over, proceeding and scourged they will kill him*. | **and spat upon** (D uses a different spelling; the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac add *in his face*): P, R, 7 others, and the Zohrab Armenian omit this (following Matthew, though Mark includes it).

**33.** **they will kill** (likewise 'd'): the Greek 'p' and manuscript 'i' use a different spelling or tense meaning "they kill" <note>Latin: *occidunt*</note>.

# 18, 34. ACCORDING TO LUKE #

...on the third day he will rise again. 34 <gloss>223. 10</gloss> And they understood none of these things, and this saying was hidden from them, and they did not know the things being said.

<margin>
35—43
Matthew 20, 29—34
Mark 10, 46—52
</margin>

35 <gloss>224. 2</gloss> And it happened, as he drew near to Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting by the road begging. 36 Hearing a crowd passing by, he asked what this might be. 37 They told him that "Jesus the Nazarene is passing by." 38 And he cried out, saying, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" 39 And those leading the way rebuked him so that—

---

33. **on the third day** <note>original: "τη ημερ. τη τριτ."</note> (found in manuscripts 'a', 'am', 'ing', 'tol'; likewise 'e', though the Latin phrase *die tertia resurget* ["on the third day he will rise"] is strangely corrupted into *deterioresurgent* <note>likely a scribal error where "the third" and "will rise" were blended into a word meaning "worse rise"</note>): ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, Δ, 1, 13, 69, 124, 131, 209, and more than 40 others, plus Latin 'b', 'c', 'f', 'g1,2', 'i', 'q' (manuscript 'l' reads "after three days"), and the Vulgate, Armenian, and Epiphanius <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> in his notes on Marcion read **the third day** <note>original: "τη τριτη ημερα"</note> (following the phrasing in Matthew) | **will rise again**: Manuscript L, about 10 others, and Epiphanius read **will be raised** <note>original: "εγερθησεται"</note> (following the phrasing used in Matthew).

34. **and they**: D <note>Codex Bezae</note>, U, and a few others, along with Latin 'e' and the Syriac and Ethiopic versions, read **but they** | **none of these things**: Manuscript D reverses the word order to **these things none** | **and it was**: Manuscripts 1, 142 (margin), 209, and several Latin versions ('a', 'b', 'c', 'e', 'f', 'i', 'q'), the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac read **but it was**... manuscript 'l' skips ahead to "what was being said" after "they understood," omitting the rest | **this**: Omitted in D, 1, 25, 131, 209, and several Latin, Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian versions | **hidden** <note>original: "κεκρυμμενον"</note>: G, Gamma, and a few others read **concealed** <note>original: "κεκαλυμμενον"</note> | **from**: Manuscript Lambda reads **upon** | **the things being said**: The Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac add **with them**.

35. **into**: Manuscripts 13, 124, 346 read **the** (manuscript 69 reads **in the**). Likewise, Epiphanius (citing Marcion's version): "And it happened as he drew near to Jericho, a blind man cried out: 'Son of David, have mercy on me,' and when he was healed he says: 'Your faith has saved you.'" | **Jericho**: Spelled *Iereicho* in B, D, P, Q (as in Luke 19:1, Mark 10:46, Hebrews 11:30)... most other editors and many uncials read *Iericho* with ℵ, A, L, R, X, etc. | **begging** <note>original: "επαιτων"</note>: found in ℵ, B, D, L, Origen, and the Dialogue of Adamantius <note>a 4th-century work against various heresies</note> (Latin 'd', 'e' and Adamantius place "begging" before "was sitting")... many other uncials and manuscripts read **asking for alms** <note>original: "προσαιτων"</note> (compare the wording in Mark). The Adamantius Dialogue says: "Since the followers of Megethius, of the Marcionite sect, are present, I read from their own gospel: 'And it happened as he drew near' up to 'and immediately he regained his sight' (v. 43)."

36. **passing by** <note>original: "διαπορευομενου"</note> (also Origen and Adamantius): D and X read **passing alongside** <note>original: "παραπορευομενου"</note>. Most Old Latin versions and the Vulgate read **the crowd passing by**, while 'e' reads **the crowds passing through** | **what this might be**: with ℵ, A, B, P, and many others; the Latin versions read **what this (or that) was**... Lachmann's edition reads **what [then] this would be** with D, K, L, M, and others, including Origen and Adamantius.

37. **they told** (Adamantius reads **it was told**) **him**: ℵ (original hand) reads **but they told** | **the Nazarene** <note>original: "ο ναζωραιος"</note>: with Latin 'b', 'd', 'f', and Coptic... D, 1, 131, 209, the Vulgate, and Origen read **the Nazarene** <note>original: "ο ναζαρηνος"</note> (a variant Greek spelling). Adamantius omits the word entirely.

38. **and**: Latin 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g' read **but he** | **cried out** (Epiphanius/Marcion has "was crying"): Manuscript 'p' has **shouted** | **Son**: omitted in several manuscripts and Origen | **David**: various Greek spellings (Daueid, Dauid, Dabid).

# ACCORING TO LUKE 18, 43 #

...should be silent; but he cried out all the more: "Son of David, have mercy on me." 40 And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be led to him. And when he had drawn near, he questioned him: 41 "What do you want me to do for you?" And he said: "Lord, that I may see again." 42 And Jesus said to him: "See again; your faith has saved you." 43 And immediately he saw again, and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, seeing it, gave praise to God.

---

39. **Omit the verse**: Manuscripts 33 (based on spacing), 57, 130, 157, 235, 258, and 433 omit this line. Also omitted in the superscript of manuscript 'b' and the Dialogue of Adamantius <note>original: "Dial⁸⁵⁸"</note> :: <term>homoioteleuton</term> <note>a scribal error where the eye skips text because of similar endings in nearby words</note> | **and those**: Manuscripts D, Old Latin 'e', and Tertullian’s work against Marcion read **but they** | **leading the way**: (Also found in Tertullian and Origen; the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac add "Jesus"): Manuscripts A, K, Π, and others read **passing by** <note>original: "παραγοντ." / Latin: "qui praeteribant"</note>, while others read **going along beside** | **should be silent**: <note>original: "σιγήσῃ"</note> (The scholar Scholz notes "this is correct for Luke, who is the only evangelist to use this specific verb") found in manuscripts B, D, L, P, X. 41. **What**: Found in ℵ, B, D, L, etc. Other editions add **saying** <note>original: "λεγων"</note> following manuscripts A, Q, R, the Vulgate, and Syriac versions. Origen uses **having said** | **said**: The R manuscript, Curetonian Syriac, and Ethiopic add **to him** | **Lord**: Some manuscripts place this after "that I may see." Two manuscripts omit it entirely | **that I may see**: The Curetonian Syriac and Armenian versions read **that my eyes may be opened and I may see**.

42. **Jesus**: (Manuscripts 1, 13, and 209 read **the Lord**; others omit it). **said to him**: (Found in the Vulgate and some Latin): Several Old Latin manuscripts and Origen read **answering, he said to him** (some add **Jesus**; the Dialogue of Adamantius reads **answering, Jesus said**).

43. The Dialogue of Adamantius, having excerpted verses 35 through 43, does not include the words from **and followed him** through **gave praise to God** | **and followed him**: Omitted in the Harclean Syriac version | **glorifying God**: Origen writes of Luke thus: "not only did he follow him, but he had something more than the rest; for he says he followed him glorifying God" | **people**: <note>original: "λαοσ"</note>. Found in some manuscripts and Origen. Other manuscripts read **crowd** <note>original: "οχλοσ"</note>. Among the Latin versions, some use **people** <note>Latin: "populus"</note> while others use **common folk** <note>Latin: "plebs"</note> | **seeing**: Omitted in manuscript K and several others | **praise**: (Also in Origen and the Vulgate <note>Latin: "laudem"</note>). 14. **this man to reign**: Omitted in Manuscript D, 254, and several Old Latin versions (b, ff², l), as well as by Lucifer of Cagliari. | **sent**: Manuscript D reads "sent forth" <note>original: "επεμψαν"</note> (alternatively "sent out" <note>original: "ενεπεμψαν"</note>). | **we want**: Manuscripts E, H, and others use a slightly different grammatical form of the verb <note>original: "θελωμεν" vs "θελομεν"</note>. | **this man**: Manuscript Delta initially added "having received the kingdom" <note>original: "λαβοντα την βασιλειαν"</note>, but the scribe corrected themselves. | **us**: Manuscript 124 reads "you" <note>original: "υμας"</note>.

15. **and it came to pass etc**: The Curetonian and Schulthess Syriac versions read: "and when he had received the kingdom and returned, he said." | **in the [act of]**: Omitted in manuscripts D and Delta; likewise, the Old Latin version (e) reads: "and it was done that he returned, having accepted the kingdom, and he commanded etc." | **returned, having received**: Manuscripts 29 and 71 read "to receive" <note>original: "λαβειν"</note>. | **and he said**: Several manuscripts and versions (including the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac) omit the word **and**. | **to him**: Manuscript D and the Old Latin version (a) read "his servants" <note>original: "αυτου"</note>; omitted by many others including the Vulgate and Ethiopic versions. | **those**: Some manuscripts read "those ones" or "his own." Omitted by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), B, D, and others. | **had given**: Manuscripts ℵ, B, D, and L use the pluperfect "had given" <note>original: "δεδωκει"</note>. The <term>Received Text</term><note>The Textus Receptus, the standard Greek text used for the King James Version.</note> and many others use the aorist "gave" <note>original: "εδωκεν"</note>. (Note: These tenses were often swapped by scribes; either could have been substituted by a later hand). | **he might know**: Variations between two forms of the Greek verb "to know" <note>original: "γνοι" and "γνω"</note>. | **what each had gained**: There is significant variation here. Most manuscripts read "what each had gained" <note>original: "τις τι διεπραγματευσατο"</note>. Latin versions vary between "what each had negotiated," "how much each negotiated," or "how much each gained." The earliest manuscripts (ℵ, B, D, L) read "what they had gained by trading."

16. **Lord**: Omitted in some manuscript traditions. | **the mina**: Most manuscripts use the singular <note>original: "η μνα"</note>. Some (B³, E, F, H, etc.) use a form that looks like a plural "minas" <note>original: "η μνασ"</note>, likely a scribal error. This occurs again in verses 18 and 20. | **earned ten minas**: The word order varies across manuscripts. Some place "ten" before the verb, others after. The Old Latin version (b) and Lucifer of Cagliari read: "your talent has acquired ten talents" <note>Lucifer uses 'talent' instead of 'mina'</note>. | **earned**: Variation in spelling between *prosērgasato* and *proseirgasato*.

17. **and**: Manuscript D and the Old Latin version (e) read "but he said" <note>original: "ο δε"</note>. | **well done**: Manuscripts B and D, and Origen use *euge* <note>original: "ευγε"</note> (Excellent!). The <term>Received Text</term> and others use *eu* <note>original: "ευ"</note> (Well), perhaps to harmonize with the wording in Matthew 25:21. | **good servant**: Most manuscripts place the adjective first ("good servant"), but others (ℵ, 1, 13, 157) place it after ("servant good"), similar to the phrasing in Matthew.

The scholarly notes detail numerous manuscript variations regarding verb tenses, word order, and harmonizations with the Gospel of Matthew.</summary>

<header>19, 18. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

18 And the second came, saying: "Lord, your <term>mina</term><note>A mina (Greek: mna) was a Greek unit of currency worth 100 drachmas, or about three months' wages for a laborer.</note> has made five minas." 19 And he said also to him: "And you, be over five cities." 20 And the other came, saying: "Lord, look, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a <term>handkerchief</term><note>Greek: soudarion, a cloth used for wiping sweat or wrapping valuables.</note>; 21 for I feared you, because you are a harsh man; you take up what you did not lay down, and you reap what you did not sow." 22 He said to him: "Out of your own mouth I will judge you, you wicked servant! You knew that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down, and—"

---

18. **the second came**: (Manuscript 157 reads "another" <note>original: "ετεροσ"</note>; Old Latin versions a, e, and s also read "another" <note>original: "alius"</note>). The word order "the second came saying" is found in versions a, e, and s; while the Vulgate and others read "the second came saying." | Manuscript D (Codex Bezae) reads: "the other, having come, said" <note>original: "ο ετεροσ ελθων ειπεν"</note>; Manuscript d reads "another" <note>original: "alius"</note>. | **Lord**: Located here in manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and L (likely also R, but the page is torn). | The Textus Receptus (ς) and Lachmann (Ln) place "Lord" before "your mina" <note>original: "η μν. σου"</note> following manuscripts A, D, and many others. This matches the wording in the parallel passage in Matthew. | The Old Latin (ff²) and Armenian (arm) omit the word "Lord." | **mina**: Manuscripts ℵ, E, F, H, and others read the plural "minas" <note>original: "μνασ"</note>. See the note on verse 16. | **made five minas**: (This order is found in the Peshitta Syriac; the Curetonian Syriac reads "five minas made"). Manuscript D reads "five made minas."

19. **be**: (Manuscripts A, B, and D use a variant spelling <note>original: "γεινου"</note>; Manuscript L and others use another form <note>original: "γενου"</note>). This is the position in ℵ, B, L, and several others. | Manuscript D and the Coptic version place "and you" before the verb. | The Textus Receptus (ς) and Lachmann (Ln) place the verb before "over" <note>original: "επανω"</note> following manuscripts A, D, and most others (Latin versions read "be over" <note>original: "esto supra"</note>). | The theologian Origen notes: "nor did he define the name of authority as he did for the first one," though in other places he seems to contradict himself by using "have authority over" instead of "be over." | **five**: Manuscript Γ reads "ten."

20. **the other**: Found in ℵ, B, D, L, R, and the Armenian version. | The Textus Receptus (ς) reads simply "another" <note>original: "ετεροσ"</note> following A, D, and others. The Latin versions (a, d, e, s, and the Vulgate) read "another" or "the other." | **Lord**: Omitted in Manuscript 243, the Curetonian Syriac, and by Lucifer of Cagliari. | **mina**: ℵ, E, F, and others read "minas."

21. **for I feared**: (The Vulgate reads "for I feared" <note>original: "timui enim"</note>). Manuscript D and most Old Latin versions read "because I was afraid" <note>original: "οτι εφοβηθην"</note>. | **you**: Omitted in some Vulgate manuscripts (am, fu). | **because a man**: Manuscript D and Old Latin e read "for a man" <note>original: "ανθρωπ. γαρ"</note>. | **you are harsh**: D and others reverse the word order to "harsh you are." | **sow**: Manuscripts U, Delta, and others add "and you gather from where you did not scatter," which is a phrase borrowed from the Gospel of Matthew.

22. **He said**: Found in ℵ, B, E, G, and the Vulgate. | The Textus Receptus (ς) and Lachmann (Ln) read "But he said" <note>original: "λεγει δε"</note> following manuscript A and others. | Manuscript D reads "But he said" <note>original: "ο δε ειπεν"</note>; other Latin versions read "and he said" or "then he said." | **I will judge**: Accented as future tense ("I will judge" <note>original: "κρινῶ"</note>) in manuscripts E, H, K, etc. | B, the Vulgate, and others read it as present tense ("I judge" <note>original: "κρίνω"</note> or "I condemn"). | **wicked servant**: The Curetonian Syriac adds "who was not faithful." | **You knew**: The Syriac and Ethiopic versions add "me." | **I**: Omitted in Manuscript L and the Ethiopic version. | **taking up**: Found in D, F, the Vulgate, and Syriac versions.

—reaping what I did not sow? 23 And why did you not give my money to the <term>bank</term><note>The Greek word "trapeza" literally means "table," referring to the tables of money-changers or lenders where interest could be earned.</note>? **Verse 21-22 continuation:** The Latin author Lucifer of Cagliari reads "I take up" <note>original: "αιρω" or "et tollo"</note> | For "reaping" <note>original: "θεριζων"</note>, Manuscript D, several Old Latin versions, and the Syriac read "I reap." | For "sowed" <note>original: "εσπειρα"</note>, Manuscripts U, A, and others add: "and gathering from where you did not scatter" <note>original: "και συναγων οθεν ου διεσκορπισα"</note>, likely adapted from the similar passage in Matthew 25:24-26.

**23.** The word **and** is omitted by manuscripts 69, 124, and several Syriac and Coptic versions. | **why**: Manuscript D reads "why then." | **my money**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and A place "my" before "money," while the <term>Textus Receptus</term><note>The "Received Text," a standard 16th-century Greek text of the New Testament.</note> (marked as ς) and many others place it after. | **bank**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and D read "a table/bank" <note>original: "τραπεζαν"</note>, while others add the definite article "the." The early church writer Eusebius quotes this freely as "you ought to have cast my money into a bank," blending it with Matthew's wording. | **I would have collected it**: Found in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The scholar Tischendorf (Ti) and the Textus Receptus use a slightly different word order for "I would have collected it." | Manuscript G and others read: "I would have brought back my own with interest." The Syriac versions follow this, mirroring the wording found in Matthew.

**24.** **And he said to those standing by**: Found in Origen and Lucifer of Cagliari. Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions read: "And he said to the bystanders." | **the mina**: Omitted by Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions. | **give**: Manuscript D uses a more forceful word for "bring it over" <note>original: "απευενκατε"</note> rather than simply "give." | **the ten minas**: This word order is found in the Vulgate and Origen. However, many other manuscripts (1, 13, 69, etc.) and Syriac versions place the phrase "the one who has" after "ten minas," mirroring Matthew 25:28.

**25.** This entire verse ("And they said to him: Lord, he has ten minas") is omitted by Manuscript D, several Old Latin versions, and the Syriac. It is likely omitted to make the passage more closely resemble the version in the Gospel of Matthew, which lacks this specific interruption. | **they said**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and L use the form "eipan," while the Textus Receptus uses "eipon." | **Lord**: Omitted in the original hand of the Vaticanus (B) manuscript but added later by a corrector.

**26.** **I tell you**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and L begin this without a connecting word. The Textus Receptus and others add the word "for" <note>original: "γαρ"</note> ("For I tell you"). Several Old Latin versions read "But I say to you." | **that**: Omitted in some manuscripts and Old Latin versions. | **will be given**: Manuscript D and its Latin translation use "will be added." Some manuscripts (13, 69) and the Syriac add "and he will have an abundance," borrowed from Matthew. | **he has**: Several manuscripts and the writer Tertullian (who notes that God is shown as a judge who not only honors but takes away what one "seems to have") read "what he seems to have" <note>original: "δοκει εχειν"</note>, matching Luke 8:18. | **will be taken away**: Manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and L conclude the phrase here. The Textus Receptus and most other manuscripts add "from him" <note>original: "απ αυτου"</note> at the end.

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 19, 41.
<sig>42*</sig>

...of the Lord; in heaven peace, and glory in the highest. **39** <gloss>235.5</gloss> And some of the Pharisees from the crowd said to him: "Teacher, rebuke your disciples." **40** And answering he said: "I tell you that if these shall be silent, the stones will cry out."
**41** <gloss>236.10</gloss> And as he drew near, seeing the city he wept over it,

---

**38.** **the king** <note>original: "ο βασιλευς"</note> with Sinaiticus* (א), H, 258 (omits it), 69, Origen (volume 4, page 182)... D, A* (first hand), 142*, various other manuscripts and versions including the Ethiopic and Methodius. **the one who comes...** likewise the <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>original: "ς" - the standard printed Greek text</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **the king who comes** with the corrected Sinaiticus (א<sup>c</sup>), A, L, R, and most other <term>uncials</term>. Vaticanus (B) and others read **the one who comes, the king**. | **in the name of the Lord:** some manuscripts omit this; D, 157, and several Latin versions add **blessed is the king** (manuscript 157, the Ethiopic, and Syriac add **of Israel**). Compare with the Gospels of Matthew and John. | **in heaven peace** with Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), L, and Origen... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Lachmann read **peace in heaven** (manuscript A uses the plural **heavens**) with A, D, R, and almost all other versions. | **in the highest:** some manuscripts read **upon the earth**; others omit the phrase entirely.

**39.** **And some:** manuscript D reads **But some**. | **they said** <note>original: "ειπαν"</note> with Sinaiticus (א), A, B, D, L, and Origen... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads **they said** <note>original: "ειπον" - a spelling variant</note> with R, Gamma, Delta, and most others. | **to your disciples:** several Latin versions and the Vulgate read simply **them** (following the command "rebuke"; the Curetonian Syriac adds **lest they cry out**).

**40.** **And answering he said:** variations in the Latin and Syriac versions include **and he answering said to them** or **but he answering says**. We have written **he said** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note> without the word **to them** following Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), L, the Coptic, and Origen... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Lachmann add **to them** with A, D, R, and most versions; additionally, the Gothic and some Syriac manuscripts add **amen** (truly). | **that:** <note>original: "οτι"</note> omitted by Vaticanus (B), Origen, and several others. | **shall be silent** <note>original: "σιωπησουσιν"</note> with Sinaiticus (א), A, B, L, R, Delta; manuscript D uses a different verb for silence. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> uses a slightly different grammatical mood <note>the subjunctive "σιωπησωσιν"</note> found in later manuscripts and Cyril of Alexandria. | **will cry out** <note>original: "κραξουσιν"</note> with Sinaiticus (א), B, L, and Origen... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and Lachmann read **will cry out** <note>original: "κεκραξονται" - a more common future form</note> with A, D, R, and most others. (Note: neither form appears elsewhere in the New Testament, but the second form is very frequent in the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, while the first form is never found there. See Stephanus's *Thesaurus* regarding this rare form).

**41.** **he wept:** <note>This is a significant textual note.</note> Epiphanius (in *Ancoratus* 31) mentions this passage, noting: "But 'he wept' is also located in the Gospel according to Luke, in the **uncorrected copies**, and Saint Irenaeus used this testimony in his work *Against Heresies* against those who say that Christ appeared only in appearance <note>the Docetists, who denied Jesus was truly human</note>. But the **orthodox removed the passage, having become afraid**..." <note>Epiphanius suggests some scribes deleted Jesus's weeping to avoid making him seem too weak or human.</note> It is often cited by Origen, Eusebius, Basil, and Cyril. | **over it** <note>the city</note> with Sinaiticus (א), A, B, D, and most others. Irenaeus uses a phrase meaning **to shed tears over it**.

<meta>This page continues the critical study of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 19. On the previous page, the text described Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem and his weeping over the city. This page (660) focuses on the specific words of Jesus’ lament and prophecy concerning the coming destruction of Jerusalem in verses 42 through 44.</meta>

<page-num>660</page-num>
# ACCORDING TO LUKE 19, 42.

saying, **42** "If you had known, even you, and especially in this your day, the things that make for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes. **43** For the days will come upon you, and your enemies will throw up a rampart <note>The Greek word "charaka" refers to a pointed stake used in building a siege wall or palisade.</note> against you and surround you and hem you in from every side, **44** and they will level you and your children within you to the ground, <gloss>237.2</gloss> and they will not leave...

---

**upon it** <note>original: "επ αυτην"</note>: Origen (vol. 4, p. 182), manuscripts 182, 192, and the 180th edition of Basel, the Ethiopic version... The <term>Received Text</term> <note>original: "ς" — the standard printed Greek text used for centuries</note> reads **upon her** <note>original: "επ αυτη"</note> with manuscripts E, G, K, M, S, U, V, Δ, and many others, as well as Origen (vol. 3, p. 750 and vol. 4, p. 180) and Eustathius.

**42. if you had known even you** <note>original: "ει εγνως και συ"</note>: The phrase **and you** <note>original: "και συ"</note> is found in several Latin versions, the Vulgate, Origen (p. 977), the Gothic, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, Eustathius, and Basil. A few sources (manuscripts a, e, i, l, s, and Armenian) read **you only** <note>original: "συ tantum"</note>. The Curetonian Syriac and some others omit **and you**. The historian Eusebius omits **especially** <note>original: "καίγε"</note>.
**especially** <note>original: "καιγε"</note>: This is supported by manuscript 'a' (using the Latin *quamquam* meaning 'although'), manuscript 'c' (*quidem* meaning 'indeed'), 'i' (*equidem* meaning 'truly'), and the Vulgate. However, it is omitted by Codex Bezae (D), manuscript 157, and several other early versions. Lachmann <note>A famous 19th-century biblical scholar</note> places it in brackets [καιγε].
**in your day** <note>original: "εν τη ημερα σου"</note>: The word **your** <note>original: "σου"</note> is supported by several Latin versions, the Vulgate, Gothic, and both Syriac versions. It is omitted by the major early manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Alexandrinus (A), and Codex Bezae (D), as well as Eusebius and Origen. The majority of manuscripts including E, G, H, K, M, R, S, U, V, and others include it. Additionally, Irenaeus (p. 92) reads **if you had known even you today the things for peace**; Origen reads **if you have known, you, the things for your peace**; and Eusebius reads **if you had known even you the things for peace for you**.
**your** <note>original: "σου"</note> after **peace**: Found in Alexandrinus (A) and the majority of manuscripts. Some read **for you** <note>original: "σοι"</note> (Codex Bezae and the Vulgate). The primary early manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and manuscript 259 omit it, as does Lachmann.
**but now... they are hidden from your eyes**: The first hand of Alexandrinus (A*) omits this.
**but now they are hidden** <note>original: "νυν δε εκρυβη"</note>: Manuscripts 'c', 'f', 'q', 's', and the Vulgate support this. Irenaeus reads **but it was hidden** <note>original: "εκρυβη δε"</note>; other Latin versions use phrases meaning **they are hidden** <note>original: "absconsa sunt"</note> or **they were hidden**.

**43. upon you**: Omitted by manuscript 28 and the Curetonian Syriac.
**will throw up [a rampart]** <note>original: "παρεμβαλουσιν"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus (א), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), L, and Eusebius. Manuscript 'a' uses the Latin *inicient* (they will cast). The <term>Received Text</term>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **will cast around [a rampart]** <note>original: "περιβαλουσιν"</note> with manuscripts A, B, and many others. Latin versions and the Vulgate use *circumdabunt te vallo* or *cingent te vallo* (they will surround/encircle you with a rampart). A few manuscripts read **will place upon** or **will throw upon**. Some sources, including Origen and Eustathius, omit the phrase **and your enemies will throw up a rampart against you** entirely, though they continue with the surrounding of the city.
**against you** <note>original: "σοι"</note> after **rampart**: Eusebius places this after "surround." It is omitted by Codex Bezae (D) and several Latin versions.
**will surround you** <note>original: "περικυκλωσουσιν σε"</note>: Supported by Eusebius and most manuscripts. Sinaiticus* (א) and L omit the word **you** <note>original: "σε"</note>.
**and hem you in** <note>original: "και συνεξουσιν σε"</note>: A few manuscripts read "will gather you." Manuscript 60 and the Latin 'd' omit **you**.
**from every side**: One manuscript reads "all" (plural). Some Latin versions omit the phrase **and hem you in**.

**44. and they will level you**: Eusebius reads **and you will be leveled to the ground**.
**within you** (the first instance): Found in Codex Bezae (D) and manuscript 124.

It compares major Greek manuscripts with early Latin, Syriac, and Coptic translations, alongside citations from Church Fathers like Origen and Eusebius.</summary>

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 19, 47.

...stone upon a stone within you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.

<margin>
Verses 45 and following:
Matthew 21:12 and following;
Mark 11:15–17
</margin>
**45** <gloss>238.1</gloss> And entering into the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling,

<margin>
Isaiah 56:7;
Jeremiah 7:11
</margin>
**46** saying to them, "It is written: 'And my house shall be a house of prayer'; but you have made it a den of robbers."

<margin>
Verses 47 and following:
Mark 11:18
</margin>
**47** <gloss>239.1</gloss> And he was teaching daily in the temple; but the—

---

<note>This section compares different ancient copies of the Bible to see where the wording of verse 44 differs.</note>
Origen (vol. 4, p. 180) and Eusebius in his *Church History* (vol. 3, p. 7) omit the end of the sentence. The phrase **stone upon a stone** <note>original: "επι λιθον"</note> is found in the <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> <note>a 4th-century Greek manuscript found at Mt. Sinai</note>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, and others. However, the <term>Received Text</term> <note>the standard printed Greek text used for centuries</note> and the editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read a slightly different grammatical form <note>original: "επι λιθω"</note> based on <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> and many later manuscripts. The phrase **in you** <note>original: "εν σοι"</note> is placed here by the oldest Greek copies, but some Latin versions and the Armenian version read **in all of you** or **in all the earth**.

**45.** **And entering** <note>original: "και εισελθων"</note>: Some manuscripts and the Syriac version add the name **Jesus**. Regarding the phrase **those selling**: The oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and the Coptic versions omit the phrase **in it** <note>meaning 'in the temple'</note>, whereas the <term>Received Text</term> and many others include it. 

<note>The following notes discuss how some scribes added extra details from the Gospels of Matthew and Mark into Luke's text.</note>
Some editors note that the phrase **and those buying** was likely added by later scribes to match the other Gospels. Several manuscripts (including <term>Codex Bezae</term> and various Old Latin versions) add a longer passage here: **and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves.** These details were likely "flowed in" <note>original: "fluxerunt"</note> from the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark.

**46.** **It is written**: A few manuscripts and some Latin versions omit this opening. 
**And my house shall be a house of prayer**: This reading is found in the oldest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and the Coptic/Armenian versions. However, the <term>Received Text</term> and the Vulgate read **For my house is a house of prayer**. The Curetonian Syriac adds **for all nations**, which is a detail found in the Gospel of Mark and the original prophecy in Isaiah.
**You have made it**: Some very early sources (like the theologian Epiphanius) use the present tense **You are making it**, though most manuscripts use the past tense **You made**.

**47.** **The daily [teaching]**: One manuscript (Codex L) and the Armenian version omit the word **the** <note>original: "το"</note> before "daily."

...chief priests and the scribes and the leaders of the people were seeking to destroy him, **48** and they did not find what they might do; for all the people were hanging on his every word <note>original: "εξεκρέμετο αὐτοῦ ἀκούων" — literally "hung from him, listening"</note>.

## XX.

<margin>
1–8
Matthew 21, 23–27
Mark 11, 27–33

**1** <gloss>240.2</gloss> And it happened on one of those days, as he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, that the priests and the scribes with the elders came upon him, **2** and spoke, saying to him—

---

**47.** **and the scribes**: The manuscripts <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Codex Zacynthius</term>, and others omit the word **the** <note>the Greek article "οι"</note>. | **and the leaders of the people**: Several sources, including <term>Codex Bezae</term> and the writings of <term>Origen</term>, change the word "leaders" <note>πρῶτοι</note> to **elders** <note>πρεσβύτεροι</note>, **rulers** <note>ἄρχοντες</note>, or even **Pharisees**. The <term>Vulgate</term> and <term>Syriac</term> versions place this phrase before "were seeking to destroy him."

**48.** **they found**: Spelled differently in various manuscripts (using an "e" or "ē" sound at the start). | **the**: Omitted by several manuscripts and the Armenian version. | **they might do**: Most manuscripts use one form <note>ποιήσωσιν</note>, while others use a slightly different future tense <note>ποιήσουσιν</note>. Additionally, <term>Codex Bezae</term> and some Latin/Syriac versions add the word **to him**. | **for all the people**: The word order varies across manuscripts like <term>Codex Bezae</term> and the works of <term>Origen</term>. | **hanging**: The spelling varies between an older form <note>εξεκρέματο</note> and a more common "vulgar" or everyday usage <note>εξεκρέμετο</note> found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> and <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>. | **listening to him**: Some versions, like the Latin and Coptic, flip the order to read **to him listening**.

**XX, 1.** **And it happened**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and an Old Latin version use a slightly different conjunction <note>original: "εγενετο δε" vs "και εγενετο"</note>. | **the days**: Some versions add the word **those** <note>εκείνων</note>, though it is missing in the oldest copies like <term>Sinaiticus</term> and <term>Vaticanus</term>. <term>Marcion</term> (quoted by <term>Epiphanius</term>) phrases this section: "so that he might be convicted out of his own mouth, it says: it happened on one of the days while he was teaching in the temple, they sought to lay hands on him, and they were afraid." | **in the temple**: Placed differently in <term>Codex Bezae</term> and the <term>Syriac</term> versions. | **preaching the gospel**: One Latin version adds the word **him** here. | **came upon him**: The <term>Syriac</term> version adds **against him**. | **the priests**: Most older manuscripts <note>such as Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus</note> read **the chief priests** <note>αρχιερεις</note>. The reading "priests" <note>ιερεις</note> is found in several later Greek manuscripts. The Latin versions translate this as *principes sacerdotum* (leaders of the priests) or *pontifices*. | **and the**: Several manuscripts omit the second **the**.

**2.** **spoke**: Different spellings of the Greek word for "said" appear in the oldest manuscripts <note>ειπαν vs ειπον</note>. Some versions omit the entire phrase "and spoke," while others simplify the sentence to "and they said to him." | **saying**: This word is placed either before or after the phrase "to him" depending on the manuscript.

<page-num>663</page-num>
<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 20, 6.</header>

...to him: “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things, or who is the one who gave you this authority?” **3** And answering he said to them, “I also will ask you a question, and you tell me: **4** Was the baptism of John from heaven or from men?” **5** And they reasoned among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ **6** But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us; for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”

---

**to him** <note>original: "αυτ."</note>: Included in <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, and several others, as well as the <term>Gothic</term> and <term>Syriac Peshitta</term> versions. It is omitted in <term>Codex Ephraemi</term>, <term>Codex Bezae</term>, various Old Latin versions, the <term>Coptic</term>, <term>Armenian</term>, and <term>Ethiopic</term> versions. | **tell us**: According to the corrected <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, and others. The scholars <term>Griesbach</term> and <term>Lachmann</term> use a slightly different form of the command "tell" <note>ειπε vs ειπον</note> based on <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> and the <term>Vulgate</term>. The original hand of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> omits it entirely, matching the style of Matthew and Mark. | **or who**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and some Old Latin and Syriac versions read **and who** instead, likely influenced by the parallel passages in the other Gospels. | **this authority**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and the Latin versions reverse the word order.

**3. But answering**: A few manuscripts and some Latin and Syriac versions add the name **Jesus**. | **to them**: The original hand of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> reads **to him**. | **I will ask**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> uses a more intensive form of the verb "to ask" <note>επερωτησω</note>, as seen in Mark’s Gospel. | **I also**: The word order varies slightly in some <term>uncial</term> <note>capital letter</note> manuscripts. | **a question** <note>original: "λογον" — literally "a word"</note>: According to <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, and several early versions. The <term>Textus Receptus</term> and others read **one question** <note>ενα λογον</note>, matching the Gospel of Mark. The <term>Vulgate</term> translates this as "one word." | **and**: Present in <term>Codex Bezae</term> and some Syriac versions, but omitted by many Latin and Coptic sources.

**4. the baptism of John**: <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> and <term>Codex Bezae</term> include the definite article **the** <note>το</note> before John’s name. Scholars like <term>Lachmann</term> and <term>Tischendorf</term> omit this article, following <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> and the majority of other manuscripts.

**5. they reasoned**: Most manuscripts use a past tense form <note>συνελογισαντο</note>. However, <term>Lachmann</term> prefers the imperfect tense **they were reasoning** <note>συνελογιζοντο</note> based on <term>Codex Ephraemi</term> and <term>Codex Bezae</term>, which aligns with the wording in Matthew and Mark. | **among themselves**: Some versions omit the word **saying** <note>οτι</note> which introduces the quote. | **he will say**: <term>Lachmann</term> adds the word **to us** <note>ημιν</note> based on <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> and some Latin/Coptic versions, mirroring Matthew. | **why**: The word **then** <note>ουν</note> is added in the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and several versions, but is omitted by <term>Tischendorf</term> based on the earliest manuscripts like <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> and <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>.

**6. but if**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and some Syriac versions read **and if**. | **all the people**: Most early manuscripts place "all" <note>απασ</note> after "the people," while <term>Lachmann</term> and later manuscripts use a different word for "all" <note>πασ</note> before "the people." <term>Codex Bezae</term> and some Latin versions reorder the sentence to say **the people will stone us**. | **for they are convinced**: Note on spelling variation in <term>Codex Regius</term>.

The critical apparatus details numerous manuscript variations, particularly showing how later scribes often harmonized Luke's wording with the Gospels of Matthew and Mark.</summary>

**9** And he began to speak this parable to the people: "A man planted a vineyard and leased it to tenant farmers, and went on a journey for a long time. **10** And at the harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they might give him some of the fruit of the vineyard—"

---

<note>This section refers to verse 6 from the previous page</note>
(**for they are convinced** <note>original Latin: "e persuasum est enim"</note>): The Greek text of <term>Codex Bezae</term> and a corrected minuscule manuscript read **for they have been persuaded**; various Old Latin manuscripts and the <term>Vulgate</term> read **for they are certain** <note>original: "certi sunt enim"</note> (as opposed to one Old Latin version which says **for it is certain**); another Old Latin version has **for they know**, while the Latin side of <term>Codex Bezae</term> has **for he knows**; the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> proceeds with **concerning John, that** | <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (both original and corrected) reads **John** | **to be** <note>original: "ειναι"</note> (the <term>Vulgate</term> reads **to be** <note>original: "esse"</note>): <term>Codex Bezae</term> and several minuscule manuscripts read **to have been**, as do most Old Latin versions and the <term>Vulgate</term>.

**7. and they answered**: One Old Latin manuscript reads **and they answered saying**, another has **and answering they said**... the <term>Curetonian</term> and <term>Peshitta Syriac</term> read **and they say to him** | **not** (omitted by the original hand of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, but supplied by a later corrector) **to know**: <term>Codex Ephraemi</term> and <term>Codex Bezae</term> add **them**... some Old Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions read **we do not know** <note>original: "nescimus"</note> | **from where**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and others include the definite article (**the from where**); several other Greek manuscripts and Old Latin versions omit the word entirely.

**8. Jesus** (according to a later corrector of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>): The original hand of <term>Sinaiticus</term> reads **answering** (one Old Latin version reads **But Jesus said to them**) | **neither** (according to a corrector): The original hand of <term>Sinaiticus</term> uses a slightly different form of **neither** | **I tell you** (The early Christian writer <term>Tertullian</term> quotes this as **and I do not tell you**): A few manuscripts reverse the order to **to you I tell**.

**9—18.** <term>Epiphanius</term> (writing in the 4th century) says regarding the heretic <term>Marcion</term>: **Again, he cut out the parts concerning the vineyard let out to farmers, and the verse: "What then is this: The stone which the builders rejected."** <note>Marcion was known for editing the Gospel of Luke to remove elements he found too "Jewish."</note>

**9. and he began to speak to the people**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> reads **and he was saying**; one Old Latin manuscript says **moreover he was also saying**; the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> reads **and he began to say to them** | **to the people** (<term>Codex Regius</term> reads **to the crowd**) at this position in the sentence according to <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and most others... The scholar <term>Lachmann</term> places it after "to say" based on <term>Codex Guelferbytanus</term> and several Latin and Coptic versions... one Old Latin manuscript omits it | **a man** (also in the editions of <term>Griesbach</term> and <term>Scholz</term>) according to the major codices... but the <term>Textus Receptus</term> (standard printed text) adds **a certain** <note>Greek: "τις"</note> based on <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term>, the Syriac, and Armenian versions | **a man planted a vineyard** in this order according to most major manuscripts and the <term>Vulgate</term>... one Old Latin version reverses it to **a vineyard a man planted**... <term>Lachmann</term> (by error) has **a vineyard planted a man** based on <term>Codex Bezae</term>, several Old Latin versions, and the writings of <term>Ambrose</term> | **leased** <note>original: "εξεδετο"</note> according to the original hands of <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>, and <term>Vaticanus</term>... but the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and <term>Lachmann</term> use a different spelling <note>original: "εξεδοτο"</note> found in later corrections and many other manuscripts | **and went on a journey** (so also in some Old Latin manuscripts): <term>Codex Bezae</term> reads **but he himself went on a journey**; several others add the word **himself** | **times** (a few add the preposition **for**) **long**: <term>Codex Cyprius</term> uses a different grammatical case for **long times** | **long**: omitted in the original hand of <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, but added by later correctors.

**10. and** (a few manuscripts add **in the** as in Mark) **at the season** according to <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, <term>Bezae</term>, and <term>Regius</term>, as well as some Old Latin versions... <term>Codex Bezae</term> reads **but at the season**... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads **and in the season** based on <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> and the majority of later manuscripts and the <term>Vulgate</term>; the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> seems to have confused the word for "in" with "one" <note>reading "and in one of the times"</note> | **that from**: one manuscript reads **away from** | **the fruit of the**: omitted by the original hand of <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, but added by a later corrector | **they would give** <note>original: "δωσουσιν"</note> according to <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and several others.

<note>The following notes refer to verse 10</note>
(**that they might give** <note>original: "δωσωσιν"</note>): ... the reading **they might give** <note>original: "δωσιν"</note> is found in <term>Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> (C), <term>Codex Bezae</term> (D), <term>Codex Nitriensis</term> (R), and most other manuscripts. | **But the tenants** (found in various <term>Old Latin</term> and <term>Syriac</term> versions): <term>Old Latin</term> and <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> manuscripts vary (some saying "they beat him," others "they flogged him"); <term>Codex Bezae</term> says **but they, beating him** without the word "tenants"; the <term>Vulgate</term> says **who, having beaten him** | The phrasing **sent him away after beating him** follows <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (ℵ), <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (B), and <term>Codex Regius</term> (L). The standard text and <term>Tischendorf</term> place **beating** before **sent him away**, following <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> (A) and many others. | **empty-handed** <note>original: "κενον"</note>: due to a frequent scribal error, <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> (A) and others write **new** <note>original: "καινον"</note>; this error repeats in verse 11.

**11. and he proceeded to send another servant**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and <term>Old Latin</term> versions read **and he sent another servant** | **proceeded to** <note>original: "προσεθετο"</note>: <term>Codex Zacynthius</term> (Q) and others add **to them**, which <term>Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> (C) adds after "to send" | **another servant to send**: the order used in ℵ, A, B, and L is supported by various Latin versions. The standard text follows the order **to send another** found in C, Q, R, and many others, including <term>Syriac</term> and <term>Coptic</term> versions. | **and dishonoring**: Omitted in ℵ and one <term>Old Latin</term> version. Furthermore, the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> omits everything from "beating and" down to "this one too" in verse 12.

**12. and** (at the start of the verse): Omitted in <term>Codex Bezae</term> and one <term>Old Latin</term> version | **he proceeded to send a third**: used in ℵ, B, L, and many others including the <term>Vulgate</term>. The standard text uses the order **he proceeded to send a third [one]** with A, C, Q, etc. <term>Codex Bezae</term> and others simply say **he sent a third**. | **but they**: Omitted in <term>Codex Bezae</term> and several <term>Old Latin</term> versions | **this one too**: found in ℵ, B, C, D, L, Q, and most others. <term>Lachmann</term> reads **that one as well** (matching the phrasing in verse 11) based on A and some Latin/Vulgate sources. | **threw him out**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and some Latin versions read **sent him away empty-handed**.

**13. then the lord of the vineyard said**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> and the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> read **but the lord of the vineyard said** | **what shall I do?**: Omitted in the original hand of <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (B) but added by later correctors | **perhaps**: <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (B) uses a different Greek word for "perhaps" <note>original: "τυχον"</note> | **they will respect [him]**: Found in ℵ, B, C, D, L, Q, etc. The standard text and <term>Tischendorf</term> (though marked as doubtful) add **seeing him** before "they will respect," following A, R, and most others. <note>The translator notes this addition likely came from verse 14, as the parallel passages in other Gospels don't match closely enough to suggest it was accidentally removed here.</note>

**14. him**: Omitted in one version of ℵ | **the tenants**: Omitted in <term>Codex Bezae</term> and one <term>Old Latin</term> source | **they reasoned** (imperfect tense): Found in ℵ, B, C, D, L, Q, etc. <term>Lachmann</term> uses the aorist tense **they reasoned** <note>indicating a specific moment of decision</note> based on A and others | **with one another**: Supported by ℵ, B, D, L, and R. The standard text and <term>Lachmann</term> read **among themselves**, matching the phrasing in verse 5 and other parallel passages, as seen in A, C, Q, and the <term>Vulgate</term>.

<header>20, 15. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

"Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may become ours." **15** And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the lord of the vineyard do to them? **16** He will come and destroy these tenants and give the vineyard to others. When they heard this, they said, "May it never be!" **17** But he looked at them and said, "What then is this that is written:
<margin>Psalm 118:22</margin>
'The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the
<margin>[Matthew 21:44]</margin>
cornerstone'? **18** Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; but on whomever it falls, it will crush him." **19** <margin>242.1</margin> And the scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very—

---

<note>The following scholarly notes refer to the variations in ancient manuscripts for the verses above.</note>

**14.** <note>Referring to "let us kill him"</note> ... the <term>Coptic</term> and <term>Armenian</term> versions, and the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> and <term>Ethiopic</term> omit this phrase | **let us kill** <note>original: "αποκτεινωμεν"</note> (manuscript $\Gamma$ and others read "we are killing") is found in <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> (A), <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (B), and others, as well as the <term>Vulgate</term> and <term>Gothic</term> versions. The scholar Schulz notes: "Luke never used this word elsewhere." The <term>Received Text</term> <note>The standard printed Greek text used for centuries</note> adds **come** <note>original: "δευτε"</note> before "let us kill," likely taken from the parallel accounts in Matthew or Mark. This is supported by <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (ℵ), <term>Codex Bezae</term> (D), and <term>Origen</term> | **so that the inheritance may become ours** (manuscript L places "become" after "inheritance"): supported by several <term>Old Latin</term> manuscripts and the <term>Syriac</term>... whereas others read **and it will be ours**, likely following the wording in the Gospel of Mark.

**15.** **throwing him out** (manuscript $\Delta$ reads "repeatedly throwing," L reads "taking him"): several manuscripts omit **him**. | **then** <note>original: "ουν"</note>: omitted by the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> and certain <term>Coptic</term> manuscripts | **to them** (found in the <term>Vulgate</term>): some manuscripts read "to those," others "to the tenants," while <term>Codex Bezae</term> (D) and several <term>Old Latin</term> versions omit it entirely to match the wording in Mark.

**16.** **the tenants** (found in the corrected <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>): omitted in the original hand of Sinaiticus | **these**: some manuscripts read **those**, while <term>Codex Bezae</term> and the <term>Coptic</term> version omit it to match Mark | **But having heard** <note>original: "ακουσαντες δε"</note> is supported by <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (ℵ), <term>Vaticanus</term> (B), and most others. The <term>Old Latin</term> reads "but hearing" or "which having been heard" | **they said** <note>original: "ειπαν"</note>: found in ℵ, B, D; whereas the <term>Received Text</term> uses a different Greek form for "they said" <note>original: "ειπον"</note> supported by <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> (A) and <term>Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> (C).

**17.** **looked at**: <term>Codex Bezae</term> (D) uses a slightly different spelling | **this**: omitted in some <term>Old Latin</term> and other manuscripts | **has become** <note>original: "εγενηθη"</note>: manuscript U reads "was born" <note>original: "εγεννηθη"</note>, a common scribal error in Greek | **cornerstone**: some manuscripts use an alternate spelling for "corner."

**18.** **everyone**: one manuscript adds **therefore**, and the <term>Syriac</term> adds **for** | **on**: manuscript $\Lambda$ reads **into**.

**19.** **sought**: supported by most major manuscripts (ℵ, A, B, L). Some manuscripts use the imperfect tense **were seeking**, matching the Gospel of Mark | **the scribes and the chief priests** (one manuscript reads "the Pharisees," another "the priests"): supported by <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> (A) and <term>Vaticanus</term> (B). The <term>Received Text</term> reverses the order to **the chief priests and the scribes**, which is the more common order in the New Testament. <term>Marcion</term> <note>A 2nd-century teacher who created his own version of Luke</note> as cited by Epiphanius seems to omit the specific titles, reading simply "and they sought to lay hands on him and they feared." The church father <term>Tertullian</term> provides no evidence on this specific wording in his writings against Marcion.

# ACCORDING TO LUKE 20, 22.

...hands on him in that very hour, and they feared the people; for they knew that he had told this parable against them.

<margin>
20—26
Matthew 22, 16—22
Mark 12, 13—17
</margin>
20 $^{243.2}$ And having watched him closely, they sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in something he said, in order to hand him over to the jurisdiction and authority of the governor. 
21 And they questioned him, saying: "Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and you show no partiality <note>Literally "do not receive a face," a Hebrew idiom for favoritism</note>, but in truth you teach the way of God. 22 Is it lawful for us to [give tribute] to Caesar...

---

**hands** <note>original: "χειρασ"</note> (manuscripts c, 240, 244, and a few others omit) **the hands**: manuscript K, Π, and a few others read **the hand** <note>singular</note> | **in that very hour**: manuscripts 47 and e omit (see also the citation in Epiphanius’s work against Marcion) ... Manuscripts D, several Old Latin versions, and the Vulgate (except for the Forojuliensis) omit **in** | **and they feared**: Manuscript D and Old Latin 'e' read **but they feared** | **the people** (so in the Peshitta Syriac and the Bodleian manuscript; a few others and the Harclean Syriac margin read **the crowd**, the printed Harclean Syriac reads **the crowds** :: likely influenced by parallel passages) with א, A, B, C, D, E, H, K, L, M, R, U, Δ, Π and many others, including the Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Coptic versions ... G, S, V, Γ, Λ and about 80 others omit this | **for they knew** (א corrected): the original scribe of א omits this. The version in Epiphanius’s *Against Marcion* skips from "the people" to "this parable" | **he said** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note> (Manuscript D reads "he had spoken") placed here in א, B, (D), G, L, and several minuscules, as well as the Vulgate and Sahidic Coptic (the Curetonian Syriac omits **this parable**) ... The Received Text places this after **this parable** with A, C, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and 7 other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, most others, the Gothic, and Palestinian Syriac.

20. **having watched closely** <note>original: "παρατηρησαντεσ"</note> (*observantes* in the Vulgate and manuscript g²; the Peshitta Syriac adds *having waited for a favorable time*): Manuscript D, most Old Latin, Gothic, and Ethiopic read **having departed** (*and when they had recessed* in f, ff², i, l, q; *and when they departed* in a; *and when they returned* in c; *and they withdrew* in e) ... the Curetonian Syriac places this later; the Sinaitic Syriac omits it | **spies** <note>original: "ενκαθετ."</note> (spelled with a 'nu' in א, D, R; manuscript 69 reads "cleansed out"; the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use the standard spelling with a 'gamma' as in A, B, C, L, and others): Manuscript e reads *one and another*, to which the reading **one by one** <note>original: "ένα καθένα"</note> written in the margin of manuscript Δ in small letters corresponds. Manuscripts c, f, g¹, g², and the Vulgate translate as *insidiatores* <note>ambushers</note>, manuscript d as *obsiduanos* <note>hostages/besiegers</note>; it is not expressed in a, ff², i, l, q | **pretending** (א corrected): the original א reads **answering** | **to be**: Manuscript D omits. Similarly, manuscript e reads *who would simulate that they were just*, q reads *who simulated themselves to be just*, c and the Vulgate read *who would simulate themselves to be just* (contrast *to be just* in ff², i, l; *being just* in g² and the Gatarianus; manuscript d reads *speaking in guile that they were just*) ... manuscript a translates only *suborfingentes se* <note>secretly shaping themselves</note> for the whole phrase | **might catch**: Manuscripts E, H, K, Δ and many others use a slightly different verb form | **his**: manuscripts c and 299 read **him**, L reads **them** | **word** <note>original: "λογου"</note> with א, A, B, Λ, Δ, Π and 7 other uncials and the vast majority (f and the Vulgate read *him in speech*) ... c, k, r and about 25 others read **a word** <note>accusative case</note>, a few others read **by a word** ... L reads **words**, D, 86, and 7 read **the words**, most Old Latin read *the words* (*e* reads *the verbs*, *d* reads *of the words*) **of him**, so also Gothic and Armenian | **so as** with א, B, C, D, L and several others ... the Received Text uses a different conjunction with A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and 8 other uncials ... c, e, f, ff², i, l, q and several versions connect this as "because it preceded that they might seize" | **him**: Manuscript Δ omits | **to the jurisdiction to the governor**: Manuscript D, e, and Curetonian Syriac read **to the governor** ... manuscript i omits.

<note>The following notes represent the "apparatus criticus," a specialist's toolkit showing where different ancient copies of the Bible disagree on specific words.</note>

**30.** <note>This section refers back to the end of verse 30, "the second took her."</note> Manuscript g$^1$, i, l, q, the Vulgate, and Armenian place after **the second** <note>original: "ο δευτ."</note>: **the second** (*Old Latin and Vulgate follow with*) **the woman** <note>original: "την γυναικα"</note> (manuscripts a, c, f, g$^1$, i, l, q, Vulgate, Armenian: **her** or **it**) **and this one** <note>original: "και ουτος"</note> (c, l, q: **that one**; 235, a, f, g$^1$, i, Vulgate, Armenian: **this one himself**) **died** <note>original: "απεθανεν"</note> (manuscript U places this after "childless") **childless** <note>original: "ατεκνος"</note> with manuscripts Alexandrinus, P, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, uncial S, and most others (Old Latin, Vulgate, Armenian), the Curetonian and Curetonian-Sinaitic Syriac, and both... manuscripts 218, 245, 435, and ff$^2$ **omitted the verse** (skipping from the first instance of "childless" to the second).

**for the seven** <note>original: "γαρ επτ."</note> (all manuscripts) **had** <note>original: "εσχον"</note> (Codex Bezae reads "have," Old Latin 'd' reads "had") **her as a wife** (Curetonian and Sinaitic Syriac omit "wife"): manuscript 229* omits.

(Similarly, Clement of Alexandria writes: "those born in this age—beget and are begotten.") But Old Latin c, e, ff², i, l, q, and others omit **marry and are given in marriage** | **given in marriage** <note>original: "γαμισκ."</note> according to Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L, 33, 36, 157, Clement, Origen, and others; the Received Text reads a different form <note>original: "εκγαμισκοντ."</note> with many uncials... 35. **to attain** <note>original: "τυχειν"</note> expressed in manuscript 'a' ("but those who have been found worthy to reach that age") and 'd' ("to obtain this age"); not expressed in other Old Latin or Vulgate copies (which read "who are considered worthy of that age") | **given in marriage** <note>original: "γαμίζονται"</note> with Sinaiticus, Bezae, Q, R, Lambda, and others; Clement writes: "the sons of that age neither marry nor are given in marriage." (It is not clear which Gospel he refers to when saying "the form of the resurrection—in which they neither marry nor are still given in marriage.") 6. **these things which**: found in <term>Sinaiticus</term> <note>Represented by the symbol ℵ, one of the oldest and most important Greek Bibles.</note>, A, B, Q, X, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, and all other <term>uncials</term> <note>Manuscripts written in large, capital letters.</note> as well as most other sources, various Latin versions, the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation.</note>, Coptic, and both Syriac versions. (The Syriac Curetonian and the Ethiopic versions read: "See these things"; one Latin version reads: "Do you not see these things?") | **upon a stone**: Sinaiticus, C, L, X, and many others read "onto a stone" <note>original: "επ. λιθον"</note> (Note: this likely comes from the Gospel of Matthew; see also the notes on Mark). Additionally, Sinaiticus, B, L, and several others add the word **here** (so Tischendorf <note>A famous 19th-century biblical scholar and manuscript hunter.</note> in his *Synopsis*). This same word **here** is added before "stone" by Manuscript X and others, or after "stone" by Manuscript D and some Old Latin versions, reading "here in the wall." We have omitted **here** (Note: because it seems to have been transferred here from Matthew, as many scribes also did in the Gospel of Mark) following A, Q, and the majority of other manuscripts and versions. | **not**: Manuscript G reads **certainly not**. | **shall be thrown down**: Manuscript 69 reads **shall be shaken**.

7. **him**: Manuscript D and others add **the disciples** (one manuscript adds **his [disciples]**). (Note: Compare this to the Gospel of Matthew). | **therefore**: Omitted by Manuscript D and several others, including the Vulgate and Coptic. (Note: Compare the parallel passages in the other Gospels). | **when [these things] are about to happen**: Manuscripts 1, 131, and 209 read "when." Manuscript D and one Latin version read **at your coming** (Note: original Latin: "adventus tui"), reflecting Matthew's phrase "the sign of your presence."

8. **Watch out etc**: The *Pistis Sophia* <note>An ancient Gnostic text from Egypt.</note> (page 280) looks to this passage or its parallels, saying: "Tell them: Beware for yourselves of the doctrines of **error** <note>original: "πλανησ"</note>, otherwise many will come in my name saying: 'I am [he],' and 'I am not [he],' and they will **lead astray** many." | **in [my name]**: Some manuscripts and the Old Latin use "in the name," as seen in Matthew and Mark. | **saying** (without the word "that"): Supported by Sinaiticus, B, L, X, and the Ethiopic. Tischendorf adds **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> following A, D, and most other manuscripts and Latin versions. | **I am**: Some Latin versions and the Syriac add **the Christ** (Note: original: "ο χς"). (Note: This is likely taken from Matthew). | **The time is near; do not**: This phrase was accidentally omitted by the original scribe of Sinaiticus but added later by a corrector. | **do not** (without the word "therefore"): Supported by Sinaiticus, B, D, L, X, and others. The Received Text <note>The standard Greek text used for the King James Bible.</note> adds **therefore** <note>original: "ουν"</note> following Manuscript A and the majority of later sources.

9. **be terrified** (many manuscripts use a slightly different spelling; Latin versions translate as "do not be terrified" or "do not be afraid"): Manuscript D uses the word **fear**. | **must**: Some Syriac versions read **are about to**. | **for** (found in most Latin versions): Omitted by the Vulgate and several others. | **these things happen first**: Most manuscripts and versions follow this order, but Tischendorf follows Manuscript A and X in reading **happen these things first**.

10. **Then he said to them**: (The Harclean Syriac reads "Then I say to you"; one Latin version reads "Then he was saying in those days").

13. **it will result** without addition with the original hand of Sinaiticus and B (*a reads "so that it may be a testimony to you"*) ... c, ff², i, l, q add *for* ... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **but** <note>original: "δε"</note> with the corrected Sinaiticus, A, L, R, all other uncials, and almost all others, e, f, the Vulgate, Coptic, etc.

14. **settle** <note>original: "θέτε" (thete)</note> with <term>Sinaiticus</term> <note>A 4th-century Greek Bible, one of the most important manuscripts.</note>, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus (original hand), Bezae, Parisinus, Regius, Monacensis, Munich, and the cursive manuscripts 33 and p... the <term>Received Text</term> <note>The standard Greek text used from the Reformation until the 19th century.</note> reads **settle** <note>original: "θέσθε" (thesthe), a different grammatical form</note> with the later hand of Vaticanus, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, most <term>uncials</term> <note>Manuscripts written in all capital letters.</note>, and most others, as well as Origen and Cyril | **therefore** (added by a later hand in Sinaiticus) : omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus and Cyprian | **in your hearts** with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and others; also in the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Coptic versions... the Received Text reads **into your hearts** with Regius, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Pi, and most others; Origen and others (though some manuscripts omit "into") | **to meditate beforehand** (Origen reads simply "to meditate") : Manuscript Bezae reads **meditating beforehand**

15. **I will give you** (also Origen, Cyril, Cyprian, etc.) : Manuscript Bezae reads **to you I will give** | **which** : Manuscript Regius reads **the ones who** (likely a scribal error) | **to withstand or contradict** (the Coptic reads "nor," manuscript 69 reads "not," the Vulgate reads "and") with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Regius, and several others; or "to contradict or withstand" (as found in the Received Text and favored by scholars like Griesbach) with Alexandrinus, Regius, and most others... The Ethiopic version translates freely as "so that they cannot contradict you, nor rise against you."

16. **and also** as in some Latin and Syriac versions and Origen : others read "for" ... several manuscripts and the Vulgate read **and** without the "also" (the Curetonian Syriac is somewhat freer; the Ethiopic reads "and they will deliver") | **parents** : the Curetonian Syriac reads **wives** | **and brothers** : several manuscripts and Origen place this **after friends**, while others place it **after relatives** ... a few manuscripts and one Latin version omit it | **and relatives** : omitted by a few manuscripts.

17. **for my name's sake** placed **after "by all"** with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and many others including the Vulgate and Coptic... Tischendorf places it **before "by all"** (noting that the later position is also found in Matthew and Mark) with several uncials and the Peshitta Syriac ... some manuscripts omit it entirely.

Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his writings against heresies.</note> says of Marcion <note>A 2nd-century heretic who created his own edited version of the Gospel of Luke.</note>: "again he cut out 'not a hair from your head shall perish.'" This verse (which Origen has) is omitted in the Curetonian Syriac :: as it is in the parallel passages of Matthew and Mark | **shall perish** : Manuscript G adds **forever**.

19. **possess** <note>original: "κτήσασθε" (ktēsasthe), an imperative command: "gain!" or "acquire!"</note> with Sinaiticus, Bezae, and most others; interpreted as "acquire" or "gain" by the Apostolic Constitutions, Basil, and Cyril... Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **you shall possess** <note>original: "κτήσεσθε" (ktēsesthe), a future promise: "you will gain"</note> with Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and various cursives; this is reflected in most Latin versions ("you will acquire" or "you will possess"), the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Tertullian, in his work against Marcion, writes: "through patience, in-" <note>The quote from Tertullian breaks off at the bottom of the page.</note>

your souls. 20 <insert>Section 252, line 10</insert> <margin>Parallel to Matthew 24, 15-19 and Mark 13, 14-17</margin> But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has drawn near. 21 <insert>Section 253, line 2</insert> Then let those in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those in the midst of the city depart, and let those in the country not enter it, 22 because these are days of vengeance, so that all things which are written may be fulfilled. 23 <insert>Section 254, line 2</insert> Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days; <insert>Section 255, line 2</insert> for there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath upon the people.

—[referring to verse 19, some manuscripts read] "you shall save yourselves" <note>original Latin: "salvos facietis vosmet ipsos"</note> :: but the word **you will gain** <note>original Greek: "κτησεσθε" (ktēsesthe)</note> seemed to agree much more with the preceding words (hence the consensus of interpreters); furthermore, it is adapted to what the primary manuscripts provide: "the one who endures to the end, this one will be saved." <note>This is a reference to the parallel passage in Matthew 24:13.</note>

20. **Jerusalem** <note>original: "ιερουσαλημ"</note> with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, <term>Bezae</term>, <term>Nitriensis</term>, and Origen... but the <term>Received Text</term> reads **the Jerusalem** <note>original: "την ιερουσαλημ", adding the definite article</note> with Alexandrinus, Regius, and almost all other uncials, as well as Eusebius’ *Church History* and *Theophania*. 21—22. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies.</note> says regarding **Marcion** <note>A 2nd-century teacher who famously edited the Gospel of Luke to remove elements he considered "too Jewish."</note>: "Again he cut these things out: 'Then those in Judea flee to the mountains,' and the rest, because of what follows: 'until all that is written is fulfilled.'" 21. **to the** [mountains]: Codex Seidelianus I and Lectionary 49 read **upon the** <note>original: "επι τα"</note> (as in Matthew) | **flee etc.**: the Old Latin manuscript *ff²* reads "let them flee from its face into the mountains" | **and those in the midst**: Regius and others write it as one word <note>original: "εμμεσω"</note> as they usually do · **of it** (manuscript H reads "of her," and Bezae and others add **not**) **let them depart**: manuscripts 262 and others omit this. | **let them [not] enter**: the *Theophania* of Eusebius uses a different form of the verb "to enter."

23. **woe** without the addition of "but" <note>original: "δε"</note> following Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius, and the Old Latin... the Received Text adds **but** (as in Matthew and Mark) with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and almost all others including the Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions | Alexandrinus reads **in the womb** <note>original: "εν γαστρι", meaning pregnant</note> | **those who are nursing**: Regius adds a prefix to the word; Bezae uses the passive form "those being nursed," whereas the Latin version *d* translates it as "those who give milk" | **for there will be**: the original hand of Sinaiticus adds **in those days**; other manuscripts add **then** | **to the people**: with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and the Coptic and Armenian versions.
