Manuscript <term>Bezae</term> reads "of the broadsword" <note>original: "ρομφαιας"</note>; **all the nations** in this order with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, Vaticanus, Regius, 124, and Coptic ... the <term>Received Text</term> reads **the nations all** with Alexandrinus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Monacensis, Γ Δ Λ Π and eight other uncials, the majority of Old Latin, Vulgate, Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac (the Scholar’s Syriac reads "into every place"), Armenian, Ethiopic, and Eusebius in *History* and *Theophania*; **until** <note>original: "αχρι (ου)"</note> (Manuscripts Ephraemi Rescriptus, Regius, and many others, Eusebius omits "ou") with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, Regius, and about 20 others, and Eusebius’ *History* (though manuscripts vary) ... the <term>Received Text</term> reads **until** without the "ou" with Alexandrinus, Monacensis, Γ Δ Λ Π and eight other uncials, and a vast majority of others, as well as Eusebius’ *Theophania* (though some manuscripts of *History* include it); **times of nations** (Eusebius’ *History* and *Theophania*): <term>Vaticanus</term> precedes this with "and they shall be," likewise Regius, Coptic, and the Peshitta Syriac in a marginal note precede it with "times, and they shall be" ... <term>Bezae</term> omits it.

25. **there will be** <note>plural: "εσονται"</note> with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, Bezae, and manuscript 229 ... the <term>Received Text</term> reads **there will be** <note>singular: "εσται"</note> with Alexandrinus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Regius, Monacensis, Γ Δ Λ Π and eight other uncials, and the majority of others, as well as Eusebius’ *Theophania* (:: in Luke 21:11, the phrase "signs will be" <note>singular</note> was written by Luke without variation); **and upon**: manuscript Δ omits **and**; **in perplexity** <note>original: "εν απορια"</note> (<term>Sinaiticus</term> spells it *apōria*): <term>Sinaiticus</term> reads "and in perplexity," the Harclean version... and through confusion ... <term>Bezae</term> reads "and perplexity" (Old Latin manuscript d reads "and the perplexity of the sounding sea, etc."). Similarly, the Curetonian Syriac (reads "and the clashing of the hands of the nations") and the Scholar’s Syriac (proceeding: "because of the stupor of the sound of the sea"; the Curetonian proceeds with "and the sound as if"); **of the roaring** <note>original: "ηχους"</note> (<term>Griesbach</term> marks this) with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, L, M, Regius, Monacensis, and about 12 others, the Old Latin, Vulgate (see below), Coptic, Scholar’s and Peshitta Syriac (Curetonian see above), Armenian (adds "as if"), and Tertullian against Marcion 4, 39 ("he relates—and on the earth distress of nations being stunned as if by the sound of the moving sea") ... the <term>Received Text</term> reads **of the roaring [sea]** <note>original: "ηχουσης"</note> with <term>Bezae</term>, Γ Δ Λ Π and eight other uncials, and the majority of others (the Ethiopic reads "the sea will sound"), and Eusebius on Luke 203. The Latin versions read: "on account of the confusion of the sound (perhaps some add 'and') of the sea and (manuscript i omits) of the waves" in manuscripts c, ff², g¹, g², l, q and the Vulgate; "in the confession of the sound of the sea and the floods" in manuscript e; "in the stupor of the sound of the sea and the waves" in manuscript a; "for the sake of the anxiety as the sound of the sea and the movement of the waves" in manuscript f; "with the stupor of the sound of the sea and the movement" in Tertullian’s *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 22; **and of the waves** <note>original: "και σαλου"</note> (also Eusebius on Luke): manuscript K reads "and of the waves" (plural) ... the Peshitta Syriac in the Greek margin reads "and of the waves" ... the Curetonian and Scholar’s Syriac do not express this (unlike the Peshitta and Harclean versions).

26. <term>Sinaiticus</term>, Monacensis, and some others read **fainting** <note>original: "αποψυχοντων"</note> (manuscript 69 reads "of those fainting"); <term>Sinaiticus</term> reads "coming upon" <note>original: "επαρχομενων"</note>; **of the heavens** (manuscript Regius reads "the [powers] of the"): manuscript <term>Bezae</term> reads "those in the heaven," likewise Old Latin manuscripts d, a, c, ff² and Ambrose on Luke 1512 "which are in heaven," e and i read "in heaven" (as opposed to f, q, the Vulgate, Tertullian against Marcion and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, which read "of the heavens").

27. **in a cloud** (also in a, Vulgate, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac text and Harclean, etc., Eusebius on Luke 202 following): manuscript c and more than ten others, as well as e, f, ff², i, l ("with clouds"), Curetonian and Scholar’s Syriac, and the margin of the Peshitta, Tertullian’s *Resurrection*, and Ambrose on Luke read **in clouds** (:: compare Mark and Matthew); **with power** (the Scholar’s Syriac adds "great") **and glory**.

32. **this generation** <note>original: "η γενεα αυτη"</note>: on the other hand, Tertullian in *Against Marcion* book 4, chapter 39 has: <note>original Latin: "adhuc ingerit non transiturum caelum ac terram nisi omnia peragantur"</note> "He still insists that heaven and earth will not pass away unless all things are completed" | **this** <note>original: "αυτη"</note>: the <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>the standard Greek text used for centuries</note> reads **to this** <note>original: "ταύτῃ"</note> (as written) | **until** <note>original: "αν"</note>: Manuscript D and manuscript 33 omit this word | **all things** <note>original: "παντα"</note>: Manuscripts D, 50, 69, 90, 124, 248, the <term>lectionary</term> l, the Coptic, and the Curetonian <term>Syriac</term> read **all these things**; manuscript q, the Peshitta <term>Syriac</term>, the Armenian, and the Ethiopic read **these all things** (compare with similar passages).

33. **will pass away** <note>original: "παρελευσονται"</note> (the first instance): found in the <term>uncial</term> <note>capital letter</note> manuscripts Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and others (though 4 manuscripts read **will be shaken** <note>original: "σαλευθησοντ."</note>); found in most Old Latin versions and the <term>Vulgate</term>... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> and manuscripts 1, 127, 131, and others read the singular **it will pass away** <note>original: "παρελευσεται"</note> | **will certainly not pass away** <note>original: "ου μη παρελευσονται"</note>: found in ℵ, B, L, 13, 33, 157... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads **will not pass away** <note>original: "ου μη παρελθωσι"</note> (mirroring the phrasing in Matthew and Mark) as found in Manuscripts A, R, X, and others.

34. **But** <note>original: "δε"</note>: found in manuscripts A, B, C, L, R, and most others, including the <term>Vulgate</term>: manuscripts ℵ, D, 1, 13, 69, 209, 346, and others omit it, as does the Latin version of Irenaeus | **yourselves** <note>original: "εαυτοις"</note>: Manuscripts C, L, V, and others read **to them** <note>original: "αυτοις"</note>... Methodius (quoting: "For the Lord says, take heed, lest etc.") and Cyril omit it | **be weighed down** <note>original: "βαρηθωσιν"</note>: found in ℵ, A, B, C, L, R, and the vast majority of manuscripts including Cyril... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads a different form of **be weighed down** <note>original: "βαρυνθωσιν"</note> found in Manuscript D and H; Epiphanius writes, "let your [hearts] not be weighed down, he says" <note>original: "μη βαρυνεσθωσαν, φησιν, υμων αι..."</note> | **your hearts** <note>original: "υμων αι καρδιαι"</note>: found in ℵ, C, D, L, R and most manuscripts; the editor Lachmann places the pronoun after the noun **the hearts of you** <note>original: "αι καρδ. υμων"</note> following manuscripts A, B, X, and the Latin versions | <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and others use the spelling **κρεπαλη** for dissipation | **come upon you suddenly** <note>original: "επιστη εφ υμ. αιφνιδ."</note>: found in ℵ, B, D, L, R, the Latin and Vulgate (the Curetonian <term>Syriac</term> reads "that day come upon you suddenly"); Methodius omits "suddenly"; Tertullian in *Against Marcion* 4, 39: <note>original Latin: "et insistat eis repentinus dies ille velut laqueus"</note> "and that day press upon them suddenly like a snare"; Eusebius reads "come upon you"... the editor Lachmann reads **suddenly come upon you** based on Manuscript A, the Coptic, and the Peshitta <term>Syriac</term>... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads **suddenly upon you come** following Manuscript C and others | **suddenly** <note>original: "αιφνιδιοσ"</note> (spelling variations exist in various manuscripts like ℵ, A, C, F, K, M, R, X, etc.) | **the day**: Manuscript D, K, and V omit the article "the."

35. **that [day] as a snare; for [it] will come** <note>original: "εκεινη ωσ παγισ· επ. γαρ"</note>: found in ℵ, B, D, L, 157, many Old Latin manuscripts, the Coptic, and Methodius ("and that day come upon you as a snare"). Tertullian (see above, after the word 'snare' he proceeds to verse 37)... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads: **that [day]; for as a snare it will come** <note>original: "εκεινη· ωσ παγισ γαρ επ."</note> following A, C, R, X, and most manuscripts, the Vulgate, and the <term>Syriac</term> versions. The Ethiopic reads freely: "that day suddenly, like a net that descends" | **will come upon** <note>original: "επεισελευσεται"</note>: found in the original hand of Sinaiticus, B, D, and some Latin versions (which use words for "enter")... the <term>Textus Receptus</term> uses a slightly different form **will come upon** <note>original: "επελευσεται"</note> following the corrected Sinaiticus, A, C, L, R, and most others (manuscript 157 uses **will stand over**).

<header>22, 1. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

## CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>
Verses 1 and following:
Mark 14, 1 and following;
Matthew 26, 1 and following
</margin>

1 Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover, was drawing near. 2 And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking a way to put him to death; for they were afraid of the people.

<margin>
Verses 3–6:
Matthew 26, 14–16;
Mark 14, 10 and following;
John 13, 2 and 27
</margin>

3 Then Satan entered into Judas, called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve. 4 And he went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers <note>Greek: *strategois*, referring to the Temple guards or commanders</note> as to how he might [betray him to them].

---

<note>The following section is the critical apparatus, which compares different ancient copies of the Bible to find the original wording.</note>

**XXII, 1.** **was drawing near** <note>original: "ηγγιζεν"</note>: (Also found in Philoponus): Manuscripts D, L, and several Old Latin versions (b, e, g¹, l, q) read **drew near** <note>original: "ηγγισεν"</note> | **now/but** <note>original: "δε"</note>: Manuscript K **omits** this.

**2.** **and the chief priests and the scribes sought** (Also in Philoponus): Manuscripts D and E read **but the chief priests and scribes sought** | **the [way]** <note>original: "το"</note>: Manuscript D and 254 **omit** this | **to put him to death** <note>original: "ανελωσιν"; Latin: "interficerent"</note>: Manuscript D reads **to destroy him** <note>original: "απολεσωσιν"; Latin: "perderent"</note> | **for they feared the people**: Manuscript G **omits** this | **for** <note>original: "γαρ"</note> (also in several Latin and Syriac versions): Manuscripts D, b, c, and the Vulgate read **but** <note>original: "δε"</note>.

**3.** From what Epiphanius <note>a 4th-century bishop</note> says when refuting Marcion <note>a 2nd-century teacher who edited the Gospels</note> and from Tertullian, it can be inferred that Marcion removed the part written here about Satan. He likely wrote it this way: **But Judas went away and conferred.** | **Satan**: Written as **the Satan** <note>original: "ο σατ."</note> in manuscript U and many others, as well as by Eusebius; most major manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, etc.) lack the word "the." | **into Judas** (also in Origen and Eusebius): Manuscript D and some Coptic and Ethiopic versions read **into the heart of Judas**. | **called** <note>original: "καλουμενον"</note>: Manuscript G **omits** this | **called**: Major manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae) use "called," while others (Alexandrinus, etc.) use a slightly different Greek word for "named" <note>original: "επικαλουμενον"</note>. | **Iscariot**: There are many spelling variations in the ancient manuscripts, such as **Iscarioth**, **Scarioth**, or **Ischariotes**. | **who was** <note>original: "οντα"</note>: Several Latin versions read **one of** <note>original: "unum"</note> or **one** <note>original: "unus"</note>. | **of the number**: Some manuscripts (b, c, f, etc.) simply say **of the twelve** without the word "number."

**4.** **with the chief priests**: Most major manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.) have this; however, some (manuscript C, P, and several Latin versions) add **and with the scribes**. | **and officers**: Omitted by manuscript D and many Old Latin versions. Conversely, some manuscripts (C, P, and some Syriac versions) add **of the temple**. This is not found in Marcion's version. | **how**: Some manuscripts use a different Greek form for "how" <note>original: "οπωσ" or "ινα"</note>. | **betray him to them**: There is a slight variation in word order between "him" and "them" across the various manuscript families (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus vs. the majority of later manuscripts).

### Critical Notes on the Text

**16.** **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> (also found in the Old Latin and the Latin translation of Origen): Manuscript C (original hand), D, and X omit this. | **no longer** <note>original: "ουκετι"</note> found with C (corrected), D, P, X, and many other manuscripts, including most Old Latin and Vulgate copies... but manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C (original hand), H, L, and others omit it. **18.** **that**: Found in ℵ, A, X, and most manuscripts and versions... <note>The following notes represent the "critical apparatus," where the editor Tischendorf lists differences found in ancient manuscripts.</note>

*A few manuscripts read* **"is,"** *others read* **"was"** | **from among them** (also found in manuscripts c, f, the Vulgate, and both Syriac versions): Manuscript D, 142, and several Old Latin versions (a, b, e, etc.) omit this. | **about to [do]:** Manuscripts D, L, and others place this after **this**; manuscripts 69 and 346 place it after **doing**. Manuscript f reads *which of them was greater*, and manuscript q reads *who then is the greatest of them.*

25. **But he [said]:** Several manuscripts and the Syriac version add **"Jesus"** (the Curetonian Syriac reads *our Lord*). | **lord it over** (also in Origen and Basil): Several manuscripts (U, X, 13, 69, etc.) use a stronger compound verb **"exercise lordship over"** (similar to the parallel passages in other Gospels). | **and those who exercise authority over them are called Benefactors** (also the corrected Sinai manuscript): The original Sinai manuscript reads **"and the rulers of the [nations] exercise authority over them and [are called] benefactors"** (this seems influenced by the wording in Matthew).

26. **let it be** (spelled **γινεσθω** or **γεινεσθω** in א, B, D, L, T): The common text and many other manuscripts (A, X, Γ, Δ, etc.) use the spelling **γενεσθω**. | **the** (omitted by D and 69) **younger** (various Latin versions use *iunior* or *adulescentior*): Manuscript D, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate read **"smaller"** or **"lesser"** (*minor*); the Coptic versions read *like a boy*. | **the one who serves:** Manuscript D reads **"the servant"** (*deacon*); several Latin versions likewise read *ministrator* or *minister*.

27. **For who** (the Sinai manuscript adds **"the"**) **is greater** (many manuscripts including A, B, and the Latin versions add the word **"is"**) **the one who reclines or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines?**: Manuscript D reads **"rather than the one who reclines"**... Manuscript X omits this section. | **Is it not the one who reclines?**: Several Old Latin versions (a, c, e, etc.) read *among the nations indeed it is the one who reclines, but among you it is not so, but the one who serves*... the Curetonian Syriac omits this, proceeding directly to *Am I not...* etc. | **But I am** through **as the one who serves** (also in Eusebius and Basil): Manuscript D reads **"For I have come into your midst not as the one reclining but as the one who serves."** Origen acknowledges this, saying: *The one who said: I have come not as one reclining but as one serving.* Similarly, another Latin translation of Origen reads: *Behold, I am in your midst not like one reclining at the table but like one serving.* This addition is also confirmed by manuscript c: *I however am in your midst not as one reclining but as one serving.*

<header>22, 28. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

[...your] midst I am as the one who serves. 28 But you are those who have stayed with me in my trials. <margin>Matthew 19:28</margin> 29 And I grant to you, just as my Father granted to me, a kingdom, 30 that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, <sup>272.5</sup> and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. 31 <sup>273.10</sup> Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded <note>The Greek verb "exetēsato" implies a formal request or demand, as in a legal trial.</note> to have you <note>Here "you" is plural, referring to all the disciples.</note> to sift you like [wheat...] <note>The text continues on the next page.</note>

***

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of differences found in ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. These notes help historians determine the most likely original wording.</note>

*...servant (likewise Sedulius <note>Coelius Sedulius, a 5th-century Christian poet</note>: "I am in your midst not as one reclining but as one serving") |* AL 69. **"in the midst"** | **"I am"** appears *after* **"your"** in the Sinai manuscript (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), L, T, and several Old Latin and Vulgate versions, as well as Eusebius... Stephens, Lachmann, and Tischendorf place it *before* **"in your midst"** based on manuscripts A, Q, X, and almost all others, along with various Old Latin versions, Basil, and Chrysostom.

28. **But you are those who have stayed** (also in Eusebius): Manuscript D reads: **"And you have grown in my service as the one who serves, those who have stayed."**

29. **I grant** (and after **"to you"**): Manuscripts A, 1, and about ten others, along with Pseudo-Athanasius, read **"I appoint"** <note>original: "διατιθημι" (diatithemi)</note>; Origen reads **"I will place."** | **"to you"** (also in Eusebius): Manuscript A, 12, 16, a few others, and the Syriac and Coptic fragments add **"a covenant."** <note>The Greek word for "grant" (diatithemai) is the root of the word for "covenant" (diathēkē).</note> Likewise Origen: **"and I will place for you a covenant, to eat and drink at..."** etc. Compare also Eusebius: **"the table, which those will partake in for whom he granted the covenant because they stayed with him in his trials, that they may eat"** etc. | **"my"** [Father]: Manuscripts D, Γ, and others omit this. Compare the Gnostic text *Pistis Sophia*: **"concerning this very thing you told us once in a parable: 'You have endured trials with me. I will establish a kingdom with you, just as my father established it with me, so that you shall eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and you will sit upon twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel.'"**

30. **that you may eat** (with manuscripts B, D, T): Other major manuscripts (Sinaiticus, A, L, Q) read a slightly different spelling of **"you may eat."** | **"you may drink"**: Manuscript L and Eusebius read **"you drink."** Additionally, manuscripts 13, 69, 346, and various Syriac and Coptic versions add **"with me."** | **"in my kingdom"** (Manuscripts D, and several Latin and Syriac versions omit **"my"**): Found in Sinaiticus, A, B, and most other versions. Origen reads: **"at the table of the Father in the truth."** | **"you will sit"** (with Sinaiticus, A, B, and others): Some versions read **"you are sitting"** or **"you might sit."** | **"thrones"** (Manuscripts D, 13, 69, etc. read **"onto thrones"**): The corrected Sinaiticus, D, X, and about twenty others, along with several Old Latin versions, the Syriac, and the Persian versions, add **"twelve"** [thrones] <note>likely harmonizing this verse with the parallel passage in Matthew 19:28</note>. Origen notes: **"the Lord promised to his disciples that he would give them to sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel."** | **"judging"**: Manuscripts B, T, and others place this after **"the twelve tribes."**

31. **Simon, Simon** (the Sinai manuscript omits the second **"Simon"**): Found without the introductory phrase **"And the Lord said"** in B, L, T, and Coptic versions. Stephens and Lachmann include the introduction **"And the Lord said"** based on Sinaiticus, A, D, Q, and almost all other manuscripts and the Vulgate. Other Latin versions read: **"Moreover, the Lord said to Peter: 'Simon, Simon...'"**

wheat; 32 but I have prayed for you <note>The Greek "you" here is singular, specifically referring to Peter.</note> that your faith may not fail. <margin>33 s</margin> And when you have turned back <note>Greek: "epistrepsas," often translated as "converted" or "returned."</note>, strengthen your brothers. 33 <margin>Matthew 26, 33-35; Mark 14, 29-31; John 13, 36-38</margin> <margin>275.1</margin> But he said to him: Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death. 34 But he said: I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know me.

<note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," where scholars list differences found in various ancient manuscripts to determine the most accurate original text.</note>

*...but the Lord said to Simon Peter: "Simon, behold..." <note>original Latin: "autem dominus Simoni Petro: Simon ecce"</note>; Manuscript 'mm' says "but Jesus said to Simon: 'Simon, behold...'" <note>original Latin: "ait autem Iesus Simoni: Simon ecce"</note>; Codex e and others read "but he said to Peter that Satan..." <note>original Latin: "ille autem dixit Petro quoniam satanas"</note>; Cyprian's writings read "but the Lord said to Peter: 'Behold, Satan...'" <note>original Latin: "dixit autem dominus ad Petrum: Ecce satanas"</note>; The Syriac Peshitta reads "But the Lord Jesus said..." etc. | **to sift you** <note>original Greek: "υμας του σινιασαι"</note> (some manuscripts add "you" in the singular; the Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac versions repeat the plural "you"): The Vulgate and Jerome read "that he might sift you" <note>original Latin: "vos ut cribraret"</note>; other Old Latin versions (b, e, f, etc.) use "that he might winnow you" <note>original Latin: "ut vos ventilet"</note>; manuscript 'c' uses "for sifting" <note>original Latin: "ad cernendum"</note>; Tertullian uses "that he might sift you" <note>original Latin: "uti cerneret vos"</note>; Cyprian uses "that he might harass you" <note>original Latin: "ut vos vexaret"</note>. Additionally, the Sinai manuscript (א) has "to sift" with a correction. Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father, c. 347–407 AD</note> asks: What does "to sift" mean? It means to lead, to lead around, to shake, to move, to agitate, to torment.*

32. **but I have prayed** <note>original Greek: "δε εδεηθην"</note>: Manuscript L reads "but I prayed" with a slight spelling variation. | **fail** <note>original Greek: "εκλιπη"</note>: Found in manuscripts א, B, D, K, L, and many others, including early versions like the Ethiopic and writers like Chrysostom and Cyril. The spelling variation "ekleipe" is found in A, E, G, H, and others. | **and when you have [turned back]**: Manuscript D and the Old Latin 'e' and Sahidic versions read "**but you, turn back and** [strengthen]." | **strengthen**: Found in most major manuscripts (א, A, B, K, L, Q); some manuscripts use a slightly different form of the verb. | **brothers**: Manuscript Δ accidentally wrote "eyes" <note>original Greek: "οφθαλμους"; Latin: "oculos"</note>. | **your** (some versions add a phrase here): Several Old Latin versions (a, b, c, e, etc.) and the Vulgate add: "and pray that you do not enter into temptation."

33. **But he said to him**: Manuscript Δ reads "But he said to him" (with a different word order); Old Latin versions and the Vulgate read "Who said to him"; several other versions specifically add the name "Petrus" (Peter) or "Simon."

34. **But he said**: Some Syriac and other versions add <insert>Jesus</insert>. | **Peter**: The Syriac Peshitta reads "Simon," while the Curetonian Syriac omits the name entirely. | **not** <note>original Greek: "ου"</note>: Most manuscripts include this, while some emphasize it with a double negative <note>original Greek: "ου μη"</note>. | **will crow**: Minor spelling variations exist between "phonesei" and "phonese." | **rooster**: The Curetonian Syriac adds "twice." | **until**: Different manuscripts use different Greek words for "until" (heos, heos hou, heos otou). Some versions (like the Vulgate and others) use "before" <note>original Greek: "πριν η"</note>, which matches the wording in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. One Latin manuscript (e) changes the order to: "in this night before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." | **deny that you know me**: <note>The Greek text here is complex because it contains a double negative that translates literally as "deny not to know me."</note> There are many variations in word order and whether "not" is included. Manuscript D reads "deny me, that you do not know me." The Sinai manuscript (א) and others read "deny to know me." Scholars note that the variation "deny to know" is likely the original, as it is a more difficult reading that later scribes might have tried to "correct."

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a technical record where the editor compares different ancient copies of the Bible to note variations in the text.</note>

35 and following. Concerning Marcion, in Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius was a 4th-century bishop who wrote against heresies; Marcion was a 2nd-century figure who edited the Gospel of Luke to fit his own theology.</note> volumes 316 and 345: *He cut out the words: "When I sent you out, did you lack anything," and the following parts, because of the phrase: "And this which is written must be fulfilled, namely: 'And he was counted among the lawless.'"* <note>original Greek: "παρεκοψε το· οτε απεστειλα υμας, μη τινος υστερησατε, και τα εξης, δια το· και τουτο το γεγραμμενον δει τελεσθηναι, το· και μετα ανομων συνελογισθη."</note>

35. **money-purse** <note>original: "βαλλαντιου"</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, B, D, L, Q, S (second corrector), T, X (second corrector), Δ, Λ (second corrector), Π, 8 other uncials <note>Uncials are manuscripts written in all-capital letters.</note> and many others... but the "Received Text" <note>represented by the symbol ς</note> reads **money-purse** with a single 'l' <note>original: "βαλαντιου"</note> with manuscripts ℵ, X, Γ, Δ, Π and many others (also found in the published edition of Origen, volumes 3 and 653) | **and sandals:** Manuscript Γ and a few others, including the Ethiopic version, omit this | **of anything** <note>original: "τινοσ"</note> (corrected ℵ): original ℵ reads **something** <note>original: "τι"</note> at the end of the verse | **did you lack:** Manuscript Γ reads a slightly different verb form; others (131, 209) read "were you lacked" | **they said** <note>original: "ειπαν"</note> with manuscripts B, D, L, T... the "Received Text" reads "they said" <note>original: "ειπον," a different spelling</note> with ℵ, Q, X, Γ, Δ, Π, 9 other uncials, and almost all others including Origen and Chrysostom. Manuscript A reads **he said** | **nothing** <note>original: "ουθενοσ"</note> with A, B, Q, X, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials and about 50 others... the "Received Text" and Lachmann read **nothing** <note>original: "ουδενοσ," a more common spelling</note> with ℵ, D, L, U, Λ, many others, Origen, and Chrysostom.

36. **And he said:** with ℵ (original hand), D, the Latin version 'e', and the Jerusalem Syriac; Chrysostom... ℵ (corrected), B, L, T and 4 others, the Sahidic and Coptic versions read **But he said**; the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac read **He said**; the Ethiopic reads **And he said**... the "Received Text," Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **He said therefore** with A, Q, X, Γ, Δ, Π, 9 uncials, and most others, including several Latin versions, the Vulgate, the Philoxenian Syriac, and the Armenian (Origen reads **He said therefore to them, Jesus**) | **to them:** Omitted by manuscript D and a few others, including some Old Latin versions and the Armenian | **money-purse** <note>original: "βαλλαντιον"</note> with ℵ, A, B, D, L, Q, X (second corrector), Δ, Λ (second corrector), Π, 8 uncials and many others... the "Received Text" uses the single 'l' spelling with X, Γ, Δ and many others | **let him take** <note>original: "αρατω"</note> (Latin: *tollat*), also Origen: Manuscript D reads **he will take** <note>original: "αρει"</note> (Latin: *tollet*). Compare Basil <note>original: "Baregg500"</note>: *"Let him take or he will take; for many of the copies have it this way—implying it is not a command but a prophecy where the Lord foretells the future"* | **let him take likewise and a bag:** (Chrysostom omits this) | **bag:** (Most Latin versions and the Vulgate read *peram*): the Old Latin 'e' reads *chilotrum* <note>A Greek-derived word for a satchel.</note> | **having:** the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, and the Ethiopic (not the Persian) add **a sword** | **let him sell** <note>original: "πωλησατω"</note> with ℵ, A, B, F, K, L, M, Q, T, U, X, Π, and many others, the Sahidic version, Origen, Basil, and Chrysostom... Manuscript D reads **to sell** (Latin: *vendat*); others (E, G, H, S, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, and about 115 others) including the Armenian and Chrysostom read **he shall sell** | **the:** Manuscript Δ reads **and the** | **his:** Manuscript U reads **his own** | **let him buy** <note>original: "αγορασατω"</note> with ℵ, A, B, G, K, L, M, Q, T, X, Δ, Π and many others, Origen, Basil, and Chrysostom... many others (D, E, F, H, S, U, V, Γ, Λ), the Armenian, and Chrysostom read **he shall buy** (Latin: *emet*).

37. **to you:** Omitted by Manuscript D and Old Latin 'b' | **that** without the word "still" <note>original: "ετι"</note> (approved by Schulz) with ℵ, A, B, D, H, L, Q, T, X, 10 others, Old Latin 'b' and 'f', Sahidic, Coptic, Jerusalem Syriac, and Ethiopic... the "Received Text" and Tischendorf add **still** with Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 uncials, and most others, including many Latin versions, the Vulgate, and Curetonian Syriac | **to be fulfilled:** Manuscript Λ and others read "to be completed" | **the** and **and:** various Latin versions (Vulgate, etc.) follow "in me" with **and with**; others (Λ, and several Old Latin) read **that also** (*quod et* or *quod ut*) | **with** (Manuscript D adds "the") **lawless:** various Latin versions use different terms: *cum iniustis* (with the unjust), *cum iniquis* (with the iniquitous), *cum sceleratis* (with the wicked). Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians, wants it translated as: *and he was reputed with those who were without law*, adding: "Although in the Latin manuscripts, due to the simplicity of the translators, it is poorly rendered as: 'And he was reputed with the iniquitous,' nevertheless it should be known that another [reading exists] among..."

"The Greeks mean <term>anomon</term><note>original: "ανοµον"</note> (lawless), which is written here, whereas another word <term>adikon</term><note>original: "αδικον"</note> (unjust) is used in the Latin volumes; for 'lawless' refers to one who is without law—but 'unjust' refers to one who is inequitable." | **and for** (Old Latin *it* and the Vulgate read *etenim*, manuscript *q* reads *nunc* [now]) **the**: [Manuscript] *τ* reads **and the for** . . . The plural **the** [plural things] is supported by Δ, Χ, Γ, Λ, Π, nine other uncials, and the majority of manuscripts, as well as the Vulgate and other Syriac versions.

<header>22, 43. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

my will, but let yours be done. 43 $^{283. 10}$ And there appeared to him

---

Many <note>abbreviated "plu"</note> [manuscripts], Dionysius of Alexandria (in a commentary according to Mai, volume 6, page 165), Basil, and the Ethiopic version (verse 283, "to pass over") ... Lachmann <note>A 19th-century editor of the Greek New Testament</note> reads **take away** <note>original Greek: "παρ-ενεγκε"</note> with the Greek Codex Bezae and about 25 others, Origen (volume 1, page 292), Dionysius of Alexandria (according to Mai), and John of Damascus; likewise, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Peshitta Syriac, and Armenian versions read **transfer** <note>original Latin: "transfer"</note>. (Also, the Apostolic Constitutions, book 5, chapter 14, section 4: "Father, take away from me this cup") ... the Sahidic, Coptic, and Curetonian Syriac, and the scholars' editions read **let it pass from me** :: compare the parallel passages. | **this cup** (so also the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, though the original hand of Sinaiticus wrote **this, the cup, this**) with Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius, etc. ... but the Majority Text and Lachmann read **the cup, this** <note>original: "το ποτη. τουτο"</note> with Codices Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and many others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Curetonian Syriac, and both Origen and Dionysius of Alexandria | **be done** <note>original: "γινεσθω"</note> (Codices Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus spell it "γειν.") with the vast majority of manuscripts, including Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and the scholars' editions ... but the Majority Text and Lachmann read **come to pass** <note>original: "γενεσθω"</note> with Codices Ephraemi, Monacensis, etc.

43. 44. **And there appeared** up to **upon the ground**: present in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and many others; however, these verses are marked with asterisks <note>indicating the scribe doubted their authenticity</note> in Codices Cyprius, Venetus, etc., and the Peshitta Syriac; they are marked with obeli <note>a symbol (÷) used by ancient scholars to indicate suspected additions</note> in Codex Tischendorfianus and others; they are also found in the Old Latin, the Sahidic Coptic, the Curetonian Syriac, and the Armenian editions. Furthermore, they are confirmed by:
Justin Martyr in his *Dialogue with Trypho* 103 ("For in the memoirs [it is written] that sweat like clots was poured out as he was praying and saying: 'Let this cup pass, if it is possible'"); Irenaeus (page 219: "Unless he had taken something from Mary... he would not have sweat clots of blood"); Hippolytus (in *Against Noetus*, "and being in agony he sweats and is strengthened by an angel"); Dionysius of Alexandria (according to Gallandi: "A 'sweat of blood' is said as a proverb regarding those who are in extreme grief and agony, just as of those who mourn bitterly it is said 'they weep blood.' By saying 'as it were clots of blood,' he did not declare the sweat to be actual clots of blood; for he did not say the sweats became blood according to literal likeness; for this 'as it were clots' presents it—thus the clots of his sweat flowed down wonderfully like drops of blood, so that he might, as it were, dry up and banish the fountain of fear from our nature... such is also that which was spoken, how an angel was standing by the Savior and strengthening him," etc. These depend on what is found in the Oxford Catena 159: "It is said as a proverbial phrase," etc.); Caesarius (in Gallandi: "And being in agony he sweat, and his sweat became as it were clots of blood, and an angel appeared strengthening him, says the divine Luke"); Arius, according to Epiphanius ("For, he says, an angel of the Lord appeared strengthening him, because he was in agony, and he sweat, and his sweat became to him as clots of blood") and again in Epiphanius ("He sweat, he says, and his sweat became as it were clots of blood falling down upon the ground; and an angel of the Lord appeared strengthening him"); and Epiphanius in his *Ancoratus* 31 ("But also 'he wept' is found in the Gospel according to Luke in the **uncorrected copies**, and Saint Irenaeus used this testimony in his work *Against Heresies* against those who say Christ appeared only in appearance. But the **orthodox removed the saying**, having become afraid and not understanding its purpose and its great power: 'and being in agony he sweat, and his sweat became as clots of blood, and an angel appeared strengthening him'"); Didymus the Blind (according to Canisius); Chrysostom ("And so that heretics might not say that he was faking the agony, for this reason there were sweats as...")

<summary>This page analyzes the textual variations of Luke 22:42-44, focusing heavily on the passage describing Jesus's "bloody sweat" and the angel's appearance. The critical apparatus documents how early "orthodox" editors may have removed these verses out of fear that they showed too much human weakness in Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the textual analysis of the "Agony in the Garden" in the Gospel of Luke. The previous page discussed the variants of verse 42 ("not my will, but yours be done"). This page focuses on the highly controversial verses 43 and 44, which describe the appearance of a strengthening angel and Jesus's "sweat of blood." These verses are absent from many of the earliest and most important manuscripts, leading to centuries of debate among scholars and church fathers.</meta>

<page-num>695</page-num>
<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 22, 44.</header>

...an angel from heaven strengthening him. 44 And being in agony

---

<note>The following section is a "critical apparatus," a dense list of historical evidence from ancient manuscripts and early Christian writers regarding whether these verses belong in the Bible.</note>

**drops of blood and an angel strengthening him appeared** <note>original Greek: "θρομβοι αιματος και αγγελος ενισχυων αυτον εφανη"</note>: This is supported by Theodoret (volume 1, page 692 and volume 4, page 271), Dionysius the Areopagite (in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 4, **concerning the angel who strengthened Jesus** <note>original Greek: "περι του αγγελου του τον ιυ ενισχυσαντοσ"</note>), Cosmas Indicopleustes (citing Bishop Theodosius of Alexandria), Leontius (in *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*), and others. It seems the Eusebian Canons <note>an ancient system for cross-referencing the four Gospels</note> also support this, as many manuscripts like M and Λ have the number 283 with canon 10 written next to these verses (though Codex Δ mistakenly places these numbers next to the phrase "nevertheless not" etc.). On the other hand, Codex L has 283 with canon 1 at the phrase "and having knelt" etc., and Codex Q has 283 at "Father, if you will," while 284 is at "and having risen." 

Regarding the Latin witnesses, support comes from Hilary (page 1061), Jerome's work against the Pelagians (book 2), and Augustine in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* (book 3, chapter 12), who wrote: "**he clearly said what those [other Gospel writers] had kept silent about: both that he was comforted by an angel while praying, and that while praying more intensely his sweat became bloody and the drops ran down to the ground**" <note>original Latin: "dixit sane quod isti tacuerunt..."</note>. Also Facundus...

Conversely, and for this reason, Lachmann <note>a prominent 19th-century editor</note> puts [**and there appeared... to the ground**] in brackets. These verses are omitted by the original hands of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Nitriensis (R), Codex Borgianus (T), and the original hand of manuscript 13 (which only has **and there appeared**, with the rest added by a much later corrector), and manuscript 69. (However, they are added in the margin of manuscript 124 and in lectionaries <note>books of scripture arranged for liturgical reading</note> after Matthew 26:39). 

Furthermore, as already indicated, the Syriac Peshitta and five other manuscripts mark these verses with asterisks, while manuscript "r" and four others mark them with obeli <note>ancient symbols used to indicate that a passage is likely inauthentic</note>. They are also omitted by various Coptic (Sahidic and Bohairic) and Armenian manuscripts (and some certainly omit verse 44). A note in the margin of a Syriac manuscript states: "**This passage is not found in the gospels among the Alexandrians, and for this reason Cyril did not include it in his 18th homily. Concerning Cyril, see below.**" 

Greek and many Latin manuscripts, according to Hilary (page 1062), omit it: "**nor should you be ignorant that in very many Greek and Latin manuscripts, nothing is found written regarding either the arriving angel or the sweat of blood**" <note>original Latin: "nec sane ignorandum a vobis est..."</note>. This is also true of most manuscripts (it seems) according to Jerome's work against the Pelagians (book 2): "**for he says: in certain copies, both Greek and Latin, it is found in Luke's writing: 'An angel appeared to him' etc.**" 

Scholion 34 <note>an ancient marginal note</note> remarks: "**It should be noted that some of the copies do not have the part about the drops of blood; however, Dionysius the Areopagite, Gennadius of Constantinople, Epiphanius of Cyprus, and other holy fathers testify that this usage is present.**" 

The Lectionaries omit this in the reading for Luke 22:39–23:1, but they include it in the reading for Matthew 26:2–27:2, where Luke 22:43–45 is read after Matthew 26:39. Athanasius, though he often could have used this passage, did not. Cyril of Alexandria, in his commentary on this place (Homily 146 in the Syriac edition), passes over it. Likewise Ambrose in his commentary on Luke (page 1517), and John of Damascus (page 464), who, when copying from "having arrived at the place" through "enter into temptation," skips from "let your [will] be done" directly to: "**and having come to the disciples he found them sleeping and said to them: pray that you not [enter into temptation] etc.**" 

Furthermore, Anastasius of Sinai testifies: "**they attempted to remove the drops of blood of the sweat of Christ.**" Likewise, the Syrians are mentioned by Photius (Letter 138 to Theodore): "**therefore do not think it is fitting for this passage of the Gospel to have been cut out for you, even if it seems so to some of the Syrians, as you said.**" The Armenians are mentioned by Nikon (concerning the impious religion of the most wicked Armenians): "**they even removed from the holy Gospels the voice saying 'and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.'**" He even adds: "**but also the story that teaches us how a woman was brought to Jesus**" <note>This refers to the "Pericope Adulterae," the story of the woman caught in adultery, which was also frequently omitted from early manuscripts.</note>. Isaac the Catholicos also writes (Chapter 5): "**these Christ-fighting Armenians [removed] his sweats from the Gos[pel]**"...

<summary>This page provides an extensive list of manuscript evidence and patristic citations regarding the authenticity of the "bloody sweat" and the "strengthening angel" in Luke 22:43-44. It documents how some early traditions and regions (like Alexandria and Armenia) omitted the verses, while others argued they were deleted by heretics.</summary>

<note>This section is the critical apparatus, used by scholars to track differences in ancient copies of the Bible.</note>

**having erased from the gospel** <note>original Greek: "αγγελίου απαλειψαντες"</note>: Others (as occurs in the *Collection of the year 881* according to Canisius) are argued to have deleted these words. On the other hand, John the Armenian (I take the name and words from Wetstein <note>Johann Jakob Wetstein, an 18th-century theologian</note>) says: "**and in the divine scriptures Saturnilus added many heresies, even into the Gospel according to Luke; there appeared etc.**" <note>original Greek: "και εν ταις θειαις γραφαις προσετιθει ο σατουρνιλος πολλας αιρεσεις, ως και εεις το κατ. λουκ. ευαγγελιον· ωφθη δε etc."</note> Furthermore, it is not sufficiently clear whether Marcion <note>a famous 2nd-century heretic who edited the Gospel of Luke</note> read these verses, as Epiphanius and Tertullian are silent on the matter.

**44.** Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) reads **becoming** <note>original: "γεναμενοσ"</note> | Codex Γ reads **he prayed** | **and it happened** <note>original: "και εγενετ."</note> is supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac versions... whereas Tischendorf and Lachmann read **but it happened** <note>original: "εγεν. δε"</note> based on Codex Bezae (D) and others | **the sweat:** Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) omits "the" | **as if:** Codex Bezae (D) and Arius-Epiphanius read **as** <note>original: "ωσ"</note> | **falling down:** <note>This notes a grammatical disagreement in the Greek between a singular form (referring to the sweat) and a plural form (referring to the drops).</note> The singular form is found in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and the Vulgate; however, Tischendorf and Lachmann use the plural **falling down** <note>original: "καταβαινοντεσ"</note> based on Codex Bezae (D), Codex L, and many others.

**45. toward:** Codex Bezae (D) and others read **upon** <note>original: "επι"</note> | **the disciples:** most manuscripts omit **his** <note>original: "αυτου"</note>, but it is added in some versions like the Ethiopic | **them sleeping:** supported by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and others.

**46. why:** omitted in Codex Bezae (D) | **that you may enter:** Codex Bezae (D) places this phrase after **into temptation**.

**47. still:** <note>A minor grammatical variant in the Greek conjunctions "still" vs "but still".</note> | **a crowd:** Codex Bezae (D) and the Syriac add **a large** crowd <note>original: "πολυς"</note> | **the one called:** Codex Bezae (D) and others use a different Greek word for **the one named** <note>original: "ο καλουμενοσ"</note> | **Judas:** Some Latin and Greek manuscripts add **Iscariot** | **one of the twelve:** omitted in some manuscripts | **was leading:** <note>Fragmentary note on the verb form</note>.

<note>The following scholarly notes (the "critical apparatus") compare how different ancient hand-copied versions of the Bible describe these events. Symbols like א (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and D (Bezae) represent the oldest surviving parchment books of the New Testament.</note>

Regarding the phrase "enough [of this]": some manuscripts omit it; manuscript 'b' reads "leave him be" <note>Latin: "dimitte eum"</note> (though after the phrase "he healed him," it adds "But Jesus said: 'Let [it be] even unto this'"). | Regarding "and touching the ear, he healed him": Manuscripts D, a, and ff² read: "and stretching out his hand he touched him and the ear was restored" <note>Latin: "et extendens manum suam... tetigit eum... et redintegrata est auris eius"</note>. Manuscript 'i' places this after the phrase "power of darkness." Manuscript 'l' adds: "thus the scriptures will be fulfilled" <note>Latin: "sic implebuntur scripturae"</note> and specifies he touched the "right ear which had been cut off" <note>Latin: "auriculam eius dextram cui fuerat amputata"</note>. Manuscript 157 reads: "and touching the one who was struck, he healed the severed ear." | The word "ear" <note>Greek: "ωτιου"</note> appears without the word "his" in manuscripts א, B, L, R, T, and the Armenian version (the Syriac version reads "the ear which had been struck")... other sources including the Textus Receptus <note>The standard printed Greek text used for centuries</note> add "his" <note>Greek: "αυτου"</note>.

**52.** The name "Jesus" <note>abbreviated as "ις" in Greek</note> is found in manuscripts א, A, B, and T... the Textus Receptus adds the definite article "the Jesus" with L, R, and others... Manuscript D and the Syriac versions omit the name here. | The preposition "to" <note>Greek: "προς"</note> is found in א and G... while the Textus Receptus and most editors use "against" <note>Greek: "επι"</note> based on A, B, D, and L. | Regarding "you have come out" <note>Greek: "εξεληλύθατε"</note>: several manuscripts use a different grammatical form of the same verb <note>Greek: "εξηλθατε" or "εξηλθετε"</note>, likely influenced by the phrasing in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. | "Clubs": some manuscripts add "to seize me" <note>original: "συλλαβειν με"</note> at the end of the verse.

**53.** "Daily": Manuscript D moves the word order. | "With you in the temple": Manuscripts D, 157, and the Sahidic Coptic version read "in the temple with you." | "Not": Some manuscripts read "and not." | "The": Manuscript L omits the article before "hands." | "But": Minor spelling variations between "αλλ" and "αλλα" <note>Both mean "but" in Greek</note>. | "Your hour": There is significant debate over the word order of "your" <note>Greek: "υμων"</note>. We have not added the word "him" <note>Greek: "αυτον"</note> following the most reliable ancient codices, though later versions include it. | "The house": Confirmed by the oldest Greek manuscripts and Eusebius.

<note>The following notes provide a "critical apparatus," which scholars use to track differences between ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. These variations help researchers determine the most authentic original text.</note>

**v. 59 about an hour** <note>original: "unius"</note> | **about**: Manuscript Λ and others omit this; it is also not expressed in the Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac translations. |
**insisted, saying** <note>original: "diischyriz. legōn"</note> (most Latin versions: **contending, he said**; the Vulgate: **he was affirming, saying**) **truly**: Codex D (Bezae) reads: **insisted, "truly I say..."** (the Latin side of D: **it was being contended: "in truth I say"**). Instead of "and after an interval," etc., manuscript *a* reads: **whom a little while after, when someone had seen him, he said: "truly this one also was with Jesus"** etc. | **he was**: Omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (א*) but added later. | **Galilean**: Omitted in Manuscript Δ.

60. **what you say**: Manuscripts א, D, and a few others read **what thing** <note>original: "ti"</note> **you say**, similar to most Latin versions and the Vulgate <note>original: "quid"</note> (though some read "quod"), following the style of the Gospel of Matthew. | **still**: Omitted in some manuscripts. | **while he was speaking** (the Syriac Peshitta adds **to these things of Peter**): Manuscripts U, 1, and 209 read **of him speaking**; several other manuscripts read **while Peter was speaking**. | **a rooster** (as edited by Griesbach and Scholz) together with א, A, B, D, L, X, and many others (plus Coptic and Armenian) ... versus **the rooster** (as edited by Griesbach and Scholz) found in several minuscules <note>handwritten manuscripts in smaller script</note> and the Sahidic version.

61. **and having turned**: Codex D and Sahidic read **but having turned**. | **the Lord** (Manuscript T* mistakenly wrote **the Peter Lord**): Codex D, 106, 124, 131, and several others, as well as Coptic and Syriac versions, read **Jesus**. | **Peter** (the Sahidic and Coptic place this before "remembered"): Omitted in Codex D, 157, and the Gatinger manuscript. | **the word** <note>original: "tou logou"</note> with A, D, Γ, Δ, Λ and many others ... versus **the utterance** <note>original: "tou rhematos"</note> in א, B, L, T, X and others (which is how it appears in Matthew and Mark). | **that** <note>original: "hoti"</note> (found in Latin versions): Omitted in Codex D and Armenian versions. | **before**: One manuscript adds **or**. | **today** with א, B, K, L, M, T, X and 25 others, Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac (some place it before "crowing," others after "deny"): The editors Lachmann and Tischendorf omit it, following A, D, and many other manuscripts and early translations. | **deny** (various spellings in Greek) **me three times**: Codex D and the Curetonian Syriac read **three times you will deny me**; the Latin versions read **three times me you will deny**; additionally, some manuscripts add **that you do not know me** or **that you know [me]**.

62. **This verse is omitted** in several Old Latin manuscripts (a, b, e, ff², i, l). | **went out** without additions in א, B, D, K, L, M, T, X and 150 others, and the Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian versions ... whereas editors Lachmann and Tischendorf add **Peter**, following A, Γ, Δ, Λ and many others including the Vulgate and Syriac (which uses the name "Simon" as it usually does). This verse is also in Matthew, but there the context seemed to require it less.

63. 64. Epiphanius (writing in the 4th century) quotes from Marcion’s version of the Gospel: **those who held him mocked him, beating and striking him, saying: "prophesy, who is the one who hit you?"** He transcribed these freely, emphasizing only what he intended to discuss. He continues his argument (Refutation 68): **that the "holding," the "mocking," the "beating," the "striking," and the "prophesy who hit you" — this was not a mere appearance <note>referring to the Docetic heresy that Jesus had no physical body</note>, but is indicative of a physical touch and a fleshly reality, as is clear to everyone.**

**Technical Notes on the Ancient Manuscripts**

**12. [with each other]**: The spelling of Pilate <note>Greek: "Peilatos"</note> follows manuscripts A, the original hand of B, and T; the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf use the spelling "Pilatos" following Sinaiticus (א), the third hand of B, D, L, and others. The word order "Pilate and Herod" <note>original: "Pilatos kai ho Herodes"</note> is found in the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf, supported by A, D, and many others; however, manuscripts א, B, L, and T support the order "Herod and Pilate." | **on that day**: Some manuscripts (209, 150ev) read "at that hour." | **with each other**: This is omitted in the Coptic and some Syriac versions. | **for they had previously...**: This entire phrase is omitted in manuscript D (Codex Bezae). | **with one another**: Manuscripts א, B, L, and T use the pronoun "themselves" <note>original: "autous"</note>, while others use "each other" <note>original: "heautous"</note>.

**13. [Pilate then]**: Spellings of Pilate vary as above. Manuscript D reads "But Pilate..." | **having called together**: Found in the original hand of B, D, and F; the Received Text uses a slightly different Greek form <note>sygkalesamenos</note> found in later manuscripts. | **and the people**: Manuscript D and the Old Syriac read "and all the people," while some Latin versions use the term "plebe" <note>original Latin: "the common people"</note>.

**14. [to them]**: Manuscript Γ uses "to themselves." | **brought**: Manuscript D uses "brought down" <note>original: "katenegkate"</note>; Latin versions vary between "presented" and "brought." | **as one who misleads**: The Old Syriac reads "whom you told me of." Some manuscripts (1, 13, 69) use "perverts" <note>original: "diastrephonta"</note> instead of "misleads." | **and behold I**: Omitted by some Greek and Sahidic manuscripts. | **having examined**: Manuscript D and the Syriac place this before "in your presence." | **no basis for a charge**: There are several variations in the Greek and Latin for "no cause/fault." Some Latin manuscripts read "I find no cause in this man" (*nullam causam invenio in hoc homine*), while the Vulgate reads "I found no cause in this man" (*nullam causam inveni in homine isto*). | **concerning the things you accuse**: Omitted by manuscript D and others.

**15. [for he sent him back to us]**: This is a major variant. Manuscripts א, B, K, L, M, and the Sahidic read "he sent him back to us." However, the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "for I sent you to him" <note>original: "anepempsa gar hymas pros auton"</note>, following A, D, and the majority of Latin and Vulgate manuscripts. The Curetonian Syriac and Armenian versions read "for he sent him to him" <note>Herod back to Pilate</note>.

**Technical Notes on the Ancient Manuscripts**

**15. [nothing... has been done by him]**: The Greek phrase for "has been done" <note>original: "estin pepragmenon"</note> is reversed in manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note>. The Latin versions (Old Latin and Vulgate) translate this as "nothing was done to him" or "nothing was found in him."

**17. [the missing verse]**: This verse—"For he was obliged to release one man to them at the feast"—is found in the Received Text <note>represented by the symbol ς</note> and some editors like Griesbach. It appears in various positions across different manuscripts. For example, some versions of the Syriac say "it was Pilate's custom," while some Latin manuscripts say "according to custom" <note>original: "secundum consuetudinem"</note>. In many early sources like the Armenian and certain Uncials, the wording varies regarding "the prisoner whom the people wanted." This verse is also recognized in the Eusebian Canons <note>an ancient system for cross-referencing the four Gospels</note>, specifically under Luke section 309, which corresponds to the release of a prisoner in Matthew and Mark. However, Tischendorf omits it here, following major manuscripts like A, B, K, L, T, and the Sahidic Coptic.

**18. [cried out]**: The form of the verb "cried out" <note>original: "anekragon"</note> is supported by Sinaiticus (א), B, L, and T. The Received Text and Lachmann use a slightly different form <note>original: "anekraxan"</note> based on manuscripts A, D, and others. | **all together**: The spelling varies slightly between "pamplethei" and "pamplethē" across the major codices. | **away with this man**: Manuscript D repeats this phrase twice for emphasis. | **Barabbas**: Manuscripts א, B, D, L, and T include the definite article "the" before Barabbas <note>original: "ton Barabban"</note>, whereas many others (A, Γ, Δ, etc.) omit it.

**19. [thrown]**: The word for "thrown" or "cast" <note>original: "blētheis"</note> in B, L, and T is replaced by "having been cast" <note>original: "beblēmenos"</note> in the Received Text and manuscripts A and D. | **into prison**: Manuscripts א, B, L, T, and X use the phrasing "in the prison" <note>original: "en tē phylakē"</note>, while the Received Text and most others use "into the prison" <note>original: "eis phylakēn"</note>.

**20. [and / therefore]**: Most major manuscripts (א, A, B, D, L, T) use "and" <note>original: "de"</note>, but the Received Text and others use "therefore" <note>original: "oun"</note>. | **addressed**: Some manuscripts (א, B, L, T) add "to them" <note>original: "autois"</note> after the verb for "addressed," while others (A, P, X, etc.) leave it implied. | **Jesus**: A few manuscripts use the pronoun "him" instead of the name "Jesus."

# 23, 22. ACCORDING TO LUKE

but they kept shouting, saying: “Crucify, crucify him!” 22 <gloss>312.9</gloss> But he spoke to them a third time: “Why, what evil has this man done? I have found in him no cause <term>aition: a legal ground or basis for a charge</term> for death; therefore, having punished him, I will release him.” 23 <gloss>313.1</gloss> But they were insistent with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed. 24 <gloss>314.1</gloss> And Pilate gave judgment <note>original: "epekrinen" — a formal judicial decision</note> that their demand should be granted; 25 and he released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, whom they were asking for, but Jesus he delivered over to their will.

***

**Textual Notes and Manuscript Variations**

**21. [they kept shouting]**: The Greek word <note>original: "epephōnoun"</note> is translated in various Latin versions as "they were shouting out" or "they were crying out." In the manuscript known as Codex Bezae (D), the word is "they cried out" <note>original: "ekraksan"</note>. **[saying]**: This word is omitted in Codex Bezae. **[Crucify, crucify]**: The word "crucify" appears twice in the oldest Greek manuscripts like Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B), and in several later versions. However, some ancient translations like the Sahidic Coptic and several Old Latin manuscripts only record the word once.

**22. [nothing]**: Some manuscripts and the Old Syriac version add the word "for" <note>original: "gar"</note>, making it "For I have found nothing." **[no cause]**: While most manuscripts say "no cause" <note>original: "ouden aition"</note>, some early versions like the Old Latin and the Syriac say "nothing worthy" <note>original: "ouden aksion"</note>—as in "nothing worthy of death." Codex Bezae (D) uses the phrasing "no single charge" <note>original: "oudemian aitian"</note>. **[found]**: Most manuscripts use the past tense "found" <note>original: "euron"</note>, but Codex Bezae and the Syriac versions use the present tense "I find" <note>original: "euriskō"</note>. **[I will release him]**: Codex Bezae reverses the word order to "release him I will."

**23. [insistent]**: The manuscript Sinaiticus (ℵ) uses a slightly different verb meaning "they lay upon" or "pressed." **[that he be crucified]**: Codex Vaticanus (B) uses an active form: "to crucify him." The Sahidic Coptic and some Latin versions simply translate this as "Crucify him!" **[their voices prevailed]**: Several ancient manuscripts, including the Alexandrian (A) and the later "Received Text" <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note>, add the phrase "and those of the chief priests." This addition might have been included by later scribes to emphasize the specific role the religious leaders played in the trial, as seen in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. However, the earliest and most reliable manuscripts (ℵ, B, L) leave this out, as "their voices" already refers to the crowd including the leaders.

**24. [and Pilate gave judgment]**: There is a minor spelling difference in "Pilate" between the oldest manuscripts. Most early sources agree on the wording here, though some later manuscripts add "the" before Pilate.

**25. [he released]**: Some later manuscripts add "to them" <note>original: "autois"</note>, likely a stylistic addition to clarify for whom he released the prisoner. **[for insurrection]**: In some manuscripts, the name **Barabbas** is explicitly added here ("he released for them Barabbas"). **[for insurrection and murder]**: One ancient manuscript (M) has a spelling error, writing "voices" <note>original: "phōnōn"</note> instead of "murder" <note>original: "phonon"</note>. **[delivered to their will]**: Some Old Latin manuscripts add a detail here found in the Gospel of John: "they took Jesus therefore, and he carrying the cross for himself was led away." This is a classic example of "harmonization," where a scribe adds details from one Gospel into another to make the story more complete.

The technical notes highlight how different ancient manuscripts recorded the intensity of the crowd and the specific legal phrasing of the judgment.</summary>

"Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing." <gloss>321. 1</gloss> And they divided his garments and cast lots. 35 And the people stood watching; <gloss>322. 2</gloss> and the rulers also scoffed <note>original: "exemuktērizon," literally "turned up their noses at him"</note> at him, saying: "Others

<note>The following section is the scholarly apparatus, comparing different ancient versions and manuscripts of the Bible.</note>

*they know what they do* <note>original Latin: "sciunt quid faciunt"</note>) Apostolic Constitutions <note>A 4th-century collection of Christian law</note> 2, 16, 1 ("as it is written in the Gospel: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do") and 5, 14, 8 (there again "what they do") Eusebius's Canon, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an influential early Church Father</note> in various volumes and often (loosely in places, such as "forgive them this sin; for they do not know etc.") Theodoret 1, 992 and 1382, John of Damascus 709, Hilary 782 etc. Confirmed also by the Clementine Homilies 11, 20: "for the teacher himself, being nailed up, prayed to the Father for those who were killing him that the sin might be forgiven, saying: Father, forgive them their sins; for they do not know what they are doing." Likewise the Acts of Pilate 10, 233. See also the words of James the Just from Hegesippus in Eusebius's History 2, 20, 16: "I beseech you, Lord God Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing..."

**[Note on verse 42: "Jesus, remember me..."]**

The reading "to Jesus" is found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> (original hand), <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, <term>Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus</term> (original hand), and Codex L (in these Greek manuscripts, the name could be read in the dative case "to Jesus," though this is not the case in the Sahidic or Coptic versions or in Origen. Otherwise, these same manuscripts do not include the word "Lord," which seems to have been introduced when the word "to Jesus" was changed into the dative case). It is also found in the Sahidic and Coptic versions, and in Origen (where it is placed after "remember me"). The Latin translation of Origen twice reads "Lord Jesus" (4,517: "who, crucified with Christ, cried out to him from the cross: Lord Jesus, remember me when..." etc.; 4,523: "just as he who confessed and said: Lord Jesus, remember me when..." etc.) ... The <term>Received Text</term> and Lachmann read **to Jesus** <note>original: "tō Iēsou"</note> with the corrected Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, and almost all other manuscripts, the Old Latin, the Vulgate (Latin: *ad Iesum*), the Curetonian, Peshitta, and Harclean Syriac, the Ethiopic, and Origen. Augustine (3,53) writes: "he said to Jesus: Lord, remember me etc." ... <term>Codex Bezae</term> reads **to him** | **remember me** without the word **Lord** according to Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, the original Ephraemi Rescriptus, and several minuscules, the Sahidic, Coptic, and Harclean Syriac versions, Origen, and Basil of Seleucia ("he offered: remember me in the..."). ... The <term>Received Text</term> adds **Lord**, and Lachmann places **[Lord]** in brackets, following Codex Alexandrinus, various other major manuscripts, the majority of versions including the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic, and Origen ("through his confession by which he said: Remember me, Lord" etc.), Hilary, and the *Acts of Pilate*. Some manuscripts (Q, e, f, etc.) place **Lord** before **remember me** | **when you come** (so Origen, Eusebius on the Psalms, Chrysostom): Codex Bezae and others read "when you shall have come," as do the Latin versions | **in your kingdom** according to the majority of manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, etc.) and Origen ... but Vaticanus, Codex L, and the Vulgate read **into your kingdom** . . . Codex Bezae reads **in the day of your coming.** Furthermore, these words of the thief are recorded in the *Descent of Christ* and the *Acts of Pilate* as: **Lord, when you reign, do not forget me.**

**43. [Note on Jesus's response]**

Epiphanius (writing against Marcion, 317 and 347) notes: "<insert>Marcion</insert> cut out the part: 'Today you will be with me in paradise'." Additionally, regarding these words, Origen (4,455) says: "This saying has so disturbed some people as being inconsistent <note>They felt it contradicted the idea of a future judgment</note> that they have dared to suspect it was added to the Gospel by certain unscrupulous hands: namely, the phrase 'today you will be with me in the paradise of God'." Chrysostom (4,788) writes: "The <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>A dualistic religious movement</note>—seizing upon this passage, say: Christ said, 'Truly, truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise'; therefore the reward of good things has already occurred, and the resurrection is superfluous. For if the thief received the good things on that day, and his body has not yet risen even today, there will be no resurrection of bodies hereafter—for if there were a resurrection of the body, he would not have said: today" etc. | **And he said to him** according to Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Codex L, and the Coptic versions; however, the <term>Received Text</term> and Lachmann add **Jesus** with Alexandrinus and the majority of versions ... Codex Bezae reads: **And Jesus, answering, said to the one who was rebuking him** (Latin: *qui obiurgabat eum*) | **Truly I say to you** with Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and Codex L ... the <term>Received Text</term> and Lachmann read **Truly, I say to you** (the usual word order) with the majority of manuscripts, versions, Athanasius, Cyril, and Chrysostom (but some versions of Athanasius, Chrysostom, and the *Acts of Pilate* read **Truly, truly**) ... Codex Bezae reads **Have courage** | **today** (the Harclean Syriac, Ethiopic, and some Coptic manuscripts add **that**) so Origen, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Epiphanius, Cyril, etc.: Hesychius of Jerusalem (Question 49) notes: "Some indeed read it this way..."

**[Critical Notes on Verse 43: Jesus's promise to the thief]**

...they read: "truly I say to you today," and they place a punctuation mark; then they follow with "you will be with me in paradise." <note>This minor change in punctuation—moving the comma after "today"—was used by some early interpreters to suggest Jesus was speaking "today" rather than promising the thief would enter paradise that very day.</note> And indeed, the <term>Curetonian Syriac</term> <note>An ancient 5th-century Syriac manuscript of the Gospels</note> distinguishes it in this way ("today that with me etc."). Similarly, it is found in the <term>scholia</term> <note>ancient marginal comments</note> 237, 239, 254. Others—they force the saying; for they say that those reading must place a punctuation mark and read: "Truly I say to you today," and then thus follow with "you will be with me etc." Theophylact says the same regarding this passage. Furthermore, the <term>Descent of Christ</term> <note>An apocryphal text describing Jesus's entry into the underworld</note> (page 310) has it this way: "and immediately he said to me: Truly, truly I say to you today, you will be with me in paradise." Compare also the <term>Acts of Pilate</term> <note>Another apocryphal work, also known as the Gospel of Nicodemus</note>: "and he said to him: today I tell you the truth, that I may have you in paradise with me." | **with me you will be** (The *Acts of Pilate* reads "with me in paradise you are") and <term>Origen</term>... the Sahidic, Coptic, and Ethiopic versions read "you will be with me." | **in paradise** (The Curetonian Syriac reads "in the garden of Eden"): Origen three times adds "of God," though his Latin translator does not, likewise with "of the Father."

**[Critical Notes on Verse 44: The darkness]**

**and it was** with <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, <term>Bezae</term>, and others. The Sahidic and Origen’s Latin translator read simply **it was**. The <term>Received Text</term> reads **but it was** with <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> and almost all others. The Old Latin manuscript *c* reads "but the hour was as if the sixth." | **already** with <term>Vaticanus</term>, <term>Codex L</term>, the Coptic versions, and Origen’s Latin translation. The <term>Received Text</term> omits this with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Bezae</term>, and the Vulgate. (The Ethiopic reads "and when it was noon at the time of the sixth hour"). | **about** (some manuscripts read "as it were"): found in <term>Sinaiticus</term>... but omitted by others. | **and darkness occurred until the ninth hour**: omitted by the <term>Harclean Syriac</term>. | **ninth** <note>original Greek: "enatēs"</note> with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>... the <term>Received Text</term> uses an alternate spelling <note>original: "ennatēs"</note>. Regarding the "sixth" hour and Mark 15:25’s "third" hour, compare John 19:14.

**[Critical Notes on Verse 45: The failing of the sun]**

**the sun having failed** <note>original: "tou hēliou eklipontos," suggesting an eclipse</note> with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, <term>Codex L</term>, several lectionaries, the Sahidic ("the sun being about to set"), Coptic ("the sun about to fail"), and the margin of the <term>Philoxenian Syriac</term>. Origen (1, 414) writes: "from the Gospels, that the earth was shaken and the rocks were split and the tombs were opened and the curtain—down to the bottom, and darkness occurred in the time of day while the sun was failing." He also writes (page 415): "and there occurred also a certain divine sign from heaven, the sun failing and the other wonders etc." Origen’s Latin translator (3, 56) notes: "But Matthew said it thus: From the hour... but Luke: It was already about the sixth hour and darkness was made over all the earth until the ninth hour, the sun failing. But also Mark: When it was the sixth hour etc."

The same Origen’s Latin translation (3, 922) notes: "regarding this text, i.e., Matthew 27:45, some slander it—and say that just as it is accustomed to happen in a failure <note>eclipse</note> of the sun, so the failure of the sun happened then. But a failure of the sun from the beginning of the world has always happened in its own proper time. How therefore could a failure of the sun happen when the moon was full? <note>Passover always occurs during a full moon, making a natural solar eclipse impossible.</note> We say therefore that Matthew and Mark did not say a failure of the sun happened then; but neither does Luke, according to most examples which have it thus: 'And it was about the sixth hour and darkness... ninth, and the sun was darkened.' In certain examples, however, it is not held as 'Darkness occurred, and the sun was darkened,' but thus: 'Darkness occurred over all the earth, the sun failing.' And perhaps [someone] dared..."

->## PAGE 716<-
->### ACCORDING TO LUKE 23:45–46<-

328. 2 And the veil of the temple was torn down the middle. 46 329. 1
<margin>Psalm 30 (31), 6</margin> And crying out with a loud voice, Jesus said: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." And having said this, he breathed his last. 47 330. 2

---

<note>The following notes discuss the debate over whether the text should say the sun was "darkened" or "failed" (eclipsed).</note>

"...someone, as if wishing to say something more clearly, put: *With the sun failing*, instead of: *And the sun was darkened*, thinking that the darkness could not have happened otherwise except by the sun failing. However, I think rather that the enemies of Christ’s church changed this word, specifically that the darkness happened 'with the sun failing' <note>original: *sole deficiente*, implying an eclipse</note>, so that the Gospels could plausibly be challenged according to the inventions of those wishing to argue against them." <note>This quote is from Origen, a 3rd-century scholar, suggesting that the word "eclipse" was inserted by critics to make the miracle look like a natural event, which would be scientifically impossible during a full moon at Passover.</note> Cyril of Jerusalem <note>4th-century bishop</note> in *Catechetical Lectures* 199 ("the sun failed because of the Sun of Righteousness") and 146 ("the sun now shining bears witness, which then—having failed—the darkness bore witness to then, etc.") and 57 ("for the sun, seeing the Master being dishonored, failed") ... the majority of manuscripts <note>represented by the symbol ς and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf</note> read **and the sun was darkened** <note>original: *kai eskotisthē ho helios*</note> along with Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, and many others, including the Latin Vulgate and Syriac versions... the Armenian and Ethiopic versions, and Origen (who notes this is found "according to most copies").

... The Palestinian Syriac text reads **the sun having failed**, and the *Acts of Pilate* <note>An apocryphal text</note> records it exactly this way. While some earlier editors omitted it, it is unlikely that Luke added nothing here, as it would be contrary to the authority of the witnesses and inconsistent with the faith, since nothing of that sort is read in the parallel passages nor would it have been randomly inserted. I do not believe that the phrase **the sun having failed** <note>original: *tou hēliou eklipontos*</note>, which is confirmed three times by Origen, was introduced by a later hand. Since the "failing of the sun" (which is the common term for an eclipse) was used by adversaries of the Christian name to explain away and diminish the event, it becomes much more probable that Luke’s original writing displeased men of "anxious piety" and was therefore "corrected" to "darkened." 

This opinion is confirmed by the fact that the phrase **and the sun was darkened** is written somewhat awkwardly in the place where it is read. Indeed, that the words **the sun having failed** were disliked and subject to abuse is proven not only by the commentary attributed to Origen—though the reliability of the old translator in this passage seems suspect since Origen himself stands against it elsewhere—but also by the so-called *Acts of Pilate*. In that text, the Jews try to soothe Pilate’s fear about the darkness by saying: "a failure [eclipse] of the sun happened according to the custom" <note>original: *ekleipsis hēliou gegonen kata to eiōthos*</note>. Furthermore, after the words "and the sun was darkened," the Syriac version adds (following Matthew's account): "and the moon hid its light, and the stars fell, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and the bodies of many saints arose and appeared to many."

| **and was torn** (the veil): found in Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Ephraemi. The majority of editors <note>Lachmann and Tischendorf</note> read **and the veil was torn** following Codex Alexandrinus and the Latin/Syriac versions. Codex Bezae (D), however, places the phrase **and the veil of the temple was torn** (omitting "down the middle") *after* the phrase "he breathed his last" in the following verse.

---

46. **Jesus**: Codices C and D, and the Coptic, Syriac, and Ethiopic versions place the name after "crying out"; the Sahidic Coptic places it before "crying out" ... it is omitted in the writings of Marcion and Epiphanius | **with a loud voice** (different word order in Greek) | **hands**: Codex Λ and Epiphanius read "hand" (singular) | **I commit** <note>original: *paratithemai*</note>: read by Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and Ephraemi.

It highlights how early Christians may have altered the text to prevent critics from dismissing the miracle as a natural solar eclipse.</summary>
