->### ACCORDING TO LUKE 23:47–49<-

47 And when the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying: "Truly this man was righteous." 48 <note>reference 331. 10</note> And all the crowds who had come together for this spectacle, having seen what had happened, returned home beating their breasts. 49 But there stood <margin>John 19:25</margin>

---

<note>The following technical notes compare different ancient versions of Jesus's final words: "Into your hands I commit my spirit."</note>

Manuscripts M, P, Q, U, X, Π and about 20 others; Justin Martyr in *Dialogue with Trypho* 105 ("For even as he gave up his spirit on the cross, he said: 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit,' as I also learned from the memoirs <note>original: απομνημονευματ., likely referring to the Gospels</note>"); Origen (volume 3, page 726); Eusebius; and Cyril of Jerusalem. Also in manuscripts D, R, and about 30 others; the *Apostolic Constitutions*; Athanasius; Basil; Epiphanius; and Theodoret. These all use the present tense: **I commit** <note>original Greek: παρατιθημι</note>. This is also supported by the Latin Vulgate, the Old Latin, and the Syriac versions.

On the other hand, manuscripts E, G, H, L, S, V, Δ, Λ and many others, along with the *Acts of Pilate*, use the future tense: **I will commit** <note>original Greek: παραθησομαι</note>, matching the wording of the Septuagint <note>the Greek Old Testament</note> in Psalm 31:5.

Regarding this verse, the scholar Ambrose <note>in *Interpretation of David* 646</note> writes: "Whence on the cross, when he was sending forth his spirit to the Father, he said: 'Into your hands I commend my spirit.' Therefore, let not some add the word **'Lord'**, as the singers do, for I have found it neither in my Latin manuscript nor in the Greek, nor in the Gospel, which is more evident." However, elsewhere Ambrose himself writes: "Into your hands, **Lord**, etc."

Regarding the phrase "And having said this": Manuscript ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, and others read **"And having said this"**. Editors Lachmann and Tischendorf note that other manuscripts like K, M, and P read **"And saying these things"**.

**47–49** Whether Marcion <note>a 2nd-century figure who edited his own version of Luke</note> included these verses is not clear, as Epiphanius and Tertullian are silent on the matter. Certainly, just because Tertullian does not quote from these verses, it does not follow that Marcion deleted them.

**47.** **And when the centurion saw what had happened:** Manuscript D reads "And the centurion, having called out."
**centurion:** Different manuscripts use slightly different Greek forms for this title <note>εκατονταρχησ vs εκατονταρχοσ</note>. Additionally, some Old Latin manuscripts add: "and those who were with him."
**what had happened:** Codex C reads "what has come to pass." Origen and others use the plural: "the things that happened."
**he glorified:** Manuscripts ℵ, B, D, L, and R use the imperfect tense (**was glorifying**), while others use the aorist (**glorified**). Some Latin versions use "magnified."
**truly:** Some versions read "that truly..."
**this man was righteous:** Origen and Cyril of Alexandria support this word order. Manuscript D and others place "was righteous" at the end of the phrase.

**48.** **come together:** Variations in the Greek prefix for "coming together" appear in different manuscript families.
**all the crowds who had come together for this spectacle:** The Curetonian Syriac omits "crowds for this spectacle." Manuscript D and some Latin versions read "all who were present at the spectacle, the crowds."
**having seen what had happened:** Manuscript A and a few others omit this phrase. Other manuscripts use slightly different verb tenses for "having seen."
**what had happened:** Some manuscripts use the plural "the things happening."

<summary>This page provides a detailed textual analysis of Luke 23:47-49, focusing on the centurion's reaction to the crucifixion and the various ways ancient scribes and Church Fathers recorded Jesus's final words and the crowds' response.</summary>

<keywords>centurion, textual variants, Marcion, Justin Martyr, Ambrose, Origen, crucifixion, apparatus criticus, manuscripts, righteous man</keywords>

The Majority text (and Griesbach and Scholz) reads **men two**, with Codex Bezae (D), Latin b, c, e, ff², l, q, the Vulgate, Curetonian, Philoxenian, and Harclean Syriac, and Eusebius in various sections | **stood by** (the third correction of Codex Ephraemi): the original hand of c* read **had stood by** (compare Acts 1:10) | **in dazzling apparel** <note>singular</note> with Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), the Old Latin, the Vulgate, and Eusebius (also the Curetonian and Philoxenian Syriac: "and their clothing was shining"), and likewise Marcion and Epiphanius read **in bright apparel** ... The Majority text and Tischendorf read **in dazzling garments** <note>plural</note> (Codex Regius L reads "white") with Codex Alexandrinus (A), Ephraemi (C), Regius (L), and almost all others, as well as the Sahidic, Coptic, Peshitta and Harclean Syriac, and Armenian.

5. **terrified** (Codex Vaticanus B*, Bezae D, Regius L, and others use a slightly different spelling; manuscript x reads "in fear").

<header>24, 18. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

looking sad. **18** Then one [of them], whose name was Cleopas, answered and said to him, "Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?" **19** And he said to them, "What things?" And they said to him, "The things concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who be—"

---

<note>The following section is the "Apparatus Criticus," a technical shorthand used by scholars to compare different ancient versions of the Bible.</note>

... The Textus Receptus, <term>Lachmann</term><note>Karl Lachmann, a 19th-century biblical critic</note>, and <term>Tischendorf</term><note>Constantin von Tischendorf, the editor of this volume</note> [read] **"and you are looking sad"** with manuscripts A, Gamma, N, P, X, Delta, Lambda, Pi, almost all other uncials <note>Greek manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and many others; also the Old Latin versions (a, b, c, f, etc.), the Vulgate, the Curetonian Syriac (which reads "while you are [sad]"), the Peshitta, Ethiopic, and Armenian... Codex Bezae (D) and Cyril of Alexandria (in his commentary on Luke 439) have nothing except **"looking sad"** (Cyril reads: "What is this that you are discussing with one another as you walk looking sad?")... the Harclean Syriac omits it entirely. Compare also Severian (in his work *The Seals* 565): "He who knows all things says to them: 'What are these words that you exchange with each other?' He who was learning everything from Him says to the One who knows all: 'Are you the only...' etc." It could not be defined with certainty what Luke actually wrote. Furthermore, the use of "to stand" <note>original: "εστηκεναι"</note> or "to be stopped" <note>original: "σταθηναι"</note> is very much in Luke's style. Similarly, in Acts 9:7, he said "they stood speechless."

**18. "One"** <note>original: "εις"</note> is found with manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and several others... but some read "a certain one" <note>original: "τις"</note>... The Textus Receptus reads "the one" <note>original: "ο εις"</note> with A, E, and most others. Furthermore, several manuscripts and ancient versions (Old Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic) and Cyril of Alexandria add **"from them"** <note>original: "εξ αυτων"</note>; hence Lachmann includes it in brackets: [from them]. But it is omitted by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most Greek uncials. | **"whose name"** <note>original: "ω ονομα"</note> with A, D, P, and almost all others; but Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others read "named" <note>original: "ονοματι"</note> (Note: Luke often uses "whose name" or just "name," as in 1:26, 8:41, etc.; but "named" is more frequent in the Acts of the Apostles. However, Greek or Latin witnesses nowhere substituted "whose name" for "named," while the reverse substitution often occurred). | **Cleopas**: some manuscripts (and the Sahidic Coptic/Armenian) spell it **Cleophas** <note>original: "κλεωπασ"</note>. Compare Origen, who says one was named Simon and the other Cleopas. 
<margin>A marginal note in the Syriac states that the one traveling with Cleopas was Simon—not Peter, but the other one.</margin> 
<margin>A marginal note in the Version states that the one with Cleopas was Nathanael, as the great Epiphanius said in his *Panarion* (67, 23). Cleopas was the nephew of the Savior and the second bishop of Jerusalem.</margin> 
A <term>Scholion</term><note>A brief explanatory comment found in the margin of a manuscript</note> (number 287) says: "The one with him was Nathanael, or as some say, the evangelist Luke himself." In Ambrose's commentary on Luke and elsewhere, they are called **Ammaon** and Cleophas. The same names are attested by the Old Latin codices for verse 13. | **"Jerusalem"** <note>original: "ιεροισαλημ"</note> with almost all major uncials and Cyril... the Textus Receptus and Lachmann read **"in Jerusalem"** with Lambda and others... The Latin versions read "are you a stranger/traveler in Jerusalem" or "do you travel from Jerusalem"... some read "into Jerusalem." | **"And"** <note>original: "και"</note> (Sinaiticus adds "these things") **"you did not"**: several manuscripts (D, a, b, c, e) and the Syriac omit the "and." | **"In it"**: Manuscripts L and e omit this; the Syriac and Severian also omit **"in these days."**

**19. "And he said to them"** (found in Latin versions and Augustine): Codex Bezae (D) reads **"But he said to him"**; others read "But he said to them." | **"And they said to him"**: some versions omit "to him"; some read "But they said," or "And they themselves said." | **"Said"**: there are minor spelling variations in the Greek for this verb <note>original: "ειπαν" vs "ειπον"</note>. | **"The"** <note>original: "τω"</note>: manuscript Lambda adds "of the." | **"Nazarene"** <note>original: "ναζαρηνου"</note>

<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 24:21</header>

...became a prophet powerful in deed and word before God and all the people, **20** and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him over to a sentence of death and crucified him. **21** But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel; and besides all this, it is now the third day [since these things happened].

---

<note>The following notes compare different ancient versions of the phrase "Jesus of Nazareth" from the previous page and the text above.</note>

[reads] "with" <note>original: "cum"</note> manuscripts $\aleph$ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, I, L, and Origen (in the Delarue edition); likewise the Old Latin versions a, c, e, and the second hand of l, and the Vulgate read *nazareno* ("the Nazarene"); version f reads *nazoreno* ...
The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **"the Nazorean"** <note>original: "ναζωραιου"</note> with manuscripts A, D, N, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials, and almost all others, along with Origen (in the Huet edition); likewise the Old Latin versions d and the first hand of l read *nazoreo*, b reads *nazareo*, ff$^2$ reads *nazaraeo*, and the Sahidic Coptic reads *nazoraeo* (*the Coptic translates this as "inhabitant of Nazareth"*) :: In Luke 4:34, the form "the Nazarene" does not vary; in 18:37, "Jesus the Nazorean" is used, which is a form also found seven times in the Book of Acts. Furthermore, John uses "Nazorean" three times, while Mark uses "Nazarene" three times. | **who** <note>original: "οσ"</note>: manuscript K, Pi, and about 20 others read "as" <note>original: "ωσ"</note> | **man** <note>original: "ανηρ"</note>: expressed in Old Latin c (but omitting "prophet"), d, e, ff$^2$, and the Vulgate ... but omitted in a, b, f, g$^2$, and l | **in deed and word**: (Manuscript A and version c read "in word [and deed]", hence Lachmann puts "in" in brackets) with manuscripts A, B, I, L, N, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all other uncials, the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Origen ... Manuscripts $\aleph$, D, the Syriac, Ethiopic, and Severian read **in word and deed** <note>Tischendorf notes the word order swap here</note> :: compare Acts 7:22, "mighty in words and deeds," and 2 Thessalonians 2:17, "in every word and deed" | **before** <note>original: "εναντιον"</note>: Manuscript D reads "in the presence of" <note>original: "ενωπιον"</note>. Among the Latin versions, a, b, f, ff$^2$, l, the Vulgate, and Augustine (*On the Harmony of the Evangelists*) read *coram deo* ("before God"); c, d, e, and Augustine (*Tractates on John*) read *in conspectu dei* ("in the sight of God").

**20.** **and how**: Old Latin ff$^2$, the Vulgate, and Augustine read *et quomodo* ("and how") ... Manuscript D reads "as", d reads *sicut* ("just as"), and a, b, c, e, f, l, and Augustine's John tractate read *quomodo* ("how") | **delivered him**: in this order with manuscripts $\aleph$, B, L, N, X, Γ, Δ, and seven other uncials, Origen, etc. ... Lachmann reads **him delivered** <note>original: "αυτον παρεδωκ."</note> (Manuscript D reads "this one", and Latin versions a, b, d, e, ff$^2$, and Augustine read *hunc* ["this one"]) with manuscripts A, D, K, Π, and others | **and our rulers**: (so in c, e, f, g$^2$, the Vulgate, and Augustine) : version b reads *et omnes populus* ("and all the people") ... a, ff$^2$, and l omit it. Furthermore, **our** (manuscripts L, U, and others read "your"): the Sahidic and Bohairic Coptic, the Peshitta Syriac, and the Ethiopic omit it.

**21.** **we were hoping** <note>The Greek tense here implies a continuous hope that has now been interrupted.</note>: (B originally had a slightly different spelling, $\aleph$ and others read "let us hope") with manuscripts A, B, D, L, N, X, Γ, and almost all others; Old Latin a, b, c, f, l, and the Vulgate (a, d, l read *speravimus* ["we hoped"], b, c, f, and the Vulgate read *sperabamus* ["we were hoping"]), all Syriac versions (the Coptic expresses it as "we hoped and we hope"), and Origen. Severian says: "**'We were hoping'** etc. See how their faith was nearly extinguished in them—he does not say 'we expect,' but 'we were [previously] expecting.'" A major collection of commentaries <note>original: "catmai"</note> says: "The voice of those who have lost hope; for he says 'we were hoping,' not 'we hope.'" Tertullian, in *Against Marcion* 4.43, writes: "**'But we thought,'** they say, **'that he himself was the redeemer of Israel.'**" ... Manuscripts $\aleph$, P, Δ, Λ, Π, and others read **we hope** <note>present tense, original: "ελπιζομεν"</note> | **is**: Manuscript D reads **was** <note>original: "ην"</note> (version d reads *quoniam ipse erat qui incipiebat salvare* ["since he himself was the one who was beginning to save"]). Likewise versions c, e, and Augustine read *quia ipse fuit* or *erat* ("because he himself was [the one]"). Others read as follows: f, the Vulgate, and Augustine read *quia ipse esset redempturus* ("that he himself would be the one to redeem"), l reads *quia ipse est salus* ("that he himself is salvation"), a and b read *ipsum esse qui redempturus esset* ("that he was the one who was going to redeem"), ff$^2$ reads *quia ipse incipit liberare* ("that he himself begins to set free") | **but indeed also**: with manuscripts $\aleph$, B, D, L, the Harklean Syriac, and the Armenian (version d reads "but also and in all these things") ... The Textus Receptus omits "also" with manuscripts A, N, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, and others. Most translators are not accurate enough here. The Latin versions read: e *simul autem* ("but at the same time"), b, c, f, ff$^2$, l, the Vulgate, and Augustine read *et nunc* ("and now"), a reads *nunc* ("now") | **with all these things**: (Some manuscripts have a variant spelling of "with") : f, the Vulgate, and Augustine read *super haec omnia* ("over/above all these things"), e reads *cum his* ("with these"). Versions a, b, and ff$^2$ move this to the next verse: "and over all these things [the] women..." | **this**: versions d, a, b, c, e, f, ff$^2$, l, the Vulgate, and Augustine omit this word | **day**: Manuscript Λ originally omitted this word.

<header>728 24, 22. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

...passes since these things happened. **22** But also some women from our group amazed us; they were at the tomb early in the morning, **23** and when they did not find his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive. **24** And some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see. **25** And he said to them: "O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that has been spo—"

---

**21.** **passes** <note>original: "αγει"</note> (omitted by the first hand of $\aleph$, supplied by the corrector $\aleph^c$) used without "today" <note>original: "σημερον"</note> in manuscripts $\aleph$, B, L, 1, the Curetonian and Sinaitic Syriac, the Ethiopic, and the Coptic and Armenian versions... Manuscript D [Codex Bezae] adds "today" <note>original: "σημεραν"</note> before "passes" (the Latin version d reads: *it acts as the third day today*)... The Textus Receptus <note>indicated by ϛ</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **today** with manuscripts A, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials, most others, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, Augustine, the Peshitta Syriac, and the Sahidic and Ethiopic versions | **these things**: l and the Curetonian/Sinaitic Syriac read "all these things" | **happened**: manuscript D reads "has happened."

**22.** **some**: The Textus Receptus omits this | **from us** (the Sahidic reads "from them"): manuscript D omits this, nor is it expressed in the Ethiopic | **having been** <note>original: "γενομεναι"</note> in $\aleph$, A, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all others... Tischendorf reads a variant spelling <note>original: "γεναμεναι"</note> with manuscript B and f | **early in the morning** <note>original: "ορθριναι"</note> in $\aleph$, A, B, D, K, L, Δ, Π... The Textus Receptus reads a different form of the adjective <note>original: "ορθριαι"</note> with K, P, X, Γ, Λ, and most others (the grammarian Phrynichus notes: *orthrinos is not used, but orthrios*). Furthermore, the Curetonian Syriac reads: *they set out for the place of the tomb where he was placed* in place of "astonished us" through to "tomb."

**23.** **they came** <note>original: "ηλθον"</note> in $\aleph$, A, B, D, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all seen... Tischendorf reads a variant spelling <note>original: "ηλθαν"</note> with manuscript B | **and a vision** (likewise in most Old Latin, Vulgate, Peshitta, and Ethiopic): D, c, e, Sahidic, Coptic, and Curetonian/Sinaitic Syriac omit **and** | **to have seen** <note>original: "εωρακεναι"</note> in $\aleph$, A, B, D, K, M, S, U, Γ, Λ, Π... Many others (E, G, H, L, P, V, X, Δ) read a variant spelling <note>original: "εορακεναι"</note>. Furthermore, the Curetonian Syriac adds *there*, and *they were astonished* (using *going and saying* instead of *who say*, as manuscript 69 has *they [the women] saying*); the Sinaitic, Peshitta, and Coptic likewise add *there*.

**24.** **And** from the beginning: the Curetonian and Sinaitic Syriac read "And also" | **went**: L reads a variant spelling... Δ reads "having gone" and omits "and" | **some**: D adds "from" <note>original: "εκ"</note>, likewise many Old Latin, the Vulgate, and Augustine ("from our own") | **just as** <note>original: "ουτως"</note> in all uncials (except Γ)... the Textus Receptus uses a slightly different form <note>original: "ουτω"</note> | **as**: D reads "how" <note>original: "ως"</note> | **also the** <note>original: "και αι"</note> in $\aleph$, A, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π... Lachmann omits "also" with B, D, Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic | **said**: D, c, e, and the Syriac/Ethiopic versions place this before "the women" | **saw**: D and e read "we saw"... the Vulgate (except manuscript gat) reads *found* <note>original: "invenerunt"</note>.

**25.** **And he** (the Curetonian/Sinaitic Syriac reads *Jesus*): D, c, e read "But he" (c, e read *he however*, d reads *but to him*). Similarly the Sahidic reads *But he said* | **to them**: manuscript A reads "to themselves" | **to believe**: manuscript D omits this (Schulz says: "not ineptly"). See on this verse the notes on Marcion in Epiphanius (317 and 348): *He [Marcion] mutilated the word spoken to Cleopas and the other, when he met them, namely "O foolish and slow to believe in [348 omits 'in'] all that the prophets spoke, was it not necessary for these things to be suffered?"; and instead of "what the prophets spoke," he made it "what I spoke to you."* Again in 349 it is read: *You have made it, O Marcion, instead of "are these not the things the prophets spoke," into "are these not the things I spoke to you."* Similarly, the Dialogue (857) reads: *He said, "O foolish and slow of heart to believe in all that I spoke to you, that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer these things."* But Tertullian differs in *Against Marcion* (4,43): "*he clearly railed against them: 'O senseless and slow of heart in believing all that he spoke to you. What things did he speak? He proves himself to be of another god, and less of a god?'*"

<header>ACCORDING TO LUKE 24, 29.</header>

...the prophets spoke. **26** Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory? **27** And beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. **28** And they drew near to the village where they were going, and he acted as if he were going farther; **29** and they urged him, saying: “Stay with us, because it is toward evening and the day has already declined.” And he entered

---

**26. was it not** <note>original: "ουχι"</note>: Manuscript D [Codex Bezae] reads "that" <note>original: "οτι"</note>; likewise the Dialogue <note>likely referring to a patristic dialogue</note>, page 857 (as just transcribed).

**27. beginning**: Manuscript D reads "he was beginning" and then "to interpret" (the Latin version d follows this: *and he was beginning, then to interpret*); likewise the Old Latin manuscripts a, b, c, g$^2$, ff$^2$, and the Gatianus, the Murbach fragments, and Augustine in his *Tractates on John* (9, 4) read "and he was" (manuscripts c and Augustine use "it was") "beginning" (manuscript a uses "commencing") "and afterwards interpreting"; manuscript e reads "and it was beginning and afterwards also interpreting." Also manuscript l reads "and beginning" (erroneously omitting "was") "and afterwards interpreting." On the other hand, manuscript f and the Vulgate read "and beginning—he interpreted" | **Moses** <note>original: "μωυσεως"</note> in manuscripts B, K, L, S, X, Π, and others... the Textus Receptus <note>indicated by ϛ</note> reads **Moses** <note>original: "μωσεως", a different spelling</note> with manuscripts $\aleph$ [Sinaiticus], A, D, E, G, H, M, P, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, and many others. Concerning these variants, see elsewhere | **and from**: Manuscript D and verse 28 in the Old Latin and Vulgate omit **from** | **all the**: Omit "the" | **interpreted**: with manuscripts $\aleph$, C, B, L, U, and others; the Murbach fragments read "he was interpreting" <note>original: "διηρμηνευσεν"</note>... Lachmann and Tischendorf read **was interpreting** <note>original: "διερμήνευεν"</note> with manuscripts A, G, P, χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, 1, 33, and many others (also the Vulgate according to Tregelles); likewise the Textus Receptus reads "was interpreting" <note>original: "διηρμηνευεν"</note> with manuscripts E, H, K, S, V, Π, and most others; likewise manuscript f, the Vulgate, and both the Curetonian and Harclean Syriac (though the Harclean reads "he began to interpret"). Concerning Manuscript D, see above; the first hand of $\aleph$ reads "and to interpret" (perhaps this should be corrected to "he was beginning," similar to Manuscript D?) | **in**: with manuscripts A, B, D, P, χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight uncials, and most others... manuscripts $\aleph$ and L (but see below), 1, and 33 read "what was in," likewise the Coptic reads "those things which are (or might be) in" | **all**: Omitted by manuscripts $\aleph$, D, g$^1$, and the Coptic | **the**: Omitted by manuscripts L, y$^{scr}$, and the Old Latin a (interpreting to them in all scriptures concerning him), e (interpreting to them in all scriptures concerning himself), c (interpreting to them all scriptures concerning himself), and the Armenian version | **himself** <note>original: "εαυτου"</note> (also in the Textus Receptus) with manuscripts $\aleph$, A, B, G, H, P, S, U, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and most others... the Textus Receptus (variant) and editors Griesbach, Scholz, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **him** <note>original: "αυτου"</note> with manuscripts D, E, L, M, V, X, and most others. Furthermore, the Latin manuscripts b, f, ff$^2$, l, and the Vulgate read "concerning him"; manuscript a reads "concerning himself"; g$^1$ reads "concerning his own self"; c reads "concerning his very self"; conversely, d and e read "concerning him."

**28. they drew near**: with manuscripts $\aleph$, A, D, L, P, χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, etc... Manuscript B reads "they have drawn near" | **he acted as if**: with manuscripts $\aleph$, A, B, D, L, 1, and a few others, and the Latin b, c, f, ff$^2$, g$^1$, and the Vulgate (all these read "he feigned"); manuscript e reads "he simulated"; manuscript l reads "he said"; likewise the Curetonian and Harclean Syriac... the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf read **he was acting as if** with manuscripts P, χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials, most others, and manuscript a ("he was affecting"), as well as the Peshitta and Philoxenian Syriac | **farther** <note>original: "πορρωτερω"</note>: with manuscripts $\aleph$, D, L, P, χ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight uncials, and most others (though P spells it *porroteron*)... Lachmann and Tischendorf read **farther** <note>original: "πορρωτερον", a slightly different comparative form</note> with manuscripts A, B, and 382.

**29. they urged** (the first hand of D reads *parabi-*, and manuscript L reads a singular form): the Murbach fragments, P, and some others read "they were urging" | **stay**: manuscript 69 reads "to stay." The Curetonian Syriac reads freely for "and they urged him" etc.: *and they began to ask him that he might stay with them, because it was near to becoming dark* | **it is and**: so in manuscript f and the Vulgate (including several specific codices)... Manuscripts D, a, b, c, e, ff$^2$, l, and others omit "and." The Latin versions read: *because the day has already declined toward evening* (e reads "evening-ward"; ff$^2$ reads "now-now"; c and l omit "already") | **already** after **has declined** (manuscripts G, H, K, P, Π, and many others read a different spelling of "declined"; D reads "has closed"): with manuscripts $\aleph$, B, L, 1, 33, 124, 258, 382, and two others; also Latin manuscripts a, b, e, f, ff$^2$ (though these five place it before "declined"), the Vulgate, and the Coptic; also the Peshitta Syriac (which places it before "toward evening"). Lachmann places it in brackets, while the Textus Receptus and Tischendorf include it.

<header>24, 30. ACCORDING TO LUKE</header>

to stay with them. **30** And it came to pass, when he sat at the table with them, having taken the bread, he blessed it and, having broken it, he gave it to them. **31** And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he became invisible to them. **32** And they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us as he was speaking to us on the road, as he was opening the scriptures to us?” **33** And rising up—

---

**30. to stay with them** <note>original: "συν αυτοις"</note>: omitted along with manuscripts A, D, P, K, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, $\Lambda$, $\Pi$, eight uncial <term>uncial: a style of manuscript written entirely in capital letters</term> manuscripts, and many others, as well as the Sahidic, Syriac (Curetonian), Armenian, and Ethiopic versions | **to stay** <note>original: "του μειναι"</note>: Manuscript D [Codex Bezae] omits "the" <note>the Greek article "του"</note>; omitted in Old Latin manuscripts ff$^2$ and l, and the Vulgate (except for the Gatianus manuscript) | **with them** <note>original: "συν αυτοις"</note>: Manuscript D reads "among them" <note>original: "μετ αυτων"</note>.

**30. sat at table**: Manuscripts E and G read a different form of "reclined" <note>original: "κατακλισθηναι"</note>; K, M, and $\Pi$ read another variation; Manuscript L reads "reclined back" <note>original: "ανακλιθηναι"</note> | **with them**: omitted in Manuscript D, Old Latin e, and the Curetonian Syriac | **the bread**: Manuscripts D, 131, and Eusebius omit "the" | **blessed**: reading confirmed by B, L, P, X, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, $\Lambda$, $\Pi$, and most others. Lachmann <note>a 19th-century biblical scholar</note> edits this as "he blessed" <note>original: "ηυλογ.", an alternative spelling</note> based on $\aleph$ [Sinaiticus], A, and D. <note>Note by the original editor: We have printed the form "ευλογ." everywhere in Luke based on the authority of the witnesses, though "ηυλογ." has several significant witnesses elsewhere, such as in Luke 2:28, 2:34, 9:16, and 24:50.</note> | **having broken he gave**: Manuscript D reads "he handed over" <note>original: "προσεδιδου"</note>.

**31. and their eyes were opened**: The Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac read "and immediately their eyes were opened." Manuscript D, Old Latin c and e, and Origen read: "But when they had taken the bread from him, their eyes were opened." Origen also notes in another place: "And when their eyes were opened and they recognized him, then the Scripture says in these very words: 'and he became invisible to them.'" | **were opened**: The spelling varies between manuscripts $\aleph$ [Sinaiticus], D, and Epiphanius. Epiphanius remarks: "it is proved that when he broke the bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized him." | **and they recognized him**: omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus, but added by a later corrector.

**32. and they said**: Manuscript D and Old Latin c and e read "but they said" | **they said**: reading "ειπαν" found in $\aleph$, B, and L; the Textus Receptus <note>indicated by ϛ</note> and Lachmann read "ειπον" with A, D, P, K, and most others | **to one another**: Manuscript D reads "to themselves" | **our heart was burning**: supported by most Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, Augustine, Ambrose, Coptic, and various Syriac versions. # ACCORDING TO LUKE 24, 39.

->“See, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.”<-

The *Dialogue* <note>original: "Dial⁸⁵⁷", likely referring to the *Dialogue of Adamantius*</note> omits “handle me and see” | **see**: Manuscript L reads “behold” <note>original: "ιδατε", a variant spelling</note> | the second **that** <note>original: "οτι"</note> (the Latin Manuscript *d* reads “because” <note>original: "quoniam"</note>): the Greek of Manuscript D <term>Codex Bezae: a 5th-century manuscript famous for its unique readings</term> reads “the” <note>original: "το"</note> | **flesh** (plural) <note>original: "σαρκας"</note> with the original hand of Manuscript ℵ <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, Manuscript D, the Latin translation of Irenaeus, and the *Dialogue* (Manuscript D reads “does not have bones and flesh,” the *Dialogue* reads “does not have bones and flesh,” the Latin Irenaeus reads “has neither bones nor flesh”) :: the plural word “flesh” <note>original: "σαρκας"</note>, being highly unusual, was rejected by most witnesses, just as John of Damascus <note>an 8th-century theologian</note>, in a passage of Irenaeus included in the *Sacra Parallela*, wrote “has neither bones nor flesh”; likewise in another place in the *Dialogue* it is written somewhat more freely: “for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having.” . . . [The scholars Tischendorf and Lachmann] read **flesh** (singular) <note>original: "σαρκα"</note> with manuscripts ℵ, D, the Latin Irenaeus, A <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term>, and B <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> (which reads “has both flesh and bones”), eight other uncials <term>uncial: a manuscript written in large capital letters</term>, almost all others, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, the rest of the versions, Cyril of Jerusalem, Cyril of Alexandria, Athanasius, and Pseudo-Athanasius. Marcion <note>a 2nd-century teacher later declared a heretic</note>, according to Epiphanius and Tertullian, reads “does not have **bones**,” omitting “flesh and”; also Tertullian and Hilary | **bones**: Manuscripts D and N, and Epiphanius (on Marcion) read a shorter form of “bones” <note>original: "οστα"</note> | **See**: some read “behold” <note>original: "βλεπετε"</note>. Furthermore, compare here Ignatius, *To the Smyrnaeans* 3: “For I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection. And when he came to those with Peter, he said to them: ‘Take, handle me and see, that I am not a bodiless demon.’” Eusebius, in his *Ecclesiastical History* (transcribing this passage from Ignatius, as did Theodoret), adds that he does not know where Ignatius obtained it. Hence Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, writes: “in which [the epistle to the Smyrnaeans] he places testimony concerning the person of Christ from the Gospel which was recently translated by me, saying: ‘But I both saw him in the flesh after the resurrection, and I believe he exists. And when he came to Peter and to those who were with Peter, he said to them: Behold, feel me and see, because I am not an incorporeal demon.’” Add Origen in *On First Principles*: “If someone wishes to bring forward to us from that little book which is called the *Teaching of Peter*, where the Savior is seen to say to the disciples: ‘I am not an incorporeal demon,’ it must first be answered to him that that book is not held among the ecclesiastical books.” Again, Jerome refers to the same passage from the *Gospel of the Nazarenes*: “For when the apostles thought him a spirit, or according to the Gospel which the Nazarenes read as the ‘Gospel of the Hebrews,’ an incorporeal demon, he said to them: ‘Why are you troubled?’ etc.” Compare also Justin Martyr in *On the Resurrection*: “When his disciples did not believe if he truly rose in the body, while they were looking and doubting, he said to them: ‘Do you not yet have faith? See, that it is I and that I have not changed.’ He offered himself to them and showed the prints of the nails in his hands. And—they invited him to eat with them—and he ate honeycomb and fish.”

**40.** We have not included this verse <note>Verse 40: “And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet”</note> following Manuscripts D, a, b, e, ff², 1, and the Curetonian Syriac (it seems to have flowed entirely from John 20:20, although the interpolator <term>interpolator: an ancient scribe who added or altered text</term>, as usually happens, adapted the Johannine text to Luke). . . . [The scholars] read “he showed,” or “he showed to them his hands and his feet” with Manuscripts ℵ, B, L, N, X, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, $\Lambda$, $\Pi$, all other uncials, almost all others, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, both Syriac versions, Ethiopic, Eusebius, Athanasius, Chrysostom, and Cyril. John of Damascus in *On the Orthodox Faith*: “The Lord says to his own disciples, when they thought they saw a spirit: ‘Handle me and see, that it is I and I have not changed, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having.’ And saying this, he showed them his hands and his side, and he stretched out to Thomas for handling.” Instead of “he showed,” [some manuscripts and scholars] read a slightly different form of “showed” <note>original: "εδειξεν" vs "επεδειξεν"</note> with Manuscripts ℵ, B, G, H, N, L, X, and others.

45. **the mind to understand**: Manuscript Λ omits this | **to understand** <note>original: "συνιεναι"</note>: Manuscript B reads a slightly different Greek form.

Manuscript 72 and others omit “thus it is written and.” Epiphanius records this freely (and he admonished them from the psalms and the prophets that thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer, etc.) | **the Christ to suffer**: Manuscript D and Latin versions read “that the Christ suffer” | **from the dead**: omitted in Manuscript D and others | **on the third day**: omitted in Manuscript b and Latin translations of Irenaeus.

47. **his [name]**: Manuscript 33 reads “my [name]” | **repentance for forgiveness** <note>original: "μεταν. εισ αφεσιν"</note> with Manuscripts ℵ, B, Coptic, and Syriac; however, the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **repentance and forgiveness** <note>original: "μεταν. και αφεσιν"</note> with Manuscripts A, C, D, N, X and almost all others, including the Vulgate. Note: both phrases are consistent with Luke’s style, as Acts 5:31 has “to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins,” while Luke 3:3 has “a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness.”

# CLOSING NOTES OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
## PAGE 738

There are **83 titles** <note>original Greek: τιτλοι (πγ')</note>, and some manuscripts also list **3,000 words** <note>original Greek: ρηματα (͵γ')</note> (or 3,073, 3,803, 3,850, etc. The Ethiopic versions count 2,800 words in the Gospel of Luke). A distinct system of notation for both chapters and numbers (perhaps the <term>Ammonian sections</term> <note>a system of dividing the Gospels into numbered sections used in ancient manuscripts</note>) is found in the **Codex Assemanianus 1** (a Syriac manuscript); it lists 104 chapters and 402 numbers (compared to 107 chapters and 426 numbers in Matthew; 50 chapters and 200 numbers in Mark; and 232 numbers in John). The **Codex Florentinus** of the same version lists 83 chapters, 348 numbers, 22 miracles, 27 parables, and 16 testimonies (compared to Matthew with 68 chapters, 360 numbers, 25 miracles, 25 parables, and 32 testimonies; and Mark with 48 chapters, 240 numbers, 22 miracles, 6 parables, and 17 testimonies). In **Manuscript B** <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, 152 sections are counted. Furthermore, many manuscripts (including the one designated as κs) have expanded closing notes in this manner: **The Gospel according to Luke** (manuscripts s etc.) or, more frequently, **The Gospel according to Luke was published fifteen years after the Ascension of Christ** <note>original Greek: το κα. λουκ. ευ. εξεδοθη μετα χρονους ιε της του χυ αναληψεως</note>. 

Also notable is this calculation (from Manuscript Δ, 262, 300, and others): **The Gospel according to Luke: written and balanced likewise in 2,677 lines; 242 chapters** <note>original Greek: ευαγγ. κατ. λουκ. εγραφη και αντεβληθη ομοιως εν στιχοις ͵βχοζ' κεφα. τμβ'</note> (Manuscript 262 says 249; Manuscript 300 says 245). Finally, in a few manuscripts, the following or similar notes are recorded: **It was written in Greek in Great Alexandria** <note>original Greek: εγραφη ελληνιστι εις αλεξανδρειαν την μεγαλην</note> (Manuscripts 9, 29, 124, 161, 163, 174, 346)... **in the Attica of Boeotia and was given to the most excellent Theophilus, who became a bishop after his holy baptism, as the great apostle Paul dictated these things to him** <note>original Greek: εν τη αττικη της βοιωταιας και επεδοθη τω κρατιστω θεοφιλω επισκοπω γενομενω μετα του θειου βαπτισματος, υπαγορευσαντος αυτω ταυτα του μεγαλου αποστολου παυλου</note> (Manuscript 293)... **it was dictated by Paul in Rome** <note>original Greek: υπηγορευθη υπο παυλου εν ρωμη</note> (Manuscripts 5, 29)... The manuscript dscr (and 18) reads thus: **A marginal note by Cosmas Indicopleustes on Luke: It should be known** (Manuscript 18 begins from here) **that the Gospel according to Luke was dictated by Peter** (Manuscript 18 says **by Paul**) **in Rome; and since it possesses a priestly character, it began with Zacharias the priest offering incense** <note>original Greek: κοσμα ινδικοπλ.. εισ λουκ. παραγραφη· ιστεον... οτι το κα. λουκ. ευ. υπηγορευθη υπο πετρου... εν ρωμη· ατε δε ιερατικου χαρακτηρος υπαρχοντος απο ζαχαριου του ιερεως θυμιωντος ηρξατο</note>... 

The Syriac Peshitta reads: **The holy Gospel of Luke the Evangelist is finished**; a Nestorian manuscript of the same version reads: **Here ends the holy Gospel of the preaching of Luke, which he preached in Greek at Alexandria**; the Philoxenian Syriac reads: **The holy Gospel of Luke is finished, which he spoke in Greek**... The Arabic version reads: **The copy of the Gospel of the apostle Luke the physician is finished, which he wrote in Greek in a certain city of Macedonia twenty-two years after the ascension of Our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven, in the fourteenth year of Claudius Caesar.**

# ACCORDING TO JOHN

## CHAPTER I.

1 ^1. 3 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, <note>original Greek: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν</note>

---

* **According to John** <note>original Greek: κατα ιωαννην</note> (Manuscript B spells it *Ioanen*) along with Manuscript ℵ <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> and Manuscript B <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>. Likewise, Manuscript **e** states: *The Gospel according to Matthew ends, the Gospel according to John begins* <note>original Latin: secundum mattheum explicit incipit secundum iohannem</note>. Nor is it written otherwise than *According to John* in manuscripts **a, b, e, q,** and the **Curetonian Syriac**; likewise Manuscript **D** <term>Codex Bezae</term> (see below) has this inscribed at the top of each individual leaf. ... The editors **Griesbach, Scholz, Lachmann,** and **Tischendorf** read **The Gospel according to John** <note>original Greek: ευαγγελιον κατα ιωαννην</note> as found in Manuscripts **A, C, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, Χ, Δ, Λ** and almost all others (Manuscript **Γ** reads *The Holy Gospel of the Gospel according to John*). ... The **Elzevir** edition of the **Textus Receptus** reads *The According to John Gospel* <note>original Greek: το κατα ιωανν. ευαγγελιον</note> with very many minuscule manuscripts; the **Stephanus** edition reads *The According to John Holy Gospel* with very many minuscules ... a few others (such as **178, 259**) read *From the According to John (178 adds "Holy") Gospel* (239 and others omit "Gospel"), and **69** reads *Gospel from the According to John* ... Manuscript **D** reads *The Gospel according to Matthew is finished, the Gospel according to John begins* <note>original Greek: ευαγγελιον κατα μαθθαιον ετελεσθη αρχεται ευαγγελιον κατα ιωαννην</note>; its Latin side **d** reads *The Gospel according to Matthew ends, the Gospel according to John begins*. At the very start of the Gospel, it repeats only *According to John* <note>original Greek: κατα ιωαν</note>. Similarly, manuscript **a** (though the editor Blanchinus only reports the inscription *It begins etc.*), **b,** and **f** read *The Gospel according to Matthew ends, the Gospel according to John begins* (Manuscript **b** omits this in the closing note but adds it when the title is repeated at the start of the Gospel, according to Blanchinus); **q** reads *Gospel according to Matthew ends, Gospel according to John begins*, followed by the heading: *The beginning of the Gospel according to John*. Likewise **c, g^1,** and the **Amiatinus** and **Forojuliensis** codices read *The Gospel according to John begins* (**g^1** omits "Gospel"); **g^2** reads *The beginning of the Holy Gospel according to John*; the **Gatianus** codex reads *Now begins the Gospel according to John*, and later *The beginning of the Holy Gospel according to John. Glory to you, O God.* ... The **Coptic** version reads *The Gospel according to John*; the **Gothic** version lacks the beginning of this Gospel as it does in Matthew, but in others where it exists, it reads *The Gospel through Mark begins*, *The Gospel through Luke begins*; the **Curetonian Syriac** reads *The Gospel of John* (which follows the end of the Gospel according to Mark); the **Philoxenian Syriac** (also the **Assemani Codex 1**) reads *The Holy Gospel (or "Holy Gospel") of John*; the **Peshitta Syriac** (at least as it is published) reads *The Holy Gospel of the Preaching of John the Herald*, to which is added: *which he spoke and preached in Greek at Ephesus*.

-2 Verse 2 is found in the **Valentinians** <note>a Gnostic group</note> according to **Irenaeus** (in the Greek and Latin), **The Peratae** <note>another Gnostic sect</note> according to **Hippolytus**, **Ignatius** (interpolated), and **Theophilus of Antioch** (who says: *wherefore the holy scriptures and all the spirit-bearing men teach us, of whom John says: In the beginning was the Word - not even one thing*). Also **Irenaeus** in the Latin translation: *In the beginning was the word - not*

[The light shone in the darkness and the darkness did not] grasp it <note>original Latin: comprehenderunt</note> and citations from: Clement of Alexandria <term>an early Christian theologian, c. 150–215 AD</term> (In the beginning - the Word was God) and the Latin translation (from verses 1, 3, 4). Theodotus in Clement (In the beginning - the Word was God; those from the school of Valentinus <term>a prominent Gnostic teacher</term> interpret it thus, etc.) and also (In the beginning - with God. That which was made — was life). Origen <term>a prolific scholar of the early Church</term>, and often in Origen's Latin translation, Hippolytus's *Against Noetus* (Lagarde edition), Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius (The [Gospel] says: In the beginning was the Word); Eusebius's *Proof of the Gospel* and likewise his *Against Marcellus* and *Prophetic Extracts* published by Mai; Athanasius; Chrysostom; Epiphanius; Cyril of Jerusalem; Basil's *Against Eunomius*; Cyril of Alexandria on John; Theodoret, and many others. Cyprian; Tertullian's *Against Praxeas* and (verse 1) *Against Hermogenes*; Hilary of Poitiers.

**1. and God:** <note>original Greek: και θεοσ</note> compare Origen, who says that in the case of "the Word" the article "the" is added, but in the case of the title "God," he sometimes places it and sometimes omits it. For he places the article when the name "God" is applied to the unbegotten cause of all things <note>referring to God the Father</note>, but is silent about it when the Word <note>Jesus</note> is named "God." Likewise Eusebius in *Against Marcellus*: "Not saying 'and the Word was the God,' with the addition of the article, so that he might not define him as being the one over all things," etc. Likewise: "Therefore he says: 'and the Word was God,' so that we may see God who is over all, with whom the Word was, and the Word himself as the Word..." Gregory of Nyssa (though not in all passages) reads: **and the God.** <note>original Greek: και ο θεοσ</note>

**3. through him:** <note>original Greek: δι αυτου</note> (also in Manuscript D): a later corrector of D wrote "through" <note>original Greek: δια</note> | **not one thing:** <note>original Greek: ουδε εν</note> with Manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, L, O, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all other uncials <term>manuscripts written in large capital letters</term>. Also the Valentinians in Irenaeus; the Naassenes in Hippolytus; the Peratae in Hippolytus; the interpolated letters of Ignatius to Polycarp; Tatian (all things by him, and without him was not one thing made); Theophilus; Clement; Origen; Hippolytus's *Against Noetus*; the *Dialogue against the Arians*; Eusebius; Epiphanius often; Cyril of Jerusalem; Basil's *Against Eunomius*; Gregory of Nyssa; Chrysostom; Theodoret, etc. ... Manuscripts ℵ*, D, and several others read **nothing** <note>original Greek: ουδεν</note> :: compare John 10:41, 15:5 and 13, Acts 4:32, Romans 3:10, 1 Corinthians 6:5. | We have joined **not one thing that was made** <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν</note> with Manuscripts C, E, G, H, K, M, U, X, Γ, Δ, Π and others, as it seems most do (as seen in Sabatier). The Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and others (Tregelles <term>a 19th-century textual critic</term> wants the opposite). One version reads: "and without him was not anything made in that which was made" <note>original Latin: et sine eo haud est quicquam factum in hoc quod factum est</note>, then continues "it was life which [was] in him." Ignatius (interpolated) adds nothing after "not one thing that was made." The *Dialogue against the Arians* (as Ignatius). Didymus the Blind in *On the Trinity*: "It becomes very clear that Didymus joined the words this way: 'That which was in him was life,' further teaching that he himself is life without beginning — wherefore he himself says: 'I am the life; I am the light.'" Ephrem the Syrian (after "not one thing that was made" continues "and the Word became flesh"). Chrysostom: "He adds that 'without him was not one thing made that was made,' that is, of created things... for we shall place the full stop at 'not one thing,' against the heretics. For those wishing to call the Spirit a created thing say: 'that which was made, in him was life.' But thus the meaning becomes unintelligible," and later he calls it absurd. Epiphanius: "without him was not one thing made; and as the reading continues it has: 'that which was made,' so that it may be known thus," etc. Hence it is of no weight that elsewhere he only cites "not one thing."

465.) That which was made in him," <note>original: παντα δι αυτου — ουδεν ο γεγονεν εν αυτω</note> that is to say, if anything was made, it was made through him. **Theodoret** 1, 808 (4, 102: "...not even one thing was made, and so forth.") **Theodore of Mopsuestia** 20: (For having said that all things were made through him, he added: "and without him not even one thing was made," that is to say, to put it briefly, none of the things that were made happened without him.) **Nonnus** (And without the Word’s labor, nothing came to be that existed; and innate life was in him, caring for all.) **Theophylact** <term>a 12th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</term> on this passage: "The Spirit-fighters <term>Pneumatomachi; a sect that denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit</term> read the present passage thus: 'and without him not even one thing was made'; then punctuating there, they read as from a new beginning: 'That which was made was life in him,' and they interpret the passage according to their own mind, saying that here the Evangelist is discussing the Spirit, saying that 'that which was made in him,' that is, the Holy Spirit, 'was life.' These things are said by the followers of Macedonius (as also testified by **Harmenopulus** *On Sects* in Wetstein's notes on this passage) etc. But we do not read it thus; rather, punctuating at 'that which was made' <note>original: ο γεγονε</note>, we read from another beginning: 'In him was life.'" Likewise **Scholion 36**: "Some also read it thus: 'and without him was made not even one thing that was made; in him...' that is, not even one of the things made through him came to be without him. But some read it otherwise: 'That which was made in him was life.' But this is false," etc. To these is added the testimony of **Ambrose** regarding the Alexandrians and Egyptians (see page 36, 35): "The Alexandrians and Egyptians indeed read: 'All things were made through him and without him nothing was made that was made,' and with the distinction <term>punctuation</term> placed between, they add: 'In him is life.' Let that distinction be safe for the faithful; I do not fear to read: 'That which was made was life in him,' and I have nothing that the Arian <term>follower of Arius, who taught Christ was a created being</term> can seize upon, because I do not consider his poisons, but I recognize the custom of the sacred reading" etc. See also *On the Faith* 3, 6: "Nor should we fear what the Arians are accustomed to compose with their cruel interpretation, saying that the Word of God was 'made' because it is written: 'That which was made was life in him.' First, let them understand... Then, how can they prove the Evangelist pronounced it so? For many learned and faithful men pronounce it thus: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made.' Others thus: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.' Finally, they pronounce 'that which was made' and then add 'in him,' that is: 'Whatever was made, however, is in him. What is "in him"?'" etc. Compare also **Jerome** on Isaiah 44, where he joins them: "and without him nothing was made that was made" (in *Hebrew Questions* 3, 306, Vallars writes only: "and without him nothing was made") etc.

<meta>This page continues the text of the Prologue of the Gospel of John, specifically concluding the discussion on spiritual rebirth in verse 13 and moving into the incarnation of the Word (verse 14) and the witness of John the Baptist (verses 15–17). # 1, 14. ACCORDING TO JOHN

...man, but were born of God. <margin>5. 3</margin> **14** And the Word became flesh and lived among us, <note>The Greek word "eskēnōsen" literally means "pitched his tent" or "tabernacled," echoing God's presence in the Old Testament tabernacle.</note> and we gazed upon his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. <margin>6. 1</margin> **15** John bears witness concerning him and has cried out, saying: <margin>1, 30</margin> “This was he of whom I said: The one coming after me has moved ahead of me, because he was before me.” <margin>7. 10</margin> **16** Because from his fullness we have all received, even grace upon grace; <note>The Greek "charin anti charitos" literally means "grace instead of grace," often interpreted as a continuous, overflowing supply of divine favor.</note> **17** because the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

---

*Regarding "of bloods" in verse 13:* Several sources (including Eusebius’s commentary on Isaiah and Epiphanius) read "from blood" <note>singular</note> instead of "from bloods" <note>plural</note>. Regarding the phrase **nor of the will of the flesh**: this is omitted by the original scribe of Manuscript E, though it was added later in the margin, and it is missing in some works of Chrysostom. | **nor of the will of a man**: Omitted by the original hand of Manuscript B (added later in the margin), Manuscript 17, and in certain citations by Athanasius and Chrysostom. <note>These omissions often occur when a scribe's eye skips between similar phrases.</note> For the Latin word "voluntate" <note>will</note>, some Latin versions read "voluptate" <note>pleasure</note>. | **of God**: Manuscript E reads "of the God." | **were born**: This plural form is found in most major manuscripts (Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.).

14. **full** <note>Greek: plērēs</note>: This reading is supported by the major codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus), as well as Origen, Eusebius, and the Latin Vulgate. Manuscript D and some scholia read "full" in a different grammatical case <note>plērē</note> to agree with "glory." | **and truth**: Manuscript B originally omitted the word "and," but it was added by a later corrector.

15. **saying**: This is present in almost all manuscripts and versions (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.). It is omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae. | **of whom I said**: Most manuscripts support this. The original hand of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read "he who said," which is likely a scribal error. Codex Bezae and some Latin versions add "to you" after "I said" <note>original: "of whom I said to you"</note>. | **The one coming**: Manuscript Δ capitalizes "Coming."

16. **Because** <note>Greek: hoti</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae, as well as the Coptic and Armenian versions. The "Received Text" <note>represented by the symbol ϛ</note> and many later manuscripts read "**And** from his fullness." | **even grace**: Some Old Latin and Coptic versions omit the word "and."

17. **Moses**: Most ancient manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) use the spelling *Mōuseōs*. Later manuscripts often use the spelling *Mōseōs*. | **Jesus Christ**: The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus <note>א*</note> omits the word "Christ," though it was added by a later corrector.

Irenaeus (Latin translation) writes: "because there is one God the Father, who contains all things and grants being to all, just as it is written in the Gospel: *No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son*" etc., and also elsewhere (*Son of God*): "for the Son, existing as the invisible Father's [revelation], being in his bosom, declares him to all." I do not believe that <term>YC</term> <note>abbreviation for "Huios" (Son)</note> and <term>ΘC</term> <note>abbreviation for "Theos" (God)</note> were swapped **carelessly** <note>In ancient manuscripts, these words were often abbreviated to "YC" and "ΘC" with a line over them; they look very similar, which often led to copying errors.</note>, but rather intentionally, which is also proven by the use of the article. While it is certain that in high antiquity a zeal for conferring the title "God" upon Christ prevailed (compare 1 Timothy 3:16), it is equally true that the same title might have offended the sensibilities of the faith. Furthermore, if you restore the word **God**, the sense of the entire passage is written somewhat awkwardly. | **who is** (Sinaiticus, second corrector): omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus, and likewise the Old Latin manuscript *a* (unless it translated "the only-begotten Son alone, being himself in the bosom of the Father, explained him." **19.** (When he sent to those who sent him—confesses, etc.): for <note>original: f οτι</note>. # 749 ACCORDING TO JOHN 1, 28.

> 26 <margin>Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; Acts 13:25</margin> John answered them saying, “I baptize in water; in the midst of you stands one whom you do not know, 27 the one coming after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.” 28 <margin>John 13:10</margin> These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

26. **answered** <note>original: απεκριθη</note> (Manuscript $T^b$ corrected, Cyprian, and the Palestinian Syriac add "and"): Manuscripts $L, T^b, U, 33, 67, 248, 249,$ and Origen read "he answered" <note>original: απεκρινατο</note> | **John** <note>original: ο ιωαννης</note> (Manuscript B spells it "Ioanes"): Manuscripts $A, 19, 433,$ and others once omit the article "the" | **saying** <note>original: λεγων</note> as in Origen: Manuscripts $1, 209,$ the Curetonian Syriac, and Cyprian omit this word | **I** <note>original: εγω</note>: Manuscripts $13, 44, 60, 69, 124, 435,$ various Old Latin versions, and the Palestinian Syriac add "indeed" <note>original: μεν</note> | **baptize** <note>original: βαπτιζω</note>: Manuscript $\Delta$, several Old Latin manuscripts (a, b, l, q), and the Armenian add "you" <note>original: υμασ</note>; some Latin versions specify "I baptize you" | **in** <note>original: εν</note> (Codex Sinaiticus first hand adds "the," but the corrector removes it) **water**: Latin manuscripts a and q read "in water unto repentance"; manuscript b reads "in the water of repentance." Against this, Origen notes that "Matthew alone has added 'unto repentance'" | **stands** <note>original: μεσοσ</note> without the word "but" <note>original: δε</note> follows Codex Sinaiticus, B, $C^*, L, T^b$, several Old Latin versions, the Armenian, and Heracleon as quoted by Origen (who says, "Heracleon says 'stands in your midst' instead of 'is already present'"); however, the majority of manuscripts including A, C, and the Vulgate add "but" | **stands** <note>original: στηκει</note> follows B, $L, T^b,$ and Origen; Codex Sinaiticus and Origen elsewhere use a different form of the verb <note>original: εστηκε</note>; most other manuscripts (A, C, and the majority) use "has stood" <note>original: εστηκεν</note>. The Latin versions generally use "stands" or "has stood."

27. **the one** <note>original: ο</note> (also in Codex Sinaiticus corrector and Origen; omitted by Codex Sinaiticus first hand and B; Chrysostom notes the phrasing "the one coming after me"). The phrase **after** <note>original: οπισω</note> without adding "he is" follows Codex Sinaiticus, B, $C^*, L, T^b, 1, 22, 33,$ the Curetonian Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Some manuscripts (G and others) add "it is he," while others like A, C, and the Vulgate include "he is the one." Latin versions and Cyprian read "he is the one of whom I said: a man coming after me who was before me." | **coming** <note>original: ερχομενοσ</note> without further addition follows Codex Sinaiticus, B, $C^*, L, T^b,$ and many early versions. However, the majority of manuscripts (A, C, and others) add **who has surpassed me** <note>original: οσ εμπροσθεν μου γεγονεν</note>, appearing also in the Vulgate and Syriac versions | **I** <note>original: εγω</note> placed after **am not** follows B, $T^b$, and Origen; whereas A and the majority of manuscripts place "I" before "am not." Several ancient sources, including Codex Sinaiticus and Coptic versions, omit "I" entirely; note the similarity to Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16 | **sandal** <note>original: υποδηματοσ</note>: A few manuscripts and the Ethiopic version add "he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire"; compare with Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16.

28. **these things**: A few manuscripts add "indeed" <note>original: μεν</note> | **Bethany**: Supported by major critical editions. <note>Some ancient manuscripts read "Bethabara" here, but "Bethany" is the older reading.</note>

# 750 ACCORDING TO JOHN 1, 29.

<margin>1, 36</margin>
**29** The next day he sees Jesus coming toward him, and says: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.”

---

<note>The following notes discuss a famous textual variant in verse 28: whether the location was "Bethany" or "Bethabara."</note>

**with** <note>Manuscripts supporting "Bethany"</note> Codex Sinaiticus (original hand), Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus (original hand), and many others—more than 130 manuscripts; the Aldine edition, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, and Peshitta Syriac versions. The text is also praised in the margins of White's edition as "in Bethany" and "in Betharaba," while the Assemani manuscript <note>A significant Syriac manuscript</note> reads "in Bethara." It is also supported by the Harclean Syriac, Armenian, Arabic, Persian, and Slavic versions. 

**Compare Origen** (Commentary on John, vol. 4, p. 140): “We are not unaware that in almost all copies it is written: ‘These things took place in Bethany.’ We also know that this appears in earlier versions, and in Heracleon we certainly read ‘Bethany.’ However, we were persuaded that one should not read ‘Bethany’ but ‘Bethabara.’ We came to this conclusion after traveling to the locations to investigate the tracks of Jesus <note>original: ιστοριαν των ιχνων ι̅ω̅</note>. For Bethany is only fifteen stadia <note>about 1.7 miles</note> from Jerusalem, while the Jordan river is far from there, about 180 stadia <note>about 20 miles</note>. Nor is there any place of the same name as Bethany near the Jordan. They say, however, that 'Bethara' is shown by the bank of the Jordan, where they record John to have baptized. Bethara is translated as ‘house of preparation,’ whereas Bethany is ‘house of obedience.’” 

**Likewise Epiphanius** (vol. 435): “in Bethabara,” though in other copies it says “in Bethany, beyond the Jordan.” **Likewise Chrysostom** (vol. 8, p. 111): “in Bethany,” but adds, “as many of the copies as are more accurate say ‘in Bethabara.’ For Bethany was not across the Jordan nor in the desert, but near Jerusalem.” The same notes are found in the Oxford Catena <note>a chain of interpretations</note> and various scholia <note>ancient marginal comments</note>.

**The received text** (following Griesbach and Scholz, though Griesbach later changed his mind) reads **Bethabara** with the corrected Ephraemi Rescriptus, and several other manuscripts including the "more accurate" copies mentioned by Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Euthymius. This is confirmed by Eusebius and Jerome in *On the Sites and Names of Hebrew Places* (p. 182), adding: “The place is shown where many of the brothers even now strive to receive the washing <note>baptism</note>.” **Likewise the Suda** <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>: “Bethany—which is written erroneously, for Bethany is on this side of the Jordan, while Bethabara [is on the other],” etc.

Other variants include **Betharaba** (found in a correction to Codex Sinaiticus, the margin of the Philoxenian Syriac, and Origen). Regarding the phrase **took place** <note>original: εγενετο</note>: Codex Sinaiticus and several Old Latin versions place this before the phrase "in Bethany." Regarding **the Jordan**: Codex Sinaiticus and the Curetonian Syriac add the word "river." Regarding **John**: Manuscripts B and Sinaiticus vary in spelling, and several major manuscripts omit the article "the." Regarding **was baptizing**: One manuscript adds "at first" <note>referencing John 10:40</note>.

---

**29. sees** <note>original: βλεπει</note> without any addition (following Griesbach and Scholz) is supported by Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus (original hand), and more than 60 other manuscripts, as well as the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, and the writings of Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril. 

**The received text** adds **John** <note>“John sees...”</note> with the corrected Codex Ephraemi and many others. Origen (vol. 4, p. 149) mentions “there John sees Jesus coming to him,” but this does not necessarily confirm the reading of the text itself.

**says: Behold** <note>original: λεγει· ιδε</note>: Manuscript 'm' reads "saying." While most use the form *ide*, Origen sometimes uses *idou* <note>both meaning 'behold' or 'see'</note> or even “This is” <note>original: ουτος εστιν</note>.

**who takes away** <note>original: ο αιρων</note>: various Latin and Coptic versions use future tense or different verbs meaning "who will take" or "who will carry away."

<keywords>Bethany, Bethabara, Origen, John the Baptist, Lamb of God, textual criticism, variants, geography of the Holy Land, Greek manuscripts</keywords>

# 752 ACCORDING TO JOHN 1, 36.

<margin>1, 29</margin> ...two of his disciples, **36** and looking at Jesus as he walked, he says: “Behold, the Lamb of God.” **37** The two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus. **38** Jesus, turning and seeing them following, says to them: **39** “What do you seek?” They said to him: “Rabbi” (which is translated as “Teacher”), “where are you staying?” **40** He says to them: “Come and you will see.” So they came...

---

<note>The following notes are part of the "apparatus criticus," a specialized system used by scholars to compare different ancient handwritten copies of the Bible. It lists which manuscripts support specific word choices.</note>

**[-John]** <note>original: -ανησ; likely the conclusion of "Iohannes" (John)</note> supported by **Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, P, T, X, Delta, Lambda, Pi**, 9 other uncial <note>capital letter</note> manuscripts, and many others; **Origen** (in various volumes), **Chrysostom**, and **Cyril**. **Lachmann** omits the word "the" <note>original: ο</note> based on **Codex Vaticanus, L**, and a few others.

**36. Behold:** <note>original: ιδε</note> Found in **Codices G and Lambda**, and minuscules **124, 230, 262**. The **Curetonian Syriac** and **Armenian** versions add "the Christ" <note>original: ο χς</note> (Syriac: "Behold the Christ, behold the Lamb of God"). | **of God:** <note>original: θεου</note> Also in **Origen** and **Chrysostom**. However, **Codex C**, various **Old Latin** manuscripts (a, ff², foss), the **Vulgate**, and **Ethiopic** versions—along with **Cyril** (who notes: "repeating the same word again, he points out Jesus to his own disciples and calls him the Lamb of God and says he takes away the sin of the world")—add the phrase **“who takes away [the sin of the world]”** <note>original: ο αιρων... την αμαρτιαν του κοσμου</note>. **Lachmann** puts this in brackets.

**37. heard:** <note>original: ηκουσαν</note> Found in the original hand of **Codex Sinaiticus** and others. **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** prefer **“and they heard”** <note>original: και ηκουσαν</note> based on **Codex Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, L, T**, and most other manuscripts and the **Vulgate**. | The word **“his”** <note>original: αυτου</note> appears after "disciples" in **Codex Vaticanus** and the **Sinaitic Syriac**. In **Codex L and T**, it appears before "disciples." **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** place it before "the two disciples" following **Codex Alexandrinus** and the **Vulgate**. Some **Old Latin** versions read "two of his disciples heard him speaking."

**38. turning:** <note>original: στραφεισ</note> Found in the original **Codex Sinaiticus** and several others. **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** add the word **“but”** <note>original: δε; Jesus "but" turning</note> following the corrected **Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus**, and the **Vulgate**. | **following:** <note>original: ακολουθουντασ</note> Several **Old Latin** manuscripts, the **Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian**, and **Ethiopic** versions add **“him”** <note>original: αυτω</note>. | The phrase **“to them”** <note>original: αυτοισ</note> is missing in the original hand of **Codex Sinaiticus**.

**39. they said:** <note>original: ειπαν</note> This spelling is in **Codex Vaticanus**. The common spelling <note>original: ειπον</note> is in **Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus**, and nearly all others. | **Rabbi:** <note>original: ραββει</note> Spelled with "ei" in **Vaticanus and Sinaiticus**. Most others use "i". | **which is translated:** <note>original: ο λεγεται ερμηνευομενον</note> Supported by **Sinaiticus, P, Delta**, and **Cyril**. **Lachmann** uses a slightly longer word for "translated" <note>original: μεθερμηνευομενον</note> based on **Vaticanus and Alexandrinus**. Note that this longer form is the standard usage in Matthew 1:23 and Mark 5:41. | **where are you staying?:** The **Curetonian Syriac** reads "where are you?"

**40. you will see:** <note>original: οψεσθε</note> This future tense is found in **Codex Vaticanus, L, T**, and **Origen**. **Origen** comments that "perhaps 'come' refers to the work of action, while 'you will see' refers to the contemplation that follows the successful completion of such actions."

# 1, 52. ACCORDING TO JOHN

*...the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these." 52 And he says to him: "Truly, truly I say to you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man."*

->II.<-

*1 And on the third day a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there; 2 and both Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding. 3 And they had no wine, because the wine for the wedding had been finished. Then the mother of Jesus says...*

---

51. **greater** <note>original: μείζω</note>: Codex Sinaiticus and Epiphanius read "greater things" <note>original: μείζονα</note>, while other manuscripts read "greater" <note>original: μείζων</note>; several Latin versions and the Vulgate read "a greater thing" <note>original: *maius*</note>. | **you will see** <note>original: οψη</note>: various manuscripts show different spellings of the future tense verb <note>original: οψει</note> as seen in the works of Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Cyril.

52. **he says**: some Latin versions and Epiphanius read "he said" <note>original: *dixit*</note>. Additionally, one manuscript omits "and he says to him." | **to you** <note>plural</note>: two manuscripts read "to you" <note>singular</note>. | **you will see** <note>without the phrase "from now on"</note>: following Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and early Latin, Syriac, and Coptic versions, as well as Origen and Cyril. However, the standard traditional text adds "from now on" <note>original: απ αρτι</note> following Codex Alexandrinus and many later manuscripts, similar to the phrasing in Matthew 26:64. | **opened**: Codex Sinaiticus uses a slightly different Greek spelling for "opened" <note>original: ηνεωγοτα</note>.

II. 1. **on the third day** <note>original: τη ημερα τη τριτη</note>: This specific word order is supported by Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and many others, as well as the Church Fathers Epiphanius and Chrysostom; the Latin versions also read "on the third day" <note>original: *die tertia*</note>. Other editors like Lachmann prefer a different word order <note>original: τη τριτη ημερα</note> found in Codex Vaticanus and several other Greek manuscripts. | **of Galilee**: after this word, the Palestinian Syriac version has a marginal note which actually refers to verse 3. | **the mother of Jesus was there**: Chrysostom adds "and his brothers," and comments: "Just as they invited her and the brothers, they also invited Jesus." In contrast, Origen writes: "One must ask why the brothers were not invited to the wedding; indeed, they were not even there, for it is not mentioned."

3. **And they had no wine, because — then she says**: following Codex Sinaiticus and several Old Latin versions. In Latin, these sources read: "and they had no wine, since <note>original: *quoniam*</note> the wine of the wedding was finished <note>original: *consummatum erat*</note>. Then <note>original: *Deinde*</note> he says." This reading is also confirmed by the Ethiopic and a marginal note in the Syriac. One Latin manuscript explains the situation further: "and it happened that because of the great crowd of guests, the wine was finished. But the mother of Jesus says to him." Another Syriac note says: "And they had no wine because the wine of the wedding failed." These various interpretations leave no doubt that the reading found in the Codex Sinaiticus was spread in high antiquity. It is superior in its truly "Johannine" character, and it seems that to avoid a certain wordiness—specifically saying the same thing twice—it was eventually exchanged for the shorter version found in most manuscripts, which reads: "And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus says..." <note>original: και υστερησαντος οινου λεγει</note> following Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, the Vulgate, and the works of Chrysostom and Cyril. | **of Jesus**: one manuscript reads "his."

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 2, 9.

...to him: "There is no wine." 4 Jesus says to her: "What is that to me and to you, woman? And they filled them up to the top. 8 And he says to them: "Draw some out now and take it to the master of the feast." And they took it. 9 When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine—and he did not know where it came from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew...

<note>The following notes provide a scholarly comparison of different ancient versions of the Bible, such as Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), and various early translations into Latin, Syriac, and Coptic.</note>

**to him** <note>original: προσ αυτον</note>: Epiphanius (vol 4, p. 443) reads "to Jesus" <note>original: του ̅ιυ</note>; Chrysostom (8, 140) reads "of him" <note>original: αυτου</note>; the Latin manuscript (a) and Armenian read "to Jesus" <note>original: *ad Iesum*</note>. | **there is no wine** <note>original: οινος ουκ εστιν</note>: This follows the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (א*); the Syriac and Ethiopic versions read "they have no wine" <note>original: *vinum non est illis*</note>. Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>scholarly editors of the Greek New Testament</note> read "they do not have wine" <note>original: οινον ουκ εχουσιν</note> based on the corrected Sinaiticus (אᶜᵃ), Vaticanus (B), and many others. Several Latin versions and the Vulgate add "son" <note>original: *fili*</note> to the mother's request.

4. **says**: Omitted the word "and" at the start, following the original Sinaiticus and several other early manuscripts. Others, including the corrected Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, add "and" <note>original: και</note>. | **Jesus**: Omitted in Codex Delta. | **woman**: One manuscript reads "O woman" <note>original: ω γυναι</note>. | **my**: Gregory of Nyssa interprets this not as a simple statement of time, but as a question: "Do you wish to command even this age of mine? Has my hour not yet come which grants authority and autonomy to my age?" <note>original: μη και ταυτης μου της ηλικιας επιστατειν εθελεις; ουπω ηκει μου η ωρα η το αυτοκρατεσ παρεχομενη τη ηλικια και αυτεξουσιον;</note>.

5. **his mother says to them etc.**: One Latin version (e) reads "and having called the servants to her, the mother of Jesus said to them." | **whatever**: Variations in the Greek particles used for "whatever" <note>original: ο τι αν, οτι ο αν, εαν</note> among Sinaiticus, Chrysostom, and Cyril. | **he says**: Some manuscripts use the present tense "says" <note>original: λεγει</note> while others use the subjunctive "might say" <note>original: λεγη</note>.

6. **stone water jars**: The word order varies; some manuscripts place "stone" before "jars" <note>original: λιθιν. υδρι.</note> while others reverse it. | **lying**: The placement of this word (indicating the jars were set there) varies significantly across the major Greek codices and the Latin, Syriac, and Coptic versions. Some manuscripts, including the original hand of Sinaiticus, omit the word entirely. | **measures**: There are minor spelling variations in the Greek word for measures <note>original: μετριτασ/μετρητὰς</note>.

7. **Jesus says**: Some versions (Sinaiticus, Ethiopic, and several Latin) add "and" at the beginning. One Latin version (e) expands this to: "and Jesus, having called the servants to him, said to them."

8. **and**: Some manuscripts replace "and" with "but" <note>original: ο δε</note> or omit it entirely. | **and they**: Some read "but they" <note>original: οι δε</note> while the standard traditional text reads "and" <note>original: και</note>. Several Latin versions replace the phrase "and they took it" with "and they did just as Jesus told them." | **took it**: One Latin version reads "they drew and they took."

9. **become**: Minor spelling variation in the Greek participle <note>original: γεγενημενον/γεγεννημ.</note>. | **where**: One manuscript (tᵇ) reads "where" <note>original: που</note> instead of "from where" <note>original: ποθεν</note>. | **who had drawn the water**: <note>Transcription ends here</note>

**19.** **Jesus** without the article: with A, B, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and eight other uncials, Origen, and Cyril... the received text (and Griesbach) add **the** [before Jesus] with Sinaiticus, K, 1, 33, 69, and a few others | **in three** with Sinaiticus, A, L, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine other uncials, and almost all Latin and Vulgate versions, Origen, Eusebius, Chrysostom, Cyril, Irenaeus, and Tertullian...
