**5.** **born**: <note>original: natus</note> The Vulgate reads **shall have been born again** <note>original: renatus fuerit</note> | **of the Spirit**: <note>original: πνευματος</note> (so manuscripts b, c, e, f, l, q, and various Vulgate editions): manuscripts a, ff², and m, as well as the standard Vulgate, the Ethiopic version, and Origen read **by the Holy Spirit** <note>original: spiritu sancto</note> | **to enter into**: <note>original: εισελθειν εισ</note> (also in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus): the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and the manuscript M read **to see** <note>original: ιδειν</note> | **of the heavens**: <note>original: των ουρανων</note> with Codex Sinaiticus, several minuscules <note>term: minuscules — Greek manuscripts written in a smaller, cursive script</note>, Justin Martyr, the Clementine Homilies, Irenaeus, Origen, and others. <note>The phrase "Kingdom of Heaven" is much more common in the Gospel of Matthew; John usually uses "Kingdom of God."</note> | **of God**: <note>original: του θεου</note> with the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Codices Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and the majority of other manuscripts and ancient versions (Coptic, Syriac, etc.), as well as Cyprian and Cyril. Note that the Docetists <note>term: Docetists — an early heretical group that believed Jesus only "seemed" to have a physical body</note> and the Clementine Homilies quote it as: "The Savior says: unless someone is born of water and spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of the heavens; because that which is born of the flesh is flesh." The Clementine Homilies (11, 26) record: "For thus the prophet swore to us, saying: Amen I say to you, unless you are born again with living water in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you shall not enter into the kingdom of the heavens." Irenaeus quotes: "As the Lord said: unless someone is born again through water and spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of the heavens."

**6.** See the Naassenes <note>term: Naassenes — a Gnostic sect known for their unique interpretations of scripture</note> (106): "That which is written: that which is born of the womb is spirit." Also the Docetists (267) continue after "kingdom of the heavens" with "because that which is born of the flesh is flesh." Hippolytus (Against Noetus 16) quotes: "That which was said by Christ, that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." Eusebius quotes: "saying: that which is born of the [Spirit] is spirit. And God is spirit. Therefore it follows to understand that also that which is born of God would be God." | **born**: <note>original: γεγεννημενον</note> used twice; Clement of Alexandria uses **being born** <note>original: γεννωμενον</note> ("Just as that which is being born of the flesh is flesh, so from the spirit it is spirit") | **is flesh**: Manuscript 161 adds **because it was born of the flesh**, as do several Old Latin manuscripts (a, b, ff², l, q) and the writings of Tertullian: **because (or since) it is born from the flesh** <note>original: quia de carne natum est</note> | **of the Spirit**: the margin of the Harclean Syriac reads **of water and spirit** | **is spirit**: Manuscript 161 adds **because it is of the spirit**, as do many Old Latin manuscripts and Tertullian. Some add **because God is spirit and moreover he is born of God** <note>original: quia deus spiritus est insuperque et ex deo natus est</note>. Furthermore, Ambrose (On the Holy Spirit 3, 11) writes: "Which passage, you Arians <note>term: Arians — followers of Arius who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God</note>, so clearly testify to be about the Spirit that you remove it from your manuscripts. And would that it were only from yours and not [from the church's...]" <note>Ambrose is accusing his theological opponents of deleting parts of this verse to support their views on the Holy Spirit.</note>

<note>This section is a "critical apparatus," a scholarly toolkit used to compare different ancient copies of the Bible. Letters like A, B, and ℵ (Aleph) refer to famous ancient manuscripts. Names like Chrysostom or Cyril refer to early Christian writers who quoted these verses.</note>

13. **who is** (The manuscript A* and several others omit this; others like the Textus Receptus and Zeno include "who was") **in heaven** (Manuscripts 80 and 88 read "from heaven") [included] with manuscripts A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials <note>term: uncials — manuscripts written in large, capital-like Greek letters</note>, and almost all others, the Old Latin and the Vulgate, the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Hippolytus (adding: "Who then was in heaven but the Word without flesh, sent so that he might show himself being on earth and also being in heaven?"); also Dionysius of Alexandria, Didymus, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Cyril, and Origen (who says: "he did not say *who was*, but *who is in heaven*"); also Novatian, Hilary ("he is not absent from heaven—he is nevertheless in heaven while saying these things"), Lucifer of Cagliari, and Jacob of Nisibis (*who was in reality in heaven*)... but omitted by ℵ, B, L, T, and others; therefore Griesbach and Tischendorf omit it. <note>This is a famous debate: did Jesus claim to be in heaven *at the same time* he was talking to Nicodemus? Older manuscripts tend to omit the phrase.</note>

14. **Moses** [spelled *Mōusēs*] with ℵ, B, K, L, S, T, Π, and many others... but spelled *Mōsēs* in A, E, G, H, M, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, and many more | **it is necessary to be lifted up** is also in the writings of the Peratics ("and just as Moses lifted up the serpent..."), Eusebius, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, Cyril, Theodoret, Origen, and Cyprian... Manuscript A and others place **it is necessary** after "lifted up."

15. **in him** [Greek: *en autō*] with manuscripts B and T, several Latin copies, and Theodoret... whereas the common reading is **into him** [Greek: *eis auton*] with ℵ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all others, including the Latin versions, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Theodoret; Manuscript A reads **upon him** [Greek: *ep' auton*] ... **may have eternal life** with ℵ, B, L, T, and several others, the Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, and writers like Cyprian and Lucifer... but many others (the common text) prefix **should not perish but**, including manuscripts A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many more.

16. **the Son** without the word "his" with ℵ and B... the common text adds **his** with A, L, T, and almost all other manuscripts and versions | **gave** (ℵ originally omitted this; manuscript 33 adds "into the world"): some Latin versions use *might send*, and one adds *might send into this world*, while others say *might give for the age* | **into him** [Greek: *eis auton*] (also in Eusebius, Chrysostom, Cyril)... while others read **upon him**... **should not perish** (some manuscripts use a slightly different spelling for "perish") **but**... **may have**: some manuscripts use a different grammatical form for "have."

17. **the Son** without the word "his" with ℵ, B, L, T, and several others, Cyril, and Victorinus... but the common text adds **his** with A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, the Latin versions, Chrysostom, and Tertullian.

-> ### 3, 18. ACCORDING TO JOHN <-

<margin>12, 47</margin> <note>This margin refers to a parallel passage in John 12:47: "I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."</note> ...that he might judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. **18** The one who believes in him is not judged; but the one who does not believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. **19** And this is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness more than the light, for their deeds were evil. **20** For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds might not be exposed. **21** But the one who does the truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be revealed, that they have been done in God.

---

To this point, the Naassenes <note>original: "huc Naass" — the Naassenes were an early Gnostic Christian sect</note> read: "For the Son of Man did not come into the world to destroy the world, but that the world might be saved through him." <note>original: "ου γαρ ηλθεν ο υιος του ανθρ..."</note>

**18. The one who believes:** <note>original: "ο πιστευων"</note> Manuscript *d* prefixes *because of this* <note>original: "propter hoc"</note>; likewise manuscript *a* and Lucifer of Cagliari <note>4th-century Bishop</note> use *therefore* <note>original: "ideo"</note> | **in him:** <note>original: "αυτον"</note> Manuscripts Λ and 7 others, Chrysostom, and Cyril read *the Son* <note>original: "τον υιον"</note>... Origen <note>An early Christian scholar, c. 184–253 AD</note> writes: "For the Lord says: 'the one who believes in *me* is not judged.' Not: 'the one who believes in *my name* is not judged.'" Origen and others read *in me* <note>original: "εις εμε"</note>; likewise the Latin translation of Irenaeus, the Latin translation of Origen, and Hilary read *in me*. | **the one not [believing]:** <note>original: "ο μη"</note> read without the conjunction "but" or "and" by manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, and others, including Tertullian and Cyprian. Lachmann <note>A 19th-century textual critic</note> reads *but the one who [does not]* <note>original: "ο [δε] μη"</note>; the Received Text and Tischendorf read *but the one who [does not]* <note>original: "ο δε μη"</note> with manuscripts A, L, T, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine other uncials <note>term: uncials — early manuscripts written in large capital letters</note>, and almost all others, including the Old Latin, the Vulgate, and the Syriac.

**19. People:** <note>original: "οι ανθρωποι"</note> (The Curetonian Syriac <note>A 5th-century manuscript of the Gospels</note> reads *the world*): Manuscript ℵ places this word *before* "loved." | **more:** <note>original: "μαλλον"</note> so read by Clement, Eusebius, and others, as well as the Latin Irenaeus and Hilary. Manuscript ℵ, Origen, Cyril, and Hilary place this word *after* "the darkness." | Manuscript *e* and Cyprian place it *before* "loved" <note>original: "dilexerunt"</note>; manuscripts 1, 118, 209, and a few others place it before "people." | **their [deeds] were evil:** <note>original: "αυτων πονηρα"</note> (According to Griesbach's assessment) found in manuscripts ℵ, A, B, G, K, L, T, U, Λ, Π, and about 120 others, as well as the Vulgate, Athanasius, Chrysostom, and Cyril. The Received Text reads *evil were their [deeds]* <note>original: "πονηρα αυτων"</note> with manuscripts E, F, H, M, S, V, Γ, Δ, and many others, including Ambrose. Other Latin versions read *their deeds were evil* or *their evil deeds*.

**20. For:** <note>original: "γαρ"</note> included by the Latin Irenaeus and Origen (though the passage is missing in some witnesses). Chrysostom uses *but* <note>original: "δε"</note>... Manuscript *E*, *a*, and Lucifer omit it; likewise (though not definitively proven) Origen. **and does not come to the light:** <note>original: "και ουκ ερχ. πρ. το φως"</note> Omitted by the first hand of ℵ and others, including Lucifer, likely due to a scribal error <note>term: homoioteleuton — a mistake where a scribe's eye skips from one word to a similar ending later in the text</note>. | **his deeds:** <note>original: "τα εργ. αυτου"</note> following manuscripts ℵ, B, L, T, Γ, Δ, Λ, most others, the Latin versions, Cyril, Irenaeus, Origen, and Lucifer. Manuscripts A, K, Π, and others read *the deeds of him*. Additionally, some manuscripts and the Coptic and Arabic versions add *because they are evil*. Manuscript *d* adds *from the light*. Origen’s Latin translation adds *and let them be seen if they are done in God*.

**21.** The first hand of manuscript ℵ <note>ℵ*</note> omits the section from **"but the one who does"** down to **"his deeds"** due to a scribal error <note>homoioteleuton</note>; it was added by a later corrector. | **his deeds:** <note>original: "αυτου τα εργα"</note> following ℵ, C, A, B, T, and most others. Manuscripts L, U, and others read *the deeds of him*. | **God:** <note>original: "θεω"</note> Manuscripts 13, 69, and 25 others add the definite article "the." | **have been done:** <note>original: "ειργασμενα"</note> The first hand of ℵ reads the singular *it has been done*. Lucifer of Cagliari translates *because it is done in God* (following "that his deeds may be manifested"); likewise the Latin Irenaeus and manuscript *a* read *because it is done in God*. Based on this, it is possible that the first hand of manuscript ℵ preserved the original reading of the Evangelist.

<summary>This page analyzes the Greek and Latin textual variations of John 3:18-21, detailing how different ancient manuscripts and Church Fathers recorded the words of Jesus regarding belief, light, and judgment. It highlights significant scribal differences, including word order changes and common copying errors.</summary>

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 3, 28.

**22** After these things, Jesus and his disciples came into the Judean land, and there he remained with them and was baptizing.
<margin>25. ³</margin> **23** Now John was also baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there, and people were coming and being baptized;
<margin>26. ⁴</margin> **24** for John had not yet been thrown into prison.
<margin>27. ¹⁰</margin> **25** Therefore a dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew concerning purification. **26** And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him." **27** John answered and said, "A man is not able to receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. <margin>28. ¹</margin> **28** You yourselves..." <note>The text breaks off here at the start of verse 28: "You yourselves are my witnesses..."</note>

***

**22.** the <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "ῑς̅" — a common abbreviation in Greek manuscripts known as a "nomen sacrum" or sacred name</note>: Manuscripts Α, Π and 5 others omit "the" | **came** <note>Latin manuscripts c, e, f, ff², q, and the Vulgate read "venit" (came); manuscript b reads "profectus est" (departed)</note>: Manuscript 33 reads: **went away** <note>original: "απηλθεν"</note>, manuscript d: **went out** <note>original: "exivit"</note>, a, l: **went out** <note>original: "exiit"</note>, foss: **was going out** <note>original: "exiebat"</note> | **and was baptizing**: manuscript b omits this phrase (manuscript l* <note>the original hand of the scribe</note> reads "and they were being baptized by him," omitting from "Now John" up to "and were being baptized"; however, a later corrector l² supplied the missing section from "Now John" up to "and were being baptized" after the phrase "and were baptized by him")

**23. John** (Codex B spells it <term>Ιωανης</term>) with ℵ, A, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 other uncials, and many others, Origen, etc. ... Codex B and manuscript 44 read "the John" | **baptizing**: manuscript 1 reads "the [one] baptizing" | **in Aenon**: manuscript e reads "in the wilderness" <note>original: "in eremo"</note>, f reads "in the desert" <note>original: "in deserto"</note> | **Salim** with ℵ, B, L, Tᵇ, Γ, Δ, Π, 8 uncials, many others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, etc., Origen, and Eusebius' *Church History* 3, 24, 11 (in the editions of Burton and Heinichen) etc: Manuscript A reads **Sallim** <note>original: "σαλλειμ"</note> ... Manuscripts U, Δ, 1, 69, 262, and over 70 others, the Aldine edition, Coptic, and most editions of Eusebius and Cyril read **Salem** <note>original: "σαλημ"</note> (noted by Griesbach)

**24. into the prison**: Manuscripts E, M (and others), 1, 22, 235, and Origen omit "the" | **John** (spelled <term>Ιωανης</term> in B) without the article with ℵ*, B, 47, and Eusebius ... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "**the John**" <note>original: "ο ιω."</note> with ℵᶜ, A, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and most others, Origen, and Cyril.

**25. Therefore there arose** (ℵᶜ): ℵ*, 47, manuscript b, the Clementine Vulgate, Coptic, and various Syriac versions read "**But there arose**" <note>original: "εγ. δε"</note> | **dispute** (ℵᶜ): ℵ* reads "**joint-dispute**" <note>original: "συνζητησις"</note> | **of John** (the Peshitta Syriac reads "his", according to Whitby): Codex B reads "**those of John**" <note>original: "των ιωανου"</note>. Furthermore, the Syriac Peshitta reads "among one of John's disciples" | **with a Jew** (also Griesbach and Scholz) with ℵᶜ, A, B, L, T, Δ, Λ*, Π*, 8 uncials, and 125 others, the Aldine edition, Syriac, Armenian, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Nonnus ... the Received Text (equal to Griesbach and Scholz, but noted by Griesbach as a variant) reads "**with Jews**" <note>original: "ιουδαιων"</note> with ℵ*, G, Λ², Π², 1, 13, 69, 124, and others, manuscript d, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic, Gothic, Origen, and Cyril (it is therefore certain that the reading "**with Jews**" stands with equal antiquity).

**26. they came and they said** with ℵ, A, B³, L, Tᵇ, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and 9 uncials ... Tischendorf reads **they came and they said** <note>original: "ηλθαν et ειπαν" — using an Alexandrian Greek spelling variant</note> with B* and Chrysostom | **to the**: manuscripts 1, 106, and others omit "the" | **Rabbi** <note>original: "ραββει"</note> with ℵ, A, B, D, E, H, Γ, Λ etc (also the Gothic and a marginal note in the Syriac) ... the Received Text and Lachmann read **Rabbi** <note>original: "ραββι" — a different spelling</note> with E, G, K, L, M, S, U, V, Δ, Π and most others | **Look**: Manuscript D and others read "**Behold**" <note>original: "ιδου"</note>

**27. John answered and said** (B spells it <term>Ιωανης</term>; manuscripts 33 and others read "the John"): The Curetonian Syriac reads "John said to them" | **to receive** (ℵ spells it <term>λαβιν</term>): L, Δ, 13, 33, 69, and others, as well as Old Latin manuscripts c and e ("to do anything of himself"), Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, Eusebius, and Chrysostom add (or place before) "**of himself**" <note>original: "αφ εαυτου"</note> :: compare with John 5:19 | **nothing**: Codex B, Chrysostom, and Curetonian Syriac read "**not even one thing**" <note>original: "ουδε εν"</note> | **if**: B reads <term>αν</term> | **to him**: Manuscript F and others omit this. Furthermore, 13, 69, 124 (and manuscript b in place of "from heaven") add "**from above**" <note>original: "ανωθεν"</note>, as does Eusebius after "from heaven."

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 3, 29.

<margin>1, 20</margin> **28** You yourselves are my witnesses that I said: ‘I am not the Christ,’ but that ‘I have been sent ahead of him.’ **29** <margin>29. 10</margin> The one who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and listens to him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This joy of mine, therefore, has been fulfilled. **30** He must increase, but I must decrease.

<margin>8, 23</margin> **31** The one who comes from above is over all; the one who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven...

---

**28.** **to me** <note>original: "μοι"</note> (Manuscripts 1, 124, 209, and a few others read **to me** <note>original: "εμοι"</note>) with manuscripts A, B, D, G, K, L, S<sup>b</sup>, U, Λ, Π, many others, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, and the remaining versions, as well as Eusebius, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Cyprian. Manuscripts ℵ, E, F, H, M, V, Γ, and more than 60 others omit it. | **I said**: Manuscript B and the Syriac (Jerusalem) version add **I** <note>original: "εγω"</note>; Manuscript T<sup>b</sup> and the Syriac (Curetonian) prefix **I**. Furthermore, from Cyprian and Firmicus (Bursian edition), add: *to those who were sent from Jerusalem to me.* | **I am not** <note>original: "ουκ ειμι εγω"</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, B, L, T<sup>b</sup>, and almost all other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and Old Latin versions b, f, ff², g, q, the Clementine Vulgate, Eusebius, and Chrysostom. Manuscripts c, am, fu, for, foss, ing, tol, and Cyril read: **I myself am not** <note>original: "εγω ουκ ειμι"</note>; Lachmann adopted this by error regarding manuscript B. Manuscripts D, a (*because I said to you I am not* etc.), l, the Syriac (Curetonian), Cyprian, and Firmicus omit **I**. | **him** <note>original: "εκεινου"</note>: The Textus Receptus and manuscript 245 read **his** <note>original: "αυτου"</note>.

**29.** **standing** <note>original: "εστηκως"</note>: Manuscript D, Theodotus, and Clement (though very freely: *but the friend of the bridegroom, standing before the bride-chamber, hearing the voice of the bridegroom* etc.) and Origen (*but the friend of the bridegroom standing rejoices with joy*) read **standing** <note>original: "εστως"</note>. | **him**: Manuscript ℵ places this after "standing" (*the one standing by him and hearing*).

**30.** **He** <note>original: "εκεινον"</note>: Manuscript ℵ adds **but**. | **but**: Manuscript G and the Syriac (Peshitta) omit this.

**31.** **the one being** <note>original: "ο ων"</note> (Corrected ℵ, Origen, etc.): The original hand of ℵ, Manuscript D, and Old Latin a, b, l, q, as well as the Syriac (Jerusalem and Curetonian) read **but the one being**. | **from** <note>original: "εκ"</note> after **being** (also Origen and a Greek commentary on Ephesians, and corrected ℵ): The original hand of ℵ and Old Latin a and e read **upon** <note>Latin: "super" or "supra"</note>. Manuscript D and others read **from** <note>original: "απο"</note>. | Manuscript Λ omits (by accident) **from the earth** before **is and**; the Syriac (Jerusalem) omits **is from the earth and from the earth** (the scribe’s eye jumped from the first 'earth' to the third). Manuscripts g, l, mm, and seemingly Origen omit **is from the earth and**, as do the Latin translations of Origen (*who do not speak heavenly things, but earthly things. He who is from the earth, speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is over all, and what he has seen and heard he testifies*), Tertullian (*he who is from the earth, he says, speaks earthly things, and he who is present from the heavens, what he has seen those things he speaks*), and his work on Baptism (*saying: he who is from the earth, speaks of the earth; he who comes from above is over all*). | **coming** without **above** etc. with the original hand of ℵ, Manuscript D, and several others, including the Syriac (Curetonian) and Armenian. Origen in his commentary says: *If therefore he who is from the earth speaks from the earth, and he who comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard, you will then seek...* though earlier he follows the standard text. Eusebius writes: *He who said: 'He who comes from above is over all, and he who comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard'*. Nonnus also follows this. Tertullian and Hilary are also cited. The Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add **above** <note>original: "επανω"</note>.

<summary>John the Baptist clarifies his role as the messenger and "friend of the bridegroom" (Jesus), emphasizing that his own mission must fade as Jesus's grows. The text highlights the contrast between the earthly origin of the witness and the heavenly origin of the Christ.</summary>

-># ACCORDING TO JOHN 3, 36.<-

**32** What he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one accepts his testimony. **33** The one who has accepted his testimony has certified <note>Literally, "set a seal"</note> that God is true. **34** For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God; for he does not give the Spirit by measure. <margin>30. 3</margin> **35** The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. <margin>5, 20</margin> <margin>31. 10.</margin> **36** The one who believes in the Son has eternal life; the one who is disobedient to the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.

---

**is over all** <note>original: "pantōn estin"</note> with the corrected Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and most other uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note> and versions, including the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic. Also found in the writings of Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Augustine. (Considering the balance of evidence, **is above all** seems to have been added here to correspond to the previous phrase **is from the earth**. This opinion is confirmed because the word **and** <note>original: "kai"</note> before **what he has seen** etc. is also omitted by important witnesses who support the inclusion of **is over all**.)

**32.** **the one who** <note>original: "ho"</note> (Manuscript ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note> corrector b or a; originally ℵ read **whom** <note>original: "hon"</note>) **has seen** <note>original: "heōraken"</note> (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and others use this spelling; other manuscripts use a slightly different spelling **eor.**) without the conjunction <note>i.e., omitting the word "and"</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and several early Latin and Syriac versions. Origen (in Huet’s edition) also omits **and** even where he retains **is over all**. Eusebius, Nonnus, Tertullian, and Hilary also lack the "and." The traditional text <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> (though Griesbach marked it as doubtful) prefixes **and**, as does Lachmann, following Alexandrinus and the majority of later manuscripts and the Vulgate. | **testifies**: Sinaiticus, Bezae, and several Old Latin and Coptic versions read this simply. The traditional text and the editions of Lachmann and Tischendorf prefix **this** <note>original: "touto"</note> (i.e., "to this he testifies") following Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and the majority of manuscripts.

**33.** **the one having accepted** <note>original: "labōn"</note>: A few manuscripts and Cyril read **the one accepting** <note>original: "lambanōn"</note> in the present tense.

**34.** **by measure** <note>original: "ek metrou"</note> (Origen [vol 2, p 595] notes: "Perhaps the measure is not named in relation to the knowledge itself, but according to the recipient, because they are not capable of receiving more. For even the rain itself is immeasurable, but it is measured [by the ground it falls on], etc."): A few manuscripts and the Aldine edition read **in part** <note>original: "ek merous"</note> | **gives**: The text stands without an explicit subject in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. The traditional text adds **God** <note>original: "ho Theos"</note> (i.e., "God gives the Spirit"), and Lachmann includes it in brackets based on Alexandrinus and the majority of manuscripts, including the Vulgate and Coptic versions and several Church Fathers. | **the Spirit**: Omitted in the original hand of the Vaticanus manuscript, but added by a later corrector in the margin.

**35.** **has given** <note>original: "dedōken"</note> (also in Eusebius): Manuscript Bezae and a few others read **gave** <note>original: "edōken"</note>.

**36.** **the one who believes**: Manuscript Bezae prefixes **that** <note>original: "hina"</note> and uses a different verb form <note>subjunctive "may have"</note>. | **the one who is disobedient**: The original hand of Sinaiticus and several Old Latin versions read this simply. The traditional text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **but the one who is disobedient** <note>original: "ho de apeith."</note> following the corrected Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and almost all other witnesses. A few manuscripts and Chrysostom read **disbelieving** <note>original: "apistōn"</note> instead of "disobedient." | **to the Son**: One manuscript adds **of him** <note>original: "autou"</note>. | **not**: A minor spelling variation exists in two manuscripts. | **shall see**: Cited thus by Sinaiticus and the letters of Ignatius.

## IV.

1 When therefore Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John, 2 (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did), <margin>32.7</margin> 3 he left Judea and went away again into Galilee. <margin>33.10</margin> 4 and it was necessary for him to pass through Samaria. 5 So he comes to a city

---

<note>This first section concludes the notes from the previous page regarding John 3:36.</note>
Ephrem <sup>5)</sup>, Apostolic Constitutions <sup>5, 20, 6</sup>, Basil <sup>2, 217. 430. 623. 469</sup> and *On Baptism* <sup>638. 657</sup>, Tertullian *Against Praxeas* etc ... manuscript ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, corrected by the first scribe, Irenaeus in Latin translation <sup>282</sup>, Cyprian <sup>296</sup> read **has** (the Latin manuscript 'e' reads **will have**) | **life** with manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, D, T<sup>b</sup> etc ... manuscripts E, F, H, L, M and about 50 others, the Latin Ignatius <sup>324</sup>, Apostolic Constitutions <sup>5, 20, 6</sup>, Basil <sup>2, 217. 430. 469. 623</sup> and *On Baptism* <sup>638. 657</sup>, Chrysostom <sup>8, 201</sup> and twice in <sup>202</sup>, Cyril <sup>4, 173</sup>, Theodoret <sup>4, 383</sup> read **the life** | **remains** with this accent [μένει] in manuscripts E, H, K, S, V etc., the Latin manuscripts a, c, d, f, ff<sup>2</sup>, l, q, the Vulgate, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac, and the Armenian ... Manuscripts M, Γ, Π and many others, Latin b, e, g, the Coptic, the Harclean Syriac, Ethiopic, Irenaeus in Latin <sup>282</sup>, Tertullian *Against Praxeas* <sup>2</sup>, Cyprian <sup>296</sup> read **will remain** <note>original: "μενεῖ"</note>, which is the future tense. The same is published in Basil <sup>2, 217. 430. 623</sup> (but not <sup>469</sup>) and *On Baptism* <sup>657</sup> (but not <sup>638</sup>), Cyril <sup>4, 174</sup> (but not Chrysostom <sup>8, 201. 202</sup>): hence Griesbach reads **will remain**. | **upon him**: ℵ and Latin 'b' place this before **remains**. Furthermore, after these things, Latin 'e' adds: *And after these things John was handed over* (marginal Syriac: *Johannes*), and the marginal Harclean Syriac provides exactly the same.

**IV, 1.** **Jesus** <term>ι̅ς̅: a "nomen sacrum" or sacred shorthand for Jesus</term> with ℵ, D, A, and minuscules 1, 22, 118, 209, 2pe and more than 20 others, Latin a, b, c, e, ff<sup>2</sup>, l, the Vulgate, Curetonian, Philoxenian, and Peshitta Syriac texts, Coptic, Armenian, and Chrysostom <sup>8, 203</sup> ... The Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **the Lord** <term>κυριοσ: the Greek word for Lord</term> with manuscripts A, B, C, L, T<sup>b</sup>, and most other uncials and minuscules, Latin f, q, marginal Peshitta, Ethiopic, Nonnus <sup>4, 1</sup> (using the poetic word *koiranos* for ruler), and Cyril <sup>4, 175</sup> (:: **the Lord** <term>κυ̅ς̅: shorthand for Lord</term>. It appears this was introduced to avoid the repetition of the same name **Jesus** <term>ι̅υ̅: shorthand for of Jesus</term>. Otherwise, for this use of the title "Lord" in John, one cannot compare any passages except 6:23 *the Lord had given thanks*, 11:2 *she who anointed the Lord with ointment*, 20:18 *that she had seen the Lord*, and 21:12 *knowing that it was the Lord*, the context of which places appears to differ somewhat from 4:1) | **that** (manuscript 69 adds **the**) **Jesus**: manuscript A, 262, and 8 others (not the same ones as those providing "Jesus" for "the Lord"), and the Philoxenian Syriac omit **Jesus** | **than** (also in B corrected): manuscripts A, B (original), G, L, Γ, 262, and a few others (also Origen <sup>4, 249</sup>) omit this.

**2.** **although** <note>original: "καίτοιγε"</note>: Textus Receptus reads **and yet** <note>original: "καιτοι"</note> | **Jesus himself** also in Latin a, b, e, f, q ... manuscripts A, D, K, Π, and 10 others, Latin ff<sup>2</sup>, l, gat, mm, Chrysostom <sup>8, 203</sup>, Cyril <sup>4, 175</sup> read **he Jesus** (ℵ and others, plus Chrysostom, add **the**) ... manuscript 251, Latin c, the Vulgate, and Curetonian Syriac omit this.

**3.** **Judea** also in Latin c, f, q, Origen <sup>4, 249</sup> etc: manuscripts D, 1, 13, 69, 106, 124, and 25 others, Latin a, b, e, ff<sup>2</sup>, l, foss, gat, mm, Armenian, and Ethiopic add (manuscripts a and d place before it) **land** :: as in 3:22 | **again** with ℵ, B (corrected), C, L, M, T<sup>b</sup>, minuscules 1, 33, 69, 124, 346, and many others, Latin a, b, c, e, f, ff<sup>2</sup>, l, the Vulgate, Coptic, Curetonian and Philoxenian Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, Nonnus <sup>4, 9</sup>, and Cyril <sup>4, 175</sup> ... Griesbach and Tischendorf omit this with manuscripts A, B (original), Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, 8 other uncials, more than 120 others, the Aldine edition, Latin q, and Harclean Syriac (Origen <sup>4, 249</sup> very freely writes *leaving Judea and going away into Galilee* etc.) and Chrysostom <sup>8, 203</sup> (*he withdrew from Judea and came into Galilee*)

**4.** **to pass through**: manuscript Λ and 124 read **to come** | **Samaria** with ℵ, C, D, E (original), L, Γ, Δ and many others ... Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **Samareia** <note>A slight spelling variation</note> with manuscripts A, B, E (corrected), F, G, H, K, M, S, U, Λ, Π and many others. Likewise in the following verses, except that in verse 5 the Textus Receptus confirms **Samareia**; but in verse 7 we gave **Samaria** with ℵ, D, F, L (original) and many others, while the Textus Receptus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **Samareia** with the rest. Compare Acts 17:11 where we published **Samaria** from ℵ, A, B (original), E, F, L, X, Δ. In Acts, the same form is maintained everywhere (seven times) by ℵ, D, E, with the addition of manuscript 'c' four times, and A and H once.

**5.** **So he comes** (manuscript C corrected, F, a few others, and the Armenian omit "so", though Latin e, f, l have it; Curetonian, Philoxenian, and Jerusalem Syriac, and Ethiopic read "and he came"): manuscript C corrected (with which the marginal ecclesiastical lectionary 'm' agrees), F, H, U, and more than 20 others, and Latin 'e' add **Jesus** |

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN 4, 8.</header>

...of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. 6 Now Jacob's well was there. So Jesus, having become tired from the journey, sat down thus by the well; it was about the sixth hour. 7 A woman from Samaria comes to draw water. Jesus says to her: "Give me a drink." 8 For his disciples had gone away into the city, so that they might buy food.

---

<margin>Samaria</margin>: see the notes for verse 4. | <margin>Sychar</margin> (also in the editions of Griesbach and Scholz) is found in the manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus, a 4th-century Greek manuscript</note>, A, B, C, D, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and most others, as well as several Old Latin versions (some reading *Esychar* or *Sycar*), the Sahidic and Coptic versions, and the writings of Chrysostom and Cyril. The variant *Sychar* (with a different spelling in Greek) appears in manuscript 69 and some others, as well as the Clementine Vulgate and Nonnus. 

<note>The following notes discuss whether "Sychar" is a misspelling of "Sichem."</note>
Jerome, in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, notes: <note>original: "hebraice Sichem dicitur... licet vitio ut Sichar legatur error inolevit"</note> "In Hebrew it is called Sichem, as John the Evangelist also testifies, although the error has grown so that it is read as Sychar by fault." He similarly notes in his work *On Hebrew Names*: <note>original: "corrupte autem pro Sichem - ut Sichar legeretur usus obtinuit"</note> "However, custom has prevailed so that it is read as Sychar corruptly instead of Sichem." But in Eusebius's *Onomasticon* (a directory of biblical places), the name is read as Sychar with this addition: <note>original: "προ της νεας πολεως πλησιον του χωριου ου εδωκεν ιακωβ ιωσηφ τω υιω αυτου..."</note> "before the new city near the plot which Jacob gave to his son Joseph, in which Christ, according to John, converses with the Samaritan woman by the well; and it is still shown today." | The word "the" (Greek: *o*) is found before "Joseph" in ℵ, A, B, C, and many others, though ℵ and B include it specifically as "to the Joseph."

6. <margin>So/Therefore</margin>: Found in many manuscripts; however, manuscript 69 and others omit it, while the Old Syriac and others use "but" or "and." | <margin>Jesus</margin>: Manuscript Δ <note>Codex Sangallensis</note> reads "the Lord." | <margin>thus</margin>: This word (Greek: *outōs*) is included in the Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic versions, but is omitted in several Old Latin manuscripts and the Armenian version. | <margin>by the well</margin>: So read Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril; however, manuscript L reads "onto the well." | <margin>hour</margin>: Some Coptic and Syriac versions add "and it was the hour." | <margin>about</margin>: The manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, D, and L read "about" (Greek: *hōs*); the later standard text reads "as if" (Greek: *hōsei*), supported by Origen and Chrysostom. Furthermore, the Curetonian Syriac version rearranges the verses so that the mention of the disciples in verse 8 follows the phrase "by the well," followed by: <note>original: "Et cum sederet Iesus erat hora quasi sexta"</note> "And while Jesus was sitting it was about the sixth hour," then: "And a woman came from Samaria etc."

7. <margin>comes</margin>: Several Old Latin and Syriac versions read "and she came"; one manuscript reads "but she came." | <margin>woman</margin>: Codex Sinaiticus and some Latin and Coptic versions read "a certain woman." | <margin>Samaria</margin>: See the notes for verse 4 regarding the spelling. | <margin>drink</margin>: The spelling *pein* is found in ℵ, B, C, D, and L. The standard text and Lachmann use *piein*, found in A and many later manuscripts. 

<note>The author cites an ancient Greek grammarian regarding this spelling.</note>
The grammarian Herodian says: <note>original: "ἁμαρτάνουσιν οἱ λέγοντες· πεῖν βούλομαι... δέον λέγειν, δισυλλάβως."</note> "Those who say 'I want to drink' (pein) in one syllable are mistaken; one ought to say it in two syllables (piein). For only in this way is it spoken among all the ancients." It also appears in the *Greek Anthology*: "To whom it is not pleasing to speak a jest, nor to drink (pein)." See also verses 9 and 10.

8. <margin>had gone away</margin>: Most manuscripts use the form *apelēlytheisan*, but manuscript L and Chrysostom use a simpler form meaning "they went away." | <margin>the city</margin>: Manuscript Δ omits the word "the."

<header>4, 9. ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

9 The Samaritan woman says to him, "How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, since I am a Samaritan woman?" 10 Jesus answered and said to her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water." 11 The woman says to him, "Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep; where then do you get that living water? 12 Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?"

---

9. **says** <note>Greek: λεγει</note> without the conjunction <term>therefore</term> <note>original: "sine copula cum"</note> in manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, v, 1, 61, 229, and others; almost in the Curetonian Syriac, Ethiopic, Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, and in the writings of Cyril. The standard text <note>indicated by ς</note> and the editions of Lachmann and Tischendorf add "therefore" <note>Greek: οὖν</note> following manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, and most others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, and Peshitta Syriac (the Harklean Syriac reads "and said"). | **the Samaritan** <note>Greek: η σαμαριτις</note>: omitted in the Harklean Syriac. | **Samaritan**: The spelling varies between *samaritis* (in ℵ, C, D, L) and *samareitis* (in A, B, and most others). The same variation occurs for "Samaritan woman" and "Samaritans" elsewhere in Luke and Acts. | **how**: In several Old Latin manuscripts (a, b, e, etc.), the Armenian version, and the Curetonian Syriac, "how" is placed after "you being a Jew" (reading: "you, since you are a Jew, how..."). | **drink**: Different spellings in the manuscripts (some use *pein*, others *pin* or *piein*). | **since [she] is**: This phrase is placed before "Samaritan woman" in several major manuscripts and the Vulgate. Manuscript D and the Armenian version omit it. Furthermore, we have not added the phrase "For [Jews have no dealings with Samaritans]" <note>original: "ου γαρ..."</note> following manuscripts ℵ and D and some Old Latin versions. Tischendorf and Lachmann include it, as it appears in ℵ, A, B, C, L, and most versions and Church Fathers (Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril), though some scholars like Wassenberg <note>a 18th-century critic</note> regarded it as a <term>gloss</term> <note>an explanatory note added by a later scribe</note>.

10. **Jesus**: Abbreviated as $\overline{\iota\sigma}$ in some manuscripts. Manuscript 69 reads "the Jesus." | **knew**: Manuscript A uses a slightly different spelling (*eideis* instead of *ēdeis*). | **drink**: Again, spelling variations (*pein* or *piein*) across the major manuscripts. | **him**: The Naassene fragment <note>a text from an early Gnostic sect</note> reads "you would have asked **of him**, and he would have given you to drink living, leaping water." | **would have given**: Omitted in manuscripts L, 69, and some others, as well as in some citations by Origen and Cyril.

11. **the woman**: Found in almost all manuscripts; however, the original hand of ℵ reads "that woman," and manuscript B omits the phrase entirely. | **neither** <note>Greek: ουτε</note>: Manuscript D reads "not even" <note>Greek: ουδε</note>. | **where**: Without "then" <note>Greek: ουν</note> in ℵ, D, and several Old Latin and Syriac versions. Lachmann and Tischendorf add "then" following A, B, C, L, and the Vulgate, as well as Origen and Chrysostom. | **the living water**: Manuscript D and others read simply "living water" without the definite article.

12. **our**: Omitted in manuscript Δ. | **Jacob**: Manuscript M mistakenly reads "Abraham." | **who**: ℵ uses a more emphatic form of "who" <note>Greek: οστισ</note>. | **gave**: Manuscript 69 and Origen use a different tense of the verb "to give." | **the well**: Several manuscripts and versions (Old Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian) add the word **this** <note>reading "this well"</note>. | **and he himself**: ℵ originally read "himself and," but was corrected. | **his livestock**: Manuscript D omits "his."

### ACCORDING TO JOHN 4, 17.

13 Jesus answered and said to her, "Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; 
<margin>7, 38</margin> <note>Cross-reference to John 7:38: 'Whoever believes in me... rivers of living water will flow from within them.'</note>
14 but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst forever; instead, the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." 15 The woman says to him, "Sir, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or have to keep coming here to draw." 16 He says to her, "Go, call your husband and come here." 17 She ans— <note>The verse breaks mid-word here in the Greek text as the scribe prepares to list the evidence for the verse ending.</note>

---

13. **Jesus** <note>original shorthand: ι̅ς̅</note>: This reading is found in the major ancient manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, B, C, D, L, and others, as well as the writings of the church fathers Chrysostom and Cyril. The "Received Text" <note>indicated by ς</note> adds the definite article, reading "**the** Jesus" <note>original: ο ι̅ς̅</note>, following manuscripts Δ and Π and Origen. | **Jesus answered and said to her**: the Curetonian Syriac version reads "Jesus replied to her."

14. **whoever drinks** <note>original: οσ δ αν πιη</note>: Found in Origen, Eusebius, Chrysostom, and Cyril. Manuscripts ℵ and D read **but the one drinking** <note>original: ο δε πινων</note>. | **that**: Manuscript E originally intended to write "of this" <note>original: τουτου</note>. | **will never thirst... [to] I will give him**: This entire section is present in most major Greek manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate. However, some early sources omit this due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>a scribal error where the eye skips from one occurrence of a word to a similar ending later, accidentally deleting the text in between</note>. Because of this omission in some versions, the editor Lachmann places this section in brackets. | **will thirst**: Variations in the Greek spelling of "thirst" appear in manuscripts ℵ, A, B, D, L, and M. | **the water that I will give him** (the second instance): This phrase is omitted by certain Latin and Syriac witnesses. | **I** (the second instance): This is included in manuscripts ℵ, D, M, and many Latin versions. It is omitted in the editions of Lachmann and Tischendorf based on manuscripts A, B, C, and L. | **him** (the second instance): Omitted in ℵ and some writings of Origen and Cyprian. | **in him**: The Old Latin manuscript "a" and others read "to him."

15. **thirst**: Codex D reads "I will [not] thirst" <note>using the future tense</note>. | **come here** <note>original: διερχωμαι</note>: This specific verb form (meaning to "come through" or "come across") is found in the earliest manuscripts ℵ and B. The editors Lachmann and Tischendorf use a more standard form of "come" <note>original: ερχωμαι</note> based on nearly all other manuscripts (A, C, D, etc.) and the writings of Chrysostom. | **coming**: There is a minor spelling variation between the forms *erchōmai* and *erchomai* across various manuscripts.

16. **He says to her**: This simple phrasing (without adding the name "Jesus") is found in the highly regarded manuscripts B and C. Manuscript ℵ and A add "Jesus," while the "Received Text" <note>ς</note> reads "the Jesus." | **your husband**: Most manuscripts place "husband" first <note>original: τον ανδρα σου</note>, but manuscript B and some versions of Origen and Chrysostom reverse the order to read "of you the husband" <note>original: σου τον ανδρα</note>.

17. **the woman answered and said**: The earliest manuscript ℵ simply reads "the woman answered." The Curetonian Syriac reads "she said to him," while Chrysostom uses a slightly different conjunction.

### ACCORDING TO JOHN 4, 18.

...the woman answered and said, "I do not have a husband." Jesus says to her, "You have well said, 'I do not have a husband'; 18 for you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband. This you have spoken truly." 19 The woman says to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. 20 Our fathers worshiped on this mountain; and you people say that in Jerusalem is the place where it is necessary to worship." 21 Jesus says to her, "Believe me, woman, that an hour is coming when neither on—

---

**17.** **she says**, says Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, volume 4, page 183</note>. **The woman says to him | and said** <note>original: λεγει αυτω η γυνη | και ειπεν</note> (compare the Latin Vulgate and manuscript *d* which read *and said*, and manuscripts *c* and *q* which read *saying*): This reading appears without further addition in manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, D, K, L, M, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and many others, as well as the Old Latin versions *e, f, q*, the Vulgate, Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, and Origen. Manuscripts B, C, E, F, G, H and about 40 others, along with Old Latin *a, b, l*, the Sahidic Coptic, and the Curetonian Syriac, add **to him** <note>original: αυτω</note>; thus Lachmann <note>Ln</note> places it in brackets [to him]. | **a husband I do not have** <note>original: ανδρα ουκ εχω</note>: Found in ℵ, C*, D, L, and manuscript 142. Also in Cyril. The "Received Text" <note>indicated by ς</note>, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **I do not have a husband** <note>original: ουκ εχω ανδρ.</note> according to manuscripts A, B, C³, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, nine other uncials, most other manuscripts, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Origen, and Chrysostom. | **you said** <note>original: ειπες</note>: Found in ℵ and B* <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, Chrysostom, and Cyril. The "Received Text," Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **you said** <note>original: ειπας—a slight grammatical variation</note> according to A, B³, C, D, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and almost all other manuscripts. (Note: The form *you said* <note>original: ειπας</note> is found in Matthew 26:25 and 64, and Luke 20:39, but the alternative *εῖπες* is never substituted there.) Furthermore, Heracleon <note>a 2nd-century Gnostic commentator</note>, as quoted by Origen, reads **you have spoken truly** <note>original: αληθες ειρηκας</note> instead of "well you said." | **husband**: manuscripts 142, 245, 247, 258, and various Latin and Coptic versions place this word after "have." | **I have** <note>original: εχω</note>: Found in almost all manuscripts including A, B, C, L, and the Vulgate. However, Heracleon (via Origen) and some Latin versions read **you have** <note>original: εχεις</note>.

**18.** **five**: Heracleon, as quoted by Origen, reads **six** <note>original: εξ</note>; he interprets this to mean that all "material wickedness" is revealed through these six husbands. | **now**: Omitted in manuscript E*. | **truly** <note>original: αληθες</note>: Found in A, B, C, D, L, and almost all others. Most Latin versions read "true" or "truly" (*verum* or *vere*). Manuscript ℵ and others read **truthfully** <note>original: αληθως</note>.

**19.** **Sir** <note>original: κυριε</note>: Omitted in the original hand of ℵ. | **you** <note>original: συ</note>: Omitted in manuscript D and several Old Latin versions.

**20.** **on this mountain** <note>original: εν τ. ορει τουτω</note>: This word order is found in ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, and most major versions including the Vulgate and Syriac. The "Received Text" <note>ς</note> swaps the order to **on mountain this** <note>original: εν τουτω τω ορ.</note> based on later minuscules and Tertullian. | **the place** <note>original: ο τοποσ</note>: Omitted in ℵ. Tertullian similarly notes: "because in Jerusalem it is necessary to worship." | **it is necessary to worship** <note>original: προσκυν. δει</note>: Found in ℵ, A, B, C*, D, L, and the Vulgate. The "Received Text" reverses it to **to worship it is necessary** <note>original: δει προσκυν.</note> based on C³, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others.

**21.** **Believe me, woman**: This order is found in ℵ, B, C*, L, and others. The "Received Text" and Lachmann read **Woman, believe me** <note>original: γυναι πιστ. μοι</note> following A, C³, D, and most others. | **Believe** <note>original: πιστευε</note>: Present imperative form in ℵ, B, C*, D, L. The "Received Text" uses the aorist imperative **Believe** <note>original: πιστευσον</note> following A, C³, and many others. | **when** <note>original: οτε</note>: Manuscripts Λ, V, Γ, Δ read "that" <note>original: οτι</note>. | **this mountain**: Read by D and several Old Latin and Syriac versions.

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN          4, 26.          775</header>

...on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father. 22 You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. 23 But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for indeed the Father seeks such people as those who worship him. 24 God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. 25 The woman says to him: "I know that Messiah is coming, the one called Christ; when he comes, he will announce everything to us." 26 Jesus says to her—

---

<meta>Catchword: Jesus—</meta>

<note>The following notes provide a technical comparison of how different ancient manuscripts and early Church writers recorded these verses.</note>

According to Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, page 804</note>: **this mountain** <note>original: τουτ. τ. ορ.</note> | **you will worship** (mistakenly written as 'you might worship'): found in manuscripts 69 and 124; also in the Coptic, Armenian, and Origen <note>volume 1, page 686 and volume 4, page 223 (though at 4, 224 he uses 'will worship' four times)</note>.

<margin>22.</margin> **is**: manuscript 69 reads **has become and is** | **what we know**: Epiphanius <note>page 677</note> reads **the things which we know**.

<margin>23.</margin> **but** <note>original: αλλα</note> with manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A, B, D ... the Received Text <note>ς</note> reads **but** <note>original: αλλ</note> with C, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials, and nearly all other manuscripts | **the Father**: manuscript 69 adds **my** | **for indeed the Father seeks such people as those who worship him** (the word **him** <note>original: αυτον</note> is also in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus ℵᶜ; the original Sinaiticus ℵ*, manuscript 254, and a few others read **for him** <note>original: αυτω</note>; manuscript Γ reads **of them** <note>original: αυτων</note>). This is also found in Origen <note>volume 4, page 229</note>, Athanasius <note>page 545</note>, Chrysostom <note>volume 8, page 220</note>, Cyril <note>volume 4, page 191</note>, and Hilary <note>page 804</note>. Manuscript 1. 22. omits this. (However, this does not apply to Tertullian <note>On Prayer, 28</note>: *the hour will come—in spirit and truth. For God is spirit, and thus requires such worshipers. For the conclusions respond to the words about which the inquiry is made.*) Furthermore, after **worship him**, manuscripts 124, a, and b add **in spirit**.

<margin>24.</margin> **God is spirit and those who worship [him]**: due to similar endings <note>a scribal error known as homoeoteleuton</note>, manuscripts G, 69, 131, 229, and a few others omit this. The entire verse in the Curetonian Syriac <note>syrᶜᵘ</note> is rendered: *For God is spirit, and those who worship him in spirit, it is also necessary for those who worship him in spirit and truth to worship.* These are indeed strangely confused. | **those who worship** without **him** <note>original: αυτον</note> according to ℵ*, D*, and Old Latin manuscripts d and ff². Heracleon <note>as cited in Origen volume 4, page 234</note> writes: *that those who worship in spirit and truth must worship, thinking it makes it clearer, worthily of the one worshiped, etc.* Novatian <note>On the Trinity, 2</note> also follows this. ... The Received Text <note>ς</note>, Lachmann <note>Ln</note>, and Tischendorf <note>Ti</note> add **him** (manuscript 251 and a few others, including Eusebius, read **for him** <note>original: αυτω</note>) according to the corrected Sinaiticus ℵᶜ, A, B, C, the second correction of D, L, and nearly all other uncials and manuscripts, most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Titus of Bostra, Cyril, and Hilary. | **in spirit and truth** (also in ℵᶜ): ℵ* reads **in the spirit of truth**. | **must worship** <note>original: προσκ. δει</note> with ℵ*, D, Old Latin manuscript a, Novatian, Victorinus, and Hilary. ... The Received Text <note>ς</note>, Lachmann <note>Ln</note>, and Tischendorf <note>Ti</note> read **it is necessary to worship** <note>original: δει προσκ.</note> with ℵᶜ, A, B, C, L, and nearly all other manuscripts, most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, and various works by Origen, Eusebius, Cyril, and Hilary. (Compare verse 20, where most also preferred "it is necessary to worship.")

<margin>25.</margin> **I know** <note>original: οιδα</note> (also Origen and Chrysostom) ... ℵᶜ, G, L, Λ, 13, 33, 69, and ten others, plus Sahidic, Coptic, later Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, Origen, Cyril, and Nonnus read **we know** <note>original: οιδαμεν; Nonnus uses εδάημεν</note>. | **Messiah** (manuscript D writes **Meiseias**) with ℵ, A, B, C, D, H, K, L, M, Δ, Π and many others ... Griesbach <note>Gb''</note> notes **Mesiah** (one manuscript writes **Meiseias**) with E, G, S, U, V, Γ, Λ, Π, and 160 others, as well as several versions. Compare also verse 1, 42. | **the one called Christ**: The Curetonian Syriac and some scholars omit this (though the Peshitta and other Syriac versions include it). | **will announce** <note>original: αναγγέλει</note> (ℵᶜ and many Origen citations): ℵ* and the Greek of D write **will proclaim** <note>original: αναγγελλει</note>. | **everything** <note>original: απαντα</note> with ℵ, B, C*, 1, and Origen ... The Received Text <note>ς</note>, Lachmann <note>Ln</note>, and Tischendorf <note>Ti</note> read **all things** <note>original: παντα</note> with A, C², D, L, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, eight other uncials, and most others (manuscript 69 reads "the all things"), Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril. | **to us**: manuscript U and others read **to you**.

<margin>26.</margin> **the Jesus**: manuscript Λ omits the article **the**.

<note>The following notes are technical scholarly comparisons of how different ancient manuscripts record these verses. Letters like ℵ, A, and B refer to specific ancient Bibles (Codices), while names like Chr and Cyr refer to early Church writers (Chrysostom and Cyril).</note>

**27.** **at this** <note>original: επι τουτω</note> with manuscripts ℵ (corrector), A, B, C, G, H, L, M, S, V, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others; also Chrysostom and Cyril ... ℵ (original hand), D, and the Coptic read **in this** <note>original: εν τουτω; Latin: *in hoc*</note> ... E, K, U, and others read **toward this** <note>original: επι τουτο</note> ... most Old Latin, the Vulgate, and Sahidic read **immediately** or **straightway**. | **they came** <note>original: ηλθαν/ηλθον</note> with ℵ, A, B, C, D, L etc., and the Vulgate ... ℵ (original) and some Latin read **they came upon him** <note>original: επηλθ-</note>. Additionally, some write the ending as **-an** (with ℵ, B) while others write **-on** (with A, C, D, L, and most others). | **they were amazed** <note>original: εθαυμαζον</note> with ℵ, A, B, C, D, G, K, L, M, Π, most Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac versions ... the Received Text <note>ς</note> reads **they marveled** <note>original: εθαυμασαν</note> with E, S, U, V, Γ, Δ, Λ. | **said** <note>original: ειπεν</note> without additions in A, B, C, L, and many others, including the Vulgate and Syriac ... ℵ, D, and some Latin add **to him**, while one Latin version adds **to the woman**, and the Armenian adds **from among them**. | **What do you seek or why do you speak with her?**: the Curetonian Syriac reads: "What did she seek? Or, what were you saying to her?"

**28.** **the water jar**: Manuscript Δ <note>Codex Sangallensis</note> omits **the**. | **her**: Manuscript D reads **her own**; others omit it. | **the woman**: Manuscript D, some Latin, and Coptic versions place "the woman" before "the water jar."

**29.** **everything that** <note>original: παντα α</note> with ℵ, B, C, and several early versions ... the Received Text reads **all things whatsoever** <note>original: πα. οσα</note> with A, C, D, L, and many others. | **this** <note>original: ουτος</note>: most Latin and the Vulgate read **he himself** <note>Latin: *ipse*</note> ... Manuscript D and some Latin read **that one** <note>original: εκεινοσ; Latin: *ille*</note>.

**30.** **They went out** <note>original: εξηλθον</note> without a conjunction in A, B, L, and many others ... the Received Text adds **therefore** <note>original: ουν</note> with ℵ, Δ, and several others; others add **but** <note>original: δε</note> ... Manuscripts C, D, and some versions read **And they went out**.

**31.** **In** <note>original: εν</note> without a conjunction with ℵ, B, C, D, L, and the Vulgate ... the Received Text adds **but** <note>original: δε</note> with A, C, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others. | **were asking/urging** <note>original: ηρωτων</note>: Manuscript Δ reads **were beseeching** <note>original: παρεκαλουν</note>. Chrysostom notes that "asked" here means "implored" in their local dialect. | **him**: Manuscripts G and Δ omit this. | **the disciples**: Several manuscripts and versions add **his**. | **saying: Rabbi, eat**: the Curetonian Syriac reads: **that he should eat bread with them**. | **Rabbi**: spelled with two 'e's <note>original: ῥαββεί</note> in ℵ, B, C, D, E, Γ, Δ ... the Received Text spells it with an 'i' <note>original: ῥαββί</note> with A, G, K, L, and most others.

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN 4:36.</header>

...[I] have food to eat that you do not know about." 33 So the disciples were saying to one another, "No one brought him something to eat, did they?" 34 Jesus says to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work. 35 Do you not say, 'There are still four months and then the harvest comes'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are white for harvest. 36 Already the reaper receives a reward and gathers fruit for—"

<note>The following notes are a "critical apparatus," which scholars use to track differences between ancient copies of the Bible. Codes like ℵ, A, B, and D refer to specific ancient parchment books (Codices), while names like Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril refer to early Christian writers who quoted these verses.</note>

**33.** **they were saying** <note>original: ελεγον</note> (in the corrected version of manuscript ℵ): the original hand of ℵ, manuscript b, and the *Questions* (6,40) read **they say** <note>original: λεγουσιν</note>; manuscript d reads the Latin *dicent* [they were saying]. | **so** <note>original: ουν</note> also in the corrected ℵ, manuscripts c, f, ff², g, 1, m, the Vulgate, the Peshitta Syriac, Sahidic, Coptic, Origen (4,245), etc.: manuscripts D, G (Greek), a, b, q, and the Harklean Syriac read **but** <note>original: δε</note> (the Ethiopic reads *and they were saying*) ... the original ℵ, d, and the Old Syriac and Curetonian Syriac omit the word entirely. | **the disciples** (the Curetonian Syriac omits "the disciples"; manuscripts a, b, c, e, ff², q, Sahidic, Coptic, and various Syriac versions add **his**) **to one another**: manuscripts 13, 69, 124, and the Coptic read **to one another the disciples** ... manuscript D (Greek) reads **among themselves the disciples**. The Latin versions translate "to one another" as follows: *ad invicem* [to each other] in a, c, d, e, f, and the Vulgate; *ad alterutrum* [to one another] in b and l; *intra semetipsum* [within themselves] in ff²; *inter se* [among themselves] in q; *inter semetipsos* [among themselves] in m. | **to eat**: the Bashmuric Coptic adds: "his disciples said to him: Rabbi, eat."

**34.** **says**: a more recent hand wrote **said**. | **to them**: manuscript Δ reads **to her**. | **to do** <note>original: ποιω</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, Γ, Δ, Λ, 7 uncials <note>manuscripts written in capital letters</note>, and many others, as well as Origen, Hippolytus, Basil, Chrysostom, and Antiochus ... The scholars Griesbach and Lachmann read **I will do** <note>original: ποιησω</note> along with manuscripts B, C, D, K, L, T, Π, and others, including Clement, Origen, Heracleon, Chrysostom, and Cyril (likely adjusted to match the future tense of the word "complete").

**35.** **still** <note>original: ετι</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, D, T, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and many others, the Latin, Vulgate, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, Origen, Chrysostom, and Hilary ... Manuscripts D, L, Π, 13, 28, 69, and others omit it, hence Griesbach marks it as doubtful. | **four-month period** <note>original: τετραμηνος</note> with ℵ, A, B, C, D, L, T, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, many others, Origen, and Cyril ... the standard received text (followed by Griesbach and Scholz) reads **four months** <note>original: τετραμηνον</note> with manuscript H and others, as well as Chrysostom. | **look, I tell you** also in Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril, Irenaeus (Latin), and Augustine ... but omitted in manuscripts 1, 22, 108, 118, 124, and some versions of Origen.

**35. 36.** **already** <note>original: ηδη</note> (manuscripts ℵ original, B, M, Π do not punctuate before or after it): we have joined this with the following words <note>reading "Already the reaper..."</note> (following the scholar Schulz) along with ℵ corrected, A, C, D, E, L, 33, and Latin manuscripts b, d, l, q (also e, for none of the Latin writers join "already" with the previous sentence), the Curetonian Syriac ("and already"), Irenaeus (who follows "white for harvest" with "For [Already?] the reaper receives a reward"), Eusebius, and Cyril (who does not address it in his commentary), and Theodoret ... however, the standard text and Lachmann join it with the preceding words <note>reading "...white for harvest already."</note> along with C, G, H, K, S, U, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, many others, the Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, Vulgate, Augustine, Origen, and Eusebius ... manuscripts a and m, the Coptic (D-Z manuscript), Harklean Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, Chrysostom, and Hilary omit the word entirely.

**36.** **the reaper** <note>original: ο θεριζων</note> starting the sentence without the word "and" in ℵ, B, C, D, L, T, 8, 17, 33, various Latin versions, Coptic, Irenaeus, Origen, and Cyril ... but the standard text (and Griesbach) reads **and the reaper** <note>original: και ο θεριζων</note>; Lachmann puts "[and]" in brackets, following A, C, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, many others, and the Vulgate, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions.

<header>4, 37. ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

...eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together. 37 For in this the saying is true, "One sows and another reaps." 38 I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor; others have labored, and you have entered into their labor. 39 Now from that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman testifying, "He told me everything I did." 40 So when they came to—

<note>The following notes represent the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of differences found in ancient hand-copied manuscripts of the Bible.</note>

**36.** **so that also** <note>original: ινα και</note> with manuscripts ℵ, A, D, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, most uncials <note>uncials are manuscripts written in capital letters on parchment</note>, and several others; also found in the Old Latin versions a, b, e, f, l, q, m¹¹² (*"likewise the one who reaps will receive a reward and gather fruit into eternal life: and the one who sows will rejoice together with the one who reaps"*), the Vulgate, the Curetonian Syriac, the Ethiopic, and the Latin translation of Irenaeus (page 259) and Chrysostom (8, 228) ... manuscripts B, C, L, Tᵇ, U, 1, 33, 67, and others, along with the Coptic, Peshitta Syriac, and Origen **omit the word "also"** <note>original: και</note>. | **rejoice together** <note>original: ομου χαιρη</note> (Manuscript D reads *chare*, see below): found in manuscripts E, K, Γ, Δ, Π* and many others as **rejoices together** <note>original: ομου χαιρει</note>. Furthermore, manuscript D, the Curetonian, Peshitta, and Palestinian Syriac, the Ethiopic, Basmuric, Armenian, and Irenaeus place **rejoice together** <note>original: ομ. χ.</note> (*"may they rejoice together"* in Irenaeus) after **the one who reaps.**

**37.** **the saying is true** <note>original: ο λογ. εστιν ετ.</note> in Old Latin versions e and g (*"the word is true"*), the Basmuric, Origen, Chrysostom, and Irenaeus ... manuscripts D, 301, pˢᶜʳ, and a few others, along with Latin versions b, c, q, and the Vulgate read **is the true saying** <note>original: εστιν ο λογος</note>. Latin versions a, d, l, m read *"is indeed the word of truth,"* and f, ff² read *"for it is the word of truth."* | **true** <note>original: αληθινοσ</note> (manuscripts A, Δ, Λ spell it *altheinos*) **without the definite article** <note>original: ο</note> according to manuscripts ℵ, B, C*, K, L, Tᵇ, Δ, Π, and others including Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril ... editors Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **the true** <note>original: ο αληθινοσ</note> with manuscripts A, C³, D, Γ, Δ, Π² and most others, including Chrysostom (*"the truthful"*). A few manuscripts and Chrysostom substitute *"truthful"* <note>original: αληθησ</note> for *"true"*. | **sower**: manuscript ℵ foolishly writes **reaper**.

**38.** **I have sent** <note>original: απεσταλκα</note> with manuscripts ℵ, D ... Editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read **I sent** <note>original: απεστειλα</note> with manuscripts A, B, C, L, Tᵇ, and almost all others including Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril (Note: *It seems John likely wrote "I have sent," although many disagree; a similar substitution of "sent" for "have sent" occurs in Acts 5:36 and other places in this Gospel.*) | **reaping** <note>original: θεριζων</note>: manuscript H **omits** this by accident. | **the** <note>original: ο</note> (also in Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril): omitted by manuscripts D*, L, and several Latin versions. | **you have labored** <note>original: κεκοπιακατε</note>: manuscript D reads **you labored** <note>original: εκοπιασατε</note>. | **others have labored**: manuscript D and Chrysostom read **others labored**. | **into the labor**: manuscripts b, l, and Irenaeus read *"into the labor"* (singular); versions a, ff², m¹¹² read *"in labor"*; conversely, c, e, g, f, the Vulgate, and others read *"into the labors"* (plural).

**39.** **in him** <note>original: εισ αυτον</note>: manuscripts pˢᶜʳ, a, e, and Origen **omit** this. | **Samaritans**: spelled with an "i" in ℵ, D, L, A; editors Lachmann and Tischendorf use the spelling with "ei" based on A, B, C, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and most others. | **because of the word etc.**: the Curetonian Syriac reads *"because of the testimony of the woman who said."* | **what** <note>original: α</note> with ℵ, B, C*, L, and various versions including Origen ... Editors Lachmann and Tischendorf read **all that** <note>original: οσα</note> with A, C³, D, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and almost all others, including the Vulgate and Chrysostom.

**40.** **So when they came** <note>original: ωσ ουν ηλθον</note>: manuscript B* originally had *"so they came together"*, then corrected it to *"so when they came together"*, and finally a later hand B³ wrote *"so they came"* or rather *"so when they came."* The Latin versions simply read *"when."*

<note>The following notes represent the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of differences found in ancient hand-copied manuscripts of the Bible.</note>

**[Notes for verse 40]** **therefore they came** <note>original Latin: ergo venerunt</note> in manuscript b; **when therefore they had come** <note>original Latin: cum ergo venissent</note> in manuscript d; **and when they had come** in manuscript q; manuscripts a, c, f, ff², g, l, and the Vulgate read **when they had come therefore**; manuscript e reads **they came therefore to him beseeching** etc. | **Samaritans** <note>original: σαμαριται</note> spelled thus in manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Bezae (D), L, and others... the scholars Lachmann and Tischendorf read **Samareitai** following manuscripts Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), and many others | Manuscripts K, L, and a few others read **erōton** <note>a slight spelling variation of "asked"</note> | **with them** <note>original: παρ' αὐτοῖς</note> (also found in Origen, volume 4, pages 240, 264, and 265, where he quotes the early commentator Heracleon saying: "He stayed *with* them and not *in* them"): the traditional Greek text <note>the Textus Receptus</note> reads **toward them** <note>original: πρὸς αὐτούς</note> | **he stayed**: manuscript H and a few others read **they stayed** | **there**: manuscript Sinaiticus (ℵ) and several others, including the Curetonian Syriac, read **with them** | **two days** (also in Latin versions c, f, g, and the Vulgate: *duos dies*; manuscript b: *biduum*; others: *biduo*): manuscript Sinaiticus (ℵ) reads **days two**.

41. **many more** (also in the Peshitta Syriac and Ethiopic): the Curetonian and Persian Syriac versions read simply **multi** <note>meaning "many"</note> | **believed** (also in Origen, Cyril, and Irenaeus): manuscript Δ and several others, along with the Vulgate and Coptic, **add "in him"** <note>original: εἰς αὐτόν</note>.

42. **and to the [woman]** <note>original: τῇ τε</note> (also in the corrected Sinaiticus and Irenaeus; the original Sinaiticus and manuscript b read **and they said to the woman**): manuscripts D, E, Λ, and several Old Latin versions (a, e, ff², l, q) read **but to the [woman]** <note>original: τῇ δὲ</note> | **that** <note>original: ὅτι</note> (found in manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae, etc.): manuscripts Vaticanus (B), 80, the Old Latin f, and Origen **omit this word**, which Lachmann places in brackets | **your speech** <note>original: σὴν λαλιάν</note> (found in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, etc. Origen quotes Heracleon as saying it "lacks the word 'only'"): manuscript Vaticanus (B) and Origen read **speech of yours** <note>original: λαλιάν σου</note>... manuscript Bezae (D), the original Sinaiticus, and some Latin versions read **your testimony** <note>original: σὴν μαρτυρίαν</note> (the scholar Scholz notes: "not inappropriately") | **we ourselves** <note>original: αὐτοί</note>: manuscript Bezae (D) reads **through him** | **we have heard**: certain manuscripts (1, 13, 69, etc.) and the Curetonian Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic **add "from him"** | **we know**: some manuscripts read **we have known** or **we recognize** | **this [one]**: one manuscript reads **thus** | **truly** <note>original: ἀληθῶς</note> (found in Origen and Irenaeus)... manuscript Sinaiticus and the Vulgate place "truly" **before "this one"**... the original Sinaiticus and a few others **omit "truly"** | **the savior of the world** <note>original: ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου</note> (found in Vaticanus, the original Ephraemi, several Latin versions, the Coptic, and early Church Fathers like Irenaeus, Origen, and Eusebius): the traditional Greek text <note>Textus Receptus, noted here as ς</note> **adds "the Christ"** <note>original: ὁ χς/χριστός</note> so it reads **the Christ, the savior of the world**, following manuscripts Alexandrinus, Bezae, and the majority of later manuscripts and versions.

43. **he went out from there** (without addition, in manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, etc.): the traditional Greek text **adds "and went away"** following manuscript Alexandrinus and many others; others read **and he came** or **and it was (it continues in Galilee)**; see also verse 3.

<note>The following notes constitute the "critical apparatus," a technical record showing where ancient manuscripts differ from one another. It compares major codices like Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Alexandrinus (A).</note>

44. **Jesus** <note>original: ι̅ς̅</note> **without the definite article** in manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), Bezae (D), and several others, as well as Origen (volume 4, page 267, four times) and Cyril (volume 4, page 202). <note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a technical list comparing how different ancient copies of the Bible (manuscripts) differ in their wording. Scholars use this to determine the most original text.</note>

**47.** **He came therefore** <note>original: ηλθεν ουν</note>, compare above for the omission of "this man" | **and asked** without the word "him" according to manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi (C), Dublinensis (L), and others, as well as the Armenian version and Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar</note> (who writes: "having come to him and asking that he would come down and heal his son; for he was about to die").
