# 824 &emsp; 7, 44. &emsp; ->ACCORDING TO JOHN<-

<margin>85. 1</margin> [a division] occurred in the crowd because of him. 44 <margin>7, 30</margin> And some of them wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him.

45 <margin>86. 10</margin> Then the officers <note>original: "ὑπηρέται" (hypēretai); these were the Temple guards or attendants under the authority of the Sanhedrin</note> came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and those men said to them: "Why did you not bring him?" 46 The officers answered: "Never has a man spoken thus, as this man speaks." 47 The Pharisees answered them:

---

Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, volume 4, page 477</note> (The Clementine Vulgate, the Peshitta Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, and manuscript ff² also have the same word order in verse 41) :: it seems <note>original: "vdtr" for "videtur"</note> to have been transposed so that the names "David" and "the Christ" were separated. For the same reason, the Latin manuscript <term>d</term>, the Sahidic, and Coptic versions transposed individual words. Similarly, Chrysostom <note>volume 8, page 347</note> reads: "The Christ does not come from the offspring of David." The preceding words, "from Galilee etc.," are shown in both ways.

**43.** **occurred in the crowd** <note>original: "εγεν. εν τω οχλ."</note>: supported by the manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), L, T, X, and others including minuscules 33, 124, 157. (The Greek of manuscript D reads "into the crowd," and 435 reads "from the crowd.") Most Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, and both Syriac versions agree. Origen <note>volume 4, page 299</note> notes: "when also a division occurred in the crowd because of him." Cyril agrees. The <term>Received Text</term> <note>original: "ϛ", referring to the standard Byzantine text</note> places "occurred" after "in the crowd," supported by manuscripts Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and seven other uncials.

**44.** **wanted** <note>original: "ηθελον"</note>: found in the corrected Sinaiticus (אᶜ). The original Sinaiticus (א*) reads "they were saying." | **laid [hands] upon** <note>original: "επεβαλεν"</note>: supported by Sinaiticus, Bezae, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and nearly all others. Lachmann <note>a 19th-century textual critic</note> prefers the shorter **laid** <note>original: "εβαλεν"</note> based on B, L, and T; the Vulgate and most Latin versions use "misit" (sent/laid). | **upon him** <note>original: "επ αυτον"</note>: B, L, T, and others. Sinaiticus originally wrote "to him" <note>original: "αυτω"</note>.

**45.** **they said** <note>original: "ειπον"</note>: supported by T and most Latin/Vulgate copies. Sinaiticus and manuscript "e" read "they say." Chrysostom reads: "For he says the officers came, and the Pharisees say to them." | **those men** <note>original: "εκκεινοι"</note>: omitted by manuscripts K, U, Π. | **bring** <note>original: "ηγαγετε"</note>: Manuscript D uses a slightly different Greek form of the same verb.

**46.** **the officers answered**: Manuscript D adds "but." Sinaiticus reverses the order to "but the officers answered." | **spoken thus [a] man** <note>original: "ελαλης. ουτως ανθρ."</note>: supported by Sinaiticus (corrected), Vaticanus, L, T, X, and others. The Sahidic and Coptic translate it as "no man ever spoke like this man." Origen and Cyril agree. The original Sinaiticus and Bezae (D) reverse it: "thus a man spoke." The <term>Received Text</term> reads: "Thus spoke a man," supported by most later manuscripts and the Syriac. | **as this man speaks** <note>original: "ως ουτοσ λαλει"</note>: found in the original Sinaiticus, the Syriac, and Ethiopian. The <term>Received Text</term> and Tischendorf omit the word "speaks" but keep "as this man," supported by many uncials and the Vulgate. Lachmann and others omit the entire phrase "as this man speaks," following the corrected Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and L. <note>The editor notes that the length of the original phrase likely caused scribes to either shorten it or remove it entirely to simplify the text.</note>

**47. answered**: without a connecting word ("and" or "then") in Sinaiticus and Bezae. The <term>Received Text</term> and Lachmann add "therefore," supported by Vaticanus, L, T, and the Vulgate. The Coptic and Gothic versions use "but." | **them**: omitted by Vaticanus and some Latin copies. | **to be led astray** <note>the beginning of the Pharisees' question in v. 47</note>

### ACCORDING TO JOHN 7, 53 ff.

...while he says: "I am the light of the world; he who follows me," etc. <note>John 8:12</note>

**Chrysostom** (Volume 8, page 351) connects 8:12 very closely with 7:52 in his commentary. For after the words "Search <note>original: "ερωτησον," likely a mistake for "εραυνησον" (eraunēson), meaning "search"</note> and see," he continues thus: "What then does Christ say? Since they were turning Galilee and the prophet upside down <note>original: "ἄνω καὶ κάτω... ἔστρεφον"</note>, freeing everyone from this foreign suspicion, and showing that he is not just one of the prophets but the Lord of the world, he says: 'I am the light of the world.' Not of Galilee, not of Palestine, nor of Judea. Why then did the Jews...?"

**Cyril** (Volume 4, page 484) again proceeds in his commentary directly from 7:52 to 8:12. Just as he says that Jesus uttered those words "If anyone thirsts," etc., as being appropriate to what was written concerning the feast, so now he makes this explanation in a timely manner—crying out: "I am the light of the world." "Going through all the holy scripture," he says, "and thinking to examine <note>original: "βασανίζειν," literally 'to test with a touchstone'</note> the things said about me through the prophets, you are far astray from the path of life," etc.

**Nonnus** (7, 193 and 8, 1) after the phrase "arises out of Galilee," continues: "And Jesus spoke, pouring out his people-saving voice: 'I am the light of the world.'"

**Cosmas Indicopleustes** <note>A 6th-century traveler and geographer</note> (in the *Topography*, Book 5, cited in Gallandi, Volume 11, page 502). He relates there which Gospel narratives John supplemented <note>The early church believed John's Gospel was written to fill in gaps left by the other three Gospels</note>, such as the wedding at Cana, Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the royal official, the man born blind from birth, Lazarus, Judas's indignation over the woman who anointed the Lord with myrrh, the Greeks who approached Jesus, etc. In this list, he could not have passed over the story of the adulteress if he had known it.

**Theophylact** (Commentary on the Oxford Catena, 272): hence it does not seem to have been found even in **Ammonius the Presbyter**, from whom many things passed into the catena <note>term: catena|A 'chain' of interpretations where a biblical text is surrounded by commentary from various Church Fathers</note>. This opinion is confirmed by what the catena brings from Ammonius regarding 8:12: "He shows that he is the one about whom it was previously proclaimed: 'Behold, I have set you as a light for the nations,' <note>Isaiah 42:6</note> and that he is not merely one of the prophets but the Lord."

**Tertullian** (On Modesty, 6): "Clearly, if you can show from what defenses of heavenly examples and precepts you open the door of repentance to adultery alone, and to fornication within it, our encounter will fight on this line. For even if we began especially from the Law by demonstrating—freedom in Christ did not do an injury to innocence—look whether the law of 'not committing adultery' is safe, to which was added 'nor shall you covet.' Otherwise, if any examples applaud into your bosom, they will not be opposed to this discipline which we defend. For in vain was the Law built above, if the pardon of adultery is granted today because it was also once <note>original: "aliquando," some editions read "aliqua"</note> granted." Now various examples from the Old Testament are added, but he urges that these preceded the age of Christ. "I prefer," he says, "to derive discipline into the glory of Christ from Christ. Let the flesh have played before Christ, or rather let it have perished," etc. In this dispute, it is utterly impossible to believe that Tertullian would have passed over the story of the adulteress if he had found it in the Gospel.

To these most certain witnesses (**Tertullian, Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril, Nonnus, Cosmas, Theophylact**) must be added others who either, like **Basil, Cyprian,** and **Hilary** (and even **Juvencus**), certainly never used these verses although they had many opportunities to use them, or are reported in ancient scholia <note>term: scholia|Ancient marginal notes or grammatical explanations in manuscripts</note> (see below) to have never used them, such as **Apollinaris** and **Theodore of Mopsuestia**.

That it was missing in antiquity is also attested by the chapter indexes in our oldest editions; for neither **Manuscript A (Alexandrinus)**, **Manuscript C (Ephraemi Rescriptus)**, nor the manuscripts **E, Λ, Π** and many others, have the chapter "Concerning the Adulteress" <note>original: "περὶ τῆς μοιχαλίδος"</note> recorded in the index, although **E, Λ, Π** and others show the story itself in the main text. Of those manuscripts that do have it in the index, the first are **Manuscripts K and M**; it was received in such a way that it was made into a tenth chapter. When this was added, the Gospel was no longer numbered with 18 chapters (as in **A, C**, etc.) but with 19 chapters. That **Ammonius** or **Eusebius** recognized these verses is not at all...

The author highlights that major commentators like Chrysostom and Cyril jump from John 7:52 directly to 8:12.</summary>

Having established that several early Church Fathers omitted the story, the text now looks at the evidence from specific manuscript traditions, numbering systems, and marginal notes (scholia) that debate whether the story of the woman caught in adultery truly belongs in the Gospel of John.</meta>

### 7, 53 ff. ACCORDING TO JOHN

---

While this is credible, nothing certain can be concluded from the numbering systems that apply here: for chapter 86 with the tenth canon in **Codex Lambda** <note>Codex $\Lambda$ is a 9th-century manuscript</note> and others is noted at 7:45 and extends to 8:19. However, the story of the adulteress itself ought to have been included under the same canon (which contains unique material for each Gospel) and chapter; and indeed, in those manuscripts that contain the story, it is included there... Some manuscripts contain the passage but mark it with asterisks <note>A star-like symbol (*) used by ancient scribes to indicate the text might not be original</note> such as **E, M, Lambda, Pi** and 15 others. (Manuscript **E** has asterisks starting from verse 2 "at dawn," **Lambda** and **Pi** from verse 3 "they brought," **M** at 7:53 and 8:11; additionally, **M** has a red cross at 7:53 and 8:3). Likewise, others mark it with obeli <note>A horizontal line (÷ or —) used to indicate that a passage is likely spurious or doubtful</note> in 30 or more manuscripts. Others transpose the passage (either 7:53–8:11 or 8:3–11) to the end of the Gospel, such as in the **Lectionary of Tischendorf** (in which 8:3–11:2 were supplied by the original scribe*, while 7:53–8:2 were added by a later writer) and 10 or more others, including most Armenian manuscripts. Manuscripts **13, 69, 124, 346** place it after Luke chapter 21; manuscript **225** places it after John 7:36... finally, various scholarly notes (scholia) testify that the passage was found in some manuscripts and omitted in others.

These notes, of which hardly any predate the ninth century, are only of minor importance in this matter, given that so many weightier testimonies exist. Nor can they be pressed for much evidence if they occasionally cite "ancient" or "accurate" or "some" manuscripts as witnesses for one side or the other.

<margin>The following notes are found in **Lambda**, manuscript **262**, and many others in the margin:</margin> "The obelized passages <note>original: "τὰ ὀβελισμένα" (ta obelismena), referring to text marked as doubtful</note> are not found in some copies, nor in those of Apollinaris <note>Apollinaris of Laodicea, a 4th-century bishop</note>; but in the ancient ones, they are found in their entirety. The apostles also mention this passage in the Constitutions <note>The Apostolic Constitutions, an early Christian collection of various precepts</note> which they set forth for the building up of the church."

<margin>Likewise, a marginal note in manuscript **1** at the end of the Gospel says:</margin> "Regarding the chapter of the adulteress: because it is not found in the majority of copies in the Gospel according to John, nor mentioned by the divine fathers who interpreted it—namely **John Chrysostom** and **Cyril of Alexandria**, nor by **Theodore of Mopsuestia** and the rest—I have passed over it at that place. But it is positioned thus a little after the beginning of the 86th chapter, following the words 'Search and see that a prophet does not arise out of Galilee.'"

<margin>In the same location, at the end of the Gospel in manuscripts **135** and **301**:</margin> "Other things have also been found in ancient copies, which we have decided to write at the end of this same Evangelist, and they are as follows."

<margin>Likewise, manuscript **259**, having supplied the text from 'they brought' to 'sin' at the end of the Gospel, adds:</margin> "In some copies, such a chapter is also found added to the Gospel according to John."

<margin>Likewise, manuscript **237** on the last leaf (containing from 'and each went' to 'sin') provides a heading:</margin> "Gospel for a penitent <note>original: "εὐαγγέλιον εἰς μετανοοῦντα." This indicates the passage was used as a liturgical reading for those seeking forgiveness for sins</note> (it is usually read in memory of **Saint Theodora of Alexandria**, see below) from the Gospel according to John," and presents it with this note: "This Gospel reading is not found in the more accurate of the copies."

<margin>Likewise, manuscript **2pe**:</margin> "The chapter about the adulteress in the Gospel according to John: as it is not found in current copies, I have passed over it. But at that place, it is positioned thus following 'has not been raised'."

<margin>Manuscript **34** has this in the margin at the actual location (7:53):</margin> "It should be known that for this reason the parts about the adulteress were placed with asterisks: because it is not included in the majority of copies; however, it is found in the older ones." There are other similar notes.

The passage is found in **D, F** (from 8:10; before a gap), **G, H, K, U, Gamma** (and in **E, M, Lambda, Pi** etc. with asterisks or obeli) and more than 300 other manuscripts, including many Greek and Latin manuscripts known to **Jerome** (who wrote in *Against Pelagius* 2, 17: "In the Gospel according to John, in many Greek and Latin copies, the story is found of the adulterous woman who was accused before the Lord"). It is also found in several old Latin versions <note>represented by codes like b*, c, e, ff2, g</note>, the Vulgate (including Vulgate manuscripts that often lean toward Old Latin readings), Ethiopic versions, and the Jerusalem Syriac.

<summary>This page catalogs the physical evidence for the story of the woman caught in adultery, noting which manuscripts omit it, mark it with symbols of doubt (asterisks or obeli), or move it to the end of the Gospel. It provides several medieval marginal notes that reveal how scribes wrestled with the passage's authenticity based on "ancient" versus "accurate" copies.</summary>

### ACCORDING TO JOHN 7:53 ff. | PAGE 829

---

(7:42 — 8:2 on page 110; 8:3 — 21 on page 460) Evidence is found in the Arabic, Slavic, Saxon, and Persian versions (in the Vatican manuscript it is moved to chapter 10); add to this the verses in which manuscripts and editions differ, namely the Syriac manuscripts 3 and P, and interpolated Coptic, Ethiopic, and Armenian versions, as well as the most recent manuscripts and the notes (scholia) written above them.

Furthermore, the *Apostolic Constitutions* (2.24.4) recognize the story: **“The elders set before him another woman who had sinned, and leaving the judgment to him, they departed; but the Lord, the searcher of hearts, having asked her if the elders had condemned her, and she saying no, said to her: ‘Go then, neither do I condemn you.’”** <note>original Greek: ἑτέραν δέ τινα ἡμαρτηκυῖαν ἔστησαν οἱ πρεσβύτεροι... This is one of the earliest references to the story, though it differs slightly from the Gospel text.</note> 

The *Synopsis of Sacred Scripture* (falsely edited from a single manuscript among the works of Athanasius) notes after John 8:20: **“Here are the things concerning the woman accused of adultery”** (which themselves seem to be the work of an interpolator <note>term: interpolator | a scribe who adds outside material into a text</note>). Euthymius <note>A 12th-century Greek commentator</note> comments on this place but adds: **“It is necessary to know that the things from here on, etc., are either not found in the accurate copies or have been marked with an obelus. Therefore they appear to be inserted and an addition; and proof of this is that not even Chrysostom mentioned them at all.”** 

Jerome (who, on the authority of manuscripts such as the Codex Amiatinus and Fuldensis, should be seen as having fully accepted it into his Latin translation, see also *Against the Pelagians* 2.17), Ambrose (Letter 26.2), and Augustine (*On Adulterous Marriages* 2.7) also acknowledge it. Augustine, in order to protect this passage from the suspicion of being a forgery, writes:

> Who would not understand that a husband ought to forgive what he sees the Lord has forgiven?

— But clearly the sensibilities of unbelievers shrink from this, so that some of modest faith—or rather enemies of the true faith—fearing, I believe, that impunity for sin was being granted to their wives, removed from their manuscripts the account of the Lord’s indulgence toward the adulteress. 

Similarly, in the 10th century, Nicon (cf. Galland 3.250) claims the narrative was cast out by the Armenians because they said **“such a reading is harmful to the masses”**: something he wrote with great ignorance of the facts. See further below on page 834.

It is absolutely certain that the passage concerning the adulteress was not written by John. However, we are taught by the authority of Codex Bezae (D) and the Old Latin manuscripts (b, e), as well as the so-called *Apostolic Constitutions* and the testimony of Jerome, that it began to be read in Greek and Latin manuscripts from the 3rd century onward. For it would be useless for someone to argue that because the *Constitutions* do not name John as the author of the story of the adulteress, it might depend on another source. 

Although this interpolation into the Gospel of John dates back to such antiquity, most copies remained uncorrupted in this section for a long time. Regarding this, Tertullian and Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril are the most brilliant witnesses, along with our oldest Greek manuscripts (א, A, B, C, T) <note>These are the great uncial codices: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and Borgianus</note> and many translations (Old Latin manuscript 'a', most Syriac manuscripts, the Sahidic, the oldest Coptic manuscripts, the Gothic, and the older Armenian manuscripts). 

The story seems to have been accepted into use earlier and more widely among the Latins than the Greeks. Among the Latins, a most eager defender arose in the 5th century: Augustine. In the year 419, in his second book *On Adulterous Marriages*, while demonstrating that marriage is indissoluble even when adultery is committed by a wife, he contended that those who first removed the story of the adulteress from their manuscripts were of "modest faith." What he said there, swept away by the heat of defending his cause, is as far removed from sound critical sense and the history of the sacred text as anything can be. Indeed, such a great boldness—which, if Augustine saw correctly, would fall near the end of the 2nd century according to the testimonies of Tertullian and Origen—that God provided that it should not run wild through the sacred books, even though a vast number of reading variations...

# 7, 53. ACCORDING TO JOHN

->D &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; D &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; D<-

<margin>7,53</margin> And each went to his own house.
<margin>8,1</margin> But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. <gloss>2</gloss> And at dawn he arrived again at the temple, and all the people came to him. <gloss>3</gloss> And the scribes and the Pharisees bring a woman caught in sin, and having stood her in the center, <gloss>4</gloss> the priests say to him, testing him so that they might have an accusation against him: "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the very act of adultery." <note>This text is transcribed from Codex Bezae, also known as "D," a 5th-century manuscript famous for its unique additions and variations in the Gospels and Acts.</note>

---

...who could doubt that the variety of the apostles' writings would allow the script to be overwhelmed, provided they are not entirely ignorant of the history of the sacred text? Let us pass over the arguments to be drawn from the style of writing and the connection of the discourse, which refute a Johannine origin. Indeed, there is little doubt as to where that story flowed from. For what Eusebius relates—who, just like Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril, most likely did not know of this interpolation <note>term: interpolation | a passage inserted into a text by a later hand that was not part of the original work</note> in the Gospel of John—in his *Ecclesiastical History* (3.39) regarding Papias: **"He has also set forth another story about a woman accused of many sins before the Lord, which the Gospel according to the Hebrews contains,"** <note>original Greek: ἐκτέθειται δὲ καὶ ἄλλην ἱστορίαν περὶ γυναικὸς ἐπὶ πολλαῖς ἁμαρτίαις διαβληθείσης ἐπὶ τοῦ κυρίου, ἣν τὸ καθ’ ἑβραίους εὐαγγέλιον περιέχει</note> is applied with the greatest probability to tracing the origin of the Johannine interpolation. 

Nor does it stand in the way that Eusebius says the woman in Papias's account was accused **"of many sins."** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ πολλαῖς ἁμαρτίαις</note> For since the ancient witnesses, in the final verse, provide the command **"from now on sin no more,"** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε</note> they clearly signify that the adulterous woman caught in a flagrant crime had sinned not once but often; I would believe this was expressed more explicitly in Papias or in the *Gospel of the Hebrews*. Furthermore, one must not overlook that Rufinus—who one might reasonably guess knew the book of Papias and that Gospel more accurately from his contemporary Jerome’s Greek and Latin translations—did not hesitate, in his translation of Eusebius's work, to substitute the story of the woman caught in adultery who was accused by the Jews before the Lord in place of the words we wrote above.

Otherwise, it is outside the scope of this section to ask whether the tradition itself is a probable supplement to the Gospel history; certainly, since it lacks apostolic authority, it cannot be held in the same status as if the hand of the Evangelists had written it.

Now, we shall provide the text as the standard edition (Griesbach) <note>original: ς (Gb⁰⁰)</note> exhibits it, indicating at the same time those points by which the older form of the passage may be restored from the authority of ancient witnesses. Beside this text, we shall add the entire passage as it is read in Codex D.

---

Manuscript Λ and 15 others have **"departed,"** <note>Greek: απηλθον</note> U and more than 35 others have **"he departed."** <note>Greek: απηλθεν</note> | **"each"**: Syriac versions add **"to."** | **"the house"**: Manuscripts 1, 25, Tischendorf, and Coptic/Armenian versions have **"the place,"** <note>Greek: τ. τοπον</note> manuscript 69 has **"his own [property]."** <note>Greek: τα ιδια</note>

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN 8, 9.</header>

⁵ Now in the law, Moses <gloss>ς</gloss> <note>The symbol ς refers to the "Textus Receptus," the standard Greek text used for centuries after the Reformation.</note> commanded us that such women be stoned; so what do you say? ⁶ But they said this, testing <gloss>ς</gloss> him, so that they might have grounds to accuse him. <meta>catchword: Je-</meta>

---

[The editor notes] ...Cato and another *without sin* <note>original: αναμαρτητον</note>, or he might express the Greek speech with a new word; or, if it has been expressed by the Latins as the truth of the interpretation holds, it is clear that *without sin* <note>original: αναμαρτητον</note> is nothing other than "without sin" <note>Latin: sine peccato</note>. | **the first**: Manuscripts E, G, H, and Λ, plus 15 others, read **first** <note>neuter: πρωτον</note> | **the stone** with Manuscripts E, G, H, K, M, S, etc.: but Manuscripts D, U, Γ, Δ, and more than 50 others omit the word **the** | **at her** with the minuscule manuscripts ... write **against her** <note>accusative: επ αυτην</note> with Manuscripts D, E, G, H, K, M, S, U, Γ, Δ, and many others | **let him throw**: Manuscripts E, G, H, K, and about 20 others read a slightly different spelling of **let him throw** <note>βαλλετω</note>. Furthermore, the word order fluctuates considerably: the Textus Receptus <gloss>ς</gloss> reads **the stone at her let him throw** with the minuscules ... but write **at her the** (Manuscript Γ and others omit "the") **stone let him throw** with E, G, H, K, S, Γ, and many others, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Augustine (in his commentary on John 33,5); Manuscripts U and Δ (and the Armenian) read **stone let him throw at her**, while the Jerusalem Syriac and others read **let him throw at her the stone**, and Manuscript D reads **at her let him throw a stone**, and so on.

8. **stooping down** (Manuscripts Γ, H, and 272 omit "stooping"): Manuscripts D and about 15 others read **having stooped down**. <header>ACCORDING TO JOHN 8:11.</header>

...[Je]sus and the woman standing in the midst. <sup>10</sup> And Jesus, straightening up and seeing no one except the woman, said to her: "Woman, where are those accusers of yours? Has no one condemned you?" <sup>11</sup> And she said: "No one, Lord." And Jesus said to her: "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more."

---

<note>The following text is the editor's scholarly commentary, originally in Latin, regarding the history of this passage in ancient Christian writings.</note>

...when he had found a version of the Latin Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible translation</note> in the *Codex Fuldensis* <note>A famous 6th-century manuscript</note> "without a title," he inquired which of the ancient writers had composed such a work. Having consulted the books of Eusebius, he believed himself to be holding in his hands the work of Ammonius, or rather (for this pleased him more) the work of Tatian. (Compare the preface of Victor <note>Victor of Capua, who discovered the manuscript</note> which has been repeated by many.) This conjecture, however unfortunate, is still repeated by some today. What of the fact that those more fond of errors even think one should proceed from Ammonius to Eusebius, having not at all understood the system of his canons? <note>Referring to the "Eusebian Canons," a cross-referencing system for the Gospels.</note> Similarly, or even more seriously, they have erred who praised *Chrysostom* <note>St. John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> as a witness to this <term>pericope</term> <note>pericope: a short extract or passage from a text</note>. For they were deceived by the Latin translation of Homily 60 (61) in Morellius’s edition, page 389, where the words "concerning the dismissal of a woman," which were written about divorcing a wife, were very poorly rendered as "whether an adulteress should be stoned." Concerning this matter, *Montfaucon* <note>Bernard de Montfaucon, a French scholar</note> has already sufficiently explained it in the preface to volume 8. 

But there is one way in which our enumeration of witnesses can truly be supplemented: I mean the liturgical testimonies, or those by which we learn that the <term>pericope</term> of the adulteress was already used for public worship from ancient times. We learn from the books that relate to this that this passage was certainly accustomed to be read in Rome at the <term>station</term> <note>station: a specific church in Rome where the community gathered for a particular day's liturgy</note> of St. Susanna, at least by the age of Gregory the Great, the famous organizer of the Roman stations. It is not incredible that it began to be read in the Roman church even a century or two before Gregory. Likewise, among the Greeks, it is certain that it has been used for many centuries for the solemnities instituted in memory of the holy women Pelagia, Theodora of Alexandria, Eudocia, Mary of Egypt, and others. For many <term>evangelistaria</term> <note>evangelistarium: a book containing Gospel readings arranged for the church year</note> testify to this use—perhaps a hundred if you seek the number, though more than thirty others are opposed <note>meaning they omit the passage</note>; likewise the <term>menologia</term> <note>menologion: a collection of lives of the saints arranged by the calendar</note>, which are a little later than the evangelistaria. From these testimonies, although it is difficult to gather exactly when the passage of the adulteress was first received among the Greeks, it becomes probable that it was received before the eighth century, which none of the hundred evangelistaria we mentioned precedes; except that more than thirty similar books which omit it entirely prove that the usage of the Greek church in this matter fluctuated for a long time. Furthermore, the Jerusalem Syriac lectionary shows that the Syrian church followed a similar practice; although we have this only in a Vatican manuscript written in the eleventh century, it seems to be derived from much older books.

And these things indeed concern the liturgical use among the Latins, Greeks, and Syrians. However, none of the testimonies that can be sought from there reaches those times in which we learn from the so-called *Apostolic Constitutions* <note>A 4th-century collection of Christian precepts</note> that the <term>pericope</term> concerning the adulteress was read in Greek in the Gospel; nor do they reach the authority of the Latin fathers, of whom there is a great number after Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, or of the Old Latin manuscripts *d*, *e*, etc.

...remain. Since these things are so, those things which we have supplied in this place can in no way undermine what we have set forth above. Nor can they be undermined further by any arguments foreign to sound criticism and a sincere zeal for divine truth—unless, perhaps, someone happens to prove that Tertullian and Origen <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) and Origen (c. 184–253 AD) were early Christian theologians whose copies of the Bible often lacked the story of the adulteress</note> were among the number of those husbands whose faith the discussion of Augustine rendered suspect. <note>original: "maritorum fuisse, quorum fidem Augustini disputatio suspectam reddidit." # 8, 21. ACCORDING TO JOHN

<page-num>838</page-num>

He spoke these things in the treasury while teaching in the temple; and no one <margin>7, 30</margin> seized him, because his hour had not yet come.

<margin>7, 33 and following</margin> **21** Then he said to them again: "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin; where I am going, you cannot come." **22** Then the Jews were saying: "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?" **23** And he was saying to them: "You are from below, I am from above; <margin>3, 31 1 John 4, 5</margin> you are of this world, I am not of this world. **24** Therefore I said to you that you will die in your sins; for if you do not believe that I am <note>The Greek "egō eimi" (I am) is a significant self-identification, often echoing the divine name in the Old Testament.</note>, you will die in your..."

---

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus." It documents variations found in ancient manuscripts of the Bible. Scholars use these codes (like ℵ, B, D) to identify specific historic books.</note>

**20.** The phrase "he spoke" appears without the name "Jesus" <term>ι̅ς</term> <note>original: "ι̅ς", a shortened "sacred name" (nomen sacrum) for Jesus</note> in manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus, 4th century</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus, 4th century</note>, D, K, L, T and about ten others, as well as the Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac versions, and in the writings of Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril. ... However, the edition by Griesbach and Scholz adds "Jesus" following manuscripts X, Γ, Δ, and many others, along with the Clementine Vulgate and certain Armenian editions. | For "treasury" (gazophylakiō): manuscripts E, S, X, Γ, Δ and many others use the spelling "gazophylakeiō". | For "had come": manuscript L reads "came," while others and Origen and Cyril use the perfect tense "has come."

**21.** "Then he said again": Manuscript ℵ reads "Then he was saying." | The text appears without "Jesus" <term>ι̅ς</term> in ℵ, B, D, L, T, X, and the Old Latin 'b' and 'e', as well as Origen and Cyril. ... Griesbach adds "Jesus" based on Γ, Δ, and almost all other manuscripts, including most Old Latin and the Vulgate. | "You will seek" (in some versions "you seek"): Manuscripts 1, 22, 209 and many others, along with the Coptic and Peshitta Syriac, add "and you will not find me." | "Where": Manuscripts U, X, 1 and about ten others, as well as the Syriac and Sahidic versions and Cyril, read "and where."

**22.** Manuscript D reads "they were saying" (elegan). | L spells "will kill" with a double 'n'. | "Himself": D, Γ, Δ and others, including Origen, use the pronoun "him" (auton) instead of "himself" (eauton). | "Because he says": Manuscript U and several others, along with the Syriac and Armenian versions, add "that" (hoti). | "Where": The original hand of ℵ adds "whenever" (an).

**23.** "He was saying" (eleghen) is found in ℵ, B, D, L, T, X and the main Latin and Syriac versions, along with Origen and Cyril. ... Scholz's edition reads "He said" (eipen) following Γ, Δ and most other manuscripts. Furthermore, versions of ℵ read "He was saying therefore" instead of "And he was saying." | "I": D, Gr, and various Latin and Coptic versions add "but" (de). | "You are of this world": Omitted in ℵ. | Regarding the first instance of "of this world": manuscripts ℵ, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, and many others, including the Vulgate, Origen, Chrysostom, and Cyril, place "this" after "world." ... Lachmann and Tischendorf <note>19th-century biblical scholars</note> read "of this world" with the words reversed, following manuscripts B and T and Origen. The Old Latin versions read "from this world." In the second instance of the phrase, most manuscripts including ℵ, B, D, L, T, X follow the standard order, while others and the Latin versions reverse it.

**24.** "Therefore I said": ℵ and several others omit "therefore" (oun). | "In your sins" (plural) occurs twice: This is found in most Old Latin versions, but the Vulgate and manuscript 'l' use the singular "in your sin" in the second instance. | "Believe": The text appears without an object in B, L, T, X, and most others, including the Vulgate, Origen, and Cyril. ... Manuscripts ℵ, D, and others add "me" (moi). | The section from "For if [you do] not" through "your sins" is omitted in manuscripts 33, 118, and several others due to the scribe's eye skipping between identical words (homeoteleuton).

# 8, 27. ACCORDING TO JOHN

<page-num>839</page-num>

...sins. **25** Then they were saying to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "What I have been telling you from the beginning. **26** I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you; but the one who sent me is true, and the things I heard from him, these I speak to the world." **27** They did not know that he [spoke to them of the Father].

---

**25.** **They were saying therefore** <note>original: "ελεγον ουν"</note> (likewise Origen, volume 4, page 307; the Old Latin manuscript *b* reads "but they were saying" <note>original: "dicebant autem"</note>; the Syriac Harclean version reads "and they answered and said to him"): Manuscripts ℵ, Γ, 249, and a few others, along with the Syriac Sinaitic, omit **therefore** | **said** <note>original: "ειπεν"</note> appears without a conjunction in manuscripts B, L, T, X, 1, 33, 69, 124, and about 15 others, as well as several Old Latin versions (a, c, d, e, ff²), the Vulgate, eight uncials, and the majority of other manuscripts; similarly, manuscript *b* reads "but he said" ... Manuscripts ℵ, D (Greek), 249, and the Emmi manuscript read **he said therefore** | **to them**: Manuscript U omits this | **Jesus**: Manuscript *b* and a manuscript of Scrivener's omit the definite article | **that which** <note>original: "ὅ τι"</note> (this spelling is not found in the uncial editions, nor is it common in the minuscule manuscripts): the standard received text (but not the editions of Griesbach or Scholz) and Griesbach's second edition read **that** <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>. The Latin versions read as follows: "the beginning (principium/initium) which" in manuscripts a, gat, mm; "the beginning which also" in c, f, ff², l, q, δ; "the principle who also" in e, and the Clementine Vulgate ... and others; "the principle because also" or "the beginning because also" in d and others; manuscript *b* reads "primarily because." Furthermore, the Syriac Peshitta and Coptic versions read "the principle which also," while the Sahidic omits "also"; the Syriac Harclean reads "the principle who also"; the Ethiopic reads "the first and (continues with 'I have spoken to you')"; the Syriac Curetonian reads "even if I have begun to speak with you, there is (nevertheless) much for me to say and judge concerning you." We have placed a period after **I speak to you**, as the standard text does; Tischendorf and Lachmann use a question mark. Regarding this passage, see **Chrysostom** (volume 8, page 357): "What he says is this: 'You are completely unworthy to hear words from me, let alone to learn who I am. For you speak while testing everything, and paying attention to nothing from me. And I could expose all these things now; for this is what is meant by: **I have many things [to speak]**'" etc.; likewise **Cyril of Alexandria** (volume 4, page 511): "'I am dishonored,' he says, 'even though I speak for eternal life—but I also suffer justly,' he says, 'because I even made a beginning of speech among you, because I addressed anything to those who know how to be helped—for I ought,' he says, 'not to have spoken to you at all from the beginning, but rather to those others'" etc. Likewise **Augustine** on John (38, 11): "And he added, 'because I also speak to you': that is, because I have descended to these words, having been made humble for your sake. For if the Beginning remained with the Father as He is, not taking the form of a servant and speaking as a man to men, how would they believe Him, since weak hearts could not hear the intelligible Word without a sensible voice? Therefore, he says, 'Believe me to be the beginning, because, so that you may believe, I not only am, but I also speak to you.'"

**26.** **many things** (Syriac Harclean: "and many things") etc.: manuscript *b* reads "although I have many things to say and judge concerning you"; manuscript *e* reads "having many things to speak and judge concerning you." Likewise, **Nonnus** (9, 61) connects this with the preceding: "'Who are you?' and Christ cried out, 'Because I have been talking to you **from the beginning**, having countless things to judge and to speak. But he is true who [sent] me'" etc. | **to speak**: Manuscript G and about 10 others read "and to speak," Chrysostom (8, 356) reads "and to say" | **the one who sent me**: ℵ adds "the Father" (see note at verse 16) | **and I**: Manuscript T reads "and I also," similarly the Coptic (but not Sahidic) reads "and I also" | **from him** (corrected ℵ), also most Old Latin and the Vulgate read "from him (that one)," manuscript *l* reads "concerning him": the original ℵ read "beside him" | **I speak** (Griesbach's second edition, approved by Schulz) with ℵ, B, D, K, L, T, U, X, Δ, and about 45 others, also Cyril (4, 513); likewise "I speak" in the Old Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, both Syriac, and Ethiopic ... the standard text reads **I say** <note>original: "λεγω"</note> with E, F, G, H, M, S, Γ, Λ, and many others | **into the world** (in manuscript *e* "into the age," in others "into the world," Tertullian against Praxeas 22; manuscripts *c* and the Vulgate read "in the world"): D (Greek) reads "into this world," likewise ff², l, q read "into this world," while a, b, d, f read "in this world."

**27.** **They did not know**: Manuscript Δ, 69, 262, and others add "therefore," while Γ, a few others, and Chrysostom (8, 357) add "but."

(Also for the Sahidic and Latin) both Syriac versions, Coptic, Gothic, Ethiopic, Cyril of Alexandria, Chrysostom, and Tertullian | **I speak** <note>original: "λαλω"</note> (also Origen and Tertullian): Codex Bezae (D), manuscript 33, and others, including Cyril, add the word **these** before it; likewise the Old Latin manuscripts *b* and *c* | **therefore** <note>original: "ουν"</note> (manuscript 71 and others read **now**): Omitted by manuscript 248, the <term>Escorialensis</term> manuscript, the Vulgate, and several Old Latin versions (though not *a, b, c, e,* or *q*), as well as Tertullian, Gothic, Armenian, and Chrysostom | **you heard** <note>original: "ηκουσατε"</note>: Found in Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and others. Origen notes: <note>original: "ζητήσαι δ' ἄν τις· πότε ἤκουσαν παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς..."</note> "One might ask: when did the Jews who believed in the Lord hear from the father? — That they heard from the father through the father having spoken through Moses and the prophets the things in the Law, etc." | Instead of "heard," many other manuscripts read **you have seen** <note>original: "εωρακατε"</note>, including Codices Alexandrinus and Washingtonianus, and the Vulgate. Apollinaris explains: <note>original: "ἑωρακέναι καὶ παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ λέγων..."</note> "By saying 'having seen with the father,' he did not mean a vision of the eyes but natural knowledge; since he also says they 'have seen' with their father [the devil], he surely does not mean they have seen with their eyes, but that they are made familiar with the counsels of the evil one by the wickedness dwelling within them." | **from the father** <note>original: "παρα του πατρος"</note>: Supported by the same manuscripts that read "heard," and also Sinaiticus (though this supports the reading "heard" even more strongly) | **the father** <note>original: "του πατρος"</note> without anything added: Supported by Codices Vaticanus and Regius. Origen observes: <note>original: "ὅρα δὲ εἰ καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο δυνάμεθα λέγειν..."</note> "See if we can also say regarding this that it does not say 'from *your* father' or 'from *our* father,' but simply 'from *the* father,' who, though he may be a father, is not at all the father of those who are not children of Abraham, etc." | Others add **your** <note>original: "υμων"</note>, including Codices Sinaiticus, Bezae, and the Vulgate | **do** <note>original: "ποιειτε"</note>: Codex Bezae adds **these things**; Tertullian also supports this.

The Vulgate reads **do!** (as a command), and some versions of Origen's text suggest the meaning "it belongs to one who understands to *do* the works of Abraham."

<header>9, 1. ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

### IX.

1 And as he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. 2 And his disciples asked him, saying: "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" 3 Jesus answered: "Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but [this happened] so that the works of God might be revealed in him. 4 We must work the works of him who se—"

---

<note>This section continues the scholarly debate on the ending of Chapter 8, verse 59.</note>
...[Jesus] departed for the healing of the blind man, proving through his works that he is before Abraham <note>original Latin: "pro του αβρ. εστιν"</note>. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century bishop</note> in his text and commentary writes: "and he was not satisfied with merely being hidden, but he also went out of the temple, sketching for us in these events a kind of pattern of things perceived by the mind." But see later... The <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>The "Received Text" used for the King James Version, marked by the symbol ς</note> adds **passing through** <note>original: "διελθων"</note> (found in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Regius, and others) **the midst of them** (Sinaiticus, Manuscript 33, Coptic, and Syriac versions) **and so he passed by** <note>original: "και παρηγεν ουτως"</note> (compare with Luke 4, 30) with the majority of later Greek manuscripts, the Latin Vulgate, and the Gothic version. Athanasius <note>A 4th-century theologian</note> and Theodore of Heraclea in the <term>Catena</term> <note>A "chain" of commentary from various Church Fathers</note> ask: "How was he hidden? Not by wrapping himself in a corner of the temple—but—by being unseen in their midst, he went out and so passed by." Pope Julius in a reply recorded by Athanasius...

**IX, 1. passed by:** Manuscript versions C, F, G, H, and others add the name **Jesus** <note>original abbreviation: "$\overline{ις}$"</note> | **saw**: Codex Vaticanus (B) and others use the spelling *eiden* ... while Codices A, C, D, K, and others use the spelling *iden* | **from birth**: most manuscripts read *genetēs* ... while others (E, F, G, H) use the spelling *gennētēs* <note>The difference is a single versus double 'n', often a scribal variation</note>. Additionally, Codex Bezae (D) adds the word **sitting** <note>original: "καθημενον"</note>.

**2. his disciples:** Codex Bezae and some Old Latin versions omit **his** | **saying:** some manuscripts omit this word | **Rabbi:** spelled as *rabbei* in the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae) ... the Received Text and editors Lachmann and Tischendorf spell it *rabbi* following later manuscripts | **born:** a few manuscripts use a slightly different verb form.

**3. Jesus:** The oldest manuscripts (ℵ, A, B, C) simply say "Jesus" ... the Received Text <note>ς</note> and editor Scholz add the article **the** <note>original: "ο $\overline{ις}$"</note>. Furthermore, some Latin and Syriac versions add **and said to them**.

**4. We** <note>The first "we" in the verse</note>: Supported by the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius), the Sahidic and Coptic versions, and Cyril. Nonnus <note>A 5th-century Greek poet</note> paraphrases this as: "it is the duty of the highest to fulfill works, the works of the living God, while the dawn still appears." This is confirmed by Origen <note>An early Christian scholar, d. 254 AD</note> who uses the "evangelical phrase spoken by the Savior" as: **"work while it is day; it comes [the night]—to work."** Jerome also follows this in his commentaries, citing the Savior’s words as: "Work while it is day." ... The Received Text and editor Lachmann read **Me** <note>original: "εμε"</note> based on later manuscripts and the Vulgate. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, known for his "golden-mouthed" preaching</note> explains this as: "that is, I must reveal myself and do those things that show me doing the same things as the Father." Similarly, for the second instance of "we," Sinaiticus and the Coptic versions support **us**.

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN 9, 7.</header>

...who sent us while it is day; night is coming when no one can work. 5 As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. <margin>8, 12</margin> 6 Having said these things, he spat on the ground and made clay from the saliva, and he smeared the clay upon his eyes, 7 and said to him: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam," (which is translated <margin>Nehemiah 3, 15</margin> "Sent"). He went away, therefore, and washed, and came [back seeing].

---

> Does he speak of things that are better left unspoken? Why, leaving aside what is appropriate for the moment, do you press to learn things beyond human comprehension? It is not a time, he says, for investigation into these matters, but for work and intense diligence; for I believe it is more necessary—and especially since he has designated us as apostles—to fulfill the works of the apostleship. The Lord, intertwining himself with those who are sent, includes himself in the number of those who must work, etc. <note>This commentary, likely from a Church Father like Cyril of Alexandria or John Chrysostom, explains that Jesus is emphasizing action over abstract theological speculation.</note>

(Origen, Jerome, and Nonnus do not address the second "us" <note>original Greek: ημασ</note>.) . . . Lachmann <note>A 19th-century textual critic</note> reads "Why me" with the same witnesses as before "me," likewise Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Bezae (D), the Sahidic Coptic, and the Jerusalem Syriac :: the reading "us" <note>original: ημασ</note> is very foreign to a corrector. Indeed, even more than "it is necessary for us to work," the phrase "of him who sent us" <note>original: του πεμψ. ημασ</note> is striking. Hence it cannot be believed that John wrote "it is necessary for us to work" and that this wording was adapted by a later hand in the Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Regius (L), etc., to match what follows. It is much more probable that in both places "us" <note>original: ημασ</note> originated from John himself, while some were satisfied with restoring "of him who sent me," and others removed "us" from both places. | **while** <note>original: εωσ</note> also in Origen, volume 3, page 201 and (from the Delarue edition) volume 4, page 27 etc . . . Codex Sinaiticus (c*), Codex Regius (L), and Manuscript 33. The margin of the Philoxenian Syriac and the Huet edition of Origen read **as** <note>original: ωσ</note>, likewise the Old Latin manuscripts *b* and *d* with "while it is day" (the other Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate have "while" or "until it is day").

**5.** **As long as I am in the world** with Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and many other uncials and manuscripts, the Latin *c, f, ff2, q*, the Vulgate (Amiatinus, Fuldensis, etc.), the Gothic, the Harklean Syriac, the Armenian, and Origen . . . Codex Bezae (D), Codex Sangermanensis (L), Codex Monacensis (X), and others read **when I am in the world** <note>original: ω εν τ. κο.</note>, as do Cyril and Chrysostom.

**6.** Codex Sangermanensis (Λ*) reads **he did** | Codex Bezae (D) reads **spittle** | **smeared** (Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Bezae write it with different vowels; others use a different verb ending): Codex Vaticanus and the original hand of Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus read **placed** | **his clay upon the eyes** with Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Regius, and others, likewise Codex Sangallensis, Manuscript 157, etc., and Cyril read **his clay upon the eyes of the blind man**, hence Lachmann reads **his clay upon the eyes [of the blind man]**. Similarly the Gothic version has "on the eyes of this blind man with this clay," Codex Bezae (D) has "the clay on his eyes," the Ethiopic has "on his eyes" (omitting "the clay"), the Sahidic has "clay upon his eyes" . . . The <term>Textus Receptus</term> <note>The "Received Text" traditionally used for translations like the King James Version</note> reads **the clay upon the eyes of the blind man** with many later uncials, the Philoxenian Syriac (which reads "he smeared the eyes of that blind man with clay"), Chrysostom, and Ammonius. Similarly, other manuscripts and the Peshitta Syriac omit "the clay," and Pseudo-Athanasius omits "the clay upon." The Latin versions for "and he smeared" through "eyes" read as follows: *c, ff2, q* have "and he super-anointed him with clay upon his eyes," *l* has "and he super-anointed him and smeared his eyes"; *e* has "and he super-anointed the eyes of the blind man," *f* has "and he super-smeared upon the eyes of the blind man"; the Vulgate has "and he smeared (or 'spread') clay upon his eyes"; *a* has "and he smeared his eyes."

**7.** **to him**: omitted by Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin manuscripts | **wash** (Latin *f, ff2, g, q* and Vulgate read "wash," *l* reads "wash yourself," *c* "and wash"; the Sahidic and Coptic add "your face"): omitted by Codex Alexandrinus and some Old Latin, hence Lachmann brackets **[wash]**, though a later hand in Alexandrinus adds "and wash" after "Siloam," and manuscript *e* adds "and wash your eyes" after "Sent" | **which is translated** (Codex Bezae: "which is interpreted") **Sent** (The Philoxenian Syriac margin has the Greek word for "Sent"): the Peshitta Syriac and Persian versions omit this | **he went away therefore** (several manuscripts and Old Latin omit this; others have "and he went away," "and he proceeded," or "but he went away") **and washed and came**: omitted by Codex Vaticanus (B) (skipping from the first "went away" to the final "came").

**20. answered then:** supported by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. <note>The word "then" was perhaps omitted or changed by other scribes because of the "then" in the previous verse.</note> The <term>Textus Receptus</term> (ς) reads "answered" without the conjunction, supported by Bezae, G, L, the Vulgate, and Sahidic. The Coptic phrases it as "his age is sufficient for him even to speak for himself." | **himself:** <note>original: "eautou"</note> most manuscripts read "himself," while the <term>Textus Receptus</term> reads "him" <note>original: "autou"</note>. | **will speak:** <note>original: "lalēsei"</note> Manuscript χ reads "will testify."

**2. is the shepherd:** (also found in **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century theologian</note> pages 698 a, e, g; the **Vulgate**; and **Lucifer** <note>Lucifer of Cagliari, a 4th-century bishop</note> 154): **Manuscript D** and the **Sahidic** <note>an Egyptian Coptic dialect</note> version read: **he himself is the shepherd**; **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching</note> 8,398 (and a Moscow manuscript 6) reads: **this one is the shepherd**; Latin manuscripts **b, c, f, ff², l, q**, the **Fuldensis**, and **Coptic** versions read: **this is the shepherd.**

The Ethiopic (Roman), Armenian, and Ethiopic versions add **to them again**, likewise with **Jesus** interposed in Codex X, and minuscules 33, 106, 32ev. 
That is: **to them Jesus again** | **Jesus** (omitted by Codex Vaticanus [B]): omitted by manuscript **b** | **I say to you**: Codex Vaticanus reads **to you I say** | 
**that** [is found] with Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Bezae (D), Codex Ephraemi (C) <note>These are major 4th and 5th-century Greek Bible manuscripts</note> and many others, the Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac (Peshitta) versions... **8. All** (also supported by **Origen** <note>A 3rd-century scholar and theologian</note> in several places and **Lucifer of Cagliari**; also recognized by the **Valentinians** <note>A Gnostic group</note> and **Hippolytus**, as well as **Clement of Alexandria**): omitted by Codex Bezae (D), Old Latin **b**, and **Didymus the Blind**; likewise in *Questions on the Old and New Testament* (page 3083, which says: "The Savior says: *I am the door; those who were before me etc., and a little later: as many as were before me*"). Additionally, Codex Gamma ($\Gamma$) adds **but**. | **came** without the phrase **before me** 
[is found] with the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph^*$), and Codices E, F, G, M, S, U, Gamma, Delta, and nearly 100 others, plus almost all Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, Gothic, Sahidic Coptic, and various Syriac versions. Also supported by **Basil**, **Chrysostom** <note>The 4th-century "Golden-Mouthed" preacher</note> (though a commentary note suggests "before me" was inserted into his words), **Cyril**, and **Theodore of Heraclea** in a collection of commentaries (page 300, which notes: "For this reason also he used the word accurately, saying: *as many as came*, but not *as many as were sent*. For the prophets of God, having been sent, arrived; but the false prophets, with no one having sent them, came for the subversion of those being deceived.") [Supported also by] **Theophylact**, **Euthymius**, **Novatian**, and **Augustine** (in *Against the Adversaries of the Law and Prophets*, Book 2.16: "he also says the Lord said: *all others as many as came before me are thieves and robbers.* However, it is not written so, but thus: *All as many as came, are thieves and robbers.* Indeed, in this place, he wanted it to be understood that those 'came' who had not been sent.") and elsewhere ("*those who came*, he says, and we understand: *except me*, that is: *Those who came apart from me, are thieves etc.*"). The **Manicheans** <note>A dualistic religious movement</note> (according to Theophylact) held a similar view, though they understood it as referring to the Old Testament prophets: "For those, wanting to show that the Old Testament was alien to God and that the prophets were not sent from God, use this saying. For behold, he says, the Lord said that *all as many as came are thieves and robbers*..." **Lachmann** and **Tischendorf** <note>19th-century editors of the Greek New Testament</note> [read] **came before me** with the corrected Sinaiticus ($\aleph^c$), Codices A, B, D, K, L, X, and about 160 others, the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, and Arabic versions, **Origen**, **Didymus**, **Isidore** (who explains it similarly to Theodore and Augustine), **Lucifer**, **Faustinus** (as cited by Augustine), and **Jerome**. Likewise the standard Byzantine text (**$\varsigma$**) places **before me** before **came** in many manuscripts and the Armenian version, the Valentinians, **Origen**, **Nonnus** ("All as many as came before with stealthy sandals, were deceitful thieves"), and **Cyril**. 
**Clement of Alexandria** seems to confirm this similarly: "Yes, they say it is written: *all those before the coming of the Lord are thieves and robbers*" and elsewhere ("all therefore those before the Lord are thieves and robbers"). 
The original Sinaiticus ($\aleph^*$) agreeing with all Old Latin, Sahidic Coptic, and Syriac versions, undoubtedly provides the reading common in the second century. At nearly that same age, although the words **before me** must be weighed by the authority of the witnesses, they nevertheless seem to have been added for the sake of explanation rather than removed out of a sense of ancient piety; for the sense hardly changes when those words are removed. the sheep [heard] them. **9** I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out and find pasture. **10** The thief comes only to steal and slaughter and destroy; I came that they may have life and have it abundantly. **11** I am the good shepherd. The evidence for those who omit the phrase **before me** <note>Referring back to verse 8</note> is much more recent; it is used by Isidore with the words retained, while Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Archbishop</note> departs from it by omitting these same words. | **they are**: manuscripts 6, 63, 71, 116, 248, 253, 254, 259, and the scribe of manuscript g, the Armenian version, and Didymus the Blind in *On the Trinity* read **they were** <note>original: ησαν</note>; Jerome reads **they were** <note>original: fuerunt</note> | **but**: Codex Bezae (D) and Codex Monacensis (X) read **but** <note>original: αλλα</note>... **10.** **I**: Codex Bezae (D), the Old Latin manuscript **a**, the Gothic version, and the Coptic (Woidius edition) and Peter’s second edition (though not in the Dietenberger or Schwartze editions) and the Ethiopic version add **but** <note>original: δε</note> | Codex Bezae (D) omits **and have it abundantly** (the Sahidic Coptic in the Mingarelli edition omits from **I came** until **abundantly**) | **abundantly**: Codex Gamma ($\Gamma$) and manuscripts 69, 157, 20ev, and Athanasius (page 854) read **more abundantly** <note>original: περισσοτερον</note>.

**11.** **lays down** <note>original: τιθησιν</note> (also found in the Textus Receptus <note>The standard "Received Text" used for the King James Version</note>, Clement pages 156 and 421, Origen in the Oxford Catena on 1 Corinthians page 167 and elsewhere, Eusebius on Psalm 106 and in *Gospel Preparation* page 614, the Apostolic Constitutions 2.20.5, Basil in his Ethiopic works page 298, Chrysostom volume 8 page 400, Cyril volume 4 page 647, Theodoret volume 2 pages 1551 and 1643 and often elsewhere, Tertullian in *On Flight in Persecution* 11, Lucifer page 189, and Hilary page 45): The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph^*$), Codex Bezae (D), and Old Latin manuscripts **b** and **c** (and likewise likely **ff²** and **g**), the Vulgate (though not in manuscripts **a, b, c, e, f,** or **l**), the Syriac Hierosolymitanum, and Augustine in his *Tractates on John* 46.5 read **gives** <note>original: διδωσιν</note> (the Old Latin manuscript **b** reads **he will deliver** <note>original: tradet</note>, and **mm** reads **he delivers** <note>original: tradit</note>). See also Theodotus in Clement page 977, who uses **to give back** <note>original: αποδιδοναι</note> (or **to give over** <note>original: επιδιδοναι</note>) :: In both verse 11 and verse 15, Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph^*$) and Codex Bezae (D) read **gives**, though not in verse 17 (nor is there much variation in the future tense **I will lay down** in 13:37-38 or 15:13); yet it is unlikely that John wrote **lays down** in verse 17 and **I give** in verses 11 and 15. The Textus Receptus reads **are** <note>original: εισιν</note> with Codices D, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, $\Lambda$, seven other uncials, and many others | **coming**: Omitted by the original hand of Codex Alexandrinus (A*) | **flees**: Old Latin manuscript **b** adds **because he is a hired hand** | **them**: Found in Old Latin **a, c, e, f**, Lucifer, Gothic, Sahidic (Woide), Coptic, and Syriac Hierosolymitanum ... by myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again; this commandment I received from my Father.

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 10:28.

23 And Jesus was walking in the temple, in the porch of Solomon. <note>Also known as Solomon's Colonnade, a covered walkway on the east side of the Temple.</note>
24 Then the Jews surrounded him and said to him: “How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
25 Jesus answered them: “I told you, and you do not believe; the works that I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness <margin>5, 36</margin> concerning me; 26 but you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. 27 My sheep hear my voice, <margin>8, 45 and following</margin> and I know them, and they follow me, 28 and I give... <margin>10, 3 and following</margin>

---

The word "and" <note>original: και</note> is prefixed to the start of the section in manuscripts A, E, F, K, M, S, U, Γ, Δ, Λ (and originally in Π but later deleted) and many others, as well as several Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, Gothic, Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian, and the writings of Chrysostom.
**23.** "was walking" <note>original: περιεπατει</note>: Manuscripts A and L read "walks" <note>original: περιπατει</note> | "Jesus": Codex B omits the article "the" | "in the porch" <note>original: εν τη στοα</note> without the article "of the" <note>original: του</note> is supported by Sinaiticus, A, D, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, seven other uncials, and many others including Chrysostom... the Received Text <note>The "Textus Receptus," a standard 16th-century Greek edition</note> and Scholz add "the" <note>original: του</note> following B, L, X, and many others. | "of Solomon": spelled "Solomōnos" in Sinaiticus (first hand), B, D, E, F, G, Λ... while the Received Text and Scholz spell it "Solomōntos" following Sinaiticus (corrected), A, K, L, M, S, U, X, Γ, Π, and very many others.
**24.** "surrounded" <note>original: εκυκλωσαν</note> with Sinaiticus, A, D, the remaining uncials, and almost all others... the Received Text reads "ekukleusan" | "him": Sinaiticus (corrected) includes it, but the first hand of Sinaiticus omits it | Codex Bezae (the Latin side) reads "they were saying" <note>original: ελεγαν</note> | "tell" <note>original: ειπον</note> according to Sinaiticus (first hand) and others... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "eipe" <note>a different grammatical form of the imperative "tell"</note> with Sinaiticus (corrected), A, B, D, and almost all others. <note>The editor notes that "eipon" was rarely retained except by the oldest editors in specific passages like Matthew 18:17 or Luke 22:66.</note> | "plainly": Codex B (first hand) and D spell it with one 'r' <note>original: παρησια</note>.
**25.** "answered" <note>original: απεκριθη</note> without any addition in Sinaiticus (first hand), Codex Bezae, and the Gothic... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add "to them" <note>original: αυτοις</note> with Sinaiticus (corrected), A, B, L, most uncials, and nearly all others... | "Jesus": Codex B omits the article "the" | "I told" <note>original: ειπον</note> (Latin: *dixi*): Various Old Latin versions and the Vulgate read "I speak" <note>original: λαλω / loquor</note> | "to you": manuscript x adds "already" | "you do not believe" <note>original: ου πιστευετε</note> (also in the Latin versions): Codex B, manuscript 157, and others read "you did not believe" <note>original: ουκ επιστευσατε</note>. Additionally, Codex Bezae, manuscripts 13, 69, and others add "me" <note>original: μοι</note> | "these": several Latin versions read "the same" <note>original: αυτα / ipsa</note> | "concerning": Codex H omits this.
**26.** "but" <note>original: αλλα</note> is used in Sinaiticus, A, B, L, Δ... while the Received Text uses the shorter form "all'" <note>original: αλλ</note> with D, X, Γ, Π and most others | "because not" <note>original: οτι ουκ</note> with Sinaiticus, B, D, L, X, many minuscules, and the Vulgate... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "for you [are] not" <note>original: ου γαρ</note> with A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and most others | "of my own [sheep]" <note>original: των εμων</note> without any addition in Sinaiticus, B, K, L, M... the Received Text and Tischendorf add "just as I told you" <note>original: καθως ειπον υμιν</note>, and Lachmann puts this phrase in brackets, following A, D, M, X, Γ, Δ, Λ... <note>Chrysostom records this as: "But I told you, he says, and you do not believe me, because you are not of my sheep."</note>
**27.** "hear" <note>original: ακουουσιν</note> with Sinaiticus, B, L, X, several minuscules, and citations from Origen, Basil, and Chrysostom... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read the singular form "hears" <note>original: ακουει</note> with A, D, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and most others.

# 10, 29. ACCORDING TO JOHN

I give them eternal life, and they will never perish for eternity, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. 29 My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. 30 I and the Father are one.

---

Clementine Homilies $^{794}$ Origen $^{3,298}$ and $^{4, 367}$ Eusebius $^{55. 106.}$ Basil $^{313}$ and $^{3, 14}$ and $^{48}$ Chrysostom $^{8,416}$ (but also using the word "follows" <note>original: ακολουθει</note>) Theodoret $^{1,690. 1375}$ and $^{2,61. 108}$

**28.** "give them eternal life" <note>original: διδ. αυτ. ζω. αιωνιον</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius, 33, 157, the Sahidic and Coptic versions, the Peshitta, Ethiopic, Armenian, and Cyril... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "eternal life give them" with manuscripts Alexandrinus, Bezae, and many others, including the Vulgate, Gothic, and the writings of Basil and Chrysostom. | "they will perish" <note>plural: απολωνται</note>: Sinaiticus originally read "he will perish" <note>singular: αποληται</note> | "will not snatch" <note>future tense: ουχ αρπασει</note> with manuscripts A, B, and many others... Sinaiticus and others read "surely will not snatch" <note>subjunctive: ου μη αρπαση</note>.

**29.** "the Father" <note>original: ο πατηρ</note> without the word "my" with Sinaiticus, several Old Latin manuscripts, the Persian Syriac, Basil, Chrysostom, Tertullian, and Hilary... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf add "my" <note>original: μου</note> with the corrected Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and almost all other manuscripts and versions. | "that which he gave" <note>neuter: ο δεδωκεν</note> with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many Latin versions, including Tertullian and Hilary... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read "who gave" <note>masculine: ος δεδωκεν</note> with Alexandrinus and many others, including Basil and Chrysostom. <note>The neuter "that which" implies the "gift" of the sheep is greater than all; the masculine "who" implies the Father himself is greater than all.</note> (Regarding Tertullian's reading *For the Father, that which he gave to me is greater than all*, Semler notes: “others read: 'For the Father, who is greater than all, gave to me.' Junius reads: 'For the Father, who gave to me, is greater than all.'”) ... Manuscript Bezae reads "the one having given." | "to me": manuscripts 13, 69, and others add "them" <note>referring to the sheep</note>. | "greater than all is" <note>original: παντ. μειζ. εστ.</note> in this order with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Peshitta... The Received Text and Lachmann read "is greater than all" with Alexandrinus and almost all others. Augustine explains this more fully: *“What the Father gave to me—that is, that I should be his Word, that I should be his only-begotten Son, that I should be the radiance of his light—is greater than all things.”* | "greater thing" <note>neuter: μειζον</note> with Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and the Latin versions... The Received Text and Tischendorf read "greater person" <note>masculine: μειζων</note> with Sinaiticus, Bezae, and many others. Even Lachmann published "greater person," but it is clear from his commentary that he intended "greater thing" :: The Old Latin reading, which enjoys the consensus of the manuscripts (except for manuscript d) and the Latin Fathers—namely, the neuter "that which" and "greater thing"—is confirmed by manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and others. Even though some of these mix the masculine and neuter forms, based on the evidence, this must be considered the most ancient reading. Everyone can see why this would have been changed to the masculine "who" and "greater person." However, it is highly unlikely that if someone had found the masculine "who," they would have intentionally changed it to the neuter "that which." | "to snatch": manuscript 69 and others add "them," as do some Latin versions with the word "that." | "of the Father" with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Origen... The Received Text and Lachmann add "my" with Alexandrinus and almost all other manuscripts and versions.

**30.** "I and the Father are one" (cited by Theodotus, Clement, and Origen): compare Hippolytus: *“But if he says, 'I and the Father are one,' let him apply his mind and learn that he did not say 'I and the Father am one' [singular], but 'we are one' [plural].”* Similarly, Cyril of Jerusalem: *“He did not say, 'I and the Father [am one]...'”*

<summary>This page documents the complex textual variations in John 10:28-30, focusing on whether "the gift of the Father" or "the Father himself" is described as "greater than all." Tischendorf argues that the neuter Greek construction is the original form, which was later modified by scribes for clarity or theological emphasis.</summary>

<keywords>Gospel of John, textual criticism, Trinity, Christology, manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Augustine, Tertullian, Hippolytus, variants</keywords>

<note>This section is the "apparatus criticus," a scholarly shorthand used to compare different ancient copies of the Bible. The letters (like א, A, B) and abbreviations (like "vg" for Vulgate) refer to specific manuscripts and ancient translations.</note>

**25.** Nothing similar is found in the Synoptic Gospels <note>original: Nil simile apud Synoptt.; the Synoptic Gospels are Matthew, Mark, and Luke</note>. | The word **that** <note>original: οτι</note> is included with manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), L, X, and others; as well as various Old Latin versions, the Vulgate, all Syriac versions, Eusebius, Athanasius, Cyprian, and Hilary... but is omitted by manuscripts A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and the majority of others, as well as the Gothic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. | **I** <note>original: εγω</note>: omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus (א*) and some Latin copies. | **I said** <note>original: ειπα</note> is found in manuscripts א, B, E, G, H, K, L, and others, as well as Eusebius and Athanasius (the Naassene fragment also quotes this as "this is what is written: I said, you are gods and all sons of the Most High," following the Psalm itself)... **36.** **sanctified** <note>original: ηγιασεν</note> (also supported by Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Tertullian, Cyprian, etc.): manuscript U and 47 read **loved** <note>original: ηγαπησεν</note>. | **you are blaspheming** <note>original: βλασφημεις</note> (supported by Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, etc.): some Latin versions read **he blasphemes**, Eusebius in one instance reads **blaspheming** <note>in the third person</note>, and Hilary in several places reads **I blasphemed**. | **because I said** <note>original: οτι ειπον</note>: manuscript G omits "I said"; many manuscripts (א, D, E, G, and others) omit the word **of God** <note>original: του θεου</note> following "Son," while Lachmann and Tischendorf include **of God** based on A, B, L, X, and the majority of others.

**37.** **not** <note>original: ου</note>: some manuscripts and Chrysostom use a different Greek negative particle <note>original: μη</note>.

**38.** **but** <note>original: δε</note>: manuscript X has this written above the line. | **not** <note>original: μη</note>: omitted by several manuscripts and John of Damascus. | The first instance of **believe** <note>original: πιστευετε</note> is supported by א, A, E, G, H, and many others; similarly manuscript D and pseudo-Athanasius read **you wish to believe** <note>original: θελετε πιστευειν</note>, which is also found in the Old Latin, Vulgate, Tertullian, and Cyprian... Lachmann uses the subjunctive **you might believe** <note>original: πιστευητε</note> based on B, K, L, and others, but this is likely a later grammatical correction. | **the works:** some manuscripts and Chrysostom add **of mine** <note>original: μου</note>. | The second instance of **believe** <note>original: πιστευετε</note> is supported by א, B, D, K, L, and others... Tischendorf uses a different tense <note>the aorist: πιστευσατε</note> based on A, E, G, and the majority of manuscripts. | **and understand** <note>original: και γινωσκητε</note> is found in B, L, X, and the Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions.

<note>This section is a critical apparatus, which scholars use to compare different ancient versions of the Bible to find the most original wording.</note>

**understand** <note>original: γινωσκ.</note> (John of Damascus, volume 1, page 568: *so that you may know and believe and recognize*) Hilary, pages 932, 933, 935 <note>original: Hil</note> (*so that you may know and recognize*) ... the Received Text <note>original: ς</note> includes "and believe" <note>original: καὶ πιστεύσητε</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and seven other uncials <note>uncials are manuscripts written in all capital letters</note> (though manuscript E adds "that you may know and believe" in the margin) and many others, including Old Latin versions f and g, the Vulgate, Gothic, and various Syriac versions, as well as Basil... Manuscript D and several Old Latin versions (a, b, c, e, ff², l), Tertullian, and Cyprian omit this (or rather do not express it), hence Griesbach <note>original: Gb⁰</note> marks it for omission. These Latin versions render "so that you may know" <note>original: ἵνα γνῶτε</note> as: *and know* (a, e, Tertullian), *and recognize* (c, l, Cyprian), *and you shall recognize* (b, ff²). | **in the Father** <note>original: ἐν τῷ πατρὶ</note> (Griesbach's preference) with manuscripts ℵ, B, D, L, X, and others; as well as Old Latin a, c, e, g, the Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, various Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, John of Damascus, and Hilary... the Received Text <note>original: ς</note> reads **in him** <note>original: ἐν αὐτῷ</note> with A, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π, and most others, including Old Latin b, f, ff², l, Gothic, and some Syriac versions. (Pseudo-Athanasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Tertullian read: *that I am in the Father and the Father is in me*).

39. **therefore they sought** <note>original: ἐζήτουν οὖν</note> with ℵ, A, K, L, X, Δ, Π and most others, including the Vulgate and Sahidic (Chrysostom reads *therefore they wished*); ... B, E, G, H, M, S, U, Γ, Λ, and others, including Coptic, Armenian, and Gothic, omit **therefore** <note>original: οὖν</note>... Manuscript D and some Syriac/Ethiopic versions read *and they sought*. | **him** without the word **again** <note>original: πάλιν</note> according to the original hand of Sinaiticus (ℵ*), D, and others. Tischendorf <note>original: Ti</note> adds **again** after **him** with the corrected Sinaiticus (ℵᶜ), A, K, L, X, Δ, Π, and others; the Received Text <note>original: ς</note> and Lachmann <note>original: Ln</note> add it before **him** with B, E, G, H, M, S, Γ, Λ and the majority. | **from the hand**: Manuscripts 1, 22, 247 read **from the hands**, as do most Latin, Gothic, Coptic, and Syriac versions.

40. **and he went away**: Manuscript A reads *therefore he went away*. | **to the place**: Omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus (ℵ*) and Chrysostom. | Manuscripts B and D spell **John** with a specific Greek variant. | **at the first**: Omitted or moved in some manuscripts; Sinaiticus (ℵ) and others read *formerly*, as do several Old Latin versions (*prius*). | **he stayed** <note>original: ἔμεινεν</note> with ℵ, A, D, L, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π... 42. **many** before **believed** with ℵ, B, D, L, M, X and others. It is omitted in the Vulgate and by Chrysostom.
