Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.” 28 And having said this, she went away and called Mary her sister secretly, saying: “The Teacher is present and is calling for you.” 29 When she heard this, she rose quickly and came to him. 30 Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha had met him. 31 The Jews, therefore, who were with her in the house and comforting her, seeing Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, thinking that she was going to the tomb in order to weep there.

<header>11, 47.    ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

...but some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. 
47 Therefore the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a <term>council<note>original: συνέδριον (synedrion) — refers to the Sanhedrin, the high court of Jewish elders and priests.</note></term>, and they were saying: "What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. 48 If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." 49 But a certain one of them, Caiaphas, being the high priest for that year, said to them: "You know nothing at all! 50 Neither do you <margin>18, 14</margin> consider that it is better for you that one man should die for the people..." <note>The text continues in verse 50 on the next page: "...than that the whole nation should perish."</note>

---

<note>The following section is the "critical apparatus," a technical record showing how different ancient manuscripts of the Bible vary in their wording. Scholars use these codes (like א for Codex Sinaiticus or B for Codex Vaticanus) to determine the most original text.</note>

**45.** Manuscript **e** reads <note>original Latin: viderunt quod est factum</note> "they saw what was done." This is also found in manuscripts **l, am, fu, for, fos, em, ing, iac, gat, mm, tol, sax, go,** and the Sahidic, Coptic, and Armenian versions, as well as Origen. The <term>Textus Receptus<note>original: ς — the "received text" used for early English translations like the King James Version.</note></term> adds **Jesus** (which manuscript **א** omits) along with several other major Greek manuscripts and ancient versions. | **in him**: Omitted by manuscript **c**.

**46.** Verse omitted by manuscript **s**. | **went away**: Manuscript **D** uses a different Greek spelling for "went." | **they told**: The Textus Receptus and various editors (Lachmann, Tischendorf) use one form of "told," while manuscripts **A, B, C, L,** and others use another. | **Pharisees**: Manuscripts **13, 69, 124** read "the chief priests and Pharisees." | **them**: Omitted by manuscript **G**. | **what**: Found in **א, B, L,** and many others. Other versions (including the Syriac and Coptic) use a variation meaning "all the things that." | **Jesus**: Accompanied by the definite article in many manuscripts (a common Greek grammatical style).

**47. Therefore**: Manuscripts **69, em, sah, go** read "But." | **council**: Manuscripts **13, 69, 124, 127, 254, 346** and 5 others add "against Jesus." | **and they were saying**: Several manuscripts read "saying" (as a participle). | **What**: Manuscript **Δ** adds "therefore." | **are we doing**: Different manuscripts use various Greek tenses (present vs. future). The Latin versions mostly read "we do" or "we shall do." | **that**: Omitted by manuscript **D**. | **this man**: Some manuscripts (and the Armenian version) swap the word order to "the man this." | **many**: The Latin versions **d, b, c, e, ff^2** read "such" instead of "many." | **performs signs**: The word order varies across the ancient copies.

**48. If**: Manuscripts **D, 235** and several ancient versions read "And if." The *Apostolic Constitutions* (an ancient Christian collection) paraphrases this as: "If we do not kill Christ, they say, everyone [will believe]." | **will believe**: A few manuscripts use a slightly different grammatical mood (subjunctive) or tense. | **both our place**: Various Latin manuscripts and the church father Origen place "our" after "place" or "nation." The Latin versions vary in how they include the word "and" between these terms.

**49. Caiaphas**: Some manuscripts (like **D**) spell this as "Chaiphas" or "Kephas." Several versions (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian) add the phrase "by name." | **being high priest**: A few Latin manuscripts translate this as "since he was" or "who was."

**50. consider**: The Textus Receptus uses a different Greek compound verb (διαλογίζεσθε) meaning "reason among yourselves," while the older manuscripts (**א, A, B, D, L**) use the simpler form (λογίζεσθε).

## XII.

<margin>11, 43</margin>
1 Jesus therefore, six days before the Passover, came to Betha-
ny, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. 2 They
<margin>Luke 10, 40</margin>
made a dinner for him there, and Martha served, but Lazarus
was one of those reclining at the table with him. 3 Mary therefore, having taken
<margin>Matthew 26, 6-12</margin>
a pound of ointment of pure, <term>pistic</term> <note>original: πιστικῆς. This Greek word is rare and debated; it likely means "genuine" or "pure," but some early scholars thought it might refer to a specific place or a liquid consistency.</note> costly nard, anointed the feet

---

<note>The following notes are part of a "critical apparatus," a technical record of how ancient manuscripts of the Bible differ from one another. Scholars use these codes—like א (Codex Sinaiticus), B (Codex Vaticanus), and D (Codex Bezae)—to reconstruct the most original version of the text.</note>

XII. 1. **Jesus therefore** <note>original: ο ουν ις</note>: Manuscript 69 and others omit this, but add **Jesus** (or **the Jesus**) after the word **came** at the start of the section. Likewise Codex Sinaiticus (א) [the scholar Tregelles testifies only to **the Jesus** after **came**] | **Lazarus** without additions in א, B, L, X, the Old Latin, the Sahidic Coptic, the Syriac, and the Ethiopic (the Persian version adds: "where Jesus had raised Lazarus from the midst of the dead"). Nonnus <note>A 5th-century poet who paraphrased John into Greek verse</note> reads: "where near the tomb he raised Lazarus from the dead." A homily attributed to Chrysostom begins: "Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, in the house of Mary etc." (See also Matthew's commentary where the phrases **the one who had died** and **from the dead** are omitted) ... The Textus Receptus and Tischendorf add **the one who had died** <note>original: ο τεθνηκωσ</note>, Lachmann brackets it, following manuscripts A, D, I, and several others, the Vulgate, the Gothic, and others. Although the common reading "Lazarus the one who had died" has a great appearance of truth, it is not incredible that it was inserted to make the story clearer. If you argue it was omitted as redundant, it is strange that the oldest and quite diverse witnesses agree on this point alone. | **from the dead** <note>original: εκ νεκρων</note> (manuscripts c and e read: "whom he raised dead"): omitted by b, the Vulgate, and the Persian version. | **Jesus** (Lachmann and Tischendorf read **the Jesus**, but א, B, 13, and 124 read **Jesus**) with א, A, B, and many others (though א and others place the name before **from the dead**). Omitted by several other manuscripts.

2. **Therefore they made**: Manuscripts D, c, e, and the Syriac read **and they made**; the Vulgate reads **but they made** ... Origen omits the connecting word. | **there** (placed before **dinner** in some manuscripts): omitted by a and e. | **and Martha served**: Manuscript D and the Armenian version read **and Martha was serving**. | **from** <note>original: εκ</note> with א, B, L, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate. Origen also includes it ... The Textus Receptus and Lachmann omit it with A, D, and others. Similarly, **from** was dropped in John 12:4. John loves the phrase "one from" <note>original: εισ εκ</note> and does not usually vary it. In other places, such as Mark 13:1 and 14:20, "from" seems to have been added later. | **reclining with him**: with א, A, B, D, and others. (Codex Sinaiticus and a few others omit **with him**). The Textus Receptus reads **reclining together with him** <note>original: συνανακειμενων αυτω</note> based on later minuscules.

3. **Mary** with א, A, D, and others ... Manuscripts B, 1, and 33 read **Mariam**. | **having taken** <note>original: λαβουσα</note>: Manuscript D reads **takes**, while the Latin versions read **took**, and add "and" before **anointed**. The Fulda manuscript <note>A famous Latin manuscript of the 6th century</note> reads: "having an alabaster jar—and having broken it, she poured it over the head of Jesus as he reclined, and anointed his feet," mixing John's account with the versions found in the other Gospels (Matthew and Mark). | **ointment of pure nard** (The Vulgate and Origen read **ointment of pistic nard**): Manuscripts D and e reverse the order to **pistic ointment**; others omit **nard** or **ointment**. | **very costly**: omitted by manuscripts a, b, and e.

**Glorify your name**: this is identical to the precision of the interpretations.
*Furthermore*, <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> adds: "in the glory which I had with you before the world was" <note>This addition is borrowed from John 17:5</note>. *Augustine seems to have read this passage as interpolated from 17:5* (Against Adimantus 8, 121): *When the Lord had said: Father, glorify me with that glory which I had with you before the world was, a voice sounded from heaven: And I have glorified, and I will glorify.* Similarly, *Epiphanius in Heresies* 42 | **so it came** (omitted by <term>Sinaiticus (ℵ)</term>, Coptic, and Armenian; "but" in Old Latin 'a' and Gothic; "and it came" in the Syriac Peshitta, Ge'ez, and Ethiopic): <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> reads **and it happened** (omitted by Latin 'd') | **from heaven**: <term>Codex Bezae</term>, several uncials, and various versions (Old Latin, Coptic, Syriac) add **saying** (not found in Latin 'b', 'f', or the Vulgate. *Furthermore, as Lucas of Bruges noted in the corrections: "Do not add Saying"*) | **and again** (also Origen and Eusebius): <term>Codex Delta (Δ)</term> reads **again and**.

29. **so** (Gothic, Sahidic, and Syriac read "but"; Syriac and Ethiopic read "and the crowd") with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus (B)</term>, <term>Bezae (D)</term>, and almost all others: <term>Vaticanus (B)</term> and Old Latin 'a' omit it, hence <term>Lachmann (Ln)</term> puts [so] in brackets | **stood** with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and most ancient manuscripts ... <term>Lachmann</term> reads a different Greek form of "stood" with <term>Codex Alexandrinus (A)</term> and others | **having heard** without a conjunction in <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Bezae</term>, and others ... <term>Stephens (ς)</term>, <term>Lachmann</term>, and <term>Tischendorf (Ti)</term> read **and having heard** with <term>Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and most others | **was saying**: several manuscripts and versions read **were saying** (the Latin 'c' and 'd' read "the crowds were saying"; 'e' reads "therefore the crowd was standing and those hearing were saying") | **that it had thundered** (also the Vulgate and Syriac): <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> and several Old Latin versions read "that thunder has happened" | **others**: some versions add **but** | **said**: several manuscripts add **that**.

30. **Jesus** (Griesbach) with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and 50 others ... <term>Stephens</term> and <term>Lachmann</term> read **the Jesus** <note>Adding the definite article before a proper name, common in Greek</note> with <term>Alexandrinus</term> and most others | **and said**: <term>Vaticanus</term> and <term>Codex L</term> place this after "answered" ... <term>Sinaiticus</term> omits it | **this voice** with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and many others ... <term>Stephens</term> reads the word order as **the voice this** with most later manuscripts and the Vulgate | **has come** (Coptic: "was made"): <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> and most Old Latin and Vulgate versions read **came**.

31. **now is the judgment of this world**: omitted by <term>Sinaiticus</term> and the Jerusalem Syriac | **of this world** in the first instance: several Latin and Coptic versions omit **this**, hence Griesbach marked it for potential removal | **now the ruler of this world**: <term>Sinaiticus</term> and a few others omit this (skipping from "of this world" to "of this world") | **will be cast** (<term>Codex Bezae</term> uses a simpler form of the verb; Old Latin 'a' and 'c' read "is sent") **out**: some sources read **will be cast down**, and several Old Latin versions read **will be sent downward** (or "will be dismissed downward," or the Sahidic "they will throw him down"). *Compare Gaudentius* (at the Sabbath): "*he will be sent downward or expelled outside, as we read in the Greek copies*" — "*In the Greek it is written 'cast out,' that is, he will be ejected or expelled outside.*" (Sermon 6: "he is ejected outside").

32. **And I**: <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> and others read "And I also" | **if** (also Origen): <term>Vaticanus (B)</term> uses a shorter form of "if"; other sources read **when** | **from** with <term>Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Alexandrinus</term>, <term>Vaticanus</term>, and most others: <term>Codex Bezae (D)</term> and a few others read **away from**; likewise the Old Latin and Vulgate read "from the earth."

49. **I** <note>original: "εγω"</note>: Manuscript D and others place this after the word "myself" ... Manuscript G and others omit it; likewise Tertullian in *Against Praxeas* 23 <note>original Latin: "quoniam scilicet a memet ipso non sum locutus," meaning "since obviously I have not spoken from myself"</note>, Ambrose in *On the Faith*, and Chrysostom (who writes "for I have not come from myself" <note>original Greek: "οτι απ εμαυτου ουκ εληλυθα"</note> etc.) | **I spoke** <note>original: "ελαλησα"</note>: Manuscript Γ and several others, along with Chrysostom, read "I have come" <note>original: "εληλυθα"</note> | **from** <note>original: "εξ"</note>: Manuscripts L, 1, 22, 69, 346, and others read "from" <note>original: "αφ" or "απ"</note>, as does the Latin "a me" in manuscripts a, e, l, and Tertullian | **himself** <note>original: "αυτοσ"</note>: Manuscript G reads "this one" <note>original: "ουτοσ"</note> | **a commandment to me** <note>original: "μοι εντολην"</note>: Manuscripts 1, 118, and others read "commandment to me" <note>order reversed</note> | **has given** <note>original: "δεδωκεν"</note>: Supported by the primary manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), and others ... but the traditional Byzantine text reads "gave" <note>original: "εδωκε"</note> as found in Codex Bezae (D) and others | **and what** <note>original: "και τι"</note>: Some Latin and Coptic versions read "or what" <note>original: "η τι"</note>. Similarly, Nonnus in his poetic paraphrase (v. 196) writes "or what I should cry out."

50. **is eternal life**: Manuscript D reads "is life eternal," while others read "life is eternal" | **I speak** <note>original: "εγω λαλω"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), and many other early witnesses, including the Latin Vulgate and Coptic versions ... Manuscript D and Chrysostom omit "I" <note>original: "εγω"</note> ... the traditional Byzantine text places "I" after the verb | **has told**: Manuscripts 13, 69, and others read "commanded," while a few others read "said."

XIII. 1. **knowing** <note>original: "ειδωσ"</note>: Some versions read "seeing" <note>original: "ιδων"</note> | **had come** <note>original: "ηλθεν"</note>: Supported by the major early codices ... the traditional Byzantine text uses the perfect tense "has come" <note>original: "εληλυθεν"</note> ... Codex Bezae (D) reads "was present" | **his own** <note>original: "ιδιουσ"</note>: In the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), this was accidentally written as "Jews" <note>original: "ιουδαιουσ"</note>.

2. **during supper** <note>original: "γινομενου"</note>: Supported by Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and others, meaning "while supper was happening" ... the traditional text and the Latin Vulgate read "supper being finished" <note>original: "γενομενου"; Latin: "caena facta"</note> | **the devil**: Manuscript A adds "both" before the devil | **that Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, should betray him**: There is significant variation here regarding the grammar of the names. Early manuscripts like Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B) suggest the devil put the intent into the heart of Judas ... while the Byzantine tradition (followed by many later manuscripts) phrases it as "into the heart of Judas" <note>possessive</note>. Codex Bezae (D) specifies Judas was "from Karyotos."

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 13, 20.

I did to you, and you should do. 16 <margin>118,3</margin> <margin>John 15:20; Matthew 10:24; Luke 6:40, 22:27</margin> Truly, truly I say to you, a servant is not greater than his lord, nor is an apostle greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. 18 <margin>119.10</margin> <margin>Psalm 40 (41):9 (10); Acts 1:16</margin> I am not speaking about all of you; I know those whom I have chosen; but let the scripture be fulfilled: “The one eating the bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.” <note>This is a quote from the Psalms, using the metaphor of a horse kicking its master to describe treachery.</note> 19 From now on I tell you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe that I am <note>original: "ego eimi" — "I am." <note>The following notes are part of the "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of how different ancient hand-written manuscripts vary in their wording. Letters like A, B, C, and the symbol ℵ (Sinaiticus) represent specific famous Bibles from the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>

**Verse 16.** Origen (volume 4, pages 405, 419, 423), Basil (page 295), Chrysostom (volume 8, page 477), Theodoret (volume 1, page 1209) | **"I"** (also found in Origen; Cyril places it after "did to you"): Manuscripts U, Γ, 33 and about ten others omit this; also omitted in Origen’s Latin translation | **"I did"** (also found four times in Origen): Manuscripts 13, 69, 124, 229, 254, 346, 440; Manuscript 440 reads "I have done" | **"to you":** Manuscript E originally read "you" (as an object) | **"you should do"** with Manuscripts ℵ, A, B, C, K, L, S, U, Γ, Δ, Π and many others, Origen (four times), Basil (three times), Chrysostom... ->Manuscripts "e", "l", the Old Syriac, Ethiopic, and Chrysostom (volume 8, page 481) support the text; manuscripts "e" and "o" also read: "He who receives me receives him whom I sent. **Verse 22.** "They looked" (without a conjunction) appears in Codices Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. (Origen notes: "Perhaps also this: the disciples looked at one another.") ... The Textus Receptus and Lachmann add "therefore" with Codices Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, and others. Other manuscripts add "and." Additionally, the original scribe of Sinaiticus (ℵ*) wrote "the Jews looked," but a later corrector (ℵa) deleted "the Jews." | **the disciples**: manuscripts 13, 69, 124, and the Sahidic Coptic add "his." | **at a loss**: Codex Bezae (D) and others use a slightly different Greek word for "doubting."

**Verse 23.** "He was" (without a conjunction) appears with Codices Vaticanus, Ephraemi (C*), and L. ... The Textus Receptus omits "of" with Codices E, F, G, and others. | **whom**: Codex Bezae (D) reads "whom also." | **Jesus**: manuscript 69 and the Old Latin "e" omit this.

**Verse 24.** "Therefore" appears in Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and others ... Manuscript 69 and some Syriac versions omit it. | **Peter**: Codex Bezae (D) spells it "Petrous." | **and says to him**: (Latin "a" has "saying," others have "and he said") **tell us who it is**: Manuscripts B, C, I, L, X, and the Latin Vulgate include "tell us who it is." The Textus Receptus reads "to inquire who it might be" (Codex Bezae adds "this man") based on Codex Alexandrinus and others. The scholar Scholz notes: John does not use this specific Greek mood (the optative) in any other single place. | **about whom he speaks**: Omitted in some Latin manuscripts.

**Verse 25.** **Falling upon**: Found in the original Sinaiticus (ℵ*), Alexandrinus, Bezae, and others. ... Griesbach, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **leaning back** based on the corrected Sinaiticus (ℵc), Vaticanus, and others. Note: the word for "leaning back" is used everywhere for those sitting at a meal; therefore, this was likely substituted by a scribe who did not notice the specific significance of the word "falling upon." This change was perhaps influenced by the wording in John 21:20.

<margin>John 13:19</margin> I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I. 29 And 
<margin>John 12:31</margin> now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe. 30 I will no longer speak many things with you; for the ruler of the world is coming, and in me he has nothing <note>original: *ouden*; "nothing" or "no claim," suggesting the devil has no power over Jesus because Jesus is without sin</note>, 31 but so that the world may know that I love [the Father]...

27. **"my peace I give to you"**: found also in Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> (vol. 1, p. 752; vol. 4, p. 100) and in Latin translation (vol. 2, p. 255), and three times in Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD)</note> (*Against Hierocles* 364, 561) and in his commentary on the Psalms (143, 171), and in his *Theophania* (129), Didymus the Blind's *On the Trinity* (book 1, p. 26), Nonnus <note>A Greek epic poet who wrote a poetic paraphrase of John's Gospel</note> (section 104), etc. ... The Scrivener transcription omits this. | **"gives"**: Codex Sinaiticus <note>A famous 4th-century Bible manuscript</note> adds "to you." Similarly Nonnus (section 105) reads "not as he gives to you," etc. | Manuscript *e* <note>An Old Latin manuscript</note> omits the section from "not as" through "give to you." | Manuscripts G, Gamma, and others spell "be troubled" <note>original: *tarassethō*</note> with a single "s."

28. **"you loved"**: (also Origen vol. 1, p. 234; Eusebius *Against Marcellus* 110; Athanasius <note>Bishop of Alexandria and defender of Orthodoxy (c. 296–373 AD)</note> p. 329; from two manuscripts; Epiphanius p. 867; Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an influential preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople (c. 347–407 AD)</note> vol. 8, p. 507; Cyril vol. 4, p. 842; Cyprian pp. 169, 230, 321, etc.) ... Codex Bezae (original hand), H, L, 69. The Received Text and Scrivener read "you love." | **"because I am going"**: along with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae (corrected), L, X, Pi, and about 12 others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Curetonian Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, Cyril, Nonnus, Cyprian, etc. ... The Received Text (endorsed by Griesbach and Scholz) reads **"because I said: I am going"** with manuscripts E, G, H, K, M, S, U, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, and most others, Athanasius, Irenaeus <note>2nd-century Bishop of Lyon</note> in Latin translation, Tertullian <note>Early Latin author</note>, Cyprian, and Hilary. Many add **"my"** [Father]. | **"the Father"**: along with Sinaiticus (corrected), Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, X, and various other manuscripts and versions, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Cyril, Irenaeus, Origen, Tertullian, Cyprian, Hilary (also "the Father who sent me" in Origen and "the Father who sent me" in Didymus) ... The Received Text (Griesbach) adds **"my"** [Father], and Lachmann puts **"my"** in brackets, based on the original hand of Sinaiticus, many other uncials, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Gothic, and Eusebius.

29. **"before"**: manuscripts 13. 69. 124. 346. read "before the time." | **"so that"**: Sinaiticus and Chrysostom use a shortened spelling. | **"when"**: manuscript L reads "if." | **"you may believe"**: Codex Bezae adds "in me"; others (33. 346. 32) add "that I told you"; Latin manuscripts *l* and *gat* read "that I am"; Chrysostom reads "that I am."

30. **"is coming"**: manuscripts *f* and *q* and Hilary read "will come." | **"for"**: manuscript 69 and the Armenian version omit this. | **"the world"** without "this": with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, L, X, and about 150 others, Syriac, Theodoret, Cyril, and Hilary ... The Received Text (Griesbach, Scholz) adds **"this"** [of this world] with manuscripts 1, 346, the Old Latin manuscript *e* ("of this age"), and the Vulgate. Additionally, many (including Origen, Basil, Macarius, Athanasius, and Chrysostom) place the word **"ruler"** before "of the world." | **"has nothing"**: (manuscript D and *a* add "to find") with manuscripts *b*, *c*, *e*, *ff²*, *g*, *l*, *q*, Vulgate, Syriac, and Origen. Griesbach notes a variation **"will find nothing"** in manuscripts K, Pi, etc., and in the writings of Hippolytus, Athanasius, Macarius, Basil, and Cyril. Origen and Epiphanius also use **"finds nothing"** or "finds nothing of his own."

## XV.

1 “I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener. 2 Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit, he prunes <note>original: *kathairei*; this Greek word means both "to cleanse" and "to prune," creating a wordplay with *airei*, "to take away"</note> it so that it may bear more fruit. <margin>John 13:10</margin> 3 You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you; 4 abide in me, and I in you. Just as the branch is not able to bear fruit

---

31. **“and just as”**: The Greek phrase *kai kathōs* is found in manuscripts A and E, and Old Latin versions *b* and *ff²*. However, some omit “and,” leading the scholar Lachmann <note>Karl Lachmann (1793–1851), a major figure in biblical textual criticism</note> to place “and” in brackets. | **“commanded me”** (*eneteilato moi*): This reading is supported by the Great Uncial manuscripts <note>Large-letter parchment bibles from the 4th-9th centuries</note> like Sinaiticus (א), A, D, and many others, as well as the Coptic, Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian, and Gothic versions. Lachmann, however, prefers the phrase **“gave me a command”** (*entolēn edōken moi*) based on manuscripts B and L, the Vulgate, and the writings of Cyril. The Old Latin versions *b, e, q* and Hilary of Poitiers read “gave a command” or “precept.” The Ethiopic version reads “and I do his command” or “just as the Father gave me his command, so I do.” It appears the phrase “gave a command” may have been altered to match the wording in John 12:49. | **“the Father”**: Manuscript D and some Latin versions omit the word “the.”

XV. 1. **“the vine”**: Found in Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, and Basil. Manuscript M* omits the definite article “the.” | **“the true [vine]”**: This is found without additions in almost all major uncial manuscripts, the Old Latin, and the Vulgate. However, some sources like Origen, John Chrysostom, and Cyril add **“you are the branches”** here, likely pulling the phrase forward from verse 5. Hilary also adds this. | **“the gardener”** (*ho geōrgos*): Manuscripts D and Δ omit the definite article “the.”

2. **“bearing”** (*pheron*): Some manuscripts (A, H, Γ²) use a slightly different grammatical form of the word (*pherōn*). | **“not bearing fruit”**: Origen paraphrases this as “remaining but not bearing fruit,” and Hilary writes “not abiding nor bearing fruit.” | **“he takes away”** (*airei*): Latin manuscripts *a, b, f, d* translate this as “he takes away” (present tense), while others (*c, e, vg*) use the future tense “he will take away.” Origen’s Latin translation uses a word meaning “he will cut off,” and Hilary uses “it will be uprooted.” Nonnus <note>A 5th-century poet who wrote a paraphrase of John</note> uses a term meaning “he will cut through.” | **“takes it away”**: Manuscript 2pe and Old Latin *b, c, l* add “the Father” as the subject. | **“that which bears fruit”**: Manuscript D uses “the fruit-bearing one.” Origen paraphrases as “remaining and producing good fruit.” | **“he prunes”** (or cleanses, *kathairei*): Supported by most early sources. Manuscript D and several Latin versions use a word meaning “he will cleanse.” | **“it”** (second instance): Manuscripts א and G use a masculine form of "it," while others omit the word entirely. | **“more fruit”**: Manuscripts א, B, L, and the Vulgate place the word “more” before “fruit.” Other manuscripts like A and D reverse the order to “fruit more.” | **“may bear”**: A few manuscripts use a slightly different verb mood (indicative instead of subjunctive).

3. 4. **“You are already...”** through **“bear fruit”**: Manuscript D and its Latin counterpart *d* omit this entire section.
4. **“just as”**: A few manuscripts add “for” to this sentence.

<header>15, 5. ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

...by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. **5** I am the vine, you are the branches. The one who remains in me and I in him, this one bears much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing. **6** If anyone does not remain in me, he is thrown out like a branch and withers; and they gather it and throw it into the fire, and it is burned. <gloss>133.4</gloss> <margin>14, 13</margin> **7** If you remain in me and my words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. <gloss>134.10</gloss> **8** By this my Father is glorified, that [you bear] much fruit...

---

**4.** **“remains”** <note>original: *menē*</note>: This form is found in manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and L, and the Old Latin *a* (reading "may remain")... However, the editors Stephanus (ς), Lachmann (Ln), and Tischendorf (Ti) use the form *meinē* based on manuscripts A, D, X, and almost all others (though manuscript G reads *meinei*), including the Vulgate (reading "should have remained" or "remained") and the church fathers Origen and Eusebius. | **“neither you”** <note>original: *oude hymeis*</note>: Found in the Vulgate and several other versions... but manuscripts *x, y* and some others, along with Eusebius, read **“and you”** (*kai hymeis*). Similarly, Old Latin versions *b* and *ff²* read "so also he who does not remain in me." | **“you remain”** <note>original: *menēte*</note>: Found in Sinaiticus, A, B, and L... while editors Stephanus and Tischendorf prefer *meinēte* based on D, X, and nearly all others including Eusebius and Cyril. It is clear that based on the evidence, one should read either *menē* and *menēte* or *meinē* and *meinēte*. Verse 7 is different.

**5.** **“I”** <note>original: *egō*</note>: Supported by Origen and Eusebius; however, manuscript D and some Old Latin versions add **“for”** (*gar*). | **“in me”**: Manuscript D (Greek text) omits **“in”**. | **“this one”** <note>original: *houtos*</note>: Some manuscripts and the Gothic version read **“so”** (*houtōs*). | **“nothing”** <note>original: *ouden*</note>: Old Latin version *a* adds "unless he remains in me." Manuscript B reads **“not even one thing”** (*oude hen*). Manuscript D and some others omit the word entirely.

**6.** **“remains”** <note>original: *menē*</note>: Found in Sinaiticus, A, B, and D... while Stephanus and Tischendorf prefer *meinē* based on L, X, and almost all others including Cyril. See the note on verse 4. | **“thrown out”** <note>original: *eblēthē*</note>: Manuscripts G, L, and others read **“cast out”** (*ekblēthē*). | **“withers”**: Manuscript L reads a slightly different form of the word. | **“it”** <note>original: *auto*</note>: This singular reading is found in Sinaiticus, D, L, X, and many others, as well as the Vulgate, Syriac, and Armenian. However, the editors Stephanus, Lachmann, and Tischendorf prefer the plural **“them”** (*auta*) based on manuscripts A, B, and most others, as well as the Coptic. The note suggests that the plural verb **“they gather”** seemed to require a plural object. | **“the fire”**: Most manuscripts (Sinaiticus, A, B, E, etc.) include the definite article **“the”** (*to*), though Stephanus and Lachmann (by error) omit it based on D, H, X, and Cyril. Compare this to Matthew 3:10, 7:19, and Luke 3:9. | **“they throw”** <note>original: *ballousin*</note>: Manuscript 33 reads **“they throw into”** (*emballousin*).

**7.** **Corruption in Manuscript 69**: This manuscript contains a scrambled reading: "If you do not remain in me and my words do not remain in you; but if you remain in me, remain [misspelled]; and whatever you wish will happen for you." | **“if”**: Manuscript D and some versions add **“but”** (*de*). | **“you remain”**: Some manuscripts use slightly different Greek verb tenses or spellings. | **“whatever”** <note>original: *ho ean*</note>: Supported by A, D, L, X and almost all others... Lachmann prefers *ho an* based on Vaticanus (B), while Sinaiticus (א) reads **“as many things as”** (*hosa ean*). | **“wish”** <note>original: *thelēte*</note>: Various manuscripts show minor spelling variations (*thelete*). | **“ask”** <note>original: *aitēsasthe*</note>: This imperative form ("ask!") is found in manuscripts A, B, D, L, and many others, as well as the Coptic and Syriac. However, the "Received Text" (Stephanus) reads the future tense **“you will ask”** (*aitēsesthe*) based on manuscripts E, G, H, and others, including the Vulgate. | **“for you”**: Manuscript D and some Latin versions omit this.

**8.** **“By this”**: Sinaiticus and L have a minor spelling variation. | **“much”**: Manuscript D places this word before "fruit." One minor manuscript omits it.

18. **"hates you"**: Sinaiticus (ℵ) reverses the order to **"you hates."** Origen’s Latin translation reads "this world hates you, because it hated me before you." | **"first"** <note>original: prōton</note> without "of you" with ℵ*, D, and several Old Latin and ancient versions... the majority of editors (Stephanus, Lachmann, Tischendorf) add **"before you"** <note>original: hymōn</note> with ℵᶜ, A, B, I, L, and most other manuscripts and versions. | **"it has hated"**: ℵ* and N use a simpler past tense **"it hated."**

*On the phrase "the word of their law which says": Origen (vol. 4, page 580) notes Cyril (vol. 4, page 908) ... the conjunction "but" is placed before "in the" by manuscripts A, E, H, I, K, M, S, U, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and many others, as well as the Gothic, both Syriac versions, and the Ethiopic.*

*26. In the second instance of "Father," many manuscripts lack "my," while D and several old Latin and Syriac versions add it ... On the word "testify," manuscript L and others use a slightly different future tense spelling.*

*27. "And you also" (in the Gothic, Coptic, and Syriac versions: "and you also"): manuscript D and 15 others omit "also," nor is it expressed in the Vulgate or Syriac ... "From" (ap): manuscript 1 reads "out of" (ex).*

*Chapter 16, verse 2. "But" (all): manuscript ℵ spells it "al." On the phrase "but an hour is coming etc.": compare the letter from the churches of Lyon and Vienne found in Eusebius' Church History (book 5, chapter 1, section 15): "the word spoken by our Lord was fulfilled, that a time will come in which everyone who kills you will think they offer service to God." On the second "you" (found in Origen, Cyprian, etc.): manuscript B omits it ... "Service" (latreian): manuscripts E, K, L, Δ spell it "latrian" ... "To God": manuscript ℵ reads "to the Lord."*

*3. "They will do": manuscript ℵ and others use a different verb ending. We have written this without additions following A, B, and the vast majority of manuscripts and early translations like the Vulgate and Syriac ... the Standard Text (ς) adds "to you" (hymin) following ℵ, D, L, and several Latin and Coptic versions.*

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN 16, 18.</header>

[The Spirit] will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. 14 That one will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and will declare it to you. <margin>John 17:10</margin> 15 All things that the Father has are mine; <margin>John 14:10</margin> for this reason I said that he takes from what is mine and will declare it to you. <margin>John 14:19</margin> 16 A little while and you will no longer see me, and again a little while and you will see me. 17 Some of his disciples then said to one another, "What is this that he says to us: 'A little while and you do not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? and 'Because I am going to the Father'?" 18 They were saying therefore, "What is this 'little while' of which he speaks?"

14. **The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus** <note>original: ℵ*</note> omits this verse | **will glorify**: manuscript y and a few others read **might glorify** <note>a grammatical variation from the future indicative to the aorist subjunctive</note> | **because**: manuscript 69 reads **and** | **he will take**: spelled *lēmpsetai* in manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and the original hand of Vaticanus... but spelled *lēpsetai* in the corrected Vaticanus, Codex Regius, and almost all others ... Codex Δ reads **he will glorify** | **to you**: Epiphanius adds **all things** <note>likely added from the context of verse 13</note>. Also manuscript 33 connects **all things** with the following phrase "will declare to you."

15. **The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus** omits this entire verse <note>due to "homoeoteleuton," an error where a scribe's eye skips from one similar word ending to another</note>, though it was added by a later corrector | **has**: Codex Basiliensis and a few others read a variant spelling | **I said**: manuscripts Sinaiticus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and others add **to you** | **he takes**: read as *lambanei* <note>present tense</note> by manuscripts Vaticanus, Bezae, and many others, including the Syriac and Armenian versions ... but the standard printed text <note>Textus Receptus</note> reads **he will take** <note>future tense</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus (corrected), Alexandrinus, and others | **will declare**: Sinaiticus and the Gothic version use a slightly different future form.

16. **no longer**: supported by manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many early versions ... but the standard printed text and Tischendorf read simply **not** with manuscripts Alexandrinus, Cyprius, and others. Additionally, a few versions read **a little while longer** | **you will see me** without additions: supported by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Old Latin ... but the standard printed text adds **because I go to the Father**, as do manuscripts Alexandrinus, Cyprius, and the Gothic and Syriac versions.

17. **they said**: the standard spelling *eipon* is found in most manuscripts, but Tischendorf prefers the variant *eipan* found in Vaticanus | **of his disciples**: manuscript Λ has a corrupted repetition of the word "their" | **to one another**: some manuscripts place this before the mention of the disciples | **The original hand of Sinaiticus** skipped from the first "little while" to the second, later corrected | **do not**: manuscript Bezae and 33 read **no longer** | **see**: manuscript Bezae and several Latin versions read **you shall see** | **and because**: a few manuscripts and the Peshitta Syriac omit **and** | **I am going**: most manuscripts; some others add the pronoun **I** specifically.

18. **They were saying therefore**: omitted by the original hand of Bezae and a few others | **What is this?**: word order variation between "What is this?" and "This, what is it?" | **of which he speaks**: omitted by the original hand of Sinaiticus, Bezae, and some Old Latin versions | **the "little while"**: omitted by Vaticanus and a few others.

<header>16, 19. ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

"...we do not know what he is saying." 19 Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, and he said to them, "Are you inquiring among yourselves about this, that I said: 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? 20 Truly, truly, I say to you that you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy. 21 Whenever a woman gives birth, she has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has brought forth the child, she no longer remembers the tribulation <note>The Greek term *thlipsis* refers to intense pressure or distress, often used for the pains of labor.</note> because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. 22 And you, therefore, now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and [your heart] will rejoice...

---

**18.** Omit **the** <note>original: "το"</note> | **what he says** <note>original: "τι λαλεῖ"</note> with manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), the corrected Bezae (D²), and others; but the original hand of Bezae (D*) reads **what he speaks** <note>original: "ο λεγει"</note> ... Codex Vaticanus (B) and the Ethiopic version omit this entire phrase.

**19.** **knew** <note>original: "ἔγνω"</note> without a conjunction <note>such as 'and' or 'therefore'</note> with Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Regius (L), and others. Origen notes "when the disciples were speaking... Jesus knowing..." | The standard text <note>original: "ς" (Textus Receptus)</note> and Lachmann (Ln) read **Jesus knew therefore** with Alexandrinus (A) and most other manuscripts ... Other versions like the Vulgate and Syriac read **But Jesus knew** or **And Jesus knew** | **Jesus** <note>original: "Ἰησοῦς"</note> with Vaticanus (B) and Regius (L) ... The standard text and Lachmann read **the Jesus** <note>The addition of the definite article is common in Greek manuscripts</note> with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus | **they wanted** <note>original: "ἤθελον"</note>: Sinaiticus and others read **they were about to** <note>original: "ἤμελλον"</note> | **to ask**: Codex Bezae (D) reads **to question him about this** | **to them**: Manuscript Alexandrinus (A) and others omit this | **about this**: Codex Λ reads **concerning this**.

**20.** **and you will lament** <note>original: "καὶ θρηνήσετε"</note>: Manuscript Λ reads **and you will mourn** | **you will be sorrowful**: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and many early versions (Latin, Coptic, Syriac) follow this ... The standard text adds **but** <note>original: "δέ"</note> after **you** with Alexandrinus and many others | **but** <note>original: "ἀλλ'"</note>: Tischendorf (Τι) uses the longer form *alla* with Bezae and others | **your**: Some manuscripts read **our** | **will turn into**: One manuscript uses a slightly different accentuation on the Greek word for **will become**.

**21.** **gives birth** <note>original: "τίκτῃ"</note>: A common spelling variation in manuscript Λ and others | **has come**: Manuscript Υ reads **is here** | **the hour** <note>original: "ἡ ὥρα"</note>: Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions read **the day** <note>original: "ἡ ἡμέρα"</note> | **brought forth**: Spelling variation in Alexandrinus | **the child**: Manuscript 1 omits **the** | **tribulation** <note>original: "θλίψεως"</note>: Codex Bezae (D) and Ambrose read **sorrow** <note>original: "λύπης"</note>; some Latin versions read **pain** | **was born**: Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C) uses a slightly different spelling of the verb. | **human being**: The original hand of Sinaiticus (ℵ*) adds the definite article **the**.

**22.** **therefore** <note>original: "οὖν"</note> in this position is supported by the Vulgate and others ... Sinaiticus places it after **now indeed** ... Several manuscripts and the Ethiopic version omit it entirely | **now indeed have sorrow**: This phrasing is found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae. The Latin translations vary, some omitting "indeed" (*quidem*). The standard text (ς) and Tischendorf (Ti) read **sorrow indeed now** with Alexandrinus and others | **you have** <note>original: "ἔχετε"</note> (present tense) with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most manuscripts ... Lachmann (Ln) reads **you will have** <note>original: "ἕξετε"</note> (future tense) with Alexandrinus, Regius (L), and various Latin and Coptic versions. Chrysostom paraphrases this as **now indeed you will be sorrowful**.

Manuscripts Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Alexandrinus (A), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), the corrected Bezae (D²), Regius (L), and others, along with many ancient versions (Gothic, Syriac, etc.) and the church fathers Chrysostom and Cyril. ... **23.** **And** <note>original: "και"</note>: Omitted by manuscripts 249, 252, and the Old Latin version (e). | **you will ask** <note>original: "ερωτησετε"</note>: Sinaiticus and others read a slightly different form <note>original: "ερωτησητε"</note>. **25.** **the hour is coming** <note>original: "ερχεται ωρα"</note>: Without the word "but" <note>original: "αλλ"</note> in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Latin Vulgate. **26. you will ask** <note>original: "αιτησεσθε"</note>: Manuscript Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), manuscript 1, and the Old Latin *a* <note>reading *petite*</note> and Coptic versions read "ask" <note>original: "αιτησασθε" (imperative form)</note>, and Sinaiticus and manuscript 1 place this before the phrase "in my name" | **not (now)** <note>original: "ου (εμ nunc)"</note>: Manuscripts H and L omit | Old Latin *a* reads "and I will ask for you" instead of "and I do not say to you... concerning you" | **Father**: Manuscript Bezae (D) adds "my" | **concerning you**: Also in Old Latin *a, f, ff², g, q*, the Vulgate, Hilary, and Augustine... Manuscripts 36, b, c, Cyril, and Augustine elsewhere omit.

**27. me** <note>original: "εμε"</note>: With manuscripts Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Bezae (D), and almost all others including Clement... **28. ...the same way as in Cyril's edition (4,942); this reasoning is favored by the Syriac <note>a translation used in ancient Eastern churches</note> (reading "believe" <note>original: *credite*</note>) which omits "now" <note>original: *arti*</note>, and likewise the Persian version (and the Persian codex) which transposes the text as follows: *Jesus said to them: The hour comes and this is the hour, have faith, that each etc.* Even the Philoxenian Syriac reads "now you have faith" without a question mark. Father**: manuscript D reads *patēr* <note>a variation in spelling/case</note>. | **which** <note>original: *hē*</note> also in ℵ (corrected), Origen, and Didymus: ℵ (original hand) and Eusebius read "which was" <note>original: *hēn*</note>. | **the world existed** <note>original: *ton kosmon einai*</note> following Origen and Eusebius... manuscript D and the Sahidic Coptic read "the world was made" <note>original: *genesthai ton kosmon*</note>, as do Irenaeus and Cyprian ("before the world was made"). | **alongside yourself** in this position following Origen, Didymus, and Chrysostom... manuscripts D, a, f, and others place it after "which I had."

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 17, 18.

> ...so that the scripture might be fulfilled. 13 But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world so that they may have my joy made full <margin>15, 11</margin> within themselves. 14 I have given them your word, and the world has hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not <margin>15, 18 ff</margin> of the world. 15 I do not ask that you take them out of the world, <margin>Matthew 6, 13</margin> but that you keep them from the evil one. 16 They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. 17 Sanctify them in <margin>11</margin> the truth; your word is truth. 18 Just as you sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world;

<note>The following section is a technical "apparatus," which lists differences found in ancient hand-copied manuscripts.</note>

The Received Text <note>original: "ς"</note> omits "and" with manuscripts AC*D(Greek)XYΓΛΔΠ and most others, including the Latin Vulgate, Gothic, and Syriac versions. | Manuscript κγ and four others read "perished" | Manuscripts ΧΥΛ and others read "of perdition" <note>original: "απωλιας"</note>

**13.** **in the world:** Manuscript d reads *in this world*, likewise manuscripts a, b, c, f, ff². (But not e, g, q, or the Vulgate) | **within themselves** with manuscripts ℵABXΠ (though the 'e' in 'themselves' was added by the first hand in ℵ) and three others; similarly C* and the Sahidic Coptic read *in their hearts* ... The Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **in them** with C³DLYΓΛΔ and most others, including Cyril.

**14.** **I have given them your word:** Manuscript D reads *But I gave your word in them* | **has hated** also in Origen: Manuscripts D, 40, 63, 73, 77, 253, 259, and Latin a, e, q read *hates* | **are** (Latin d: *sunt*) **of:** Manuscripts D, a, c, f, q add *this* | **just as I** (also ℵ corrected, but the original ℵ omitted it; f, g, Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac, and Origen read *and I*) **am not** (Manuscripts M, 248, and others place *am not* after *world*) **of the world** (Latin a, f, q and Origen: *from this world*) also Origen's Latin translation (*and these are not of this world, just as I* etc): Manuscript D, Π*, and others omit this. One cannot include Origen here <note>original: "Huc trahi non licet"</note> (who writes: "one must consider the earthly place... this is clearly indicated by 'and the world hated them, because they are not of the world.' For it hated" etc).

**15. 16.** Manuscripts 33 and 225 omit these verses (skipping from the first "of the world" to the second "of the world"). <note>This is a common scribal error called 'homoeoteleuton,' where the eye jumps between similar words.</note>

**15.** **I do not ask that you take** (Manuscripts UΛ, K and others have spelling variations of 'take') **them out of the world:** Manuscript Y omits this | Manuscript B* omits *out of the world, but that you keep them*, which was added by a later corrector B³. Similarly, manuscript 'a' jumped from the first *out of the world* to the *out of the world* at the start of verse 16. Several other witnesses do the same.

**16.** **of:** Manuscripts D, b, c, f, q add *this* | **I:** Manuscripts D, 69, 97, c, f, and the Vulgate read **and I** | **am not** in this position with ℵABCDLX and others, including the Latin, Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac ... The Received Text places it after *of the world* with YΓΔ AΠ and most others.

**17.** **Sanctify** (Cyril reads *Keep*, which he repeats in his commentary): Manuscript Δ, Cyril, and Didymus add **Holy Father**, likewise the Syriac and Persian versions | **the:** Manuscript B omits, as does Cyril's text, though his commentary adds *your* | **truth** without "your" with ℵ* (though it skips from one 'truth' to the next) ABC*DLΠ² and most Latin, Vulgate, Gothic, and Sahidic versions ... The Received Text and Tischendorf add **your** with ℵ corrected, C³, and most other manuscripts and versions | **is truth:** Manuscript B adds the definite article *the*.

**18.** **into** (twice): Manuscripts d, a, b, c, f, q add *this* | **sent:** Manuscript Δ* has a spelling variation.

# 17, 19. ACCORDING TO JOHN

<margin>Hebrews 2:11</margin>
19 And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth. 20 Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word; 21 That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
<margin>11</margin>
22 And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one

---

<note>The following section is a critical apparatus, a technical shorthand used by scholars to compare different ancient versions of the Bible. It lists variations in the Greek text found in famous manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus (א) and Codex Vaticanus (B), as well as quotes from early Church Fathers.</note>

**19.** **I sanctify** <note>Greek: αγιαζω</note> without the word **I** <note>Greek: εγω</note> according to manuscripts א, A, and others... <note>The translator is noting that some ancient copies omit the emphatic "I" before "sanctify."</note> Tischendorf includes **I** before it, Lachmann puts **I** in brackets... <note>Ti and Ln refer to 19th-century editors of the Greek New Testament.</note> **that they also** <note>Greek: ωσιν και αυτοι</note> according to א, A, B, C, D... while the "Received Text" <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> reads **and that they** <note>Greek: και αυτοι ωσιν</note>.

**20.** **of those believing** <note>Greek: των πιστ.</note>: some manuscripts add **all** <note>Greek: παντων</note>... **believing** <note>Greek: πιστευοντων</note> according to א, A, B, C, D... while the "Received Text" uses the future tense **those who shall believe** <note>Greek: πιστευσοντων</note>.

**21.** **all one**: manuscript C omits **one**... **Father** <note>Greek: πατηρ</note> according to B, D... while the "Received Text" and Lachmann use the vocative form **O Father** <note>Greek: πατερ</note>... **in us**: without the word **in** <note>Greek: εν</note> according to B, C, D... while the "Received Text" adds **in**, and Lachmann puts it in brackets... **that [the world] may believe** <note>Greek: πιστευη</note> according to א and B... Tischendorf uses a different Greek tense <note>aorist: πιστευση</note> found in A, C, D, and others.

**22.** **And I** <note>Greek: καγω</note> according to א, B, C, D... the "Received Text" writes it as two words **And I** <note>Greek: και εγω</note>... **thou hast given** <note>Greek: δεδωκασ</note> according to א, B, C, L... Lachmann uses a different past tense <note>εδωκασ</note>... **I have given** <note>Greek: δεδωκα</note>... **may be one**: manuscript D reads **may be the one**... **we are one**: some versions omit the word **are** <note>Greek: εσμεν</note> following manuscripts B, C, D... while the "Received Text" and Lachmann add **are**.

# ACCORDING TO JOHN 17, 26.

...just as we are one; 23 I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them just as you loved me. <margin>12, 26<br/>14, 3</margin> 24 Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may also be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world. <margin>16, 3</margin> 25 <gloss>154.3</gloss> Righteous Father, even though the world did not know you, <margin>17, 8</margin> I knew you, <gloss>155.10</gloss> and these men knew that you sent me; <margin>15, 9</margin> 26 and I made your name known to them and will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them and I in them.

*just as we are one*) <note>Latin: sicut sumus nos unum</note> Vulgate, both Syriac versions, Sahidic, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Eusebius *Against Marcellus* pages 192 and 193, Cyril volume 4 page 1000, Origen (Latin translation) volume 1 pages 70, 82, 152, Hilary page 954.

23. **I in them and you in me** (also Clement page 140, Hippolytus *Against Noetus* 7, Eusebius *Against Marcellus* 192, 193 etc., Origen (Latin translation) volume 1 page 70 etc.): Manuscript D and 59 read **you in me and I in them** | **into one** (also Clement, Hippolytus etc.): Manuscript D, Eusebius *Against Marcellus* twice, Chrysostom volume 8 page 553b read **into the one** | **that** (the second occurrence) with Manuscripts B, C, D, L, X, 33, 69, 124, 249, some others, Old Latin (a, e, g), Coptic, Persian (Origen volume 3 page 599 notes "the 'that the world' etc. is said twice" etc.), Hippolytus *Against Noetus*, Eusebius *Against Marcellus* twice, Chrysostom, Cyril volume 4 page 1900, Ambrose *On the Faith* book 5 ... ### Critical Notes on the Text

<note>The following section lists variations in ancient manuscripts. Letters like A, B, C, and D refer to famous parchment bibles from the 4th and 5th centuries (Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc.).</note>

**Verse 4.** Manuscripts 90, 124, 157, the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, and Nonnus. In line 25, manuscript $\sigma$ reads "seeing" <note>Greek: idon</note> instead of "knowing." | **all the things:** manuscript $y$ omits "the." | **coming upon:** manuscript $\Delta$ reads "coming against." | **went out and said:** follows manuscripts B, C, D, and several Old Latin versions (a, c, e, g, q). The Vulgate reads *processit et dixit* (he went forth and said), though some versions read *dicit* (says). Also supported by Sahidic and Syriac versions, Origen, and Chrysostom. The majority of later manuscripts <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> read "having gone out, he said" <note>Greek: exelthon eipen</note>, supported by Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Alexandrinus (A), and others.

**Verse 5. they answered:** manuscript x and the Ethiopic add "and said." The Gothic and Coptic versions read "answering him, they said." | **the Nazarene:** Manuscripts D, a, c, e, and the Vulgate read "the Nazarene" <note>Latin: nazarenum</note> with a slightly different spelling. | **says:** Origen adds "but." | **Jesus [says] to them:** follows Codex Sinaiticus. The majority of manuscripts read "Jesus says to them" with the article "the." Tischendorf <note>the editor of this volume</note> omits "Jesus" here, following Codex Vaticanus (B) and Bezae (D). | **was standing:** follows B, C, L, and others. Sinaiticus and others use a slightly different Greek spelling for "standing" <note>istekei vs eistekei</note>. (Note: the spelling of this word often fluctuates in the manuscripts; see notes on verses 16 and 18).

**Verse 6. therefore:** omitted by Codex Alexandrinus (A). | **to them:** omitted by the original scribe of Sinaiticus. | **I am:** without the introductory "that" <note>Greek: hoti</note>, following $\aleph$, A, B, D, L. Origen describes this moment as "by his divine power they went backward." The majority of manuscripts (ς) and the Armenian/Syriac versions include "that." | **they drew back / they fell:** The manuscripts vary between two different Greek forms of the past tense (the "-an" ending vs the "-on" ending).

**Verse 7. he asked them:** The word order varies between manuscripts. Some use "he asked them" while others use "them he asked." The versions (Latin, Coptic, Syriac) generally support the standard order. Manuscript D and the Syriac add "saying" (and he said to them). | **they said:** Most manuscripts agree; D and Origen add "again." | **the Nazarene:** Latin versions use *nazarenum*.

**Verse 8. answered:** Most omit "to them," but manuscript D, the Coptic, and Syriac versions add "to them." | **Jesus:** Most manuscripts include the name; some later ones add the definite article "the."

**Verse 9. you have given:** Manuscripts D, 42, and 122 use a different past tense form of the verb "to give." | **I have lost none of them:** Manuscript A begins a variation here...

<margin>Matthew 26:51 ff; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:50 f</margin> ...none of them. **10** $^{160.1}$ Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear; and the servant’s name was Malchus. <note>The name Malchus is unique to John's Gospel; the other Gospels mention the injury but not the name.</note> **11** $^{161.1}$ Jesus therefore said to Peter: “Put the sword into <margin>Matthew 26:42</margin> the sheath. <margin>Matthew 26:57; Mark 14:53; Luke 22:54</margin> **12** $^{162.1}$ Then the cohort <term>speira: a Roman military unit, often a detachment of several hundred men</term> and the commander <term>chiliarchos: a military tribune in charge of 1,000 men</term> and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him, **13** $^{163.10}$ and they led him to Annas first; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas,

### Critical Apparatus
<note>This section lists variations in ancient manuscripts. Letters like א (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), and D (Bezae) refer to specific famous codices.</note>

**of them) none:** Codex D reads *I lost none of them*; Latin manuscript *e* reads *I lost no one from those*; manuscript *a* reads *I lost no one from these*.

**10. then Simon:** Codex D reads *then Simon*; other versions read *But Simon* or *Truly Simon*. | **drew:** Various codices (א, L) show slight spelling variations in the Greek verb for "drew." | **the servant of the high priest:** Most manuscripts (A, B, C, L) place "servant" after "high priest," while others (א, D) reverse the order. | **ear:** <note>original: "ωταριον" (otarion)</note> Scholars note this diminutive form for "ear" is likely correct here, though some later manuscripts use the standard word <note>original: "ωτιον" (otion)</note>. Most versions simply translate as *ear*. | **name:** Some manuscripts add the definite article *the* name. | **to the servant:** Some manuscripts add *that* servant.

**11. the sword:** Most ancient copies (א, A, B, C) omit the word *your*, simply saying *the sword*. Later versions (influenced by Matthew 26:52) add *your*. | **sheath:** Some manuscripts add *its* sheath. One specific manuscript (254) adds the famous line from Matthew: *for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword*. | **has given:** Minor variations between the perfect tense *has given* and the aorist *gave*. | **the Father:** Some versions add *my* Father.

**12. seized:** Minor grammatical variation in the Greek middle/active voice.

**13. led:** Most early manuscripts (א, B, D) use the simple *led*, while later ones (influenced by Matthew and Mark) use *led away*. Some manuscripts include the word *him*, others omit it. | **Annas:** One manuscript (G) spells it *Anas*. | **for:** One manuscript uses *but* instead of *for*. | **for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas:** The Palestinian Syriac version omits this, while other Syriac traditions rearrange the sentence or add a note that *Annas sent Jesus bound to Caiaphas*.

### Critical Apparatus
<note>This section lists variations in ancient manuscripts. Letters like ℵ (Sinaiticus), A (Alexandrinus), and B (Vaticanus) represent major codices.</note>

**21.** **what I said** <note>original: α ειπον</note> : manuscript κ reads **what I spoke** <note>original: τι ελαλησα</note>

**22.** **but/and** <note>original: δε</note> : omitted by κ, minuscules 69, 237, 440, and a few others, including the Coptic and Armenian versions (the Syriac, Ethiopic, and others read "And these things" etc.) | **one of the officers standing by** : found in ℵ, B, and Latin versions (Vulg. *unus adsistens ministrorum*). The majority of later manuscripts (A, C, D, etc.) read **one of the officers who stood by**. | **answer** <note>original: απο- κρινή</note> : some manuscripts (M, U, 69) use a slightly different spelling of the verb.

**23.** **Jesus answered him** : ℵ, 13, 69, 124, and Armenian read **But Jesus said to him**... Sahidic, Coptic, and Syriac read *Jesus answered and said to him* | **Jesus** <note>original: ις (nomen sacrum)</note> : with manuscripts b, c, L... the majority read **the Jesus** | **I have spoken** <note>original: ελαλησα</note> : ℵ reads **I said** <note>original: ειπον</note>; Augustine notes "I spoke falsely," though most Latin texts follow "I have spoken."

**24.** **Then Annas sent** <note>original: απεστειλ. ουν</note> : found in B, C, L, and several Latin/Syriac versions. ℵ and others read **But Annas sent**; others read **And he sent** or **Then he sent**. | **Annas** : Manuscript D and a few others omit the definite article "the." | **Caiaphas** : minor spelling variation in manuscript Λ. | **high priest** : Manuscript H has a minor spelling variation.

**25.** **Simon** : omitted by manuscript x and Chrysostom | **they said** : Manuscript Δ and one Latin version read **he said** | **of him are you** : variations in Latin manuscripts include "are you of that one" or "are you of that man." | **denied** (without a conjunction) : found in ℵ, A, B, C, D, and many others. Later manuscripts add **Therefore he denied**. Other versions (Latin, Coptic) read **But he denied** or **And he denied**. | **said** : Manuscript A and 33 read **says**.

**26.** **says** : some manuscripts add **therefore** | **being a relative** : Manuscripts L, X, 33, and Syriac read **the relative**; Latin versions vary between "relative" and "neighbor." | **I saw** <note>original: ειδον</note> : spelling variation between **ειδον** and **ιδον** across various codices.

**27.** **Peter** : found in A, B, C, D, and others. The majority of later manuscripts (following ℵ) add the definite article **the Peter**.

33. **as** (versions 'a' and 'et') **they saw** (the reading 'they saw' is found in manuscripts $\aleph$, B, L, $\Gamma$, $\Lambda$, $\Pi^2$, and most others; $\aleph^c$, D$^{supplement}$, K, M, X, Y, and $\Pi^*$ have the same) and afterward **not** and. Manuscript $\aleph^c$ ... $\aleph^*$ reads **they found** and afterward **and not**, likewise 'f' and Coptic manuscripts 'they found—and' (though Coptic does not have the 'and'); similarly the Sahidic version reads **they saw**, the Syriac (Harklean) reads **they recognized** (but neither adds 'and'; thus it reads: 'they saw him already dead, they did not break etc.') | **already him** with manuscripts B and L (Syriac Harklean reads 'immediately they already recognized him to be dead,' see also Syriac Peshitta) Origen <note>original: "Or^{4,176}" refers to a specific volume and page in a 19th-century edition of Origen's works.</note> (:: which order seemed to need correcting ... the Received Text and Lachmann read **him already** with $\aleph$, D$^{supplement}$, X, Y, $\Gamma$, $\Lambda$, 7 other uncials <note>term: uncials|Early Greek manuscripts written in large, capital-like letters.</note>, and almost all others, the majority of Old Latin manuscripts (against ff$^2$, q, Armenian, and Prosper of Aquitaine who omit 'already,' nor is it expressed in the Ethiopic), the Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac (Schaf), and Cyril.

34. **but**: D$^{supplement}$ reads **but [alternative spelling]** | **of the soldiers**: manuscript 69 adds **having come forth** | **his side**: 69, 346, Old Latin, Vulgate, Origen ... manuscript $\Lambda^*$ omits this. Compare regarding this verse Eusebius: **when one of the soldiers, according to the Gospel of John, pierced the side of the Lamb of God with a spear, and immediately water and blood came out.** | **pierced** ($\Upsilon^*$ has **pierced [plural]**, manuscript 225 and others have **opened**): 56, 68, and others have **opened** or **unlocked**. Likewise the Latin 'f', 'g', Vulgate, Syriac Peshitta, and Ethiopic have **opened**; against this, manuscripts confirm **pierced** (as do Origen and Eusebius), while Old Latin 'a' and 'ff$^2$' and Syriac (Schaf) have **struck**, 'b' has **pricked**, 'c', Sahidic, and Coptic have **pierced through**, 'e' has **inserted**, 'q' has **struck and pierced through**. (Likewise the Ethiopic reads **pierced his side, which was the right side, with a spear.**) | **immediately came out** in this order with $\aleph$, B, L, X, 33, 'a', 'b' ('e' omits 'immediately'), Syriac (Harklean), Origen, and Eusebius ... the Received Text and Lachmann read **came out immediately** with A, D$^{supplement}$, $\Gamma$, $\Lambda$, 7 other uncials, and most others, 'e', 'f', 'ff$^2$', 'g', Vulgate, Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac (Schaf), Ethiopic, etc., and the Paschal Chronicle (Cyril: **and blood immediately came out and water**) | **immediately [Greek: euthys]** with $\aleph$, A, B, E, H, K, L, S, X, $\Delta$, $\Pi$, and most others, Origen, Eusebius, and Cyril ... Griesbach reads **straightway [Greek: eutheos]** with D$^{supplement}$, M, U, Y, $\Gamma$, and 60 others, and the Paschal Chronicle | **blood and water**: 'y', 'e', Sahidic, and Coptic read **water and blood**.

35. D$^{supplement}$, E, G, H, K, $\Pi^2$, and many others have a variant spelling | **true**: $\aleph$, 122, and Chrysostom read **truthful** | **his is the testimony** with the Received Text, A, B, D$^{supplement}$, L, M, X, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, $\Pi$, and most others, and Origen ... E, G, K, S, U, $\Delta$, and 30 others, the Amiatinus, Ingoldstadt, and Caesarius manuscripts read **is his the testimony**, while 'h', 'y', and 60 others, 'b', 'c', 'f', 'ff$^2$', 'g', the Clementine Vulgate, etc., Chrysostom, and Cyril read **is the testimony of him** ('a' reads **and his testimony is true**) | **and he [Greek: kakeinos]** with $\aleph$, A, D$^{supplement}$, L, X, $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, $\Pi$, 7 other uncials, and most others, and Origen ... Nonnus reads **we know** | **and you** with $\aleph$, A, B, D$^{supplement}$, H, K, L, U, X, $\Delta$, $\Pi$, 25 others, Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic, Armenian, both Syriac versions, and Ethiopic, Origen, and Cyril ... the Received Text omits **and** with E, G, M, S, U, Y, $\Gamma$, and far more others, and the Coptic | **you may believe [present tense]** with $\aleph^*$, B, and Origen ... the Received Text, Lachmann, and Tischendorf read **you may believe [aorist tense]** with $\aleph^a$, A, D$^{supplement}$, L, X, 11 other uncials, and almost all others, Chrysostom, and Cyril.

1. **the** | **from** (Tischendorf's 69th and 229th manuscripts and others including Dionysius of Alexandria use <note>original: "απο"</note>, as do several Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate; as opposed to manuscripts a, e, and the Dublin manuscript which use <note>original: "εκ"</note>) **the tomb** (also used by Dionysius, Eusebius, Chrysostom, and Cyril): Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), and manuscripts 1, 19, 22, 157, 209, as well as several ancient versions like the Sahidic and Coptic, read **from the door** <note>original: "απο της θυρασ"</note> (Sinaiticus adds **out of**) **the tomb**.

Sinaiticus originally skipped from the first mention of "the linen cloths lying" to the same words in the next verse. | **but**: some manuscripts add **at least** or **and**.

# 952 20, 7. ACCORDING TO JOHN

...him, and he entered the tomb, and he saw the linen cloths lying there, **7** and the face cloth, which had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. **8** Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed; **9** for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. **10** Then the disciples returned to their homes. **11** <insert>211.1</insert> But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb. Manuscripts Γ Δ Λ Π, seven other uncials <note>term: uncials|Early manuscripts written in large, blocky Greek capital letters</note>, most others, and Old Latin versions b, c, d, e, f, ff², g, q, the Vulgate, both Syriac versions, Ethiopic, and Cyril: ... **8. and** (Manuscript D omit, but not its Latin translation 'd') **the other**: manuscripts c, d, e, ff², q read *and the other*; b, g, and the Vulgate read *and he*; f, gat, and mm read *and that other*; manuscript 'a' reads simply *and* | **saw** with Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, A, B, and most others (manuscripts 61, 69, 124 read **they saw**) ... **9. they knew** (so also Codex Sinaiticus, and manuscripts a, d, f, ff², g, Vulgate): Codex Sinaiticus (original hand), b, c, e, q, gat, mm read **he knew** (Latin: *sciebat* or *noverat*) | **to rise from the dead**: manuscripts x, d, e, Sahidic, Coptic, both Syriac, and Ethiopic read **from the dead to rise**.

**10. to themselves** <note>original: "πρὸς αὑτοὺς"</note> with Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L ... others read **to their own [homes]** with Codex Sinaiticus (corrected), A, D, R, Q, X, and almost all others including Chrysostom and Cyril. # 957 ACCORDING TO JOHN 20, 28.

...into the place of the nails and put my hand into his side, I will never believe." 26 <gloss>Section 217, Canon 9</gloss> And after eight days his disciples were inside again, and Thomas with them. Jesus comes, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst and said: "Peace to you." 27 Then he says to Thomas: "Reach your finger here and see my hands, and reach your hand and put it into my side, and be not faithless but believing." 28 <gloss>Section 218, Canon 10</gloss> Answ—

---

<note>The following technical notes compare the Greek text with ancient translations and writings from early Church leaders. They focus on whether Thomas said he wanted to see the "place" of the nails or the "mark/print" of the nails.</note>

"unless I see in his hands the places <note>Latin: *loca*</note> (the Persian Polyglot <note>a 17th-century multi-language Bible</note> reads 'the place' <note>Latin: *locum*</note>) of the nails and put into them (the Persian Polyglot says 'again into the place of the nails') my fingers and extend my hand into his side." Likewise, the Jerusalem Syriac version <note>an ancient translation from the 5th or 6th century</note> reads: "unless I see in his hands the place of the nails (omitting the words 'and put' and following) and put my hand into his side." | The phrase **and put** <note>original: "kai balō"</note> up to **of the nails** <note>original: "tōn hēlōn"</note> is omitted by manuscripts Δ, 69, 235, and others, as well as the Sahidic <note>Coptic language of Upper Egypt</note> and certain versions of the Latin Vulgate. Manuscript D <note>Codex Bezae</note> places it after the phrase **into his side**. | The phrase **my finger** <note>original: "mou ton daktylon"</note> is found in the major 4th-century manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, and L. Other versions, including the one edited by Lachmann, read "the finger" or "my finger" in a different order. | The reading **into the place of the nails** <note>original: "eis ton topon tōn hēlōn"</note> is supported by manuscripts A and I, several Latin versions, the Peshitta <note>Standard Syriac Bible</note>, and early writers like Origen, Hilary of Poitiers, and Augustine. Origen writes: "Wherefore he did not merely say: 'If I do not see, I will not believe,' but added also: 'If I do not put my hand into the **place** of the nails and touch his side, I will never believe.'" 

By contrast, the majority of manuscripts (including ℵ, B, D, and L) read **the mark of the nails** <note>original: "ton typon tōn hēlōn"</note>. The Sahidic version translates this as "into the holes of the nails," while the Ethiopic reads "into his nails." This version is also supported by Cyril of Alexandria and Nonnus. In manuscript ℵ, the original scribe wrote "into his hand" (implying "if I do not put my finger into his hand"). The placement of the word **my** <note>original: "mou"</note> before **the hand** is supported by ℵ, B, D, and L, while others place it after. | Additionally, compare *On the Resurrection* by Justin Martyr (chapter 9): "And he permitted them to touch him and showed them the **marks** <note>original: "typous"</note> of the nails in his hands." See also the surrounding context there. 

Also compare Clement of Alexandria (page 999) in his *Sketches* <note>original: "Adumbrationes"</note> on the First Letter of John 1:1: "It is related in traditions that John, touching the body itself which was external, sent his hand into the depths, and the hardness of the flesh in no way resisted him, but gave way to the hand of the disciple." <note>This strange tradition suggests that to John’s touch, Jesus’s resurrected body might have seemed ghost-like or permeable, though the Gospel text emphasizes his physical solidity.</note>

**26.** The phrase **his disciples** is found in ABCDLX and most manuscripts, as well as the Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac. Manuscript ℵ and several others omit the word **his**. | **Thomas**: Manuscript D and 69 add the definite article "the." | **comes**: Manuscripts D and 1 add the word "therefore." | **said**: Manuscript Δ reads "said to them," and others read "says to them."

**27.** **be not** <note>original: "mē ginou"</note> is also supported by Origen, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Cyril. A passage in the *Dialogues* reads: "He said: put your finger into the **places** (so Delarue reads, though I suspect an error for 'marks') of the nails and your hand into the side, and be not," etc. In the writings of Epiphanius, after the words "be not," etc., it is added: "For he showed the mark of the nails and the place of the spear, and he left those very scars upon his body..." Manuscript D uses a different Greek verb for "be not" <note>original: "mē isthi"</note>, which matches the Latin "noli esse."

**28.** The word **answered** <note>original: "apekrithē"</note> appears without a connecting "and" in manuscripts ℵ, B, C, D, G, L, X, and most Latin and Coptic versions.

# 963 ACCORDING TO JOHN 21, 18.

<margin>17</margin> ...Shepherd my little sheep. <gloss>230.10</gloss> He says to him the third time: "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" <note>original: "φιλεῖς με;" (phileis me). <note>The following section is the "Critical Apparatus," a technical list where the editor, Tischendorf, compares different ancient handwritten manuscripts to show where they vary from one another.</note>
