# 966 21, 25. ACCORDING TO JOHN

(the leaf that preceded the last one ends, and a colon, not a period, is placed.) Furthermore, one must compare the scholarly notes <term>scholia: explanatory notes written in the margins of ancient manuscripts</term> of several manuscripts, such as the one Matthaei brought forward from manuscript 237: *“Others say that this is an addition <note>original: ἄλλος δὲ προσθήκην εἶναί φησι</note>, someone diligent having placed it on the outside <note>on the margin</note>, to demonstrate that the miracles performed by the Lord were more than those written; but later, perhaps through the ignorance of the first scribe, it was placed inside by another <note>moved from the margin into the main text</note>... and it became part of the Gospel writing, which time and custom prepared to be carried through all the Gospels.”* Concerning the phrase "through all the Gospels," manuscript 36 reads: *“Then, as time and custom prepared it to be carried through all the Gospels, it gained such firm standing among all the faithful that it truly became one part and the end of the things written by the Evangelist, lest we should seem to divide or even falsify the God-inspired words of the Evangelists.”* (Let us omit the rest) ...... The editors Lachmann and Tischendorf have the text thus: *“But there are also many other things that Jesus did, which if they were written one by one, I suppose even the world itself would not contain <note>original: χωρήσειν</note> the books that would be written”* according to the Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and many other manuscripts, including the Vulgate and the writings of Origen, Eusebius, and Chrysostom. 

But several details differ. For as has already been indicated, the word "which" <note>original: α (short form)</note> should be read instead of "as many as" <note>original: ὅσα</note> according to manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others... though the Received Text <note>represented by the symbol ϛ</note> uses "as many as" following the Alexandrinus and most other uncials. Likewise, instead of "Jesus," manuscript D reads "the Christ Jesus." Furthermore, manuscript 76 and others add "before his disciples," and the Old Latin manuscript b adds "which are not written in this book." Likewise, "nor" <note>original: ουδε</note> should be read according to Sinaiticus and others... though the Received Text reads "not even" <note>original: ουδε</note> with different accentuation. Likewise, "will contain" <note>future tense: χωρήσειν</note> should be read with the oldest manuscripts... though the Received Text and the editors Lachmann and Tischendorf use "to contain" <note>aorist infinitive: χωρῆσαι</note> following the majority of later manuscripts and versions like the Vulgate.

At the end of the book (that is, after the word "books"), the Received Text adds "**Amen**" following many manuscripts and the Syriac version... but we have omitted it <note>as the editor</note> following the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae), many early translations (Sahidic, Coptic, Syriac), and the fathers Origen and Chrysostom.

### End-Titles <note>original: Subscriptiones</note>
The manuscripts Sinaiticus, K, M, U, and others have no end-title (but regarding the Sinaiticus, see the Prolegomena)... Manuscripts A, C, E, and others read: **The Gospel According to John** ... Manuscripts H and others read: **The End of the Gospel According to John** (some add "**Holy**" Gospel) ... Manuscript D reads: **The Gospel According to John is finished, begins—** <note>This indicates the manuscript was moving on to the next book in its collection.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical collation of biblical manuscripts, moving from the final verses of John to the "subscriptions"—the concluding notes added by ancient and medieval scribes to mark the end of a book and record historical traditions about its origin.</meta>

<page-num>967</page-num>
<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN: Subscriptions.</header>

...[The] Gospel according to Luke <note>original Greek: "ευαγγελιον κατα λουκαν"</note>. Similarly, Latin manuscripts **a, b, d, e, f, ff²,** and **q** record: *the Gospel* (omitted in **q**) *according to* (using the word "cata" in **e**) *John* (spelled "iohannem," "ioannem" in **ff²**, or "iohanen" in **d**) *ends* (placed before "Gospel" in **a**, adds "amen" in **q**, adds "in God" in **b**); *the Gospel* (so in **d** and **f**; omitted in **a, b, e, ff²,** and **q**) *according to* (using "cata" in **e**) *Luke begins* (manuscript **a** says "Lucanum," **ff²** says "Lucanum, amen") ... manuscripts **g, gat, mm,** and **mt** record: *the Gospel according to* ("cata" in **gat** and **mm**) *John ends*; manuscript **e** records: *the Gospel of John ends*. 

Furthermore, manuscripts **H, S, A,** and many others add the number of <term>stichoi</term> <note>lines of standard length used by ancient scribes to measure the size of a book and calculate payment</note>: **H, S,** and many others say 2,300; **Λ** and many others say 2,210; others say 2,010, 2,024, or 1,300, or "two thousand three hundred" (as in manuscript 246) and other variations. 

Likewise, **Λ** and many others list the number of <term>kephalaia</term> <note>ancient chapter divisions, which were different from our modern ones</note> (232, as do **Δ** and many others; the marginal notation in manuscripts **C, K,** etc., proceeds to this same number; in **A** and **M**, the last chapter is 231). 

Likewise, they list <term>titloi</term> <note>the descriptive titles or headings for the chapters</note> (which in most ancient editions, except for the famous manuscripts **Sinaiticus, Vaticanus,** and **Bezae**, are placed before each Gospel: they number 18 in **Δ, C,** and **Δ**, or 19 in **K** and **M**. This difference depends on whether the scribe included the story of the woman caught in adultery, see the discussion above). 

Some also list the number of <term>rhemata</term> <note>individual words or phrases</note> (2,600 or 1,331 or 1,338. Athanasius <note>a 4th-century church father</note> records 2,600 words). In manuscript **B** <note>the Codex Vaticanus</note>, 80 chapters are counted.

Moreover, many manuscripts (as already mentioned above) have expanded <term>subscriptions</term> <note>formal closing statements</note> (such as "The Gospel according to John" or "The according to John Gospel") with these details: *It was published 32 years* (others say 30 or "thirty," and one says 20) *after the ascension* <note>original Greek: "αναληψεωσ"</note> *of Christ* (manuscript **G** uses "departure" <note>original Greek: "αναλυσεωσ"</note>. Indeed, the word written in that manuscript, with the letters added by abbreviation, is more likely "departure" than "ascension," unless we assume the scribe used the letter "u" instead of "e" due to a similarity in sound).

It is also notable what is marked in manuscript **Δ**, number 262, and others, as we have seen above: *It was written and compared likewise from the same copies in 2,210 verses and 232 chapters.* 

Finally, in several manuscripts, these and similar notes are added: *It was written in Greek at Ephesus thirty years* (manuscript 237 adds "but others say thirty-two years") *after the ascension of the Lord, under King Domitian* (as in manuscript 160). 

Similarly, the Syriac Peshitta <note>the standard Syriac version of the Bible</note>: *The holy Gospel of the preaching of John the Evangelist, which he spoke in Greek at Ephesus, is finished.* 

Likewise, the Syriac Philoxenian <note>a more literal Syriac translation</note> in the very ancient Assemani manuscript 1: *The scripture of the holy Gospel of John ends; he spoke and wrote it in the Ionic dialect in Ephesus* (the scholar White translates this more simply as: *the description of the holy Gospel of John, which he spoke in Greek, is finished*) ... *it was published 32 years* (manuscript 246 adds "after the ascension of our God") *after the ascension of Christ, on the island of Patmos* (as in 246 and 252) ... *it was composed by this John when he was in exile on the island of Patmos under King Trajan, and it was published in Ephesus through Gaius, the host of the apostles, 32 years after the ascension of Christ* (so in manuscript 145).

Regarding these traditions, compare the <term>Suidas</term> <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry "John," where it is read: *that the Theologian and Evangelist, having returned from his exile on Patmos, composed the Gospel when he was 100 years old, and he lived until the age of 120...* 

*...The Gospel of John, son of Zebedee, one of the twelve apostles, is finished. It was written in Greek for the people of the city of Ephesus after the ascension of our Lord into heaven in the body, in the thirtieth year, during the reign of Nero, the Roman Emperor. With it, the four holy Gospels are finished, like the four rivers of life, and glory be to God.* 

Similarly, the Persian version refers to all four Gospels: *The four glorious Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John are finished.* 

Furthermore, at this place, it does not seem right to pass over what is read in the prologue of the Gospel according to John, as found in the Vatican-Alexandrian manuscript number 14 from the ninth century (compare my book: *When were our Gospels composed?*, 4th edition, 1866, page 118 and following): *the Gospel of John was revealed and given to the churches by John while he was still living in the body, just as Papias...*

<page-num>968</page-num> <header>Subscriptions.</header> <header>ACCORDING TO JOHN</header>

A Hierapolitan by name, a dear disciple of John, related [this] in his exoteric works, that is, in the last five books. Indeed, he wrote down the Gospel correctly, with John dictating. With these, a prologue in Corderius, prefixed with an anonymous note, must be compared: "For John, the last of these – he having become very old, as Irenaeus and Eusebius and others handed down to us – at that time (at that time?) terrible heresies having arisen, dictated (sic) the Gospel to his own disciple Papias Eubiotos the Hierapolitan, for the completion of those who had preached the word before him."

LEIPZIG, PRINTED BY GIESECKE & DEVRIENT.
